15938-the-yankee-tea-party-or-boston-in-:
A children's history of the Boston Tea Party by Henry C. Watson, telling Boston in 1773 for young readers. The tale follows the quarrel over tea, tax, and liberty to its famous night in the harbour. Watson writes in plain, stirring prose for boys and girls. Pictures from the University of Florida's children's collection join this edition.

Ships lie at anchor, patriots disguise themselves, and chests of tea splash into the water. Boston's streets, meetings, and anger fill the background. Watson keeps the story clear and patriotic, without hiding the risk. The book still serves as a first history of a famous night: a tax resisted, a harbour full of tea, and a revolution begun.
16916-the-fatal-jealousie-1673:
Henry Nevil Payne wrote this 1673 drama, The Fatal Jealousie, here reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society in November 1948 with an introduction by Willard Thorp of Princeton. The series, drama number two, was lithoprinted at Ann Arbor and sold for one dollar. General editors from Michigan, California, and Los Angeles oversaw the series.

Payne's play turns on jealousy as a fatal passion, in the high, formal style of Restoration drama. Thorp's introduction sets the play in its age and stage. The reprint gives modern readers a rare, short Restoration play, useful for students of drama history and for those who want a taste of 1673 theater in a clean, scholarly text.
29940-dogfight-1973:
Mack Reynolds wrote Dogfight 1973 as a first-person tale of air combat at extreme speed. The pilot flies at 1600 miles per hour, acts with split-second timing after sighting the enemy, and is allowed only one mistake: his last. His radar picks up the foe five hundred miles to the north-northeast and forty-five miles above him. He switches on the velocity calculator at once.

The enemy ship runs at sixteen, perhaps sixteen and a half, and the pilot guesses an Ivar Interceptor. He punches out an evasion pattern with one hand and snaps an Ivar K-12 card into his calculator with the other. His nearest squadron mate is a good minute and a half away, which might as well be a century. The whole fight takes less than sixty seconds to happen, though it takes far longer to tell.
4820-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
In this nineteenth volume, covering 1572 to 1573, The Rise of the Dutch Republic continues. Its file header numbers it as the twentieth Gutenberg volume. Chapter eight opens with affairs in Holland and Zealand, and the siege of Tergoes by patriots, whose importance and position are weighed. An audacious plan sends succour across the Drowned Land, and a brilliant expedition by Mondragon raises the siege.

A horrible sack of Zutphen and base conduct of Count Van den Berg follow, with Naarden's refusal to surrender and an unsuccessful deputation to Don Frederic. Don Frederic before Naarden, treachery of Romero, and admission of Spaniards bring general massacre of garrison and burghers, with the city burned to the ground. Warm reception of Orange in Holland and secret negotiations with the Estates follow, amid desperate struggle between Spain and the provinces. Readers get Motley's account of siege, massacre, and Orange's rising cause.
4821-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Alva's long rule ends in 1573, and John Lothrop Motley follows the sieges and quarrels that mark its close. Spanish troops mutiny, the duke feuds with his would-be successor Medina Coeli, and the town of Alkmaar prepares to resist a siege it cannot win on walls alone.

The first assault fails, soldiers refuse a second storming, and Orange orders the surrounding country flooded to break the siege. Motley then turns to secret talks with France, the dismissal of the cruel De la Marck, and the arrival of Requesens as governor. The narrative shows a turning point: Spanish terror losing its grip while Dutch resistance gains method and resolve.
6856-the-great-riots-of-new-york-1712-to:
J. T. Headley tells the great riots of New York from 1712 to 1873, with a full account of the four days' draft riot of 1863. Headley dedicates the book to the metropolitan police. Their fidelity and courage in the past promise what they will do for the city in future. The book lists pictures of burning offices, hospitals, asylums, and fights between rioters and militia. A hanging in Clarkson Street and a dead sergeant mark its grim pages.

From early slave revolts to doctors' riots and the draft, Headley traces mob violence in a growing city. His tone is that of a Victorian historian, earnest and detailed. The Great Riots of New York is a vivid, if dated, chronicle of urban disorder.
arxiv-2412-01273:
Jiazhou Liu and five co-authors explore head-mounted augmented reality as a safety tool on high-rise building sites. Their work-in-progress paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. It was written with industry experts. The focus is the safety screens set around each floor's edge. These screens stop people and objects from falling, so gaps in them are a real hazard.

The team tracks which parts of the screens a worker has already checked. Machine learning spots gaps that need a closer look and repair. Reports are then produced with less manual effort. The paper also faces a hard question: watching workers raises privacy worries. It weighs ways to cut those risks. The project is early, and the authors report first progress and open concerns.
arxiv-2412-01473:
Naimy and co-authors work out exact formulas for two measures of quantum information in a three-qubit state, in a 2024 paper. The measures matter because quantum sensing uses odd quantum links to sharpen how well a value can be guessed. Noise that breaks those links, called decoherence, can spoil the gain, so the team tracked how the measures change under three kinds of noise.

Closed formulas are given for each noise type. The team then tested a well known three-way linked state under each kind of noise. Phase-type noise left better guessing power than the third kind, which scrambles the state more fully. The results may help users pick noise settings that keep sensing sharp.
arxiv-2412-02373:
Xichen Ye and colleagues present a training method that resists wrong labels in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Deep networks learn well from clean data, but real data sets often carry label errors. Networks can memorize the noise and fail on new data. Loss functions built to shrug off noise help. One known design pairs an active loss with a passive one, using mean absolute error as the passive part.

The authors show a flaw in that pairing. Mean absolute error treats clean and noisy samples the same, which slows learning. They propose a new family of passive losses, called normalized negative loss functions. Plugged into the same frame, these losses speed training while keeping noise resistance. The work targets image and pattern tasks where labels cannot be fully trusted.
arxiv-2412-02773:
Chung and co-authors speed up the tuning of unknowns in Bayesian inverse problems. Such problems often carry several settings that shape the prior and the noise model. The team focuses on linear problems with Gaussian noise and Matérn-style priors. The target is the most probable setting under the data. Reaching it needs log determinants, which are costly to compute. Their fix swaps the exact goal for a sampled average version.

A Lanczos method, aided by a fresh preconditioner, approximates the goal and its slope cheaply. The preconditioner updates at low cost when settings change. Gradient parts get reused across steps. The result is a faster route to the same estimates.
arxiv-2412-02973:
Jane Hsieh, Angie Zhang, Mialy Rasetarinera, and five colleagues study worker-led data sharing in the gig economy in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Platform companies hold most work data, creating power imbalances that leave drivers and couriers managing overheads and isolation alone. Sharing data among workers could support collective action and mutual aid, and could inform regulators. The team interviewed eleven United States policy experts and ran co-design workshops with fourteen active gig workers across four domains.

The results map what policymakers want, what information they need, and where their priorities misalign with workers' own concerns about data collectives. Workers and experts sometimes wanted the same system to serve different ends. From these findings the authors derive design recommendations for data-sharing systems. The aim is technology that supports worker needs while moving legislation toward more equitable gig work.
arxiv-2412-04773:
Xiaoyu Zhang and three co-authors made tensor fitting methods that stand up to wild, heavy-tailed data, in a paper published in 2024. Tensor models pack multi-way data into low-rank form and see wide use. Most fitting methods rely on tame distribution assumptions, which real data often break. Their method runs gradient descent with the extreme steps clipped, so one unusual point cannot wreck the path.

The team proves that the method settles as claimed. They also prove its error reaches the best known rates, under a loose local condition on the spread of the data. That condition reads the data only where the low-rank shape points. Tests on synthetic data support the claims. The authors present the method for real datasets where tails run heavy. It keeps the speed of gradient methods while removing their weak spot.
arxiv-2412-04973:
Raffaela Capitanelli and Mirko D'Ovidio study the Laplace equation when the wall of the region reacts and stores, with memory spread along the boundary, in a paper from 2024. Such conditions model walls that are not passive: they trade material or heat with the inside and respond over time. Non-local terms let distant wall points influence each other.

The paper works from two sides at once, formulas and chance. On the formula side, the solution gets a compact closed form. On the chance side, the same solution reads as the average path of a boundary process, a walker that lives on the wall with its own rules. The twin view aids both proof and intuition. Applications include diffusion in coated domains.
arxiv-2412-05073:
Zhan Bai, Xiangyan An, Yuqi Chen, Baifei Shen, Ruxin Li, and Liangliang Ji propose making axions, hypothetical dark matter particles, by firing a laser into a crystal, in a 2024 paper. When the laser and axion fields march in phase inside an ionic crystal, the crystal emits axions coherently. Stacking thin crystal layers, each half a wavelength thick, strengthens the effect further.

The team estimates the scheme beats the classic light-through-a-wall setup by up to a hundredfold in conversion chance over the same length. A ten-meter rig with today's lasers could push the coupling limit down to a stated bound. The authors offer the design as a new terrestrial route in the hunt for axions.
arxiv-2412-05673:
Saptarshi Chakraborty, Kshitij Khare, and George Michailidis build a robust regression method in a 2024 paper. Regression with many predictors is fragile when errors have heavy tails or repeat in patterns over time. Standard Bayesian tools also demand careful tuning choices.

Their framework rests on a smoothed loss that blends squared and absolute error. That blend handles both light and heavy tailed data well. A working likelihood built from the loss gives stable estimates and honest uncertainty for each parameter. Priors can suit either modest or very large predictor sets. The method avoids ad hoc tuning while adapting to the tail shape found in each data set.
arxiv-2412-06473: Tatsumi Aoyama and co-authors check a disputed piece of one of physics' most precise calculations in this 2024 paper. Two teams computed a tenth-order part of the electron's magnetic moment and disagreed by about five times the stated uncertainty. The authors split the part into hundreds of diagram pieces and compared each one. No single diagram explained the gap; small differences in one diagram family added up instead. Extra Monte Carlo sampling firmed the numbers.
arxiv-2412-07873:
Steve Butler and co-authors study a classic parking puzzle in a 2024 mathematics paper. Cars arrive one by one on a one-way street, each with a preferred spot. Each car takes the first free spot at or past its choice, and a parking function is a set of choices where every car still parks.

A car that lands exactly on its chosen spot is called lucky, and so is the spot. Lucky cars have been studied before and fit a neat pattern found by Pollak. Lucky spots turn out to be messier and had not been studied. The authors give chances that the first few spots are lucky and how those chances settle as the street grows. The paper adds a fresh angle to a beloved counting problem.
arxiv-2412-07973:
G. Bruce Berriman made the case in 2024 that astronomy's Virtual Observatory is an equity instrument as much as a technical one. The observatory is not a place but a global ecosystem. Archives worldwide expose their data through shared links built by the members of an international alliance founded in 2002. So any astronomer can query the sky's data as if it sat in one library. It was built around open, FAIR data rules from the start.

That design hands the same public data sets to a small university in an underserved country as to a major data center. This lets research staff everywhere join the big questions of the decade. One example is the flood of transient events coming from the Rubin Observatory. Berriman describes the alliance's agreement with the International Astronomical Union's development office, which carries these tools into training and capacity building where astronomy is growing.
arxiv-2412-08773: John Donoghue answers a short question in a brief 2024 note: do the cosmological constant and Newton's constant run in real reactions? Running would mean changing with energy. His answer is no. The note is written as a teaching piece. It lays out in plain terms why these two constants should not be treated as running parameters when physicists compute what actually happens in a physical process.
arxiv-2412-09173:
Jiashu Yao and co-authors study whether language models can follow formatting instructions faithfully, in work from 2024. Producing well-structured output on demand, such as wrapped text or code in a set style, is a basic skill that models often miss. Their benchmark covers many task types, chat styles, and format kinds, each with an automatic checker.

Tests showed even leading open and closed models fail format rules often. The team then proposes a reinforcement method that trains on checker feedback, needing no human labels. It raised format faithfulness sharply on test tasks while holding general quality steady. Mixed with labelled data, it improved both faithfulness and quality at once. An analysis section explains how the training changes model behaviour.
arxiv-2412-09873:
He-bin Zhang, Yuanjiang Tang, and Yong-Chun Liu propose a way to make light whose photons arrive in unusually strong bunches in a 2024 paper. How photons correlate in time is central to quantum optics and its technologies. Past methods could not reach the extreme bunching the authors target.

Their scheme rests on two effects in a cascaded quantum system, where an emitter feeds a filter or a cavity. One effect, electron shelving, pauses emission at random times. Adding up the fluorescence over time then amplifies the correlations far beyond past reach. Both the strength of the bunching and the color of the light can be tuned over wide ranges. The authors say current lab techniques can build the setup, opening doors for strong-correlation studies and devices.
arxiv-2412-10073:
Bester and ten co-authors release imaging software for radio astronomy in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Radio interferometers build images from scattered measurements, a hard inverse problem. The CLEAN algorithm dominates through maturity, speed, and robustness. Alternatives rarely win adoption: they cost more compute, lack mature code, or expose obscure parameters.

Their library, pfb-imaging, supplies the scaffolding for building new imaging algorithms. It handles the shared machinery so researchers can focus on the reconstruction method itself. As a demonstration, they implement a sparsity-based technique known as SARA within the framework. The goal is mainstream usability in the big-data regime of modern arrays. Readers in radio astronomy get infrastructure meant to lower the barrier between a published algorithm and a working pipeline.
arxiv-2412-11173:
Lizhong Wang, Xingzhong Xu, and Jiping Zhang sharpened a rule on which subgroups control a group's prime fusion, in a mathematics paper published in 2024. Fusion asks how parts of a group fuse into one class in the whole group. Earlier work set a bar for which small subgroups can control it. For odd primes, their bar is lower.

They prove that flat subgroups built from prime-order steps, of rank two or more, are enough to control the fusion. The gain tightens a named earlier theorem for the odd prime case. The even prime case sits outside this claim. Group theorists use such rules to cut large fusion checks down to small subgroup checks. The paper is short and dense with proof, aimed at specialists in that field.
arxiv-2412-12473:
The Adam optimizer trains neural networks fast, but models it trains often do worse on new data than they should. Long Jin and co-authors add an integration step to Adam to steer it toward flatter resting points. Flat spots in the loss surface tend to mean the model handles new data better. The added term works like a filter that smooths sharp dips during training. Theory from diffusion models backs the idea.

Tests show the new optimizer generalizes better and resists noisy labels. It keeps Adam's fast convergence while beating Adam and its variants on standard benchmarks. The team also studies how the added term changes convergence itself. Better generalization without slower training is a rare win for optimizer design.
arxiv-2412-13073:
Dimitrios Konstantinides and Charalampos Passalidis estimate ruin risk for an insurer holding many lines at once. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. Claims arrive in vectors across the lines, returns on reserves jump over time, and the worst claims are heavy-tailed.

The model renews claims through one shared counting process. Claim vectors share a heavy-tailed law, depend weakly on each other, and mix dependence inside each vector. The authors derive uniform estimates for the chance that discounted claims enter rare danger sets within a set horizon. Ruin probabilities follow directly. Under a stricter tail class, the estimates hold across the whole time horizon at once. The results serve pricing and capital planning under extreme joint losses.
arxiv-2412-13173:
Siqi Li and co-authors detect openable parts of objects in this 2024 paper. Robots must spot drawers, doors, and lids and predict how they move. Earlier methods tied themselves to single categories or narrow datasets. Their transformer framework uses two kinds of prior knowledge in two stages.

Stage one adds perceptual grouping features, which sharpen part detection through cross attention. Stage two adds geometric features to predict motion parameters like axis and angle. Both detection and motion scores beat prior methods in their tests. Foundation model priors supply the general knowledge that small datasets lack. The code and models are public. Kitchen and warehouse robots both need this skill to work unseen objects.
arxiv-2412-13673:
Manuel Del Piano, Stefan Hohenegger, and Francesco Sannino present a 2024 physics paper on black holes changed by quantum effects. In earlier work they built a model-free way to describe such black holes near the horizon, the point of no return. That method used series expansions that work well nearby but lose accuracy farther out.

Here they extend the reach of the method with a math tool called a Padé approximant, which stretches a series into a ratio that stays accurate over a wider range. With it, they can write clear formulas for things that can be observed, such as the dark shadow a black hole casts. In the limit, they get a closed formula for the shadow of the fully changed black hole. Tests on known models matched well in all cases.
arxiv-2412-13773:
Daigo Mugita and co-authors give a new algorithm for finding the settled states of a packed disk system, in a 2024 paper. Glassy materials relax through rare hops between such states. For hard disks the flat energy floor makes the usual descent methods fail.

Their method moves each disk toward the center of its free area, again and again, until the pack settles. Compared with rival methods, it caught the push of entropy more faithfully. The states it found showed sane shifts and picked out string like hops in a squeezed two kind disk pack. The tool serves work on how dense matter slows and ages.
arxiv-2412-14073:
Tiago de Lima, Emiliano Lorini, Elise Perrotin, and François Schwarzentruber wrote a paper in twenty twenty-four that sets out a formal language for the mental attitudes of agents, human or artificial. The language covers beliefs, what an agent holds to be true, and wants and likes, what an agent is drawn to or away from.

Meanings rest on belief bases, plain data structures a computer can hold, rather than on abstract possible worlds. Five modal operators state full belief, full attraction, full repulsion, and more realistic forms of the last two. The four give rules for the system and prove that none of the five can be swapped for the others. Mixed together, the operators can state mixed feelings, no preference, and being spurred on or put off. A further part of the language tracks how attitudes change.
arxiv-2412-14373:
Han, Duan, Rosenberg, Liu, and Zhao present ECG-Byte, a tokenizer for heart signal language models in twenty twenty-four. Language models can describe electrocardiograms in words. Older systems first train a separate signal encoder, then a language model. That two stage process is slow and hard to interpret.

ECG-Byte adapts byte pair encoding to compress heart signals into tokens. Text and signal tokens then train one model end to end. Tokens map back to the original signal, aiding interpretation. Performance matched the older approach on text generation tasks. Training ran three times faster than the two stage route. It also used less than half the training data. The authors argue direct tokenization is the cleaner path.
arxiv-2412-15273:
Vipula Rawte, Deja Scott, and Gaurav Kumar ask whether official voter information pages actually answer the questions voters have. State election commissions are the main source of voting FAQs in the United States, with nonprofits filling gaps. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team gathered voter FAQs from all fifty states into the first national data set of its kind. They built a quality score covering the questions asked, the answers given, and how well answers match their questions, then graded each state.

Only a small share of states scored as leaders, and a similar small share lagged badly, with most in the middle. Separate leader and laggard lists appear when scoring is tuned for voters versus for developers. The authors close with concrete steps states at every level can take to raise FAQ quality and strengthen the wider information ecosystem around elections.
arxiv-2412-15473:
Ge Gao, Amelia Leon, and colleagues ask how early software logs can forecast student success in a 2024 education study. Schools care most about rare, delayed outcomes such as end-of-year state exams. Waiting a full year to spot struggling students wastes the chance to help them, and testing new tools becomes slow.

Earlier work predicted outcomes from a full year of usage logs, or forecast only the next hour from minutes of data. The authors instead use short-term logs to predict long-term results. Finding signal early could let teachers intervene while change is still possible. It could also speed fair evaluation of learning products.
arxiv-2412-15973:
Recommender systems often train their content encoders apart from the behavior models that use them, which wastes what the content itself can teach. Qijiong Liu, Lu Fan, and Xiao-Ming Wu present Legommenders, a software library that trains content encoders jointly with behavior and interaction modules inside one pipeline. The library lets researchers build and compare more than a thousand distinct models across fifteen datasets with little setup effort.

The library also plugs in large language models in two roles, as feature encoders that read item content and as generators that create synthetic data. By keeping everything in one tested framework, the authors aim to make content based recommendation studies easier to run, easier to reproduce, and easier to extend. They frame the tool as a platform for developing stronger and more personal recommendation models.
arxiv-2412-16273:
Zafar Normatov sets out a new kind of algebra and lists all its smallest cases in a 2024 paper. The objects are called compatible anti-pre-Lie algebras. Each one carries two operations of a set kind that must fit together in a fixed way. Questions of this sort link several branches of modern algebra.

Normatov shows how these algebras connect to two nearby topics: anti-O-operators and special cocycles on compatible Lie algebras. Those links let results proved in one setting carry over to the others. He then lists every example with just two dimensions, building on a known list for the plain version of these algebras. Full lists in small sizes give later researchers test cases for new ideas.
arxiv-2412-16473:
Jonathan Crall, writing alone in 2024, introduces ScatSpotter, a dataset for spotting dog waste in photos. Small, shapeless droppings hide easily in cluttered outdoor scenes. Yet they matter for clean streets, public health, and cleanup robots. Crall gathered images mostly in city settings under a strict photo protocol.

Each site was shot three ways: with the waste, after removal, and a nearby clean scene with look-alikes. The set holds over nine thousand images and six thousand outlined annotations. A community-shot test set adds shots from other hands and places. Off-the-shelf detectors struggled, and a top vision model failed cold. Tuned versions did best, showing the dataset's challenge and value.
arxiv-2412-16573:
Huidong Xie and a large team build a diffusion reconstructor for perfusion scans that works across dose and view settings without retraining. SPECT imaging checks blood flow to the heart muscle, but cutting radiation dose or camera angles degrades the pictures. Earlier deep learning fixes were locked to the setting they trained on. Writing in twenty twenty-four, their framework generates three-dimensional images while a consistency strategy forces every sampling step to agree with the projections, the image data, and the scanner geometry. Detail from CT scans and a smoothness constraint guide the process, and a two-and-a-half-dimensional trick supplies whole-volume context within memory limits.

Validation covered over a thousand stress and rest studies from hundreds of patients, each rendered at several reduced-count levels. The authors report one model handling the range of settings, a flexibility clinics need when protocols vary by patient.
arxiv-2412-17273:
James MacLaurin and Pedro Vilanova derive, in twenty twenty-four, the large-scale limit equations for balanced neural networks. Balanced networks are a popular explanation for the brain's highly variable, noisy activity. Their model has two neuron classes, excitatory and inhibitory, each connected to all others. Each neuron's synaptic response follows a differential equation. Spikes arrive as random Poisson events, with rates set by a sigmoid of the sender's state. Interactions scale more strongly than in classic particle systems.

They show the system does not blow up as the neuron count grows, because excitation and inhibition stay balanced. The limiting population dynamics are Gaussian. The mean is set by the balance point; the variance follows from a central limit theorem. The limit reduces to ordinary differential equations for means and variances.
arxiv-2412-17973:
Abhijat Sarma wrote a paper from 2024 on layered materials whose two crystal patterns clash on purpose. A honeycomb sheet, such as graphene, sits on a base with a different symmetry. Chosen with care, the base folds the sheet's two electron valleys close together. Sarma starts from a tight-binding picture of the atoms and derives a smooth low-energy model of the pair.

Two base shapes are worked through in full. The first grows a hidden time symmetry of its own. Across a wide range of settings it behaves like a stack of one-way wires, a phase called a sliding Luttinger liquid. The second grows a three-fold turn symmetry from a rectangular base. It yields flat bands with honeycomb and kagome patterns, both topological.
arxiv-2412-18673:
Xingjian Zhang and co-authors published a 2024 paper on generating new content from the maps scientists draw of their data. Projection maps squash huge datasets into two-dimensional pictures, where clusters of similar items appear. People read these maps to understand a field, and the empty regions hint at what is missing. Until now, no systematic method turned a point on such a map back into content.

Their task, MapExplorer, asks a model to take coordinates from any projection map and produce text that belongs there, coherent with the neighborhood. Point at a gap between clusters, and the system drafts what could fill it. The authors demonstrate the idea as a knowledge discovery tool: the map stops being a picture and becomes an instrument you can play. Applications range from literature surveys to design spaces. The work reframes visualization as a two-way street, from data to picture and back.
arxiv-2501-00173:
Lewis Bowen and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 proving that a long-standing conjecture about networks is false, by way of an undecidability result. The conjecture asked whether every symmetric random network can be approximated by finite ones. The team attacks a tailored class of nonlocal games, puzzles that also model quantum experiments and proof systems.

They show no algorithm can tell whether such a game admits a perfect play of a special kind or whether every play falls far short. A bridge built in their companion paper turns that undecidability into a counterexample network. As a side result, the proof again settles a famous embedding problem from operator algebras.
arxiv-2501-01073:
Chen and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about a transformer model that generates graphs by predicting tokens in sequence. Graph generation supports molecule design and network analysis. Most models build adjacency matrices directly, which can be wasteful. Their approach writes a graph as a sequence of node and edge sets. That encoding is compact and order-friendly for a transformer. The model, called G2PT, learns structure through next-token prediction like a language model.

Fine-tuning adapts the pretrained model to downstream jobs. Goal-oriented molecule generation and property prediction were tested. Experiments across many data sets showed superior generation quality. Both generic graphs and molecules benefited from the approach. The model showed strong versatility between generation and prediction tasks. The authors present it as a foundation model for graphs. Code is released for public use.
arxiv-2501-03273:
Md Shoaibur Rahman, a solo author, presents a computing study from 2025 on shrinking large language models. Cutting whole layers from a model saves size and cost, but picking which layers to cut is tricky. Single clues, like layer activity or weight size, each miss part of the picture.

Rahman tested fourteen cutting plans across nine data sets. Twelve plans used one clue each, drawn from signals like attention and gradients. Two fusion plans merged the clues, one by regression and one by random forest. The forest fusion won on seven data sets and nearly won the other two. A teaching step then restored lost accuracy, even beating the base model on six sets. Size-to-accuracy gains averaged near nineteen-fold.
arxiv-2501-03473:
Masaya Endo and Rei Kurita study how foam behaves when scraped in this two thousand twenty-five soft matter paper. Foams, colloids, emulsions, and biological tissues all jam, and spreading them takes force applied with a blade or plate. Scraping foam with a rigid plate behaves in complex ways unlike simple liquids. The authors quantitatively analyzed the transition between partial scraping and slender scraping regimes, tracking internal structure and spreading lengths.

They found that partial scraping arises from bubble rearrangements propagating one after another through the foam. The scraping length in the partial regime diverges near the transition point, with a critical exponent near zero point six one. That value matches directional percolation theory, suggesting foam scraping belongs to that universality class. The results advance understanding of flow and deformation in jamming systems generally.
arxiv-2501-04873:
Alexander Valverde, Luis Solano, and André Montoya built a system that tells confiscated seashells' home coast in a 2025 paper. Illegal souvenir collecting strips about five tonnes of shells from Costa Rican beaches each year. Once seized, shells cannot be returned because officers cannot tell which coast they came from.

The team assembled BackHome19K, a set of about 19,000 shell photos across 516 species, each labeled Pacific or Caribbean. Their light pipeline sorts a shell's origin on a plain phone-grade processor. It reached about 86 percent balanced accuracy, and a screening filter rejected most non-shell images. A web app has already processed 70,000 shells for wildlife officers.
arxiv-2501-06473:
Chunbing Cai, Jordan Roulleau-Pasdeloup, and Zhongxi Zheng solve stuck-interest-rate models in this two thousand twenty-five paper. When central bank rates hit their floor, standard economics models grow hard to solve. Earlier methods handle special cases with pencil and paper. The authors give a perfect-foresight method that contains those cases and goes beyond them. Their version lets today's effects linger endogenously, a feature the older tricks lack.

They prove the method always yields stable spending multipliers. A model with habit formation is fit to expectations data from the Great Recession. The fiscal multiplier comes out near one for both the United States and Japan. Macroeconomists who study recessions at the rate floor are the audience.
arxiv-2501-06873:
Prashant Garg and Thiemo Fetzer map causal claims across economics in two thousand twenty five. Economics papers make claims that resist easy comparison at scale. Their claim graphs turn each paper into a directed network. Nodes are standard concepts, edges are stated relationships.

Each edge is labeled by its evidentiary basis. Causal designs are marked apart from non causal support. A multi stage AI workflow built graphs for over forty four thousand papers. Causal edges rose from under eight percent in nineteen ninety. They passed thirty percent by twenty twenty. Causal structure links to top journals and lasting citations.
arxiv-2501-06973:
Stars can be born inside the dense gas disks around giant black holes, live fast, and collapse there. Chris Fryer and five co-authors model what those stars leave behind in a 2025 paper. Fed by the disk, the stars grow massive and spin fast, then explode or collapse into neutron stars and black holes.

Even stars that form black holes can fling out much iron, thanks to disks spun off during collapse. Those chemical traces might show up in the glow of the disk itself, giving observers a way to count how many such systems form. The authors call this a first study and note the models need widening.
arxiv-2501-07473:
Edoardo Di Martino, Matteo Cinelli, Roy Cerqueti, and Walter Quattrociocchi compared measures of political polarization in twenty twenty-five. Polarization drives social fragmentation, but quantifying it inside an ideological distribution is methodologically unsettled. The authors put five widely used measures through their paces on synthetic data, where the truth is known. They also used a real case: YouTube discussions around the twenty twenty United States presidential election.

Each measure showed distinct strengths and failure modes. Building on the diagnosis, the team adapted Kleinberg's burst detection algorithm — originally for spotting surges in streams — to detect modes in polarized distributions more faithfully. The paper offers both a critical review for researchers choosing a measure and a new tool for reading ideological patterns in social media discourse.
arxiv-2501-08373:
Water barely absorbs visible light, yet experiments show sunlight can boil it off a surface far faster than heat alone allows. Michael Landry and co-authors propose a theory for this photomolecular effect. At the surface, they argue, a photon's energy can cleave whole clusters of water molecules free in one event, rather than warming them loose one by one.

The puzzle pieces fit: evaporation runs two to five times above the thermal limit, and the rate peaks at green wavelengths even though absorption does not. The model explains how light couples to the interface strongly enough to snip the clusters. If right, the effect matters for clouds, desalination, and drying technology.
arxiv-2501-08573:
Iago Nascimento Barros and Marcelo Lobato Martins simulate how taxes and redistribution shape wealth inequality, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Their start point is stark: wealth can pile up with no cap at all. The pair asks which rules can soften the gap that grows out of that fact.

They build on a past agent-based model. New parts are non-uniform redistribution policies and tax evasion. The runs go on till wealth settles into a steady state. The results back two claims with force. Well-made rules cut the gap in a real way, and tight control of tax planning and evasion is just as much a must. Both are key tools for a society that is more equal and can last.
arxiv-2501-08773:
Rydberg atoms, atoms excited to huge orbits, are a favorite platform for quantum computers because neighbors interact strongly. Jun Wu and co-authors use a rhythmic tuning method, called Floquet frequency modulation, to shape those interactions into flexible logic gates. Their scheme builds gates that add any chosen phase.

A key gain is that no laser needs to aim at single atoms, which simplifies the hardware. The method can also merge with gentle control techniques that raise accuracy and stability. As a proof of use, the team runs a search algorithm variant that finds its target with zero failure rate in their tests. The authors argue the approach suits large, reliable machines. It joins two active toolkits: Rydberg hardware and rhythm-based control.
arxiv-2501-08973:
Takashi Kurumaji and a large team gauge the band form of YAuGe, a pick for a seam-like state. The work came out in 2025. The stuff is thought to host Kramers seam lines. Those are one-step seams where bands touch. The seams are kept safe by the frame's own flip rules.

Thought says such seam lines rise in each frame that lacks a core and lacks a hand twist. Math puts them on a set plane of this stuff's push space. The team checks with two tests. One test snaps shots of the band form with light. One test probes the form with pull fields and waves. Both show marks that match the called hole bands. The full name of the work flags one more trait. An odd Hall shift shows up when rare-earth bits with pull take the place of some bits in the stuff.
arxiv-2501-09373:
Black holes in anti-de Sitter space matter because of the AdS/CFT correspondence, which links gravity to a boundary field theory. Nashed studies charged, stationary, and rotating four-dimensional solutions in f(Q) gravity, a theory built on non-metricity rather than curvature. He uses a power-law form for the theory, chosen because it fits observations. The resulting solutions form a new class: they have no uncharged version and do not reduce to general relativity.

He computes curvature and non-metricity invariants and finds a central singularity that is softer than in Einstein gravity, an effect he credits to f(Q). The holes show an outer event horizon plus inner Cauchy horizons, but a large enough charge strips the cover and leaves a naked singularity. He also derives a rotating charged solution that is asymptotically anti-de Sitter, and he examines the holes' thermodynamics.
arxiv-2501-09673:
Álvaro Rodríguez Echarri and co-authors build a general theory for electron energy-loss spectroscopy in cylinder-shaped structures, in a physics paper from 2025. Fast electrons passing near metal wires or holes shake loose plasmons, and the energy they lose reveals those modes. Most theory handles electrons flying along the cylinder's axis.

The new work gives closed-form solutions for electrons crossing at right angles to the axis, the missing geometry. Two heavy numerical methods confirm the formulas. The numerics also handle finite rods, where ends change the picture. The framework serves both reading spectra and designing hybrid devices that couple free electrons with light in fibers, wires, and holes.
arxiv-2501-09973:
Jize Han and seven colleagues wrote a paper in twenty twenty-five that fixes key constants of the ytterbium-171 ion. The ion is a top system for microwave quantum frequency standards, the atomic clocks that keep the most exact time. Its Landé g-factor states how the ion's energy levels shift in a magnetic field. Exact values are needed to correct clock readings for magnetic upsets.

The team worked out the g-factor by two separate advanced methods and got the same value both ways, about 2.002615. From it they drew the first- and second-order Zeeman coefficients, which state how strongly the field moves the levels. With these numbers, clock builders can cut magnetic error and sharpen the clocks. The results may also help tests of whether nature's basic constants change over time.
arxiv-2501-10773:
Xinyue Cheng and Yalu Feng wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on Finsler manifolds, spaces where distance depends on direction as well as position. The authors study such spaces when curvature is controlled only in an averaged, integral sense. That weaker control is harder to work with but covers more cases.

They first prove comparison theorems for the Laplacian and for volumes, the basic rulers of the field. From those, they draw a volume growth estimate and a compactness result for families of such spaces. A local estimate of the isoperimetric constant follows, which measures how area fences volume. That estimate then yields bounds on the first eigenvalue of bounded regions and on gradients of harmonic functions. The paper builds a toolkit for rough-curvature geometry.
arxiv-2501-11173:
Karianne Calta, Timothy Goldberg, and Lauren Rose present a 2025 mathematics paper inspired by a card game. Quad-128 is a pattern-matching card game played on a seven-dimensional board over a two-symbol alphabet. A cap is a set of points where every four sit in general position, with no hidden flat pattern among them.

The authors classify all caps of size ten or more in this geometry, up to symmetry. There are two kinds of ten-point caps and one kind of eleven-point cap, none of them complete. The twelve-point caps form a single class, and they are both complete and as large as possible. The result answers how many cards can be laid out before the pattern rules force a stop.
arxiv-2501-11773:
Katharine Fisher and Youssef Marzouk ask whether Bayesian neural networks can make confident predictions, in two thousand twenty-five. Such networks promise a principled way to state how unsure a prediction is. In practice, the full spread of plausible network settings is hard to map, and its meaning is murky.

Under a stepped prior on the inner weights, the pair can write the prediction spread exactly as a mix of bell curves. That form lets them group settings that give the same training error. They find settings where unlike settings fit training data equally well yet predict unlike outcomes. They also chart when the prediction spread tightens as more data arrives.
arxiv-2501-12273:
Maosong Cao and colleagues generate synthetic conversation data to fine-tune chat models, using stored world knowledge and self-critique to keep quality high. Human-written fine-tuning data is scarce and expensive, yet model manners depend on it. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their two-stage framework first grows a tree of world knowledge topics to seed diverse questions. Answers, then runs a self-reflection stage where the model revises its own drafts. The pipeline is designed to scale without armies of annotators.

A base model trained on only a modest set of the synthetic examples outperformed counterparts trained otherwise, by the authors report. The refinement stage also let models of many sizes, up to the largest tested, improve themselves iteratively. A side study of how performance scales with synthetic data volume suggests large headroom remains.
arxiv-2501-13073:
José Rodríguez-Ortega, Francisco Pérez-Hernández, and Siham Tabik wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It locates anatomical landmarks on 3D dental scans in one end-to-end pass, skipping the slow tooth-by-tooth segmentation that earlier systems needed.

Orthodontists place these landmarks by hand, slowly and expertly. The method, CHaRM, encodes the scan's point cloud, then predicts heatmaps for each landmark. A companion head reports which teeth are present, and a novel module feeds that knowledge back in, steadying detection when teeth are missing. The team trained and tested it on a new public set of 1,214 annotated scans, using five different point cloud backbones. The best variant beat prior state-of-the-art systems on accuracy and speed. Dataset and code are released to give orthodontics the open footing other fields enjoy.
arxiv-2501-14373:
Lingwei Zhu, Han Wang, and Yukie Nagai present a 2025 paper on learning safe policies from logged data in reinforcement learning. Sparse policies assign truly zero chance to some actions, unlike the usual bell-curve policies. That matters in fields like medicine, where some options must never be picked. Offline learning from records is attractive, but existing methods need to evaluate actions the sparse policy rules out, which breaks them.

Their method, Fat-to-Thin Policy Optimization, keeps two policies. A broad, heavy-tailed one learns from the data set, then passes its knowledge to the sparse policy that acts in the world. Tests covered a safety-focused treatment simulation and a standard robot control suite. The method performed favorably against rivals in both. The authors release their code for others to try.
arxiv-2501-14773:
Zlatan Ajanović and co-authors study how well-run research institutes are organized, in work from 2024. They look at institutes that stand out for both scientific quality and benefit to society. Small countries and the field of artificial intelligence get special focus.

The team defines key practices on three fronts: how research results are judged, what money terms an institute needs, and how topics are chosen. The aim is a recipe for institutes that can sustain themselves while serving the public. Traits that enable high innovation are named and weighed. The paper speaks to founders and funders who build institutes outside the largest research nations.
arxiv-2501-16273:
Mohamed Elfeki, Rui Liu, and Chad Voegele make the case for bringing back the two-part form of language model for small models. Big one-part models rule the field, yet they spend much at each step. The two-part form reads the input once, then writes, which should cost less. The team timed both forms on three kinds of chips used in small gear.

For models of a billion parts or less, the two-part form cut the wait for the first word by near half. It also pushed through more than four times the work on edge gear. A new way to pour skill from big one-part teachers into small two-part students won back about six score points on the whole. With fresh tricks added, the old form looks like the sane path for models that must run on the gear itself.
arxiv-2501-16573:
Girnar Goyal, Philipp Holl, Sweta Agrawal, and Nils Thuerey wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It shows that a neural network can learn the treacherous landscape of a physics fitting problem and smooth it, so the search for the right parameters stops falling into traps.

Inverse problems, recovering hidden causes from observed effects, are solved by climbing down an error surface. For systems governed by partial differential equations, that surface is chaotic, pocked with local minima and flat dead zones. The authors feed networks the trajectories of simulations and find they reproduce the wild landscape faithfully. Regularization during training then irons the landscape to a chosen smoothness. Optimizing on the smoothed proxy beat a standard momentum optimizer, BFGS, on several hard problems. The approach treats the optimizer's map, not the territory, as the thing to engineer.
arxiv-2501-16673:
Li Yin and Zhangyang Wang automate prompt tuning for multi-step language model workflows in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Crafting prompts by hand is slow, and it gets harder when a pipeline chains many model calls with tools like search and formatting.

Their framework, LLM-AutoDiff, treats each text input as a trainable setting. A frozen second model writes feedback, like a gradient in text form, that steers prompt updates step by step. The design handles tool nodes, repeated calls in loops, and split sub-prompts, and it spends compute on error-prone samples. Across sorting, multi-hop question answering, and agent pipelines, it beat earlier text-gradient methods on both accuracy and training cost.
arxiv-2501-17273:
Jasper Timm, Chetan Talele, and Jacob Haimes measure how well language models can persuade people in a 2025 study. Models can now tailor arguments to a reader using personal data, which raises the scale at which disinformation could work. The team set up debates in which a person argued with model-made text meant to change their view.

Thirty-three people took part. The researchers measured each person's agreement with the debate claim before and after, and tracked both how far views moved and whether they moved the model's way. They compared several tactics: arguments shaped by the reader's traits, arguments backed by invented statistics, and a mix of both. The study names itself with a warning: tailored text plus fake numbers is a potent mix, and knowing its strength is a first step to defense.
arxiv-2501-17573:
Jinmian Li, Takaaki Nomura, and Kei Yagyu hunt for multi-lepton jets from an exotic Higgs decay. Their twenty twenty-five particle physics paper studies the LHC collider. The Higgs boson could decay through a new scalar into four new gauge bosons. Light masses would boost those bosons strongly.

Leptons from such boosted decays bunch into jets, not isolated tracks. The team simulated signals and backgrounds for that signature. Muon-based jets set strong limits on how often the decay can occur. Electron jets help when the new boson is very light. The limits convert into bounds on mixing between the Higgs and the new scalar.
arxiv-2501-18173:
Paolo Nason and Giulia Zanderighi refine the value of the strong coupling from jet shapes. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, extends an earlier fit. The coupling sets the strength of the force that binds quarks. They fit it with a partner term for effects outside standard perturbation theory, using three-jet events.

The earlier work used data from one machine at one energy. The new fit adds many machines across a wide energy span. The central value barely moves, which is a good sign. Spread across energies helps split the two kinds of corrections apart. Error bars split into test-based and theory-based parts. The result matches the world average well.
arxiv-2501-18673:
Tyler Volkoff and Giri Gopalan study how to gauge the length scale of a stirred quantum oscillator. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Heavy oscillators are eyed for fine sensors and weak-force hunts. Their phase space is stretched, and the stretch is set by a length scale that can itself be the target.

They show that squeezed and rung-up states of one oscillator hit Heisenberg scaling for that scale as the rung count grows, with unbiased gauges to match. Two oscillators tied in a chain gain as much as a third plain one would add. A chain of many shows the same scaling with total energy.
arxiv-2501-18773:
David Martínez-Rubio and Sebastian Pokutta present new ways to make a classic optimization method work better, in a research paper from 2025. The method, called Frank-Wolfe, solves problems step by step and is used when each step must stay simple. Past work often used short steps that lean on how smooth the target function is.

The authors add an optimistic version of the method, which uses past steps to plan the next one. They prove that this version closes the gap between the current answer and the best answer at a good rate. They also give a broader short-step rule based on a gap that a computer can check. Tests show the new method beats older ones in practice, and the step rule also helps plain gradient descent.
arxiv-2502-00873:
Subhash Kantamneni and Max Tegmark present a 2025 study that reverse-engineers how language models add numbers. Math skill is a key test of such models, yet their inner method was a black box. The team studied three mid-sized models. Numbers, they find, are stored as a twisted spiral code, a shape they call a generalized helix. That code is shown to drive addition and subtraction, and to serve division and remainders too.

Addition runs by turning the two number spirals into the answer spiral, a routine they name the Clock. They model the outputs of layers, heads, and single neurons with the spiral code. Direct tweaks to the code change answers as the theory says. The work gives a first part-level account of model math.
arxiv-2502-01273:
Students now code alongside AI assistants, and educators want to know what that help does to learning. Naman Agrawal and co-authors follow 126 undergraduates through a thirteen-week software project in this 2025 study. They log the students' chats with the assistant and track how much of its code survived into the final work.

Students preferred a chat assistant over an in-editor one. The chat tool also produced simpler code, and talking through problems yielded better code than accepting automatic completions. The authors argue that early, guided practice with AI tools is now part of becoming an engineer, and courses should teach students how to work with these assistants well.
arxiv-2502-01673:
Arpita Vats, Rahul Raja, Mrinal Mathur, Vinija Jain, and Aman Chadha apply state space models to question answering in Indic languages, in a 2025 paper. India's languages pose hard problems for language tech: rich word forms, tangled syntax, and scarce training data. State space models track long and short links in sequences well, which suits these traits. The team tested several such designs on question answering data sets across Indic languages.

Their results show the models catch subtle language cues and align questions with context more soundly. Answer quality improved over earlier approaches in their comparisons. The authors call this the first use of these models for Indic question answering, setting a benchmark for later work. They also propose tweaks to fit low-resource and multilingual settings better.
arxiv-2502-01773:
Xupeng Zhu and co-authors improve, in twenty twenty-five, keyframe imitation learning for robot manipulation by exploiting symmetry. Imitation from keyframes can teach many tasks, but ignoring symmetry wastes training samples. Their setting has a double symmetry: moving the workspace or the grasped object should move the action the same way. They analyze that symmetry and build a Keyframe Transporter policy. It scores actions by cross-correlating features of the grasped object with features of the scene, in the spirit of transporter networks.

A coarse-to-fine scheme then evaluates combined translation and rotation actions efficiently. The method beat strong baselines by over ten percent on average across simulation tasks. In four real robot experiments, it won by about fifty-five percent on average.
arxiv-2502-02673:
Adibvafa Fallahpour and four colleagues introduce MedRAX, an AI agent for interpreting chest X-rays, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Chest X-rays drive critical decisions in disease management and patient care. Specialized models exist for many interpretation tasks, but they usually work in isolation. That limits their usefulness in real clinical practice.

MedRAX integrates leading chest X-ray analysis tools and multimodal large language models into one framework. It calls these tools dynamically to answer complex medical queries, with no extra training. To test it, the authors built ChestAgentBench, a benchmark of twenty-five hundred complex queries across seven categories. MedRAX reached state-of-the-art performance against both open-source and proprietary models in their experiments. The authors present it as a step toward practical automated X-ray interpretation.
arxiv-2502-02873:
T-H Hsieh and co-authors mapped gas temperatures and carbon forms around a pair of forming stars using the ALMA telescope array, in a 2025 paper. Twin young stars are common, but how material streams from the wide envelope onto the pair, and how that shapes heat and chemistry, is poorly seen. Their target holds two infant sources close together.

They observed two forms of a probe molecule, one normal and one with a rarer carbon type, at fine detail. Careful modeling that includes dust blocking the light proved essential to read the signals. The team sorted six gas motions, including a possible stream falling onto the brighter, bursting source. Heat from shocks and from the binary's motions likely sculpts the region, and the carbon ratio came out below the usual space value.
arxiv-2502-03773:
Chhavi Yadav, Evan Monroe Laufer, Dan Boneh, and Kamalika Chaudhuri make AI explanations provable in a 2025 computing paper. Rules increasingly demand that models explain their decisions. But when the parties distrust each other, explanations can be cooked: a lender could show a flattering reason that is not the real one. The authors bring in zero-knowledge proofs, cryptography that proves a claim without revealing the secrets behind it.

Their system, ExpProof, adapts the popular explanation method LIME so its output can be proven against a hidden model. They test it on neural networks and random forests and release the code. Provable explanations could let regulators check fairness without companies surrendering their models.
arxiv-2502-03973:
Alan Tsz-Lok Lam and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on whether neutron stars that spin at wild, uneven rates can hold together under a theory that tweaks gravity. In the tweaked theory, merged stars could keep about ten times the spin that standard theory allows. Such extremes are pointless if they fly apart at the first wobble.

The team evolved these stars in computer models that keep the setup symmetric around the spin axis. A classic turning-point rule still signaled where stability ends. The survivors raise a sharp question: can two such tweaked stars merge and leave a short-lived, ultra-fast remnant? The work gives merger modelers a stability map to test.
arxiv-2502-04173:
Juraj Vladika, Stephen Meisenbacher, and Florian Matthes study word replacement in this two thousand twenty-five natural language processing paper. Lexical substitution swaps one word in a sentence for another that fits the context and grammar, not merely a dictionary synonym. Recent methods use masked language models to propose replacements. The authors' approach, ConCat, feeds the original sentence back in as extra context to steer those proposals.

Quantitative evaluation using sentence similarity and task performance showed ConCat guiding models toward more contextually relevant substitutes than existing approaches. A qualitative human study confirmed that users preferred its suggestions. The team also tested on CoInCo, the prevailing benchmark for the task, and found potential pitfalls in how the benchmark scores systems. Those findings ground a critical discussion of how lexical substitution should be evaluated, beyond the paper's own method.
arxiv-2502-05073:
Rupert Li and Elchanan Mossel wrote a 2025 theory paper on why some structured functions are hard for computers to learn. Many successes of deep learning involve data built in layers, like a tree. The authors study functions with that tree structure, where each layer combines the outputs of the one below. They measure how steady such a function is when its inputs are slightly scrambled by noise.

They show that if each piece of the hierarchy is not close to a simple linear rule, the whole function becomes extremely sensitive to noise. Its steadiness shrinks at an exponential rate as the tree deepens. That fact has direct payoffs. It yields strong lower bounds on what a common class of learning algorithms can achieve. It also bounds how many examples gradient-based training needs. A related result covers crossing events in a physics model of spreading through a grid.
arxiv-2502-05173:
A team of co-authors wrote a machine learning paper in two thousand twenty-five on how video models should encode position. Rotary position embedding is a popular way to tell a model where each token sits, prized for handling long inputs. Video adds time and space together, and stretching the one-dimensional trick to video is not obvious.

The authors first name four traits a good video version needs. They build a hard test in which moving distractors are planted in a visual search task, and older variants fail it. Their design, VideoRoPE, uses a three-dimensional layout with slow time frequencies and a diagonal arrangement to keep space and time relations intact.
arxiv-2502-05573:
Teams of learning agents, like squads in a strategy game, often share one policy to keep training cheap, but sharing everything can dull each agent's special skills. Beining Zhang and co-authors propose LoRASA in this 2025 paper, giving each agent a small personal tweak on top of the shared policy.

The tweaks are tiny low-rank matrices added at each layer, which keeps memory and compute costs low while letting agents specialize. Bolted onto two popular training methods, the approach matched or beat rivals on game and robot benchmarks. Tests of tweak size and placement confirm the design is flexible, and the authors pitch it as a new default pattern.
arxiv-2502-05773:
Junbo Li, Zhangyang Wang, and Qiang Liu recast the alignment of language models as a statistics problem with a prior, in a 2025 paper. Offline preference methods like DPO train models from ranked answers without costly reinforcement learning, but the family of methods lacked one story. Their framework, PIPA, frames alignment as maximum likelihood estimation with prior constraints. Paired or unpaired data, whole answers or single steps, all fit.

Two famous methods fall out as special cases with different priors. Two new variants built on richer priors gained three to ten percent on grade-school and competition math benchmarks. The gains cost no extra training or compute. The authors offer the framework as the missing common language for alignment research.
arxiv-2502-05973:
Shengwen Gan, Danqing He, Xiaochun Li, and Shukun Wu prove sharper estimates for how wave motion smooths itself out over short distances and times. The local smoothing question, open since the late nineteen eighties, asks how much extra regularity wave solutions gain when watched in a bounded region. It sits where wave equations, harmonic analysis, and geometry meet, and hard cases are tied to Kakeya-type configurations of thin tubes. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team works both on flat spaces and on curved compact spaces.

For odd dimensions they reach estimates that are sharp, meaning no better bound of that form exists. In even dimensions they improve what was known. The route goes through smoothing bounds for a class of Fourier integral operators. Results for ordinary flat space improve as well, as a byproduct of the general method.
arxiv-2502-06173:
Sanket Jantre and co-authors adapt large language models to predict which proteins interact, while keeping track of how sure the model is, in a 2025 paper. Knowing protein partnerships explains how cells work and where diseases strike, and language models can mine the vast biomedical literature for clues. Their weakness is shaky confidence: answers may not repeat, which is dangerous in medicine.

The team fine-tuned two models, a general one and a biomedical one, for the interaction task. To grade confidence, they added two uncertainty tools built on small adapter modules, one using ensembles and one using Bayesian reasoning. The system matched rival tools at finding interactions across several disease settings. More importantly, its confidence scores were calibrated, so users can tell which predictions to trust. The authors frame this as a step toward precision medicine tools that know their own limits.
arxiv-2502-06573:
A large detector collaboration characterizes a new pixel sensor chip for particle physics in a 2025 paper. A fresh 65-nanometer chip process packs more logic into each pixel than older lines allow. Their test chip ports a proven hybrid detector design into a single monolithic piece.

The matrix holds about a thousand square pixels, each with its own pulse processing. The study focuses on how response varies inside a single pixel, a detail that affects position accuracy. Bench measurements map that non-uniformity across the array. Monolithic sensors promise lighter, cheaper tracking detectors for future colliders. Knowing the in-pixel quirks early lets designers correct them in the next chip revision.
arxiv-2502-08773:
Running big language models costs money, so services keep a pool of models and send each prompt to the cheapest one that can handle it. Wittawat Jitkrittum led a team that tackles the harder case: brand-new models arriving at test time, never seen during training. Their method, UniRoute, describes each model by a fingerprint, its answers on a fixed set of sample prompts.

Routers built on those fingerprints come in two forms, one grouping models into clusters and one learning a map to them. Both are shown to shadow the ideal routing rule, with a bound on their error. Tests across public benchmarks, with more than thirty unseen models in the pool, showed the approach picks well without retraining.
arxiv-2502-08873:
Sawyer Jack Robertson and four co-authors make graph learning hold its nerve when labels are few or dirty. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Semi-supervised methods spread labels across a network, but scarce or corrupted labels poison the spread.

Their method, p-conductance learning, generalizes two earlier approaches under one objective. An affine loosening of the label constraints keeps bad labels from ruling. The math links the programs to randomized cuts, effective resistance, and distribution distances. A Newton-style solver, extended to use class-size estimates, turns the continuous answers into labels. On vision and citation graphs, accuracy topped rivals exactly where labels were rarest or most corrupted. Partial labeling regimes showed the same edge.
arxiv-2502-09173:
Jin Cui, Alexander Capstick, Payam Barnaghi, and Gregory Scott published this health data paper in 2025. It analyzes movement and activity data recorded in the homes of people living with dementia. Such high-frequency records are rich but hard to read. The authors propose a two-stage, self-supervised learning method that squeezes the data into a compact form that keeps the meaningful patterns.

In the first stage, activity sequences are turned into text-like strings and encoded by a pre-trained language model. A PageRank-based step then extracts a low-rank summary of how one activity state follows another. That summary supports clustering and transition analysis. The patterns it revealed lined up with clinical scores of cognitive function. The authors say the approach could support predicting cognitive status, tailoring care, and monitoring many patients at scale.
arxiv-2502-09373:
Kyu-Hyun Chae tests gravity at very weak pull using pairs of widely spaced stars, in a research paper from 2025. Wide binaries act as natural labs for this test, since their slow orbits feel tiny accelerations. Past studies used only the motion seen across the sky.

Chae built a Bayesian orbit method that also uses motion along the line of sight, then applied it to 312 pairs from the Gaia DR3 data. At stronger pull, the results matched Newton's law well. At the weakest pull, gravity looked stronger than Newton predicts, by a factor near 1.4 in the broad weak range. That boost closely matches what MOND theories of gravity predict for this regime.
arxiv-2502-11073:
Ming Shan Hee and Roy Ka-Wei Lee present IntMeme, a system that spots hateful memes and explains its calls. Their paper appeared in 2025. Memes can hide hate in jokes and context, so detection is hard. Older systems classify well but cannot say why, which weakens trust. The new system uses a large model that reads both image and text to write a plain account of each meme.

The system encodes the meme and its written account apart, then joins them for the final call. This mix raised accuracy while keeping decisions open to inspection. The authors test the system against older fine-tuned models and report gains on both fronts. They argue that moderation tools should show their reasoning, so human reviewers can check calls and users can appeal them.
arxiv-2502-11173:
Armando Bellante and co-authors assess whether quantum machine learning could change cybersecurity, in work from 2025. Quantum computing threatens current encryption, and defenders are building post-quantum tools. Less clear is how quantum learning methods might affect everyday security tasks such as spotting network intrusions.

The team surveys where quantum methods might beat classical learning on security problems. They then set out a method to quantify the future impact of fault-tolerant quantum algorithms on real tasks. As a case study, they apply the method to standard intrusion detection methods and datasets based on a classic compression technique. The results spell out what hardware and software advances would be needed for a real quantum edge. The work aims to guide investment before such machines exist.
arxiv-2502-11673:
Adrian Müller and four co-authors asked if one learning rule can be both safe and sharp in games. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with online learning with bandit feedback. Two aims clash: lose near naught next to a set fixed plan, and lose slow next to any plan. Past work left if both can hold at once in doubt. They give the first yes, when the fixed plan can play each move.

In zero sum games with value zero, the same math lets a player risk a flat small loss. Yet it can still take a haul that grows with time from a weak foe. That joins the perks of no regret play and of minimax play. Readers in game learning get a best of both form.
arxiv-2502-12873:
The BESIII Collaboration reports a first measurement of a phase effect in particle decays in a paper from 2025. The work uses data from a detector in electron and positron collisions. It studies a charm particle and its antimatter twin decaying into two kaons and two pions. The phase gap between the two paths matters for a key angle in particle theory.

Measurements were made in four paired slices of the decay pattern, chosen for best sensitivity. The team also found the share of the decay with even symmetry. A new decay rate value came out twice as precise as earlier ones. The results feed into sharper tests of matter and antimatter differences.
arxiv-2502-12973:
Marino Kühne and five co-authors tune social networks against polarization in twenty twenty-five. Platforms widen access to ideas yet are blamed for splitting opinions. Handcrafted fixes and heuristics dominate current responses. The authors instead treat the network itself as the design variable.

Interaction weights between users, such as contact frequency, become the controls. User opinions evolve under the classical Friedkin-Johnsen model. The goal is optimizing a metric like polarization reduction. That yields a large, non-convex optimization problem. Their hypergradient-based algorithm is simple, scalable, and accepts varied objectives. Readers in control and network science get a principled alternative: design the recommender's connection strengths directly, rather than patching content rules one by one.
arxiv-2502-13373:
Swati Kar, Soumyabrata Dey, Mahesh Banavar, and Shahnewaz Karim Sakib published this artificial intelligence paper in 2025. It trains a fighter jet agent inside a custom game-like simulation built with Pygame. The jet must do three things at once: navigate the space, reach a target, and choose when to fight or flee from an enemy. A reward function balances the three goals while the agent learns by deep reinforcement learning.

The trained agent completed more than eighty percent of its tasks. To make its choices understandable, the authors compare the reward of the action the jet picked against the rewards of the actions it passed over. That factual-versus-alternative check shows why the agent acted as it did. The study is offered as a small demonstration of multi-goal learning with built-in explanation.
arxiv-2502-13873:
Hui Wang and a large team of co-authors built a runahead trick to feed sparse neural nets on NPUs. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a speed flaw: sparse models cut math but their wild memory paths miss the cache oft, so wall time stays high. Past fixes rework the memory layout at high cost and poor port. Their tool, NVR, runs ahead in vector form to fetch data before the main core stalls.

It is a light, split off hardware add that needs no compiler or algorithm change. That makes it fit many sparse loads. Readers who build AI chips get a cache cure that rides on the chip, not on the model.
arxiv-2502-14873:
Wensrich and six co-authors examine a stress measurement problem in twenty twenty-five. Eigenstrain methods infer residual stress inside a material from measured data. The authors ask whether those inverse problems are well-posed. They focus on non-uniqueness: many eigenstrain fields can fit the same measurements.

Through the null space structure, they show a trivial solution exists for every such problem. All other solutions differ from it by an unobservable null component. That sounds fatal, yet the framework still has use. It enforces equilibrium while estimating stress from incomplete data. Two examples use measured data, one on ancient Roman medical tools. Readers get a clear-eyed account of what eigenstrain analysis can and cannot reveal.
arxiv-2502-15673: Guillaume Blanc and Alice Contat find how fast a solution grows without bound for a generalized Blasius equation, in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. The equation came from their work on a chance model they call Poissonian burning in Euclidean space. Their proof tracks the solutions of a Lotka-Volterra system over long stretches of time. That system is a classic model of groups that act on each other.
arxiv-2502-15873:
Stephen Casper, Luke Bailey, and Tim Schreier propose principles for AI cost and compute accounting in a 2025 paper. Lawmakers increasingly use training cost and compute as stand ins for AI capability and risk. Some rules trigger duties once a model passes a set threshold, so how the numbers are counted matters greatly.

Ambiguity creates loopholes that firms could game, weakening the rules. The authors offer seven principles for accounting standards. Their goals are to cut gaming, avoid punishing firms for safety work, and keep practice consistent across companies and countries. Clear accounting, they argue, is basic infrastructure for AI governance.
arxiv-2502-16473:
Chenyang Yin and co-authors present TerEffic in 2025, hardware that runs large language models with ternary weights on a reconfigurable chip. Edge devices lack the memory and power budget for standard models. Ternary quantization, where each weight takes one of three values, slashes memory while keeping much of the accuracy.

General processors waste that advantage because they still move and multiply data the wide way. Their FPGA design is built around ternary arithmetic from the start. The result is fast, low-power inference suited to phones, robots, and offline devices. Efficient local models matter for privacy and for places with poor connectivity, two growing limits on cloud-based AI.
arxiv-2502-17173:
Xueru Wen and colleagues built Chinese reward models from scratch in a 2025 guidance paper. Reward models grade language model answers to steer them toward human taste, but nearly all research uses English and machine-made data. For Chinese, that leaves training sets and test sets thin and shaky, so models may learn the wrong lessons about what readers want.

The team offers a fully human-checked test set for Chinese contexts and a large preference dataset labeled by people and machines together. Leading open models scored poorly on the human test, showing real gaps. A model trained on their data topped the test, which argues that careful human supervision still beats piles of synthetic labels.
arxiv-2502-18073:
Manca and a team of colleagues reported in twenty twenty-five on a candidate transitional millisecond pulsar and its gamma-ray match. Such pulsars switch between spinning power and feeding on a companion star. In their active state they are the only low-mass X-ray binaries seen at very high energies by the Fermi telescope.

The X-ray source they studied sat near a faint gamma-ray source in the Fermi catalog. The team reanalyzed Fermi data from two thousand eight to twenty twenty-three, rebuilding the background model. Their sharper position matched the X-ray source at the ninety-five percent confidence level. The gamma rays followed a simple power-law shape. The match supports the source's status as a transitional pulsar.
arxiv-2502-19473:
Pierre Kervella and co-authors search for faint infrared glow from a nearby dormant black hole. Their 2025 paper targets Gaia BH3, a black hole of about thirty-three solar masses found by its pull on a companion star. It sits close enough that interferometry can separate it from that star.

Using four large telescopes linked as one instrument, the team looked for near-infrared emission from gas falling toward the hole. They found none, down to a contrast of a small fraction of the companion's light. Nor did a hydrogen line show emission. The upper limit caps how much material the hole is currently swallowing. A quiet result still informs theory, since a truly dormant hole should glow far below this bound, and any future brightening would stand out.
