arxiv-2502-20073:
Haochen Sun leads a team of nine on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It grades language model agents as teammates, in a cooking game where two cooks must share a cramped kitchen.

The benchmark, Collab-Overcooked, grows out of the Overcooked-AI game. Agents chat in plain words to divide the work. New scores grade the fine grain of teamwork, not just the final soup count. Thirty open tasks ship with the test bed. Thirteen well-known models are run through it. All read the goal well enough. The weak spots are the live parts of teamwork: speaking up, pitching in, and reshaping the plan as things shift. The authors map the strengths and gaps for the field.
arxiv-2502-20273:
Varshini Reddy and three co-authors ask how much training data a tokenizer needs in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Tokenizers split text into pieces before a language model reads it. Their quality depends on settings like vocabulary size and the algorithm used. One setting is rarely studied: how much text the tokenizer itself trains on. The team trained three kinds of tokenizers across many vocabulary sizes.

Their training corpora ranged from one gigabyte to nine hundred gigabytes of English text. Gains in tokenizer quality faded once data passed roughly one hundred fifty gigabytes. Past that point, more data bought little. The authors trace why the returns flatten. The finding gives model builders a sane budget for tokenizer training.
arxiv-2502-20373:
Zhang and co-authors prove a learn plan for mixed quantum sets at the best pace cap. Mixed sets pair unlike grain kinds in one quantum frame. Such sets ground work in stuff and facts fields in labs. Their plan reads an unknown spin-boson drive form in full. It hits the Heisenberg cap for all tie marks to a set flaw. Whole time runs as one past the flaw in their proof.

Read counts run as a soft log of that flaw count in step. Small prep and read flaws fail to break the plan in tests. A twin plan spreads reads to cut time per read a lot. Tests span mixed drive learn and range learn in the work. Use spans light, stuff, and high-force fields in the close.
arxiv-2502-20473:
Power grids run on sensor readings, and an attacker who quietly alters those readings can steer operators wrong. Mohammadreza Iranpour and Mohammad Rasoul Narimani study false data injection against the alternating-current model of the grid, the realistic one. Such attacks can slip past the bad-data detectors that guard control rooms.

Using the PowerWorld simulator on a standard thirty-nine-bus test grid, they compare attack designs head to head. Attacks tuned to be maximally stealthy changed the targeted readings less than crude attacks did. Counterintuitively, their physical impact on the grid was also often smaller. The authors frame attack design as a trade-off between hiding and harming. Their unified approach lets defenders test both kinds of attacks in one place.
arxiv-2502-20673:
Pegah Mohammadipour and Xiantao Li analyze a popular quantum error trick with fresh rigor, in a 2025 paper. Zero-noise extrapolation runs a quantum circuit at several boosted noise levels, then extends the trend back to zero noise. The standard version leans on polynomial fitting, as in Richardson extrapolation. The authors dissect its three headaches: real noise is not polynomial, high-degree fits overfit, and measurement noise grows fast along the way.

They derive bounds on both bias and variance and estimate how many samples a target precision needs. The analysis extends to least-squares fitting, which softens the overfitting. Error mitigation is what makes today's small quantum machines useful at all, so knowing its true cost in samples tells users when to trust the trick.
arxiv-2503-00373:
Arunima and co-authors present an astronomy paper from 2025 on tracing star orbits in our galaxy. To rebuild a star's past path, scientists assume some of its motion values stay fixed. But the galaxy disc churns with spiral arms and gas clouds that tug on stars.

The team ran a fine simulation of a galaxy like ours, with gas and star birth included. They tracked how the motion values of young stars drift over time. The drift acts like a random walk that grows slowly with time. Upward motion drifts faster than outward motion. Spiral arms drive the outward drift, while gas clouds drive the upward drift. The rates cap reliable orbit tracing at about one hundred million years. The authors urge care in studies of galaxy history.
arxiv-2503-00473:
Chavez and co-authors compute, in a 2025 physics paper, the condensation energy of a superconductor modeled as a gas of electron pairs stacked in many layers. Boson-fermion models treat some electrons as paired composite bosons, which carry the superconductivity, alongside unpaired ones.

The mixture sits in a comb-like potential that mimics the layered planes of high-temperature superconductors. For the bosons the team gives the condensation temperature; for both parts, the chemical balance, internal energy, and entropy across temperatures. From these they build the free energy and extract the condensation energy for several wall strengths. The results feed theories of layered superconductors.
arxiv-2503-00773:
Yakun Zhang computed algebraic K-theory groups in twenty twenty-five for several rings built over the integers modulo prime powers. K2 captures subtle relations among units of a ring; its reduced part connects to cyclic homology and differential forms. Zhang treats three algebra families within one framework.

For cyclic p-group rings and truncated polynomial rings, he determines the reduced K2 structure explicitly. For abelian p-group rings over the p-adic integers, he extends a known isomorphism between reduced continuous K2 and first cyclic homology to all finite abelian p-groups. The proof constructs a generalized Artin-Hasse map giving an explicit splitting, realized by extending Oliver's p-adic logarithm. He also characterizes the map to linearized K2, clarifying the web of connections.
arxiv-2503-01173:
Yujie Qin, Mustafa Kishk, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini studied how user speed affects information freshness for ground and aerial users in two thousand twenty-five. Age of information measures how old the newest received update is. Its peak value matters for systems that need timely data, like drones and vehicles.

Their framework starts from the strongest interferer at a base station and approximates the signal quality distribution from two key distances. They then compute how success chances correlate across space and time as users move. Ground users showed higher correlation than aerial users, so speed hit their performance harder. The approximation matched well even under a complex fading model.
arxiv-2503-02273:
Simulating waves or fields on a fine grid can take hours, so engineers shrink the model, but a shrunk model that leaks fake energy gives wrong answers over time. Harsh Sharma, Juan Diego Draxl Giannoni, and Boris Kramer present a shrink method in a 2025 paper that keeps the books balanced. Their trick adds helper parts that turn messy energy terms into neat squared ones.

Once the energy is in squared form, the shrunk model can hold it exactly, even on the full grid. The team tried the method on four wave-style systems, from a one-line wave to coupled field pairs. Results matched the best rival method in speed and accuracy during runs, while the setup stage ran much faster. For design shops that rerun models often, the saving lands where it counts.
arxiv-2503-02473: Davydov and Rotar prove a limit theorem for triangular arrays of point processes built from random variables that do not share one distribution. They then apply the result to two problems. One is the limiting behavior of the argmaximum of independent random variables, the point where a maximum is reached. The other is the behavior of certain step processes. The work links a general point process result to concrete questions about extremes and stepwise random motion.
arxiv-2503-02773:
Francesco Panelli and co-authors propose a scientific-method approach to explaining how neural networks behave. Rather than probing one network at a time, they suggest forming a mathematical model from observed behavior, then using it to predict new behavior. They test the idea on a controlled case they call the Prime Convolutional Model. The network reads blocks of consecutive whole numbers, drawn from the first million, and learns to name each number's remainder class for a given divisor.

By varying the divisor and the block size, the team charts when the model succeeds and how it fails. A mathematical model fitted to those results captures the pattern in terms of the two settings. The model explains both success and the shape of the errors. The authors present the case as groundwork for a theory of explainable AI.
arxiv-2503-03073:
Black hole binaries sometimes fire off jets of matter at near light speed, but catching the launch moment is rare. Callan Wood and co-authors use a radio telescope array to film one such outburst in the binary Swift J1727.8-1613 during its bright 2023 flare. Fast-moving jets blur ordinary imaging, so they fit a model that changes over time directly to the raw data.

In a single four-hour look they found a compact core plus three blobs racing downstream. They measured each blob's motion, brightness changes, and even its swelling during the observation. That let them date the launches, one to within forty minutes. Each launch lined up with an X-ray flare and a sudden change in the inflow's X-ray behavior, the tightest such link yet seen.
arxiv-2503-04573: Christoph Ternes, Giulia Pagliaroli, and Francesco Villante set limits in a 2025 paper on neutrino behavior. Neutrinos from a star that exploded in 1987 reached Earth and were recorded, giving a rare long-baseline test. The authors use those records to bound quantum decoherence, a fading of the neutrino's wave nature that some models predict. Their bounds come out far stronger than those from reactor experiments or neutrino telescopes, by many orders of magnitude. The paper is short and aimed at specialists in particle astrophysics.
arxiv-2503-05173:
Vincent Cohen-Addad and co-authors wrote a 2025 computer science paper on fair clustering in a sliding window stream. Fair clustering splits data so each group holds a fair share of each type. In streams, old points drop out as new ones arrive, which strains both speed and fairness.

In the plain insert-only stream, fast fair methods exist. The authors prove a sharp split: in the sliding window, no method can keep a finite quality ratio while holding the fairness rule exact. Loosen fairness by a hair, though, and a near best method exists in small space. Its space grows in a mild way with cluster count and slack. Tests on real data sets round out the theory.
arxiv-2503-05273:
Paula Alvarez Cartelle and co-authors show a second job for particle detectors at the LHCb experiment in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The RICH detectors there usually name charged hadrons across a wide speed range. The upgraded set can also count luminosity, the collision rate measure experiments live by.

The team describes the electronics model, the powering plan used in running, and the calibration steps. A novel counting technique is proven in principle. Early precision figures from the two thousand twenty-three run are reported for both live and offline counts. The authors present the method as a separate check on the experiment's main rate measure.
arxiv-2503-05473:
Noah Mamie and Susie Xi Rao organize swarms of foundation models into a cooperating society in a 2025 study. Single large models are powerful but costly and hard to scale to every user. Groups of models that divide work, modeled loosely on animal swarms and evolutionary ideas, might share the load better.

Their Society of HiveMind framework orchestrates how member models interact and improve together. Tests find little benefit on tasks that mostly need real-world knowledge. Gains appear significant on other task types the authors examine. The split result is useful: it tells builders where collective arrangements pay and where a single strong model suffices.
arxiv-2503-06173:
Soheila Emamyari and co-authors track a polymer chain squeezed through a tiny pore, in work from 2025. The chain starts cooped in a narrow channel, then is driven through the pore into open space. The team pairs live-style simulations with a tension-spread theory to read both local and whole-chain motion.

The theory matched the simulations well at every channel width tried. Where the channel rivals the chain's free span, crossing time scales with both chain length and channel width. In very tight channels the chain runs like a stiff rod, and time scales with length alone. The split traces to how much the chain can wiggle inside.
arxiv-2503-06373:
Soares and co-authors study how gravity bends light in this 2025 paper. Einstein's theory predicts the bend, which astronomers use as a natural lens. Loop quantum gravity suggests small corrections to the shape of space near dense objects. The team works out the bending for two such corrected space shapes.

They treat both gentle bends from far passes and strong bends from near passes. Formula expansions cover each case in turn. From those formulas they derive what telescopes might actually measure. For the second model, the predicted values fall within reach of current tools. A measured mismatch with the classic values would hint that quantum corrections are real.
arxiv-2503-06873:
Huy and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-five on an explainable network for medical image analysis. Clinicians need to see and steer why a model decides as it does. Concept methods explain at whole-image level, too coarse for pinpointing regions. Prototype methods compare patches but leave their meaning murky. Their network grounds each concept's prototypes on exact image patches. Doctors can also interact at the level of image regions. Accuracy rises over prior explainable methods on three biomedical datasets.

Patch-level grounding makes explanations local and readable. Spatial interaction lets users probe specific areas directly. Code is released in public for reuse. The authors pitch the tool for transparent diagnosis support.
arxiv-2503-07073:
Krzysztof Stempak studies the Grushin operator, a differential operator used in analysis, in a 2025 paper. He builds a new transform for it that blends a partial Fourier transform with one based on scaled Hermite functions. The transform turns the operator into a simple multiplication on a matching dual space, which makes its behavior much easier to read.

From that link, Stempak defines a self-adjoint extension of the operator as the multiplication itself. He also defines other extensions through sesquilinear forms and compares the two families. Last, he gives a closed formula for the heat kernel of the related heat flow. The results give analysts a cleaner handle on an operator that shows up in several hard problems.
arxiv-2503-08473:
Yang, Liang, Guo, and Jensen give in 2025 a tutorial on data driven decision making with time series and place linked data. Such data record traits that change over time, and over space as well, across science, medicine, industry, and the environment. Digital growth now yields huge volumes of both.

The tutorial follows a chain from data to governance, analysis, and decision. It covers data quality work, then analysis under five aims, automation, generalization, robustness, explainability, and efficiency. A traffic forecasting case shows greener transport as a pay off. The authors close with decision strategies and open research paths.
arxiv-2503-09673:
Elisa Cali and co-authors build a code editor plugin that asks a language model to spot and fix web accessibility flaws while developers write, in work from twenty twenty-five. Accessibility problems are usually caught after a site is finished, when fixes cost most. Moving checks into the editor could prevent that.

The Visual Studio Code extension calls a large language model on code in progress. In evaluation, the plugin produced working fixes whenever it had detected the error correctly. Detection was the weak link: one generic prompt, meant to fit many code shapes, missed or misread many issues. The authors call the results promising but accuracy bound, and point to sharper tuning as next work.
arxiv-2503-10573:
Afrar Jahin and four co-authors grade the math of language models in twenty twenty-five. Mathematical reasoning needs multi-step logic and abstract generalization. It remains one of the hardest skills for large language models. Prior evaluations were often narrow, covering few models or one benchmark.

This study compares eight leading models, including two recent DeepSeek systems. Three independent benchmark data sets supply the tests. The analysis works at fine grain, splitting performance by domain. DeepSeek-R1 performs competitively with OpenAI's o1 across most domains. It achieves the highest accuracy on the MMLU formal logic benchmark. Readers get a detailed map of where today's models reason well in mathematics, and where they still fail.
arxiv-2503-10973:
Shuchen Wu's thesis asks how minds carve raw sensation into reusable parts in a 2025 dissertation. Perception arrives as a high-dimensional stream, yet cognition swiftly finds chunks within it and relations among them. Wu treats a sensory stream as a sequence and studies chunking, the split of sequences into learned parts. Reaction-time experiments showed people adapt to hidden chunks while trading speed against accuracy.

Wu then built models that learn chunks and read sequences chunk by chunk. Chunking is framed as a rational way to find repeating patterns and nested layers. Learned chunks become building blocks for transfer and mental simulation. A second part moves to abstract patterns, sorting motif types and testing their role in memory. A learning model that adds abstract variables matched human behavior and stood apart from large language models. The thesis offers chunking and abstraction as twin principles of structured learning.
arxiv-2503-11173:
The gas in a galaxy disk mostly rotates in orderly fashion, but fountains and inflows ride on top of that flow. Se-Heon Oh and Jing Wang present a 2025 method for separating the orderly bulk gas from the rest in radio data cubes.

Their approach splits each line-of-sight velocity profile into Gaussian parts, then labels them bulk or non-bulk using gas density, spread, energy, and rotation speed. A tilted-ring fit of the disk refines the split. Tested on the galaxy NGC 4559 from a major survey, the method classed about half the hydrogen gas as non-bulk, possibly stirred by star formation feedback. Upcoming sensitive surveys, the authors say, need exactly this kind of careful separation.
arxiv-2503-11873:
Li and co-authors squeeze a kagome metal to see how its superconductivity changes in this 2025 physics paper. The compound LaRu3Si2 superconducts near 7 kelvin and hosts charge density wave order at higher temperatures. Kagome lattices, with their corner-sharing triangles, attract wide interest.

The team measured electrical transport up to 65 gigapascals and crystal structure up to 35 gigapascals. The transition temperature first rose to about 8.7 kelvin near 8.5 gigapascals, then fell in stages, tracing a dome shape. Two structural changes appeared under pressure, near 11.5 and 23.5 gigapascals, shifting the crystal to lower symmetry. The structural breaks line up with features in the transport curves.
arxiv-2503-12573:
Yi Teng, Orazio Scarlatella, Shiyu Zhou, Armin Rahmani, Claudio Chamon, and Claudio Castelnovo wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It proposes a standard test for many-body coherence in gate-based quantum computers, a trait at the heart of quantum edge.

The test uses anyon-like interference in a spin chain, which mirrors a particle on a ring with or without flux through it. The longest ring on which the flux can still be told apart sets a grade for the machine's coherence. The authors show how to run the test on gate platforms and grade gear from five named makers. They aim for a live web board that tracks coherence gains over time, in the spirit of Moore's law.
arxiv-2503-12673: Andre Nies edited the joined Logic Blog for 2023 and 2024, published as one file in 2025. Much of the blog treats particular classes of groups and how they relate to logic. Other entries take up ergodic theory and questions in foundations, and a short part near the end turns to AI proving. The file joins the two yearly blogs into a single record, so readers get both years of short research notes in one place.
arxiv-2503-12973:
Colin Prieur and four co-authors tackle a consistency problem in mapping tropical forests from the air in a 2025 paper. Hyperspectral cameras read each tree's light signature, but the same species can look different on different flights, which breaks classifiers. The team asks whether self-supervised learning can build features that shrug off that variation.

They trained a Barlow-Twins model on repeated spectral passes over the same forest. The learned features held steadier across dates than raw reflectance. Classifying forty tropical species with them gained about ten points of accuracy across acquisition dates. The authors present self-supervision as a practical path to reliable species maps for ecology and forestry.
arxiv-2503-14973:
Rishav Rishav and co-authors explain reinforcement learning agents by finding the behavior patterns they repeat, in work from twenty twenty-five. Trust in such agents needs clear reasons for their choices, most of all in robotics, health, and finance. Past tools explain one step or a whole run, but miss habits in between.

Their frame works offline and needs no reward data. It groups state and action runs into coherent behavior clusters that recur across many runs. Each action is then credited to a cluster, giving a fine but readable account. Tests in four settings found clear behaviors and beat whole run methods on fidelity and human choice. Code was shared in public.
arxiv-2503-15573:
Da Ma and co-authors pick training data for a target task by reading a model's own neuron activity, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Instruction tuning teaches models to follow orders, but the best data for one task is hard to choose. Past pickers lean on surface features or messy embeddings that miss how the model really processes a sample.

Single neurons fire for many ideas at once, muddying raw activity. A sparse autoencoder untangles that activity into single-meaning units. A matching score in that clean space then finds task-relevant samples. Wide tests across data sets, models, and pick rates beat prior pickers in stability and task gains.
arxiv-2503-15773:
Liam Dunn and six co-authors search data from the LIGO gravitational wave observatory for continuous waves from spinning neutron stars in five globular clusters. Their paper came out in 2025. A slightly lopsided neutron star should broadcast a faint, steady hum of gravitational waves as it spins.

Their search used a hidden Markov model tracking the signal's frequency and phase from one data segment to the next. That phase tracking is a first for this kind of LIGO search. After vetoes removed artifacts, no significant candidate survived. The team reports how faint a signal they would have caught, and what that implies about how deformed the neutron stars can be. The best sensitivity came for one nearby cluster, at a frequency in the low hundreds of hertz.
arxiv-2503-15973:
Zichen Liu and co-authors present a prompting method in two thousand twenty-five that adapts image-language models to video. Models like CLIP learn from huge image-text collections and transfer well to new image tasks. Video is harder: labeled clips are scarce and training is costly.

Earlier video prompting used one fixed prompt for every clip, ignoring how scenes change over time. Their model, STOP, works on two levels. Prompts inside each frame steer attention to regions that change and matter. Prompts between frames mark the frames with the biggest shifts, so key moments get priority. Together the two levels capture fine detail and time flow. Tests across several video benchmarks showed strong results, which the authors credit to the dynamic design.
arxiv-2503-16173:
A large team of cosmic-ray scientists lays out a ten-year plan for better reaction data in a paper from 2025. Space detectors now measure cosmic rays with great precision. Reading those data, though, is limited by poor knowledge of the nuclear reactions that create antimatter and secondary nuclei. The report sums up a 2024 workshop at CERN, the third in a series on the problem.

The authors map the most urgent gaps in cross-section data and how to close them. Better data would sharpen studies of cosmic sources, travel through the galaxy, and dark matter searches. The report also covers space radiation protection and cancer therapy with beams. Shared needs link fields that rarely talk.
arxiv-2503-16973:
Wentao Jiang and colleagues present a method for generating how a person reacts to another person action, for uses such as virtual reality and social robots. Earlier diffusion-based systems built reactions from noise through tangled conditioning steps, and their motions often broke physics, with bodies passing through each other. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team instead learns a direct flow from an action to its reaction. A physical guidance step steers sampling away from body overlap, and a corrected sampling scheme plus added randomness improve both realism and variety.

Tests on three public human interaction data sets showed better motion quality and more varied reactions than prior methods. Collisions dropped sharply under new measures the authors introduce for overlap volume and frequency. Readers get a clear example of how adding simple physical guardrails can fix a common failure of generative motion models.
arxiv-2503-17073:
Jonas Wallat and co-authors tested how well large language models stand up to questions that turn on time, in a paper published in 2025. Models hold much factual knowledge about the world, but dates trip them up, because they miss the time span of a fact or ignore the time aspect altogether. The team built eight time-based tests of factual strength and ran six well-known models with no task-specific training.

Models lacked temporal robustness across the board. Reworded time frames and shifts in date granularity hurt most. A selection of the tests can score a model's temporal robustness on the fly, as user questions come in. The authors then used the findings to raise scores on time questions by up to 55 percent. The work gives the field a yardstick for a weak spot that plain fact tests miss.
arxiv-2503-17273:
Benjamin Biaggi, Jan Draisma, and Sarah Eggleston study the subrank of real three-way arrays, a measure of how much clean diagonal structure hides inside a tensor. Subrank over the complex numbers can exceed the real one. The paper lower-bounds the real subrank in terms of the complex subrank. It then shows every value between the minimal and maximal typical subranks actually occurs typically.

Small formats with several typical subranks get close attention. The authors build a three by three by five tensor whose subrank is exactly two. The quaternion multiplication tensor, four by four by four, also has subrank two. Componentwise complex multiplication yields a tensor with real subrank equal to its size. Informally, no device doing that many complex multiplications can squeeze out extra real ones. A version for other real division algebras follows.
arxiv-2503-17473:
Cathy Mengying Fang and co-authors present a 2025 study of how long chatbot use shapes mental well-being. People increasingly turn to chatbots for company and emotional support. The team ran a four-week chance-based trial with 981 people and over 300,000 messages. Arms varied by mode, text or voice of two kinds, and by chat type, from open to personal.

Four outcomes were tracked: loneliness, real-life social time, emotional dependence on the bot, and problem use. The assigned arms showed no firm effects on any outcome. Yet people who chose to chat more, in any arm, fared worse across the board. Strong trust in and pull toward the bot also tracked with dependence. The results shift focus from bot design to user habits.
arxiv-2503-17773:
Reinier Sorgdrager, a solo author, studies a special class of representations in a 2025 paper. The setting is the mod p Langlands program, which links number theory to symmetry groups over p-adic fields. Two groups are treated: a matrix group and a quaternion unit group. Other researchers had carved out a full subcategory of smooth representations for special study.

His result says membership in that subcategory can be read off locally. Whether a representation belongs is fully decided by how it behaves when restricted to any small open subgroup, however tiny. The paper is a short, technical note for specialists in the Langlands program.
arxiv-2503-18273:
Raza Ul Mustafa and co-authors used language models to decode semi-coded Islamophobic speech online in a 2025 paper. Extremist platforms circulate slurs respelled to look harmless out of context. Human moderators and automated filters both miss them.

The team gathered posts from platforms such as 4chan, Gab, and Telegram that use these terms. They first tested whether large language models understand the coded words, and found that the models do grasp them. A toxicity service also scored Islamophobic posts higher than other hate categories. Topic modeling then mapped the recurring themes of this discourse. The results argue models can help moderation, though detection still needs work.
arxiv-2503-21173:
Meghana Bhat, Saipriya Dubey, and Shreedevi Masuti extend an algebra tool in a 2025 paper. The Hilbert function counts the size of a graded algebra layer by layer. For a special class of algebras, that count splits into symmetric parts. Iarrobino introduced that split in 1989 as a sorting tool.

The authors define the same split for any ideal inside such an algebra. Ideals are the substructures that define most objects in the field. Their hope is a fuller catalog of possible count patterns. As a test, they list all short patterns of one narrow kind. Each listed pattern is shown to arise from a real ideal. The paper is technical and aimed at algebra specialists.
arxiv-2503-22573:
Kar Balan, Robert Learney, and Tim Wood propose a framework for proving, with cryptography, that an AI system was built and run as claimed. As AI spreads into regulated industries, calls grow for safety laws that demand transparency and audit trails. Their framework covers the whole pipeline, from sourcing data through training and inference to unlearning, and sorts the existing cryptographic tools that can vouch for each stage. Proofs attached to AI outputs could let others check where content came from and whether it was made correctly.

The catch is linkage: tools that verify one stage in isolation exist, but chaining proofs across stages efficiently is the open problem. The authors argue research should aim at linkable tools, not just faster single steps. The paper is a map and agenda, meant to guide builders and regulators toward AI that can show its work.
arxiv-2503-22873:
Senbei Du, Merav Opher, and Marc Kornbleuth study newborn pickup ions in the heliosheath, the region past the shock where the solar wind slows, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. These ions matter because they help make the neutral atoms that the IBEX spacecraft maps.

The authors focus on ions born inside the heliosheath itself, when neutral solar wind atoms swap charge with local ions. They find this group can supply much of the signal IBEX sees at modest energies. The newborn ions also keep a lopsided spread of speeds for a long time. The usual waves that would smooth them out stay weak once the wind has slowed. Computer runs point to the mirror instability as the main wave at work. The result changes how maps of the Sun's bubble should be read.
arxiv-2504-01373:
Emadeldeen Eldele and co-authors present UniFault, a foundation model for machine fault diagnosis from bearing data, in a research paper from 2025. Fault diagnosis catches machine damage early for planned repair. Past models fit one operation and fail to transfer, since fault data sets are small and mixed, with varied sampling rates and channel counts across systems.

UniFault starts with a data harmonization pipeline that unifies varied inputs into a standard form. The model then learns features that transfer across data sets. Few-shot and zero-shot use are the goals, as with foundation models in vision and language. The design targets robust extraction from diverse bearing signals in real plants.
arxiv-2504-01673:
Perrier extends in twenty twenty-five a geometric method for fast quantum control into quantum neural networks. The fastest ways to steer a quantum system often follow shortest paths on curved spaces, found through a split of motions called a Cartan decomposition. He builds network layers from that split, inside designs that respect the system's symmetries.

He shows a shallow network with such layers can copy the known best paths for a family of control problems. With the right training cost and mild conditions, gradient training settles on globally fastest solutions for some problem classes. The work generalises older geometric control results. It also clarifies how best-path estimates can be done inside quantum machine learning.
arxiv-2504-01973:
Christoph Brunken and co-authors present a transferable coarse-grained force field learned by a neural network in a 2025 paper. Coarse-graining lumps atoms into beads so huge biomolecules can be simulated at all. Hand-built rules tie older methods to narrow system types. Their algorithm instead learns the grouping from graphs of the molecule, tuned to keep statistical noise in the true forces low.

That quiet training signal improves the learned model sharply. The force field rides on a modern architecture for atom-level models. Its training set came from fragmenting large biosystems across protein, RNA, and lipid chemistry. In dynamics runs, the model produced stable, qualitatively sound trajectories for varied systems. The authors are candid about cases where reliability still lags. They present the work as the first deep coarse-graining that travels across biosystem types.
arxiv-2504-02073:
Hristo Djidjev wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about extending quantum annealing to problems with continuous values. Quantum annealers shine on yes-or-no problems written in a standard binary form. Many real tasks, though, involve real numbers, and rewriting them fully as binary problems is awkward and costly.

The proposed method blends quantum annealing into simulated annealing, a classic search method. The quantum device picks discrete search directions, which then steer the classical search through the continuous space. Tests used box-bounded quadratic programming, a common hard problem class. The hybrid beat classical baselines in solution quality, above all on larger and poorly conditioned problems, at competitive speed. The author sees the method scaling as hardware matures.
arxiv-2504-02173:
Eric Bittner and Bhavay Tyagi wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies anyons, odd particles found in flat systems. Their exchange rules fall between those of bosons and fermions, and the paper asks how they settle and sync when open to their surroundings.

The authors build a Lindblad model for anyon oscillators. By tuning the exchange phase and the links to the bath, they show some modes can be shielded from decay. They also find exceptional points in the decay spectrum, and see coherence split as heat shifts. Light-based probes can read the phase from the response. The phase thus acts as a knob for making quantum states that resist loss.
arxiv-2504-02973:
Cassandra Jacobs and Morgan Grobol model how people learn pronouns and neopronouns in this 2025 paper. Using a person chosen pronouns matters for equity in queer communities. Speakers often blame errors on habit or on expectations from appearance. The authors build a probabilistic model of individual learning instead of static word meanings.

Their graphical model grows from a nested restaurant process used in cognitive science. It learns referring forms without relying on word co occurrence statistics. People differ in how fast a new name or pronoun enters their knowledge, and the model captures that spread. Simulations reproduce varied learning speeds across speakers. Respectful language technology needs exactly this flexibility, the authors argue.
arxiv-2504-03073:
Andre Rodriguez and William Osborn analyze locking methods that keep shared data consistent across many machines, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Locks stop two writers from clashing, but coordinating them costs time. The team compares classic central locks with modern spread-out protocols.

Speed, delay, and scaling were graded under varied workloads. Tuned spread protocols beat central ones by up to sixty-eight percent under heavy contention. Strong consistency held throughout the tests. Fresh tuning ideas cut coordination cost for systems spread across the globe. The work guides concurrency design for modern platforms.
arxiv-2504-03473:
Prelovsek and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on exotic particles made of four quarks, studied through lattice QCD. Their focus is a doubly charmed tetraquark, a particle built from two charm quarks and two light antiquarks. Computer studies of it rely on how two mesons scatter off each other.

Most past work used only meson-meson operators to probe the system. This team added diquark-antidiquark operators, which treat paired quarks as units. The added operators shifted some energy levels and pulled the particle's pole a bit closer to the threshold. They place the particle just below threshold, as a shallow resonance. For a heavier cousin with bottom quarks, the added operators mattered even more, letting a deeply bound state appear.
arxiv-2504-04373:
Shenyang Liu, Yang Gao, Shaoyan Zhai, and Liqiang Wang published this paper in 2025. It tackles prompt recovery: reconstructing the hidden instruction that produced a language model's output. Their test bed is style transformation, where a prompt asks the model to rewrite text in a new voice.

They built StyleRec, a benchmark data set for this task, assembled with model help and checked by several quality techniques. Attack strategies ranged from plain zero-shot guessing to fine-tuned recovery, jailbreak tricks, and a fallback that substitutes a canonical prompt when recovery fails. One-shot examples and fine-tuning recovered prompts best. A deeper finding concerns grading: standard sentence-similarity scores judged recoveries poorly, rewarding surface echoes over true reconstruction. The authors say the field needs recovery metrics as much as recovery methods. Their data set and experiments give prompt recovery research a firmer footing.
arxiv-2504-04573:
Jieyi Zhang and five co-authors teach a robot hand to grasp objects the way a task demands, in a 2025 paper. Picking up a tool is not one problem but many: the right grip depends on what you will do next. Two-finger grippers dominate earlier work, but dexterous hands face a huge space of valid poses and many correct answers per task. Their framework, DexTOG, uses a diffusion model to generate grasp poses guided by language instructions.

A data engine feeds the learner, and the team releases an eighty-thousand-example dataset built with a shadow robot hand on eighty objects in five categories. Language-conditioned dexterity is a step toward robots that can be told, simply, how to pick something up.
arxiv-2504-05273:
Tammy Mackenzie and co-authors review what research actually knows about GPT use in business and management, in a 2025 paper. They searched peer-reviewed studies from the first 22 months after GPT's release. For all the public talk, they found only 42 studies that fit. The work spreads thinly across finance, marketing, human resources, strategy, operations, production, and analytics.

No sector or subfield yet has enough evidence for firm claims about how the tools are used. The authors list open questions on jobs, productivity, energy costs, fairness, and small firms. They also suggest how consultants and journalists can help fill the gaps. The paper closes as a call for much more research, including work on control systems for AI risks in firms.
arxiv-2504-05473:
A ninth planet may lurk far beyond Neptune, betrayed only by odd orbits of distant icy bodies. Hector Socas-Navarro and Ignacio Trujillo report a targeted hunt for it in a patch of sky about 98 square degrees wide. The patch sits in a high-probability zone from simulations, yet earlier searches covered it poorly.

Their method watches for tiny position shifts between consecutive nights, the parallax a nearby slow object should show. They found no believable candidate down to about magnitude 21.3, an 85 percent confidence limit. A candidate could hide if star glare spoiled one night's image, but they estimate that chance at about 0.4 percent. The authors discuss why the planet may have escaped, including the chance it is fainter than their limit. Deeper searches with stronger instruments come next.
arxiv-2504-05773:
Yongle Yu studies events where many atoms in a gas take up laser photons at the same time, one photon each. The paper from twenty twenty-five sets set frequency terms for these joint jumps. Each atom is excited through its own photon uptake. The events are natural high-order effects of quantum electrodynamics. They need no atom-to-atom interplay to occur.

A set length scale emerges from the analysis. It bounds the range over which these joint effects show themselves. Yu proposes lab tests to display the core traits of the process. The work is theoretical, with the tests sketched rather than run. Such multi-atom, multi-photon events stretch the usual one-atom picture of light-matter interplay. The paper gives them a clean frame and a path to proof.
arxiv-2504-06373:
Giacomo Bastianel and co-authors published a review paper in 2025 on giant offshore power hubs that gather wind energy in the North Sea and send it ashore. Such projects pack many gigawatts into a small sea area with several links to land grids. Planners lacked a shared, precise word for the thing they were building.

The paper coins a formal definition, Electrical Energy Hub, and spells out what such hubs do. It then walks through the hard problems they pose for control, planning, and fault protection. A list of live and planned projects is checked against the new definition. Clear terms, the authors argue, must come before sound grid codes and support rules.
arxiv-2504-07173:
Nishchhal Verma and three co-authors present a 2025 perspective on quantum geometry, a hidden structure in the electrons of advanced materials. Simple models describe such materials by how electron energy varies with motion. Yet mixing between electron bands adds new length and time scales, set by how the wave patterns twist in momentum space. These scales are the material's quantum geometry.

The authors argue these hidden scales change both straight and nonlinear responses of a material. They can even help decide its ground state at very low temperatures. The piece reviews fresh experiments that have begun to measure these effects on several platforms. It also explains how separated scales let researchers estimate when geometry matters most. The perspective aims to move quantum geometry from a niche idea to a working tool in materials science.
arxiv-2504-07373:
Yuanyun Zhang and Shi Li present ChronoFormer, a transformer design built to model clinical events with their timing, in a 2025 paper. Health records unfold over time, and that time structure makes outcome prediction hard for standard models. Their design encodes time directly, using time embeddings, layered attention, and masking shaped by medical knowledge.

The team tested it on three benchmark tasks: predicting death, predicting readmission, and forecasting the onset of long-term conditions. ChronoFormer beat the current best methods by clear margins, they report. Reading its attention patterns showed it catching long-range links between events that carry clinical meaning, a sign the time handling works as intended.
arxiv-2504-07573:
Urban Jezernik and Špela Špenko wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It frames a measure called additive diameter for group representations, which joins a family of Waring-type problems in noncommutative algebra.

Given a representation and a subspace that spans the whole space under the group's action, the diameter is the least count of shifted copies of the subspace needed to cover the space. The authors show every irreducible representation of one key group has the best possible diameter. They give sharp bounds for another group's action on its own Lie algebra. Links to maps between varieties round out the work, tying the new gauge to older ones.
arxiv-2504-08173:
Tathagata Karmakar and Andrew Jordan set optimal control rules for quantum systems that are watched nonstop, in work from twenty twenty-five. A watched system follows a random path set by its readout stream. A known path integral method gives the most likely path for simple cases.

The authors extend that method to any watched system by adding a costate operator. They then state a quantum form of the classic Pontryagin control principle. The most likely path turns out to be a case of that principle, with readout odds as the cost. Tests on a watched oscillator cover code word prep, cooling, and state transfer. Optimal control raised high fidelity run counts by large margins.
arxiv-2504-08273:
Chiral magnets twist their atomic compasses into spirals and soliton trains, and Kentaro Nishimura and Ryosuke Yoshii ask what quantum entanglement sees in such a chain. Their 2025 simulations of a one-dimensional chiral ferromagnet use a powerful matrix method to compute how much one part of the chain knows about the rest.

The entanglement rises and falls in waves along the chain, and an outside magnetic field retunes the waves. Local magnetization and twist measures confirm the waves trace the soliton pattern. The authors propose entanglement itself as a detector for a magnet's hidden vacuum structure, a probe beyond ordinary magnetization.
arxiv-2504-08773:
Jeunen wrote in twenty twenty-five about causal inference for recommender systems that learn by Thompson sampling. Recommenders choose content step by step under uncertainty. Thompson sampling picks actions probabilistically to balance trying new options against using proven ones. Offline evaluation asks what would have happened under a different policy. Standard estimators need the probability of each action taken, called its propensity. Those probabilities are not readily available under Thompson sampling.

Jeunen derives exact formulas for the propensities that are cheap to compute. The formulas cover a variety of parameter and outcome distributions. With them, off-policy estimators become usable in Thompson sampling settings. That enables unbiased offline evaluation of recommender systems. Applications extend to online advertising and personalization more broadly. The work fills a practical gap in causal inference for adaptive systems.
arxiv-2504-09073:
Akanksha Mehndiratta and Krishna Asawa present a framework that helps chat programs pick the best reply in a multi-turn talk. Their paper appeared in 2025. Many systems treat all past turns as equal, or ignore how turns relate to each other. The framework first encodes each turn with meaning, word order, and grammar features. It then learns tokens that capture how a turn links to the turns around it.

The two steps build a picture of the flow of the talk, not just its words. The team tested the framework on the Ubuntu Dialogue Corpus, a large set of tech-support chats. It beat older methods on standard scoring measures. The authors argue that tracking how turns connect helps a system choose replies that fit the talk so far.
arxiv-2504-09273:
Maciej J Capiński and Marian Gidea published a paper in 2025 proving a strong form of chaos in the motion of three bodies under gravity. The three-body problem has resisted full solution for centuries because some motions are wildly unstable. The authors show that energy can drift between parts of the system by a fixed amount, a behavior called Arnold diffusion.

They treat the flat three-body problem as a blend of the two-body problem and a restricted version with one tiny body. Their proof uses a topological method checked by computer. As a concrete case they use a Neptune, its moon Triton, and an asteroid, with explicit bounds on sizes and time. The result confirms deep instability in a physically real system.
arxiv-2504-09373:
Ramya Namuduri and co-authors present QUDsim, a measure of similarity between texts, in this 2025 paper. Large language models write fluently on many topics, yet their texts often feel repetitive. Standard similarity scores count shared words or sentence shapes. Those scores miss sameness in how a text unfolds.

QUDsim instead tracks the questions each text raises and answers as it goes. That structure comes from linguistic work on questions under discussion. Two texts score as alike when their question paths run in parallel. With this measure, model texts reused discourse structures more than human texts did. They also diverged from human patterns. The tool gives researchers a way to measure a subtle kind of model sameness.
arxiv-2504-11373:
Zhu and co-authors show that language models often swallow false assumptions hidden in cancer patients' questions instead of correcting them, in a paper from 2025. Patients increasingly ask models for medical guidance. A question can smuggle in a wrong premise, and a model that answers around it can mislead care.

Three cancer doctors first judged real patient questions and found answers broadly accurate but blind to false premises. The team then built an expert-checked set of nearly six hundred such questions. No top model corrected the false premise more than about two fifths of the time. Guardrail prompts pushed accuracy up on the trap set but made models flag false premises where none existed. The authors call premise checking a safety gap.
arxiv-2504-13073:
Lara Koehler, Markus Eder, and colleagues propose a new way to control self-assembling structures in a 2025 study. Building complex shapes from engineered pieces is a central goal of nanotechnology. Keeping the final size under control gets harder as assemblies grow, and older strategies need many piece types or exact shaping of each piece.

Their approach uses identical pieces whose bonds favor crystals yet also encourage defects. Topology limits how far those defects can spread in a large crystal. As a result, the strength of the defect-inducing interaction sets the assembly size. Theory supports the mechanism, offering a simpler control knob for nanoscale construction.
arxiv-2504-13173:
Ali Behrouz, Meisam Razaviyayn, Peilin Zhong, and Vahab Mirrokni rethink how sequence models store and recall facts. Their two thousand twenty-five paper draws on attentional bias, the human habit of favoring some events over others. They view transformers and newer recurrent networks as memory modules. Each one learns a map from keys to values under an inner goal.

The authors find that most models use one of just two inner goals. One is dot-product similarity, and the other is a squared-error fit. They propose fresh choices for this inner goal, with stable ways to train them. They also recast forgetting as part of the same frame. The paper links test-time memory, retention, and online learning into one shared picture.
arxiv-2504-13773:
Cory Nunn and a team of co-authors synchronize two lasers to within picoseconds over city-scale fiber, in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum networks need light sources at distant sites to produce matching photons. That demands tight timing between the pump lasers at each site, far tighter than ordinary network clocks give.

The team locked two mode-locked lasers using a precise time protocol over one hundred twenty kilometers of working fiber. Pulse-to-pulse timing stayed better than three picoseconds. The spread of timing error stayed below four picoseconds over averaging times up to ten seconds. With the sources' planned coherence time, that timing implies near-perfect overlap when the photons meet.
arxiv-2504-14073:
Da Costa and Neves estimate photon qudit states ptychographically in two thousand twenty five. Ptychography images by overlapping projections and iteration. Its quantum version estimates pure states from partial subspace data. Photons here encode qudits in angle and orbital angular momentum.

Angular slits discretize the photon profile into D path states. Binary spatial filters perform the overlapping projections. Fourier basis measurement postselects matching orbital angular momentum modes. An iterative algorithm rebuilds the state from the counts. Simulations show the scheme works for this encoding. Lab feasibility is discussed for real setups.
arxiv-2504-14473:
Md Badrul Hasan, Meilin Yu, and Tim Oates present a 2025 paper on machine learning models for the fine swirls inside hurricane boundary layer winds. Large simulations cannot resolve the smallest eddies, so a sub-grid model must stand in for them. The flow both drains energy downward and, in places, pushes it back up, and a good model must capture both.

Their model pairs a classifier, which flags zones of strong energy transfer, with a regression step that sets stress values there. Built-in physical and geometric symmetry features lifted classification scores by about seventeen percent over versions without them. Tests reported here cover model building and offline checks, ahead of full simulation trials.
arxiv-2504-14873:
Karen Abe presents an augmented reality artifact that brings Japanese wartime oral histories to younger generations. Her position paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The work grows out of her own family and standpoint. Its core material is interview footage of her grandmother and grandaunt.

In the footage, the two women recall the nineteen forty-five Tokyo air raids firsthand. The artifact layers such accounts into an archive meant for teaching as well as keeping. Abe walks through its features and weighs what the medium adds. She also names the barriers: cost, access, and the care owed to painful memories. A list of questions for a workshop closes the piece. The paper asks how immersive tools can carry memory without flattening it.
arxiv-2504-14973:
Haonan Zheng and co-authors study ultra-diffuse galaxies in a computer universe in a 2025 paper. These galaxies spread their stars over a large volume, making them remarkably faint. Using the highest-resolution run of the EAGLE simulation, the team found 181 of them and compared their traits with real observations.

The simulated galaxies matched observations well and proved to be dwarf galaxies, not failed giants, forming one continuous family with normal dwarfs. Field galaxies grew diffuse because their star-forming gas carried high spin, possibly after galactic fountains flung gas outward to gain rotation. Among satellite galaxies, about sixty percent were diffuse before falling into a host, while the rest were stretched by tides afterward.
arxiv-2504-18673:
Jiayi Li and co-authors ask whether third parties can truly read the emotions in someone's writing. Emotion data sets are usually labeled by outside annotators, and models learn from those labels. The team ran human experiments comparing outside labels, from both people and large language models, against the authors' own labels for their texts.

Both kinds of outside labels diverged significantly from the authors' private states. The models still beat human annotators nearly everywhere. Two fixes helped: matching annotators to authors by demographic background improved human labels. Feeding the author's demographic details into the model prompt also helped, slightly but significantly. The authors offer a framework for measuring the limits of third-party labeling. They call for annotation practices that respect how private inner states really are, rather than assuming they can be read off the page.
arxiv-2504-19973:
String theory has a famous shortcut: hard closed-string problems can be rebuilt from easier open-string ones, a link called the KLT relations. Luis Alday, Maria Nocchi, and Aurélie Strömholm Sangaré carry that link into anti-de Sitter space, a curved setting where strings are much harder to handle. The basic pieces there form two endless towers of integrals, broad versions of classic functions from math.

The team shows the open and closed pieces still join through a KLT-style link, and they compute the joining kernel exactly. They also pin down the open-string pieces as a known family of special functions, writing them out in closed form up to a certain depth. The result gives a firm base for string work in curved space.
arxiv-2504-20273:
C Pallis studies F-term hybrid inflation in a unified theory, with metastable cosmic strings and low reheating, in light of fresh telescope data. The strings form in a left right unified frame, while twin poles are thinned by the inflation stage. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The setup sits in an extension of the standard model with two symmetry groups and a global R symmetry. Its hidden sector has a curved space with a de Sitter vacuum that breaks supersymmetry without fine tuning. Inflation fits the data, new telescope reads included, when a soft term stays in a set range. Strings made then match wave background hints from pulsar timing arrays.
arxiv-2504-21073:
Michel Gondran and Alexandre Gondran rebuild a classic attempt to derive quantum mechanics from particle motion in a 2025 paper. Nelson's stochastic processes aimed to produce the Schrödinger equation from random motion. The authors replace randomness with deterministic but pseudo random processes, and replace the point particle with an extended one: a tiny vibrating elastic string of four interacting points.

Creation and annihilation alternate in each vibration period. From this structure, spin and the uncertainty relations emerge. A complex version of the least action principle then yields a complex Hamilton Jacobi equation, whose phase solves the Schrödinger equation. The particle's center follows the guided trajectories of the de Broglie Bohm picture. Two new mathematical tools underpin the construction.
arxiv-2504-21373:
Tonghua Liu, Xiaolei Li, and Jieci Wang put three dark energy models through the newest cosmic data together, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The question is whether dark energy is a fixed constant or evolves as the universe expands.

They confront the standard ΛCDM model, a flexible two-parameter evolving model called CPL, and an emergent dark energy model, GEDE. The data combine galaxy distance measurements from DESI, the Pantheon Plus supernova catalog, and time-delay lensing from TDCOSMO. The evolving CPL model improves the fit by a statistically notable margin, favoring quintessence-like behavior that weakens over time. The emergent model also fits slightly better than the constant. Neither margin closes the case, but both point the same way. Joint analyses like this are how a constant could eventually fall.
arxiv-2504-21473: Semenov wrote a solo math study in twenty twenty-five on a fixed link among four terms in a row of a fading split form. The form drops by half each step and flips sign as it goes. He proves a blend of the four terms, scaled by their spots, is the same for all steps past a point. That bridge can rebuild a lost term, check a stream for flaws, and cut waste in data flows at low cost.
arxiv-2504-21573:
Yi Zheng and five co-authors present a quantum imaging method in a 2025 paper. Imaging with linked photon pairs offers sharper pictures and strong noise resistance. Yet paired photons pick up distortions that blur the result. Older fixes probe the distortion source with classic light or scan corrections slowly. Their method reads the distortion directly from the pairs themselves.

They adapt a classic wavefront sensor, using a tiny lens array and the pairs' strong position link. From where the pairs land, the added phase pattern is rebuilt in a single shot. Tests corrected imaging through a disturbed plastic film. The authors see a direct route to quantum adaptive optics for microscopy and remote imaging.
arxiv-2505-00373:
Ghara and co-authors turn radio telescope non-detections into limits on the infant universe's gas, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Ten nights of LOFAR data capped the 21-centimeter signal at three early eras. A model code plus a Bayesian frame mapped which gas states those caps rule out.

Ruled-out worlds had big, rare hot or lit zones. At the middle era, mean lit-plus-hot share stayed under about half, and mean gas heat under a set low cap. A strong extra radio glow beyond the cosmic background is hinted at the tighter level. The caps bite mainly on extreme models. Readers get first fences around dawn-era gas from silence.
arxiv-2505-01673:
Jeremy Mould reports a search for primordial black holes in the Gaia star archive, in a 2025 research note. Such black holes could supply dark matter. They might also ease a tension in cosmic expansion measures. As supermassive forms, they could seed the brightest early quasars. Hawking doubted they could ever be detected. Einstein likewise doubted his own lensing idea would prove practical. The author searched for lensing events among Gaia's faintest stars.

The search came up empty. Local dark matter density is high, so the null result carries weight. It narrows where these objects can hide. The author points to a coming telescope as the better tool. Its lensing surveys may open the asteroid-mass window. The note is short and candid about the miss. Negative results, it implies, still guide the hunt. Future surveys will test smaller masses.
arxiv-2505-02073:
Yi Han defends time series classifiers against adversarial attacks in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Classifiers for sequences are used more and more, and small made-up shifts can fool them. In computer vision, defenses are well studied. For time series, the field has leaned on adversarial training. That path costs much compute. Han builds five defenses on data augmentation. They are fit to time series and plain to put in place.

The most costly of the five lifts compute cost by about fourteen percent. That is set off against the model. Of two joined defenses, one pools all five methods. That pool defended better than adversarial training based on projected gradient descent. It also made the model generalize better, as a gain. It cost less than a third of the training-based defense. Han talks through how defenses could plug into pre-trained foundation models for time series.
arxiv-2505-02173:
Chutiphan Charoensuk and Nathakhun Wiroonsri present a 2025 paper on a new way to judge how different two time series are. Clustering time series groups series with like behavior, a task used from health care to energy. Most measures track either raw distance or correlation, and each misses something the other catches.

Their measure blends the two: it averages the largest ranked gaps between series, weighted, and mixes in the classic Pearson correlation gap. Plugged into hierarchical clustering, it beat rival methods on hard cases with shifting seasons, trends, and peaks. The authors then clustered a sample of Thai electricity customers into seven groups with distinct usage styles. Utilities can use such groups to design tariffs and forecasts.
arxiv-2505-03073:
Easthope presents a musical controller driven by the heartbeat in twenty twenty-five. Biofeedback is growing as a control method for human computer interfaces. Breath has been used for new musical instruments, but the heart has drawn less attention. The author argues the heart shapes our sense of time and thus of music.

A light based pulse sensor measures heart rate as a one dimensional control signal. It warps audio buffers in real time by time scaling before playback. The listener wears the sensor, closing a loop from sound to heart to sound. The paper discusses what such a loop affords for control and performance ambience. Generative latent spaces are floated as a way to extend the single control dimension.
arxiv-2505-03173:
Sameer Malik, Moyuru Yamada, Ayush Singh, and Dishank Aggarwal gave video models a retrievable memory in a 2025 paper. Large multimodal models choke on long videos: even minutes of footage overflow their context, and they lack any explicit memory to search. Their setup, RAVU, converts a video into a spatio-time-based graph whose nodes and edges record entities and their relations across frames. Then answers questions by decomposing each query into thinking steps executed over that graph, retrieving only the relevant pieces.

Questions needing multi-hop thinking and object tracking across time benefit most. On the NExT-QA and EgoSchema benchmarks, RAVU beat prior state-of-the-art methods and usual tests while retrieving only a handful of frames. Form, the authors argue, can substitute for brute-force context.
arxiv-2505-03673:
Huajie Tan and co-authors release an open robot operating framework that lets unlike robots plan together under one brain and skill library, in work from twenty twenty-five. Single robot systems struggle to switch bodies, schedule long jobs, and fix errors live. Layered vision language models plan well but rarely coordinate teams.

Three parts do the work: a brain model for global seeing and decisions, a plug in skill library for execution, and a shared memory that syncs team states in space and time. Cloud links speed the chatter for large deployments. Real world trials across scenarios showed the system running mixed robot bodies on long tasks. The authors frame it as a shift to multi agent embodied intelligence.
arxiv-2505-04573:
A black string is what you get by stretching a black hole along a circle: take the Schwarzschild solution and multiply it by a round loop of length L. Emma Albertini and Daniel Platt ask whether that object is the only one of its kind nearby. Earlier work had turned the uniqueness question into a nonlinear elliptic equation, and they build on that setup.

For small circle length, they show the black string is infinitesimally rigid as a Ricci-flat metric, meaning no tiny deformation keeps it Ricci-flat except the string itself. A fixed point theorem then upgrades that fact to local uniqueness: in a neighborhood whose size they bound, no other Ricci-flat metric exists. They also revisit a simpler scalar-field toy problem, where the same method yields a global uniqueness statement, stronger than the local one. The contrast shows where the method's power ends.
arxiv-2505-04673:
Jindal and Deshpande introduce REVEAL, a framework for testing image-based harms in vision language models over long chats. Models that see and read raise new safety risks. Old safety tests assume text-only, single-turn exchanges. REVEAL mines images on its own and builds adversarial cases from them. It stretches attacks across many turns with a crescendo strategy. Judge models, including GPT-4o, then grade the harm in replies.

Five leading vision models were put through the pipeline. The tests show how guardrails erode as a chat wears on. Single-turn checks miss that slow slide. The frame is built to scale across models and image sets.
arxiv-2505-05273:
Alexander Soen, writing alone in 2025, links two ideas in machine learning: teaching models to abstain, and measuring gaps between probability laws. A model that can reject a case avoids risky guesses. One way to build the rejector compares an ideal data law with the true one. Soen studies an ideal law over both inputs and labels.

He shows that thresholding certain gap measures yields the rejector. With a variant of the log-loss, the right measure is a skewed Bhattacharyya divergence between class odds. The classic rule, Chow's rule, instead thresholds a different gap. Rejecting by the Bhattacharyya route turns out less aggressive than Chow's rule. The link gives designers a new dial for how cautious a model should be.
arxiv-2505-06873:
Howlader, Das, and Kumar published this physics paper in 2025. It simulates how ordered regions grow inside a magnet spoiled by a random field from impurities. After a sudden cooling from a scrambled state, patches of aligned spins form and eat their neighbors; how fast they grow is the question.

The team runs spin-flip simulations where the impurity field fades with distance in a power-law pattern, rather than being noise. Snapshots of the patchwork obey the scaling rules, and large-scale views match the Porod law for sharp domain walls. The surprise is the growth law: average patch size creeps upward as a double logarithm of time, far slower than the usual logarithmic crawl of random-field systems. Correlated disorder, the authors conclude, nearly freezes coarsening. Such sluggish dynamics matter for magnetic materials that must hold their state, and for understanding glasses and stuck systems.
arxiv-2505-07173:
Xu, Ding, and Bao cut read noise in proof qubits by task shifts in time. Proof fix is a must for trust-worthy quantum work at scale. Face codes give high fail bars and lean gear in that role. Yet noise in one-shot reads caps how true proof reads can be. Their plan shifts read tasks from shaky qubits to firm nodes. Shallow tied loops do the shift work in the plan.

That shift trades gate flaws for read noise in a fair split. Picks rest on shape weight and flaw marks per node. Time caps from fade and fix needs bind the plan in real runs. A learn tool then steers the shifts to fit those caps. Sims show proof flaw rates fall by up to 34 percent. Gains span code spans from three to 11 in the sims.
arxiv-2505-08073:
Explaining why a reinforcement learning agent acted as it did is hard because its choices unfold over time. Madhuri Singh, Amal Alabdulkarim, Gennie Mansi, and Mark Riedl use world models, which predict how the world changes when the agent acts, to generate counterfactual trajectories showing what could have happened instead. They add a reverse world model that predicts what the world would have needed to look like for the agent to prefer a different action the user had in mind.

Explanations showing what the world should have been like raised users' understanding of the agent's policy significantly. The authors suggest such explanations can also teach users how to steer an agent by changing its environment.
arxiv-2505-08273:
Nibir Chandra Mandal and nine co-authors release a large open data set for mapping how farms irrigate, in this 2025 paper. Knowing whether fields use sprinklers, drip lines, or flooding matters for water planning, but labeled examples were scarce. IrrMap gathers satellite imagery at several resolutions, plus crop type, land use, and vegetation measures.

The set holds over a million image patches covering about 1.7 million farms and fourteen million acres across western American states, spanning 2013 to 2023. Patches are standardized and packaged with loaders and set train test splits for machine learning. Analyses chart how irrigation methods vary by crop and region, and how the two satellite sources differ. A full pipeline is published so others can extend the mapping to new regions.
arxiv-2505-08873:
Abdallah Alsammani, Gassan Farah, Mohammed Mohammed, and Mehmet Yavuz model cholera control in this 2025 paper. Cholera spreads both person to person and through dirty water, so single fixes often fail where sanitation is poor. Their model tracks susceptible, infected, and recovered people plus the water reservoir.

The team adds three levers: household sanitation, water cleanup, and vaccination. They split the spread number into direct and waterborne parts and measure each lever's pull. Math proofs show the disease-free state is stable below the threshold. Simulations reveal that paired sanitation steps reinforce each other, cutting the burden more than either alone. Sensitivity checks name the strongest drivers of outbreaks.
arxiv-2505-09373:
Federico Ferrari and Ole Sigmund use near-buckling theory to shape trusses and frames that act well just past the point where they would buckle. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A frame's path just past buckling can be steered by two terms: the first slope and the curve of its load path. The team puts both terms in the design task. That also makes the design less frail to small flaws in its shape. The same near form can stand in for the frame's full bent path, to design for a set mark of bent work. Tests on size and shape tasks for trusses and frames show the way works.
arxiv-2505-10773:
Maxine McCarthy and David Whittaker present a 2025 physics paper on topology in small chiral structures. Topology sorts materials by traits that resist smooth change. The authors ask a fresh question: can the border between two topological phases itself hold distinct phases?

For chiral systems, their answer is yes. They define phase borders by a forced rise in zero-energy states sitting at fixed points in space. By repeating the question, they build a method they call sequential topology. It finds the largest slice of a disordered parameter space that keeps a set order of zero-energy states. Those states change how waves spread and settle in the structure. Tests with a coaxial cable platform backed the theory, which works for any finite chiral layout.
arxiv-2505-11273:
Yuxin Xia and co-authors published a 2025 paper on planning growth of the electric grid under wind power's uncertainty. Grid planners must decide years ahead which new lines to build. Their choices shape the market that later matches power supply with demand. Wind output is unknown when that market clears a day ahead, which complicates every step.

The authors build a two-level model. At the top, the planner invests while looking ahead to market results. Below, the market clears with rules that keep power flows safe with high probability, even under wind swings. Their model also counts how network charges feed into the true costs faced by market users. A new approximation method handles the tough chance constraints without adding extra caution or numeric trouble. In tests, the plan met its safety targets on fresh data. The method also ran much faster than older approaches.
arxiv-2505-11673:
Livia Popa, Sumanta Basu, Myung Hee Lee, and Martin Wells present statistical methods in two thousand twenty-five for finding biomarkers in omics data. Clinical teams increasingly hunt for markers in short-term repeated measurements, where uncertainty and false discovery must be controlled. Their toolkit, BLOG, is Bayesian and built for such longitudinal data.

One approach scores single variables with a special prior and Bayes factors, with two ways to set its tuning value. A second approach selects whole groups of variables with a group lasso and spike-and-slab prior. Both work on changes between time points. Tests on simulated data and a tuberculosis metabolite study picked the right markers with high accuracy. The methods beat standard mixed models.
arxiv-2505-11973: Alireza Shirmarz and three co-authors built a tool to record and replay cloud gaming traffic, in a short paper from twenty twenty-five. Cloud gaming study is held back by wild game engines and closed trade platforms with locked logs. Their tool, CGReplay, records player commands and the frames that come back, in step as an action and reaction loop. Replay then lets labs grade user feel and service quality under set network states. The code is public.
arxiv-2505-12173:
Christopher Ryzowicz, Richard Bertram, and Bhargav Karamched gave a mathematical account in 2025 of how living systems hold steady while oscillating. Homeostasis is usually defined for static equilibria, quantities that refuse to move when parameters change, yet much of physiology pulses: hormones surge, neurons burst, hearts beat. In such systems what stays constant is not the instantaneous value but the average over a cycle, a dynamic form of stability the authors call homeodynamics.

Their framework treats systems with two or more separated time scales and shows how homeostasis can appear in the time average of a chemical species. The key is the response of the slow variable: when it reacts to parameter changes in the right compensating way, the fast oscillations rearrange themselves while their average holds still. The result gives relaxation and bursting systems, from pancreatic cells to neural circuits, a shared mathematical language.
arxiv-2505-12673:
Three iridium oxides host a rare state of matter where electrons move like light, report Zhi-Ming Yang and Huan Li in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their crystal symmetry protects the state, called a Dirac semimetal, but these materials also carry strong electron interactions and spin orbit coupling.

The authors combined two simulation methods, with the interaction strength computed rather than guessed. The fast electrons come from a spin orbit split state of iridium, and they grow heavier from the interactions. Surface bands and Fermi arcs appear on one face, clear of the bulk states. The paper presents the oxides as a meeting point of symmetry, correlation, and topology.
arxiv-2505-13373:
Anne-Lena Moor and colleagues clarified a measurement puzzle in biochemical networks in 2025. Researchers often quantify how much information one part of a cell's chemistry carries about another using trajectory mutual information. A popular shortcut, the linear-noise approximation, computes it through Gaussian channel theory and should be trustworthy for large systems. Yet in some cases its answers disagreed qualitatively with exact calculations, even for large molecule counts.

The authors show the mismatch comes from two different ways of describing a trajectory. In chemical systems the information lives in the sequence of reaction events, which the exact jump-process description records. The Gaussian shortcut can instead lump separate reaction channels into a single combined noise term, a state-based view that loses event detail. Naming that distinction explains when each calculation should be believed.
arxiv-2505-13473:
Luc Chabassier, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, presents a graphical interface for doing group theory proofs inside the Coq proof assistant. Group theory is powerful but abstract, and proof assistants are normally text-based.

Graphical languages already exist to tame categorical abstraction, yet they had not been brought into proof assistants. Chabassier's Coq plugin lets users both visualize proofs as diagrams and interact with them graphically. The goal is educational as much as useful: students can practice diagrammatic thinking on concrete proofs they already know. The paper describes the use of the plugin.
arxiv-2505-14573:
