The tower is branched and indexed by p-adic integers. They also tie a key algebraic object, the characteristic ideal of an Iwasawa module, directly to the Ihara L-function. The result roots a graph theory firmly in classical number theory methods.
arxiv-2508-08173:
Chongke Bi, Xin Gao, Jiangkang Deng, Guan Li, and Jun Han sharpen time-varying 3D simulation data while barely using any high-resolution examples, in a 2025 paper. Big simulations are costly at full resolution, so researchers upscale cheaper low-resolution runs. Older upscalers need piles of high-resolution training data. Their framework, CD-TVD, first studies past simulations to learn how detail degrades, using contrastive learning paired with a diffusion model.

Fine-tuning then needs just one fresh high-resolution time step. A local attention tweak helps the diffusion model restore fine detail. On fluid and weather datasets, the method delivered accurate, cheap upscaling. The authors call it a step toward practical data augmentation for large simulations, and they release the code.
arxiv-2508-09573:
Michał Rzepka and Piotr Chołda propose metrics for judging how flows change the state of a network, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Traffic in data networks fluctuates, and peak rates strain resources. Operators need measures that show which flows matter and how much load the network carries.

The authors analyze link and flow data using percentiles and sample distributions. They introduce a Utilization Score metric for network load. A modified Shapley value approach measures each flow's individual influence. Eleven metrics are reviewed and compared across network scenarios. Three of them gave broad insight while staying easy to maintain. The methodology is offered as a framework for future metric research.
arxiv-2508-09673:
Damiano Abram, Giulio Malavolta, and Lawrence Roy build a cryptographic primitive in twenty twenty-five. Two parties hold vectors and want a secret-shared tensor product of them. Their notion, succinct oblivious tensor evaluation, uses just two simultaneous messages. Message and setup sizes do not grow with the vector dimension.

They construct the primitive from the standard learning-with-errors problem, with optimal complexity. That one tool then unlocks a family of applications. Adaptively secure laconic function evaluation becomes possible, where communication stays near the input and output sizes. Trapdoor hash functions for all functions follow. So do succinct homomorphic secret sharing and efficient laconic oblivious transfer. Readers in cryptography get a single new building block that pays off across many protocols.
arxiv-2508-09773:
Andrei Zabolotskii constructs number tilings that are as wild as possible, in a short mathematics paper from 2025. An SL2-tiling is a grid of numbers where every two-by-two block obeys a fixed rule tied to the group SL2. Tame tilings connect to classic objects such as the Farey graph and frieze patterns.

Wild tilings, which break the tame rules somewhere, were far less understood. The author defines a wild density: the share of the grid where wildness shows. For integer tilings, he proves the highest possible wild density is two fifths, and exhibits tilings reaching that bound. Over clock-arithmetic number systems, he builds tilings that are wild everywhere. The note pins down how untamed these grids can get.
arxiv-2508-12173:
Suyash Gupta, Dakai Kang, Dahlia Malkhi, and Mohammad Sadoghi present a 2025 protocol for getting a network of computers to agree on one shared order of records. Such atomic broadcast is the core of blockchains and replicated databases. The hard case comes after a burst of faulty leaders, when an attack called tail-forking can stall progress by discarding the work of honest leaders.

Their design, Carry-the-Tail, is the first of its kind to promise, once the network settles, that a fixed share of honest leaders' blocks are kept. It does so without giving up the best known worst-case message cost, and steady traffic stays lean. The core trick, called Carry, drops into a known family of protocols. It blunts the attack and clears most leader-caused stalls.
arxiv-2508-12973:
Monika Bahl and six co-authors introduce a single score for swirling light beams in a 2025 paper. Light can carry orbital angular momentum, a twist used in optical tools, fast data links, and quantum work. Real beams often mix many vortices, so their total twist is hard to state.

Their R-index captures the twist content of any structured field in one number. It also gauges beam purity, which shows how clean the generation was. The score applies from pure textbook modes to messy multi-vortex mixes. A shared measure lets labs compare beams across very different setups. It should help designers pick the best beam shapes for tools and communications alike.
arxiv-2508-13773:
Tian Sun, Yuqi Chen, and Weiwei Sun argue that transformers forecast long horizons better when their attention knows the calendar. Long-term time series forecasting remains contested ground for the architecture. Real series carry nested rhythms, daily inside weekly inside yearly. Standard attention must discover those cycles from scratch.

Their mechanism, PENGUIN, builds periodicity straight into attention. A periodic-aware bias in the attention scores rewards matches at cycle lags. Grouped multi-query attention lets several cycles coexist, each with its own group. The design stays simple and drops into existing transformer forecasters. Across diverse benchmarks it consistently beat both multilayer perceptron models and fellow transformers. Code is public. The lesson: a little explicit structure about time's rhythm goes a long way.
arxiv-2508-14073:
Qian Zhang and four co-authors present MCLPD, a method that spots Parkinson's disease from brain wave records and works across distinct data sets. Brain wave tests can catch the disease early, but labeled records are costly and sets differ in how they were made. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The method first learns without labels from one large set, using paired views of the same record changed in time and in wave rates. It then fine tunes on a tiny share of labeled records from two other sets. With very few labels it scored well on both sets, and scores rose more with a bit more labeled data. The authors report clear gains over past methods.
arxiv-2508-14173:
Tanmoy Chattopadhyay and co-authors report tests of readout electronics for sensitive X-ray detectors in a 2025 paper. The detectors, called SiSeRO devices, sit on chips and can sense single electrons, which makes them sharp tools for astronomy. A first version showed low noise and fine energy detail, and repeated reading pushed noise lower still.

To run the next round of detectors, the team built a compact eight-channel chip that uses little power and reads fast. The paper shares first results from pairing the chip with the detectors. It also lays out designs for improved detectors, including one with many amplifiers for fast repeated reading and a pixel sensor proof of concept. The work moves the technology toward real instruments.
arxiv-2508-14273:
Krishna Garg, Firoz Shaik, Sambaran Bandyopadhyay, and Cornelia Caragea test whether language models can write the opening section of a research paper. Their twenty twenty-five study sets a new task: given a title, an abstract, and related works, the model must draft a full introduction.

The team built data sets from two twenty twenty-five venues and tested five top models, both open and closed. They scored the drafts on word overlap, meaning match, content cover, faithfulness, citation care, and story flow, with both auto scores and model judges. LLaMA 4 Maverick led on most counts, and giving three worked examples beat fewer. Code and data are shared.
arxiv-2508-14873:
Kamal Panigrahi and Balbeer Singh study the thermodynamics of a deformed black hole, on both sides of the holographic mirror. The object is a Schwarzschild black hole in anti-de Sitter space, deformed by a gravitational decoupling method. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they work in the extended thermodynamics where the cosmological constant acts as pressure. The bulk shows two transitions: the classic Hawking-Page change and a liquid-gas style first-order transition in the right parameter range. Its critical exponents match mean-field predictions. The holographic dictionary then carries the analysis to the dual field theory on the boundary.

Three boundary ensembles reveal distinct behavior. One mirrors the Hawking-Page transition. In another, the deformation destabilizes most branches, leaving a single stable phase. The authors stress the deformation parameter's grip on the confinement story throughout.
arxiv-2508-16673:
Pooja Rao and co-authors audited language models used to score job interviews in 2025, looking for cultural bias. Machine-run hiring tools more and more rate candidates, and a model trained mostly on one culture's speech may quietly penalize another's. The team weighed model scores on one hundred interview transcripts from United Kingdom candidates and one hundred from Indian candidates, covering hireability and related traits.

Indian transcripts received every time lower scores than British ones, even after identifying details were anonymized. The gap tracked traits of the language itself, such as sentence hardness and vocabulary diversity, rather than who the person was: when the authors swapped names signaling gender, caste. And region inside the Indian transcripts, the substitutions did not produce major score changes. The findings expose a subtler, linguistic channel through which hiring models can disadvantage a whole culture's applicants.
arxiv-2508-16773:
Hugo Camacho, Kaja Rotermund, and a large team describe map-making for a radio telescope bound for the far side of the Moon in a 2025 astronomy study. The instrument, a pathfinder called LuSEE-Night, will listen to faint cosmic radio signals shielded from Earth's noise. Turning its raw measurements into a sky map needs care because the telescope's response mixes directions and frequencies.

Linear map-making writes that response as a matrix problem and solves it directly. The authors lay out the method for this lunar instrument and its data pipeline. Clean maps of the radio sky at these frequencies could reveal conditions in the early universe.
arxiv-2508-17273:
Shiguang Feng and Lvzhou Li complete a rule set for reversible circuits in twenty twenty-five. Reversible circuits matter for quantum computing and design automation. Rule-based rewriting is a standard way to optimize them. Whether any proposed rule set is complete had been a longstanding open problem.

The authors present five fundamental transformation rules. They claim the set is complete: any two equivalent reversible circuits can be transformed into each other using only these rules. The proof introduces a canonical circuit form for reversible functions. Every function has a unique circuit in that form. Any circuit can be rewritten into its canonical form with the rules. Readers in quantum design automation get a finished foundation for rule-based optimization tools.
arxiv-2508-17373:
Zhi-Gang Wang and Qi Xin published a research paper in 2025 on exotic five-quark particles that may hide in a bump seen when a J/psi particle pairs with a Lambda baryon. Experiments have spotted two candidate states there, but their makeup is debated. The pair model them as two diquarks bound with an antiquark, with zero isospin, separating this charge family for the first time.

Using a standard approximation scheme of quantum chromodynamics, they isolate the negative-parity states cleanly and compute their masses for three spin options. The resulting spectrum accommodates both observed candidates naturally. The work gives experimenters firmer mass targets and a template for sorting real pentaquarks from look-alikes.
arxiv-2508-17473:
Krishna, Khorrami, and Tzes design a consensus rule for agents that move as rigid mechanical systems in twenty twenty-five. Such agents, from drones to robot arms, live on curved spaces of poses, not flat grids. Classic consensus rules were built for flat space with double step motion. Their rule extends those ideas to a broad class of curved pose spaces.

An error score compares the poses of two linked agents on the curved space. The control law needs only neighbor poses, not speeds or mass data. A broad form of stability theory proves the group settles at one shared pose. Tests on the pose sync of many rigid bodies back the design.
arxiv-2508-17573:
Yunze Xiao, Lynnette Hui Xian Ng, Jiarui Liu, and Mona Diab say that to make language models seem like men and women is a design pick. The work came out in 2025. It should be seen as a knob that can be tuned, not just a risk. Models show more and more traits like ours in view, speech, acts, and thought. That makes chats feel smooth and plain. It also calls up too much trust and false shows.

Past work lists those risks for the most part. It gives scant help with design picks. The team sets out a tiered frame drawn from more than one field. In it, the human-like feel of a model grows from cues that staff build in. It grows from the sense that users make of those cues too. Design and sense meet at each tier of the good, from face words to seeming thought.
arxiv-2508-17973:
Miriam Anschutz, Thanh Mai Pham, and Georg Groh introduce a German data set for rewriting texts at set reading levels in this 2025 paper. Clear texts must be tailored to readers with different skills. Their set, German4All, holds aligned versions of the same paragraphs at five levels. It covers more than twenty-five thousand samples. A large AI model made the versions, and both human and AI judges checked them.

The team then trained an open rewriting model on the set. That model reached the best scores reported for German text simplification. It allows finer control of level than a simple easy-or-hard switch. The authors share both the data and the model in public. Such tools can help schools, offices, and health services reach more readers. The paper also details how the set was checked for quality.
arxiv-2508-19473:
Stephen Arndt and co-authors present a 2025 paper on coloring the common ground of several matroids. Matroid intersection coloring asks for the fewest colors so that each color class stays independent in every matroid at once. It models scheduling and assignment problems where many constraint systems must hold together.

The authors give a fast algorithm for one general matroid combined with several partition matroids. The coloring uses only a modest multiple of the obvious lower bound on colors. Since most standard combinatorial matroids reduce to partition matroids at small cost, the result covers them too. For just two matroids, the best earlier method lost a logarithmic factor through a set cover detour. The new bound is a plain multiple of the number of matroids. That is a clean step for approximation theory.
arxiv-2508-19973:
Helena Schreder and three co-authors studied how small rods drift in a flow. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, asks if size and shape alone can make rods gather in some spots more than others. Past work tied this effect to particle weight. Here the rods have no weight effect at all. Shape gives them forces that shift with how they point.

The team first proved the effect needs three things at once. The rods must have size, have a long shape, and sit in a flow that is not plain. They then ran tests in a steady two cell flow. The work helps explain how real bits in water or air, from plankton to waste, may cluster.
arxiv-2508-20773:
Christoforos Spartalis and three co-authors present SAFEMax, a method that makes image generators forget banned classes, in a 2025 study. Owners of such models may need to erase a class, such as a face or a style, without retraining from scratch. SAFEMax pushes the model to output plain noise when asked for a banned class. It does so by raising the entropy, or disorder, of what the model makes for those prompts.

The method acts on the early steps of image formation, where class traits are strongest. That focus lets it forget the banned class while keeping other classes sharp. Tests show it matches or beats prior erasure methods on quality checks. It also runs much faster than those methods. The authors ground the design in information theory and report strong gains in efficiency.
arxiv-2508-21273:
Sensors pour out data streams that drift over time, and yesterday's anomaly detector quietly goes stale. Ashok Devireddy and Shunping Huang present CALM, a framework that keeps retraining itself as the stream flows. A forecasting model flags odd points; the system then fine-tunes on fresh data in a closed loop. A large language model acts as judge, deciding which flagged points are noise and which mark a real shift worth learning from.

Built on a distributed processing engine, the system runs in near real time. On a broad public benchmark, the ever-updated model beat the frozen starting model on most datasets. The team argues that self-refresh, guided by a judging model, is the way to watch changing streams.
arxiv-2508-21373:
Niladri Halder and Chandra Murthy present a 2025 study on hearing data through underwater sound channels. Underwater links smear signals in both delay and scale, which blurs the data. A receiver must first learn the channel, then read the bits. The pair build one frame that does both jobs for four kinds of signal design.

Their frame states one shared input-output rule for all four designs, so the contest stays fair. They add fresh methods: a learning loop that refines channel guesses, a soft decoder that rates each bit, and a scheme that reuses read data as extra guide posts. Tests show the methods sharpen both channel learning and data reading. Among the designs, one led with a simple equalizer, while a common design trailed. The work aids sonar and subsea links.
arxiv-2508-21473:
Daniil Vostrikov and six co-authors study maximum extractable value, profit that block producers can take by reordering transactions, on the Polygon blockchain. Their paper came out in 2025. They focus on atomic arbitrage, a risk-free trade that buys and sells across prices inside one transaction.

The team set rules to spot such trades and analyzed nearly two years of blocks. They compared spam strategies, which flood the network with attempts, against auction strategies, which bid for priority. Spam attempts were more common, but auction trades earned more profit. Their analysis also traces how network design and transaction ordering shape these profits. The findings support stronger rules for ordering transactions.
arxiv-2509-00173:
Shahiduz Zaman, Tanzima Hashem, and Sukarna Barua define a new query in 2025 for picking group meetup spots that fit each person's existing trip. Group outings are hard to plan when days are packed. Each user's trip is a sequence of stops, and the user may detour to a meetup point from any stop in that sequence.

The Trip-based Group Nearest Neighbor query finds the meetup point and the best detour stop for each user. The goal is to minimize total extra distance across the group. Fast computation methods for the query are the paper's focus, in this full version. Trip-aware picks could make group plans fairer and easier to keep.
arxiv-2509-00273:
Saeed Tafazoli and Jaap Top study hyperelliptic curves built from Chebyshev polynomials in 2025, with a focus on when such curves are maximal over finite fields. A hyperelliptic curve generalizes an elliptic curve to higher genus. Maximal means the curve has the most rational points a curve of its kind can have over the squared field in question, a prized trait in coding and cryptography.

Starting from a prime-degree case, they present new degree and field pairs where maximality holds. They also give new conditions that rule maximality out for other pairs. Arguments mix Frobenius slope data, complex multiplication on the curve's Jacobian, and a two-descent technique. One maximality method, for a prime case in set characteristics, departs from earlier arguments.
arxiv-2509-00373:
Sihao Wu, Gaojie Jin, Wei Huang, Jianhong Wang, and Xiaowei Huang present a two-stage defense in 2025 against jailbreak attacks on vision-language models. Such models fuse visual and textual input for reasoning, but they stay highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks that coax out harmful output. Activation steering can suppress harm, yet prompt-tied steering vectors generalize poorly and can degrade visual grounding.

Their method, SPO-VLM, first computes adaptive, layer-specific steering vectors from diverse data for broad suppression at inference. A second stage adds sequence-level preference optimization at the policy level. The pairing targets robustness without sacrificing grounding. Stronger built-in defenses matter as such models enter open use.
arxiv-2509-00473:
Vladimir Sokolov studies charged black points. A black point is a charged black hole whose horizon has shrunk to a point. The horizon is the surface past which light cannot escape. In this state the horizon meets the singularity. He works in a theory that changes the rules for strong electric fields.

Sokolov shows that black points obey a key heat law in Planck's form. The classic charged black hole does not obey it in the same way. He also shows that forming a black point is not a first-order phase change. He then studies a case where two horizon surfaces merge. That case is much like an extreme black hole.
arxiv-2509-01073:
Brain signals picked up from the scalp, called EEG, are weak and easily spoiled when a person moves. Yuhong Zhang, with six co-authors, aims to clean such motion noise by also recording motion itself. Sensors that track movement, known as IMUs, record how the head shifts while EEG is gathered.

Zhang and the team fine-tune a large brain model so it learns links between motion data and noise in brain channels. The tuned model has about nine million parts and trained on under six hours of paired records. It beats older cleaning methods that used EEG alone. Cleaner signals would help brain-computer links work outside the lab, where people move freely.
arxiv-2509-01173:
Chenjian Wang studies a type of maximal operator linked to moment curves in spaces of dimension three or more. Maximal operators measure the largest average of a function over a family of shapes, and they are central tools in harmonic analysis. Here the averages follow a curved path rather than straight lines or balls.

Wang derives mapping properties that state how these operators act between function spaces, measured in L p norms. In a special case, the estimate obtained is sharp, meaning it cannot be improved. The short note adds a precise piece to the theory of operators tied to curves.
arxiv-2509-02073:
Davide Ghio, Fabrizio Boncoraglio, and Lenka Zdeborova infer spreading processes on graphs when starting states depend on node covariates. Spreading models cover epidemics and other dynamics where each node changes state over time. Observers see only some nodes at some times and must reconstruct the rest. Past work assumed random starting states, ignoring side data that shape them.

Here a single layer neural network maps covariates to each node starting state inside a Bayesian frame. A hybrid belief propagation and message passing algorithm handles dynamics and covariate data together. It beats estimators that use only spread data or only covariates. In some regimes, first order phase transitions create gaps where perfect recovery is possible in theory yet the algorithm fails. The gap highlights hard inference zones.
arxiv-2509-02273:
Chenhao Wang leads four co-authors with RS-OOD, a sight and speech frame to flag out of range shots in remote sense work. To flag new or odd patterns is key for self led watch, flood aid, and green checks. Ways built for plain shots move poorly to sky shots, with thin data, multi scale scenes, and stark drift. Their frame fits sight and speech models to those sky shot traits.

Space trait boosts first sharpen how scenes split from each other. A dual prompt match cross checks scene sense with fine text sense for one voice. A trust led self train loop mines fake tags to grow data with no hand tags. On a range of sky shot tests, the frame beats past ways each time. Few tagged shots are all it takes to fit new tasks.
arxiv-2509-02473:
Ziting Wang and five co-authors present a 2025 benchmark paper, FDABench, for data agents that answer analytical questions across mixed data sources. Such agents must reason over databases, documents, web pages, images, video, and audio together.

Older benchmarks test single skills or few data types, so coverage stays thin. FDABench holds about two thousand tasks spanning six data modalities, scored under one multi-level evaluation framework. Its tasks were built with PUDDING, a construction pipeline that pairs model generation with repeated expert checks for reliability. The authors run several agent designs, including general analytical agents, semantic operator frameworks, and retrieval-based methods. Comparisons reveal where each design struggles and offer guidance for building stronger data agents.
arxiv-2509-02673:
Hanbit Oh, Hui Yang, and Ya-Hui Zhang wrote a 2025 review of theory for new superconductors. The materials may arise by doping a spin-one Mott insulator. In such a material, electrons sit localised with spin one. Interest centres on a recently found bilayer nickelate superconductor.

The reviewed model couples mobile electrons in one orbital to localised spins in another. A strong Hund coupling links them. It favours aligned spins. In that limit the model reduces to a t-J type model. It mixes two kinds of states. Numerical results on chains and ladders show a Luther-Emery liquid phase. On a bilayer lattice, strong coupling between layers drives pairing. An ideal version shows kinetic-energy driven superconductivity. It also shows a pseudogap metal phase, like underdoped cuprates.
arxiv-2509-02873:
Zhantong Qiu, Mahyar Samani, and Jason Lowe-Power presented a 2025 computer science paper on testing processor designs without slow, full simulations. Their framework, called Nugget, picks small but telling slices of a program's work. Those slices can run on real machines as well as in simulators.

Nugget works at an intermediate level of code that sits between human-written programs and machine instructions. At that level it can study stretches of work without tying itself to one program file. It then builds light, portable snippets that researchers can check on hardware first. The payoff is faster testing across different chip designs, program libraries, and simulators. Architecture teams can try new ideas sooner and with less wasted effort.
arxiv-2509-03073: M. Ibrahim and 4 co-authors wrote a 2025 quantum optics paper on several two-level atoms coupled to a single light mode. The mode is held in a Fock state, meaning a fixed count of photons. They gauge shared quantum links with global quantum discord and quantum Fisher information. The second measures how sharply a quantity can be pinned down. Their model adds a Kerr effect, where light changes its own medium, plus parametric amplification. It also adds intrinsic decoherence, the slow loss of quantum behavior from within.
arxiv-2509-03173:
Mingfeng Lin introduced a 2025 self-teaching method for outlining coronary arteries in X-ray angiography images. Coronary artery disease is a leading killer, and tracing these vessels by hand is slow work. Automated segmentation, painting the arteries pixel by pixel, still struggles with accuracy and with generalizing to new patients.

Knowledge distillation normally trains a small student model from a larger teacher. Lin's version turns the model's own layered outputs into the teacher, a deep self-knowledge scheme. Two losses guide learning: one matches probability distributions loosely, the other supervises single pixels tightly. That double pressure improved scores for overlap, accuracy, and sensitivity on two public datasets. The method also aims for robustness when image conditions change.
arxiv-2509-03373:
Elizabeth Coda, Ery Arias-Castro, and Gal Mishne proposed a modular visualization method in 2025 that clusters data before embedding it. Dimensionality reduction squeezes high-dimensional data into two dimensions for viewing. Popular tools like t-SNE and UMAP group points while embedding them, giving well-separated clusters, but they tend to distort the overall geometry.

The new approach separates the steps for transparency. It groups the data first. Each group is then embedded on its own, and the pieces are aligned at the end into one global picture. Tests on synthetic and real-world datasets showed performance competitive with the established tools. The authors emphasize that each stage can be inspected and swapped, unlike the single opaque step of the standard methods. That clarity helps users judge what a visualization actually shows.
arxiv-2509-03473:
Mitchell J. Walker and seven co-authors describe a 2025 research paper on loading large optical tweezer arrays. Such arrays trap single neutral atoms in focused light beams for quantum computing, simulation, and precise frequency measurement. More usable sites mean stronger machines, so filling wide arrays matters.

Their method, called painted loading, sweeps the cooling light frequency so the atom supply drifts across the strontium-88 array. Arrays taller than 100 micrometres are filled, over three times the height reached from a still reservoir. Average temperature across the array stays very low. Adjusting the sweep also shapes how atoms are spread, allowing uniform fills or chosen regions only, and a simple rate model matches the pattern.
arxiv-2509-03773: Co-Higgs bundles of Schwarzenberger type and the determinant morphism attached to them are examined in a 2025 mathematics paper by Kuntal Banerjee. A co-Higgs bundle pairs a vector bundle with a special endomorphism-like field, and Schwarzenberger bundles form a classic family built from projective geometry. The determinant morphism maps such bundles to simpler determinant data. Working with trace-free co-Higgs bundles modelled on rank two Schwarzenberger bundles, Banerjee identifies the images of that morphism. The result describes exactly which values the determinant map attains for this family.
arxiv-2509-03873:
Jiajun Song and one co-author devote a 2025 research paper to recognising food dishes never seen during training, even in new cuisine and ingredient mixes. New dishes appear all the time, so a recogniser cannot require examples of every category. Their new task frames cuisines as attributes and ingredients as objects, matching the structure of compositional zero-shot learning, where known parts recombine into unseen wholes.

Three obstacles are named: distracting backgrounds, mix-ups between staple and side dishes, and semantic bias toward a single attribute. Their method, SalientFusion, answers with two components. SalientFormer strips background redundancy and resolves role confusion using depth features. DebiasAT reduces that bias by aligning text prompts with visual features. Two new benchmarks are introduced, with categories numbering in the hundreds. SalientFusion reaches leading results on those benchmarks and on the most popular general datasets as well. Code is released publicly.
arxiv-2509-03973:
SAC-MIL, a method for classifying whole slide histopathology images, the digitised microscope slides used in cancer diagnosis, occupies a 2025 research paper by Yu Bai and thirteen co-authors. A slide is far too large to feed a network at once, so multiple instance learning treats it as a bag of small patches and labels the bag. Patch positions matter, yet many methods ignore them.

One module encodes each patch's actual coordinates in the slide, capturing spatial relationships instead of relying on sequence order. That choice also solves length extrapolation, where test slides produce longer patch sequences than training slides. A second block computes full correlations between all instances with a simple multilayer perceptron design, in time linear in sequence length. Avoiding transformer machinery means no graphics kernels are needed for deployment. On three standard datasets covering lymph node, lung, and breast cancer slides, it reaches leading classification performance.
arxiv-2509-04073:
L Lacroix and thirty-eight co-authors give a 2025 status report on measuring exploding stars well enough for cosmology, meaning the study of the universe's expansion. The Zwicky Transient Facility, a sky survey, released records for thousands of confirmed Type Ia supernovae. Such explosions can reveal dark energy only if their brightness is measured with extreme care. A technique called scene modeling photometry separates each blast from its host galaxy.

Star measurements repeated to better than one percent in tests. One catch surfaced: a sensor flaw the team calls the pocket-effect warps star images depending on brightness. Fixing it needs pixel-level corrections that are still being built, so the release cannot yet support precise cosmology.
arxiv-2509-04373:
Bufan Gao and one co-author, Elisa Kreiss, show that gender-bias scores for language models wobble depending on how tests are framed in a 2025 research paper. Bias evaluations often use carefully built prompts that quietly signal their testing purpose. The authors vary two things: how salient the evaluation context is, and how salient the gender content is. Four task formats are scored both by token probabilities and by forced discrete choices, letting the measurement methods themselves be compared.

Prompts framed more clearly as bias tests produced different gender output patterns than neutral ones. Forced-choice scoring also amplified apparent bias compared with probability measures. Benchmarks may be triggering a special testing mode in models, the authors warn, which threatens real-world validity.
arxiv-2509-04473:
Jaekwon Yoo and four co-authors link speech to language models cheaply for low-resource settings in a 2025 research paper. Joining a speech encoder to a large language model usually demands heavy data and compute. Their parameter-efficient adapter converts speech embeddings, numeric sound summaries, into tokens the language model can read. Three spoken tasks are targeted together: transcription, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis. A language model also labels synthetic training data, cutting annotation costs.

With seven times fewer trainable parameters, the adapter still improved all three tasks substantially on standard measures. Extra gains came from a classifier regularizer and low-rank adaptation of the main model. Scores on the SLUE spoken understanding benchmark rose clearly. Smaller teams can now attempt unified speech systems.
arxiv-2509-04573:
Ancy Anna John and sixteen co-authors hunt the boiling-granulation signal of a quiet dwarf star in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Stars' surfaces bubble like soup, and that granulation jitters the radial velocity measurements used to find exoplanets, now precise below one meter per second. The team watched HD 166620, a K dwarf in a magnetically quiet Maunder-like phase, for two intense nights with the HARPS-N spectrograph. After correcting a newly spotted instrument flaw from uneven detector illumination, structure functions and Gaussian process models isolated the granulation.

Its timescale landed near forty-four minutes with an amplitude matching predictions. Splitting spectral lines by formation temperature showed deeper, cooler layers tracking theory best. Exoplanet hunters gain a cleaner noise budget.
arxiv-2509-05273:
Energy use and carbon cost vary sharply between learning algorithms, Jason Gardner and four co-authors show in a 2025 study of deep reinforcement learning on classic video games. Training these systems takes heavy computing, yet their power bills and emissions are rarely measured.

The team trained seven well-known algorithms for a million steps each on ten Atari games, measuring power in real time. Costs are then estimated from United States average electricity prices. Some algorithms matched others on performance while using far less energy and emitting much less carbon. The trade-offs between score, time, energy, and money point to greener design choices that do not sacrifice learning.
arxiv-2509-05473:
How large can special arithmetic functions grow at their central point? João C. C. Vargas gives a lower bound in a solo 2025 number theory paper on class group L-functions, series attached to imaginary quadratic fields that encode deep facts about their arithmetic.

Vargas bounds the maximum value of these functions at the centre of their critical strip. On average over the field size, that maximum is at least a stated exponential quantity whose exponent grows like a square root of logarithms. Lower bounds of this kind are hard-won evidence about extreme values, complementing average behaviour results. They matter because L-function peaks are linked to class numbers and the distribution of prime ideals.
arxiv-2509-05573:
Pairs of bright light beams with linked fluctuations yield shared random numbers in a 2025 quantum optics paper by Anirudh Shekar and three co-authors. Random number generators built on quantum effects are vital for secure communication and encryption.

Using four-wave mixing in rubidium vapour, the team produced twin beams whose intensity fluctuations matched extremely closely at the test frequency. Squeezing of the intensity difference certifies the quantum link between them. From the fluctuations they extracted several bits of entropy per sample. After selecting matched data and hashing, the two sides held identical random strings at a useful rate, passing standard statistical test suites.
arxiv-2509-05673:
A new class of rings that generalises two earlier ones is introduced by Peter Danchev, Mina Doostalizadeh, and Ahmad Moussavi in a 2025 algebra paper. Rings here are algebraic systems with addition and multiplication, and nil-clean style properties describe how elements split into well-behaved parts.

The authors define weakly strongly 2-nil-clean rings and explore the notion in depth. They prove every such ring is strongly pi-regular, a stability property for powers of elements. More concretely, each one decomposes as a direct product of a strongly 2-nil-clean ring and a ring of residues modulo a power of two. The result organises several variants from earlier literature under one roof.
arxiv-2509-05773:
Ancient Chinese oracle bone characters are set as a visual test for large multimodal models by Zijian Chen and six co-authors in a 2025 paper. These pictographic characters are the oldest attested written Chinese, and matching them to the real objects they depict is a step toward decipherment.

Their dataset, PictOBI-20k, pairs twenty thousand character and object images into more than fifteen thousand multiple-choice questions. Human annotations check whether people and models use the same reference points when reasoning visually. General models showed early decipherment skill, but mostly leaned on language priors rather than the image itself. The authors hope the set will sharpen visual attention in future oracle bone models.
arxiv-2509-05973:
A dying massive star could betray hypothetical axion particles through its neutrino glow, according to long-term simulations by Masamitsu Mori and Kanji Mori in a 2025 paper. Axion-like particles, if they couple to photons, would drain energy from a core-collapse supernova and cool it. The authors run general-relativistic radiation-hydrodynamic simulations that include that cooling channel.

Two production routes are modeled, photon coalescence and the Primakoff effect, for a particle mass and a range of coupling strengths. The cooling shows up late rather than early, and axion brightness stays below the neutrino brightness throughout. Counting expected events in the Super-Kamiokande detector for a nearby supernova, the authors conclude the long neutrino signal could still reveal axions below existing limits.
arxiv-2509-06173:
Magnetic fields in a galaxy's gas layer can buoyantly rise and reorganize the whole layer, and Yasin Qazi and three co-authors simulate that instability in a 2025 paper. They solve non-ideal isothermal magnetohydrodynamic equations for rotating and non-rotating layers. The field is imposed at the boundaries or maintained by an alpha effect, and cosmic rays enter as a weightless pressure source.

Without rotation, an imposed field decays to a very weak state as the layer thins, while an alpha-maintained field survives. Rotation changes everything: the system oscillates nonlinearly, the field direction can switch, and parity can flip from quadrupolar to dipolar through dynamo action outside the layer. A secondary alpha effect at altitude, with anomalous sign, drives the switch. None of the classic analytic assumptions about the Parker instability survive the simulations.
arxiv-2509-06373:
Dissipation, usually the enemy of quantum control, becomes the tool in experiments by Tao Chen and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. The team builds a tunable, state-resolved laser-induced loss channel for individual Rydberg atoms, in quiet and strongly interacting settings alike. Loss can then prepare, transfer, and stabilize quantum states on purpose.

Interaction shifts move the exceptional point dividing quantum Zeno behavior, where watching freezes change, from its anti-Zeno opposite, and interactions enhance decay measurably. A configuration-selective two-body Zeno effect freezes chosen spin states while neighbors evolve. Theory extends the trick to many-body chains, where unwanted spin configurations could be distilled away dissipatively. The work opens routines for preparing correlated states in Rydberg arrays.
arxiv-2509-07173:
S. Vaidya and 19 co-authors report an experimental study in 2025 of a magnetic chain with a twist. The material holds nickel atoms in a line, each with spin one, and the chain orders as an antiferromagnet, where neighboring spins point in opposite directions. The nickel sites turn in a four-fold chiral pattern, meaning the structure twists like a screw as it runs.

Muon spin rotation shows long-range magnetic order sets in below about 1.82 kelvin. Neutron diffraction reveals that the chiral order comes from a twisting direction of the easy-axis anisotropy, the preferred spin direction set by each ion, rather than from the usual interaction suspects. Neutron scattering maps the spin waves, and simple theory fits them well with a few measured constants. Extra flat bands in the data hint at further effects beyond that simple picture, leaving a clear target for later work.
arxiv-2509-07473:
Qin Chen and 5 co-authors present SheetDesigner in 2025, a system that lays out spreadsheets automatically with a multimodal language model. Spreadsheet layout is skilled manual work: components must sit on a discrete grid, not at free coordinates, and cells carry semantic links such as data dependencies that generic layout tools ignore. The authors first formalize the layout generation task itself.

They supply a seven-criterion evaluation protocol and a dataset of 3,326 spreadsheets. SheetDesigner then works zero-shot, with no training, combining rule-based reflection and vision-based reflection to place components and fill content. It beats five baselines by at least 22.6 percent. The study also finds that models handle overlap and balance well through vision but struggle with alignment, which is why both reflection types are needed. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2509-07573:
Oxana Shaya and 3 co-authors study quantum complexity when random operations come from smaller symmetry groups in a 2025 paper. Typical quantum states and circuits are often modeled by sampling from the full unitary group. Here the operations come instead from the symplectic and special orthogonal groups. These are structured subsets with their own geometry. The question is whether that structure makes typical states simpler.

The authors use concentration of measure, the fact that random quantities cluster near their average. They show that states from these groups still carry exponentially large strong complexity. The states also sit nearly at right angles to each other. The same behavior holds for designs over these groups. They also prove that learning circuits built from such gates is hard on average. In short, structured subgroups can match the full unitary group in complexity.
arxiv-2509-07773:
Sebastian Macaluso and 6 co-authors lay out a vision in 2025 for quantum computing in large-scale network optimization. Future 6G-and-beyond mobile networks need multi-objective optimization over vast search spaces, a task often intractable for classical methods. Quantum computing promises new leverage, and many network problems share a graph-centric representation, with nodes and links carrying the constraints.

By analyzing common features across problem classes, the authors propose a unified strategy built on quantum algorithms. Two routes are outlined in detail: optimization by quantum annealing, which lets a quantum system settle toward low-energy solutions, and quantum reinforcement learning. The article is a vision and agenda paper rather than a benchmark study. It closes with the main challenges quantum algorithms and hardware must overcome before they can effectively optimize future networks.
arxiv-2509-07873:
A robot that nods and reacts at the right moments may draw people into deeper conversation, report Hieu Tran and 2 co-authors in a 2025 human-robot interaction paper. Their social robot, powered by a large language model, uses sentiment-based backchannels, the small sounds and gestures that signal listening, together with active listening behaviours.

Backchanneling done well can encourage self-disclosure, create a sense of empathy, and build rapport between person and machine. The study compares the robot's listening style against alternatives to see how much people open up and engage. As social robots enter homes and care settings, listening well may matter as much as speaking well, and this work measures that skill directly.
arxiv-2509-07973:
Elena Silvestre-Rosello and 6 co-authors ask what fourth-order lensing stats can teach us, in a 2025 cosmology paper. Gravity from dark matter bends light and slightly stretches galaxy shapes. This stretch is called shear. Two-point stats of shear miss part of the signal, the part that is not shaped like a bell curve.

Four-point patterns hold that missing part. The paper builds the theory for reading them through aperture stats, which sum the shear in round patches. It also builds the code to compute the values. Last, it forecasts how much new information the fourth-order stats will add. Survey teams can now judge if the hard extra work is worth the gain.
arxiv-2509-08273:
N. M. Jiménez Cruz and 2 co-authors propose a fresh test for modified gravity in a 2025 paper. Einstein's theory allows just two kinds of gravitational wave stretch. Many rival theories add a third, scalar kind. The team hunts that scalar kind in the faint hum of waves from the whole sky.

Three-point patterns are the key. Averaged over angles, those patterns vanish for the two known kinds. The scalar kind leaves a trace that does not vanish. The team works out the response for ground detectors, for pulsar timing arrays, and for star-position watches. They also build the best estimator for the job. A scalar find would break Einstein's theory in its home ground, so a clean test is worth having ready.
arxiv-2509-08473:
Vincent Bagayoko and Vincenzo Mantova show that Taylor expansions exist for functions on fields of generalised series in a 2025 maths paper. Generalised series allow far wilder growth than plain polynomials. They can stack logs and exponentials many layers deep. Such series are the native script of asymptotic analysis, where one asks how a function behaves at extreme size.

The main result gives both existence and convergence of the expansions. It needs two tools on the field: a derivative and an exponential map. The result then covers the standard fields of transseries, both the log-exp kind and the omega kind. Calculus moves that students take for granted are now licensed in that wilder world.
arxiv-2509-08673:
Different teams counting galaxy clusters reach different cosmologies, and simply comparing their final numbers hides where they clash. G. Aymerich and 6 co-authors take a more physical route in a 2025 research paper. They ask what two recent cluster cosmologies, from the SPT and eROSITA surveys, would predict for the older Planck cluster sample. Galaxy clusters trace the growth of cosmic structure, so their counts test the universe's matter content.

With mass calibration fixed, one cosmology predicts roughly the observed Planck count, while the other predicts more than double. Refitting forces very different values of the hydrostatic mass bias, a known systematic fudge factor. The predicted microwave background distortion signal also overshoots Planck's measurement under one cosmology. The authors argue that comparing predicted observables, not just parameter summaries, exposes tensions that headline numbers conceal.
arxiv-2509-08773:
Rowen I. Glusman and 32 co-authors search for giant planets around small M-dwarf stars in a 2025 paper. These planets, called GEMS, are rare on short orbits. The team uses TESS and Gaia light curves for stars within one hundred parsecs.

A custom package called TESS-miner plus vetting steps scans a huge sample. Tens of millions of fake planet tests measure how complete the search is. Occurrence rates are estimated by stellar subtype and rise with stellar mass in a pattern that fits core growth theory. Rates stay well under one percent in each group. The work sets a base for later occurrence studies.
arxiv-2509-08873:
Jonas M. Schmid and 3 co-authors find the sound traits of room surfaces from sparse measures in a 2025 paper. Sound work in enclosed spaces needs the impedance of walls, a value for how much sound a surface takes in or sends back. Old ways rest on simple views of the sound field.

A Bayesian frame, which weighs odds for each guess, infers impedance from a few pressure measures. Neural nets map fake data straight to odds for the true values, with no slow sampling. Tests on a box room, a tube, and a car cabin all give sound results. Checks show the stated doubt is well matched to real error.
arxiv-2509-08973:
Harshit Agrawal and 2 co-authors achieve ultrafast scatter estimation in cone-beam CT in a 2025 paper. Scatter blurs cone-beam scans and lowers image quality. Deep learning can estimate scatter, but large networks use too much memory for mobile or edge devices.

The team studies reconstruction error across six resolutions and four interpolation methods. A leading method is then trained at five resolutions and compared on operations, time, and memory. A much smaller input cuts operations about seventy-eight fold while error actually improves slightly. Inference runs far faster with far less memory. Tests on simulated and real phantom scans confirm robustness.
arxiv-2509-09073:
Gianlucca Zuin and 1 co-author propose the Rashomon Ensemble in a 2025 paper on model selection. The Rashomon effect means many different models perform almost equally well on the same problem. Picking just one can hurt performance on new data.

Models are grouped by both performance and explanations, then selected to maximize diversity while keeping accuracy. Each chosen model handles its own part of the solution space. That makes the ensemble more robust to shifts in data distribution. Tests on open and proprietary real world datasets show large gains where the Rashomon ratio is high. Business uses are also demonstrated.
arxiv-2509-09273:
Biswajit Maji and 2 co-authors uncover a crystal of vortex triplets in an active-spinner fluid in a 2025 paper. Active fluids of spinning rotors can self organize into exotic steady states. Their model couples a binary fluid description with a velocity field and a torque driven activity term.

An order parameter distinguishes clockwise from counter-clockwise spinner regions. As activity rises past dissipation, a triangular crystal emerges with spinning vortex triplets at its vertices. The authors characterize it as a nonequilibrium counterpart of an equilibrium plastic crystal. Statistical properties of the new state are described in detail. Possible experimental realizations of this active matter state are suggested.
arxiv-2509-09873:
James Jewitt and 4 co-authors audit software licenses across the open-source AI ecosystem in this 2025 paper. Models and datasets posted on Hugging Face often carry limits on use, and those limits can quietly vanish when the work is reused in applications on GitHub. The team traced hundreds of thousands of datasets, well over a million models, and a large set of downstream projects.

Their central finding is that more than a third of the moves from model to application dropped restrictive license terms and relicensed the work under looser terms. They also built a rule engine covering nearly two hundred license clauses. It flagged most conflicts in applications. They released their data and the prototype for others to use.
arxiv-2509-10073:
Irving Gómez-Méndez and 3 co-authors benchmark six survival models in a 2025 clinical paper. Survival analysis gauges how long it takes for an event to occur. Such events include discharge from care or relapse. The line-up spans three eras of method. It holds classic Weibull and Cox models. It holds a random survival forest. It holds a deep learning model called DeepSurv. It also holds Bayesian forms with frailty terms. Those terms soak up hidden gaps between patients.

The test used a public breast cancer data set. Scores tracked agreement and error. DeepSurv predicted best overall. Readable rivals stayed close behind it. The frailty models earned praise for honest doubt. Standard libraries barely support them, so they were hand-built. The authors frame the choice plainly. It is raw accuracy against bedside clarity.
arxiv-2509-10273:
Sahil Sethi and 2 co-authors build a learning system that predicts the properties of ionic liquids in this 2025 paper. Ionic liquids are salts that stay liquid and can be tuned for many jobs, from solvents to process fluids. Their design space is huge, while measured data are sparse, so picking the right liquid for a task is slow.

Their method pre-trains neural recommender models on simulated data at fixed conditions, then fine-tunes small networks on real measurements at varied temperatures and pressures. Five properties are covered, from density and viscosity to melting point. Knowledge moved both within and across properties, and the final models can screen hundreds of thousands of candidate liquids for process design.
arxiv-2509-10573: Christophe Parisel, writing alone, asks which way the Voynich script reads in this 2025 paper. The famous undeciphered manuscript was almost surely written left to right on the page. Whether the underlying script or cipher itself runs left-to-right or right-to-left is a separate question, and it has had little measured attention. Parisel introduces a statistical test based on how predictable character sequences are in each direction, using n-gram perplexity asymmetry to detect a directional bias in the text.
arxiv-2509-10673: Ivan Hetman, writing alone, presents ten Steiner systems in this short 2025 note. Six have the form S(2,8,225). Four have the form S(2,9,289). A Steiner system sorts points into blocks. Each pair of points falls in just one block. Finding such systems for a given size is a classic hard problem. These two cases were still open. They were two of 129 open cases for block sizes eight and nine. The cases are listed in the Handbook of Combinatorial Designs. This note closes both of them.
arxiv-2509-10773:
Alexander Plakhotnikov, writing alone, studies the spectrum of squared distance matrices in this 2025 mathematics paper. Take points in a space and tabulate the squared distances between every pair; the resulting matrix has a spectrum, a set of eigenvalues that encode the shape of the point set. Plakhotnikov asks what happens when the point set becomes infinite, drawn from points spread over a curved surface.

His approach trades the discrete problem for a continuous one based on walk matrices. From that switch he describes how the spectrum is structured and studies the behavior of spectral flows, the paths eigenvalues trace as the setup changes. The work extends a finite-size tool of geometry into the infinite setting.
arxiv-2509-10973:
Akshay Vegesna and Samip Dahal split neural network training into search and learning in this 2025 paper. Gradient descent settles into a single low point of the training loss and never explores other basins that might generalize better. Searching the full weight space for alternatives is hopeless, so the authors search somewhere smaller: the space of internal activations.

Evolutionary search there finds varied, high-fitness patterns of activity, and more search compute yields better and more diverse ones. Ordinary gradient training can then be aimed at those patterns by regression, reaching near-standard accuracy on standard image benchmarks. The resulting networks also travel different internal paths during training, which the authors offer as a route past gradient descent's narrow habits.
arxiv-2509-11373:
Hadi Zayyani and three co-authors speed up a famously secure link scheme in this 2025 paper. The scheme is KLJN communication. Two sides trade bits with strong security by comparing thermal noise on resistors. A resistor hopping variant raises the bit rate and keeps the security.

The team adds small bias voltages to the hopping scheme. The two sides can then be told apart by noise means, not just by spread. The biases stay tiny, so power use stays low. A maximum-likelihood detector is derived for the receiver. A simpler threshold detector comes with a proof of the best threshold. Tests show a higher data rate and fewer errors than classic KLJN. The cost is more complex gear.
arxiv-2509-12173:
Bayesian tempering warms a hard probability distribution into an easier one, and many algorithms walk a chain of in-between distributions to reach the target. Mengxin Xi and four co-authors show in 2025 that the walk may not need to finish: the in-between steps already know the answer.

Under stated conditions, expectations under the true posterior are fixed by their tempered versions over any stretch of the chain. The authors turn that fact into a post-processing tool for sequential Monte Carlo samplers, extrapolating and smoothing the tempered values to cut variance. The appeal is practical: cheaper partial runs can still yield sharp final estimates.
arxiv-2509-12273:
Travelers state trip wishes in plain words, with several goals at once and hard limits on time. Liangqi Yuan and three co-authors present LLMAP in 2025, a route planner that lets a language model read the request while a graph algorithm does the actual searching.

The model parses the prompt, extracts preferences, and spots dependencies between tasks. The solver then builds the route step by step, weighing place quality and task completion against distance, while respecting time budgets, opening hours, and task order. Trials on a thousand prompts spanning many countries and cities show stronger performance than direct model planning or plain graph search.
arxiv-2509-12373:
Yuxiao Hang and Stephan Haas map the phases of interacting chain models in a 2025 physics paper. Their models are Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains, one-dimensional chains with alternating links that can host protected states at their edges. They study versions with two-site and three-site repeating units.

Using density matrix renormalization group simulations, a powerful numerical method for such chains, they swept interaction strength and dimerization, the unevenness of the links. In the two-site model, a new antiferromagnetic phase appeared between the trivial and topological regimes, and edge modes stayed protected up to a finite interaction strength. The three-site model showed no intermediate phase and displayed asymmetric edge localization. Entanglement and magnetization measurements located the transition lines.
arxiv-2509-12473:
Survival analysis usually follows one outcome per patient, yet diseases strike paired organs and clustered sites together. Yael Travis-Lumer and four co-authors extend the famous Cox regression to the plane in 2025, modeling two survival times at once through Lehmann-type forms of the joint survival function.

A simple version keeps the classic structure, while a generalized version carries three regression parameters and contains the first as a special case. Effects read directly as statements about survival probabilities and their dependence, with no copula or frailty distribution assumed. Estimation uses pseudo-observations in two steps, with consistency and normality proved, and a retinoblastoma study illustrates the method.
arxiv-2509-12573:
Knowing when to hand a case to a human expert is a skill most AI systems must be taught with piles of expert-labeled data. Tim Bary and two co-authors skip the teaching in 2025 with a training-free deferral framework built on conformal prediction, which wraps any classifier's output in a set of plausible labels.

For each case, a segregativity score judges which expert best separates the plausible labels from the rest. Across three models and two labeled datasets, the method cuts the training labels needed per expert by up to about nine tenths while holding accuracy in low-data regimes. It also runs roughly a hundred times faster than trained alternatives.
arxiv-2509-12773:
Laura Koesten, Peter Ferenc Gyarmati and five co-authors describe PLUTO in 2025, a tool to judge the public worth of a data project. Groups from firms to charities often use data with mixed gains and harms, and they need a shared way to weigh both sides.

PLUTO grows from the idea of data solidarity, where use should serve the common good. It walks users through gains, risks, and hard choices, and asks them to reflect as they go. Early user trials suggest it can guide fair choices and shared duty, though turning word-based scores into fair number scores stays hard.
arxiv-2509-12973:
Aamer Aljagthami and 4 co-authors test large AI models at translating code from one programming language to another, in a 2025 paper. Turning old code into a new language helps teams move software, maintain it, and let systems work together. Yet solid comparisons are scarce. Little shared evidence shows how the choice of model, the way a prompt is written, and the language of the prompt itself each affect the quality of the result.

Their study was systematic. It covered translations among C++, Java, Python, and C#, and it set a traditional benchmark system alongside the AI models for comparison. The team tried two prompt styles, a brief instruction and a full specification. They also wrote the prompts in two languages, English and Arabic. Full prompts brought steady gains, for every model and in every direction. English prompts beat Arabic ones in their tests.
arxiv-2509-13373:
M. Pradosh Keshav and Arun Kenath build in 2025 an f(R) gravity model that unifies early inflation with late cosmic speedup in one frame. High curvature gives a Starobinsky-like flat top for inflation. Low curvature settles to a stable dark energy phase.

In scalar form the Jordan potential is hilltop-like, mapping to an exponential in the Einstein frame. A log loop correction flattens the late potential with no fine tuning. Field mass drops to the Hubble scale, which yields thawing acts off a constant by under one percent. Joint supernova and distance data fit local expansion values. General relativity returns at low curvature.
arxiv-2509-13473:
Jack Cook widens in 2025 a result on line bundles for real groups. A line bundle is a family of lines over a space. Broer showed that high cohomology, a tool that counts holes, is zero for some bundles on a fixed cone. Real groups need a new cone built from a Cartan part.

Cook builds a smooth cover of that cone. For weights in a set cone, all high cohomology of the bundles is zero. The proof joins a count of the base bundle with a known vanishing rule. The plain sheaf case then tells the shape of the cone norm. For one class of groups, the ring matches an induced module.
arxiv-2509-13973:
Davide Ferri proves a split lemma and a first isomorphism theorem for groupoids in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. Groupoids generalize groups by allowing multiplication only between matching arrows, and they are staples of topology and representation theory. In the category of all groupoids, the first isomorphism theorem, a basic bookkeeping result for groups, famously fails.

Ferri recovers a universally lifted version of the theorem by defining virtual kernels, substitutes that behave like kernels where none exist. He also defines crossed products for groupoids and proves they match split epimorphisms exactly, making them the correct categorical analogue of semidirect products. Over a fixed vertex set, where a first isomorphism theorem was already known, his split lemma collapses to the simpler known one.
arxiv-2509-14073:
Gefei Cai and three co-authors derive an exact formula in a 2025 probability paper. The puzzle is a Brownian motion on an annulus, the region between two circles. A wandering Brownian path may or may not separate the inner boundary from the outer one. The question is the probability that it never disconnects them.

The leading behavior of that probability is governed by a disconnection exponent. Lawler, Schramm, and Werner found it through Schramm-Loewner evolution, a theory of random curves. Cai's team build their exact formula on that connection, coupled with Liouville quantum gravity, a random geometry framework. Along the way, they pin down a precise relation between Brownian motion stopped at a disk's boundary and the loop measure of a specific random curve. They describe the quantum surfaces the stopped path cuts out.
arxiv-2509-14173:
Hao Li and four co-authors compare superconducting contact materials for germanium quantum devices in a 2025 materials paper. Superconductor-semiconductor hybrids built on strained germanium quantum wells could extend quantum circuit capabilities. They need transparent contacts of that kind. A platinum contact of that family was recently demonstrated. Its critical temperature sat below one kelvin, limiting its use.

The team fabricated germanide and germanosilicide films of platinum, palladium, rhodium, and iridium by solid-phase epitaxy. They characterized them side by side. Iridium films got an in-depth look with electron microscopy and X-ray checks. The films show a many-grained layer with a sharp interface to the base layer. Under optimal growth, the iridium compounds reached critical points of a few kelvin. That is a clear improvement for contact applications.
arxiv-2509-14373:
Huy Le and six co-authors introduce CodeLSI in 2025, a framework for generating code with foundation models inside a company. Firms want code tuned to their domain, at low cost, without sending data to outside services. Generic models and paid application interfaces miss those needs.

CodeLSI pairs low rank optimisation with instruction tuning on domain material. Low rank methods cut the cost of training and fine tuning sharply. Domain instructions then steer output toward company style and tasks. Models run on company infrastructure, so no third party interface is needed at use time. Tests assess code quality for the target domains. The design speaks to teams that need custom code help under tight security and budget rules.
arxiv-2509-15073:
Shaoang Li and Jian Li study learning with scarce feedback in changing environments in a 2025 machine learning theory paper. Multi-armed bandits model the choice among options with unknown rewards, and non-stationary versions let those rewards drift over time. Most algorithms assume the learner sees the reward after every round, which many real systems cannot afford.

Their new model restricts how often feedback may be requested, under a fixed query budget. They propose the first algorithm that needs no prior knowledge of how fast the environment changes. It still achieves near-optimal dynamic regret, the gap against an oracle that always picks the best arm. The regret bound depends on the number of arms, the total variation of the environment, the time horizon, and the budget. Limited feedback, handled well, need not cripple adaptation.
arxiv-2509-16173:
Training large neural models takes great time and cost, and the size of each training batch shapes both speed and quality. Yuen Chen, Yian Wang, and Hari Sundaram present DiveBatch, a method that adjusts batch size on the fly. It watches how varied the update signals are across the batch and grows or shrinks the batch to suit.

Small batches tend to teach well but run slowly, while large batches run fast but can teach worse. Tests on made-up data and three image sets show faster training than standard methods, with only a slight loss in final quality. The idea builds on a firm theory base.
arxiv-2509-16273:
Hunting for active drug-like compounds in huge libraries is hardest when only a few known actives exist to learn from. Jungseob Yi and three co-authors build SubDyve, a network method that links compounds by shared substructures tied to activity. Signals from the known actives spread across this network to rank new candidates.

When seeds are few, the method grows the seed set step by step, with a local error check to curb false hits. On ten standard targets and one huge library test, it beat fingerprint and embedding methods by wide margins. Careful growth keeps the search sharp despite sparse labels.
arxiv-2509-16373:
Tiny head-mounted microscopes let scientists watch brain cells fire while animals move freely, but their lenses are bulky or flawed. Zhihao Zhou and eight co-authors swap the lens stack for flat meta-optics, thin layers etched with tiny structures that bend light. Their miniscope gains a wide view, a deeper focus range, and depth sensing in one small package.

The objective shrank from near seven millimeters to two and a half, with better imaging at the same time. Such compact scopes could widen what behavior studies can record. The work grows the toolbox for portable brain imaging in living animals.
arxiv-2509-16573:
Teeradej Kittipassorn and Peerawit Suriya solve a coloring puzzle on an endless grid in a 2025 math paper. The grid is a diagonal one that runs on without bound. Colors must keep same-colored points far apart, with gaps set by a fixed list. The list here starts with a small gap and then repeats a larger one.

The pair prove that the least number of colors needed is forty. Their proof must handle a grid with no edge to lean on. Packing rules like these show up in channel assignment and code design. An exact answer for an endless case is a firm anchor for nearby finite puzzles.
arxiv-2509-16973:
Behdad Khodabandehloo and Reza Rajimehr compare deep designs for brain scan time series in a 2025 paper. Functional MRI records brain activity over time, at rest or during a movie. Which built-in bias a model carries shapes what it can learn from such data. Small datasets make that choice matter even more.

At the dataset size they study, local spatial patterns carry the key signal. Links between regions matter as well. Those traits favor convolutional designs over rivals. The findings guide model choice for labs that cannot gather huge scan sets. Picking the right bias early can save a study from chasing noise in scarce data.
arxiv-2509-17073:
Yansheng Ma, Peter Y. H. Pang, and Yifu Wang wrote a 2025 arXiv paper in applied mathematics about microbes that drift through a fluid. The model tracks three things at once: the microbes, the chemical signal they chase, and the flow of the liquid around them. How fast the microbes spread depends on the strength of the signal, and the spread shuts off when the signal is absent.

For smooth starting data, the authors prove that solutions exist for all time and stay smooth in two space dimensions. With no growth term, the proof needs the starting signal to be small in a set sense. With growth, the solutions stay bounded and can settle to a steady state. The results extend earlier work on the same system without a fluid to the case with flow.
arxiv-2509-17173:
Tahereh Sadat Parvini, writing alone, studies a magnetic material that could link light and spin in future quantum devices. Her 2025 arXiv paper looks at bilayer cuprate antiferromagnets, with the compound YBa2Cu3O6+x as the main case. Such hybrid setups join microwave photons to group spin waves, but common magnets force a trade-off among strength, coherence, and control.

Using a spin model checked against neutron data, Parvini works out the full set of spin-wave modes at the zone center. One mode stays gapless and shifts in a straight line with a magnetic field, while a second mode can be tuned across a wide frequency range. Linked to a microwave cavity, the two modes give two distinct channels for control. The setup can move from weak to strong coupling with one knob, and the predicted light patterns give clear targets for lab tests.
arxiv-2509-17573:
Mina Doostalizadeh, Ahmad Moussavi, and Peter Danchev define a new class of rings in a 2025 arXiv paper. The class, called unit uniquely clean rings, joins two older notions: uniquely clean rings and strongly nil clean rings. A common generalization can clarify how those families relate and where each one ends.

The authors show that abelian rings of the new class are uniquely clean, and that members with a nil Jacobson radical are strongly nil clean. The class also covers two families defined by Calugareanu and Zhou in 2023. A neat test emerges: a ring is of the new class exactly when it is an exchange ring and Boolean modulo its Jacobson radical. The paper tracks how the property behaves under group ring and matrix ring constructions. Examples mark the borders of each claim.
arxiv-2509-17873:
Saudamini Nayak, Nabin Kumar Meher, and Sudhansu Sekhar Rout count symmetry types for a small Lie algebra. Their 2025 paper works on so(5), whose basic blocks come in sizes set by two whole numbers. They ask how many such blocks have each size, summed up to a bound.

Their count rests on the divisor function, a classic count of ways to split a number. A known sum rule for that function sets the main term and its error. The team derives a like sum rule for the so(5) block count. Such rules help number work that uses sums over block sizes.
arxiv-2509-18073:
Bart van Rossum and Twan Dollevoet set a maths task for allocations that must be Pareto-optimal. Their 2025 paper deals with shares such as houses, school places, and kidney swaps. A Pareto-optimal share leaves no swap that helps one person and hurts none.

Their task, Max-Pareto, seeks the best such share by total welfare. A fresh result, that split shares keep the same trait, lets them prove the task is hard in the NP sense. A two-level program form is given for the task. Tests check how that form runs on welfare-max cases.
arxiv-2509-18173:
Hongyi Luo and 9 co-authors bench language models on reversing a route from words. Their 2025 set, TurnBack, asks a model to give the way back along a path told in text. Humans swap such route facts with ease, while model skill there was little tested.

Routes come from a dozen world cities, in the tens of thousands. A tool, PathBuilder, turns route text into map paths and back. Eleven top models were tested on the reverse task. Most of their return routes did not reach the start or match the best way back. Models were also shaky on fresh routes, yet sure of wrong answers.
arxiv-2509-18273:
Steffen Gielen and Sofie Ried study a quantum-fixed black hole that cycles through white hole phases. Their 2025 paper checks a smooth, non-singular solution built in a small model of unimodular gravity. One new term sets a least radius, where a black hole flips to a white hole.

Far from that radius, the space sits very close to the classic Schwarzschild form. The full extension stacks endless Kruskal spaces in a chain, linked by those flips. Heat and light traits of the outer space match the classic case in the team's checks. The price is a break of a classic energy rule.
arxiv-2509-18673:
Fair division asks how to split items so no one envies another's share, while waste stays low. Siddharth Barman and Paritosh Verma study that pairing for mixed manna in this 2025 paper. Mixed manna means a pool holding both goods people want and chores people shun. For goods alone and chores alone, fairness up to one item can pair with efficiency. For the mixed case, a recent result says they clash.

The pair restore the pairing by softening the fairness rule in two principled ways. One rule lets an agent erase envy by adding an item to its own bundle, or by dropping one from it. The other lets envy be checked by adjusting the other's bundle instead. They prove efficient allocations exist under both rules with additive values. The proofs lean on a classic fixed-point theorem. The results also yield a fresh proof for the divisible case.
arxiv-2509-18773:
A graph's Laplacian matrix encodes how its nodes connect, and adding the identity matrix makes it invertible. Enide Andrade and Geir Dahl study that inverse in this 2025 paper. The inverse turns out to be doubly stochastic: each row and column sums to one. The question is how its entries reflect the graph beneath.

The pair prove a general monotonicity property for the entries. For path graphs, the property sharpens, and the entries can be written with Fibonacci numbers through a matrix factorization. For trees, they bound the diagonal entries using distances between vertices. They also give a simple, efficient algorithm for the tree case. In any graph, each diagonal entry is strictly the largest in its row and column. A link to heat-type equations closes the paper. The results tie graph shape to a concrete matrix.
arxiv-2509-18873:
Jacobi matrices, endless grids of numbers with three busy diagonals, model many vibrating and quantum systems. A. S. Mikhaylov and V. S. Mikhaylov derive a new formula for their Weyl function in this 2025 paper. The Weyl function is a key analytic object tied to such a matrix. It encodes spectral data in one complex-valued package.

Their approach leans on a discrete-time dynamical system linked to the matrices. That link yields the new representation in both the finite and the semi-infinite cases. New formulas for classic objects often unlock cleaner proofs elsewhere, from inverse problems to scattering theory. The paper is brief and addressed to specialists in spectral theory. It adds a tool rather than a sweeping claim. The dynamical view of Jacobi matrices is the paper's stated engine.
arxiv-2509-19373:
Elijah Gadsby, writing alone, surveys a notion from provability logic called selector proofs. A serial property is a numbered list of formulas. It is selector provable when a single computable function can hand back, for each formula, a proof of it that the system itself verifies.
