From the estimated channels, they derive rate bounds. These are lower bounds on achievable data rates. Two standard combining schemes are covered. The atomic receiver beat conventional radio equipment. This held under both fading models tested. The atomic system has its own noise quirks. Even so, the result supports quantum receivers for future satellite networks.
arxiv-2510-15873:
Hengyuan Chang, Xiaoxuan Xie, Syuhei Sato, and Haoran Xie present a poster paper in 2025. It turns an artist's sketch into animated smoke. The method has two stages. Smoke adds expressive motion to illustrations. Making it normally means running physics fluid simulations. Illustrators cannot easily art-direct those simulations.

Their pipeline first converts the sketch into a stream function. That is a mathematical description of flowing motion. Diffusion-based generators then produce a velocity field. The field guides a smoke simulation as a driving force. The smoke follows the sketched shape. It still moves like real smoke. Artists gain control with far less technical overhead.
arxiv-2510-16073:
A. Golebiewska, S. Rybicki, and P. Stefaniak study when symmetric Newtonian systems hold whole connected sets of periodic solutions. The systems are autonomous and symmetric under circle actions. The solutions sought are non-stationary and repeat after one full period. An energy-like parameter ranges over positive values for each family.

The three authors state necessary conditions for such closed connected sets to exist. They also state sufficient conditions for the same sets. Closed means the family has no loose ends in the space of periodic paths. Their main tool is the degree for equivariant gradient maps. That tool counts solutions while respecting the symmetry of the system. The result gives a two-way checklist for researchers. It says when symmetric mechanical systems must carry continua of periodic motions, not just isolated ones.
arxiv-2510-16173:
Aria Pessianzadeh and five co-authors measure how much the public trusts generative AI, using years of Reddit talk. Trust shapes whether people adopt these tools and how they should be governed, yet it is rarely tracked at scale over time. Their data covers thirty-nine Reddit forums and more than two hundred thirty thousand posts from 2022 to 2025.

Human labels on a sample trained sorting models that scored the full set. Trust and distrust came out nearly even, with trust a bit ahead, and both swung when big new models launched. Talk focused most on how well the tools work and how easy they feel to use. Personal stories were the most common reason people gave for their stance. The study offers a reusable way to watch public trust shift as AI spreads.
arxiv-2510-16273:
Jingyue Huang and six co-authors present MuseTok, a way to chop written music into tokens that AI models can learn from. Tokenizing worked well for images, speech, and text, but music has its own symbols and structure. MuseTok cuts scores bar by bar and squeezes each bar into a short code with a trained autoencoder.

The codes rebuild the music faithfully and also carry music theory sense. Models using them beat older methods at reading tasks like pulling out the melody, naming chords, and spotting the mood. At writing new music, they match the best older methods. Probes of the codes show they capture real musical ideas from big collections. A shared token scheme like this could let one model both write and understand music.
arxiv-2510-16373:
Federico Ravenda and three co-authors steer a language model toward mental health work by nudging its inner states. Small models often stumble on specialist tasks, and full retraining is costly. Their method applies a simple linear shift to the activity of one layer. Steering vectors guide the shift toward the desired behavior.

Two tasks test the trick on Reddit posts. One asks whether a post helps detect signs of depression. The other completes a standard depression screening questionnaire from a user's post history. With only the cheap nudge, the model improves on both tasks, with no heavy training runs. The results suggest steering hidden states is an untapped, low-cost way to adapt models for sensitive fields like mental health.
arxiv-2510-16473:
Dario A. Bini, Massimiliano Fasi, and Bruno Iannazzo study a matrix task in their 2025 paper. A matrix is a grid of numbers that can stretch or turn vectors. Their task takes a function of a paired matrix set, called a pencil. One grid is firm and sure, and one is mirror-even in form. Such tasks show up in control, waves, and sound work.

They first gauge how touchy the task is to small input shifts. Then they give methods that split the pencil with a clean split step. Some use a matrix square root, and some use a Cholesky split. Tests show the Cholesky forms win on speed and on exactness. Their cost counts help users pick the right method per task.
arxiv-2510-16673:
Yuki Ohnishi and three co-authors estimate causal mechanisms inside cluster-randomized trials, where whole groups, not single people, get a treatment. Mediation analysis asks how much of an effect flows through an in-between variable. Trials of this kind add interference between units, confounders that appear after treatment, and layered covariates.

Their Bayesian nonparametric framework handles all three problems at once. A Gaussian copula with one dependence parameter replaces a strict cross-world independence assumption, which builds in a sensitivity check. A nested prior shares information across clusters while adjusting for covariates without disturbing the outcome model. The authors derive the prior's partition structure and convergence guarantees to support the method.
arxiv-2510-17373:
Parkinson disease often flattens the face, a symptom called the masked face, and Yintao Zhou with four co-authors uses that clue to grade how severe the disease is. Judging severity matters for catching patients early and tailoring care. Older methods leaned on a single facial expression, which can mislead, and they struggled when some disease stages had far fewer examples than others.

Zhou and his co-authors merge several kinds of expression features through an attention based fusion step, which learns which features deserve more weight. A balancing method then adjusts how much each training example counts, based on how common its class is and how hard it proves to classify. Their tests show promising grading accuracy.
arxiv-2510-17473:
Dark matter remains unseen directly, yet the hunt for it is changing fast on every front, Milena Crnogorčević reports in a conference summary. Direct searches, which wait for a dark matter particle to strike a detector, have entered an era where ordinary solar neutrinos now form a limiting background. Indirect searches, which look for products of dark matter meeting itself, have become genuinely combined efforts across gamma rays, neutrinos, cosmic rays, and radio data.

Crnogorčević also notes that candidates beyond the classic heavy particle idea are moving to centre stage, including axions, very light particles, primordial black holes, and larger relic objects. Progress, the report argues, now depends as much on shared data and common analysis methods as on new hardware. The summary distils how assumptions have shifted since the previous conference and where decisive steps may come next.
arxiv-2510-17773:
Enamul Atiq and Shaikh Anowarul Fattah build a skin cancer classifier that explains itself. Early detection greatly improves patient outcomes in skin cancer. Sorting lesions from microscope-style skin images is hard and error prone. Many deep learning tools act as black boxes, which limits clinical trust.

Their system first outlines each lesion with a custom segmentation network. Two encoders then read the full image and the outlined lesion separately. An attention step fuses both views, focusing on the diseased region. Patient details like age, sex, and lesion site join the prediction. Heat maps confirm the model looks at lesions, not background.
arxiv-2510-17873:
Tadesse K Bahiru and three co-authors audit the data behind gender classification systems and find a shared flaw. All five widely used data sets they checked leave out many mixed groups of age, race, and gender. Models trained on the two most balanced sets still erred more on female faces and skewed by race.

To fix the data, the team built BalancedFace from real, unedited photos drawn from several sources. It evens out shares across many age, race, and gender groups. A plain classifier trained on it cut the largest racial gap in correct rates by over half in their tests.
arxiv-2510-17973:
Michael Unger, writing alone, reports measurements that help track how cosmic rays spread through our galaxy. When cosmic rays smash into gas, they break into lighter pieces, and the rates of that breakup shape what detectors see. The NA61/SHINE setup at CERN is well placed to measure those rates at high energy.

New results cover carbon breaking into two boron forms and one carbon form. They come from a pilot run and feed into reading the boron-to-carbon ratio in space data. A much larger 2024 campaign, spanning many light nuclei, promises the full reaction network that transport models need.
arxiv-2510-18173:
Ritam Upadhyay and four co-authors test how well language models turn long sports tables into faithful written summaries. Common recipes lean on heavy prompt tricks, pipeline splits, or entity scaffolding, all costly and opaque. Their SporTabSet benchmark spans two sports and demands tracking many players while adding numbers under each sport's own rules.

Splitting the task into parts raised accuracy and number fidelity a lot. The gains came mostly from untangling multi-entity interference, not from better arithmetic. Shuffled and stressed inputs also exposed fragility. Data-to-text researchers get a clear diagnosis of where long-context summarizers wobble.
arxiv-2510-18273:
Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian and Sergio Pequito design resilient resource sharing algorithms in a 2025 paper. Distributed resource allocation means many linked devices divide a shared supply without one central boss. Real networks drop links, delay messages, and distort signals, which breaks many older methods.

Their algorithm keeps total supply and demand balanced at every moment, even if work stops early. It still converges when links carry nonlinear distortions like quantization, meaning rounding of values, and saturation. It also needs only uniform connectivity, meaning the network must reconnect over time, not stay linked always. Simulations show optimal results despite delays and heavy link failures.
arxiv-2510-18473:
Yuya Sasaki, writing alone, benchmarks methods meant to keep graph neural networks fair when they learn from knowledge graphs. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities and power tools such as recommender systems, yet no earlier study had tested fairness-aware versions of these networks on them. Sasaki built new test graphs from three large public sources, YAGO, DBpedia, and Wikidata, each far bigger than the graphs used in past fairness work.

The study compared fixes applied before training and during training, across several network designs and stopping rules. Knowledge graphs behaved differently from older test data: the trade-off between accuracy and fairness showed up more clearly. Results depended not only on the fairness method but also on the network design and on when training stopped. Early data fixes often improved fairness, while in-training fixes tended to protect accuracy.
arxiv-2510-18673:
Sungtae Cho and Su Houng Lee compute charm-strange meson production. The setting is nuclei colliding at nearly light speed at the Large Hadron Collider. Matter melts into a quark-gluon plasma there. As it cools, quarks recombine into particles. Each meson in their study pairs a heavy charm quark with a strange quark. Several excited versions are included.

First they pinned down the momentum spread of charm and strange quarks. Measured phi and D-zero mesons served as guides. Their recombination math then matched both the momentum pattern and the yield of the basic meson well. They studied a ratio comparing charm-strange output with D-zero output. It shows how light and strange quarks shape charmed output. They also computed an exotic candidate two ways, as a four-quark state and as a two-quark state.
arxiv-2510-18773:
Jannis Fleckenstein and his five co-authors apply a geospatial foundation model to the urban heat island problem, where cities run hotter than their surroundings. Planning shade and green space requires detailed temperature maps, but conventional models trained on scarce local data often predict poorly, especially in underserved neighborhoods. Foundation models, pretrained on global data, promise strong general performance with only a little local fine-tuning.

The team first built an empirical picture of real heat patterns by measuring how much green spaces cool their surroundings, and checked the model's predictions against it. They then fine-tuned the model to predict land surface temperatures under future climate scenarios. A simulated inpainting exercise, where a changed landscape is painted into the data, showed how planners could test mitigation ideas before spending on them. The authors argue such models are a powerful tool for data-scarce regions aiming at climate-resilient cities.
arxiv-2510-18873:
Ziang Zhang and his seven co-authors benchmark how well vision models understand scenes where both the camera and the objects are moving. Static and two-dimensional skills do not guarantee a model can track dynamic three-dimensional relationships. Their benchmark, DSI-Bench, contains nearly one thousand dynamic videos and more than one thousand seven hundred hand-annotated questions, organized around nine separated motion patterns for observers and objects.

Symmetric designs in space and time reduce biases and let evaluators isolate reasoning about self-motion from reasoning about object motion. Testing fourteen vision-language and specialist models exposed recurring failures: models confuse the observer's motion with the object's, fall back on semantic expectations, and misjudge relative relationships in moving scenes. The authors offer the benchmark as a diagnostic for building models with genuine dynamic spatial intelligence.
arxiv-2510-19073:
Sebastian Nagies and eight co-authors test whether dynamical decoupling can protect quantum annealing from local field noise. Annealing offers a route to hard optimization problems on quantum hardware, yet noise in real devices steadily degrades the quality of the answers it returns.

Periodic pulses that flip all spins together suppress that noise in their scheme. Test problems include small object-tracking and cutting-stock cases built for industry-style use, plus a classic spin glass model where the method stays robust across size and structure. The results point toward annealing protocols that survive contact with real machines.
arxiv-2510-19273:
Zhang Nengbo and Ho Hann Woei present MobiAct, a lightweight system for recognizing the actions of micro air vehicles from video. Drone swarms need fast motion recognition on tiny platforms, but accurate models are usually too heavy, forcing a trade between recognition quality and speed.

MobiAct uses a compact MobileNetV4 network as its backbone and adds a stage-wise distillation strategy that transfers motion features from a larger teacher network into the small student. Contrastive learning further sharpens the features. The result aims for high accuracy at low cost, so small drones can perceive and coordinate in real time.
arxiv-2510-19373:
Basavasagar Patil and four co-authors propose temperature sampling to fix a hidden imbalance in robot training data. Robot datasets keep growing, yet many differently named tasks share nearly the same physical motions, so common actions dominate while rare actions are scarce, and policies trained on such data generalize poorly.

Sampling with a temperature rule rebalances which examples the policy sees during training. The change takes only a few lines of code in existing systems. The authors test it both when pretraining small models and when fine-tuning large foundation models, finding better generalization in each case from the same collected data.
arxiv-2510-19673:
Julen Expósito-Márquez and four co-authors test whether a neural network recovers galaxy mass profiles better when it can see both gas and star motions. Astronomers weigh galaxies by watching how their material orbits, but combining two kinds of kinematic maps is hard for traditional methods. The team trained a probabilistic convolutional network on mock maps from several cosmological simulation suites.

Models were trained on gas-only, stars-only, and combined maps so the comparison is direct. The combined input cut the scatter in recovered mass profiles by up to a factor of about one and a half. The network clearly extracts complementary information from the two tracers, though performance dropped when a model trained on one simulation suite was applied to another.
arxiv-2510-19873:
Junfeng Gong and four co-authors help small language models write optimized GPU code like large ones, without sending code to the cloud. Big models generate good CUDA, but cloud APIs risk leaking code and local deployment is costly; small models run privately yet reason too weakly for complex optimization. Their framework, ReGraphT, needs no additional training.

ReGraphT stores recorded optimization sessions as a reasoning graph, where combined optimizations become transitions between states, and searches that graph with Monte Carlo methods to guide the small model. A tiered CUDA benchmark supports the evaluation. On two benchmark suites the method averaged a speedup of about two and a third times, beating fine-tuned specialist models and other retrieval approaches and bringing small models close to large-model quality.
arxiv-2510-19973:
Hatim Chergui and three co-authors write a tutorial on cognitive biases in the AI agents proposed to run future 6G networks. Language-model agents that negotiate across network domains inherit human-like biases from their design and training. Those biases can distort decisions. The tutorial catalogs well-known biases with their mathematical forms, how they emerge in telecom systems, and tailored countermeasures.

Two case studies validate the ideas. In inter-slice resource negotiation, a randomized starting anchor replaced a fixed one. Agents then used contract slack intelligently, and energy savings doubled, peaking at twenty-five percent. A small local model kept decisions fast enough for near-real-time use. In cross-domain negotiation, a debiased collective memory cut latency fivefold. It also raised energy savings by roughly forty percent over memoryless agents.
arxiv-2510-20073:
Swaroop Hegde proves an inverse and stability result for Ruzsa inequality on triple sumsets in additive combinatorics. The inequality bounds the size of a triple sumset by a power of the size of the double sumset for any finite set in a commutative group. Ruzsa own examples show the bound is nearly sharp, which raises the question of what near-extremal sets look like.

Hegde shows that if a set comes close to the bound, within a factor set by a parameter, then it must resemble the sets in Ruzsa construction. New families of examples suggest that description is likely best possible in qualitative terms. The method extends to higher sumsets, with an almost exact stability version included.
arxiv-2510-20373:
Gabriele Riccio and eleven co-authors present FAST-SBF, an automatic Python pipeline for measuring galaxy distances with the Surface Brightness Fluctuation method. That method is among the most reliable and efficient distance tools for galaxies within one hundred megaparsecs, and it still works on ground-based data when seeing is sharp and fields are wide. Upcoming surveys will offer thousands of suitable galaxies.

The pipeline is built for automation with minimal user intervention and aims at large datasets from surveys such as LSST, Euclid, and Roman. The authors validate it on high-quality Hyper Suprime-Cam imaging of luminous early-type galaxies and fainter dwarfs. Their measurements agree excellently with recent Virgo cluster results and with stellar population synthesis models, supporting its readiness for survey-scale use.
arxiv-2510-20573:
Amartya Chakrabortty, Georges Griso, and Julia Orlik run three limit steps at once on a mixed plate in bend: grain growth, flat cut, and line fit. The plate sits in non-linear bend with load on it, and its full bend power scales by a set law of two small marks. Part one runs all three steps at once with no link set on the pair of small marks.

Part two draws line bend as a sound limit of the non-linear case for small warps and loads. The end power stays the same if the line step runs first or all steps run at once. A Gamma-form proof gives one sole solve for the end task. Marks stretch to pierced plate forms as well.
arxiv-2510-20673:
Jinhee Kim, Jae Jun An, Kang Eun Jeon, and Jong Hwan Ko tackle the training cost of networks that must run at several numeric precision levels in one shared model. Past training repeats full data passes for each level, so cost grows in step with the number of levels offered.

Two fixes drive the work, a bias fix that aligns layer outputs across levels so shared scaling layers work without extra fine tuning. A smart sampling plan that trains each level on a small but rich subset of data. Tests on image tasks with two major network types match or beat prior accuracy while cutting training time by up to near eight fold. Code is shared for others to use and check.
arxiv-2510-20773:
Elaine Cozzi, Nicholas Harrison, and Zachary Radke extend a landmark negative result on the two dimensional Euler equations, which govern ideal fluid flow. Bourgain and Li showed the equations are strongly ill posed at a borderline smoothness level, meaning tiny changes in starting flow can defeat any stable solution theory there.

The trio pushes the result into slightly smaller, log refined spaces that still contain all smoother spaces above the borderline. These spaces add a fractional log derivative to the critical norm, tightening the allowed roughness. For log powers up to one half, strong ill posedness still holds. The finding narrows the hope that a mild log fix could restore good behavior at the critical level.
arxiv-2510-20873:
Shanhe Su leads five co-authors on how quantum togetherness changes heat based doubt bounds, which trade current precision against entropy output in driven systems. Whether genuine quantum effects can loosen or reshape those classical bounds has stayed unsettled.

Their framework folds togetherness into the bounds for open quantum systems with memoryless dynamics, joining a quantum estimation limit with an expansion of the deformed dynamics. The resulting bound carries a togetherness sensitive correction drawn from the off diagonal parts of the state, cleanly split from classical terms. The split shows where quantumness helps precision at a given dissipation cost, a guide for tiny engines and sensors.
arxiv-2510-21073:
Mark J Ablowitz leads two co-authors on spiral wave solutions of linear and weakly nonlinear irrotational water wave equations. The spirals grow from suitable starting conditions without outside forcing, unlike driven wave patterns.

Stationary phase analysis gives a long time asymptotic form that matches the exact solution well and reveals a hyperbolic spiral structure. Simulations show the spirals survive when weak nonlinearity is added. Spiral waves are famous in reaction diffusion media, so finding them in water waves widens the family of systems where such coherent rotating patterns arise naturally.
arxiv-2510-21273:
Naomi Desobry, Elnura Zhalieva, and Souhaib Ben Taieb address calibration in forecasts that predict several outcomes at once. A calibrated model is right about its own uncertainty, but checking and fixing that property for many outputs at once is much harder than for a single output.

Older tools only diagnose problems, using summary scores called pre-ranks that compress each forecast and outcome pair into a single number. The authors turn diagnosis into training: a penalty term pushes those summaries toward the pattern expected from a calibrated model. Their penalty covers both single outputs and joint behavior, and a new summary based on principal components tracks directions of greatest spread. Across eighteen real data sets, the penalty improves calibration without hurting accuracy.
arxiv-2510-21573:
Matthew Crawford, Pavan Kartik, and Reese Lance compute integrals of stable envelopes, geometric classes that organize how a torus symmetry acts on the cotangent bundle of a Grassmannian. These classes, introduced by Maulik and Okounkov, sit at a crossroads of geometry and mathematical physics, including three-dimensional mirror symmetry.

The integral they define uses equivariant localization, a method that rebuilds global quantities from data at fixed points of the symmetry. Each integral turns out to be an integer times a power of a formal parameter, and the main result is a combinatorial formula for those integers. In the smallest case the integers are plain binomial coefficients, while for larger Grassmannians they appear to be new. The authors conjecture links to curve counting on the mirror-dual space and to richer quiver and bow varieties.
arxiv-2510-21773:
Van Nam Dinh reviews the solvers that legged robots rely on in real time. These solvers plan motion and keep the robot balanced. Many core tasks are framed as quadratic programming problems. The robot must find the best answer under firm limits, many times each second. It does so on small onboard computers with tight energy budgets.

Solvers are grouped into four families, including interior-point and active-set methods. Dinh compares them on speed, accuracy, and energy use. He also weighs how well each handles warm starts and problem structure. Summary tables turn the comparison into practical advice. They match solver types to jobs like long-horizon planning or fast balance control. The review closes with trends toward harder problem forms and ready-made solver code.
arxiv-2510-21973:
Arnaud Salvador and Tyler D. Robinson ask what a future space telescope could learn about an Earth twin. Such a planet shows up only as a faint dot of reflected light. Direct images will have narrow color coverage and noisy spectra. Planners need to know which measurements are worth the exposure time.

The pair uses a retrieval tool that works backward from a spectrum to the planet behind it. They test bandpass choices and signal quality levels. The tests cover seventeen properties of a habitable Earth analog. The properties span air, surface, bulk makeup, and orbit. For each one, they lay out what detection takes. The results assume a Habitable Worlds Observatory style mission. Instrument designers and observing strategists gain a concrete shopping list.
arxiv-2510-22173:
Wei Ni, Yangfan Qiu, and Yanyan Xiao design a flow for hard optimization problems. The problems mix a nonsmooth term with equality and inequality constraints. The standard trick projects gradients back onto the allowed set. That trick is awkward to analyze and clumsy to simulate. The authors drop projection entirely.

Mirror descent shapes the primal-dual dynamics instead. The variables and their constraint prices move as a pair. An extended proximal augmented Lagrangian handles general convex constraints. The joint dynamics turn strongly convex in one block and strongly concave in the other. That pairing is the recipe for exponential convergence. The error shrinks by a constant factor per unit time. Earlier guarantees were weaker. They ignored constraints, allowed only flat ones, or promised only eventual arrival.
arxiv-2510-22473:
Jing Yang and co-author Yufeng Yang propose DynaPose4D for turning one still image into moving four dimensional content. Making high quality dynamic scenes from a single picture is hard because motion over time and changing camera views must stay consistent. Their method builds a three dimensional model with Gaussian splatting and then predicts pose key points across views.

A pose alignment loss ties the predicted motion together, using guidance from one chosen view as support. Experiments show strong coherence, consistency, and smooth motion in the generated scenes. The authors point to uses in computer vision research and in animation production.
arxiv-2510-22573:
Pulsars orbiting the giant black hole at our galaxy's center could act as precise clocks for testing dark matter. Jiang-Chuan Yu, Yan Cao, Zexin Hu, and Lijing Shao present in 2025 the first study of how ultralight dark matter structures would tug those pulsar orbits.

Such dark matter might form dense boson clouds or self gravitating soliton cores near the black hole, called Sgr A*. The team builds a practical framework covering black hole and orbital settings. Long term timing, a goal of the future SKA telescope, could detect a cloud near one solar mass and probe many lighter soliton cores.
arxiv-2510-22873:
Success runs in coin like trials can be split by gaps. S J Dilworth and S R Mane study that pattern in 2025. Trials are Bernoulli, meaning each has two outcomes. Runs follow a Type II binomial law of order k. A gap is a failure plus some arbitrary outcomes.

Most prior work used a gap of one only. Their main results give the probability mass function. Two derivations are presented. They also give the law of the longest success run. Cleaner formulas cover factorial moments. Results extend to a negative binomial version. There, the number of runs is fixed and trials vary.
arxiv-2510-22973:
Bohan Li leads a team of twelve researchers working to generate realistic driving scenes for self-driving cars. Occupancy-based methods, which map space as filled or empty, give steady control across frames. Their weakness is a lack of labeled occupancy data, which is costly to make by hand.

The group built Nuplan-Occ, described as the largest semantic occupancy data set so far, from the NuPlan benchmark. They also present a unified method that creates high-quality scenes across sensors. The larger data set should help teams test perception and planning with more varied and consistent scenes.
arxiv-2510-23073:
Zishang Li, Changqing Ye, and Eric T Chung propose an iterative multiscale method for contact problems where material properties vary sharply. Contact of Signorini type models bodies that can touch but not overlap, common in engineering. High contrast between stiff and soft regions breaks standard solvers.

Their framework merges an energy-minimizing multiscale finite element method with a primal-dual active set strategy from semismooth Newton methods. Local spectral problems build basis functions on oversampled patches, updated only at the contact edge as the active set evolves. Analysis backs the method, which promises robust reduced models for hard contact simulations.
arxiv-2510-23573:
Kyle Celano and three co-authors prove a pattern result for words, meaning finite strings of natural numbers where values may repeat. A repeat is any occurrence of a value after its first appearance. They ask how many repeats a word can carry before one of several fixed patterns must show up inside it. A pattern shows up when some scattered subword matches the pattern's ordering of values.

They show that any word past a certain count of repeats must contain one of seven listed patterns. Those patterns range from long flat runs to rising and falling staircase shapes, and the count depends on the pattern size. For the smallest case of their parameter, the bound is exactly right. They prove that by building a word that reaches the lower count of repeats while dodging every one of the patterns.
arxiv-2510-24073:
Xinwei Wu and seven co-authors build a new test for made up content in machine translation by large language models. Models can add facts not in the source, drop the task, or drift from the text, yet old tests do not catch these faults well in many languages. The team sorts faults into two types: drifting from the instruction and drifting from the source.

Using that sorting, they built HalloMTBench, a checked set of 5,435 cases across eleven translation directions from English. Four top models made the draft cases, judges and experts screened them, and seventeen models were then tested. Results show distinct triggers tied to model size, source length, language bias, and training style.
arxiv-2510-24173:
Yiheng Du and Aditi S. Krishnapriyan introduce EddyFormer, a transformer model that speeds up simulations of three dimensional turbulence. Fully resolving turbulence is a central problem in fluid dynamics because motion spans many scales at once. Direct simulation at large scale costs far too much, which drives interest in learned alternatives.

EddyFormer blends spectral element methods with attention, splitting the flow into grid scale and subgrid scale parts as tokens. This lets it capture both local eddies and global patterns. The team built a new dataset of isotropic turbulence and trained the model to reach direct simulation level accuracy at a large grid size, with much lower cost at scale.
arxiv-2510-24673:
Alp M Sunol, James V Roggeveen, Mohammed G Alhashim, Henry S Bae, and Michael P Brenner learn how thick fluids act, straight from partial flow reads. Laws that link stress to shape change guide work on plant and body fluids. Old ways need neat, ideal flows that miss traits seen in real shapes.

Their frame runs a full physics code that can learn from any flow read. A net inside the code learns the local law with no set form picked in advance. Since the law is local, it can move to new shapes with no new training. They then turn the net law into a short sign form.
arxiv-2510-24773:
Ziyang Xu, Olaf Wysocki, and Christoph Holst gauge how unsure each point is in a laser scan made from a moving rig. Such scans feed maps, models, and change checks, so trust in each point matters. Old ways to gauge doubt need costly high grade ground truth at large scales.

Their frame learns from local shape traits of the cloud how large point errors tend to be. Two group learn tools were trained on split parts of a real scan set, so no leak crossed the split. Both tools caught the shape to error links well. Height shift traits stood out as key clues. The frame needs no ground truth at the site of use.
arxiv-2510-25273:
Sandipan Majhi and Paheli Bhattacharya study Hindi tourism question answering. Their 2025 paper uses small language models. Hindi counts as a low-resource language here. That means labeled training data is scarce. General models also know little about tourism. Both gaps make accurate answers hard to get.

The pair describe a multi-stage fine-tuning plan. It mixes real data with synthetic data. Large models made the synthetic question and answer pairs. Those large models were LLaMA-70B and Phi-14B. The pairs were added to the small original set. The authors test several training methods. They also check how well each method generalizes. Their results suggest large models can supply useful data. Small models can then learn that data well. This offers a practical path for other narrow fields.
arxiv-2510-25373:
Janik Pinter leads four co-authors on battery scheduling. Maximilian Beichter, Ralf Mikut, and Frederik Zahn helped. Veit Hagenmeyer closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper studies residential prosumer battery systems. Prosumers both produce and consume electricity at home. Photovoltaic panels charge batteries for later use. Owners schedule grid exchange to minimize costs.

They compare model predictive control with rule-based control. Research often averages results over fifteen to sixty minutes. Net billing and battery degradation were included here. They simulated five months for fifteen buildings. Buildings were located in northern Germany. Costs were computed at one-minute resolution ground truth. Time-averaged tests made predictive control look always better. Finer testing shrank its reported advantage sharply. The shrinkage averaged about sixty-nine percent for hourly schedulers. For some buildings, conclusions even reversed completely.
arxiv-2510-25673:
Kyle G Miller led five co-authors controlling laser intensity. Tomas E Gutierrez, Archis S Joglekar, and Amanda Elliott helped. Dustin H Froula and John P Palastro complete six. Their 2025 paper uses differentiable programming for pulses. Optical techniques produce pulses with custom form. Structured pulses usually follow forward design methods.

Inverse methods enable discovery of new pulse forms. Superior results may result from such discovery. Gradient-based tuning designs structured pulses from goals. Uniform longitudinal intensity over extended regions is first. A superluminal intensity peak traveling far is second. It keeps constant duration, spot size, and amplitude. A pulse ionizing gas into uniform plasma is third. Tuning full spatiotemporal form better results fifteenfold. Spatial or time tuning alone performed worse.
arxiv-2510-25773:
Andy Bruce, Alexander Aghili, Razvan Marinescu, and Daniel Sabo derive latent Langevin changes. Their 2025 paper concerns coarse-grained molecular changes potentials. That limits families of usable coarse-graining functions. Machine learning coarse-grained potentials face that restriction. They derive a general family of embedding functions.

Correct sampling is the key trait they establish. Non-geometric coarse-graining features become usable with Langevin changes. Principal part features are one such example. Latent embeddings from neural networks are another. Molecules can be represented in learned latent spaces. Changes there must still sample correct distributions. Their family ensures that correctness mathematically. Coarse-graining reduces run cost by removing detail. Sampling guarantees are needed for scientific validity. The work paves way for neural latent runs.
arxiv-2510-26373:
Juan David Álvarez-Cuartas and John H Reina study quantum batteries, small devices that store energy using quantum effects. Such batteries might charge faster when many parts act together than when each part acts alone, an effect tied to superabsorption. The pair use two standard models of atoms linked to light in a cavity, and they add noise and loss to match real setups.

Álvarez-Cuartas and Reina track how stored energy, charging time, and peak power grow as the number of qubits rises. One model grows faster than plain size would suggest, with power rising well above the linear rate. They also find that some loss can help, steadying the growth of entanglement, which is the link between quantum parts. Their results give targets for labs building such batteries.
arxiv-2510-26473:
Junya Shiraishi, Shashi Raj Pandey, Israel Leyva-Mayorga, and Petar Popovski tackle wasted energy in small connected devices. Such devices store machine learning models in DRAM, a fast memory that must be refreshed again and again to keep its data. Refreshing burns power even when the device sits idle, a real cost for battery-run sensors.

Shiraishi and his three co-authors propose two fixes. One wakes memory up over the air only when a task needs it. The other stores a rough, lighter copy of the model when an exact one is not needed. Their tests show lower energy use than an always-on setup, while the answers the device pulls back stay accurate enough. The idea suits task-specific data fetching in the internet of things.
arxiv-2510-26773:
Alice Colpani Serri and five co-authors present a 2025 tool for particle physics. It adds a new part to MadGraph, a program that computes how particles collide and form. The tool handles quarkonium, a bound pair of a heavy quark and its anti-partner. It also handles leptonium, a like pair made of lighter particles.

Work runs in two frames, named NRQCD and NRQED, which treat slow bound pairs in steps. Tests on known cases show the tool is sound and can bend to new tasks. It links with shower tools, programs that trace how particles spread after a hit. It also fits models beyond the standard one through a shared interface. The authors warn that small terms can matter more than simple rules suggest.
arxiv-2510-27173:
Jiaxin Yuan, Haizhao Yang, and Maria Cameron present a new tool in 2025 for fast tests of systems that move and jitter. Such systems are written as stochastic differential equations, math rules that mix steady drift with random kicks. Solvers grind through them step by step, trading speed for accuracy. Training a fresh AI model for each new case is also costly.

Their model, FMint-SDE, learns one general fix instead. It reads rough solver runs plus text notes about the case, then corrects the errors. It builds on a transformer, the design behind chat models, trained to learn from examples in context. Tests span molecules, machines, finance, and living systems. The model beat classic solvers on the speed and accuracy balance.
arxiv-2510-27273:
Maurizio Palesi, Enrico Russo, and five other co-authors tackle message traffic inside future quantum computers in this 2025 paper. Such machines may link many small chips that must swap both quantum and plain signals. Plain signals steer the work and support tricks like teleportation, the transfer of a quantum state. In cold chips, a wireless net may carry the plain traffic.

Old rules pass a token, a pass granting a turn to talk, from chip to chip in a ring. Idle chips waste turns and slow the rest. Their rule, ID-MAC, plans talk turns ahead of time from the program itself. Only chips with something to send get turns. In simulations, message time fell by up to seventy percent, and total run time fell sharply too.
arxiv-2510-27473:
Carles Roch I Carceller and Armin Tavakoli ask when entanglement helps under a tight energy budget, in this 2025 paper. Entanglement is the quantum link that ties two systems' fates. Their setting is prepare-and-measure tests where the sent signal's energy is capped. Such caps suit semi-device-independent setups, where devices are only partly trusted.

For classical signals, they derive a test that any unlinked resource must pass, then show linked pairs can still fail to help in standard tasks. For quantum signals, they study the basic job of sending one bit with some chance of success. Help appears only when the encoding purposely blurs the linked state, and richer links help more. They also probe quantum random number generation, a standard use. Attacks in the low-energy range leave its security mostly intact.
arxiv-2510-27573:
Aleksandra Kowalska proves a number theory result in 2025 for polynomials over a field with two elements, written as F2[x]. The work mirrors a known result for whole numbers by Green, which held only if a major open guess, the Riemann idea in broad form, is true. Here no such guess is needed, and the bound is stronger.

For a large set of such polynomials, the proof shows two members must differ by one less than a prime-like element. The size bound uses an exponent of seven eighths, plus a small extra term. Results of this kind show how number patterns persist when whole numbers are swapped for polynomial rings.
arxiv-2511-00073:
Harald Kristen, Daniel Kulmer, and Manuela Hirschmugl compare AI architectures for detecting habitat and land cover change in Gesaeuse National Park, an Austrian alpine protected area. Climate change demands frequent monitoring, but manual mapping is too expensive at the needed rate. Long-term alpine habitat data, with fuzzy class boundaries and highly imbalanced classes, tests geospatial foundation models.

Two paradigms are compared: detecting change after classifying each date, versus detecting change directly. A Prithvi Earth observation model is among the systems evaluated for post-classification change. Environmental monitoring readers get guidance on applying foundation models to complex natural terrain rather than tidy urban scenes.
arxiv-2511-00273:
Sander de Jong and five co-authors study what the public gets wrong about gig work, jobs arranged through apps and platforms. Behind myths of freedom and fair pay sit hidden risks: unclear pay, health and safety dangers, and privacy breaches. In the first phase of their study, more than two hundred crowd workers rated five common myths, and nearly all believed at least one.

In phase two, each person had to defend their view against a counterargument written by an expert or a language model. The exercise exposed how little workers know about shared risks in gig jobs. The authors discuss which persuasion styles worked best and how better public understanding could support fairer rules for platform work.
arxiv-2511-00573:
Wei Feng and Zongyuan Ge tackle category discovery when the data itself shifts domains. Generalized category discovery uses labeled examples of known classes to cluster unlabeled data that may hide new classes. Under distribution shift, performance usually crumbles, and unlabeled samples may also come from unknown domains. Their framework, FREE, reads the problem in the frequency domain, where domain signatures show clearly.

Those amplitude gaps first separate known from unknown domains. Two perturbation strategies follow: swapping amplitude parts across domains to teach adaptation, and perturbing within the unknown domain for robustness. Extended contrastive and clustering losses guide training, and a resampling step focuses effort on groups that are hard to cluster. Across benchmarks, the method finds known and new categories more steadily under shift.
arxiv-2511-00673:
Dominik Drexler speeds up automated planning for tasks with numbers. Most planners translate a task written in a first-order-like language into ground facts before searching, and that grounding step can explode exponentially on hard tasks. Drexler extends a leading lifted successor generator, which works with the compact lifted form, to handle numeric preconditions on actions for the first time.

The method enumerates maximum cliques in a substitution consistency graph, where each clique yields one ground action, now augmented with numeric checks. The generator is proved exact under stated conditions. When conditions fail it may over-list actions, but a final applicability filter restores completeness, and in practice the failure is rare across benchmark domains. Rich numeric planning fragments become searchable without the grounding blowup.
arxiv-2511-00873: A. Puhalskii proves tightness and exponential tightness for the stationary queue lengths of generalised Jackson networks, a standard model of linked service stations where jobs move between queues. The abstract states the scope only: uniform proofs covering several setups concerned with large, normal, and moderate deviations of the queue length sequences.
arxiv-2511-01073:
Marco Buratti and colleagues construct additive Steiner 2-designs, highly symmetric arrangements of points and blocks used in combinatorics. A design is additive over a group when its points are group elements and every block sums to zero. Nearly all known manageable examples live over elementary abelian groups.

The authors give general constructions that unify the known ones and produce new designs. Among them are a resolvable design on fifty two points over the group of order two hundred fifty six. Three pairwise non-isomorphic designs on one hundred twenty one points, none equal to the classical point line design of the projective space. They also prove a negative result: a sought design on five hundred eleven points cannot be cyclic, ruling out one natural construction route.
arxiv-2511-03673:
Shubham Rohal, Dong Yoon Lee, and Shijia Pan turn everyday surfaces into touch displays with a folding origami structure called OriFeel. Tables, chair backs, and armrests invite passive touch all day, yet past haptic skins needed dense actuator grids that bulk large and drain power. OriFeel instead folds in the Miura-ori pattern, where linked units move together.

Embedded cables pull the fold network so one drive spreads across many contact points. Touch output can be steered across the surface without an actuator per point. That structural trick cuts hardware and power while keeping spatial control. Ambient furniture could thus whisper directions or alerts through touch, a channel that stays private in shared rooms.
arxiv-2511-03973:
Changfeng Gui, Jun Wang, Wen Yang, and Yong Zhang prove existence of Stokes waves with piecewise smooth vorticity in deep water. These travelling waves move over sheared currents in a semi-infinite domain, and vorticity may jump across internal streamlines, adding features absent from earlier steady wave studies.

A hodograph transformation turns the free boundary problem into an elliptic boundary value problem, then a height function casts it as a transmission problem. A singular bifurcation approach joins global bifurcation theory with a topological lemma, while an exact mean-flux identity controls the closing Fourier mode. New difficulties include an internal interface, an unbounded domain, and a non-Fredholm linearized operator.
arxiv-2511-04473:
Alberto Cattaneo and two colleagues build ground-truth data for knowledge graph question answering. Language models grounded in knowledge graphs promise more factual answers. Yet few datasets reveal the exact facts a system should retrieve, so methods are hard to compare.

Their SynthKGQA framework generates questions from any knowledge graph with full ground-truth fact sets. Applied to a Wikidata-derived graph and checked against a current Wikidata dump, it yields the GTSQA dataset. The set is built to test zero-shot skill on unseen material. With known targets, retrieval methods can finally be scored on what they fetch, not just final answers.
arxiv-2511-04773:
Shirin Ermis leads ten authors with a framework for three-dimensional cloud reconstruction around tropical cyclones. Forecasting these storms is hard because satellites rarely probe their inner structure. Cloud properties tied to intensification are especially tough to resolve.

Machine learning has rebuilt clouds in 3D elsewhere, but regions with frequent cyclones were left out. Their pipeline pre-trains on multi-satellite global data, then fine-tunes for storm work. Flat satellite images become 3D maps of key cloud properties. A custom cyclone dataset tests the model where it matters most, on intense storms that earlier methods validated poorly.
arxiv-2511-04873:
Jordan Eckert and two colleagues select training prototypes using topological data analysis. Prototype picking shrinks a dataset while keeping its decision structure intact. Existing method families ignore the multi-scale shape of the data.

Their Topological Prototype Selector runs two Rips sweeps in sequence. It keeps both boundary-relevant points and typical interior points for the shrunk set. A boundary-conscious variant weights its filtration to hold points near the decision edge. Both face seven classical baselines across fifteen real datasets. Keeping the shape of the data, not just its density, may preserve accuracy with far fewer examples.
arxiv-2511-05173:
Sushil Kumar and co-authors analyze secret key exchange between two users over free-space optical links with many antennas. They study discrete-variable quantum key methods in both one-way and two-way forms, using weak pulses and decoy states.

The work assumes an attacker who splits off photons, and a receiver that uses threshold detection across its antennas. For both protocol forms, the authors derive fresh formulas for the secret key rate and the error rate. Those formulas let designers weigh antenna count, link loss, and attack strength before they build such a system.
arxiv-2511-05473:
Agnieszka Janiuk and co-authors model how winds from a post-merger accretion disk could make the heavy elements whose decay powers a kilonova, the glow seen with some gamma-ray bursts. Such bursts have lately been tied to kilonova light, and the source of that glow needs a firm account.

They run time-based magnetohydrodynamic models of a new black hole eating merger debris. In the disk wind, they track r-process building of heavy nuclei for a range of start values and merger types. The wind traits they find set how bright and long a kilonova can shine.
arxiv-2511-05573:
Ziyang Liu, Kevin Valencia, and Justin Cui tackle a weak spot of text-to-video models: words inside the video often come out garbled. Even short phrases can break apart or drift over time. Past fixes tend to be heavy and costly to run.

Their approach builds training data in a cheap, synthetic way. First a text-to-image model makes pictures rich in text. Then an image-to-video model animates them without seeing the text. Those pairs fine-tune a video model with no change to its design. Short text became clearer and steadier across frames, and longer text showed early structure, hinting that weak synthetic supervision can teach better lettering.
arxiv-2511-05773:
Zishuai Liu and co-authors recognize what people are doing at home from ambient sensors, in real time and without pre-cut clips. Smart home activity recognition is hard because sensor streams run on, activities blend, and most methods ignore the home's physical layout. Their framework, named MARAuder's Map, works straight from raw streams.

Sensor firings are projected onto the floor plan, making image-like sequences that trace how a person moves through rooms. A hybrid deep model reads both the spatial pattern and its timing, helped by a learned embedding for hour and weekday. An attention step picks out the informative parts of each window. On real smart home data sets the method beat strong baselines.
arxiv-2511-05873:
Tong Chen and co-authors restore endoscopic images damaged by several problems at once: dim light, smoke, and bleeding during surgery. Such flaws hide details clinicians need. Older restoration tools each handle one flaw type and often must be told which flaw is present, which limits real-world use.

Their system, EndoIR, handles all flaw types with one diffusion model and no prior label. A prompter extracts features from both the image and its frequency view. Clean and degraded inputs run through separate streams and are fused in a structured way. A routing block picks only noise-relevant features to save compute. On two data sets EndoIR beat strong baselines with fewer parameters, and follow-up segmentation tests confirmed clinical value.
arxiv-2511-06473:
Janosch Fuchs and co-authors add a new move to the coloring reconfiguration problem. Given two proper colorings of a graph, can one be reshaped into the other through legal intermediate colorings? The new rule, color swapping, lets two neighboring vertices exchange colors whenever the result stays proper, a move unlike the single-vertex and Kempe chain rules studied before.

Complexity splits cleanly at three colors: swapping is solvable in polynomial time for at most two colors and becomes PSPACE-complete from three colors up. Hardness survives even on bipartite, split, and bounded-degree planar graphs. Polynomial algorithms do exist for paths with three colors, split graphs with fixed colors, and cographs with any number of colors.
arxiv-2511-06573:
Biswajit Kumar Sahoo and co-authors hide encrypted audio inside ordinary images using a spiking neural network. Steganography must balance secrecy, capacity, and how natural the carrier looks, a balance that clever generative attacks keep disturbing. Their system, SteganoSNN, converts sound samples into spike trains through leaky integrate-and-fire neurons, mimicking brain-style signaling.

The spikes are encrypted with a modular mapping, then tucked into the least significant bits of image color channels with dithering to hide distortion. Built with a neural simulator and run on a small programmable chip, it embeds eight bits per pixel in real time. Image quality stayed high on a standard photo dataset, ahead of a GAN-based rival on efficiency.
arxiv-2511-06673:
Joel Kemp and colleagues present a family of soft air-driven actuators that telescope outward like an extending spyglass. Soft robots promise free-form motion in any direction, but the design space is too vast to search directly. One class with tunable settings makes that space manageable, letting designers dial in dimensions and watch behavior follow.

These units lengthen along their axis when inflated, suiting deployable structures and work in tight spaces. A geometry generator builds models from high-level choices, and careful tests mapped how parameters govern extension, bending, expansion, and stiffness. A soft quadruped with deploying legs shows the payoff, walking after unfolding itself to fit through confined spaces.
arxiv-2511-06773:
Junyan Cao, Ya Deng, Christopher D Hacon, and Mihai Paun revisit classic results about the cohomology of complex manifolds, aiming to prove them inside one unified system. The targets are the generic vanishing theorems of Green and Lazarsfeld and the work of Budur and Wang on cohomology jumping loci. Their unifying tool is a suitable version of the partial-bar lemma from Hodge theory.

The paper's main labor is building the machinery that approach requires: an L2 Hodge theory for the cohomology of rank-one local systems on quasi-compact Kähler manifolds. Local systems encode how cohomology twists as one moves around the manifold, and the L2 methods control that behavior near infinity. Higher-rank local systems and geometric applications are deferred to a companion paper, briefly outlined in the introduction.
arxiv-2511-07173:
Tao Hao, Ying Hu, and Jiaqiang Wen establish the theory of mean-field backward stochastic Volterra integral equations. In these equations, the solution at each time depends on its own future path and on the distribution of the whole population. Such systems arise in large-population control and finance. The authors prove existence and uniqueness of solutions in two regimes for the generator's growth in the control variable: linear growth and quadratic growth.

They then connect the system to particle systems, finite populations whose collective behavior should approximate the mean-field limit. This propagation of chaos is proved under both growth conditions, with convergence rates derived in each case. The quadratic case requires the generator to be independent of the law of the control variable. The rates quantify how large a particle system must be before it faithfully represents the mean-field equation.
arxiv-2511-07673:
K. Zhao reports the latest hunt for neutrinoless double beta decay with the CUORE experiment in Italy. Finding that rare decay would prove neutrinos are their own antiparticles and that lepton number can break. CUORE watches tellurium nuclei inside nearly a thousand crystals chilled below fifteen thousandths of a kelvin.

More than seven years of running gathered close to three tonne-years of exposure. Results set a leading limit on the exotic decay and a precise half-life for the ordinary two-neutrino version. The follow-up experiment CUPID aims higher with better background rejection. Each tighter limit narrows what neutrino mass models may claim.
arxiv-2511-07873:
Shan-Xia Bao, Ren Zhao, and Yun-Zhi Du compute the thermodynamics of a five-dimensional de Sitter black hole with hair. Mass, charge, a hair parameter, and the cosmological constant serve as state variables under a universal first law. Effective thermodynamic quantities follow for the region where black hole and cosmological horizons coexist.

Heat capacity plotted against temperature, or against the horizon position ratio, can develop a peak-like Schottky anomaly. Such peaks signal Schottky-type behavior familiar from two-level systems, here emerging from spacetime itself. Two-horizon thermodynamics tests whether horizon statistical mechanics mirrors ordinary matter, a clue physicists chase toward quantum gravity.
arxiv-2511-08373:
Henrik Daniel Christensen, Saverio Giallorenzo, and Jacopo Mauro improve pod placing by adding constraint coding as a fallback to the default placer. Kubernetes runs app parts as pods on cluster nodes, keeping rankings and resource requests. Its fast heuristic placer can fragment resources and leave deployable pods unplaced, above all higher priority ones, wasting cluster capacity.

Their plug in uses the OR-Tools solver to find optimal allocations when the default attempt fails. Within a one second window on small to mid sized clusters, it improves placing in many scenarios where the default placer fails and certifies optimality in others. A ten second window raises the improvement share substantially.
arxiv-2511-08573:
Shanaka Liyanaarachchi and four co-authors build a model that reads two kinds of cancer tissue data at once: gene activity maps from spatial transcriptomics and structure from pathology images. The goal is to mark tissue regions accurately, including tumor substructures tied to drug resistance.

Earlier methods leaned too far toward one data type, either drowning in transcriptomic noise or smoothing away functional detail. Their architecture, SENCA-st, uses a shared encoder with neighborhood cross-attention so both data types keep their own features. It highlights spots that look alike in images but differ in gene activity. The authors report it beats prior methods at finding tumor variation and micro-environment regions.
arxiv-2511-08973:
Junkang Huang, Z. D. Wang, and Tao Zhou find an unconventional superconducting state hiding inside a Weyl semimetal, a material whose electrons behave like massless Weyl particles. The material is a type-II, time-reversal-symmetric version, modeled with two orbitals, and the pairing is worked out self-consistently rather than assumed.

The pairing that emerges is a hybrid: singlet s-wave on one surface and triplet p-wave on the other, with the surface Fermi-arc configuration deciding which wins where. The resulting superconductor is also topological in a higher-order sense, carrying protected hinge states along its edges. Because the ingredients are intrinsic to the material rather than engineered in a heterostructure, the authors nominate these semimetals as a promising natural platform. The prize is unconventional and topological superconductivity, a combination hunted for future quantum devices.
arxiv-2511-09373:
Adam Štorek and eight co-authors build Routesplain. The router sends each software task query to the language model best suited for it. Model performance varies sharply across tasks like code generation, repair, and computer science questions, so choosing well saves money and improves answers. Earlier routers were general-purpose black boxes trained on raw queries.

Routesplain first extracts human-readable concepts from a query, such as its task, domain, and reasoning complexity, and routes using only those concepts. That design yields faithful, intelligible reasons for each routing decision. Across 16 leading models and eight software tasks, it beat individual models on accuracy and cost and matched or beat black-box routers. Users can also intervene on the concepts to steer routing.
arxiv-2511-09573:
Valentino F. Foit, David W. Hogg, and Soledad Villar remind machine learning practitioners that exact symmetries can be imposed on any trained model for free. Many physics tasks are precisely equivariant under some symmetry group, yet models are often left to learn the symmetry imperfectly. Group averaging fixes that at test time, with no retraining or structural changes.

The trick is to average the model's predictions over the symmetry group when evaluating. The authors apply it to established benchmark models of differential equations whose solutions obey known symmetries. Evaluation loss fell in every test, improving by up to about 37 percent on their error measure. Predictions for continuous dynamics also looked visibly better, making group averaging an easy default for physics applications.
arxiv-2511-09873:
Nikunj Gupta, Bill Guo, Rajgopal Kannan, and Viktor K. Prasanna present HierRouter, a system that answers each query by chaining specialized small language models instead of calling one giant model. Large models are capable but costly in compute and memory, which hurts real-time and resource-limited use. HierRouter treats pipeline building as a sequential decision problem and learns it with reinforcement learning.

A Proximal Policy Optimization agent picks which model to invoke at each stage of multi-hop inference, watching the evolving context and the cost spent so far. With three open-source candidate models across six benchmarks covering questions, code, and math, response quality rose up to about two and a half times over single models. The added inference cost stayed minimal on average.
arxiv-2511-09973:
Satoshi Suzuki and nine co-authors propose DiVE, a fine-tuning method that adapts vision-language models such as CLIP to a target data set without wrecking their zero-shot reach. Earlier robust fine-tuning reused contrastive learning, but the authors found that this distorts the geometry of the embedding space, which is exactly what generalization depends on. DiVE instead constrains how far embeddings move during fine-tuning.

For each sample, a difference vector records the gap between pretrained and fine-tuned embeddings. Two losses push those vectors to agree: one globally, toward their weighted average, and one locally, for consistent multimodal alignment. Tests showed the geometry largely preserved, with strong results on in-distribution, out-of-distribution, and zero-shot measures alike.
arxiv-2511-10073:
Yuhao Ren and six co-authors speed up global placement, the chip design step that decides where millions of cells go before detailed routing. Analytical placers solve a nonlinear optimization in which the starting arrangement strongly shapes both convergence and final quality. Area-aware initializers model cell sizes well but are slow, while fast point-based ones ignore area and start the solver from a misleading picture.

Their co-optimization framework adds heuristic area hints into a signed graph signal, using virtual nodes and negative-weight edges to keep the start spectrally smooth. A macro-schedule procedure then restores the full area constraints gradually. On academic and industrial designs the method improved wirelength in eleven of twelve cases while running about a hundred times faster than the leading area-aware initializer.
arxiv-2511-10273:
Dieter Vandesande, Jordi Coll, and Bart Bogaerts bring proof logging to branch-and-bound MaxSAT solvers, so a solver's answer comes with a checkable certificate. Satisfiability solvers already log proofs, guarding against bugs in complex code, but the optimization variant MaxSAT lacked a comparable breakthrough until recently. This extended paper shows how to certify the advanced machinery inside state-of-the-art branch-and-bound MaxSAT solving.

Covered techniques include look-ahead methods and clausal encodings of pseudo-Boolean constraints built on multi-valued decision diagrams. The ideas are implemented in the leading solver MaxCDCL. Experiments show proof logging is feasible with limited overhead, though checking the proofs remains a challenge, an honest caveat the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2511-10373:
Robert Davis and five co-authors, including Jesús A. De Loera and Josephine Yu, work in Ehrhart theory, which counts lattice points inside stretched copies of a geometric shape called a polytope. Their paper rebuilds that counting so the answers carry algebraic labels from a group ring, not just plain numbers. The richer counts record far more structure than a single integer can.

The authors show that the central results of Ehrhart theory still hold in this setting, through a generalized form of Brion's theorem. Rational generating functions, reciprocity, links to volume, and vertex cone decompositions all carry over. The framework also unifies several known refinements, including weighted and q-based counts, as products of one algebraic mechanism.
arxiv-2511-11273:
Jin-Yang Shen, Xin-Yi Liu, and their colleagues build a holographic model of the phase structure of quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons, for two light flavors plus the strange quark. Their Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton model with flavor reacts fully on itself and is tuned to lattice simulations with machine learning help. A holographic model trades a hard strong-force problem for a gravity problem in higher dimensions.

The model reproduces the equation of state and chiral dynamics with quantitative accuracy and maps the Columbia plot, finding its tri-critical point. At finite density it predicts a change from smooth crossover to a sharp transition, ending at a critical endpoint within reach of heavy-ion experiments.
arxiv-2511-11373:
Shulin Liu, Dong Du, and their colleagues present MarsRL, a reinforcement learning framework that trains a whole team of reasoning agents together. Single models hit a length limit on how deep one answer can reason, so teams split the work among a solver, a verifier, and a corrector that refine answers in rounds. Open models often lack the critic skills to make that loop work, which MarsRL targets directly.

Agent-specific rewards cut reward noise, and a pipeline-style training scheme handles long trajectories efficiently. Applied to a mid-size open reasoning model, MarsRL lifted scores on two hard math benchmarks past those of a much larger sibling model.
arxiv-2511-11473:
Guilin Hu, Malek Itani, and their colleagues introduce proactive hearing assistants that find and isolate the wearer's conversation partners with no explicit prompts. The system listens through two-ear, wearer-centered audio and anchors on the wearer's own speech. Turn-taking patterns and dialogue dynamics then reveal who is in the conversation and who is background to suppress.

Two models share the work for real-time, on-device use. A light streaming model runs every few milliseconds to extract partner voices at low delay, while a slower model reads longer-range conversational flow. Tests on real two- and three-speaker recordings from eleven participants show the system generalizes across multi-conversation settings.
arxiv-2511-11573:
Christopher R. Lee-Jenkins builds a first bridge between machine learning and modern differential geometry by reimagining the softmax step, which turns raw scores called logits into probabilities. Two descriptions based on potentials, one from negative entropy and one from log-sum-exp, are shown to meet along a geometric seam.

That seam sits as a Legendrian curve on the probability simplex, viewed as a contact screen inside a folded symplectic collar. Shifting all logits by a constant appears as Reeb flow, and a known equality gives a measurable distance to the seam. Two- and three-class cases make the picture concrete, with links to information geometry sketched for later work.
arxiv-2511-11673:
M. A. Gameiro classifies song lyrics by fusing two kinds of evidence: deep semantic embeddings from a sentence transformer, which are rich but opaque, and simple structural features that a human can interpret. Neither source alone tells the whole story about what a lyric is doing.

A gated Synergistic Fusion Layer lets the structural cues modulate the deep features, deciding how much each should count. The task separates one dominant, uniform cluster of lyrics from everything else, a split derived from clustered embeddings. The gated model edges out a strong random forest baseline on accuracy and F1 score. The design shows how interpretable signals can steer, rather than merely accompany, deep representations.
arxiv-2511-11773:
Ruchira Dhar, Ninell Oldenburg, and Anders Soegaard argue that AI tests should measure generality, not intelligence. Famous tests in the style of ARC or Raven's matrices are treated as intelligence tests. Yet intelligence has no stable meaning in this field. It also predicts real work poorly, such as answering questions, summarizing, or coding.

Three assumptions behind such testing are examined. They are generality, stability, and realism. Only generality survives close scrutiny, the authors contend. Chasing intelligence scores can steer the field away from useful systems. A focus on breadth of skill would change which models get built. It would also change which claims buyers should believe.
arxiv-2511-11873:
Damien A. Easson works out, fully analytically, how a Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole evaporates when quantum backreaction is included. These black holes sit in a universe with a positive cosmological constant, so two horizons, the black hole's and the cosmological one, radiate at different temperatures and the system never reaches equilibrium.

A two-dimensional dilaton gravity model, reduced from four-dimensional Einstein gravity, captures the whole causal and thermodynamic structure exactly. Adding the trace anomaly of conformal matter through the Polyakov action yields the evolving mass, the steady nonequilibrium Hawking flux, and what static observers measure locally. Exact nonequilibrium evaporation is rare theoretical ground.
arxiv-2511-11973:
Xinming Gao, Shangzhe Li, Yujin Cai, and Wenwu Yu revisit Extreme Q-Learning, an offline reinforcement learning method that learns from a fixed dataset using extreme value theory to model Bellman errors. Offline learning matters where fresh interaction is dangerous or costly, but the method and its stabilized variant demand heavy per-dataset tuning and can train unstably.

Quantile regression supplies a principled estimate of the temperature coefficient that previously had to be hand-tuned, under mild assumptions. A value regularization technique with a generalization argument further steadies training. Removing fragile knobs is what turns a clever offline algorithm into one practitioners can trust on a new dataset without a tuning expedition.
arxiv-2511-12273:
Mario Bertaina and thirteen co-authors report first performance results for MIZAR, a readout chip built for a balloon mission that will hunt ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos. The chip reads optical Cherenkov light from air showers seen from high altitude. It must handle many channels while using little power.

MIZAR is a 64-channel circuit that reads an eight-by-eight array of silicon photomultipliers. Each event is stored in analogue memory cells, converted to digital form, and sent to a programmable gate array that runs the trigger logic. The design samples at a fast rate and aims at a new generation of low-power front-end electronics for the PBR mission.
arxiv-2511-12673:
Matteo Maltoni's doctoral thesis studies how to spot physics beyond the Standard Model at colliders like the LHC when no new particles show up directly. If new states are too heavy to produce, their effects can still be captured by extra operators in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. The catch is that the leading signal, the interference between known and new amplitudes, is sometimes suppressed by a helicity mismatch or by cancellations between contributions.

Maltoni introduces quantities that tell the two suppression cases apart and develops a strategy to revive the hidden interference. He applies it to specific operators in three-jet production and in electroweak processes such as vector boson fusion. A final chapter sets limits on ten four-quark operators using multijet events. The work gives collider analysts practical observables for squeezing information out of signals that first looked muted.
arxiv-2511-12773:
Andreas Thom asks whether flat slices can reveal a three-dimensional shape, using the regular dodecahedron as a test case. The question is motivated by microscopy of biological structures such as organoids, where imaging gives two-dimensional sections whose orientation is unknown. Thom replaces the solid with its twenty vertices and records the shapes that planar cuts produce. If that distribution fixed the subset up to symmetry, sections would determine structure.

He shows they do not. Two different seven-vertex subsets, not related by any symmetry of the dodecahedron, produce exactly the same planar statistics. It follows that two polytopes can share the full distribution of their two-dimensional intersection shapes while not being congruent themselves. The result mirrors classical non-uniqueness findings in geometric tomography, the mathematics of reconstructing shapes from slices. It is a caution for anyone inferring 3D form from 2D sections.
arxiv-2511-13473:
Alix Deruelle and 3 co-authors find conditions under which a singular Kähler metric can start a smooth Kähler-Ricci flow. Their input is a closed positive current on a compact Kähler manifold, which induces a distance structure on the space. The question is when that rough structure is truly the limit of smooth geometries.

They give sufficient conditions for the space to arise as a Gromov-Hausdorff limit of compact Kähler manifolds, either at rest or at the starting time of smooth flows. In dimension one they extend earlier work, showing any compact oriented Alexandrov surface with bounded total curvature and no cusp can serve as starting data for such a flow.
arxiv-2511-13573:
Joseph Naor and five co-authors improve correlated sampling for the hypersimplex, a tool that lets separate parties draw sets that overlap as much as possible. Correlated sampling from the simplex has served theoretical computer science since the two thousands as a shared building block. The hypersimplex version asks for sets of bounded size whose expected gap stays within a factor of the input distance.

Earlier work reached a factor that grows with the full ambient dimension. The new algorithm brings that factor down to one that grows only with the set size, removing the dimension from the bound. It also samples fast on sparse inputs and supports quick updates. Uses include online paging, metric multi-labeling, and welfare reallocation problems.
arxiv-2511-13773:
Cynthia A. Huang and Tina Lam synthesize a framework for documenting and judging web-scraped datasets, called PRITES. Scraped data now feed research across government, industry, and universities, yet the literature on its quality is scattered across computing, statistics, and applied fields with clashing definitions. Their six stages run from planning and retrieval through investigation, transformation, and evaluation to summarizing.

Each stage is tied to known technical and statistical pitfalls of collecting and analyzing online data, with quality factors to watch while scraping or before reusing an existing set. A case study turns scraped retail alcohol prices from an industry partner into analysis-ready data for public health policy work, showing the reporting the framework supports.
arxiv-2511-13873:
Hang Thanh Nguyen, Bart Van Der Holst, Phuong Hong Nguyen, and one co-author tackle grid balancing in power systems with growing renewable supply. Some countries reward firms that passively adjust their power use to help the grid, but profit-driven responses can bunch up and strain the link between transmission and distribution networks. The authors build a two-stage model of this behavior under price uncertainty.

They compare three existing pricing schemes for imbalances, then propose a new one that depends on congestion. Their design keeps the reward for helpful passive balancing while respecting grid limits.
