Lea S. Schimak and eleven co authors test red clump star models with a rare binary system. Binaries where both stars pulsate are rare but extremely valuable. Their system pairs a core helium burning red clump star with a red giant branch star. The binary is cataloged as KIC 10841730, and it pulsates in ways seismology can read.

Theirs is the first study of an asteroseismic binary of this exact makeup. Asteroseismology uses star vibrations to probe interiors that light cannot reach. Two pulsating stars in one system give cross checks no single star can. Red clump stars serve as standard candles for galactic distances. Testing their models sharpens the distance ladder of astronomy.
arxiv-2601-13173:
Leonardo Grimaldi, Elisa Maggio, Lorenzo Pompili, and Alessandra Buonanno test Einstein's theory with a loud black hole crash. The signal, named GW250114, is the clearest wave of its kind yet caught. Its last stage, where the merged hole rings down, is a sharp probe of strong gravity.

The team asks how well that stage fits Einstein's rules for holes that spin and wobble. They use a wave form model that can bend away from Einstein's form in set ways. It sits in the effective one body frame, a way to map two body motion to one body terms. Tight bounds here would be a strong pass for the theory in its most harsh realm yet.
arxiv-2601-13473:
A. Koley, A. M. Stutz, and co-authors map magnetic fields in the G327.29 star forming cluster two ways. Fields and churn may steer how such clusters make dense cores and stars. To test that role, the field's shape in space must be known with care.

One read uses the velocity gradient technique on molecular line light. A next read uses polarized light from dust in the same sky. The team sets the two maps side by side. Where they match, trust grows. Where they part, the part marks a limit of one tool. ALMA data drives both reads. Such a head to head test firms up field maps for all cluster work.
arxiv-2601-14173:
Paris Karakasis and Nicholas Sidiropoulos study smoothness penalties for low-rank tensor models in 2026. Their models are low-rank tensor-product B-spline models for regression tasks. They investigate Dirichlet energy as a measure of smoothness. They show these models admit a closed-form expression for that energy.

They also reveal scenarios where perfect interpolation is possible with tiny Dirichlet energy. Exponentially small energy can accompany an exact fit in those cases. That renders global Dirichlet energy regularization ineffective as a guard. Local penalties, per the title, offer a way to restore control. The fix is to charge for rough spots where they sit, not for the whole field. That local charge keeps good fits sharp while it curbs the cheat.
arxiv-2601-14473:
Danny Butvinik, Nana Boateng, and Achi Hackmon study financial crime queues in this 2026 paper. Detection systems turn a continuous stream of risk scores into decision thresholds. Scores must be split into priority classes for investigators. The catch is that score distributions are non-stationary: they drift over time, so fixed thresholds go stale.

The team proposes adaptive kernel density estimation for real-time thresholding. KDE is a way to estimate the shape of a score distribution from live data. Their system builds prioritized queues for financial crime investigation. Readers get a method that keeps alert queues stable and sorted even as fraud patterns shift under them.
arxiv-2601-14573:
M. N. Chernodub, V. A. Goy, and A. V. Molochkov simulate the electroweak model in a strong magnetic field in this 2026 paper. They use numerical Monte Carlo simulations on a lattice. Their goal is the mass spectrum of the bosonic sector of the model. The external field has electroweak-scale strength, about 10 to the 20th tesla. The temperature is zero.

Fields that strong exist only in extreme settings, such as the early universe or magnetars. The paper's title asks a pointed question: are there acoustic phonons in a magnetized vacuum? Phonons are sound-like waves in a medium. Readers get lattice results on how the vacuum itself behaves as a material under such a field.
arxiv-2601-14673:
Yogesh Pipada Sunil Kumar and four co-authors bring neural networks into power system optimization in this 2026 paper. The decarbonisation of power systems drives growing reliance on distributed energy resources. Those resources introduce complex, nonlinear interactions. Conventional optimization models struggle to capture them. Machine learning based surrogate modelling has emerged as a promising approach.

The catch comes at integration time. Embedding ReLU deep neural networks directly into optimization often results in nonconvex and computationally intractable formulations. The team develops efficient reformulations of such networks for surrogate modelling. Reformulation rewrites the network so solvers can handle it. The point is use. A net that no solver can read is a dead end for grid work, no matter how well it fits past data. That is the goal of the work. Readers get a bridge between trained neural surrogates and the optimizers that run real grids.
arxiv-2601-14773:
Haizhou Liu, Yiming Wang, Haodong Jin, and Hui Yu summarize videos with AI in this 2026 paper. Video summarization enables efficient browsing of massive multimedia content and extraction of key information from social platforms. Most existing unsupervised summarization methods rely on Generative Adversarial Networks. GANs enhance keyframe selection and generate coherent summaries through adversarial training.

The team's method is semantic-guided unsupervised video summarization. Semantic guidance means the summary follows meaning, not just visual change. Unsupervised means no human-made summaries are needed for training. The use is plain. A long clip can be cut to its key frames, so a viewer saves time. Readers get a summarizer aimed at social video, where meaning matters more than motion: the key moment may be a quiet one.
arxiv-2601-14873:
Youssef El Khatiri works in the algebra of operators, the math behind much of quantum theory. His 2026 arXiv paper studies C*-algebras, a key class of these algebras. He looks at maps that keep the order between elements of the algebra.

El Khatiri gives a full account of such order-preserving maps. He covers maps between the self-adjoint parts of two C*-algebras. He then extends the result to general operator intervals in a wider class of algebras. The account rests on Jordan maps and on closed operators in rings tied to the algebra.
arxiv-2601-15173:
Katarina Krivokuća bounds a covering quantity for convex bodies. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with the covering minima of a convex body, a gauge from the geometry of numbers. She gives two new upper bounds for that quantity.

Each bound leans on simpler pieces of the body. One uses the covering minima of its projections. The other uses its intersections with flat subspaces. She shows one bound is sharp for direct sums of two bodies. That sharp case extends earlier results on covering radius and on lattice width for such sums.
arxiv-2601-15473:
Fahd Seddik and four co-authors tackle a tooling gap in deep learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Training large models strains GPU memory and compute budgets. Methods from randomized numerical linear algebra, or RandNLA, can help shrink these models. Yet no single, production-grade library has pulled those methods together. That gap, the authors argue, has slowed wider use.

Their answer is Panther, a library that works with PyTorch. Panther gathers known RandNLA methods into one fast framework. The title promises faster and cheaper computation as the payoff. For model builders, the point is plain. Tricks that once took custom code now sit in one shared tool, ready to use.
arxiv-2601-15673:
Qilong Yan and four co-authors improve recommendation with diffusion models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Sequential recommendation predicts what a user will want next. Methods have grown more complex over time. Many now use diffusion-guided generation instead of plain classification. These methods lean on user information as guidance. Real user sequences have missing data, though. Gaps in that guidance hurt the quality of what gets generated.

The title names the focus: enhancing guidance when data are missing. Better guidance should steer generation toward items the user truly wants. Missing history is the norm in real platforms, not the exception. Users skip, pause, and browse off the record. A recommender that copes with holes serves both users and sellers better.
arxiv-2601-15773:
Yuanyuan Qi and six co-authors blend several language models into active learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Active learning picks which data humans should label. Language models now join these pipelines as annotators. Their labels cut annotation costs. Quality is the catch. Labels from models often fall short of real-world needs. One model alone can be biased or brittle.

The title names the fix: a mixture of LLMs in the loop. Several models label together, checking each other's weak spots. Diversity among annotators is a classic route to better labels. The authors aim for annotation that stays cheap without going sloppy. Labeled data feed nearly every applied AI project. Cutting its cost while holding quality is a broad win.
arxiv-2601-16473:
Wei Song and coauthors strip deepfake marks with no query to the guard. Their 2026 preprint, named DeMark, deals with marks hid in fake pics. Marks let teams spot fakes and trace their source. The guard case holds that marks stand firm to clean tricks. Past tests oft need asks to the guard model to find a path.

DeMark needs no such asks to strip the mark. A no ask attack is far more hard to spot or block. If marks fall with ease, mark guards need a rethink. The work tests mark strength in a harsh, real case. It warns teams that marks alone may not hold.
arxiv-2601-17373:
Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors study privacy fears in smart home assistants. These tools now act as social agents in the home. User worry turns on where data goes and who can hear it. The team uses Privacy Boundary Theory, a frame from interpersonal talk. A three-phase early study grounds their work. It first maps how data moves in these homes.

From that base, they probe how risk feels across sharing ranges. A chat kept in one room feels unlike one sent to the cloud. Design that shows those ranges could calm real fears. It could also stop over-sharing by default. The work links social theory to device design.
arxiv-2601-17673:
Weiyu Zhang, Yuan Hu, Yong Li, and Yu Liu present Uni-RS for remote sensing. Unified models both understand and generate images. The authors name a flaw they call the spatial reversal curse. Models can describe object locations in images with care. Yet they fail to use the same spatial relations when they generate. In remote sensing, those relations are core meaning.

A map-like image with wrong left-right layout is useless. Uni-RS aims for spatial faithfulness in both directions. Better spatial truth serves land use, disaster, and defense maps. Generation that respects layout can also augment training data. The work names a clear failure mode. Naming it lets the field measure progress on it.
arxiv-2601-17973:
Yuan Bian, Grace Y. Yi, and Wenqing He extend boosting to data where event times are only partly known. Their 2026 preprint deals with interval-censored data. In such data, an event is known to fall inside a window, but the exact time is unseen. The setup is common in survival analysis and in studies of time to an event, like relapse or failure. Classic boosting was built for full data and often struggles here.

Boosting builds a strong model by joining many weak ones in steps. The authors adapt that idea for both regression and classification with censored inputs. Sound tools for windowed data matter in medicine and reliability work. The paper gives those fields a modern learning option.
arxiv-2601-18173: N. B. Huamaní studies vertex degrees in grid graphs built from permutations that avoid the pattern 213. His 2026 preprint builds the graph column by column, with each column's height set by the permutation entry. Vertical edges join levels inside a column, and horizontal edges join equal levels in neighboring columns. The paper works out how the degrees of the vertices behave in this family.
arxiv-2601-18273:
Lorenzo Verzichelli works on scaling normalizing flows to bigger problems in condensed matter. His 2026 preprint studies the Hubbard model, a basic model of electrons in a lattice. Normalizing flows have recently learned the Boltzmann distribution of that model. That success opens a new route to generative modeling of quantum materials. The open question is how to reach larger lattices and lower temperatures without the training falling apart.

Verzichelli studies the steps needed for that scale-up. Stability and efficiency are his twin focus. Flows that stay sound at low temperature could sample states that other methods reach slowly. The work maps the path from a proof of concept to a working tool.
arxiv-2601-18573:
Frederik Glitzner and David Manlove study match tasks in which some who take part break ranks and some hold firm. The base tasks pair up people by what they like best, in a way no pair would both gain by a swap. In one form of the task such a firm match is sure to exist and can be found fast. In the next form it may not exist at all, though one can tell fast if it does.

Real match tasks must weigh size next to firm-ness: a big match that some would break, or a small one that none would. The team add two kinds of folk to that mix. Some will break a match for a small gain. Some will hold firm at a cost. Their maths maps how those kinds shift the best trade. Match maths serves dorms, jobs, and organ swaps.
arxiv-2601-18873:
A study sets out a new kind of skyrmion that is born of heat, not of cold calm. A skyrmion is a knot in a field that can't be smoothed out. It acts like a lone bit and can be quite firm. In the maths of the bits that fill atom cores, such knots stand for the cores them-selves. They may also live in the field that gives mass to all bits, if set cross terms are at play.

The new kind is tied to heat: its form and firm-ness shift with how hot the field runs. That tie could change where such knots can live and what they do. Heat-born knots may have played a role in the hot young cosmos. The work is a maths study, with no lab test in view. It adds a fresh form to a prized class of field knots.
arxiv-2601-19073:
Jessica Eskew and eight co-authors study how a split in a magnetic island changes the spread of electrons. In magnetized plasmas, islands are closed loops of field that can trap or guide particles. When an island splits, its inner points and borders move, and the paths for sideways diffusion change with them.

The team tracks that effect under controlled splitting of the island shape. Diffusion across the field sets how fast heat and particles leak in fusion and space plasmas. Knowing how island shape steers that leak helps read experiments and may help keep hot plasma penned in longer.
arxiv-2601-19473:
Lucia Varbaro and thirteen co-authors report superconductivity that returns, driven by magnetism, in a nickel based crystal. Infinite layer nickelates are thin structured cousins of the famous cuprate superconductors. Doping this one with europium adds magnetic atoms to the mix.

In such a setting, superconductivity can vanish and then come back, a re-entrance, as conditions shift. The team traces that return and links it to the paramagnetic response of the dopants. Re-entrant cases are stress tests for theories of how magnetism and superconductivity share one material, a puzzle at the heart of the field.
arxiv-2601-19973:
Andrew R. Casey and five colleagues rethink a routine step in analysing starlight. To infer a star's temperature and chemistry, astronomers forward-model its spectrum. That usually requires a synthesis code or an emulator trained on curated examples. Before modelling, the spectrum is normalised: its continuum level is set by a preprocessing step kept separate from the stellar parameters.

That separation biases results and makes them inconsistent across signal-to-noise levels. The authors propose a constrained linear model that folds continuum normalisation into the analysis itself. A joint treatment should give abundances that agree no matter how noisy the data are. Chemical surveys of millions of stars depend on such consistency. The work cleans up a quiet source of systematic error. The bias is small but it does not go away.
arxiv-2601-20173:
Zeyang Huang and four colleagues present MAPLE, a method that squeezes high-dimensional data down to a low-dimensional map for visual analysis. It builds on UMAP, a widely used tool for this task. MAPLE adds self-supervised learning to model the shape of the data manifold more efficiently.

At its core are maximum manifold capacity representations. These pull together points that are locally similar while pushing apart points that differ. The result is a map where tangled structure is easier to see. Better maps help analysts explore data in fields from biology to social science, where clusters and paths guide the next questions.
arxiv-2601-20473:
Weichen Wang and a large team report a quiet galaxy. It sits inside a gas-rich knot of the cosmic web at redshift about three, when the universe was young. Space telescopes have recently found many quenched galaxies at that era, which challenges models of galaxy formation. Since star formation feeds on gas flowing in from outside, the gas around such a galaxy is the key clue.

This galaxy sits where filaments of the web meet and gas is plentiful, yet it has stopped forming stars. Studying its circumgalactic gas may show how quenching can win even where fuel is abundant.
arxiv-2601-20673:
Felix Janda and Xin Wang study deep patterns in the geometry of curves in this 2026 math paper. Their subject is topological recursion relations on the moduli space of curves. That space collects all curves of a given genus with marked points. Recursion relations are formulas that tie complex cases to simpler ones. The paper looks at the basic structures these relations can take.

One focus is the coefficient of the bouquet class on that space. That coefficient gives the answer to a conjecture in the field. The authors map out the structures one by one. Their work is pure geometry, aimed at readers who study how these spaces are built. It adds basic facts that later work on curve spaces can build on.
arxiv-2601-20773:
Rubén Jiménez and Oriol Pujol copy deployed AI models using nothing but questions and answers. Their 2026 paper studies black-box model copying with signed-distance supervision. Deployed systems must evolve as data, architectures, and regulations change. Often the original training data and model internals are gone. Black-box copying offers a practical refactoring path. A replica is learned from input-output queries alone. The legacy model is upgraded without ever being opened.

The authors smooth that copying with signed-distance supervision. A signed distance says how far an input sits from a decision boundary, and on which side. That richer signal guides the replica beyond bare labels. Better copies preserve behavior where it matters most. The method serves teams stuck with models they cannot retrain. It turns a black box into a maintainable asset.
arxiv-2601-20873: P. J. Rijken and Th. A. Rijken give a new way to find the eigenvalues of the Heun equation. Eigenvalues are the special values at which an equation has clean solutions. The Heun equation is a broad form met across physics. Its eigenvalues are hard to pin down. The 2026 paper tests the method on the Breit equation, a two-particle equation from atomic physics.
arxiv-2601-21273:
Tianchen Hu and ten co-authors test how a layered crystal handles very strong light pulses. The crystal belongs to a family with built-in electric order and strong responses to light. Earlier work focused on its simpler response, where light comes out at twice the input frequency.

The team measures stronger effects, where the output reaches much higher multiples of the input frequency. Such high harmonics can serve as tiny light sources and probes of the material itself. The crystal's layered form makes it a good fit for small devices. The results support its use in compact photonics, where strong light effects must fit on a chip.
arxiv-2601-21373:
V.L. Martinez-Consentino, J.E. Amaro, and J. Segovia compute how nuclei answer when neutrinos scatter off pairs of particles inside them. Two particles can be knocked out together by exchange currents between nucleons. That two-body response is a key input for reading neutrino experiments.

The authors study how the response scales across many nuclei, from helium up to uranium. Their model treats proton and neutron densities with separate momentum scales. Asymmetric nuclei, where the two counts differ a lot, get special care. The scaling rules help experiments predict signals without a fresh heavy calculation for every target.
arxiv-2601-21473:
Zaifeng Pan and eight co-authors make large multi-agent simulations cheaper to run. Simulations where each agent is a language model are spreading across many fields. Each agent keeps private state on the graphics chip, and memory fills fast as the agent count grows.

The authors notice two helpful traits of these workloads. Only a few agents are active at any moment, and the order of future calls can be estimated. Their system, ScaleSim, manages memory based on how soon each agent will be called next. That foresight keeps the chip from choking as simulations scale up.
arxiv-2601-21573:
Masaki Miyashita studies how a firm should spread its products across features that buyers care about. The work builds on a hedonic model where a single representative buyer values product characteristics. A monopolist selling several products chooses where each one sits in feature space.

The striking result is that the monopolist's choice matches the social planner's optimum. That holds even though the firm produces too little overall. In other words, the range of products is right even when the volume is wrong. The finding separates two questions policy often mixes: variety can be fine while quantity is the true distortion.
arxiv-2601-21673:
Dexuan Ding and eight co-authors compress brain scans into compact surrogates for Alzheimer's classification. Structural MRI is widely used to spot the disease. Most learning methods use heavy three-dimensional networks, slice-by-slice features, or frozen features from general image models.

Each route has costs in compute or in fit to the task. The authors build multimodal visual surrogates that summarize the scans more directly. A compact summary could make scan-based screening faster and cheaper to deploy. It may also travel better across hospitals, where scanner types and image quality vary a lot.
arxiv-2601-21873:
Jinhang Chai, Xuyuan Liu, Elynn Chen, and Yujun Yan study transfer learning for structured matrices. Learning systems often grow over time: new features arrive and internal representations expand into larger spaces. Earlier representations end up embedded inside bigger ones, with only limited new structure added.

The team studies how to transfer an estimate from a well-solved source task to a larger target task. Their matrices combine a low-rank part, which holds the main pattern, with a sparse part for exceptions. The 2026 preprint develops theory for this transfer as both the ambient dimension and the inner representation grow. Such results guide fields like recommendation and imaging, where models are retrained on ever wider data.
arxiv-2601-21973:
Erin Dawson extends a counting theory in tropical geometry. Tropical Tevelev degrees arise from maps between tropical moduli spaces of curves, counting how curves meet given conditions in a simplified, combinatorial version of geometry. Dawson and Cavalieri defined and computed these degrees in one specific case.

That case used a particular relation between the degree of the maps and the genus of the curves, with a fixed count of marked points. Dawson's 2026 preprint adds a new integer parameter to the theory, widening the family of degrees that can be defined and studied. Tropical counts often mirror classical algebraic geometry results, so each extension enlarges a dictionary between combinatorics and geometry.
arxiv-2601-22773:
Sung Une Lee and a team give builders a reusable template for safety cases for AI systems. A safety case is a structured argument that a system is safe enough. Their 2026 preprint notes that classic cases, from aviation and nuclear work, assume fixed bounds and known failure modes.

Modern AI breaks those assumptions: it shifts, learns, and acts on its own. Their template framework adapts the case form to that reality. Reusable parts can lift the floor for AI governance. The work serves regulators and builders alike. It turns a craft into a kit.
arxiv-2601-23173:
Chris Sherlock, Andrew Golightly, and Anthony Lee fix a failure mode in particle filtering for hidden Markov models. Sometimes every simulated particle scores zero likelihood for an observation, so the filter collapses. Then the filtering distribution cannot be estimated and the parameter likelihood reads zero.

Their partially alive scheme, nicknamed the Frankenfilter, keeps such runs going in a principled way. It slots into particle Metropolis-Hastings, a standard inference method. Robust filters matter for tracking, epidemiology, and finance, where zero-likelihood steps occur in real data. Partially alive particles keep the filter estimable through stretches where a naive particle set would collapse to zero.
arxiv-2602-00073: Yurui Wu and coauthors study test time adaptation for time series that drift, where a model trained on past data loses accuracy as conditions change. Their light method freezes the main model and updates only normalization affine terms from recent unlabeled windows. For classification it cuts entropy and enforces time consistency. For regression it cuts variance across weak time preserving changes, with an optional teacher, a drift penalty, and a fallback for safety.
arxiv-2602-00173: Shuozhe Li and colleagues train robust reasoning through guided adversarial self play, called GASP. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards yields strong reasoners, yet those models can fail badly when context is flawed. Flaws include corrupted chains of thought, misleading partial solutions, or slight input shifts. GASP builds a self play game inside one model: a polluter learns to induce failure with locally coherent corruptions, while an agent learns diagnosis and recovery. An imitation term on self generated repairs raises early recovery rates while preserving prior skills.
arxiv-2602-00273: CMS Collaboration searches for heavy scalar resonances decaying to Lorentz boosted Higgs and Higgs like bosons in the bb4q final state at 13 TeV. The search targets a heavy scalar X that decays to a Higgs boson H plus a Higgs like scalar Y. H decays to two bottom quarks, while Y decays through vector bosons to four quarks. X masses run 900 to 4000 GeV, and Y masses run 60 to 2800 GeV. Jet finding and mass rebuilding use machine learning, including a novel attention based particle transformer.
arxiv-2602-00373: Amartya Chakrabortty and Abu Sufian study homogenization of control for nonlocal semilinear elasticity with soft inclusions. The domain holds a matrix phase and a soft phase, with small parameters for periodicity and contrast, and control only in the inclusion region. With an L2 tracking cost on displacement, they analyze the limit as both parameters tend to zero, their ratio tending to a finite or infinite constant. They derive the homogenized limit state system and prove microscopic controls converge to a limit control for the limit problem via Gamma convergence.
arxiv-2602-00473: Jin-Long Chen and colleagues build a hybrid quantum-classical attention model for recognising phases in many-body systems. Conventional tools struggle with tangled correlation patterns in large systems, so the model reads correlations in quantum states via swap tests and a parameterised circuit, then sorts ground states. Trials on the cluster-Ising model at 9 and 15 qubits reach high accuracy with fewer than 100 training examples and stay steady when the training set changes. The model also picks out phase-sensitive features and characteristic length scales.
arxiv-2602-00573: Zheng Zhang and colleagues formalise stage-aware learning, where a class is learned through stages rather than treated as static. In practice one class can change form, as a larva becomes a butterfly, so a model must separate classes and track within-class change. They introduce Stage-Bench, a two-stage benchmark for forgetting and degradation, and STAGE, a baseline that splits identity from evolution dynamics via a memory pool. Conventional reductions and continual-learning baselines fall short, while STAGE beats rivals, showing explicit evolution-aware modelling pays off.
arxiv-2602-00673: Jiří Kabát and colleagues study how the plasmonic response of vanadium dioxide nanoparticles changes with size and with the insulator-metal transition. They track the dipole peak, higher modes, breathing modes, and bulk losses as size varies, using in-place spectroscopy at high resolution that records electron energy loss. Through the transition, near-infrared absorption switches on and off gradually, with the peak shifting by 0.18 eV for a 120 nm particle. The authors suggest the effect should extend to larger, higher-aspect-ratio structures, widening tunability for vanadium dioxide devices.
arxiv-2602-00773: Huiqian Lai investigates the Keep4o backlash after OpenAI replaced GPT-4o with GPT-5, a clash between fast platform iteration and deep user attachment to AI systems. Analysing 1,482 social media posts with mixed methods, the study finds two roots of resistance. One is instrumental dependency, with the AI woven into professional workflows. The findings suggest that for companionship and deeply integrated systems, preserving user agency during change can matter as much as the technology itself.
arxiv-2602-00873: I. A. Aleksandrov and colleagues compute the induced electron-positron current, momentum-resolved particle yields, and energy and angular momentum tensors. They study vacuum change in a changing outside electric field of any polarization with quantum kinetic equations. They extend a revised equation set from earlier work, using an adiabatic basis of Hamiltonian functions in a uniform field. They detail the charge-renormalization step removing log divergences, and show a match with Dirac-Heisenberg-Wigner results. The analysis gives a firmer theory base for nonperturbative strong-field effects.
arxiv-2602-00973: Avinash Ajit Nargund and colleagues test radar-based warnings for people walking in outdoor virtual reality. Millimeter-wave radar spots obstacles without filming faces, guarding bystander privacy, but its sparse maps need display. The team rebuilt WaveWalkerClone to prove radar plus GPS-IMU sensing works in varied outdoor light. A study with 18 users compared three displays: story-fit alien avatars, out-of-story human avatars, and plain point clouds. All three aided safety and awareness, yet differed on effort, frustration, and taste, so no single design fits all users.
arxiv-2602-01273: Xun Zhang and co-authors build Q-DiT4SR, the first low-bit quant plan made for diffusion-transformer super-resolution. Past quant plans aim at U-Nets or text-to-picture nets, and slapping them onto super-resolution nets wrecks textures. Their H-SVD plan pairs global and local rank branches under a single size budget. A variance-wise mixed-bit plan then sets layer and step bit widths from rate-distortion lore and dynamic programming. Tests show top scores under tight W4A6 and W4A4 bit plans.
arxiv-2602-01373: Wen-Zhong Li and co-authors track quasi-periodic oscillation lag modes in RE J1034+396 across 10 XMM-Newton looks. The oscillation flips between two lag modes, hard and soft, that swap into each other. Though lag traits differ, the root-mean-square amplitude shape matches in both modes, hinting at one engine. Spectral reads tie lag modes to spectral states: soft-lag times pair with harder X-ray spectra and hotter glows. A relativistic precession model of the corona offers a plausible tale for the flips and spectral shifts.
arxiv-2602-01473: Romain Branchereau studies a geometric theta correspondence linking a modular curve's first homology to weight 2 modular forms. From Stevens' account of that homology, he tracks where the map sends three kinds of objects. Modular symbols go to products of weight one Eisenstein series; caps go to weight 2 Eisenstein series, while hyperbolic cycles go to diagonal restrictions of Hilbert-Eisenstein series. He then uses it to revisit Borisov and Gunnells and clarify its link to a theorem of Li. The payoff is a geometric proof of relations among Eisenstein series.
arxiv-2602-01573: McAlinn and Takanashi ask when updates from a loss count as Bayesian. They split updates into belief based ones, backed by Savage and Anscombe Aumann foundations, and decision based ones, backed by tastes over choice rules. Their result says the two match ordinary Bayes exactly when the loss equals negative log likelihood, apart from a scale change and a term that uses only the data. They warn that for decision based updates, the generalized marginal likelihood carries no weight as proof, and Bayes factors lack meaning without structure.
arxiv-2602-01673: Enguang Fan tests NetVLAD as a loop closure for SLAM, where recognizing places lets pose constraints correct drift. Bag of words methods run fast but degrade under appearance change and aliasing, while place descriptors resist them yet cost too much for real time. Fan compares NetVLAD against DBoW on KITTI. He introduces a top K precision recall curve for cases where a query may have zero or several matches. With Faiss search, NetVLAD reaches real time speed and beats DBoW on accuracy and robustness, making it an alternative for SLAM.
arxiv-2602-01973: Muli Yang and colleagues fix bias in AI image detectors, which often misclassify fake images as real. Models overfit surface artifacts that fail across generation methods, misaligning decision thresholds under shift. The team offers a post hoc calibration framework from Bayesian theory, adding a scalar correction to model logits, tuned on a small target set with the backbone frozen. This adjustment offsets output shift, realigning the boundary without labels. Benchmark tests show improved robustness without retraining, a light fix for reliable adaptive detection.
arxiv-2602-02173: Jiancheng Tu and others propose a mixed-integer programming method for learning globally optimal classification trees under nonlinear metrics such as the F1 score. Optimal trees are prized for clarity. Global tuning has only recently become real on real data, and standard methods handle class imbalance poorly. The method pairs flexible mixed-integer models with a tailored branch-and-cut method, instance reduction, and warm-start plans. On fifty benchmark data, it optimizes nonlinear metrics efficiently with strong predictive results and shorter answer times than current methods.
arxiv-2602-02373:
Andrés Franco-Grisales and 1 co-author connect three lines of research on how the universe could begin at a calm big bang, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A quiescent singularity is a big bang where the geometry stays controlled rather than chaotic. Past work derived long-time behavior in symmetric cases, built spacetimes from data placed on the singularity itself, and proved big bangs form without symmetry.

The missing link was whether the spacetimes in the third line actually induce data on the singularity, as the second line requires. Franco-Grisales and his co-author prove that solutions from a recent general formation result do induce such data. The argument is more general than that single case. It may apply in other gauges, meaning other choices for labeling time and space in the equations.
arxiv-2602-02573:
Haonan Dong and 2 co-authors rebuild neural network design on algebra, treating multiplication as the basic act, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Convolutional, attention, state-space, and equivariant networks are usually built as separate crafts despite sharing recurring principles. Their scheme, product interactions, treats data as algebraic elements and builds networks by stacking multiplication operators.

How inputs act on themselves sets the order. Within the scheme, convolutional and equivariant networks emerge as symmetry-bound first-order cases. Attention arises as a third-order interaction from reusing the same operator. The Mamba design is recovered by raising a state-space model's interaction order from one to three. Such rules produce familiar structures: translation symmetry yields convolution, and rotational fit yields the Clebsch-Gordan product. A new simple layer built from these ideas beat Mamba on CIFAR-10 in both accuracy and throughput.
arxiv-2602-03173:
Georgi Bebrov, in solo work dated 2026, aims to push quantum key spread to still longer distances. Sending-or-not-sending plans already achieve the longest known transmission distances for sharing secret keys through quantum signals. Bebrov offers a variant that combines that principle with phase matching, improving tolerance to phase mismatch, which otherwise degrades the key rate as distance and instability grow in long optical links.

Security is analyzed in the asymptotic, infinite-key regime under collective attacks. Results is compared with standard phase-matching plans, theory-based and experimental twin-field variants, including an test spanning about a thousand kilometers. The new plan achieved greater transmission distances than those earlier methods in the analysis. Bebrov presents it as a option for long-distance quantum communication.
arxiv-2602-03373:
Watermarking methods that look alike but behave differently are unified by Jiale Meng, leading 5 other authors, through a dimension-aware mapping view. Deep watermarking systems share similar encoder-decoder architectures yet differ substantially in functional actions. Their system, DiM, formulates watermarking as mapping payloads between dimensions, where information can be a one-part binary message, a two-part spatial mask, or a three-part spatiotemporal form in video or other media.

Dimensional setup of vector and extraction largely determines actions, the authors find. Same-part mappings preserve payload form and support fine-grained control. Cross-part mappings enable spatial or spatiotemporal localization. Instantiated in video, varying only those dimensions produced other capabilities, including tamper localization, local vector control, and recovery of time order under frame disruptions, without architectural changes.
arxiv-2602-03473:
Meng Lou and 2 co-authors push continual learning to sequences of more than 300 tasks in a 2026 paper. Their learner, CaRE, builds on a pre-trained model and must add new classes over time without erasing old ones. Long sequences strain both feature quality and the balance between stability and plasticity.

The core is a bi-level routing mixture-of-experts design. One stage activates the routers relevant to a task, and a second stage selects and blends the experts, injecting richer features at every layer. The authors also release OmniBenchmark-1K, a dataset built for very long class-incremental sequences. CaRE leads on standard benchmarks and, the authors report, is the first learner to scale past 300 tasks.
arxiv-2602-03773:
Ian Wu and 3 co-authors ask whether a model can keep improving far past the horizon it was trained on. Their 2026 paper introduces Reasoning Cache, an iterative decoding algorithm that replaces plain autoregressive decoding in both training and inference. Standard reinforcement learning pins the model to fixed problem distributions and budgets, which limits such extrapolation.

The method exploits an asymmetry: models summarize better than they generate. Reasoning chains are built that improve consistently across iterations, each round conditioning on a summary of the last. A four-billion-parameter model trained with a sixteen-thousand-token budget climbs from forty to nearly seventy percent. The benchmark is a hard mathematics test, and the climb uses half a million test-time tokens. It also stacks well with existing scaffolds.
arxiv-2602-04073:
A classic completeness proof in conditional logic may rest on a technical shortcut. Alexander W. Kocurek and 2 co-authors examine the logic C2, which reasons about if-then statements with quantifiers. The known proof lets selection functions operate on formulas. But the theory's founder insisted they should operate on propositions, meaning sets of possible worlds.

The authors prove the result cannot be extended: under the propositional reading, the logic is frame incomplete. The failure survives changes in domain assumptions and added predicates. Their result reopens basic questions about how conditional logic should be built and what its semantics really commits us to.
arxiv-2602-04273: The smallest galaxies known break a tidy rule linking mass and motion. James Chi Chung Wong's 2026 paper is part eight of a series on variable modified Newtonian mechanics. It takes up the velocity dispersions of ultra faint dwarf galaxies in the Milky Way. Their measured motions depart markedly from the baryon Tully-Fisher relation that massive galaxies obey. Wong proposes that his variable modified Newtonian dynamics model explains the deviation. The note is brief, offering a modified-gravity account of why these faint systems move as they do.
arxiv-2602-04673:
Nathanaël Berestycki and Isao Sauzedde prove a long-standing conjecture about Brownian motion in a 2026 probability paper. Brownian motion is the random wandering path seen in pollen grains and stock charts alike. Their construction builds it from simpler random objects.

Take a radial SLE path, a random curve from conformal geometry, and add every loop from a Brownian loop soup that the curve meets, in time order. The authors show the resulting stitched path is continuous and has exactly the law of planar Brownian motion. This settles a conjecture by Lawler and Werner. The same coupling appears as the scaling limit of a random walk and its loop-erased version, tying discrete and continuous models together.
arxiv-2602-04773:
Bernhard Schmiedmayer and 3 co-authors predict a tensor property of materials using only scalar machine learning models in a 2026 paper. The target is the Born effective charge tensor, which describes how polarization shifts when atoms move. Tensor targets often demand specially designed tensorial inputs.

Their trick uses the definition: the tensor is a derivative of polarization with respect to atomic displacement. Scalar kernel models, called monopole models here, can thus capture its tensorial nature. The authors compare this with past tensorial dipole kernel models that encode structure directly. Both support charge partitioning into monopole and dipole parts. As a test, they computed finite-temperature infrared spectra for several complex materials.
arxiv-2602-04873:
Diffusion models can now generate images direct from the patch features of a self-supervised encoder, but those dense patch grids carry heavy redundancy. Ramón Calvo-González and François Fleuret built FlatDINO, an autoencoder that compresses that representation into a short one-dimensional run of continuous tokens. The squeeze cuts sequence length eightfold and total size far more.

A large diffusion transformer trained on those latents scored well on ImageNet generation while using a fraction of the compute per step of the uncompressed version. The authors are plain that these are preliminary results and the work is in progress. Even so, the savings point to a cheaper route for feature-space diffusion.
arxiv-2602-05073:
Language model agents act over many turns, so knowing when they are unsure matters more than in one-shot question answering. Changdae Oh and 10 co-authors argue in this 2026 paper, accepted at ACL 2026, that uncertainty research has not kept pace with agents. Most current methods still target single-turn setups and lack a principled frame for interactive systems.

The paper lays three pillars for later work. First, a general form of agent uncertainty that holds earlier setups as special cases. Second, four named hurdles: picking an estimator, handling uncertainty across mixed kinds of entities, tracking how uncertainty shifts during interaction, and the lack of fine-grained benchmarks. Numerical study on a real agent benchmark shows them in action. Third, a talk of practical effects and open problems. The aim is reducible uncertainty, doubt that better modeling can truly shrink.
arxiv-2602-05473:
A new kind of hybrid particle is predicted by M. Nursagatov, Xiyin Ye, and 3 co-authors, formed when light couples with waves inside a ferroelectric layer. The stack they study places that layer between two superconductors, and the coupled waves are called ferrons on the material side and Swihart photons on the light side. Together they form what the authors name a ferron-polariton.

The coupling is reported to reach the ultrastrong regime, with an energy gap in the terahertz range that is far larger than in magnetic counterparts. That strength reflects how strongly electric dipoles interact compared with magnetic ones. Beyond the prediction itself, seeing this effect would give direct evidence that ferrons exist. The authors present the layered structure as a new platform for extreme light-matter coupling. They also point to fast, ferroelectric-based quantum devices working at terahertz speeds as a long-term goal.
arxiv-2602-05773:
The traveling salesman problem asks for the shortest tour through a set of cities, and Yılmaz Arslanoğlu presents a short note linking it to a tree problem. He defines a constrained Group Steiner Tree Problem on a simplicial incidence graph built from the complete weighted graph of cities. The graph is bipartite, joining triangles to edges.

Choosing an admissible, disk like set of triangles in that graph induces a unique boundary cycle. With global connectivity and local regularity constraints added, maximizing net weight in the tree problem is exactly equivalent to minimizing the tour length in the salesman problem. The note is a brief communication, four pages with three figures, prepared for submission to an operations research journal. It is a structural result rather than a new algorithm. Its interest lies in recasting a classic routing problem in the language of Steiner trees and incidence geometry.
arxiv-2602-05973:
Quantum theory usually keeps its math Hermitian, a rule that keeps probabilities sane. Oem Trivedi and Alfredo Gurrola ask what happens if that rule is loosened inside quantum cosmology, by extending the Wheeler-DeWitt frame beyond strictly Hermitian dynamics. In their version, anti-Hermitian terms act like damping or gain, shaping both early ripples in the universe and later growth of structure.

They test the frame against inflation data, growth of structure, and the near flatness of the universe. The result is a set of strong infrared limits that push non-Hermiticity down across cosmic history, with early and late tests agreeing. The limits can ease a little in theories beyond general relativity. The paper turns cosmology into a test bed for a basic rule of quantum mechanics, and hints that Hermiticity itself may emerge as the universe evolves.
arxiv-2602-06473:
Wind pushing on the ocean's surface drives drift currents, and the classical theory of them flattens Earth into a plane. Christian Puntini and 2 co-authors derive a model that keeps the planet's spherical geometry. Starting from the full flow equations in rotating spherical coordinates, they allow depth-varying density and eddy viscosity.

A careful scaling produces two small parameters, tied to rotation and to the thinness of the wind-driven layer. Expanding in both gives simple leading-order equations with nonlinear boundary conditions. The leading dynamics are linear; energy input and loss enter only at higher order. For Ekman-type flows they prove the leading solution exists, is unique, and keeps the classical spiral structure for any viscosity profile. Comparisons with Sverdrup's classic theory follow.
arxiv-2602-06573:
Quantum dots made from indium antimonide nanosheets are a promising platform for topological superconductivity, and Xingjun Wu and 8 co-authors built one coupled to superconductors on both sides. A bottom bilayer gate defines the dot and tunes its coupling to the leads. The dot showed large magnetic response factors and strong spin-orbit coupling.

Transport measurements revealed Coulomb diamond patterns with alternating even-odd sizes and sharp features tied to the superconducting gap, confirming a few-electron regime. At odd occupation, Kondo signatures appeared, including a zero-bias peak that split in a magnetic field and faded logarithmically with temperature. As coupling strengthened, Andreev bound states switched from crossing to anticrossing, marking a doublet-singlet quantum phase transition.
arxiv-2602-06673:
Xin Hu, Yuya Ominato, and Mamoru Matsuo give a theoretical study of a hybrid device that joins a thin transition metal dichalcogenide layer to a ferromagnetic insulator. A heat-driven effect, the spin Seebeck effect, excites spins in the magnet, and the question is whether the paired valleys in the thin layer can sort that spin flow. A magnetic field applied across the layers splits the valley energy levels unevenly.

The authors show that spin-valley locking in the thin layer, together with the uneven level structure, can generate a spin current that is also valley-polarized. They compare currents arising from the conduction and valence bands and explain their different microscopic origins. Their clearest prediction is a set of quantum oscillations in the valley-polarized current, a measurable fingerprint of the quantized valley states.
arxiv-2602-06873:
Shaoshi Chen and four co-authors study how to integrate functions in fields that hold Weierstrass-like quantities. Those quantities obey a first-order equation that is not linear, so they sit beyond the reach of plain integration theory. Computer algebra can handle many functions, but elliptic-style builds need their own rules.

The team extends the old idea of special polynomials to these Weierstrass-like fields, then builds step-by-step reduction rules on top of that extension. Reduction is the core move in deciding whether an integral can be written in closed form. As a payoff, they derive new closed formulas for integrals of powers of the Weierstrass function itself.
arxiv-2602-07073:
Nardine Basta and five co-authors build a proactive defense for enterprise networks against zero-day attacks. In today's firms, perimeter plus distributed firewall rules govern connectivity. Automated tools now generate those rules and access policies, yet risks from dynamically generated policies, above all exposure of critical assets, remain hard to manage. Networks keep shifting too, with remote users, personal devices, and cloud links.

Their system, Pro-ZD, uses a graph neural network to find weighted shortest paths through the network. Those paths reveal misconfigurations and high-risk links that could threaten critical assets and be exploited through undisclosed flaws. Pro-ZD then tunes firewall rules and access policies on its own to close high-risk links and block unauthorized access. Tests show robustness and transferability, with over 95 percent average accuracy at spotting high-risk links across settings.
arxiv-2602-07473:
Partially observable Markov decision processes model choices under uncertainty, but computing optimal reachability probabilities for them is known to be impossible in general. Nathanaël Fijalkow and four co-authors carve out a tractable class: posterior-deterministic POMDPs.

For that class, the best chance of reaching a target set can be estimated to any precision, in sharp contrast to the general no-method result. Verification and synthesis teams get a new island of solvable cases in POMDP theory, with a precise setting marking where estimates become possible. The new class thus opens checking problems that were out of reach before for partly observable systems.
arxiv-2602-07573:
Graph domain adaptation moves knowledge from labeled source graphs to unlabeled target graphs, but most methods assume both graphs are homophilic, where neighbors share labels.  Ruiyi Fang and ten co-authors drop that assumption with a homophily-agnostic method that handles varying homophily on both sides.

A divide-and-conquer strategy reconstructs highly homophilic and heterophilic variants of source and target graphs separately, then aligns knowledge between matching variants.  Experiments on five benchmarks show superior results where homophily varies.  Graph learning teams get adaptation that works whether neighbors agree or disagree, a common reality the field long assumed away.
arxiv-2602-07873:
Soft policies in reinforcement learning balance exploration and exploitation by sampling actions in proportion to their estimated values, but implementing that sampling is awkward. Donghyeon Ki and three co-authors realize soft-policy sampling directly with Langevin dynamics, which follows the gradient of the action-value function to draw samples without an explicit policy network.

Plain Langevin sampling mixes slowly in high-dimensional, rugged value landscapes, so they add multi-scale noise conditioning to the value function, yielding Noise-Conditioned Langevin Q-Learning. The resulting method samples from the target Boltzmann distribution more effectively while keeping entropy estimates tractable. Reinforcement-learning teams gain a more expressive, principled alternative to parametric and diffusion-based policies.
arxiv-2602-07973:
Neurosymbolic learning trains neural classifiers whose hidden labels must satisfy a logical formula, but the number of label combinations that satisfy the formula can explode. Aaditya Naik and four co-authors propose CLIPPER, a technique that prunes that space using the intuition that inputs with similar internal representations likely share labels.

Because logical constraints couple labels together, pruning is formulated as an integer linear program that discards inconsistent combinations while respecting the formula's structure. The method works alongside existing training algorithms rather than replacing them. Across sixteen benchmarks on complex tasks, it makes neurosymbolic learning tractable where exhaustive enumeration would stall, giving researchers a scalable tool for combining neural perception with logical reasoning.
arxiv-2602-08273:
Fixed-wing drones need reliable pose and airspeed gauges from motion sensors and Pitot tubes, with guarantees that hold from almost any starting state. Melone Nyoba Tchonkeu and two co-authors build a cascade watcher: a Riccati-type filter first gauges body-frame air speed and tilt from motion data with Pitot outputs. Then a curved watcher on the spin group mixes tilt with compass data for full pose.

Under mild input, the gauging errors are flatly seen, and strict analysis shows almost global long-run calm of the whole cascade. Validation on real flight data confirms the theory. Aerospace engineers gain an estimator with strong guarantees for a safety-critical drone subsystem, not just good results in model.
arxiv-2602-08673:
Branch-price-and-cut solves vehicle routing exactly, but its column generation follows linear-relaxation signals that may mislead integer solutions. Lukas Eveborn and Elina Rönnberg propose a primal heuristic based on pricing for integrality to find good integer solutions earlier. Their arXiv paper targets electric vehicle routing with time windows and charging slots.

The heuristic builds a partial integer solution from the column pool, then iteratively searches for columns that complement it, guided by modified pricing, dual information, and previously generated columns. Tests show it closes thirty to forty percent of the root-node gap on average versus a restricted-master heuristic. Readers get a practical accelerator for exact routing solvers.
arxiv-2602-08973:
Thanawuth Thanathibodee and six co-authors catch a young star's disk changing fast. A 2024 JWST observation of the transitional disk around CVSO 1942 shows mid-infrared light at wavelengths under 10 microns doubled versus the near-photospheric level Spitzer saw in 2005. Longer wavelengths, above about 15 microns, show no significant change.

Comparing the new spectrum with NEOWISE photometry pins the brightening to a span of just two weeks. The pattern fits warm dust near 1,400 kelvin, optically thick and made of grains at least a micron across, sitting near the dust sublimation radius. The authors propose fresh dust forming in place, possibly from planetesimal collisions in the inner disk.
arxiv-2602-09073:
Sagar Mandal and one co-author count sum-dominant, difference-dominant, and balanced subsets of the dicyclic group Dic-4n. For subsets of size two, exact counts show the sum-dominant and balanced families grow equally fast as n increases. Size three is richer: for odd n, exact counts depend on whether n is divisible by 3.

In that size-three case, sum-dominant subsets asymptotically outnumber each of the other two kinds six to one. A lower bound for the boundary case of size 2n completes the picture. The results map the sum-versus-difference landscape of dicyclic groups with unusual precision.
arxiv-2602-09173:
Small, specialized language models can reason surprisingly well when trained with verifiable rewards, and Ryozo Masukawa and ten co-authors ask whether teams of them can do better together. Their n-Musketeers design links several frozen, heterogeneous expert models through their internal hidden states, joined by a trainable attention interface, a scheme called soft hidden-state collaboration.

On Reasoning Gym and GSM8K, the latent team competes with strong single-model baselines. Ablations reveal two regimes: on simpler arithmetic, gains mostly reflect static expert preferences, while harder settings drive increasingly concentrated, structured attention, a sign of emergent specialization. The design offers both a compact way to reuse frozen experts and a window into how collaboration evolves under training.
arxiv-2602-09373:
Translation tools still serve African languages poorly, and heavy models fit badly on the modest devices many users own. Yasmin Moslem and two co-authors present AfriNLLB, a 2026 family of lightweight translation models for African languages in both directions. The suite covers fifteen language pairs, thirty directions in all, from Swahili and Hausa to Zulu, Lingala, Wolof, and Egyptian Arabic, plus wider official languages.

Training spans English paired with thirteen languages and French paired with two more. The models start from a six-hundred-million-parameter base, then shrink through iterative layer pruning and quantization, with fine-tuning on curated parallel texts and distillation from a larger teacher. Performance matches the baseline while running far faster. Two versions are released, one for further fine-tuning and one for fast inference, along with the training data.
arxiv-2602-09873:
Qudit-based quantum computers have lacked their own native rules for proving when two circuits match. Colin Blake closes that gap in his 2026 paper with a first finite schematic theory for exact unitary qudit circuits. It works for every finite dimension of two or more, and it is both sound and complete.

Circuits combine local gates in sequence and side by side, plus controls tied to a chosen basis value. For each dimension, the theory rests on a short finite set of local axiom schemata with bounded arity. The diagram shapes stay the same across dimensions. Two circuits can then be proved equal exactly when their standard unitary meanings agree. The local rules also yield the internal algebra of controlled operations inside the circuit PROP. The result is a finite basis, uniform across dimensions, for exact reasoning about qudit circuits.
arxiv-2602-10273:
Thought gains in large language models are often credited to distribution sharpening, which piles output probability onto high-likelihood sequences. A 2026 paper led by Seyedarmin Azizi, with four co-authors, offers Power-SMC, a training-free sampling method aiming at the sequence-level power distribution at close to standard decoding latency. Earlier Metropolis-Hastings sampling reached the same distribution only with tenfold slowdowns.

Power-SMC keeps several candidate sequences side by side, scoring each by an importance weight measuring fit to the power distribution, then regularly pruning low scorers for high scorers. Theory backs the design. Among next-token strategies ignoring future tokens, one sampling temperature alone removes per-step weight variance. The method thus delivers sharpened thought without retraining or heavy latency cost.
arxiv-2602-10573:
Ruisheng Shi and seven co-authors detect hidden cryptomining in encrypted traffic in a 2026 paper. Blacklists and deep packet inspection fail against encrypted mining streams and suffer high false-positive rates, leaving networks exposed to resource theft. The paper proposes a useful two-stage finding system.

Machine learning first classifies traffic at fine granularity, then active probing cuts false positives from the classifier. The system reports a very high F1 score and identifies exact cryptocurrencies with near-perfect scores in the authors' tests. Extensive testing across mining pools supports the claims. The work offers network defenders a more precise instrument against mining that hides inside ordinary encrypted flows.
arxiv-2602-10773:
Tomás Caraballo and two co-authors develop a second-order random number scheme in a 2026 paper. The goal is a random transfer of the well-known deterministic TR-BDF2 method. Most random methods lose order compared with their deterministic counterparts, so keeping second-order scores in the random setting is nontrivial.

The paper constructs the scheme, proves its second-order scores and A-steadiness, and analyzes mean-square steadiness across parameter ranges. Comparisons with the Ito-Taylor approximation of order two reveal scenarios of interest. For certain step sizes, the new method is mean-square stable while the older approximation is not. The work gives builders a stable, exact integrator for random differential rules where order and steadiness both matter.
arxiv-2602-10873:
Yue Zhang and nine co-authors experimentally study matter-wave four-wave mixing in potassium condensates in a 2026 paper. Using Bose-Einstein condensates of potassium-39 with contacts tuned via Feshbach resonances, they study mixing in two shaped shapes. In the single-spin configuration, yield grows with larger scattering length.

For the two-spin configuration, the team explores both droplet and gas parameter regimes, finding yield peaks near the key region between gas and droplet phases. The research can help optimize mixing yield for matter-wave amplification and entangled atom pair making, with uses in quantum information processing and sharp measurement. The tests map where uneven matter-wave mixing works best.
arxiv-2602-10973:
Quark masses look other depending on the scheme used to define them. Long Chen and three co-authors compute three-loop mixed strong and electromagnetic corrections to on-shell quark mass and wave-function factors. Their scope covers every split of three loops between the two forces.

From those factors they derive the three-loop link between pole mass and the standard modified minimal-subtraction mass for a heavy quark, with full mixed terms included. They also extract the mass anomalous dimension when both forces act, and give conversion rules to a trace-anomaly subtracted mass at the same order. The results feed precision quark physics, where small mass shifts change forecasts.
arxiv-2602-11473:
Reconfigurable surfaces can bend radar around corners, but practical phase tuning matters. Kainat Yasmeen and two co-authors compare two surface configurations for around-the-corner radar: analogue phase tuning that realizes idealized single beams, and low-hardness one-bit quantized tuning that yields dual symmetric beams. Both are benchmarked against a metal plate of similar size.

Simulations and measurements test how rounding affects radar cross-section and coverage at non-specular angles. The study clarifies what is lost and gained when moving from ideal analogue control to cheap quantized control, guiding designers who must balance beam quality against hardware simplicity in reconfigurable radar surfaces.
arxiv-2602-11673:
Searching a large library of 3D objects by text is hard when objects arrive in random orientations and span hundreds of categories, since most methods demand canonical poses and cover few classes. Khanh Nguyen and three co-authors propose RI-Mamba, the first rotation-invariant state-space model for point clouds. It defines global and local reference frames to separate pose from geometry, orders points with Hilbert sorting to build geometrically meaningful token sequences, and recovers spatial context through orientational embeddings.

Training uses cross-modal contrastive learning with automatically generated triplets, so diverse datasets need no manual annotation. The model runs in linear time and proves robust across more than 200 object categories under arbitrary orientations, setting a new best on the OmniObject3D benchmark. For virtual reality and gaming libraries, that means text search that works on objects as they are found, not as they were posed.
arxiv-2602-11773:
For a directed graph with a linear order on its vertices, the backedge graph links pairs that appear as backward arcs under that order. The directed clique number is the smallest possible size of the largest clique in such a backedge graph, minimized over all orders. Grzegorz Gutowski and one co-author ask how hard it is to decide whether that number is at most a given value.

The problem has a fast algorithm when the target is one, and it is known to be NP-complete for every fixed target of three or more, even for tournaments. This note closes the remaining gap: when the target is given as part of the input, the problem is complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. The classification pins down exactly where the problem sits in complexity theory.
arxiv-2602-12073: Tove Dahn considers hypoelliptic symbols over a very regular Lie group and discusses monodromy for a spectral stratification, drawing on results of Nilsson and Bäcklund. The short note places monodromy phenomena for hypoelliptic symbols in the setting of highly regular groups and stratified spectra. The discussion builds on results of Nilsson and Bäcklund for hypoelliptic symbols, applying their work to the monodromy question in this regular-group setting.
arxiv-2602-12373:
Opioid policy is hard to test before rollout, because policies interact in a dynamic system where fixing one risk path can worsen another. Yijun Ma led this work with six co-authors, presenting Policy4OOD, a knowledge-guided world model for simulating policy interventions against the overdose crisis. Good evaluation needs three skills: forecasting under current policy, counterfactual reasoning about past choices, and optimisation over candidate interventions.

Policy4OOD joins policy knowledge graphs, state-level spatial links, and socioeconomic time series in a policy-conditioned transformer that forecasts opioid outcomes. Once trained, it simulates by forward pass, swaps policy encodings for counterfactuals, and searches interventions with Monte Carlo tree search. Built on a state-level monthly data set from 2019 to 2024, it shows spatial links and structured policy knowledge both sharpen forecasts.
arxiv-2602-13173:
Staying near a target while a flow pushes you away and noise jostles you costs work, and the price of sharpness is the question here. Till Welker and Patrick Pietzonka study optimal control of a propelled particle in finite time, tuning swim velocity and diffusivity over time, without feedback. Closeness, measured by mean squared deviation from the target, trades against energetic cost, complementing the sharpness-cost trade-off known in random thermodynamics.

Closeness beyond a threshold demands active driving, with cost rising as closeness lifts. Optimal protocols jump discontinuously between passive drift with vanishing diffusivity and active propulsion. Time-linked diffusivity thus enhances optimal control, and the results set cost-closeness benchmarks for artificial self-propelled particles navigating noisy, flowing settings.
arxiv-2602-13273:
Merging expert language models avoids retraining, but current tools treat weights as plain files and merge in one blind pass, wasting disk reads and rescanning parameters as experts pile up. MergePipe treats merging as a data management problem instead, with a catalog of parameters, merge plans, and execution history. A cost-aware planner models expert reads against a user-set input-output budget, and a streaming engine then builds the merged model with transactional safety.

The key insight is that expert reads, not base reads or output writes, dominate merge cost, and budgeting them tames the linear growth of naive pipelines. In tests, total input-output fell by up to tenfold, with end-to-end speedups up to 11 times over leading pipelines. Yuanyi Wang leads the work with eight co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13673:
Agent-based network models show rich large-scale behavior, but finding simple laws for that behavior is hard. This framework combines shape-based data analysis with the Equation-Free Method to explore large-scale dynamics of complex networks, shown on Erdos-Renyi-type random networks. A filtering process driven by the density of active nodes yields a coarse-grained large-scale shape measure defined through persistent Betti numbers, compressing data while retaining essential shape features.

Within the Equation-Free framework, a lifting step is achieved from shape properties, and a data-driven evolution law is derived for the large-scale variable. A numerical split-and-stability analysis then probes global behavior and qualitative shifts of the emergent large-scale dynamics, linking tiny agent rules to large-scale patterns. Konstantinos Spiliotis leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13773:
Models trained on smaller, high-quality data sets can beat those trained on much larger noisy corpora, yet systematic methods for large-scale data selection in instruction tuning remain underexplored. This paper studies selection through semantic representation similarity and finds a key limitation of state-of-the-art language-model encoders: they produce highly redundant semantic vectors. Compressed Representation Data Selection addresses that redundancy with two variants: CRDS-R, using Rademacher random projection plus joining of transformer hidden-layer vectors, and CRDS-W, using whitening-based size reduction.

Both variants greatly enhance data quality and beat state-of-the-art representation-based selection. Notably, CRDS-W performs strongly using only 3.5 percent of the data, beating the full-data baseline by an average of 0.71 percent across four data sets. The result shows that removing representation redundancy can beat simply adding more data. Youwei Shu leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14373:
Osvaldo Guzman and one co-author continue a 2026 arXiv investigation of square-bracket operations from chapter 5 of Walks. An operation has the Ramsey club property when, for every club subset of omega-1, some uncountable subset maps entirely into the club under the operation. The second author previously showed the Proper Forcing Axiom gives this property for operations from Aronszajn trees.

This paper extends that result to the other two classes of square-bracket operations. It follows that both the claim that all such operations have the Ramsey club property, and the claim that none do, are consistent with ZFC. In other words, ZFC cannot decide the property for any square-bracket operation. The paper also analyzes the property under Martin's Axiom and the Continuum Hypothesis.
arxiv-2602-14573:
Marcel Moosbrugger and three co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv algebra checker for loops, called Polar. The setup fully autos study of old and chance loops through algebra thought, centered on algebra repeats that grasp loop meaning exactly. Tricks work out exact closed forms of repeats over higher-order moments of values, infer invariants, and derive loop sense to unknown knobs.

Polar handles chance loops with if-statements, poly math, and common chance spreads. Turning loop study into linear repeat cracking lets Polar work out the strongest poly invariant or infer knob sense from closed forms. The system is sound and full within well-set coding model limits, with hardness limits when limits lift. Patchy but sound tricks also work out moments of joined loops deftly.
arxiv-2602-14873:
Linlin Li and colleagues measure the bar fraction in paired galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, testing how interactions affect galactic bars. Close pairs show a significantly reduced bar fraction at projected separations within twenty-five kiloparsecs, compared with isolated galaxies.

The drop is driven almost entirely by systems with clear merger or disturbance signatures, showing tidal interactions suppress bars, and it comes mainly from weak bars while strong bars hold steady. Suppression tracks major mergers most strongly, especially in massive hosts, with a weaker signal in minor mergers for massive galaxies with small bulges. Galaxy encounters, it seems, can erase a bar.
arxiv-2602-15173:
Ge and colleagues compare risky choices between reasoning and conversational language models, minding the description-history gap. Large language models now serve as decision support and agentic workers, yet how they choose under uncertainty remains poorly understood. The team studies choices along two axes: prospect representation, explicit or via outcome history, and decision rationale in the form of explanations. Twenty frontier and open models take part, alongside a matched human experiment and a payoff-maximizing rational agent model as reference points.

Models split into two camps. Reasoning models lean rational, ignore prospect order, gain-loss framing, and explanations, and behave alike for explicit prospects and outcome histories. Conversational models are less rational, slightly more human-like, and sensitive to ordering, framing, and explanation, showing a large description-history gap. Paired tests of open models suggest training for mathematical reasoning is a key factor behind the split.
arxiv-2602-15273:
De Lima and colleagues study regimes for framing-sensitive fine-tuning in language models. Simulation offers a partner to direct study, with fine-tuned language models enabling agent studies. Fine-tuning often induces broad shifts, including bias drift, broken shortcuts, and base task changes, hurting trust. The central challenge is inducing local decision shifts while preserving overall behavior outside the target.

The team studies how steady supervised fine-tuning is, lowering loss on chosen training slices to shift false-claim belief. They offer FrameRef, a dataset of same-meaning claims with controlled surface framings across five dimensions: Authoritative, Consensus, Emotional, Sensationalist, and Prestige. They present a method for finding per-model steady zones where aimed error shifts can be induced while preserving overall accuracy and tuning. A stepwise showing task over FrameRef shows small framing-linked shifts build into very different total results under replies, but largely disappear without replies.
arxiv-2602-15373:
Dilsiz and colleagues offer a review of street grasp in India English and Aussie English across seven top word models. They build two sets: WEB, with 377 web-taken cases from Urban Dictionary, and GEN, with 1,492 made usages of street words. They test models on three jobs: target word guessing, led guessing, and target word choice.

Findings show better scores on choice versus guessing jobs, with hits rising from three hundredths to about forty-nine hundredths. Scores are better on WEB versus GEN sets, with likeness rising by three hundredths and five hundredths across guessing jobs. India English jobs beat Aussie English jobs when mean across models and sets, with choice showing the top gap, increasing hits from forty-four hundredths to fifty-four hundredths. These results stress gaps between making and picking skills for variety-own word use, notably for street phrases in a deep word such as English.
arxiv-2602-15673:
Tahir and colleagues revisit Leicester City famous 2015-16 Premier League title through expected goals modelling. Probabilistic models are good tools for judging team strength, but an open question is whether they can reflect real performance while giving sensible odds to freak outcomes. The team builds an inference-based frame on expected goals, turning shot-level data into season simulations of points, ranks, and outcome chances.

The frame captures the league table shape well, naming the top four and the relegation candidates and explaining much of the variance in final points and ranks. Over the full season it rates Leicester title win as a statistical anomaly, giving it low probability. Using only first-half data, however, Leicester ranks among the top teams by expected goals. The team earns a small but notable title chance, suggesting the triumph was unlikely yet not detached from underlying performance.
arxiv-2602-15773:
Jiang and colleagues propose a new query for transaction flow networks, motivated by fraud detection at Grab, a digital payments leader in Southeast Asia. Such networks matter for spotting wash trading, credit card fraud, cashback arbitrage, and money laundering, and industry fraud detection leans heavily on finding dense flows. The S-T densest flow query asks for source and sink subsets, of size at least k, whose maximum flow between them is densest.

Recognising that the query is NP-hard, the team builds CONAN, an efficient divide-and-conquer algorithm, plus an approximate flow-peeling algorithm that optimises CONAN performance on large networks. The approach has been integrated into Grab fraud detection with significant gains in identifying fraudulent activity. Experiments show CONAN beating baselines by up to three orders of magnitude in runtime and finding densest flows more effectively, with applications also shown on NFT transaction networks.
arxiv-2602-16473:
Hongjian Jiang, Matthew Hague, Philipp Rümmer, and Anthony Widjaja Lin develop new techniques for synthesizing and verifying transformer programs. C-RASP is a simple programming language recently shown to capture concepts expressible by transformers. The paper establishes a connection between checking C-RASP programs and checking synchronous dataflow programs in Lustre, letting the authors exploit state-of-the-art model checkers built on highly optimized SMT solvers.
