The second contribution addresses learning a C-RASP program in the first place, with a new algorithm that learns one from examples using local search. The authors demonstrate their implementation on benchmarks of C-RASP programs from the literature, particularly for two applications: program optimization and constrained learning of programs from a partial specification. The report thus covers both verification and learning of programs.
arxiv-2602-16573:
Antonios Tziorvas, George Theodoropoulos, and Yannis Theodoridis propose MoDE-Boost, a pair of gradient boosting models for forecasting shared mobility demand, one for classification and one for regression. The models blend time and context features to predict demand at horizons from a few minutes to an hour, feeding routing, dispatch, and congestion work in intelligent transport systems. Evaluation uses open e-scooter and e-bike data from five metropolitan areas.

Against state-of-the-art methods and a generative AI model, the approach proves effective at capturing the tangled patterns of modern urban mobility. City planners and shared-mobility operators get forecasts that can place vehicles where riders will soon need them, easing the strains of rapid urban growth toward more livable streets.
arxiv-2602-16873:
Geunbin Yu presents AdaptOrch, a formal frame for task-adaptive multi-agent teamwork. It fits an era when language models from varied providers converge on comparable benchmark scores. When no single model clearly wins per task, picking one best model yields diminishing returns. How agents are teamed now drives system scores more than single-model skill. Teaming means how agents are coordinated, run side by side, and merged.

AdaptOrch dynamically picks among four standard team shapes: side-by-side, in sequence, layered, and mixed. Picks rest on task link graphs and by tests derived domain traits. Gains include a convergence scaling law, a routing code running in linear time on graph size, and a synthesis protocol with provable ending and heuristic accord scoring. Tests across coding, reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation show team-aware coordination lifting scores by twelve to twenty-three percent.
arxiv-2602-17573:
Konstantinos Foteinos and team built a data set to help first responders steer ground robots by hand gesture in disaster zones. Voice and screens may fail there, so gestures offer a robust backup. The team drew twelve commands from gestures responders already use and from tactical hand signals, then refined them with seasoned responders.

The FR-GESTURE set holds thousands of paired color and depth shots, taken from two viewpoints at seven distances. It is billed as the first set made for gesture-guided robot control by first responders. Set test rules and baseline scores come with it, as a start point for better models. Field robotics teams gain a public, task-specific resource.
arxiv-2602-17773:
Noah Trupin and team present a generative frame for physically feasible two-dimensional incompressible flows under varied obstacle shapes and edge settings. Past diffusion-based flow makers ignore physical constraints, impose soft costs that fail to guarantee fit, or narrow to fixed shapes. The new approach joins three pieces.

An edge-led diffusion model works on speed fields. A physics-led training goal adds a spread cost. A projection-constrained reverse process enforces exact incompressibility through a shape-aware Helmholtz-Hodge tool. The method amounts to a discrete take on constrained Langevin sampling on the space of divergence-free vector fields. Tests on analytic Navier-Stokes data and obstacle-bounded flows beat free, projection-only and cost-only rivals on spread, spectral scores, spin stats and edge match.
arxiv-2602-17873:
Shaobing Yuan and Salvatore Torquato sharpen the long-time asymptotics of diffusion spreadability for two-phase media. Spread probes inner structure across length scales in two-phase mixed media. When spectral density follows a power law at low wavenumber, normalized excess spread scales as a power of time in the long-time limit. That scaling reveals the infinite-wavelength exponent.

A prior method reliably extracted that exponent from long-time spread data. This paper improves it further with higher-order correction terms and smoothness traits of spectral density at the origin. Tests cover hyperuniform, typical nonhyperuniform and antihyperuniform models. Combining large-time and small-time series yields a two-point Padé formula for all times with few knobs. The work aids inner structure study from number or NMR relaxation data and inverse design of targeted spread.
arxiv-2602-17973:
Phan The Duy and colleagues present PenTiDef, a decentralized framework that spots intrusions across industrial internet-of-things networks without any central server. The design joins three parts at once: guarding privacy, fighting poisoned updates, and blockchain coordination. It targets settings where many devices learn as a group without trusting each peer.

On each device, Distributed Differential Privacy adds stochastic Gaussian noise to shield gradient leakage. A light latent-space defense module compresses penultimate-layer representations into stable Latent Semantic Representations with an AutoEncoder, then uses Centered Kernel Alignment and K-Means clustering to flag hostile updates with no extra data. A permissioned blockchain layer with smart contracts runs on-chain checks, secure FedAvg aggregation, and an audit trail that cannot be altered. In tests with hostile shares up to forty percent, PenTiDef beat the FLARE and FedCC baselines on detection accuracy and F1-score with lower training overhead.
arxiv-2602-18173:
A large team led by C. Duffy built a prototype that pairs Rubin Observatory alerts with Euclid space telescope views. Their 2026 paper faces a flood: Rubin is set to send ten million transient alerts each night, while Euclid scans wide sky fields in visible and near-infrared light. The system matches alerts to Euclid images on its own, joining light curves and image cutouts across both sets.

Tested with Zwicky Transient Facility alerts as a stand-in for Rubin, the system proved useful whether or not Euclid caught the event. When Euclid had seen it, earlier space views tightened the blast time, as with one supernova spotted about three days before ground telescopes. When Euclid missed it, its images still sharpened the host galaxy's shape and match. The prototype shows joint Rubin-Euclid data can add value on both sides of a detection.
arxiv-2602-18573:
Amy Vennos and two co-authors make probability predictions trustworthy. Their 2026 paper notes machine-made probability predictions are vital in modern classification such as image classification. A model counts as calibrated when predictions match observed rates. Existing multicategory recalibration methods are weak: they compare models rather than testing one model, require under-the-hood model access, and produce output hard for analysts.

The team proposes Multicategory Linear Log Odds recalibration, which includes a likelihood ratio test for calibration, needs no under-the-hood access and thus applies widely, and can be easy to read. They demonstrate effectiveness through simulations and three case studies: image classification with convolutional networks, obesity analysis with random forests, and ecology with regression models. Compared with four recalibration techniques using their test and Expected Calibration Error, the method works well alone and with others.
arxiv-2602-18673:
When must a team actually talk to get a job right, and when is that talk just waste? Harang Ju, writing alone in 2026, takes up coordination in organisations, a question made sharper by multi-agent AI systems where the cost of talking can outrun the cost of the work itself.

The answer turns on monotonicity: coordination is needed when new facts can overturn earlier conclusions, but not when conclusions only grow. Mapping an older taxonomy of interdependence onto that test gives a decision rule, checked against 65 real workflows and thousands of job tasks. The finding is that much coordination spending may be needless for correctness alone.
arxiv-2602-18773:
Pathology diagnosis is moving from coarse image-text matching toward agents that call tools and check molecular facts. Haoyang Su, with two co-authors, presents LAMMI-Pathology in 2026. It is a tool-first, bottom-up agent frame for molecularly informed work in pathology.

Tools built for the domain form the base. They group by style into component agents. A top planner then runs them in layers. That avoids the overlong contexts that cause task drift. Reasoning paths are built from Atomic Execution Nodes. These are small, composable units that capture true agent-tool steps. A fine-tuning method that follows those paths aligns the planner's choices with them. The goal is sturdier diagnosis and smarter use of the toolset.
arxiv-2602-19373:
Deep reinforcement learning often wobbles because its targets and data keep shifting during training. Ali Saheb Pasand and four co-authors show that isotropic Gaussian embeddings, in which representations spread evenly in all directions, are provably helpful under such non-stationary targets. They support stable tracking of changing targets for linear readouts, maximize entropy for a fixed variance budget, and encourage balanced use of every dimension.

Building on that insight, the paper proposes Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization, which shapes representations toward an isotropic Gaussian during training. Across varied domains, this simple and cheap method lifts performance under non-stationarity while cutting representation collapse, dormant neurons, and training instability. Readers get a lightweight stabilizer for agents facing shifting objectives.
arxiv-2602-19573:
Mickaya A. Razanaparany and Christian Rakotonirina look at three operator tools in quantum theory: the Chrestenson operator, the Weyl basis, and the Kronecker-Pauli basis. The setting is d-size Hilbert spaces in Dirac symbols, for prime d greater than 2. Seeing them side by side sets up a match across bases oft treated apart.

The authors set out a new algebra link tying these operators, joining the three tools in one formula. The cases d equals 3 and d equals 5 show the link in action. Readers get a tight bridge between operator bases in prime-size quantum theory, with small cases showing how the broad link works.
arxiv-2602-19873:
Simulating particles that interact only at short range needs a neighbour list, and building that list fast on graphics hardware, with little memory, is a practical bottleneck. A 2026 arXiv paper by Felix Thaler and Sebastian Keller presents a compressed, GPU-native neighbour list built on a space-filling-curve memory layout and particle clusters.

The list stores roughly two hundred neighbours per particle in only a few bytes each, and it runs on both major graphics hardware families. Against a highly tuned neighbour list in the molecular dynamics code GROMACS, it shows comparable overhead and similar speed in a neighbourhood pass. Its layout also handles varying interaction radii and sharp density contrasts well, suiting astrophysical problems. It integrates with octree domain decomposition and long-range methods, as shown in a large Evrard collapse test.
arxiv-2602-19973:
Programs proved in proof-oriented languages are often extracted to everyday languages for use in larger codebases, but extraction itself is rarely fully proved. A 2026 arXiv paper by Cezar-Constantin Andrici and five co-authors advances secure extraction for F-star programs with input-output effects.

The hard step is quotation, turning a shallowly embedded program into a deeply embedded form, which has resisted proof. Earlier work certifies single extractions by checking translations. The authors limit checking to a first step, relational quotation, where a metaprogram builds a typing outline following the original program's structure. Once that outline checks out, a proved syntax generator produces code guaranteed related in meaning to the original. Applied as SEIO-star, the method carries a machine-checked proof of a very strong secure-compiling standard, beyond prior work focused on correctness alone.
arxiv-2602-20073:
In the two-dimensional Hubbard model, magnetism, charge order, and superconductivity compete and coexist. A 2026 arXiv paper by Robin Scholle and three co-authors studies that interplay with a renormalized mean-field approach. It improves on mean-field theory by capturing high-energy fluctuations through a renormalization group framework.

That framework yields magnetic and d-wave pairing interactions. They permit an unbiased survey of coexisting phases at weak and moderate strengths. Mean-field calculations on finite lattices join analyses in the thermodynamic limit. The result is a phase diagram with coexistence regions. On the electron-doped side, d-wave superconductivity sits with Néel order. On the hole-doped side, superconductivity sits with spiral or stripe magnetic orders. Inside the stripe region the superconducting order parameter varies in space, tracking the stripes' charge modulation. Below van Hove filling, pairing supplies the energy gain, stripe order only a small extra lowering.
arxiv-2602-20173:
A honeycomb built from two materials can shrink sideways when stretched and shrink when heated, two negative responses at once. That combination makes hybrid-honeycomb lattices useful for heat-elastic uses. A 2026 arXiv paper by Xiang-Long Peng and Bai-Xiang Xu designs such structures backward: start from wanted properties and find the structure that delivers them, using machine learning.

High-throughput simulation builds a large dataset. Computational averaging covers structures with varied geometry and base materials. A forward model learns to predict effective thermoelastic traits for a given design, fast and well. Inverse models then suggest geometry and base materials for desired targets. Six inverse models cover different cases, set apart by which target traits and which design knobs they use. Users can thus work backward from properties to structures.
arxiv-2602-20273:
Zhuofan Josh Ying and three co-authors test how large language models represent truthfulness. Their 2026 study starts from a puzzle: earlier work reported that models encode truthfulness along a straight line, yet newer work doubts how general that finding is. They propose a spectrum view: the model space holds truth directions from broad and domain-general to narrow and domain-specific.

They test probes across five truth types, definitional, empirical, logical, fictional, and ethical, plus sycophantic lying, expectation-inverted lying, and existing honesty benchmarks. Linear probes transfer well across most domains but fail on the two lying styles. Training on all domains together restores strong performance. Probe geometry explains the pattern: similarity between probe directions predicts transfer almost perfectly. Concept-erasure tools isolate general, specific, and shared directions. Causal tests show specific directions steer better. Post-training, the authors find, pushes sycophantic lying further from other truth types.
arxiv-2602-20373:
Joseph Moscoso and five co-authors present the first lattice calculation of a two-particle matrix element of a local current. The calculation uses a leading pionless effective field theory of two nucleons in a finite volume, where the Hamiltonian can be diagonalized exactly. Across couplings that support a deuteron-like bound state, the team determines spectra and matrix elements of the local vector current.

Using the Lüscher formalism, they constrain the infinite-volume hadronic amplitude, then map finite-volume matrix elements to scattering amplitudes for two-particle states coupled through a current insertion. A relation then links those amplitudes to the bound-state elastic form factor, constraining it directly. Varying the coupling shows deep bound states need little finite-volume correction, while shallow ones need it critically. The analysis also yields the bound-state charge radius, and shallow results match the anomalous-threshold prediction.
arxiv-2602-20573:
Molecules are often written as SMILES strings, which convert to graphs with atoms as nodes and bonds as edges for neural net training. Rajan and Ishaan Gupta note that graph neural nets for molecular property prediction still lack a rigorous benchmark. Their paper proposes MolGraphBench, a benchmark of four common graph neural net models for molecular regression tasks, judged on absolute performance, training speed, transfer learning, and prediction quality.

Results point to graph convolutional nets and graph isomorphism nets as the best architectures for molecular graph regression. The study also finds that molecular fingerprints add nothing complementary in fused graph-fingerprint models. The models match or beat current state-of-the-art graph baselines across three data sets. The paper concludes that the choice of graph layer should be treated as a tunable setting rather than a fixed design choice.
arxiv-2602-20673:
A free-viewpoint, tunable, high-quality driving sim matters for training and testing end-to-end autonomous driving systems. Hao Zhang and seven co-authors present GA-Drive, a simulation system that makes camera views along user-chosen novel paths through shape-look split and diffusion-based making. Given images from a filmed path plus scene shape, GA-Drive builds novel pseudo-views from shape information.

Those pseudo-views are then turned into lifelike views by a trained video model. Splitting shape from looks enables look editing through state-of-the-art video-to-video editing techniques while keeping base shape, so edits stay steady across first and novel paths. Broad tests show GA-Drive clearly beats current methods on NTA-IoU, NTL-IoU, and FID scores.
arxiv-2602-20773:
Sachin Dudda Nagaraju and three co-authors study how hospitals can train one image-segmentation model together without pooling raw scans. The snag is that CT and MRI scans look different, so a model trained on one type often falters on the other, in this case for abdominal organs and the whole heart.

They test several fixes inside federated training, including spatial warps, frequency tweaks, and a global intensity method called GIN. GIN proved most steady across scan types: pancreas scores rose from 0.073 to 0.437 when CT data joined, and a 3D heart model gained on unseen CT and MRI centers, keeping 92.4 percent of pooled-data performance on unseen CT data.
arxiv-2602-21073:
Active automata learning usually assumes a teacher who answers every query fully. Daniel Stan, Adrien Pommellet, and Juliette Jacquot relax that assumption in this 2026 arXiv technical report. Their IdMAT teacher answers with respect to any language in a target class at once, which suits problems like language separation and invariant synthesis that admit many correct answers.

Such a teacher may answer don't know, yet also supply inductive facts of the form: if one word is accepted, so is another. The companion algorithm LIndA encodes all uncertainty as a single SAT instance without forking, uses incremental solving with unsatisfiable-core analysis, and handles both kinds of counterexamples frugally. A prototype is evaluated on language separation and regular model checking.
arxiv-2602-21273:
Generating multi-frame visual stories without fine-tuning strains three goals at once: faithful action text, stable subject identity, and continuous backgrounds. Jinghao Hu, Yuhe Zhang, GuoHua Geng, Kang Li, and Han Zhang balance them in this 2026 arXiv paper with StoryTailor, a zero-shot pipeline running on a single high-end graphics card. It turns a long narrative prompt, per-subject references, and grounding boxes into coherent image sequences.

Three modules cooperate. Gaussian-centered attention focuses on each subject core and eases box overlaps, action-boost reweighting amplifies action directions in text embeddings, and a selective forgetting cache keeps transferable background cues across scenes. Experiments show text alignment gains of ten to fifteen percent with competitive identity scores, at faster inference than a leading baseline on matched hardware.
arxiv-2602-21373:
Yifan Liu and nine co-authors test separate cores of a multicore erbium-doped fiber amplifier in a noise-canceled link for ultrastable optical frequency transfer. Such links carry precise time and frequency signals, and multicore fiber could fold that job into future communication networks.

The stabilized amplifier alone reached a fractional frequency instability of 5 times 10 to the minus 19 at 1,000 seconds of averaging. Joined to a 40-kilometre, 7-core spooled fiber, the link reached 1.4 times 10 to the minus 18 at the same averaging time. The authors present this as a step toward building precision time and frequency distribution into multicore fiber infrastructure.
arxiv-2602-21673:
Kazuya Saito alone authors a paper on the odd-even effect in the dominant order of self-assembly of cross junctions in space dimension d at least 3. The work extends a prior study for dimension 3 to general dimension d. The problem equals building a d-dimensional hypercubic jungle gym, at every junction of which 2d rods with different colours meet.

Analysis reveals a unique trait of dimension 3. At least one perfectly ordered, singly coloured direction or axis is forced to exist there. That contrasts with its possible absence in dimension 4 and above. Yet uniaxial order proves overwhelming not only in dimension 3 but also for dimensions 4 to 7 and odd dimensions 9 and above in a sufficiently large system. For even dimensions 8 and above, isotropic states dominate, giving alternation of dominant states between uniaxial and isotropic orders depending on parity of dimension 7 and above.
arxiv-2602-21773:
Machine unlearning lets a model forget specific data, a key tool for privacy and reliability, yet its power can collapse when models absorb unintended biases from spurious correlations. JuneHyoung Kwon and five co-authors study unlearning from such biased models and identify shortcut unlearning. Bias-aligned samples picked up quickly prove resistant to removal. What gets erased is the bias feature rather than the class feature, so accuracy on the category targeted for erasure can unexpectedly climb.

Their CUPID framework starts from the observation that samples with different biases show distinct loss landscape sharpness. It splits the forget set into causal- and bias-approximated subsets by sample sharpness. It disentangles model parameters into causal and bias pathways, and routes refined causal and bias gradients to their matching pathways. Tests on biased datasets including Waterbirds, BAR, and Biased NICO++ show state-of-the-art forgetting and effective mitigation of shortcut unlearning.
arxiv-2602-21973:
Future phone networks may use thousands of antennas at once, working so close to users that signals vary with distance as well as direction. Ahmed Hussain and four co-authors tackle how to get strong service from fewer active antennas. Instead of moving antennas by hand, they switch only a chosen subset on, shaping a sparse array on the fly to match where users actually are.

The paper first checks when unwanted extra beams, called grating lobes, appear, and finds they vanish along the range direction. It then builds two tuning methods, one that quiets those extra beams and one that lifts total data speed for many users at once. Tests show the switched arrays can rival full arrays while using far less hardware.
arxiv-2602-22173:
Mixed-integer programs drive choices in finance, logistics, energy, and network design, but standard solvers strain on large or tightly constrained cases. Antonio A. Chaves and five co-authors test the Random-Key Optimizer, a search method that works in a continuous random-key space while decoders map candidates to workable integer solutions. Search and feasibility checks are thus kept separate.

The method is tested on two very different benchmarks, including a mean-variance portfolio problem, where it delivers high-quality solutions. Its flexibility comes from problem-specific decoders, letting one search engine serve many problem shapes. For teams facing solver-hostile cases, it offers a usable backup route to strong solutions.
arxiv-2602-22273:
Testing whether language models truly understand finance needs more than trivia: it needs exams and realistic business scenarios. Xiyuan Zhang and ten co-authors introduce FIRE, a benchmark covering both. Its theory side curates questions from recognized financial qualification exams, while its practice side organizes complex financial domains into an evaluation matrix spanning essential subdomains and activities.

From that matrix the team collects three thousand scenario questions, mixing closed-form decisions with rubric-graded open questions. Comprehensive evaluations of leading models, including a new financial-domain model, show where finance knowledge holds and where it breaks. For builders of financial AI, FIRE offers a yardstick that tests both textbook knowledge and desk-ready judgment.
arxiv-2602-22373:
Scientific theories live at many levels of abstraction, and category theory offers a language for stacking those levels. Leo Lobski and Fabio Zanasi study layered monoidal theories, a framework built on string-diagram algebra. They introduce models for three related classes: fibrational, opfibrational, and deflational theories.

For each class, the authors prove soundness and completeness with respect to its models. The work also reveals links between layered theories and familiar category structures, including Grothendieck fibrations and displayed categories. Workers gain a solid bridge between layered science models and standard category theory.
arxiv-2602-22473:
Cosmic inflation in the early universe may have been driven by Higgs fields, and supergravity offers a natural home for that idea. Pallis studies a renormalizable extension of the minimal supersymmetric standard model, endowed with an R symmetry and a gauged B minus L symmetry. The model pairs chaotic inflation from a quartic potential with Higgs superfields that break the B minus L symmetry on their own.

Consistency with recent ACT data comes from a fractional shift-symmetric Kaehler potential with two free parameters kept within tight ranges. The model also explains the mu term of the supersymmetric standard model when a related parameter stays small, and baryogenesis proceeds through non-thermal leptogenesis as the inflaton decays to right-handed neutrinos. It ties inflation, particle masses, and the matter surplus into one framework.
arxiv-2602-22673:
Md Tanvir Hasan Turja forecasts bacterial drug-resistance trends from WHO tracking data to guide policy. Drug-resistant germs threaten global health, and the WHO GLASS system sets a standard for drug and use data, yet large-scale machine-learning outlooks remain rare. The study used nearly six thousand records from 44 countries and five WHO regions across 2021 to 2023, testing six models on one-year-ahead outlooks.

Readers should trust the corrected version, not the first headline. A version-3 correction reports that a leakage audit found flaws in feature building. On the corrected panel, a simple persistence outlook beats XGBoost, and the first claim of a large error cut over the naive guess is withdrawn. The local lookup-based system still turns outlooks into source-tagged policy guidance without fake citations.
arxiv-2602-22773:
Bibhash Kumar Das and one co-author open a study of bilateral weighted backward shift operators on spaces of analytic functions over an annulus, a ring-shaped region of the complex plane. These Banach spaces carry a normalized Schauder basis built from simple polynomial-like pieces.

The team gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a weighted shift to be bounded, and conditions under which it resembles a compact perturbation of a shift on sequence space. They also examine hypercyclic, supercyclic, and chaotic behaviour, showing the zero-one law of orbital limit points fails here, unlike for shifts on sequence space. Most proofs run through the matrix form of the shift.
arxiv-2602-22873:
Eduardo Paluzo-Hidalgo and one co-author connect multi-chart auto-coders with vector bundles and characteristic classes. Rather than forcing one global flat placing, they treat locally trained encoder-decoder pairs as a learned atlas on a shape, a standard shape viewpoint applied to machine learning.

Any reconstruction-consistent atlas canonically defines transition maps obeying the cocycle condition. Linearizing those maps yields a vector bundle that matches the tangent bundle when latent dimension equals intrinsic dimension. That construction unlocks differential-topological invariants: the first Stiefel-Whitney class falls out of Jacobian signs of learned transition maps, giving an algorithmic orientability test. Nontrivial classes also block single-chart representations, and the minimum chart count follows the manifold's good cover structure.
arxiv-2602-23073:
Yaacov Pariente and one co-author speed up risk-averse scoring for partly seeable Markov choice tasks. Risk-averse choice under doubt is central to self-run agents, and CVaR is a key risk measure. Yet solving POMDPs is compute-wise unsolvable, and rough methods rely on expensive run-throughs of future paths.

The work derives bounds on the CVaR of a number using a helper number, under assumptions on piled-up spread and thickness. The bounds yield readable bunching rules that settle as the spread gap closes. Upper and lower bounds on the CVaR function, computable from a trimmed belief-MDP, feed gauges with chance promises and enable speedup via action cutting. Actions whose bounds show weakness under the trimmed model are dropped while keeping agreement with the POMDP. Test-based scoring across domains confirms that the bounds cleanly separate safe from dangerous policies with large speedups.
arxiv-2602-23273:
Sanjay Sarkar and two co-authors build a unified theory of extrinsic spin-splitter currents in altermagnets. Altermagnets show motion-linked spin splitting while keeping zero net magnet pull. That quirk enables a spin-splitter effect, in which an outside charge field drives lateral spin currents by sorting carriers of opposite spin.

The theory covers linear extrinsic currents and folds in two impurity effects, side-jump and skew scattering. Applied to the d-wave altermagnet FeSb2, it shows asymmetric impurity collisions as the dominant channel. Strikingly, the resulting spin conductivity is even under time reversal, unlike prior spin-splitter responses from symmetric scattering, marking a distinct transport signature for these materials.
arxiv-2602-23373:
Pavel Chernakov and two co-authors build an agentic language-model system for adverse media screening in anti-money-laundering compliance. Adverse media screening is a critical part of anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer checks at financial institutions. Traditional keyword searches generate high false-positive rates or demand extensive manual review.

The system pairs large language models with RAG in a multi-step workflow. An agent searches the web, retrieves and processes relevant documents, and computes an Adverse Media Index score for each subject. Tested with multiple language-model backends on a data set of politically exposed persons, regulatory watchlist persons, sanctioned persons from OpenSanctions, and clean names from academic sources. The system distinguishes high-risk from low-risk individuals, offering a path to faster, more accurate compliance screening.
arxiv-2602-23473:
Alif Aqsha and two co-authors solve many-variable linear-quadratic random control problems with a signature-based numeric scheme. Their key insight is that linear signature readouts are dense among admissible controls, so the original random problem becomes a fixed convex quadratic polynomial problem.

To support cutoff signatures in practice, they prove the value function can be matched by finite-size polynomial estimates when cutoff levels are high enough. Remarkably, experiments show decent accuracy even at small truncation levels. The analysis rests on three tools. First, the algebra form of controlled random rate equations and costs as linear readouts of path signatures. Second, the settling of the cutoff readouts. Third, density of signature controls.
arxiv-2602-23973:
Prasoon Kumar and two co-authors simulate how electron-electron interactions affect ultrashort voltage pulses traveling through a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The 2026 paper targets electronic flying qubits, which require pulses shorter than the flight time through the device, a regime where interaction physics must be treated carefully.

Using time-resolved simulations with interactions handled at the time-dependent mean-field level, the authors find that the main effect is a renormalization of pulse velocity. Interactions rescale how fast pulses move, rather than scrambling them. Crucially, interference effects prove robust to interactions, surviving the treatment intact. That robustness supports the interferometer as a platform for flying-qubit experiments, since the quantum signal that carries information is not washed out by electron-electron repulsion. That speed change is the whole story.
arxiv-2602-24073:
Narges Kakavand and Anupam Sengupta study ecological memory of hydrodynamic cues in motile microorganisms, asking whether past flow exposures shape later growth and migration. The 2026 paper introduces flow-induced memory as a lasting imprint of prior spatio-temporal cues, a form of ecological memory.

Using millifluidic flow control, high-resolution cell tracking, and tunable flow cues, the team follows a model microbe across growth stages under two perturbation orders. One order is flow after static conditions. The other is flow before static growth. That design separates exposure history from exposure duration and reveals legacy effects: prior flow modulates sensitivity and alters growth timing relative to static controls. Repeated hydrodynamic exposure thus leaves a multigenerational imprint, suggesting that aquatic microbes carry their flow history into future behavior. In short, past flow leaves a mark that lasts.
arxiv-2602-24273:
Borja Requena and four co-authors propose a minimal agent for automated theorem proving. The 2026 paper implements the core features shared by leading systems, stripped to a simple design: library search, context management, and iterative proof refinement.

Tests on different benchmarks, comparing frontier language models and design choices, show competitive performance against state-of-the-art approaches, at a fraction of their cost and with a significantly simpler architecture. The study also demonstrates advantages for iterative proving over multiple single-shot generations. Released open-source, the minimal agent serves as an accessible prover and future research as a reference. It clarifies which ingredients of complex prover systems actually drive performance.
arxiv-2603-00073: Kim, Lee and Choi give exact rules for when a quartic polynomial stays above zero, using a split-apart method. Since rules for Gram-Charlier densities rest on such a polynomial, their result gives briefer exact formulas for the densities' valid range. Past work gave number-based rules in 1952, and exact formulas in 2019 and 2022, but those formulas stayed hard to untangle. The new rules clear up that picture while keeping full exactness.
arxiv-2603-00173: Ryu and Han describe training Summer-22B, a video foundation model built from scratch on about 50 million clips. They combine metadata curation, multi-stage filtering, μP parameterisation and hypersphere-constrained optimisation, run via the Lavender Data system with inference-aware architecture. Dataset work took most of the effort, design variants mattered less than hoped, and μP transfer worked even under geometric constraints. The report shares lessons for others scaling similar projects.
arxiv-2603-00273: Dorken Gallastegi and colleagues tackle reflected downwelling light, a long-standing spoiler of passive long-wave infrared ranging from thermal radiation. Their quadspectral method uses four narrowband readings, two at a water vapour line and two at an ozone line, for a simple closed-form range. A hyperspectral method uses a wider band for better accuracy plus temperature, emissivity and downwelling estimates across zenith angles. Tests cut error from over 100 metres to about 7 metres with the first method and about 1 metre with the second.
arxiv-2603-00373: Sartor, Dörfler, and Lanzetti study how to steer a spread of agents with only a few controlled actors, using a coupled equation pair for the crowd and its drivers. Standard terminal costs based on transport distance turn rough at finite agent counts and sit outside common cost classes. Under stated regularity conditions they prove how the state responds to control changes, build an adjoint system with an explicit cost gradient, and derive Pontryagin style necessary conditions. A splitting test shows the adjoint method in action.
arxiv-2603-00973: Nigri, Shang, and Ungolo build a mortality framework that keeps cause-of-death forecasts consistent with total deaths, a coherence separate models often break. Totals follow a Poisson law, cause splits a multinomial law, and cause probabilities a Dirichlet law, with age and year patterns in both parts. Applied to United States and French data from 1979 to 2023, it matches the standard Lee-Carter model on accuracy while keeping projections coherent and uncertainty well calibrated.
arxiv-2603-01073: Fu and five colleagues speed cardiac MRI registration with FlowReg, a flow-matching method strong in as few as two steps that refines further with more. A warmup-reflow scheme lets a single-step teacher train a student from any middle state, with no pre-trained model needed. An initial-guess trick feeds each prediction back as the next start. It wins five of six tasks across two sets, cuts heart-function error by about two and a half points, and needs almost no extra parameters or labels.
arxiv-2603-02373:
Taylor Daniels studies signed partition numbers in this 2026 mathematics paper. Partitions split a whole number into a sum of smaller parts. Signed versions weight each part by a function that returns zero, one, or minus one. Daniels uses the Legendre symbol, a classic sign from number theory, as that weight.

Series formulas in the style of Rademacher are derived for several small primes. The primes covered are five, thirteen, and seventeen, all one more than a multiple of four. Derivations make clear how the method extends to all such primes. For the prime seventeen, deeper tools enter, including Dedekind sums and their twisted versions. The signed counts turn out to vanish exactly on certain arithmetic progressions modulo thirty-four.
arxiv-2603-02473:
Boqin Yuan, Yue Su, and Kun Yao diagnose where memory-augmented agents fail in this 2026 paper. Such agents store past interactions and retrieve them to answer later questions. Teams debate whether better writing or better retrieval matters more. Their diagnostic framework crosses three write styles with three retrieval methods.

Write styles range from raw chunks to extracted facts and summaries. Retrieval spans cosine matching, keyword search, and a hybrid reranker. On a long-conversation benchmark, retrieval choice swung accuracy by about twenty points. Write style moved it by only a few points. Raw chunks, needing no model calls, matched or beat costly lossy options. Failures clustered at retrieval, not at use of retrieved text. Better retrieval, they argue, beats fancier writing today.
arxiv-2603-02573:
Jiahao Lu, Jiayi Xu, Wenbo Hu, and colleagues track every pixel in 3D from a single video in this 2026 paper. Knowing each pixel's 3D path unlocks full understanding of video dynamics. Prior methods track only sparse points or rely on slow per-video optimization. Their feedforward model, Track4World, aims for dense tracking at practical speed.

A transformer first encodes the global 3D scene from the video. A novel 3D correlation scheme then estimates dense 2D and 3D flow between any frame pair. Scene flow plus rebuilt geometry yields the 3D trajectory of every pixel. Tracking happens in world coordinates, not camera coordinates, which suits reconstruction. Across multiple benchmarks, the method beat existing approaches on flow and tracking. Robustness and scale suit real-world four-dimensional reconstruction tasks.
arxiv-2603-02673:
Baptiste Ferrere, Nicolas Bousquet, Fabrice Gamboa, and colleagues solve a long-standing gap in model explanation math. Their 2026 paper concerns functional ANOVA, which splits a model's output into single-feature effects and interactions between features. For linked categorical features, no exact formula existed, so teams relied on slow sampling estimates.

By linking the problem to an extended form of discrete Fourier analysis, they derive a closed-form split that assumes nothing about the links. The formula is fast to compute and reduces to the classic result when features are independent. It also yields a natural extension of SHAP values, a popular explanation score, to the general categorical case. Exact answers replace rough estimates for a wide class of models.
arxiv-2603-02773:
Zhen Zhang, Zihan Wang, Xinyu Ma, and colleagues help search models absorb new documents without full retraining. Their 2026 paper concerns generative retrieval, where a model answers a query by generating a document's ID directly. Such models often fail on documents added after training, and retraining is costly and can erase old skill.

Their method, DOME, edits the model in three stages: find the key layers, tune edit vectors, then apply the update. A mixed-label training trick keeps edit vectors distinct even when documents share ID parts across queries. On the NQ and MS MARCO benchmarks, new-document retrieval improved a lot while old results held. The update took only about sixty percent of the time of incremental retraining.
arxiv-2603-02873:
Tianyou Liu, Ziqiang Li, Xurui Liu, and colleagues argue that the TeX typesetting system holds back AI-assisted science writing. Their 2026 paper examines LaTeX compilation in an era when language models draft much of the text. They cite slow builds, weak meaning in the output, hard-to-locate errors, and a costly token footprint.

As an alternative they present Mogan STEM, a structured editor that shows the document as it will look while editing. Tests favor Mogan on build and rendering time and on language model task performance. Its file format also carries less redundant information, making model fine-tuning cheaper than with TeX files. The authors call for larger trials of training models on the new format.
arxiv-2603-03173:
Hassan Abdelraouf and Jeff Shamma ask whether choosing the wrong good learning rule can itself be a mistake. No-regret algorithms guarantee that, over time, a learner does about as well as the best fixed strategy. Yet that promise says nothing about how high the final average actually is, and different no-regret rules can land at different heights.

Framing generalized replicator dynamics as control systems, they compare variants by reshaping one internal block. Near equilibrium, a passivity test ranks the variants. Globally, an anticipatory variant provably dominates the standard rule across every payoff environment, with an optimal-control argument showing the reward gap can reach zero. A genuine free lunch exists among no-regret dynamics, at least in this family.
arxiv-2603-03573:
Daiheng Zhang and five colleagues post-train language models to edit biological sequences step by step. Optimizing proteins and molecules means revising a string under strict syntax rules, a job needing long-horizon planning. Diffusion models refine gradually but hide their edits; ordinary language models expose edits yet plan poorly. Their 2026 framework, STRIDE, makes the model write out an executable trail of atomic edits: insert, delete, replace.

Training first imitates shortest-edit demonstrations aligned by edit distance, then applies group-based policy optimization to align the trails with task rewards. On protein fluorescence and instruction-guided molecular tasks, editing success leapt from about two fifths to nearly nine tenths. Novelty of the outputs more than doubled as well. Validity and controllability beat a diverse set of baselines, and the code is public.
arxiv-2603-03673:
Sophia Sklaviadis and four colleagues extend a workhorse identity of statistics beyond the Gaussian world. Stein's identity converts expectations into gradient formulas and powers generative modeling and stochastic optimization, but it was built for Gaussian distributions. Their 2026 paper derives the identity for q-Gaussians with bounded support, a flexible family that lives on a finite interval instead of the whole line.

The proof extends earlier Bonnet and Price type theorems and simplifies them using escort distributions, close cousins of the original law. The resulting gradient estimators look nearly identical to the Gaussian ones and are just as easy to implement. Experiments add a practical lure: bounded-support distributions can lower the variance of gradient estimators. The authors point to Bayesian deep learning and sharpness-aware minimization as likely beneficiaries.
arxiv-2603-03973: Soochul Park and Yeon Ju Lee present Dual-Solver, a generalized ODE solver for diffusion models with dual output. Classical ODE numeric methods have been adopted to reduce evaluations, but output type and integration domain choices lead to varied sampling behaviors. Parameters are learned through a classification-style objective with a frozen pretrained classifier. For ImageNet class-conditional output and text-to-image output, Dual-Solver lifts FID and CLIP scores in the low-tests regime across backbones.
arxiv-2603-04273: Maire and colleagues model a chiral fluid with spinning disks in two dimensions. Chirality comes only from a sideways kick at contact, while collisions dissipate energy and add orbital angular momentum. A Boltzmann Enskog description yields nonlinear equations for density, momentum, and temperature, plus an antisymmetric stress with nonzero torque density. In the dilute limit, Chapman Enskog theory predicts odd viscosity, odd heat conduction, and odd self diffusion, matching simulations. The model thus gives a clean test bed for odd transport.
arxiv-2603-04673: Kc and colleagues assess hallucinations in medical repair with sFRC. Deep learning restores images from sparse and undersampled takes, yet outputs may hallucinate. Few easy tools or robust metrics exist to spot hallucinations. The paper performs Fourier Ring Correlation analysis over small patches, scanning DL outputs and references to detect hallucinations, termed sFRC. Tests on CT super-resolution, sparse view CT, and subsampled MRI show sFRC detecting hallucinated features for CT and matching theory maps for MR. Hallucination rates for in-distribution versus out-of-distribution data characterize DL robustness.
arxiv-2603-05273: Clemens Eisenhofer and team offer a new way to solve string equations, building on Nielsen changes as extensions of them. Three ways combine in the approach: a power operator for strings, generalizations of Parikh images, and equality decomposition. As one these methods solve complex string equations, including the less commonly encountered SMT inputs over strings.
arxiv-2603-05473: Jarman and colleagues explore neural radiance fields for three-dimensional reconstruction from longwave infrared hyperspectral images, aimed at gas plume detection and analysis. Few views of a scene are usually available and analyzed separately, so combining them into one representation adds context. Built on Mip-NeRF with hyperspectral and sparse-view techniques plus a novel adaptive weighted loss, their method needs around 50% fewer training images than standard Mip-NeRF. Gas plume detection on rendered test views reaches an average AUC of 0.821 against ground-truth masks.
arxiv-2603-05573: Heo and team look at how error behaves when large sequence models work outside their power ranges, through Lie algebra control. Large models such as Transformer kinds and state-space designs often trade power for parallel work to train fast. Their theory links model depth to a tower of Lie algebra extensions and describes fixed-depth models with their power bounds. It derives an error bound showing error shrinks by a fixed factor with each added layer. Tests on symbol word and smooth state-tracking problems back up the guesses.
arxiv-2603-06273: Chatterjee studies how a rotating Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton-Axion black hole yields energy and speeds up particles, with a focus on dilaton hair near the horizon against Kerr. For the Penrose process, analytic expressions for top efficiency show negative dilaton hair can strongly lift ideal gain at extremality, reaching about 91 percent. Irreducible mass falls as the hair parameter grows more negative, while rotationally extractable energy rises, giving a larger spin reservoir. At extremality, about 0.63 of mass is drawn from rotation for EMDA, against the Kerr value.
arxiv-2603-06373: Baroudi and his team study Hindi English code switched doctor patient conversations from DISPLACE-M, and DASHA, which chains diarization, speaker tagged transcription, and LLM based extraction. A neural system with vector clustering on a multilingual encoder cuts error rate to 7.76 percent. A Qwen3 ASR model adapted to Hindi with Devanagari normalization cuts time constrained word error rate a lot, with further gains from optional LLM correction. Such gains lift that work only with adapted ASR, and DASHA ranked first among 25 DISPLACE-M participants.
arxiv-2603-06673: Pande and team address imaging of artefacts, where scope records a spectrum per pixel, but mixed species in worn samples make manual library matching slow. They propose a self-taught autoencoder for blind splitting, gauging endmember spectra and abundance maps while using spatial structure through patch-based model. A weighted spectral angle distance loss with weights from spatial flatness, neighbour agreement, and roughness reduces feeling to flaws across more than 1500 bands. Next to angle training, it improves clarity in contamination-prone regions, shown on a Ghent Altarpiece section.
arxiv-2603-06873: Zhou and colleagues present PICS, pairwise image editing that keeps space links across later edits. Diffusion editing often breaks those links, since later inserts cover earlier content and disrupt order, despite strong single turn results. PICS composes objects at once by a decomposition method, modeling links among seen objects and background. A model routes background, solo, and overlap regions to masked experts. Blending fuses overlap objects in a fitting way while keeping edges sharp, and geometric tweaks covering pose changes improve strength.
arxiv-2603-06973: Guo and colleagues propose T2SGrid, a temporal-to-spatial grid method for video temporal grounding. Video temporal grounding finds the segment matching a plain query, needing a grasp of temporal motion. Current vision-language models read temporal motion through position codes, text time labels, or frame numbers. Each approach has limits: time labels add cost and thin focus, position codes miss exact timing, and frame numbers harm spatial detail. T2SGrid reframes video temporal reading as a spatial task, using clips, with overlapping windows splitting the video.
arxiv-2603-07273: Hallin, Werker and Zhou tackle a wrinkle in statistical theory: the largest nuisance-free slices of an experiment are usually not unique. They build a sequence-based version of maximal ancillarity inside locally asymptotically normal limits and show efficient procedures can be rewritten to live on those slices. That removes the nuisance exactly in finite samples, with no need to estimate it. Classical tangent-space methods, by contrast, only wash the nuisance out asymptotically and still demand an estimate.
arxiv-2603-07673: Huang and colleagues build a factor-graph framework for distributed quantum optimization that is structure-aware. Circuit cutting saves qubits at exponential classical cost, while search-space splitting weakens Grover's squared speedup. Writing objectives as factor graphs and cutting along natural seams yields loosely coupled subproblems linked by shared entanglement. The design keeps Grover-like scaling up to seam factors, with layered divide-and-conquer and two running modes for different hardware eras.
arxiv-2603-07773: Mann backs and sharpens a basic approach for colimits in Cat. The approach, while evident in idea, was never made fully explicit. He first shows the homotopy category functor from simplicial sets to Cat exists exactly when certain weighted colimits in Cat exist. He then constructs these weighted colimits from simplex properties and the nerve functor. Consequently the Cat map into simplicial sets is reflective, implying Cat is cocomplete. Finally he uses this approach to redo coequalizers and localizations in Cat.
arxiv-2603-07873: Crowley and colleagues study graded Ehrhart theory, a q-version of lattice-point counting built on orbit harmonics, for unimodular zonotopes. Building on a 1991 Stanley result, they prove the graded count is a q-value of the Tutte polynomial. The graded series is therefore rational and meets a graded reciprocity law. They also show the harmonic algebra is a coordinate ring of an arrangement Schubert variety, is finitely generated and Cohen-Macaulay, and say when it is Gorenstein.
arxiv-2603-08373: Cuypers gives a uniform mathematical approach to dynamical Lie algebras built from Pauli strings. Such algebras, Lie subalgebras of su(2^n), have recently been studied intensively, and are also called Pauli or Hamiltonian algebras. The paper gathers various recent results on Pauli algebras into one framework. It also presents an algorithm that, given a set of Pauli strings, determines the isomorphism type of the dynamical algebra they span. Its running time is cubic in the larger of n and the size of the generating set.
arxiv-2603-08473: Islami and colleagues prove the Banach, Newton-Raphson and Brouwer fixed point theorems for generalized smooth functions. This framework is a minimal extension of Colombeau theory and of classical distribution theory, and it models nonlinear singular problems. It keeps key traits of usual smooth functions, including closure under composition and classical calculus theorems. The results let us handle equations of the form F(x)=0 where F is such a function, including Sobolev-Schwartz distributions. The authors give singular cases that the classical versions of these theorems do not cover.
arxiv-2603-09173: Sneha Paul and colleagues present SAGE, a multimodal model that reads raw point clouds directly with no pre-trained 3D encoder. Encoder-based rivals suffer semantic mismatch between geometry and language, resolution sensitivity, and heavy compute. SAGE instead uses a light 3D tokenizer that samples and groups points, then quantizes them into tokens like words of a foreign language. A preference training scheme with a semantic reward sharpens its answers on open-ended 3D questions.
arxiv-2603-09373: Wanchun Li and colleagues quantify and extend the coverage of spatial categorization datasets built on the Topological Relations Picture Series. Such datasets record how languages label spatial relations in standard scenes, but coverage of possible scenes is thin. They show labels from large language models align fairly well with human labels and can guide which scenes and languages to add. Their extension adds 42 scenes and covers the scene space better than two earlier extensions.
arxiv-2603-09673: Anh Thuan Tran and Jana Kosecka introduce VarSplat, an uncertainty-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting system for RGB-D SLAM. Existing splatting SLAM handles measurement reliability only implicitly, so pose estimates and global alignment drift in low-texture regions or on tricky surfaces. VarSplat learns per-splat appearance variance and renders a per-pixel uncertainty map in one pass using the law of total variance and alpha compositing together. That map steers tracking, submap registration, and loop detection toward reliable regions, improving robustness on standard datasets.
arxiv-2603-09973: Raghunathan and coauthors look ahead to how next wave surveys will test physics past the standard model of the cosmos. Type Ia star blasts probe the late cosmos, sound waves frozen in galaxy maps probe the middle ages, and the microwave glow probes the early one. Mixing the planned Rubin LSST star blast set with DESI and planned microwave data, they use Markov chain sampling to bound dark energy traits and total neutrino mass. The star blast gains alone roughly double current precision.
arxiv-2603-10073: Alex Shvets studies how to estimate a binary count privately when each person's answer passes through a shuffle. Privacy must hold for every neighbouring data set at fixed global parameters, and biased estimators are allowed. Shvets derives Poisson and Skellam approximations and pins down the limiting minimax risk. Binary randomised response turns out optimal only under one equality condition; otherwise a marked response scheme beats it, with a certified finite sample example.
arxiv-2603-10373: Yasuyuki Fujii and co-authors propose a few-shot way for robots to adapt when the world shifts in ways they cannot directly observe. Instead of retraining model weights, which risks forgetting and costs compute, their method estimates a small latent Trend ID while the model stays frozen. Temporal regularization and a state transition model keep that latent state smooth over time. On a food grasping task, learned Trend IDs formed distinct regions with steady paths, and the robot adapted to new settings from few examples, with no weight changes.
arxiv-2603-10573: Faris Chaudhry and Siddhant Gadkari ask what algorithm a transformer runs when it learns in context. Their test bed is binary hypothesis testing, where the best policy is a known likelihood-ratio test, giving rare ground truth. Trained on tasks with distinct geometries, models approximated the Bayes-optimal statistics from context, matching an ideal oracle in nonlinear cases. Probing suggested no fixed smoothing trick: decisions became readable at shifting depths, ensemble-like for linear tasks, more sequential for nonlinear ones.
arxiv-2603-10773: Bahare Riahi and co-authors study K-12 teachers' views of AI-generated rubric tools, in a summer workshop with twenty-five teachers. Teachers rarely build rubrics from scratch, since the work is slow and level distinctions are hard to phrase. After hands-on use of MagicSchool.ai and a chatbot, they called the AI rubrics strong starting drafts that clarified vague criteria. Oversight stayed essential: wording could be generic or pitched at the wrong grade, and editing criteria was the weakest part. Teachers would adopt them if customization stays easy.
arxiv-2603-11073: Md Nasir Uddin Shuvo and coauthors report on a small full-stack team's production experience with vibe coding. They build software conversationally with code-generating tools, under explicit architectural constraints. They built two systems. One is a multi-project agent learning platform with isolated projects and structured memory. The other is an academic retrieval system giving citation-grounded answers with role-based access. Generation sped up scaffolding and integration. But isolation rules, access control, and memory policies kept needing deliberate design. Engineering effort shifted toward specifying and auditing constraints.
arxiv-2603-11273: Darshan Makwana and coauthors schedule speech recognition serving by expected duration. They attack the head-of-line blocking that first-come-first-served queues suffer when workloads drift. Audio duration turns out to predict processing time well for models like Whisper. They integrate two policies into a serving engine. These are shortest job first and highest response ratio next. Shortest job first slashes median latency at high load but starves long requests. The response-ratio policy keeps the median gain. It has bounded tail damage and no throughput penalty.
arxiv-2603-11473: Zou and co-authors present KProxNPLVM, a new soft sensor that sidesteps a flaw in latent variable training. Soft sensors infer hard-to-measure values, with a sense of uncertainty built in. The usual route lets neural nets set the variational posterior, which turns a function-space problem into a finite parameter one and leaves an approximation error. KProxNPLVM instead relaxes the objective, using Wasserstein distance as a proximal operator. The team proves the old error and shows gains on synthetic and industrial data.
arxiv-2603-11573: Fujimura and co-authors free projection mapping from its dark-room constraint with a target-excluding light system. Projection mapping paints images onto real objects, yet bright rooms wash it out. Their setup lights the room around the target, leaving the target dark. An LED display panel and an optimized aperiodic lens array create that light field. The array acts as a large, soft source with natural shadows and fine spatial control. A placement method cuts crosstalk dark spots, and a prototype keeps contrast high in bright rooms.
arxiv-2603-12273: Kleine Buening and co-authors learn alignment directly from multi-turn user interactions. Follow-up messages often reveal that a reply missed the mark, yet training usually discards them. Models can already use such follow-ups in context to revise their behavior. Their method conditions the model on the follow-up and compares its new token distribution with the old policy. That hindsight distribution becomes a target, distilled back into the current policy. Training on real WildChat conversations improved alignment scores and enabled personalization without explicit feedback labels.
arxiv-2603-12573: Pedro Melo asks how much information one observed outcome can carry about an unknown parameter. He derives upper bounds on pointwise mutual information that use stochastic Fisher information. The bounds cover bounded ranges and smooth priors, with clear cases where they saturate. Averaging his result recovers a known link between mutual and Fisher information. He then tests the ideas on a Langevin particle and on a thermal qubit that senses a field.
arxiv-2603-12673: Trung Loc Tang and co-authors study a weakly coupled system of structurally damped wave equations with critical nonlinearities. The nonlinear terms carry moduli of continuity whose powers sit on the critical curve. The team seeks a sharp condition on those moduli. They prove global existence for small data Sobolev solutions in some cases. In others, solutions blow up in finite time. For blow-up cases, they also give sharp lifespan estimates for local solutions.
arxiv-2603-12873: Jiale Meng and co-authors propose TRACE, a document watermarking method that encodes data in character shapes. Older methods rely on edge traits or fixed codebooks, which noise can disturb. Character structures stay stable and share one form across many glyphs. Their diffusion system finds handle and target points, moves chosen points, then repairs the region. Tests gained over 5 dB in PSNR and 5% in extraction accuracy after cross-media transfer. The method works across languages and fonts.
arxiv-2603-13073: Manuel Hagelueken and co-authors test how the cost of adaptive variational quantum eigensolvers scales with system size. VQE hopes to find ground states that classical machines cannot reach. A Rényi entropy from classical runs predicts the needed iteration count with high accuracy. Tests covered more than 20 molecules with active spaces of four to ten orbitals. Iteration counts, and thus circuit depth, grew exponentially with size. Large molecules with high fidelity thus look out of reach for current VQE forms.
arxiv-2603-13173: I de Zarzà and co-authors test whether language model agents keep their answers under meaning-preserving changes to a problem. Fixed benchmark forms cannot catch this kind of fragility. Their metamorphic frame applies eight such changes, from paraphrase to fact reordering and context shifts. Seven models from four families faced 19 multi-step problems in eight science domains. Scale did not predict stability: a smaller Qwen3 model proved most invariant. Larger models broke down more often under the same shifts.
arxiv-2603-13573: Reda Elwaradi and co-authors present a weakly supervised pipeline for high-resolution sea ice topology retrieval from SAR imagery. Operational ice charts give only coarse region-level polygons, so models struggle for pixel-level accuracy. Their U-Net fuses Sentinel-1 SAR and AMSR-2 radiometry data with a region-based loss. An Analytical Logit Scaling step then fixes under-confident outputs after inference. It sets temperature and bias from latent space percentiles of each scene. The method reveals fine sea ice fractures at 40-meter resolution with no manual pixel labels.
arxiv-2603-13673: Mingchen Shao, Yuzhang Xie, Carl Yang, and Jiaying Lu propose LLM-MINE to mine Alzheimer's phenotypes from clinical notes. Alzheimer's and related dementias data sit in free text, not tables, so they are hard to extract with accuracy. Their framework uses a large language model to pull phenotypes from two expert-defined lists. Chi-square tests confirm significant phenotype differences across cohorts, and memory impairment is the strongest discriminator. Few-shot prompting with both lists gave the best clustering for unsupervised disease staging, well above NER and dictionary baselines.
arxiv-2603-13773: Seungbin Yang and co-authors introduce LiveWeb-IE, a benchmark for online web information extraction. Prior benchmarks use HTML snapshots from a single point in time, which misses how the web evolves. Performance on static benchmarks often fails to generalize to dynamic real-world settings, they note. LiveWeb-IE evaluates systems directly against live, permission-granted websites with natural language queries. Queries span text, images, and hyperlinks at four complexity levels. They also propose Visual Grounding Scraper, a multi-stage agentic framework that visually narrows page content to extract data.
arxiv-2603-14073: Kim, Um, and Ye boost motion in text-to-video models with a method called MotionCFG. Standard guidance leans on negative prompts like static or blurry, which can bend content and break objects. The authors name that failure Content-Motion Drift. MotionCFG instead adds Gaussian noise to concept embeddings, which makes soft negative anchors near the target idea. Those anchors mark poor motion variants without shifting the scene's identity. A stepwise schedule limits the push to early denoising, which lifts motion at tiny cost.
arxiv-2603-14173: Shanivendra joins classic machine learning with large language models to tailor bank marketing to each customer. Banks must guess what a customer wants and still write messages that obey the rules. One part sorts customers into groups, infers intent, and picks the best product and channel. A second part drafts the message with facts pulled from bank documents, which cuts made-up claims. Tests use a made-up dataset with behavior over time. Time and intent cues lift accuracy, and cited sources help audits.
arxiv-2603-14273: Xiang, Zhang, and Feng test whether large language models can run sensitivity checks in causal inference. Tools like the Cornfield inequality and the E-value gauge how strong hidden confounding must be to explain a result away. Clinicians often find these tools hard to compute and read. The authors feed four published studies to ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, and Gemini with structured prompts. They score E-value math, plain readings of robustness, and guesses at hidden confounders.
arxiv-2603-14373: Ji studies whether motivational framing in system prompts changes how AI coding agents debug code. Two studies compare trust-framed guidance, a fear-framed variant, and a plain baseline. Trust-framed agents took far more investigative steps and found many more hidden bugs. They found fewer surface issues, a depth-over-breadth trade. Fear-framed agents beat the baseline on no measure in the second study. The author concludes that trust framing deepens agent investigation while fear framing does not help.
arxiv-2603-14473: Tong and co-authors ask whether AI can learn scientific taste. Taste here means judging which research ideas will matter over time. Such judgement sits with a few senior experts in narrow fields. Their method, RLCF, learns from community feedback such as citations. One model, Scientific Judge, scores ideas and beats strong language model baselines, they report. Its scores also hold for future papers and unseen fields. A second model, Scientific Thinker, proposes ideas rated higher than baseline ideas.
arxiv-2603-14573: Dandi, Gamarnik, Pernice and Zdeborová make the dynamical cavity method rigorous. Physicists use the method to derive mean field equations for system dynamics. Past math proofs relied on other tools, such as Gaussian conditioning. The team now formalizes the cavity method itself. With it, they give a fresh proof of the DMFT equations. The proof covers General First Order Methods, a broad algorithm class. Gradient Descent and Approximate Message Passing both sit inside that class.
arxiv-2603-14673: Xu and co-authors bound regret for nonstationary online linear programming from a single sample. Orders arrive one by one with shifting reward and resource profiles. Each call to accept or reject is final. Only one sample from each order distribution is known up front. Their re-solving algorithm blends dynamic programming with dual methods from the stationary case. With resources scaling in the order count, regret grows as the square of log n. Strong drift and thin data still allow polylog regret, they prove.
arxiv-2603-14873: Edet and co-authors build an English-Efik corpus and translation system for digital inclusion. Efik, a smaller Nigerian language, barely appears in translation research. A community-curated set holds 13,865 parallel sentence pairs. Two multilingual models get fine-tuned on that base. NLLB-200 beats mT5 in both directions, they report. BLEU reaches 26.64 for English-Efik and 31.21 for Efik-English. Matching chrF scores back the fluency gains. Practical tools for low-resource languages look feasible here.
arxiv-2603-14973: Popowski, Schramma, Lerner and Jalaal dissect cage breaking in a minimal active-matter setup. Three self-propelling disks move inside a circular cage. An entropic landscape for rearrangements is built exactly for the trio. The passive twin landscape offers a clean comparison. Low activity keeps the landscape near bistable. High activity adds basins tied to frustrated clusters at the wall. Escape runs fastest when persistence length matches particle radius. Probability currents swirl in the two-dimensional landscape view. Detailed balance breaks at both fine and coarse levels.
arxiv-2603-15273: Bosco and co-authors describe a flash lamp that produces vacuum ultraviolet light for testing light sensors. Noble liquids such as argon and xenon glow in this band when particles pass through, so dark matter and neutrino detectors depend on such sensors. The lamp mimics the wavelengths seen in those detectors. The authors detail the design choices behind it. They also report results from a prototype run at room temperature.
arxiv-2603-15473: Wright and co-authors present the Agent Lifecycle Toolkit, open-source middleware that hardens AI agents for enterprise use. Agent faults can corrupt data, hide errors, or breach policy, yet most frameworks leave safeguards to each builder. The toolkit marks six intervention points, from the raw user request to final response assembly. Modular parts detect, repair, and soften common failure modes at those points. Shared interfaces drop into current pipelines, and low-code tools like Langflow are supported. The aim is production-grade agents with far less bespoke safety code.
arxiv-2603-15573: Howarth and co-authors simulate turbulent lean premixed hydrogen jet flames with direct numerical simulation and detailed chemistry. Slot and round jet shapes run at several pressures, all at the same jet Reynolds number of 10,000. Big-picture measures like flame length look alike across shapes. Deeper measures split: mean local reactivity fades downstream as the Karlovitz number drops, faster in round jets. Pressure sharpens how displacement speed answers local curvature. That raises flame stretch and wrinkling near the nozzle at high pressure.
arxiv-2603-15873: Hilman and Ramzi build multiplicative norms on equivariant algebraic K-theory. Norms in the plain case rest on localizing motives machinery. Their work lifts that machinery to genuine equivariant settings. Perfect G-stable categories supply the base objects. A new motive view handles non-exact functors along the way. The main theorem says norms of stable categories preserve motivic sameness. A unique equivariant multiplicative K-theory refinement follows. A genuine equivariant THH with Dennis trace also results. Every genuine G-spectrum becomes K-theory of some category.
arxiv-2603-15973: Spera proves that safe parts can join into an unsafe whole. Capability-based AI systems grant agents bundles of single capabilities. Two agents may each lack any path to a banned capability. Combined, a conjunctive dependency can still open that banned goal. His formal framework makes the gap precise and provable. The result marks safety as non-compositional in such systems. Checks on single agents cannot certify the joined system. System-level audits must hunt emergent combined paths.
arxiv-2603-16173: Friedlander and Suen study a family of active scalar equations with two diffusion controls. One control damps the scalar, and the other sets the strength of a fractional Laplacian. They prove results on how solutions behave in key regimes. Averaged over long times, the solutions lose no energy in an anomalous way. A single global attractor is shown to exist. The results cover the surface quasigeostrophic and magnetogeostrophic equations.
arxiv-2603-16673: Liu and co-authors teach robot agents when to think and when to act. Calling a language model costs time and can stall motion. Too much reasoning delays action; too little invites errors. Their RARRL framework learns an orchestration policy, not low-level control. The policy picks whether to reason, which role to use, and what budget to spend. It reads observations, history, and remaining resources. Tests with ALFRED latency profiles raised success rates. Latency fell and robustness improved.
arxiv-2603-16873: Bujack and co-authors propose a way to grade charts that AI systems draw from text prompts. One shot generated charts often fall short, and human grading is costly at scale. Their metric needs no large set of human labels. Instead, it treats the source data as ground truth. A reconstruction step tries to recover the original data from the chart itself. How well that recovery works becomes the quality score. The authors argue this gives a scalable stand in for careful human review.
arxiv-2603-17173: Piland and co-authors test whether general multimodal models can detect iris presentation attacks with help from human experts. Building specialist models is hard: future attacks are unknown, data are costly, and sharing biometric data raises privacy issues. They find that vision encoders in these models already cluster many attack types without task training. Where clusters overlap, prompts carrying human salience, meaning verbal notes on attack signs, resolve the ambiguity. On 224 iris images, Gemini with expert prompts beat a specialist baseline and human examiners.
arxiv-2603-17473: Han, Zhang, and Luo study a plactic-like monoid built from the stalactic congruence and its dual. They equip this monoid with several involutions and sort them into types by alphabet size. A faithful representation comes with each involution type. Clear combinatorial rules then describe which identities hold under each one. That settles both the finite basis problem and the identity checking problem for these monoids.
arxiv-2603-17573: Zheng and co-authors present HeiSD, a faster decoding scheme for robot vision-language-action models. Speculative decoding drafts ahead, but drafter-based and retrieval-based forms each have weak spots. HeiSD mixes both and adds a verify-skip step plus looser sequence-level acceptance. A kinematic score sets the switch point between the two modes on its own. Speedups reached 2.45 times in simulation, they report, with task success intact.
arxiv-2603-17673: Normann, Happe, Cito, and Arp train a small local model to run Linux privilege escalation tasks. Big cloud agents are hard to audit or use on sensitive code. Their recipe fine-tunes a 4B model on traces from staged escalation setups first. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards then sharpens it further. The tuned model hit 93.3 percent success on held-out cases, they report. Cost per success fell by more than eightyfold.
arxiv-2603-17773: Caccavale and co-authors report on a language-model chatbot inside a university course. The assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation to stand in for a teacher-led exercise. Three iterative studies with mixed methods, one a crossover, test the swap. They probe student drive, response quality, and grades, plus how the bot feels versus a human teacher. Hallucination and shallow topic knowledge frame the risks. The results weigh where such tools fit specialized teaching.
arxiv-2603-17973: Alonso, Yovine, and Braberman present TDAD, an open tool that warns coding agents which tests a patch may break. It maps links between source code and tests before a change is made. On SWE-bench Verified, TDAD cut regressions from 6.08% to 1.82% in their tests. Plain test-driven prompts without this map made regressions worse. As an agent skill, TDAD also raised the fix rate from 24% to 32%.
arxiv-2603-18073: Yang's thesis takes three steps toward AI that keeps improving itself beyond human caps. First, synthetic data methods amplify small corpora so models can learn new knowledge with less waste. Second, a model can self-generate data to bootstrap pretraining without a tuned teacher model. Third, scaling test-time search lets AI explore learning algorithm designs past human reach. Each chapter breaks one dependency on human creators.
arxiv-2603-18173: Lee and co-authors present GRAFITE, a platform for tracking and testing issues in large language models. Benchmark exposure during training can inflate scores over time, they note. GRAFITE builds a growing repository of model problems from user feedback. A pipeline tests models against these issues with LLM-as-a-judge quality checks. Side-by-side views across releases help teams spot regressions as models change.
arxiv-2603-18273: Pan and co-authors present EDM-ARS, a multi-agent system that automates educational data mining research.
