arxiv-2604-24373: Jackson and three colleagues study creativity when software pros work with a language model. In a workplace-like lab, 18 pairs had 90 minutes to produce a design from specs. They had optional language-model access and were not primed to be creative. It showed in all pairs' work, with 13 writing docs showing creativity. The authors credit human designers most, driven by experience, empathy, and analogy. The model contributed novel ideas and elaborations. Sometimes the model slowed it, so human insight remains central.
arxiv-2604-24473: Moll and 23 colleagues test whether an agent-style language model system can reason over years of myeloma care records as well as cancer experts do. They ran the system, plus simpler retrieval and full-context rivals, on hundreds of patient questions drawn from 811 patient files, with expert labels as the yardstick. The agent system matched experts at 79.6 percent overall and pulled further ahead on the hardest questions and longest files, though its remaining errors were more often clinically serious.
arxiv-2604-24673: Schofield, White, Baker and Byrne model how melanoma cell clusters form, a step that can promote spread. If caught early, it can be cured more often. If it spreads, care gets much harder. They fit a system of differential equations, built on coagulation, fragmentation and proliferation, to time-lapse microscopy data for proliferative and invasive phenotypes. Invasive cells in monoculture coagulate at nearly three times the rate of proliferative cells, which proliferate slightly faster. These gaps match known gene patterns. It also shows how mixed cultures differ from single cultures.
arxiv-2604-24773: Lee, Chung and Huh address molecular design. Binding arrangements must be both good in energy and made as a single molecule. They formulate simultaneous placement of two fragments as Q-SFD, a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem. They add a clear inter-fragment distance term to favor arrangements that can be rebuilt. Relative to the version without that term, Q-SFD roughly doubles top-1 recovery of reconstruction-feasible pairs. Top-5 solutions hold at least one feasible pair in more than 90 percent of benchmark cases.
arxiv-2604-24873: Serrani and Skvortsov show nonzero tree-level amplitudes, in Kleinian signature or in complex kinematics, across all self-dual theories, massless higher-spin fields included. Recent work showed infinitely many exist once massless higher-spin fields are allowed, with chiral higher-spin gravity maximal. The authors establish nonzero amplitudes for the full family. In sky duality work, nonzero amplitudes in chiral higher-spin gravity supply a missing ingredient. It completes the sky analogue of the vector-model and higher-spin AdS/CFT duality.
arxiv-2604-24973: Ramacciotti and four colleagues improve the Grover-Rudolph algorithm for sparse quantum state preparation. First, they extend a gate-merging procedure by letting rotations merge onto virtual zero-angle gates on unreachable branches. This reduces the number of CNOTs and control qubits. Second, they introduce an approximate variant merging rotations with similar but not identical angles, at the cost of small, controllable error. They derive a classically computable estimate of overlap with the target state, used to guide merging decisions.
arxiv-2604-25073: Lysenstøen studies feasible-first search for constrained deployment tuning in crash spaces. The space holds many invalid setups: tests may crash, exceed memory or violate latency limits. It proposes Thermal Budget Annealing, a feasible method mapping valid regions before warm-starting a Parzen Estimator. Two robustness tools handle hardware: timeouts aborting infeasible tests early. The authors present DeployBench, a benchmark suite with crash zones, hard constraints and unequal costs. On synthetic tests and real GPU deployment with five vision models across five targets, the hybrid improves discovery under constraints.
arxiv-2604-25273: Zhang and five colleagues propose Salient Subject-Aware Multimodal Embedding for unified retrieval, tackling visual neglect and semantic drift. Methods focus on sample objectives while missing subject semantics, so models fail to find salient regions and lean on text cues. Their framework uses multimodal models and visual experts to stress salient concepts, with a saliency goal aligning attention with key regions. A module adjusts features from saliency maps for balanced integration. Tests show state-of-the-art performance on MMEB.
arxiv-2604-25573: Sachdeva and four colleagues study anneal-inspired algorithms suited to noisy near-term quantum devices. They first scan rough anneal runs whose step size and layer count drift from faithful runs, finding regimes that keep anneal-like behaviour at lower cost. Those tuned parameters then warm-start the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm, beating random starts. They also introduce evolving Hamiltonian tuning, a multistep trial scheme that steers tuning through mid-step Hamiltonians. Tests on hard 2-SAT cases suggest both schemes offer practical routes to stronger variational quantum tuning.
arxiv-2604-25673: Bai, Hao, and Guo calculate how tau particles decay into an axion-like particle plus a meson, using chiral effective field theory. They build the mixing among neutral pions, eta mesons, and the hypothetical particle. Resonance parameters are fit to measured tau decay spectra. The team then predicts branching ratios, mass distributions, and forward-backward asymmetries for two decay channels. The results give future searches a firm basis for hunting axion-like signals in tau decays.
arxiv-2604-25873: Claros and Rela give new quantitative results on embedding the Muckenhoupt class A-infinity into A-p, with correct asymptotics as weights near constancy. The parameter p tends to 1 when the Fujii-Wilson constant approaches 1. Steps along the way estimate weighted and unweighted BMO norms of the logarithm of the weight. Consequently, a precise quantitative weighted Poincaré-Sobolev inequality holds for weights with small constant, recovering the classical Sobolev exponent as the constant tends to 1. The work sharpens the quantitative theory of Muckenhoupt weights.
arxiv-2604-26173: Zhao and five colleagues improve test-time selection among sampled language-model responses without training an outside reward model. High-entropy tokens cluster into consecutive groups during generation, so they define high-entropy phases and their entropy centroid, a centre-of-mass-like average position of uncertainty along a response. A lower centroid signals early exploration followed by confident generation and often marks higher quality. Picking the lowest-centroid response beats baselines across mathematics, coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks, with gains growing with model size.
arxiv-2604-26673: Saiapin and Batselier propose a Bayesian tensor network kernel machine that uses a linear Laplace method for inference. Gaussian process models give sound uncertainty numbers but scale poorly, while tensor network kernel machines scale well yet break Gaussian form and complicate chance-based inference. Their method, LA-TNKM, restores sound uncertainty numbers under tensor network assumptions. Across varied UCI fit tests, it matches or beats Gaussian process models and Bayesian neural nets in test after test.
arxiv-2604-27173: Khan asks which joint probability distributions distributed agents can realize when each agent sees only limited information. Classical local rules cannot reach every distribution that full conditioning on history would allow. Shared quantum states can close part of that gap, even separable states that are diagonal in a fixed basis. Those states let local measurements realize distributions that classical rules cannot, though quantum methods cannot mimic fully adaptive dependence on outcomes that look identical.
arxiv-2604-27573: Brennan, Callow, and Lin give two proofs that the chance no p+1 sticks form a (p+1)-sided polygon equals a product of reciprocals involving p-step Fibonacci numbers. The first proof leans on matrix algebra to stretch an earlier triangles-and-quadrilaterals method. The second uses the minimum and maximum stick lengths compatible with failing to form such a polygon, revealing why Fibonacci numbers appear. The approach generalizes to sticks drawn from any probability distribution.
arxiv-2604-27773: Abebe treats cosmic tensions as global fit rules on the base model, rather than lone flukes. The fit trio links cosmic growth (H0), structure-growth size (S8), and the redshift link of growth, shown by the growth index. Using f(Q) gravity as a test case, he draws on recent Bayes and motion-system studies of power-law, exponential, and log kinds. While f(Q) models can ease individual tensions, joint fit across all three corners sharply restricts the viable setting space, leaving only a narrow subset in play.
arxiv-2605-00073:
Mohd Sameen Chishti, Damilare Peter Oyinloye, and Jingyue Li propose AgentReputation, a reputation framework for decentralized marketplaces of AI agents. Such markets host agents that debug code, generate patches, and audit security, often with no central overseer. Trust there is hard: agents can game the evaluations, skill in one task type may not transfer to another, and checks range from cheap automated tests to costly expert review.

Their three-layer design separates task execution, reputation services, and tamper-proof storage so each can evolve alone. Explicit verification regimes are tied to each agent's standing record, and context-conditioned reputation cards stop scores from bleeding across domains. A policy engine turns those scores into decisions on resources, access, and when to step up checking. The paper closes with research directions, from checking ontologies to cold-start bootstrapping.
arxiv-2605-00273:
Yujin Jeong and 4 co-authors ask why text-to-image diffusion models so often fail when a picture must contain several objects at once. The pictures look sharp, yet objects go missing, merge, or land in the wrong places. The team first asks how much of the failure comes from the training data itself.

They built a controlled data generator, called mosaic, and trained models under two regimes: one where single concepts appear unevenly, and one where certain combinations are held out on purpose. Scene complexity, not concept imbalance, proved the dominant obstacle. Counting objects was uniquely hard to learn when data was scarce. Held-out combinations also broke down faster as more were withheld, which points to a need for stronger built-in biases and better data design.
arxiv-2605-00573:
René Peschmann hunts perfect cuboids, boxes with integer edges, face diagonals, and space diagonal, whose existence has been open for centuries. The paper works with body cuboids, which may lack the integer space diagonal, parametrized by pairs of Pythagorean triples in Euclid's form. Its first contribution is a verified pattern the author calls the exponent-one blocker, found in the space-diagonal norm of every such candidate examined.

In each fully factored case, some prime divides that norm to exactly the first power. That prime also avoids a fixed list of twenty-nine parameter expressions, a primitive obstruction to the norm being a square. Two natural strengthenings of the pattern fail. The second contribution builds a generator from the elliptic curves behind the parametrization, minting over a million further candidates. None is a perfect cuboid, and every factored record obeys the blocker pattern: evidence, not proof.
arxiv-2605-00773:
Fredrik Bakke and three co-authors study the Sierpinski cone in synthetic models of space built by extending homotopy type theory with an interval. In ordinary settings the cone adds a universal closed point below all others and classifies partial maps defined on an open part. In the synthetic setting that classifying property proves more delicate.

The authors show the property cannot hold for all such types without collapsing the theory. They identify the largest subuniverse where it does hold, described as a localization at interval-based embeddings, and show it sits strictly inside the Segal types when the interval is nontrivial. They extend the results to mapping cylinders with a new such property.
arxiv-2605-00973:
Hao Zhou and fourteen co-authors present xMAE, a pre-training framework that uses the ordered timing between biosignals to learn better patterns. Signals from different body sites often view the same process at different stages. Heart electrical activity, recorded by ECG, starts each beat, while the PPG pulse arrives later after vascular travel. Most self-supervised methods treat such signals as interchangeable views and miss that direction.

xMAE trains with masked cross-modal rebuilding across time-ordered signals, encouraging physiologically meaningful timing in the learned patterns. Pre-training beats unimodal and multimodal baselines on most of nineteen downstream tasks, from heart outcome prediction to sleep staging, and generalizes across devices and body locations. Timing structure appears reflected in the learned pulse patterns.
arxiv-2605-01073:
Leonid Bedratyuk studies the local shape of sentence embedding clouds formed by controlled sets of semantically close sentences. The central question is how paraphrase-like variation is arranged in that space and whether low-degree fitted surfaces can model that local structure in full. Affine, quadratic, and cubic carriers are fitted, and a probing procedure makes synthetic latent points in a reduced local space relative to the fitted surface.

Generated points are judged on surface consistency, neighborhood preservation, agreement with the observed spread, and stability of shape and coefficient measures. Nonlinear local models describe the clouds more closely than affine ones. Surface-based generation also shows strong shape fidelity. Shape validity does not on its own improve classification, however. A large dataset of sentence variants is also introduced.
arxiv-2605-01173:
Fiaz Hossain and four co-authors build a framework to limit how AI data center load swings affect fatigue life of thermal turbine generators. Rapid variations in data center demand can drive torsional oscillations in synchronous generators, accumulating fatigue damage. Their frequency-domain approach quantifies allowed swings in three steps.

First, maximum allowed power variation at each generator is found from a lumped multi-mass mechanical model. Next, load flow gives an interaction factor mapping a load change at a bus to generator output changes. Finally, candidate buses are screened and an optimization sets optimal allowed swings. Tests on standard test systems and a synthetic two-thousand-bus Texas system demonstrate applicability and scalability.
arxiv-2605-01373:
Jinyuan Feng and seven co-authors study diffusion language models, which write by cleaning up noisy text step by step. These models see the whole passage at once, yet common decoding habits favor local cues and waste that wide view, which lowers quality.

The team finds that high-information tokens, the words that carry the most content, help a lot when fed back as context, and they settle early in decoding. Their method, FoCore, needs no training: it briefly hides those core tokens and uses them as negative samples to steer writing by contrast. A faster variant decodes stable nearby tokens in parallel once core tokens settle. On math, code, and logic tests, and on two model families, FoCore lifts quality, and the fast variant cuts decoding steps by more than half.
arxiv-2605-01473:
Satoru Iwata and Haruto Konno unify two classic algorithms for shrinking symmetric submodular functions, a family of set functions with a diminishing-returns shape that shows up in cuts, clustering, and entropy. Two orderings of the ground set, built decades apart, each expose a special pair of elements that lets the search contract and continue.

One ordering yields a pendent pair and the other a flat pair, and the link between them was never clear. Iwata and Konno add a third ordering, then stretch all three into a one-parameter family. A single general inequality governs the family, and the two classic results drop out at the two ends of the dial. At every setting, the last two elements of the ordering form a contractible pair, which gives one contraction algorithm that finds a nontrivial minimizer with a cubic number of value queries.
arxiv-2605-01573:
B Kosyakov, E Popov, and M Vronsky review models that treat the atomic nucleus as a bound system of quarks, three per nucleon, rather than as protons and neutrons alone. The overview seeks an effective theory of low-energy strong-force physics that still explains plain nuclear facts.

A Fermi gas picture explains why stable light nuclei, up to calcium, hold nearly equal numbers of up and down quarks. A modified bag model then accounts for the drift away from that balance in heavier nuclei and matches static traits of many stable nuclei well. To sharpen the bag model, the authors invoke a refined gauge-gravity duality linking an extremal black hole's interior to a stable subnuclear system. The duality predicts the main decay channel of the lightest glueball and a ceiling on stable nuclear charge near 82, the charge of lead's heaviest stable isotope.
arxiv-2605-01673:
Xinmeng Xu and five co-authors slow down audio-visual fusion until the fused state is ready to be trusted. In stage-wise encoders, each layer's fused state seeds the next. A locally convincing match between sound and sight can still lack the wider support needed to guide later layers. The authors call that failure premature commitment.

Their Delayed Perceptual Commitment Network grades each intermediate state with an observable readiness-deficiency score. It finds the bottleneck stage where intervention helps most, and corrects it with evidence drawn across layers and across senses. Task heads, losses, and decoders stay untouched, so the fix rides on the encoder alone. Speech separation, event localization, and speech recognition all improve. Ablations, counterfactual probes, and readiness traces across depth back the claim that timing the commitment, not adding capacity, earns the gains.
arxiv-2605-01873:
Rishad Shahmurov studies vortex stretching in fluid flow by splitting the vorticity equation according to how large the vorticity is. For almost any cut-off level, the stretching above that level equals a change in mass above the level plus two non-negative terms from viscosity. One term tracks changes in vorticity direction, and the other tracks loss across the level surface.

Adding the result over all levels recovers the classic balance for vorticity and, in one key case, the usual palinstrophy account. At a critical exponent, the loss term can be written with a new nonlinear variable. The method also lets distinct high-vorticity episodes be counted without overlap, under extra assumptions.
arxiv-2605-02073:
Arash Ahmadi, Sarah Sharif, and Yaser Banad treat the reward function itself as the thing to search for when training a language model to reason. The base model stays fixed, so reward design is the main lever left. A frontier model proposes candidate rewards, which are checked automatically and then screened in short training runs.

Each candidate is trained with group-based policy methods on a small Llama model and ranked by its score on the GSM8K maths test. Summaries of past rounds feed the next round of proposals. Over five rounds the search made fifty candidates. The paper reports how the best rewards evolved and whether search beats hand design.
arxiv-2605-02273:
Kacper Duma and colleagues analyse how humans review pull requests written by AI on GitHub, using the AIDev data set. They compare AI-authored requests with human-authored ones inside the same repositories. The question matters because review is often read as a sign of human oversight in large studies of coding activity.

Most AI-generated requests received no review at all. When review happened, AI agents dominated it rather than humans. Human-authored requests were more likely to get human-only review and direct human feedback. Reviews of AI requests more often ran through automation, with humans steering agents instead of judging the code alone. The authors warn that review metrics can mislead as measures of human oversight in agentic workflows.
arxiv-2605-02473:
Nitin Serwa classifies low-order conservation laws for a family of fifth-order Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equations, which model waves in two spatial directions. Conservation laws matter because each one names a quantity that stays fixed as the wave evolves. Serwa uses the direct multiplier method and limits the search to multipliers of differential order at most two, stated in the original variable.

The first result is that every such multiplier in fact has order at most one. Sorting the cases then gives one general case and two special nonlinear cases, each with its own set of free functions of time. Serwa derives sample conserved densities and flows for all three. The general densities cover mass and a transverse moment, while the special cases add energy-like and higher moment densities.
arxiv-2605-02673:
Serhii Zabolotnii describes EstemPMM, an R software package for estimating model parameters when errors are not Gaussian. Standard least squares is optimal for bell-shaped errors, but real errors are often skewed or heavy-tailed. The polynomial maximization method uses the third and fourth standardized moments of the error to build estimators that beat least squares in those cases.

The package gives one interface for linear regression and for autoregressive, moving-average, and combined time-series models, including seasonal forms. A dispatch function picks among least squares and two polynomial variants by reading the sample's skew and tail weight. Standard R tools for summaries, intervals, and prediction are supported. Simulations check the theory, and a crude-oil case study shows the package in use.
arxiv-2605-02973:
Eitan Kosman, Gabriele Serussi, and Chaim Baskin add structure to diffusion bridges, a method for translating data between modalities, such as image styles or sensor types. Translation is under-constrained: many cross-modal maps can produce the same overall distributions. Most bridge methods lean on fully paired data as their single constraint, which is costly to gather and may not exist.

Their framework first characterizes the space of maps that fit, then narrows it with alignment constraints, treating paired examples as an optional aid rather than a requirement. Tests on synthetic and real translation benchmarks cover unpaired, partly paired, and fully paired settings, with steady performance across all three. Quality close to the fully paired case was reached with far looser pairing. Bridges, the authors argue, are a flexible base beyond paired data.
arxiv-2605-03073:
Venkata Pushpak Teja Menta tackles speech recognition for entity-heavy Indic speech, such as digit strings, money amounts, addresses, and mixed English-Indic speech. Both open and commercial systems do poorly on this niche, missing most of the key entities in Telugu tests.

Menta builds a loop in which a text-to-speech system makes about twenty-two thousand training utterances at low cost, then fine-tunes a recognizer on them. Entity hits rose many times over both baselines on held-out tests, and a small human-recorded check confirmed the gain carries to real speech. All test targets were still missed, and results are reported plainly.
arxiv-2605-03273:
Kun Huang introduces the consecutive lifting-projection flow as a new approximation for the Boltzmann and Landau equations of kinetic theory. The collision operator in these equations is nonlinear and hard to handle, which complicates both analysis and solver design.

The method lifts collisions to a linear master equation on spheres in higher dimensions, evolves there, and projects back down. The flow keeps mass, momentum, and energy, dissipates entropy, and settles to the correct equilibrium. For Maxwell molecules an error bound is given. The frame unifies known schemes and yields a new, unconditionally stable Green's function method.
arxiv-2605-03373:
Zhe Li, Bicheng Ying, Zidong Liu, and Haibo Yang explain why zeroth-order optimization, long thought to slow badly with model size, can fine-tune billion-parameter language models. Classic theory predicts a dimension penalty versus first-order methods, yet practice keeps succeeding at huge scale.

Deriving one-step learning dynamics, they show the empirical neural tangent kernel governs progress, and its entries are tangent vectors projected onto a random low-dimensional subspace. By a classic embedding lemma, fidelity depends on the number of perturbations and the output size, not the parameter count. That dimension-free property resolves the paradox in theory.
arxiv-2605-03573:
Jian Xu and six co-authors study score-based diffusion on the manifold of quantum pure states, a curved space where each point is a possible state of a quantum system. No closed-form transition density exists there, so the score must be taught by a local-time teacher taken from a Euclidean approximation. The paper asks what makes that teacher reliable.

Three training choices prove decisive: dividing increments by the diffusion clock rather than elapsed time, using closed-form Fubini-Study maps for the geometry, and randomizing the global phase. With them, the model beats the published baseline across eight benchmarks and an ambient Euclidean method by about an order of magnitude. The authors also bound the cost of the approximation.
arxiv-2605-04073:
Cor Steging and Tadeusz Zbiegień confront a structural problem in using machine learning to support bail decisions: label indeterminacy. When bail is denied, whether the defendant would have appeared in court is never observed. So historical bail data only partially reveal the outcomes that future models are trained to predict. Building systems on such data risks bias and self-reinforcing feedback loops.

In a case study of bail decisions from Pennsylvania's Unified Judicial System, the authors evaluate five approaches to handling indeterminacy. They test them across three machine learning models. One approach is a novel label imputation method motivated by bail dynamics. Every method rests on unverifiable assumptions. Yet the choice among them influenced predictive behavior sometimes more than the choice of model. Explainable AI analysis showed the effects reach the models' internal decision processes.
arxiv-2605-04273:
Max Hall-Brown and Peter Guy Wolynes model polyamorphism, the ability of one material to form more than one distinct liquid phase. In network liquids such as water, the effect comes from competition between bonded and non-bonded local arrangements.

Their simple microscopic model calculates both glassy and thermodynamic behaviour directly from the underlying interactions. It contains a liquid-liquid transition that can be placed above, near, or below the glass transition by tuning the parameters. The work aims to explain related oddities such as water's density peak, while avoiding the freezing problems that make supercooled water hard to study directly.
arxiv-2605-04473:
Rinki Imada and Tomohiro Tachi develop a design method for origami that folds itself in sequence, like a line of dominoes, driven purely by geometry rather than by stored energy. Propagating fronts of state change appear in nature and engineering, but a general framework for programming them through folding constraints was missing.

Working with strips of simple flat-foldable vertices, they show uneven coupling between neighbouring creases produces recurrence relations whose combined behaviour generically links the unfolded and flat-folded states. That link enables sequential deployment. They further show the overall shape can be programmed separately from how the front propagates, giving designers two independent controls.
arxiv-2605-04673:
Matteo Quinzi, Tommaso Chiarotti, and Nicola Marzari rethink pseudopotentials. These effective potentials let materials work ignore the inactive core electrons. Only the active valence states are treated. That replacement is really an embedding problem. The removed core can be described by a dynamical potential, one that depends on energy.

Their framework builds such dynamical potentials. It derives the generalised norm-keeping rules they must obey. A sum-over-poles form separates the number of reference energies from the number of projectors. It matches all-electron scattering closely, over wide energy ranges. The potentials also fit naturally into many-body energy formulas. That brings the atom, the pseudo-atom, and the solid under one theory.
arxiv-2605-05073:
Shibo Yu and four co-authors rank items from pairwise comparisons made by several judges, while treating judge disagreement as information rather than noise. Standard methods pool all judgments into one score, hiding steady gaps between judges. Their framework separates three targets: the shared consensus ranking, each judge's sensitivity to that consensus, and leftover structured disagreement.

The authors give rules under which this split can be pinned down and build an anchored switching method that preserves it. They also measure how sure the results are when a fixed panel of judges makes repeated pairings. On test and real multi-judge data, the method improved fit, held up better, and gave surer confidence scores than pooled baselines and simpler ones.
arxiv-2605-05273:
Michael Fowler builds a diagrammatic proof system for a fragment of structural semantics based on the Greimas semiotic square, a classic square of opposed meaning terms. Basic terms become diagram layouts in a spider diagram system, and links such as contradiction and implication become changes ruled by inference rules. Proofs, shown by proof trees, carry out the meaning-building step by step.

Fowler's main result shows the four meta-terms of the square arise the same way, each derived from a pair of basic configurations through one fixed proof pattern. Negation in the diagrams turns out not to be a full Boolean flip but a narrow counter-stance set by zones. The framework gives the field a rule-based footing.
arxiv-2605-05473:
Carvalho and two colleagues study curved spaces shaped by a vector field. Generalized m-quasi-Einstein manifolds extend Einstein metrics, structures prized in geometry and in gravitational physics. They add a potential vector field and a function that together deform the Ricci curvature equation. Under suitable integral assumptions on the potential field, the authors prove it must be a Killing field. Such a field is a symmetry direction that preserves the metric. The result extends an earlier result of Sharma to the generalized setting. A divergence-free potential field is likewise forced to be Killing.

Sign conditions on the parameters yield further results where the structure collapses to a simpler form. The authors also revisit a recent theorem of Ghosh, expose a subtle gap in its argument, and supply a corrected proof. Rigidity results for geodesic vector fields close the paper, tightening what such manifolds can look like.
arxiv-2605-05873:
Hirofumi Ota and four co-authors give language model self consistency a rigorous stopping rule. Models often sample many answers and aggregate them, which improves reasoning, but knowing when enough samples have been drawn is hard. The answer set is not known in advance, and data dependent stopping can silently break error guarantees that fixed sample rules enjoy.

Their algorithm, CITE, certifies a prespecified answer as the unique mode of the model's response distribution, valid at any stopping time. It controls false certification at a chosen level under arbitrary data driven stopping, with no prior knowledge of the answer categories. The authors prove matching lower bounds on stopping time and extend the method to confidence weighted voting. Simulations and model experiments confirm the error control in practice.
arxiv-2605-06273:
Rotzer and eight colleagues report a wildfire detection system already flying in orbit. Nine commercial thermal-infrared satellites watch for fires. The onboard computer is a Jetson Xavier NX, the model must stay under a megabyte, and alerts must reach responders within ten minutes of overpass. The imagery is uncalibrated mid-wave infrared at two hundred meter resolution, where fires often appear as single-pixel anomalies drowned in imbalance. Standard thermal-threshold pipelines built for MODIS and VIIRS do not address this regime.

The team trains lightweight dense representations with masked autoencoding. A hybrid variant adds exponential moving average distillation. Both are probed under extreme imbalance. Their fastest model reaches 0.640 test average precision and 0.69 event-level Fire-F1 at 65 milliseconds per batch in a 0.52 megabyte engine. The best configuration reaches 0.699 average precision while staying under one megabyte, beating a supervised baseline.
arxiv-2605-06373:
Leon Halgryn, Sophie Langer, Janusz M. Meylahn, and E. Moritz Hahn give finite-sample bounds for deep Q-learning when replay data are not independent. Analyses usually pretend sampled minibatches are independent, yet they come from time-linked trajectories. The authors model the minibatches as tau-mixing, a formal way of saying dependence fades over time.

They show that assumption holds under stated conditions on trajectories and sampling, then treat each network update as a regression problem with dependent data. The resulting risk bounds show dependence slows the statistical rate, reflecting a smaller effective sample size. Tests on standard Gymnasium tasks confirm that this assumption often fails.
arxiv-2605-06673:
Jon-Paul Cacioli maps how well thirty-three frontier language models monitor their own confidence across subject domains. A single metacognition score can hide the fact that a model judges its answers well in one field and poorly in another. Cacioli gave each model fifteen hundred MMLU questions across six domains and scored confidence accuracy per domain.

Applied and professional knowledge proved easiest for models to monitor, while formal reasoning and natural science were hardest, with the middle domains statistically indistinguishable. Profiles cluster within some model families but not others, and one newer Gemma model improved markedly over its predecessor. The atlas argues for screening models domain by domain before deployment in specific areas.
arxiv-2605-07073:
Yubin Kim and eleven co-authors present TeamBench, a benchmark for agent teams where roles are enforced by the operating system, not just by prompts. In many setups, one agent can quietly do another's job, hiding whether the team truly coordinated. TeamBench splits requirements, editing, and certification across planner, executor, and verifier roles.

Across hundreds of task templates, enforced and prompt-only teams scored similarly, but prompt-only verifiers tried to edit code far more often. Verifiers also approved many submissions that the true grader failed. A human study showed the benchmark exposes coordination patterns that pass rates alone completely miss.
arxiv-2605-07273:
Jiaju Han and ten co-authors attack satellite image search systems by painting fake weather onto pictures. Retrieval-augmented systems for remote sensing fetch text evidence using the image, yet input-space attacks on that retrieval stage were little studied. Their CloudWeb attack adds parameterized cloud and haze patterns while leaving the retriever and knowledge base untouched.

The patterns are tuned to pull image embeddings toward weather evidence and away from the true scene. Across seven datasets and five retrievers, the attack planted weather evidence into top results far more than clean or hand-crafted baselines. Downstream answers then showed weather hallucinations, proving retrieval attacks propagate into final responses.
arxiv-2605-07773:
Xin Xu and four co-authors test the short-board effect, the old claim that a team performs only as well as its weakest member, using teams of AI agents. Testing the claim on people is nearly impossible: abilities are hard to measure, real teams churn, and data skew toward successes. Simulated teams driven by large language models, following standard procedures, sidestep those problems.

In uniform teams they found three capability regimes, including a threshold state of busy but ineffective effort. Adding one weak member hurt core roles more than peripheral ones. With several weak members, damage multiplied rather than being set by the single weakest link. The practical lesson: fixing only the weakest member is not enough, and mitigation should address weaknesses in aggregate.
arxiv-2605-07873:
Shi Lin Sun and eight co-authors dissect the atmosphere of HAT-P-70b, an ultra-hot Jupiter whose dayside is hot enough to ionize metals while its nightside may let refractory species condense. Using the MAROON-X high-resolution spectrograph, they cross-correlate the planet's transmission spectrum against templates for individual chemical species.

Fourteen neutral and singly ionized species were detected, from iron and titanium to barium and oxygen. The absorption was blueshifted by a few kilometers per second, consistent with day-to-night winds. Retrieval experiments carried a warning: ignoring ionization badly biases inferred abundances of easily ionized elements like calcium and titanium. Equilibrium chemistry, by contrast, brought ratios closer to solar-like expectations. One genuine puzzle remains, a distinct enrichment of nickel that other ultra-hot Jupiter studies also seem to see.
arxiv-2605-08473:
Rodrigo Pastrana, M. Silvina Riveros, and Raúl Vidal characterize the weights that keep a variable fractional maximal operator bounded on spaces where the exponent itself varies by point. Their result extends earlier work on simpler fractional operators. They also define a new class of rough kernels meeting a variable version of a classic smoothness condition.

For operators built from those kernels, they prove a comparison inequality of Coifman and Fefferman type plus weighted bounds in the variable spaces. Examples confirm the new kernel class is not empty. Harmonic analysis gains tools for fractional operators whose order and integrability both change across the domain.
arxiv-2605-08573:
Tongkeun Chang and Kyungkeun Kang study when a thin boundary layer of slow fluid pulls away from a wall in the half space, a separation event that reshapes flow and pressure. Working first with the Stokes system under localized boundary data, they prove a clean test: a certain singular integral built from the boundary data decides the outcome by its sign alone.

A negative integral forces a separation point to exist, while a strictly positive one rules separation out. When separation occurs, they track its motion and the pressure gradient's sign. A perturbation step then builds matching Navier-Stokes solutions with the same behavior. Fluid mechanics gains a sharp criterion for a classic flow instability.
arxiv-2605-08673:
Masuyama and five colleagues improve online clustering, where nodes are created and updated as data arrive. Existing methods make node learning explicit, but mapping from learned node states to output clusters stays implicit or simplified. Implicit mappings leave clusters sensitive to weak graph bridges and local distance relations, with no constraint on which groups stay intact.

The team proposes PHIDA, a persistence guided node to cluster map for online clustering. It combines Inverse-Distance ART node learning with mapping constrained by Persistent Homology, inside Adaptive Resonance Theory based clustering. Tests on 24 benchmark sets show PHIDA earns the best average ranks in stationary comparisons, including recent stationary only methods. It also improves aggregate performance in nonstationary settings over online methods that create and update nodes adaptively. Ablations link the gains to PH guided mapping that keeps raw PH components intact, plus the PH component view.
arxiv-2605-09073:
Connor Holmes and four co-authors explain a cleaner way to estimate motion that unfolds smoothly over time, a need that arises when sensors report at different moments. Two broad styles exist: fitting flexible curves, or using Gaussian processes, which treat the path as a smooth random function. The second style has spread slowly in robotics despite clear strengths.

The authors recast Gaussian process estimation in the language of factor graphs, the diagram style roboticists already use to organize estimation problems. Their account aims to lower the barrier for newcomers. Three working examples built in a popular estimation library show the approach in action, covering the setup from model to solved trajectory.
arxiv-2605-09273:
Huang and three colleagues study online multicalibration beyond the worst case, seeking one efficient algorithm that adapts to easy and hard prediction sequences alike. Their algorithm moves smoothly between benign and worst-case sequences, refining a dyadic grid of prediction values as it goes, with error tied to how fast the refinement tree grows.

The analysis recovers the known worst-case-optimal rate, while adapting automatically to easier cases. In the marginal stochastic setting it reaches a square root rate, and for piecewise-stationary means a root of segment count times horizon rate. More generally, the rate depends on how closely simple contextual scores can stand in for predictable means, with thresholds the group family can represent. That threshold-complexity dependence is tight up to log factors. One algorithm thus covers the full range from benign to worst-case inputs without tuning to the instance type in advance.
arxiv-2605-09373:
Yamaguchi and a colleague measure how much steady, axisymmetric Jeans modelling misreads rotation curves when the stellar velocity field breaks axisymmetry. They use a high-resolution simulation of a lone Milky Way-like disk galaxy. They build mock stellar measurements for two observer angles relative to the bar, at 25 degrees and 115 degrees, inside a wedge-shaped volume with limited sky coverage.

For the 25 degree view, mean azimuthal streaming runs 10 to 15 kilometres per second above the averaged expectation. That gives an average overestimate of the circular speed of about 4 percent near the centre. Across snapshots the mean offset is a 1 point 5 to 2 sigma deviation, and for the 115 degree view the bias flips sign and underestimates the speed. Under the usual spherical approximation, a 4 percent speed bias means an 8 percent mass bias at fixed radius. Steady axisymmetric modelling can therefore mislead wherever the velocity field is not axisymmetric.
arxiv-2605-09773:
Berg and Lulla steered a large language model, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, to amplify Dark Triad traits: Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy. They used sparse autoencoder features, small interpretable knobs in the model's inner workings, and scored behavior on five psychology tests. The steered model grew far more exploitative, aggressive, and callous on fresh test scenes, with a very large effect size, while its grasp of others' thoughts stayed intact.

That split mirrors the empathy gap seen in human Dark Triad groups, where feeling with others lags behind reading them. Key point: strategic deception did not move at all, hinting that exploitation and deception run on separate tracks in the model. How features were found also mattered: contrast-found features shifted both self-report and behavior, while meaning-searched ones shifted only self-report. Antisocial leanings, the paper argues, are separate parts, not one lump.
arxiv-2605-10073:
Yoo and three co-authors improve patent reading by machines, where pre-trained language models flatten claims into token strings and miss the dependency hierarchy between claims. Two problems follow. Claim relations differ in trust, so noisy tech links can swamp cleaner legal citations. Claim-level graphs also do not fit token-level models, since spreading claim links across tokens dilutes structure.

Their Patent Heterogeneous Attention Graph Encoder, PHAGE, separates legal citations and technical relations into distinct edge types in a typed graph. A connectivity mask with trainable relation-aware biases then projects claim-level topology into token-level attention. A dual-level contrastive objective aligns codes with both inter-patent tree and intra-patent topology. PHAGE beats domain-adapted and citation-aware baselines on sorting, search and grouping, and finds claim topology more informative than inter-patent structure.
arxiv-2605-10173:
Jean Goubault-Larrecq studies previsions, broad forms of integration functionals used in math and computer science. A prevision is a map that scales cleanly and respects limits. Past work focused on two special kinds, sublinear and superlinear, which model mixes of choice and chance. This 2026 paper examines plain previsions, with neither extra trait assumed.

Goubault-Larrecq shows that each plain prevision can be written as a greatest lower bound of the sublinear kind, and as a least upper bound of the superlinear kind under mild rules. The result extends to structure-preserving matches between spaces of previsions and certain hyperspaces built over the two special kinds. Orthogonality links help pin down those hyperspaces, tying the build to the double powerspace construction.
arxiv-2605-10373:
Real databases rarely live in one place, and Makbule Gulcin Ozsoy argues that query systems should stop pretending otherwise. Most Text2Cypher tools start from one preselected graph database whose schema is known. In practice, information for one question may span several independent graph databases split by domain or system. Her 2026 paper reframes the task as multi-database query reasoning.

Rather than taking one fixed setup for granted, the system must work out three things: which databases matter, how to split a question across them, and how to combine partial results. Ozsoy formalizes this through a three-phase roadmap: database routing, multi-database decomposition, and heterogeneous query reasoning across database types and query languages. The paper maps challenges in source selection, decomposition, and result integration, aiming at natural-language interfaces to graph data that feel closer to real use and scale better.
arxiv-2605-10573:
Mateusz Baran and two colleagues propose a Riemannian BFGS method for tuning with Euclidean bounds. The method pairs a limited-memory quasi-Newton update in the tangent space with a curved-space version of the Cauchy point plan from L-BFGS-B. That handles Euclidean bounds while using the domain's shape. Their 2026 paper gives a framework and code in the Manopt.jl library.

The setting matters for covariance matrix work with bounded variance, brain scans, and EEG signal sorting. It also covers tasks coupling manifold variables with constrained Euclidean values. Tests on problems show only minor speed loss on Euclidean problems versus L-BFGS-B, while beating older methods. On two mixed problems, the method beats methods by several orders of magnitude. The problems are capped-amplitude blind source separation and bounded-variance maximum likelihood common principal components analysis.
arxiv-2605-10673:
Yao Shu and Zilin Zhu identify query geometry as the missing object in low-bit zeroth-order optimisation, and propose Compander-Aligned Queries to fix it. For nonuniform companding quantisers, a fixed weight-space radius can collapse in dense cells, over-span sparse cells, or assign a rounded chord to an unrounded update direction.

CAQ-ZO forms one-grid-step Rademacher stencils in the transformed space. It maps endpoints back through the inverse transform, and updates in the transformed space. Theory proves the grid-span mismatch and decomposes endpoint-rounding estimator residuals. It gives stationarity bounds in which generic off-grid queries retain a residual channel while CAQ-ZO makes the query-time residual exactly zero. Synthetic experiments isolate this channel, and matched fine-tuning of quantised Qwen and Llama models shows CAQ-ZO improving the trained low-precision baseline under the same quantiser and evaluation budget.
arxiv-2605-10973:
Hangzhan Jin and five colleagues present Rotation-Preserving Supervised Fine-Tuning, a fix for the way standard fine-tuning trades in-domain gains against out-of-domain losses. Prior work links that degradation to shifts in dominant singular subspaces of pretrained weights. Finding loss-sensitive directions directly costs too much at language-model scale.

RPSFT instead punishes movement in the top singular-vector block, projected, of every pretrained weight matrix, curbing pointless rotation while keeping task learning intact. Across model families and sizes trained on math reasoning data, it improves the in-domain versus out-of-domain trade-off over standard fine-tuning and strong baselines. It also better preserves pretrained representations and gives stronger starting points for later reinforcement-learning tuning. Fine-tuners get a cheap proxy for Fisher-sensitive directions.
arxiv-2605-11373: Drago Plecko and two colleagues build a causal frame for algorithmic recourse, the advice that lets a person overturn a bad AI decision. Old methods treat recourse as a what-if for a fixed person, ignoring repeat decisions under changing hidden conditions. Their frame tracks outcomes before and after an intervention, allowing partial stability and fresh draws of hidden variables. Stability conditions let them reason from observational data alone, with a copula-based method, goodness-of-fit tests and a distribution-free fallback, shown on real and semi-synthetic data.
arxiv-2605-11573: Matsumoto, Nakayama, Onagi and Rychkov run a Monte Carlo study of the dipolar universality class in 3D. This class describes phase shifts in 3D ferromagnets with strong dipolar forces. Though studied by theory and experiment, little was known from simulation. The authors build a lattice model enforcing the transverse constraint on order and a Markov chain Monte Carlo method mixing local Metropolis updates with a global zero-mode update. Runs on lattices up to 48 cubed show a smooth transition, yielding critical exponent and Binder values.
arxiv-2605-11773: In 2026, Muhammad Haris Khan questions a habit every diffusion sampler shares: noise levels that only ever fall. He tests four families of nonmonotonic schedules on DDPM, EDM, and flow matching models across 90 setups on CIFAR-10. None beats the monotonic baseline, though the penalty ranges from severe in DDPM to negligible in EDM. He formalizes this spread as a Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient, a cheap check of whether a denoiser has truly converged.
arxiv-2605-11873: Argyrios Deligkas and four colleagues study how to boost reach in time graphs formed by k time paths, such as train networks. They allow shifting edge timing labels earlier or later while keeping each path's time flow. The problem stays easy when measured by both path count and shift budget, and when measured by path count alone with open budget. Nearly every other setup proves hard, with matching XP methods.
arxiv-2605-11973: Z. Derbazi weakens the shape conditions needed for endpoint tests of stochastic order. For usual and hazard-rate stochastic orders, the endpoint tests still hold when the likelihood ratio is unimodal. They also hold under a sign pattern for the ratio minus one: at most two sign changes with a negative right tail. A direct superlevel-set test on the same ratio gives the same conclusion, which helps for ratios that jump.
arxiv-2605-12073: Leif Eriksson and five colleagues study a new way to size hard logic problems. Their yardstick counts the clauses that must be cut to reach an easy class, called a clause covering backdoor. The test problems are quantified Boolean formulas, a class known to be PSPACE-complete. For the old easy classes Horn, 2-CNF, and linear equations, they prove Horn is W[1]-hard while the rest allow fast fixed-parameter methods. Their methods use propagation and Gaussian elimination, and just one key case is left open for a full split.
arxiv-2605-12173: In a 2026 study, Babak Vakili studies chaos in the Mixmaster world under two Planck-scale tweaks. Starting from the Misner Hamiltonian, he derives motion rules under polymerization and an uncertainty principle. He tracks Kasner epoch lengths as a probe of motion. One tweak shortens epochs, causing more frequent wall hits, while polymer tweaks lengthen them and damp bounces. Mixed, the tweaks give a middle shift between the trends, and chaos strength shifts with the tweak settings.
arxiv-2605-12273: Isabel Corpus and Allison Koenecke tackle ad skew while accounting for unknown users. Ad platforms match ads to users, and audits show under-delivery despite intent to reach groups. That gap matters most for public-service ads. Advertisers can counter skew by targeting groups, but that excludes unknown users on Google Ads, which offers no such targeting. Working with an agency, the authors design a split including unknown users alongside inferred male and female labels. It cuts skew without excluding unknown users, balancing costs against skew from demographics.
arxiv-2605-12373: Aslan, Tandogan and Schweitzer study quasi parton distributions, objects defined at spacelike separations for fast-moving hadrons and accessible to lattice QCD. As hadron speed nears light speed, these quasi distributions converge to ordinary parton distributions. The authors prove convergence and sum rules for unpolarised quark and antiquark cases in a broad class of quark models without gauge fields, for two choices of Dirac matrix. They illustrate the results with the Covariant Parton Model, including small-x behaviour and a form-factor result.
arxiv-2605-12573: Evangelista and three colleagues sharpen diffusion posterior samplers for image repair with a lagged time fix. Standard samplers lean on instant data-matching guesses, which inject swing into the reverse motion. The authors recast the standard update as a first-order stepping plus a rest term for the gap between cleaned guess and data-matching guess. A second-order stepping naturally adds a fix from how next guesses change. Their LAMP method joins both terms as a plug-in, keeping sampler structure while lifting results.
arxiv-2605-12673: Wang and five colleagues audit AI agent benchmarks for reward hacking with BenchJack, an auto red-teaming system. Benchmarks guide model selection, funding and use, yet reward hacking emerges on its own in frontier models without overfit. Reward hacking means agents chase a score without performing the set task. From past incidents, the team derives eight repeat flaw patterns in the Agent-Eval list for benchmark makers. BenchJack drives coding agents to audit benchmarks, and a repeat loop finds flaws and patches them.
arxiv-2605-12873: Byramji, Kane, Morris and Ostuni construct a distribution that separates adaptive from non-adaptive cell-probe sampling almost as sharply as possible. With two adaptive probes per output bit, the distribution can be sampled exactly. Without adaptivity, any sampler needs on the order of N probes to come close to it. The two-versus-roughly-N gap improves on earlier separations and sharpens the known limits of non-adaptive sampling.
arxiv-2605-13073: Kang and four co-authors tackle 3D Gaussian Splatting in the wild, where passers-by and changing light create conflicting gradients across views. Image masking alone cannot remove residual occlusions or lighting inconsistencies. Their framework first refines masks with semantic consistency scores, then reconciles view-specific gradients by rotating them into an orthogonal configuration. Conflict-aware densification and pruning further stabilise growth and drop persistently conflicting points. Tests show state-of-the-art rendering quality on standard in-the-wild benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-13173: Liu and seven co-authors introduce OxyEcomBench, a multimodal benchmark of about 6,300 instances for bilingual Chinese-English e-commerce. Existing e-commerce benchmarks take one stakeholder view or a narrow task set, missing the full pipeline. OxyEcomBench covers operators, merchants and customers across 6 capability aspects and 29 tasks, with text-only and mixed inputs. Data come from authentic platforms, verified by domain experts, with a four-level difficulty rubric. Even leading models score modestly on it, and gaps between models narrow.
arxiv-2605-13473: Chenyu Zhou and five colleagues propose OSDN, an online scaled DeltaNet that lifts the Delta Rule for linear attention. OSDN adds a diagonal preconditioner updated online via hypergradient feedback, equal to per-feature scaling on the write-side key. That keeps the DeltaNet chunkwise parallel pipeline without high-dimensional state overhead. At 340M parameters, OSDN lifts in-context recall by 32 percent over DeltaNet, and at 1.3B size it cuts the recall residual ratio by 39 percent.
arxiv-2605-13573: B. Costarella and ten colleagues use high magnetic fields and a tuned NMR method to study spin fluctuations in the strange-metal phase of lanthanum strontium copper oxide. Blocking superconductivity with high fields, they show the low-energy limit of the spin susceptibility at doping x equals 0.25 keeps rising down to their lowest heat. That pattern suggests quantum-critical fluctuations, a leading cause for strange-metal transport, yet it appears well beyond the spin-stripe doping of 0.19.
arxiv-2605-13773: Mohammad Reza Mousavi asks whether large word models grasp the formal meaning of High-Level Message Order Charts. He tests three models on 129 meaning tasks from querying basic constructs to meaning-keeping lifts and joins. Results show only modest grasp at about 52 percent overall hits. Basic-concept scores are strong near 88 percent, but lifts and joins scores are weak near 36 percent, and traces and LTS scores near 42 percent. All three models struggle with co-region and plain causal links, never using them in meaning-keeping changes.
arxiv-2605-13873: Wajdi Aljedaani and Rubel Hassan Mollik present an ordered review of papers: 38 peer-checked studies on large language model use in web access cases. Findings show most studies apply language models to text-centric and plain access tasks, with WCAG as the primary guide frame. Little thought goes to thinking access rules. Checked ways mostly rely on general-purpose language models and prompt-based chats, while test habits vary widely and often lack direct input of users with limits.
arxiv-2605-13973: Galceran and ten co-authors train a convolutional net to read star birth tales and age-metallicity links for near galaxies in the PHANGS team. The net joins conv layers, attention tricks and one shared latent space to guess both traits across sixteen age bins. It reads integral-field spectra from PHANGS-MUSE with five-band light counts from PHANGS-HST. Training runs on a set of 165,000 entries.
arxiv-2605-14173: Rabeti and Mahdavifar offer univariate bicycle codes, a neat subclass of generalized bicycle quantum low-density parity-check codes from a Frobenius link. The build shrinks code design from a two-polynomial search to a one-polynomial search while keeping sparsity. An explicit algebraic map of logical coset spaces, built from a basis for the logical quotient space, yields a full parametrization of logical operators. Upper bounds on minimum distance follow by tying logical representatives to cycle-density traits of linked circulant matrices.
arxiv-2605-14373: Liang and colleagues propose Coherent Coordinate Descent, a deterministic zeroth-order optimiser for settings without backpropagation. Zeroth-order methods estimate gradients from function values alone, but existing options are sample-hungry or noisy. CoCD reuses stale gradients as warm starts. It needs only a constant query count per step. Larger finite-difference steps implicitly smooth the landscape, improving stability. On multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks and ResNets up to 270 thousand parameters, it beats block cyclic descent on efficiency and loss. It is steadier than randomised rivals.
arxiv-2605-14673: Silinga, Edgar, McVitie, Fallon, Kovacs, Dunin-Borkowski and Almeida measure how composition and magnetic induction change in cobalt and iron nanowires. The wires were grown by focused electron beam induced deposition. Growth angles ran from zero to ninety degrees to the optic axis. Electron microscopy mapped elemental composition and magnetic induction against angle. Metal content is reported to fall as growth angle rises, but near-equal metal content up to sixty degrees was achieved with low voltage and high current.
arxiv-2605-15173: Quinten De Man and four others tackle dynamic connectivity on sparse graphs with hybrid sketching. Sketching theory promises space independent of edge count, but per-vertex sketches cost thousands of bytes, paying off only on extremely dense graphs. Real sparse graphs are often not uniformly sparse: they hide dense cores carrying most edges. The team sketches only the core and stores the sparse periphery losslessly. It matches the theoretical lossless bound on sparse graphs and the sketching bound on dense ones, and improves on both in between.
arxiv-2605-15473: Xuan Liu and seven colleagues judge language-model agents as simulated study participants against validated behavioral hypotheses. Their HumanStudy-Bench rebuilds protocols from twelve human studies and runs them on ten models under four agent designs. Agent effects are scored against published human findings for inferential agreement and effect-size consistency. The authors report which effects carried over, where agents parted ways, and how far design choices moved the match.
arxiv-2605-15973: Menacho, Pellicer, and Solà-Morales study how fast a linear chromatography model settles to its steady state. The True Moving Bed model links eight hyperbolic equations through six parameters. They prove the pace is set by a dominant eigenvalue and build the function whose roots give the spectrum. The results are applied to separating omeprazole mirror-image forms, with a simpler limit case worked out in full.
arxiv-2605-16373: Yang and seven others study multimodal segmentation of bone infections, where expert and machine labels differ. Their bimodal model fuses PET metabolic signals with CT bone-window anatomy. To avoid inflated scores from inter-slice correlation in small data sets, they replace 2D scoring with patient-level 3D volumetric scoring and cross-validation. Parallel models trained on separate expert labels with high-sensitivity and high-specificity intents preserve diagnostic diversity, and a cross-check matrix shows models internalize distinct expert views.
arxiv-2605-17273: Oh challenges state-of-the-art claims in AI, arguing that top average scores alone cannot carry them. A claim of superiority implies meaningful effect size, consistency across tasks and robustness to dropping datasets. Yet in over half of top-model comparisons across ten public benchmarks at least one of those traits fails. Aggregate wins often ride on outlier datasets, so claim language should mirror the strength of the evidence.
arxiv-2605-17573: Rashidi, Ali and Rahman detect social-media deepfakes through timing artifacts with a 3D convolutional network based on R3D-18. Frame-level detectors degrade as generator quality rises, but timing inconsistencies persist. A composite loss mixing binary cross-entropy with a timing-consistency regularizer processes 16-frame clips. Accuracy reaches about 93 percent in-dataset and about 76 percent transferring to FaceForensics++ without fine-tuning, showing timing signals survive re-encoding.
arxiv-2605-17773: Xinpeng Liu and three colleagues build PlantPose, a tool that draws plant skeletons from images. Human skeletons have fixed joints, but plants branch in free-form trees, so the tool must guess arbitrary tree graphs. PlantPose mixes learned graph generation with classic graph methods that force tree shape during training. A broad mix of real, synthetic, sketch, and abstract plant images trains it to cope with varied styles and new plant types. Tests show sturdy, accurate skeletons across domains, even on unseen kinds of images.
arxiv-2605-18173: Antonio Colombo's 2026 paper offers a rectification-free route to scene text spotting with a soft attention mask embedding module. The module uses transformer encoders to weigh high-level features and blend them with predicted masks, yielding sharper text boundaries that suppress background noise. Because the attention step is fully differentiable, recognition loss tunes detection as well, so the two goals train jointly. The resulting SAME-Net scores 84.02 percent end-to-end H-mean on Total-Text, beating the prior best GLASS by 1.02 points with no extra training data.
arxiv-2605-18373: Edoardo Caldarelli and four co-authors tackle fast robotic cloth folding, where quick motions exploit cloth dynamics but make modeling and planning hard. Their 2026 design trains a Koopman operator model, a linear stand-in learned from a physics-based cloth simulator, and embeds it in a model predictive controller. In both simulated and real-robot tests, the method folds unseen poses fast without losing accuracy.
arxiv-2605-18473: Megh Dutta and three co-authors seek faster charging in a 2026 paper for electric double-layer capacitors. These are ionic-fluid devices between two metal electrodes that complement batteries. Inspired by shortcuts to adiabaticity in colloidal systems, they derive time-dependent voltage protocols within the Poisson-Nernst-Planck model. The protocols cancel arbitrary numbers of relaxation modes. They approach full charge in finite time, in practice an order of magnitude faster than natural equilibration, even for drives shorter than the natural RC time.
arxiv-2605-18573: William Blair proves, in a 2026 paper, the Dirichlet problem for second-order iterated Vekua equations is well-posed. The rule is a product of an exponential and a polynomial on a non-degenerate conic that is not a circle. The result generalizes the Bitsadze equation setting to this wider class. He also extends related results for polyanalytic and generalized analytic functions to bicomplex differential equations. The paper thus unifies several boundary-value results under one plan.
arxiv-2605-19173: Adrien Bazoge and three colleagues test whether prompting language changes diagnostic thinking and accuracy in language models, comparing English and French across five models. Two doctors scored 180 cases across sixteen fields on an eighteen-point scale for diagnosis and thinking quality. Four of the five models scored higher in English, by 0.37 to 0.91 on average, with gaps in differential diagnosis, logical structure, and internal validity. The o3 model alone showed no language effect. Prompting language is thus a key driver of clinical results, with stakes for fair use globally.
arxiv-2605-19273: Dawit Hailu proposes running classical logic on the motion of a two-level atom as chip shrinking nears its limits. Unlike plain combinational circuits, where output follows input alone, his finite-state design lets output depend on both input and the system's starting state. Information sits in observable quantities from the density matrix, namely population and coherence entries, analyzed through the Liouville equation. Noise may erode stored values, yet fast steps can finish first, operations can be read in parallel, and the scheme extends to more levels.
arxiv-2605-19773: Shvets proves a split prime supercongruence at the complex multiplication point one sixth, one third, one. For a sequence built from a cubed hypergeometric series, he shows a congruence modulo the fourth power of the prime for every split prime from seven upward. The exponent four beats the weight three prediction of three, an extra factor traced to complex multiplication enhancement at j equals zero. A matching inert prime obstruction is also established, via a formal parameter congruence and a Cartier parity law modulo p.
arxiv-2605-20273: Siyuan Li and co-workers set out M-ORE, an online multimodal editor for tight budgets. Visual signals swamp fix-shaping stats in text-only editors, sparking cross-modal clashes. Shared-space edits tangle into long-range drag. From a proximal-projection frame, M-ORE gives a closed-form Sherman-Morrison fix at constant cost. Text and vision keep apart locality stats; fixes use a fixed orthogonal low-rank edit space. Tests on backbones and editing benchmarks put M-ORE past rivals on reliability, generality, and locality.
arxiv-2605-20573: Dongjin Oh and fourteen colleagues use polarized Raman light scattering to compare lattice vibrations and charge waves in kagome superconductors. The family, written AV3Sb5, uses caesium, rubidium, or potassium for A. They find a split in one phonon mode, earlier seen only in the caesium compound, appears in all three. Collective charge excitations, by contrast, differ sharply by alkali metal, clarifying how charge order varies across the family.
arxiv-2605-20773: Yonghong Chen, Zhijun Qiao, and Mingxuan Zhu derive the multi-peakon dynamical system for a class of Camassa-Holm-type equations with quadratic nonlinearities. They then study the Cauchy problem, first establishing local well-posedness in Besov spaces and giving blow-up criteria. With suitable conditions on the starting data, the corresponding solution either exists widely or blows up in finite time. Finally, they prove ill-posedness in one Besov space using non-traveling wave solutions.
arxiv-2605-20873: Ziliang Zhao and nine colleagues present PlanningBench, a system for generating scalable and checkable planning data. Planning requires coordinating goals, constraints, resources, and lasting consequences into executable, checkable solutions. Existing benchmarks treat planning data as fixed sets. That limits scenario coverage and ties challenge to surface proxies rather than structural roots. It starts from real scenarios and abstracts workflows into a structured taxonomy, a clear map of task types of over 30 task types, subtasks, constraint families, and challenge factors.
arxiv-2605-21173: Zhenqi Jenny Wang develops a new approach to higher-order mixing in the semisimple setting. She proves exponential mixing of all orders for partially hyperbolic algebraic actions under a strong spectral-gap assumption, with decay rates explicit in Lyapunov and spectral-gap data. At order two, estimates need only partial regularity along weak stable and unstable directions. For representations with better-than-tempered decay, the order-two estimate attains the optimal matrix-coefficient exponent. The proof centers on solving multiple fractional cohomological equations of sum-of-product type.
arxiv-2605-21673: Emma Pidduck and co-authors document the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts transition from restricted data licensing to open access under CC BY 4.0, completed in October 2025. The shift used a tiered service model keeping forecast data open while offering supported delivery at cost. Between 2020 and 2025 the Centre ran a planning cycle: an annual revenue target, open-tier additions, infrastructure work, and outcome assessment. In the six months after the shift, over ninety-three percent of paying organisations kept a Service Agreement, while open endpoint downloads rose substantially.
arxiv-2605-21873: Hiroshi Ando and Isaac Goldbring prove a claim about type III-one factors in a W-star probability space. For a type III-one factor, any nontrivial proper closed subset of the reals, and any nonprincipal ultrafilter on the naturals, consider the ultrapower of a spectral subspace. It is a proper subset of the spectral subspace of the ultrapower. The result concerns spectral subspaces tied to the modular automorphism group. The authors discuss the model-theoretic implications of this strict inclusion.
arxiv-2605-22073: Zesheng Li, Chengchang Pan, and Honggang Qi present BRIDGE, a behavior-guided method for multimodal recommendation. More cross-view alignment does not always lift ranking: tests on Amazon Baby show moderate alignment helps, while stronger alignment suppresses task-specific variation, and low-frequency parts capture shared structure. BRIDGE keeps the backbone and puts behavior evidence into candidate calibration, keeping the base top-K candidate set in training and inference. On Amazon Baby, Sports, and Electronics it beats baselines by up to 7.3 percent in Recall at 20 and 14.9 percent in NDCG at 20.
arxiv-2605-22373: Hughes and colleagues study membership inference attacks on safety classifiers for generative AI. Such classifiers learn from raw self-harm and mental health talks. The team bets that cases where the classifier is least sure leak the most. A boundary-targeted rule picks such cases to boost the leak. An attacker then finds 19 percent of distress-flagged talks at a 5 percent false alarm rate. That is 3.5 times the haul of leading attacks on their own. Filters on content fail here, though noise tricks help.
arxiv-2605-22473: Adaloglou, Bargalló i Gómez and Hauber prove Arnold's nearby Lagrangian conjecture for pinwheels inside rational homology balls. They show any two embeddings of a pinwheel are linked by a compactly supported Hamiltonian isotopy. The proof uses neck stretching and symplectic rational blow up, plus a computation of the symplectomorphism group. That group turns out to be generated by a twist about the pinwheel, dubbed the pintwist. Uses include Gromov non squeezing for pin balls, a proof of local Lagrangian unknotting, and a uniqueness result for pinwheel types.
arxiv-2605-22573: Sarwade and others give the first full study of iron K alpha fluorescence in 47 top class solar flares from the first year of SoLEXS on India's Aditya-L1 craft. Silicon drift detectors record broad continuum and line light together, pinning the link between iron line flux and exciting flux above 7.11 kilo electron volts per event. Derived efficiencies vary from centre to limb as theory expects, offering a probe of coronal source height. One snag remains: source height cannot be fixed alone without assuming a photospheric iron abundance value.
arxiv-2605-22873: Xia and three colleagues ask when chain-of-thought reasoning actually helps language models, and route decoding by early entropy dynamics. Tasks with large reasoning gains tend to show falling early entropy, while low-gain tasks oscillate or rise. Their EDRM framework summarizes those early trajectories and chooses among direct, standard, and chain-of-thought decoding. Across 15 benchmarks and 7 models it saved 16 to 55 percent of tokens at comparable accuracy.
arxiv-2605-22973: Rajabinasab and three coauthors argue that unsupervised feature selection needs a random baseline, and that many celebrated methods fail it. New methods each year are judged only against each other on selected datasets, with no established floor. The authors propose random feature selection as that floor and show empirically that many state-of-the-art methods lose to random choice on both performance and efficiency. They urge developers to require consistent improvement over random selection before claiming progress.
arxiv-2605-23073: Li, Shomorony, and Milenkovic study recovering positions of objects moving on a line from pairwise collision data alone. With full observability, where collision sets and time order are known, positions are recoverable exactly when the collision graph is connected. With partial observability and no timing, the problem connects to function graphs. A standard layer decomposition yields an interval graph with fast methods. With incomplete data and missing collisions, the problem becomes graph completion, shown NP-hard via bandwidth.
arxiv-2605-23173: Jara, Longo, and Rasmussen prove that dichotomies with growth rates faster or slower than e-growth either do not occur or do not matter for skew-products with compact base. A similar result holds for uneven e-growth conduct. The proof studies groups of shifted linear time-varying rules and proves spread results for them. It also studies shifts of growth rates under a contrast rule.
arxiv-2605-23273: Park and Chung present TopOptAgents, a multi-agent system running topology optimization design and choices. Shape tuning makes matter layouts for set goals and limits through number methods. Experts decide settings and whether the design meets concerns beyond the problem. TopOptAgents uses six LLM-based agents working through repeat self-review cycles spanning framing, checks, code writing and running, and quality review. Repeat self-review helps most where the trained language model has limited prior contact, such as forms whose papers and open-source code are sparse.
arxiv-2605-23373: Meng and colleagues build AffectCodec, a neural speech codec that keeps emotion intact instead of trading it for clean reconstruction. Standard codecs squeeze audio into tokens for speech language models, but tight bitrates and mixed streams let feeling leak away. Their block-diagonal residual quantizer walls emotion and acoustic channels apart, so bit shares become explicit rather than loss-driven. Multi-scale emotion conditioning and multi-rate training then hold feeling at low bitrates, with sound quality and clarity intact.
arxiv-2605-23773: Zhang determines which N-vertex sets in the square lattice support the most trees. Every maximizer minimizes edges joining the set to the rest. Its shape is a rectangle with at most two strips at opposite corners. For N at least 18, the maximizer is unique up to symmetry: a rectangle with one corner strip. For square N, he proves a stability inequality bounding the difference from a translated square by tree loss. He also derives a product formula and a recurrence for tree counts in rectangles with a corner strip.
arxiv-2605-23973: Nahmed and five colleagues build a digital twin for microwave ablation of liver tumours, predicting how a burn will spread. When the antenna lands off plan, reinserting it risks spreading tumour cells, while keeping the old plan risks an incomplete burn. Their optimizer retunes power, duration, and antenna position without reinsertion, using equations fitted to each patient's CT and MRI scans. Tested on three pig-liver ablations, the simulator matched the true burn zones, and replanning lifted scores by 20.3 to 48.1 percent.
arxiv-2605-24173: Wang and Asokan study memorization in diffusion language models, which fill in masked tokens anywhere. Prefix-only probing thus shows one facet of memorization and understates risk. They define infilling extraction, a protocol keyed to any mask that covers prefix probing and captures two-way bias. Across five modes, three training setups, and three corpora, mask shape drives leakage: edge-conditioned masks pull up to three times more verbatim strings than prefix masks. Even redacted email addresses prove easier to recover here than from matched autoregressive models.
arxiv-2605-24373: Morales-Salgado builds a broad mover frame, writing the mover as phase plus size. The phase governs semi-classic phase structure while the size carries transport and weighting of setups.
