Their library, jvenn, draws diagrams from up to six lists inside any web page, in the classic layout or the Edwards design for many sets. Readers can click regions to see the shared items, and page builders can restyle the display freely. The package is open source, documented, and ships with an example. It aims at the everyday lists thrown off by high-throughput experiments, where the interesting story often sits in the overlap.
europmc-pmc4322573:
George Rosenberger and eleven co-authors publish a library of measurement assays covering more than ten thousand human proteins. Their data paper appeared in Scientific Data in 2014. Mass spectrometry is the deepest tool for reading the proteome, but targeted measurement needs a ready assay for each protein, built in advance.

The library supports SWATH-MS, a method that records all proteins in a sample and then mines the data for chosen targets. Each assay tells the instrument exactly which fragments prove a given protein is present and how much of it there is. Shared openly, the compendium lets labs quantify most of the human proteome in patient or research samples without building assays one by one.
europmc-pmc4327973:
Nathaniel P Katz, Florence C Paillard, and Evan Ekman explain how to judge whether a treatment for painful bone and joint conditions helps enough to matter to patients. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research in 2015. Trials report statistical significance, but a tiny average gain can clear that bar while leaving patients no better in daily life.

The authors describe a two step yardstick: fix the smallest change on a measure that patients count as important, then apply it to each patient's results. They review how such thresholds, including the minimum clinically important difference, are derived and where they mislead. The guidance is meant for trial designers and clinicians reading orthopedic evidence.
europmc-pmc4530473:
Erica L. Scheller leads a twelve-author team showing that fat inside bone marrow is not one tissue but two, in Nature Communications in 2015. Marrow fat builds up in many conditions yet stays poorly understood. Comparing sites along the mouse tibia, the team found the fat near the knee and the fat near the ankle differ in size, fuel mix, gene activity, and control.

Proximal fat sits scattered among active blood-forming cells and vanishes after 21 days of cold exposure. Distal fat forms earlier, holds larger cells richer in unsaturated fats, and endures system-wide challenges. Rats and humans show the same distal pattern. The authors name the two types regulated and constitutive marrow fat, and argue studies must treat them apart.
europmc-pmc4538573:
Jiabei He, Ying Hu, Mingming Hu, and Baolan Li review an immune escape route in lung cancer, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Non-small cell lung cancer makes up about 85% of lung cancers, the world's top cancer killer. Surgery, chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and radiation still leave poor outlooks, so new angles are needed.

Tumors exploit the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway, a brake that normally keeps immune cells from over-firing. By engaging that brake, cancer cells hide from attack and shape a friendly local setting. Blocking it can release the body's own antitumor response, and early trials in this lung cancer showed gains. The review covers the pathway's biology, the inhibitors in development, and the open problems for wider use.
europmc-pmc4574473:
Raphaël Etournay leads a twelve-author team on how a fly wing takes shape, in eLife in 2015. A tissue's final form emerges from thousands of cells dividing, swapping neighbors, and changing shape, but the accounting was missing for any real organ. The team studied the pupal wing of the fruit fly Drosophila as it reshapes under pull from the contracting wing hinge.

Live measures let them tally exactly how much of the blade's reshaping comes from division, rearrangement, and cell shape change. Cells both create stress and answer it, and that feedback sets how the junction network remodels. Anchoring patterns from the surrounding matrix force the tissue into the right outline. A continuum model reproduces the whole interplay.
europmc-pmc4574773:
Federico Costa leads a ten-author team giving leptospirosis its first global toll, in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2015. The disease spreads from animal urine through water and soil, striking rural farmers and urban slum dwellers hardest. It can kill and causes lung bleeding outbreaks, yet no worldwide counts of illness and death existed, which kept it neglected.

The team reviewed 80 incidence studies from 34 countries that met quality bars, then modeled rates by age and sex for every country and region. Case fatality ratios were folded in to estimate deaths. Data were thin for regions such as Africa, a gap the authors flag. The estimates hand health agencies a baseline for control planning.
europmc-pmc4586373:
M. Loretto Munoz leads a twelve-author team asking how short a heart recording can be, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Heart rate variability, the beat-to-beat wobble in pulse timing, carries health information, but standard measures assume recordings of four to five minutes. Routine clinic electrocardiograms last only ten seconds, so the team tested whether such scraps suffice.

In 3,387 adults, two variability measures from 10-second strips were compared with the long-recording standard. Single strips already agreed substantially; averaging three ten-second strips raised agreement further, and longer shorts did still better. One measure, RMSSD, held up especially well at ten seconds. The results open variability screening to the ECGs clinics already record.
europmc-pmc4603273:
Nicola Doebelin and Reinhard Kleeberg presented a 2015 program called Profex, a graphical front end for the BGMN refinement program. BGMN analyses X-ray diffraction patterns to pin down crystal structures, a method called Rietveld refinement. Like much academic software, it lacked a friendly interface. The paper appeared in the Journal of Applied Crystallography.

Profex runs on multiple platforms and is open source. It wraps BGMN's number-crunching in windows, menus, and plots that are easier to learn and use. The authors describe how independent developers often step in to add such interfaces once a tool proves popular. For diffraction users, Profex lowers the entry barrier to a powerful but previously plain program, without changing the science underneath.
europmc-pmc4615873:
Li Song and Liliana Florea presented a 2015 program called Rcorrector, which fixes errors in RNA sequencing reads. RNA-seq reads are short, and random sequencing errors complicate alignment and assembly. Genome read correctors fail on RNA because gene activity levels vary so widely. The paper appeared in GigaScience.

Rcorrector builds a compact graph of short DNA words from the reads. Instead of one global cut-off, it judges each position in a read against local evidence to decide which words are trustworthy. Accuracy matched or beat rival tools, while speed and memory use improved. It handles 100 million reads in about five gigabytes of memory, so an ordinary desktop can run it. Cleaner reads mean more reliable gene activity studies downstream.
europmc-pmc4633473:
A 2015 study linking changes in bacterial surface charge to membrane damage came from Sounik Halder and colleagues. The surface charge measure, called zeta potential, might serve as a quick marker of harm from membrane-attacking agents. The team treated Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus with two positively charged chemicals. The work appeared in SpringerPlus.

As the chemicals shifted surface charge, membranes grew leakier and the cell population grew more varied in size. Past a critical point, the shifts ended in cell death for both a Gram-negative and a Gram-positive species. Microscopy backed the measurements. The results suggest drug hunters can use surface charge readings to screen compounds that attack bacterial membranes, a route of growing interest as antibiotic resistance spreads.
europmc-pmc4642273:
Preparing samples for viral metagenomics, the study of all viruses in a sample is the subject of a 2015 protocol by Nádia Conceição-Neto and colleagues. Gut virus research lacked validated preparation methods. The team tested each preparation step on a mock community of nine diverse viruses plus four gut bacteria. The work appeared in Scientific Reports.

Their tuned protocol, called NetoVIR, recovered every virus in the mock mix. Viral reads jumped from 43.2 percent to 96.7 percent of the data, while bacterial reads collapsed. The tests also warned that fine filters and hard spinning in common protocols can throw away large viruses. NetoVIR runs fast and reproducibly, mainly for faecal samples, and should help labs compare virus studies on equal footing.
europmc-pmc4672173:
Joanna M. Morrow and colleagues published a 2016 study testing MRI measures as markers of neuromuscular disease progression. Trials in these disorders lack sensitive outcome measures. Muscle water shifts and later fat build-up can both be measured by MRI. Patients with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease 1A or inclusion body myositis were scanned at a London centre. The work appeared in The Lancet Neurology.

Patients and matched healthy controls were assessed at baseline and again after one year. Measures included muscle fat fraction and a water signal called T2. The study compared how responsive each MRI measure was over the year and how well each matched functional clinical scores. It also tested whether water changes appear before fat exceeds the healthy range, which would let trials detect treatment effects earlier.
europmc-pmc4686873:
Mirjana Kessler, Karen Hoffmann, Volker Brinkmann, and nine colleagues grew human fallopian tube organoids, reporting in Nature Communications in 2015. The fallopian tube lining is vital for reproduction and is suspected as the starting site of a deadly ovarian cancer. The team grew small three-dimensional copies of the lining from single stem cells. The organoids held both ciliated and secretory cells, like real tissue.

Growth depended on two signal systems, Wnt and Notch, working side by side. Blocking Notch slowed growth, cut stem-cell gene activity, and raised the share of ciliated cells. The organoids also answered to the hormones estradiol and progesterone in a natural way. Because the cultures stay stable long term, they give researchers a living model of this hard-to-study tissue. Future work can test disease changes and drug effects in it.
europmc-pmc4699073:
Can Ince argued for watching the smallest blood vessels during shock care, in a solo viewpoint in Critical Care in 2015. Standard resuscitation targets whole-body numbers like blood pressure and cardiac output. Ince's point is that fixing those numbers helps tissues only if the tiny vessels actually carry the flow. In infection and inflammation, that link often breaks: the body-wide numbers look fine while organs stay starved of oxygen.

Four failure patterns are named, from uneven capillary flow and diluted blood to squeezed vessels and swollen tissue. Hand-held microscopes can now show the vessels under the tongue at the bedside, making each pattern visible. Ince also proposes how to tune fluid volume so the microcirculation carries the most oxygen. The piece urges intensive care to judge success where oxygen is delivered, not only at the pump.
europmc-pmc4709873:
Wing Sun Faith Chung, Alan W. Walker, Petra Louis, and five colleagues fed gut microbe communities two dietary fibres in BMC Biology in 2016. Fibre supplements are widely hoped to steer gut microbes toward health, but which species answer which fibre was poorly mapped. The team grew three human gut communities in controlled fermentors, feeding them apple pectin or inulin while stepping acidity up and down. Community membership was tracked by gene sequencing.

Each fibre enriched its own cast. Of the leading Bacteroides types, two rose on inulin and six on pectin, and one Firmicutes species surged on pectin alone. Acidity tipped contests too: at the most acidic setting, one species displaced Bacteroides as the dominant type. Pectin, the more complex fibre, supported richer communities. The lesson is precision: fibre effects play out species by species and shift with gut conditions, so blanket predictions will fail.
europmc-pmc4773773:
Bethany N. Smith and four co-authors review the EMT cell change in the Journal of Clinical Medicine in 2016, focusing on spread and drug resistance. EMT turns fixed surface cells into loose, moving ones. It builds the embryo, but tumors use it to break away, travel, and settle elsewhere in the body.

The review maps the signals that drive the change, among them TGF-beta and growth factor paths, and the switch proteins they wake. It gives special weight to prostate cancer, where tumor cells and the support cells around them trade signals that push the change. That crosstalk also dulls therapy, so tumors return after treatment that first worked. The authors survey the types of EMT and where blocking the talk between cells might help.
europmc-pmc4776673:
Simon Mitternacht, writing alone in F1000Research in 2016, presents a free software library called FreeSASA. Structural biologists often need the solvent accessible surface area of a molecule: the area a rolling water-sized ball can touch. The figure gauges how a protein folds and how much surface gets buried when parts join. Many tools compute it, but none was free-standing and open for easy use in other programs.

FreeSASA fills that gap as a C library with command-line and Python faces. It runs both classic methods for the measure and lets users tune molecule settings, precision, and output detail. It rests only on standard libraries, so it builds almost anywhere. The author reports speed and accuracy on par with or better than the closed tools labs have long relied on.
europmc-pmc4804173:
Hiromu Monai leads a broad author team in Nature Communications in 2016 watching what a weak electric current does to the mouse brain. Passing gentle direct current through the skull, called tDCS, eases several brain conditions and can sharpen memory in people, yet its working mechanism was murky. The team used mice whose support cells glow when calcium rises inside them.

Stimulation set off large calcium surges in astrocytes, the brain's support cells, across the whole outer brain, while plain electrical activity barely moved. Afterward, the cortex answered sensory input more strongly. That boost vanished in mice whose astrocytes could not mount the surges, and it depended on an adrenaline-type receptor. The authors propose the current retunes the cortex through its support cells, not its neurons alone.
europmc-pmc4811773:
Casey M. Schneider-Mizell leads a broad author team in eLife in 2016 on how to proofread wiring maps of the fly brain. Tracing neurons from electron microscope stacks is slow, and single tracers make mistakes. Repeating the work several times and merging the copies fixes errors but multiplies the labor, so the team looked for rules in the anatomy itself that predict where connections sit.

In larval sense-motor and adult visual circuits, input connections clustered on many small twigs that sprout from a neuron's main backbone. Missing a twig caused nearly all tracing errors. Strong connections, though, spread their contacts over many twigs, which makes them hard to erase by one miss. Using these rules, a single careful pass, checked against anatomy, matched the quality of merged multi-pass maps.
europmc-pmc4814573:
J. Tyler Mefford leads eight authors in Nature Communications in 2016 probing how a class of ceramic catalysts splits water. Perovskite oxides are cheap, sturdy candidates for the oxygen-making half of water splitting, the bottleneck step in storing renewable power as fuel. Why some perovskites excel was unclear, because three traits vary together: empty oxygen slots, bond sharing between metal and oxygen, and the lattice oxygen's own readiness to react.

By swapping strontium into a cobalt perovskite in graded steps, the team tuned those traits apart. Computer modeling pointed to lattice oxygen taking part in the reaction itself, not just watching. One tuned mix stood out with high activity at room temperature for its weight and area. The study gives catalyst design a firmer rule book.
europmc-pmc4817673:
Roberto Berni Canani leads ten authors in The ISME Journal in 2016 on formula feeding and milk allergy in infants. Babies allergic to cow's milk often outgrow it faster on a broken-down formula spiked with the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG. Whether the benefit runs through gut microbes was the open question, so the team read stool microbes before and after feeding.

Allergic infants started with a gut mix ruled by two broad families. After the probiotic formula, three genera known for making butyrate, a gut-soothing compound, rose sharply. Babies who became tolerant mostly showed higher butyrate, and the enriched strains differed at fine scale between tolerant and allergic babies. One genus alone separated the groups weakly. The authors read the tolerance effect as partly a reshaping of the infant gut.
europmc-pmc4827373:
Raj N. Kalaria, Rufus Akinyemi, and Masafumi Ihara review dementia after stroke in Biochimica et Biophysica Acta in 2016. Stroke survivors face more than weakness: a quarter to a third develop thinking problems or dementia, at once or in the months after. The review gathers who is at risk, what brain scans show, and what the tissue itself reveals.

Risk climbs with age, family history, low schooling, prior mini-strokes, and depression. Scans tie dementia to silent strokes, white matter change, and shrinkage of a memory region. Under the microscope, tiny infarcts, leaky small vessels, and patchy neuron loss outweigh the classic Alzheimer's changes in most cases. Since no direct treatment exists, the authors press prevention: controlling vessel risk factors is the standing defense.
europmc-pmc4839673:
Eric Talevich, A. Hunter Shain, Thomas Botton, and Boris C. Bastian presented CNVkit in 2016, a software method that finds copy number changes from targeted DNA sequencing. Copy number gains and losses matter in inherited syndromes and in cancer. Targeted tests read only chosen genes, leaving gaps and uneven coverage that make copy number hard to judge from read depth alone.

CNVkit uses both the on-target reads and the stray off-target reads that targeted tests also produce. That mix gives fine detail inside genes and a usable view across the rest of the genome. The authors showed a genome-wide view at fine scale from a test aimed at as few as 293 genes, a gain for cancer and clinic labs.
europmc-pmc4853773:
Xiaoguang Xu and co-authors built a CRISPR-based tool in 2016 to strip methyl marks from chosen DNA spots. Methyl marks help switch genes off, and faulty marks drive disease. Their system guides a Tet1 enzyme piece, which removes methyl marks, to a target gene using reshaped guide RNAs that carry docking tags for the cargo.

Three target genes, RANKL, MAGEB2, and MMP2, turned on more strongly after treatment. Nearby DNA spots in their control regions lost methyl marks in step with the rise. Off-target effects stayed faint. Aiming mark removal at single genes gives researchers a clean way to test what each mark does and, in time, may guide new treatments.
europmc-pmc4889773:
Claire D. Bourke, James A. Berkley, and Andrew J. Prendergast argued in 2016 that immune dysfunction is both a cause and a result of malnutrition. Poor nutrition, too little or too much, drives huge illness and death worldwide. Malnourished people suffer repeat infections and lasting inflammation, signs of a broken immune system, not just an empty plate.

Marks set before birth, through gene-control changes in malnourished parents, may pass the cycle to children. The review draws on animal, lab, and human cohort proof, with childhood undernutrition at the center. Gaps in knowledge get named plainly. Treating immune paths directly could cut deaths that food alone has not stopped, the review proposes.
europmc-pmc4891873:
Monika Puzianowska-Kuźnicka and a large PolSenior team linked two inflammation markers to aging and death in 2016. Lasting low-grade inflammation, nicknamed inflammaging, raises disease and frailty risk in old age. Blood levels of interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein were measured in several thousand Eastern Europeans aged 65 and over, among them 3,496 people for interleukin-6, and tied to body and mind performance.

Both markers rose steadily with age, even in elders aging well. Higher levels tracked weaker strength and thinking and foresaw higher death risk. Inflammation thus climbs with age itself, not just with illness. The markers may help spot elders who need closer watch and early support.
europmc-pmc4908773:
Luis O. Chavez, Monica Leon, Sharon Einav, and Joseph Varon reviewed rhabdomyolysis for clinical practice in Critical Care in 2016. The syndrome is skeletal muscle breakdown that spills cell contents into the blood, risking kidney failure and rhythm trouble. Past literature clashes on its definition, causes, and best care. The review searched three databases for work from 2006 to 2015.

Causes span crush injury, hard exertion, drugs, infection, and inherited muscle faults. Care rests on fast, large fluid volumes, watching kidney markers, and treating the trigger. Standard definitions would sharpen both research and ward practice. The review hands intensive care teams a shared map for a syndrome seen across many wards.
europmc-pmc5014473:
Darren P. Martin, Ben Murrell, Michael Golden, Arjun Khoosal, and Brejnev Muhire present RDP4 in Virus Evolution in 2015. RDP4 is a Windows program that hunts for recombination in virus genomes, the swapping of genome stretches between related viruses. Such swapping creates much of the variety that natural selection then acts on, and it can mislead family trees built from the sequences.

The new version handles up to 2,500 sequences as long as ten million letters. That is twice the count and three times the length of older versions, which also makes it fit for full bacterial genomes. New tools tell recombination apart from segment swapping, give error ranges for swap points, and build family trees that allow for swapping. Charts show single events and their combined effect. Users can run it fully on its own or explore results by hand in a rich visual display.
europmc-pmc5020873:
Richard Tran and six co-authors publish a database of crystal surface energies in Scientific Data in 2016. Surface energy measures how costly it is, in energy terms, to expose a given face of a crystal. It shapes how crystals grow, how their faces react, and how they work as catalysts, and it matters most in tiny particles where surface dominates. Measured values are scarce, so the team computed them for the elements.

The database holds surface energies for more than 100 crystal forms of about 70 elements, covering the main flat faces and known rebuilt surface patterns. Each entry was checked against earlier lab and computer values where those exist. The methods are set out in full so the set can grow and improve over time. Designers of catalysts, coatings, and nanomaterials can draw ready, comparable numbers from a single source.
europmc-pmc5043373:
Kosuke Tanaka and Hideshige Takada report microplastics in fish from Tokyo Bay in Scientific Reports in 2016. Plastic pieces under five millimeters now spread through the oceans, and small plankton-eating fish are a likely entry into food webs. The team opened the digestive tracts of 64 Japanese anchovies caught in the bay and checked every particle with infrared analysis.

Plastic turned up in 49 of the 64 fish, seventy-seven percent, at an average of 2.3 pieces per fish and up to fifteen in one. Most were fragments of polyethylene or polypropylene, the plastics that float. About seven percent were beads, some matching the microbeads used in facial cleansers. Most pieces were far smaller than those usually counted at the sea surface, likely because anchovies feed below it. Since anchovies feed many people and animals, the authors flag both ecosystem spread and the need to study chemical exposure from swallowed plastic.
europmc-pmc5069773:
Jessica A. Bryant and nine co-authors survey the microbes living on ocean plastic in mSystems in 2016. Plastic debris collects in the North Pacific Gyre, and while its harm to birds and mammals is well known, its effect on microbes, the drivers of ocean chemistry, was barely studied. The team sequenced the communities on plastic pieces and compared them with the free-floating microbes in the surrounding water.

The plastic dwellers differed from the open-water community in both membership and working genes. Their dominant cyanobacteria even harvested light with different machinery than the water's usual Prochlorococcus. The study is among the first molecular surveys of this new habitat, and it shows plastic is not a neutral raft: it hosts a distinct cross-domain community with its own functional potential. The work reframes marine plastic as a microbial habitat, not just litter.
europmc-pmc5075173:
Lukasz P. Kozlowski presents a software tool in Biology Direct in 2016, writing alone. The tool, called IPC, estimates a protein's isoelectric point from its amino acid sequence alone. That value, the pH at which a protein carries no net charge, guides lab methods such as gel separation and focusing, and it helps plan protein crystallization.

IPC runs as a free web service and as a standalone program. It offers several sets of the acid constants the math depends on, including two new sets Kozlowski tuned by computation. In his benchmarks the new sets beat older algorithms, cutting average error for proteins and peptides and producing fewer wild misses. He also supplies ready-made estimates for a protein structure database and for several widely used proteomes. The paper closes with open reviewer reports and his replies, an unusual window into how the work was judged.
europmc-pmc5141373:
Marc K. Etherington, Jamie Gibson, Heather F. Higginbotham, Thomas J. Penfold, and Andrew P. Monkman tested a model of delayed fluorescence in Nature Communications in 2016. Certain molecules for organic light-emitting diodes recycle dark triplet states into light, and the team's model says the recycling runs through a local triplet state coupled by molecular vibration.

They tuned the energy levels of the relevant states in and out of alignment across a series of molecules. Delayed fluorescence peaked exactly at the alignment point the model predicts, and light-absorption measures tracked the singlet, triplet, and local triplet populations as expected. The results back the spin-vibronic coupling picture and give designers a rule: match the local triplet energy to the charge-transfer states for the fastest recycling.
europmc-pmc5149073:
Joel Chappell and seven co-authors traced the cells that build artery plaques in mice, reporting in Circulation Research in 2016. Smooth muscle cells from the artery wall pile up in plaques and in the thickened lining after vessel injury, and they can change character, even resembling immune cells. Whether every such cell can multiply, or only some, was unsettled.

Using lineage tracing that marks individual cells, the team worked in injury and atherosclerosis models. They found that a small subset of mature, contractile smooth muscle cells does most of the dividing. Those cells expand into large clones that form much of the new tissue. These few cells stay flexible, switching into several other cell types. The result reframes plaque growth as the work of a rare, plastic minority rather than the whole wall.
europmc-pmc5153673:
Lucy Yardley, Ben Ainsworth, Emily Arden-Close, and Ingrid Muller described a person-based approach to health interventions in Pilot and Feasibility Studies in 2015. The approach studies the beliefs, needs, and daily situations of future users early on, then shapes the intervention to fit real lives rather than theory alone.

They give three worked examples. For an asthma website, a review of beliefs produced guiding design principles. For an asthma booklet, think-aloud interviews showed users preferred positive, non-medical messages and images. For a diabetes activity planner, repeated think-aloud rounds caught users entering data wrongly and getting bad tailored advice, which was then fixed. The authors present the approach as a systematic partner to theory-based and evidence-based design.
europmc-pmc5207773:
Barbara J. Hunnicutt, Bart C. Jongbloets, William T. Birdsong, Katrina J. Gertz, Haining Zhong, Tianyi Mao, and David C. Van Essen mapped the wiring of the mouse striatum in eLife in 2016. The striatum is the main input hub of the basal ganglia, a brain system that helps control movement and action choice. It receives strong excitatory signals from the cortex and the thalamus, but how those signals sort into its zones was poorly known.

Their tracing produced a full input map for the whole structure. The map shows clear borders between the known sensorimotor, associative, and limbic zones, and it points to the rearmost striatum as a likely fourth zone. The dorsomedial part takes in an unusually mixed set of inputs. Light-based tests then showed that synapses from cortex and thalamus differ in strength by subregion, giving later studies a circuit guide.
europmc-pmc5239573:
Anthony Cheung and a large team of colleagues reviewed folate receptor alpha as a cancer treatment target in Oncotarget in 2016. The receptor helps cells take in folate, a vitamin needed to build DNA. It appears at high levels on tumours of the ovary, breast, and lung, yet only sparsely in healthy tissue, and its level tracks with patient outlook.

The review sums up what the receptor does in cancer growth and weighs its use as a diagnostic and prognostic tool, a way to spot disease and judge its likely course. Treatment approaches covered include drug-linked targeting agents and, with special focus, monoclonal antibodies designed in the lab to home in on the receptor. Because fresh findings also link the receptor to tumour-promoting activity, the authors argue that aiming at it could give tailored options to patient groups poorly served by standard therapy.
europmc-pmc5267473:
Mandeep Sekhon, Martin Cartwright, and Jill J. Francis built a framework for the acceptability of healthcare interventions in BMC Health Services Research in 2017. Whether patients and staff find a treatment appropriate shapes whether it gets used, yet the literature used the word acceptability loosely, with little guidance on defining or measuring it.

An overview of 43 reviews found none that defined or theorized the concept outright; measures in use leaned on behavior such as dropout rates, on feelings, or on perceptions. The authors propose that acceptability is a multi-sided judgment of appropriateness, based on expected or experienced thoughts and feelings about an intervention. Their framework names seven parts: emotional attitude, burden, perceived effectiveness, ethical fit, coherence, opportunity costs, and confidence in one's own ability to take part. It can be applied before or after people experience an intervention.
europmc-pmc5323873:
Guofa Cai, Jiangxin Wang, Kai Qian, Jingwei Chen, Shaohui Li, and Pooi See Lee built a new kind of motion sensor in Advanced Science in 2017. The sensor is a soft gel laced with paths that carry electric current. When the gel stretches or bends, its resistance shifts in a steady, readable way. Such sensors can track body motion for health checks, sports, and robots.

Most past sensors tore or failed past twice their length. This gel can stretch to ten times its length and still give a clear signal. Cuts heal on their own, in both strength and current flow, at room conditions with no help. Tests of finger bends, twists, and other human motions showed a fast, stable, and repeatable response. The team sees wearables that survive the rough use of daily life.
europmc-pmc5357473:
Kenji Ikeda and co-authors tested a drug for late liver cancer in phase two trials, in the Journal of Gastroenterology in 2017. The drug, lenvatinib, is a pill that blocks a clutch of growth switches that feed tumor blood supply and growth. Patients whose tumors could not be cut out took a set daily dose in month long rounds across Japan and Korea.

Forty six patients were treated. By an outside scan panel's read, the middle time before tumors grew again passed seven months. More than a third of patients saw their tumors shrink, and most of the rest held stable. The middle survival span ran past a year and a half. High blood pressure, sore hands and feet, lost appetite, and protein in urine were the most common side effects. Most patients needed a dose cut.
europmc-pmc5359373:
Philippa D. Darbre reviewed hormone-mimic chemicals and obesity in Current Obesity Reports in 2017. The body's hormone web runs fuel storage and use, and keeps blood sugar steady. Some man-made chemicals can jam that web. A subset, dubbed obesogens, seem to push the body to build fat and gain weight. People meet them daily in farm sprays, plastics, detergents, and skin care goods.

Animal tests and population studies point to the womb and the first weeks of life as the touchiest time for such exposure. Since these chemicals love fat, more fat gives them more room to stay, which stores up more of them and of kin pollutants. That spiral may help explain why obesity raises the risk of so many other ills, cancer among them. Darbre urges that risk tests for new chemicals weigh this fat path.
europmc-pmc5361673:
Austin Quach and co-authors tested lifestyle ties to a DNA aging clock in Aging in 2017. New blood tests read age from chemical tags on DNA. Those clock scores foretell death, long illness, and loss of function. Whether daily habits move the clock was less clear. The team used data from more than four thousand older women in a United States health study, plus a smaller Italian aging cohort.

One form of clock speed tied to fish intake, mild alcohol use, schooling, body weight, and blood signs of fruit and vegetable intake. A second form tied to poultry intake and body weight. Both forms tracked the cluster of blood sugar and fat ills called metabolic syndrome, which seemed to carry their weight links. A top diabetes drug showed no clock gain in this look. Weight gain over time also came with a faster clock on both forms.
europmc-pmc5367273:
Waldan K. Kwong, Amanda L. Mancenido, and Nancy A. Moran tested how gut microbes stir bee immunity in Royal Society Open Science in 2017. Gut mixes shape host health in part by tuning the immune system. For key insects like the honey bee, that link stayed dim. The team asked if the bee's own resident gut bacteria switch on its germ-killing proteins.

Bees with their normal gut mix read out two such proteins, apidaecin and hymenoptaecin, at higher levels in gut tissue than bees with bare guts. Fine protein tests found apidaecin in the gut channel and in the blood, richer in normal bees. The resident strains bore the proteins' attack better than a standard lab germ. In some tests, bees with full gut mixes lived better after a germ shot. The flora seems to prime the bee's guard.
europmc-pmc5408373:
Tri-Long Nguyen and six co-authors tackle a statistics choice in a 2017 paper in BMC Medical Research Methodology. In studies without random assignment, matching on a summary score can balance two groups. When balance still falls short, analysts can adjust again in a second model, but they cannot always include every factor. The team ran computer trials on fake populations to find how much leftover imbalance should trigger that second adjustment.

Adjusting for every factor whose group gap passed a set cutoff removed nearly all of the leftover bias. Adding factors below that cutoff gained almost nothing, and errors in the estimates were at their lowest under the same rule. The authors advise reshaping the match until most gaps fall below the cutoff, and only then using the double adjustment for what remains.
europmc-pmc5412373:
Vig and co-authors review progress in lab-grown skin for wound care. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Skin is the body barrier and its largest organ. Shallow wounds can regrow on their own. Deep burns and chronic wounds cannot. Grafts help, but donor skin is scarce. Foreign tissue also risks infection and rejection. Engineered substitutes aim to fill that gap.

The review surveys substitutes made from several sources. Some use no cells at all. Others draw on the patient's own cells, donor tissue, animal tissue, or synthetic materials. Each type has strengths and limits. No product yet matches full natural skin. Fast blood vessel growth stays a key hurdle. The authors also press for cheaper, easier products with longer shelf life. Readers get a map of current options and their trade-offs.
europmc-pmc5428673:
Nekrasov and co-authors breed a mildew-proof tomato in under ten months, with no foreign DNA left behind. Their research article appeared in Scientific Reports. Powdery mildew is a fungal disease of tomato. A working gene called SlMlo1 makes plants prone to it. Broken copies of that gene give resistance. Normal breeding can move the broken copy into fine varieties. That path takes years of crosses.

The team used CRISPR/Cas9 to break SlMlo1 directly. Two guide RNAs cut the gene at paired spots. The cuts removed a short stretch of DNA. Whole-genome sequencing checked the result. The new variety, named Tomelo, carried only that deletion. No foreign DNA remained. No off-target mutations were found. The deletion looks like a natural mutation. The authors say elite local varieties could gain such traits within a year.
europmc-pmc5440673:
Nardone and co-authors show that a gene switch called YAP also builds the anchors that set a cell's stiffness. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Cells grip the matrix around them at focal adhesions. YAP and its partner TAZ sense matrix stiffness. They then move into the nucleus and switch genes on. Past models put adhesions above YAP in a one-way chain. This team found traffic in both directions.

Cell spreading and the signal protein RhoA drive adhesion growth through YAP. Active YAP turns on genes for integrins. It also turns on genes for adhesion docking proteins. Those parts anchor the actin skeleton to the membrane. Tuning YAP changed cell force, adhesion strength, and shape. It also changed how cells move and mature. The authors cast YAP as a master dial of cell mechanics. Matrix cues turn the dial. The dial then rebuilds the grip itself.
europmc-pmc5467173:
Cho and co-authors build tiny balls of cells that mimic the blood-brain barrier for drug screening. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Most drugs cannot cross into the brain. That barrier blocks treatment of many brain diseases. Lab models of the barrier exist, but their traits vary from run to run. A steadier model would speed the search for brain-penetrating drugs.

The team's spheroids assemble themselves from three cell types. Astrocytes fill the core. Vessel-lining cells and pericytes coat the surface. That surface acts like the real barrier. It shows tight seals between cells and active pumps that push drugs back out. It also ferries a known carrier peptide across. A standard flat culture model performed far worse. It could not tell that carrier from a control peptide. The team used the spheroids to screen peptide candidates. They found several that cross the barrier well.
europmc-pmc5506473:
Tian, Wang, and Zhang present a review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity on oxidative stress in bowel disease. Inflammatory bowel disease covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Both are chronic, incurable, and rising worldwide. Reactive oxygen species appear central to how the damage unfolds. Such species can breach the gut lining and invite bacterial invasion.

The review traces where these species form in the gut. It links them to gene risk, immune response, and gut microbes. Defense systems that quench them get equal space. Antioxidant drugs, natural and synthetic, are weighed as future therapies. Exact mechanisms still need proof, the authors caution.
europmc-pmc5536073:
Senthebane and co-authors present a review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences on why chemotherapy fails. Drug resistance kills more cancer patients than any other treatment problem. Genes inside tumor cells explain only part of it. The tissue around a tumor, its microenvironment, actively shelters cancer cells. Stromal cells and the matrix between cells feed that protection.

Cutting off that support could restore drug power, they argue. Targets include stromal cells, their secreted proteins, and the matrix itself. New lab models mimic the real setting: spheroids, scaffolds, and organoids. Cancer cells survive by keeping these neighbors close, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc5585273:
Liu and co-authors present a software advance in Nature Communications. Many proteins carry sugar chains that shape their function. Naming those sugars at exact sites is hard. Their tool, pGlyco 2.0, reads intact sugar-bearing peptides in one mass spectrometry step.

Older methods needed several tools and steps to check both parts. The new search engine checks error rates at three levels. Those levels cover sugars, peptides, and the paired matches. A labeled-sample test gave a fresh way to judge accuracy. The team then mapped over 10,000 distinct sugars in five mouse tissues. They sat on 1,988 sites across 955 proteins. Readers get a faster, more careful route to sugar maps.
europmc-pmc5585373:
Gulen and co-authors report an immunity study in Nature Communications. Cells sense loose DNA inside them through a pathway called cGAS-STING. In most immune cells, that alarm turns on antiviral genes. The team asks what the same alarm does in T cells.

T cells carry high levels of STING, so their response runs stronger. Instead of mainly making interferons, they switch on death genes. The cells then die by apoptosis. Cancerous T cells kept this response. Drugs that activate STING stopped T-cell tumors growing in mice. The effect did not depend on STING's usual helper role for vaccines. Readers learn that signal strength, not just signal presence, shapes the outcome.
europmc-pmc5602073:
Jacob and Smith review intron retention in Human Genetics. When genes are read, introns are usually cut out. Sometimes an intron stays in the final message. That event, intron retention, was long dismissed as noise.

Deep sequencing changed the verdict. Clear retention patterns now show in development, stress, and disease. Plants and yeast use retention as a main control dial. Mammals, it turns out, use it widely too. Retention can change which protein form gets made. It can mark an RNA for decay instead. Some retained introns splice later, giving fast gene switches. The review pulls these findings into one picture. Common threads run through the retention networks. Readers see a once-ignored mechanism take its place in gene regulation.
europmc-pmc5671473:
Baker, Maass, and Jagust present a data and code article in Data in Brief. It supports correction of tau PET brain scans. The tracer AV-1451 measures tau pathology in Alzheimer's research. It also binds off target in several places. Examples include the skull, meninges, and choroid plexus. Such binding bleeds into regions of real interest.

The authors share Matlab code for partial volume correction. It applies the Rousset geometric transfer matrix method. The code builds a cleaner reference region from lower cerebellar gray. It splits the choroid plexus by binding level. Subject-specific hotspot regions are created as well. A companion paper used this pipeline to compare tau measures.
europmc-pmc5753373:
Lefkowitz and co-authors describe the virus taxonomy database kept by the ICTV. The International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses builds and maintains a universal virus taxonomy. It classifies species and higher groups by genetic and biological traits. It also names taxa and keeps the approved listing.

The website gives the current taxonomy in online and downloadable forms. A full history of virus taxa reaches back to the first release in 1971. The ICTV Report gives deep accounts of structure, genomes, and biology for all taxa. The tenth report is being published online as an open, updated work.
europmc-pmc5809573:
Watanabe and co-authors present Japan's 2016 colorectal cancer guidelines. Deaths from this cancer in Japan passed 49,000 in 2015. New treatments have grown fast. The JSCCR wrote shared rules to level care across hospitals.

The guidelines rest on a careful search of the proof. A committee weighed that proof against Japanese practice and insurance. Hard cases became formal clinical questions. Each answer carries a grade for proof strength and advice force. Topics span surgery, drugs, and follow-up care. Readers get the standard playbook Japanese teams use, here in English for wide access.
europmc-pmc5833873:
Allocati and co-authors survey glutathione transferases, enzymes that disarm toxins by tagging them for disposal. Their review appeared in Oncogenesis. The same shield can backfire in cancer. Tumors overstock these enzymes and shrug off chemotherapy.

The review spans what the enzymes act on and what blocks them. Gene variants in the family track with neurodegenerative diseases. One blocker, NBDHEX, aims to strip the tumor shield. Other work flips the trick: pro-drugs stay inert until a transferase switches them on inside cancer cells. The family thus cuts as both obstacle and tool.
europmc-pmc5847173:
Ólafsdóttir, Bush, and Barry review hippocampal replay, the brain's habit of rerunning its own routes. Their review appeared in Current Biology. Place cells in the hippocampus fire for spots along a path. During rest and sleep they refire in sequence, replaying the journey.

Replay has been cast as memory's filing clerk. It may cement fresh memories into long-term store. It may also serve recall, working memory, and planning ahead. Rodent evidence links it to reinforcement learning as well. The authors argue its job shifts with the task at hand. Arousal and demand tune what replay does moment to moment.
europmc-pmc5858873:
Katzelnick and co-authors study antibody levels and severe dengue in children. Their article appeared in Science. Dengue viruses come in four types and spread by mosquitoes. A second infection with a new type raises the risk of severe disease. The team used a long-running child cohort in Nicaragua. More than 6,600 children gave antibody measures over many years.

The authors report that severe disease risk peaked in a narrow antibody range. Mid-level antibodies seemed to help the virus enter cells and grow. High levels, by contrast, protected against illness of any kind. The team used several statistical methods to check the pattern. Their findings matter for vaccine design, where weak immunity could add risk.
europmc-pmc5871973:
Kumar and co-authors review antimicrobial peptides and ways to improve them. Their article appeared in Biomolecules. These small peptides occur in nearly all forms of life. They kill microbes, and bacteria rarely resist them for long. That makes them attractive as antibiotic alternatives. The review covers their diversity and long research history. It explains the varied ways they attack target cells.

Few peptides have won drug approval so far, the authors note. Toxicity, enzyme breakdown, and short life in the body block progress. Recent fixes include chemical tweaks to the peptide chain. Delivery systems that shield peptides are also reviewed. The authors weigh activity gains against safety in living tissue.
europmc-pmc5960473:
Wang and Zhao review gut microbiota derived metabolites in cardiovascular health and disease. Their review appeared in Protein & Cell. Trillions of microbes live in the human gut. They supply nutrients and energy from food. They also release bioactive molecules that signal through the body. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Several of these metabolites bear on its course.

The review covers trimethylamine-N-oxide and uremic toxins. Short chain fatty acids, bile acids, and lipopolysaccharide also feature. So do phytoestrogens and anthocyanins. Each can support healthy heart function when balanced. When dysregulated, they may help cause disease, the authors note.
europmc-pmc5989173:
Huang and co-authors review the role of macrophages in acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Their review appeared in Mediators of Inflammation. These lung conditions kill many patients in intensive care. Their inner mechanism still needs fuller explanation. Macrophages are central to the inflammatory process here. They play a two-sided role across the illness. Setting and disease stage decide their stance.

In the acute phase they shift to the M1 state, the authors explain. They then release strong pro-inflammatory mediators. Later they swing back to M2 to clear dead cells. That later work also feeds fibrosis. Steering macrophage function may treat these syndromes.
europmc-pmc5989473:
Markowiak and Śliżewska review the roles of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics in animal nutrition. Their review appeared in Gut Pathogens. Livestock breeders want feed additives that speed growth and guard health. Antibiotic growth stimulators were banned in 2006, they note. These microbial products are a leading hope to replace them. They mainly keep gut microbiota in balance. That balance helps animals fight pathogens that threaten consumers too.

The paper sets out definitions for each product type. It lists the criteria such formulas must meet. Common probiotics and prebiotics used in feed are named. Study results on animal health effects are summed up.
europmc-pmc6008573:
Luan and Yao review the clinical significance of C-reactive protein in chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases. Their review was published in Frontiers in Immunology. CRP is a fast-rise protein made by liver cells. It answers to cell signals during infection and swelling. It comes in two shapes with distinct acts. One shape can calm or stir swelling by context. The other stirs it strongly in blood and vessel cells.

CRP is best known as a mark of sharp swelling. Big studies also tie it to long-term swelling states. The review covers heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Eye decay, brain bleeding, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's follow. New finds may turn into tests and care for these ills.
europmc-pmc6019073:
Namiki and co-authors map descending neurons in fruit flies. Their research article appeared in eLife. Descending neurons carry signals from brain to body. They run through the neck to the nerve cord. Their activity starts and shapes movement and behavior.

The team built over 100 transgenic fly lines. Each line targets a single cell type. They identified about half of all descending neurons. They then mapped links between sensory and motor regions. The nerve cord proved to be a layered system. Separate layers support walking and flight. Readers get a basic wiring map of fly movement control. The lines also give tools for future circuit studies.
europmc-pmc6088173:
Brembilla and co-authors review the IL-17 cytokine family in psoriasis. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease. New drugs target the IL-23 and IL-17A pathway. They clear skin symptoms better than older care.

IL-17A is one member of a six-part family. The other members can mimic, differ from, or oppose its effects. Their actions vary by tissue. They also amplify other inflammatory signals. The review sums up each member's role in skin. It then asks what this means for drug design. Readers get the wider family picture behind a hit therapy target.
europmc-pmc6120873:
Sun and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on gut bacteria products and immune balance. T cells help keep the gut calm and healthy. Bacteria in the gut make short-chain fatty acids as they ferment food. How those acids steer T cells was not clear.

The team studied Th1 cells that react to a gut microbe antigen. The fatty acids pushed these cells to make IL-10, a calming signal. A receptor called GPR43 sensed the acids. Mice given cells that lack the receptor got worse gut inflammation. Treated cells made more IL-10 and caused milder disease. The work shows one way gut microbes keep peace with their host.
europmc-pmc6163673:
Zhu and co-authors wrote a review in Biomolecules on research progress linking atherosclerosis and inflammation. Atherosclerosis hardens and narrows arteries with plaque. It is now seen as a chronic inflammatory disease. When unstable plaque ruptures, clots can block the vessel and trigger acute heart disease.

The review explains how inflammation drives plaque formation. Signals involved include pro-inflammatory cytokines, signaling pathways, bioactive lipids, and adhesion molecules. These factors recruit immune cells into the vessel wall. The authors then assess prospects for treating the disease by blocking inflammation. Targets in these pathways are already under study. The review connects basic mechanisms with possible therapies.
europmc-pmc6193173:
Kim and co-authors present a research article in Advanced Science on a wearable sensor that reads two body fluids at once. Wearable biosensors usually sample just one fluid, such as sweat. Interstitial fluid, the fluid between cells, carries other useful markers. No single platform had sampled both on demand.

Their flexible skin platform stimulates sweat at one electrode by delivering pilocarpine through the skin. At a second site it extracts interstitial fluid. Separate sensors then measure the matching biomarkers in each fluid. Tests tracked glucose and alcohol after a drink, in sweat, fluid, and blood. The design points toward richer, needle-free health monitoring from one patch.
europmc-pmc6212673:
Bohmwald and co-authors review nerve harm from respiratory viruses. Viruses that infect the lungs can also reach the brain. Such spread can leave lasting nerve problems. The review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. It covers four virus groups.

The groups are respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, coronavirus, and metapneumovirus. They mainly strike young children and older adults. Reported nerve signs include seizures and encephalitis. All four viruses have been found in spinal fluid. That suggests they travel from lungs to the brain. The authors review possible entry routes. They also cover effects seen in animal models. They note that knowledge of these routes is still scarce.
europmc-pmc6232773:
Amarante-Mendes and co-authors review sensors that link germ detection to cell death. Pattern recognition receptors spot molecules from germs. They also spot molecules freed by damaged cells. These sensors belong to the innate immune system. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology.

Sensor signals switch on germ-killing and inflammatory responses. Controlled cell death is also part of defence. Each death form shapes inflammation in its own way. Death can remove infected or damaged cells. The authors discuss how death machinery and sensor signals interact. Signals from germ patterns and damage patterns both feature. The interplay affects later adaptive immunity too. The review connects two fields that are often treated apart.
europmc-pmc6269473:
Rice and co-authors show how tumour driven neutrophils switch their energy source to keep suppressing immunity. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Neutrophils defend the body, but in cancer they can help tumours grow. They release oxygen radicals that blunt T cell action. Such cells were long thought to run only on sugar burning. Tumours often starve their surroundings of glucose, though.

A young subset of neutrophils can burn fat in their mitochondria instead. That backup keeps radical output going when glucose runs low. In tumour bearing mice, this fitness was driven by a growth signal called c-Kit. Blood neutrophils from cancer patients showed the same pattern. More young cells, more mitochondria, and more oxygen use were all seen. The findings recast how tumours hold local immunity down.
europmc-pmc6321673:
Moullin and co-authors systematically review uses of the EPIS implementation framework. The review appeared in Implementation Science. EPIS maps four phases of putting practices into use. They are Exploration, Preparation, Implementation, and Sustainment. Many fields use it to plan evidence-based programs. The team searched seven databases for studies applying it.

They screened 762 full-text articles. Sixty-seven articles covering 49 projects qualified. All projects ran in public sector settings. Most studied one specific practice being implemented. Inner setting factors drew the most attention. Depth of framework use averaged moderate. The authors urge sharper definitions in future work. Bridging factors between systems need more study, they say.
europmc-pmc6324073:
Carvalho-Silva and co-authors report two years of updates to the Open Targets Platform. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The platform scores links between drug targets and diseases. It blends genetics, genomics, and drug evidence. Animal models and literature add further weight. Scores help labs rank targets for drug discovery.

Eight releases shipped since the first paper. New sources added target-disease evidence. Causal variants from targeted arrays joined the mix. Fresh visualizations aid target and disease pages. A batch search tool handles up to 200 targets. The programming interface dropped its authorization need. Training workshops and forums grew the user base. Data are free by download or interface.
europmc-pmc6356973:
Tocher and co-authors review the supply gap for omega-3 oils EPA and DHA. Their review appeared in Nutrients. These long-chain fats support development and health. They help against a range of diseases. Traditional supply comes from marine fish oil and fishmeal. That supply cannot meet global human needs.

Aquaculture both uses and provides much of the supply. Twenty years of research hunted for alternatives. Microalgae and engineered oil crops are among the options. New sources made de novo are now reaching market. The review tracks each candidate source's progress. It weighs how much each could realistically add. The authors frame the gap as solvable, with effort. Demand will keep rising with health guidance and fish farming.
europmc-pmc6378273:
Jessen and Mirsky present a review in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience on Schwann cells after nerve injury. These glial cells wrap peripheral nerve fibers in two forms, myelin-making and Remak cells. After injury, both types convert into a repair form that gives peripheral nerves their strong regrowth power.

Repair cells clear broken myelin, keep neurons alive, and guide new axon growth. The review explains the switch, driven in part by the c-Jun program. It also shows why repair fails over time: the repair state is unstable and the cells slowly die off. Human nerve repair often takes months, so keeping repair cells active is the key treatment challenge.
europmc-pmc6416573:
Chocholata and co-authors review scaffolds for bone repair in Materials. Bone tissue engineering joins material science, medicine, and genetics. Its goal is to restore lost bone function with a scaffold that cells can grow on.

A good scaffold mimics the bone's natural setting as closely as possible. The review surveys materials now in use, from ceramics to polymers. It also covers the ways scaffolds are built, such as printing and spinning. Cell-plus-scaffold pairs are the most promising route, they say. Mouth and jaw repair uses many of the same methods.
europmc-pmc6488573:
De Falco and co-authors put laundry under the microscope, washing commercial garments at real scale in a household machine. They measured the microfibers synthetic clothes shed, a leading source of primary microplastics in the oceans. Wastewater was filtered through sieves of decreasing pore size and the fibers counted and measured.

Release ran from 124 to 308 milligrams per kilogram of fabric depending on the garment, translating to roughly 640,000 to 1,500,000 fibers per wash load. Yarn construction and twist changed the shedding rate, and polyester-cellulose blends released plenty of cellulosic fibers too. The commonest fibers, 360 to 660 micrometers long, are sized to slip through wastewater treatment and reach marine food webs.
europmc-pmc6489173:
Waltz and co-authors test a seductive idea in implementation science: that experts can match fixes to barriers the way doctors match drugs to diagnoses. They asked 169 implementation researchers and practitioners to pair strategies from the ERIC compilation against 39 barriers defined by the CFIR framework, ranking up to seven strategies per barrier.

Agreement was strikingly absent. For each barrier, an average of 47 different strategies earned at least one endorsement, with wide scatter in what experts considered the right lever. Rather than forcing false consensus, the team built a tool that aggregates all endorsements into a prioritized shortlist, giving practitioners structured breadth instead of a single brittle prescription.
europmc-pmc6494973:
Mars and co-authors follow a British birth cohort to learn which teenagers who think about suicide or harm themselves go on to attempt it. In the Avon study, 456 adolescents reported suicidal thoughts and 569 reported non-suicidal self-harm at age 16. By 21, about 12 percent of each group had made a first attempt, meaning most had not.

Among those with suicidal thoughts, prior self-harm was the strongest single predictor, odds ratio 2.78, followed by cannabis and other illicit drug use and exposure to others' self-harm. In the self-harm group, drug use and insufficient sleep led. Many textbook risk factors failed to predict transition at all, sharpening where clinicians should probe.
europmc-pmc6518373:
Billionnet and co-authors assess birth risks linked to gestational diabetes in France. Their study appeared in Diabetologia. It draws on hospital and health insurance data for births in 2012. The cohort held 796,346 deliveries. Of those mothers, 57,629 had gestational diabetes.

Risks with gestational diabetes were far lower than with pre-existing diabetes. They still rose above the non-diabetic group. Odds rose for preterm birth, Caesarean section and pre-eclampsia. Odds also rose for large babies, breathing distress and birth trauma. Insulin-treated cases carried higher risks than diet-treated cases. In term births, perinatal death risk rose as well. The authors call the added risk moderate.
europmc-pmc6523673:
Gurunathan and co-authors review exosomes, from isolation to therapy. Their review appeared in Cells. Exosomes are small vesicles shed by cells. They carry proteins, lipids, RNA and DNA. Cells use them to send signals to other cells. They also seem to serve as a waste disposal route.

The authors cover the history and birth of exosomes. They detail release and the factors that shape it. Isolation methods include centrifugation, filtration and immunoaffinity capture. Testing methods check purity and cargo. Later sections treat roles in health and disease. That promise makes exosomes candidates for diagnosis and new treatments. The review ends with open challenges and outlook.
europmc-pmc6532273:
Cenini, Lloret and Cascella review the role of oxidative stress in brain aging and disease, writing in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Age is the top risk factor for Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and ALS, all marked by slow neuron loss. The authors view these diseases from the mitochondrion, the cell's power plant.

Neurons lean almost wholly on mitochondria for energy. The brain burns much oxygen, holds weak antioxidant defenses, and is rich in fats that rust easily. When reactive oxygen output outruns those defenses, mitochondria are hit first and damage builds. The review covers this damage in aging, then disease by disease, plus shifts in mitochondrial shape and movement. The authors hope these pathways point to ways of protecting the aging brain.
europmc-pmc6538573:
Kret and Sjak-Shie offer practical guidance on cleaning pupil size data before analysis, writing in Behavior Research Methods. Pupil size shifts with arousal, effort, interest and emotion, and clinics use it to gauge brain function. Standard eye trackers record it easily, but their output carries heavy noise.

Untreated noise can sink a pupillometry study, so the authors first review the measure and its uses. They then name the main noise sources and show how to spot each one, from blinks to tracking loss. Step-by-step rules follow for handling bad stretches before resampling and baseline checks. An open MATLAB script ships with the guidelines, so labs can apply the same routine to their own data.
europmc-pmc6550273:
Mathews and co-authors argue that digital health needs a proper validation path, writing in NPJ Digital Medicine. Apps, wearables and remote care tools now number in the hundreds of thousands, backed by billions in funding. Yet patients, clinicians, payers and regulators have no trusted way to tell which products actually work.

The authors propose judging each product against end-user requirements in four domains. Technical checks ask whether it measures what it claims. Clinical checks ask whether health outcomes improve. Usability and cost checks ask whether it fits real lives, workflows and budgets. They set out the plan as a scorecard and a route to a clearer market, where quality is easier to spot and to buy.
europmc-pmc6669473:
Gruber-Dorninger and co-authors report a ten-year global survey of mycotoxins in animal feed. Their study appears in Toxins. The team analysed 74,821 samples from 100 countries. Samples covered 2008 to 2017. Six major fungal toxins were measured in each. Eighty-eight percent held at least one mycotoxin. Sixty-four percent carried two or more together. Climate emerged as a key driver of the patterns. Rainfall and temperature during grain development explained yearly swings.

Most regions largely met European Union limits. Aflatoxin B1 breaches clustered in warmer regions. South Asia exceeded the maximum in 41.1 percent of samples. Sub-Saharan Africa followed at 38.5 percent. Mixtures of deoxynivalenol, zearalenone, and fumonisins dominated.
europmc-pmc6689873:
Djoumbou-Feunang and co-authors present BioTransformer, software for predicting small molecule metabolism. Their paper appears in the Journal of Cheminformatics. Existing tools suffer limited scope and availability. BioTransformer combines machine learning with knowledge-based rules. It forecasts how tissues and the gut break molecules down. Breakdown by soil and water microbes is covered. Tests pitted it against two commercial tools. Precision and recall ran up to seven times better. It reproduced every EAWAG pathway forecast tested.

A rat epicatechin study validated its naming mode. All 39 known metabolites were recovered. Twenty-eight further options were offered. Seventeen matched masses not reported before. The tool is free as software and web service.
europmc-pmc6707173:
May and Gossage review how researchers count cases of fetal alcohol syndrome. Their summary appeared in Alcohol Research & Health. It looks at studies done since the late 1970s in the United States. It also covers related birth defects and brain disorders linked to drink in pregnancy.

The authors compare three ways to find cases. One uses existing records. One uses clinic-based studies. One seeks cases out in a set group. They weigh the strengths and flaws of each way. They report a rate of 0.5 to 2 cases per 1,000 births. They also list risk factors in mothers, such as older age and binge drinking.
europmc-pmc6805573:
Von Meijenfeldt and co-authors present CAT and BAT, tools for classifying uncharted microbial sequences. Metagenomics now assembles long sequences and whole genomes from mixed samples. Naming them is the hard part. The usual best-hit method often assigns names that are too specific. That error bites hardest for novel, deep lineages with no close database relatives.

Their Contig Annotation Tool and Bin Annotation Tool combine multiple signals across a sequence. When close relatives exist, classification goes to low taxonomic ranks. When they do not, it stops at higher ranks instead of guessing. Voting across many gene signals keeps precision high. Resolution is traded for accuracy exactly when the evidence is weak, which suits unexplored microbial diversity.
europmc-pmc6838673:
Benabdallah and co-authors report a study in Molecular Cell on how genes are switched on. Enhancers are DNA stretches that boost a gene's activity from far away. The standard picture says an active enhancer loops the DNA to touch its gene. That picture rests on assumption more than proof. The team tested it on a well-known case.

They followed the Sonic hedgehog gene as stem cells turned into nerve precursors. With high-resolution imaging and contact mapping, they watched enhancer and gene positions. As the gene switched on, the pair moved apart, not together. That result clashes with the simple looping model. The authors argue enhancer action must involve a subtler rearrangement of the chromosome.
europmc-pmc6853173:
Jackstadt and co-authors report a study in Cancer Cell on how bowel cancer spreads. Colorectal cancer kills mainly by metastasis, and good treatments for that stage are scarce. A signalling pathway called NOTCH helps run the gut lining. The team switched on NOTCH1 in the gut lining of mice already prone to a serrated form of this cancer.

Every such mouse developed metastases, most of them in the liver. The tumours reshaped their surroundings into a pattern matching the worst-prognosis human subtypes. They did so by calling in neutrophils through the signal TGF-beta. Blocking that recruitment is possible with existing drugs. The work names a route by which a whole tumour type turns aggressive.
europmc-pmc6957273:
Guerrero-Ferreira and co-authors solve two new atomic structures of alpha-synuclein fibrils. Their study appeared in eLife. Clumps rich in this protein mark Parkinson's disease and related disorders inside brain cells. The shape of the fibrils matters for understanding how they form and spread.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team resolved two forms, called polymorphs 2a and 2b, at 3.0 and 3.4 angstrom resolution. Both differ radically from earlier structures. Each fibril is 10 nanometres wide, built from two filaments joined by salt bridges between specific amino acids. A region long thought exposed is fully buried by new contacts. A water-shy cleft holds sites of known family mutations. The new maps, the authors say, suggest fresh ideas about fibril growth and stability.
europmc-pmc7003173:
Subramanian and co-authors review how to combine many kinds of molecular data into one picture. Their review appeared in Bioinformatics and Biology Insights. Health and disease play out across layers: genome, gene activity, proteins, and metabolites. Studying one layer alone misses how they connect.

Fast, high-throughput methods now produce all these data sets, called multi-omics, for large sample groups. The authors collect tools and methods that integrate them, step by step or all at once. Uses include sorting diseases into subtypes and predicting useful biomarkers. They explain each method's approach, strengths, and limits. Data repositories and viewing portals get a tour. Closing challenges cover the sheer size and messiness of multi-layer data, and the skill needed to read it well.
europmc-pmc7027373:
Zhang and co-authors review T cell dysfunction and exhaustion in cancer for Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. T cells should hunt down tumour cells, and they anchor most cancer immunotherapy. Inside tumours, though, many T cells slip into an exhausted state. They keep displaying inhibitory receptors and lose the killing power of healthy effector cells.

The review explains how the tumour microenvironment pushes T cells into that state and what defines it at the molecular level. Signals from surrounding tissue and tumour cells rewire the T cell's gene programme. The authors then survey immunotherapies designed to reverse the process, including checkpoint blockade and combined strategies. Understanding these mechanisms, they argue, could sharpen treatment for patients with advanced cancers.
europmc-pmc7055373:
Zivanov, Nakane, and Scheres improve cryo-electron microscopy software in the journal IUCrJ. Cryo-EM reconstructs molecular structures from very noisy images, because samples can only tolerate a small electron dose before damage. As resolutions sharpen, the microscope's own optical flaws become the limiting factor. The authors present methods, built into RELION-3.1, that estimate those flaws from the data itself.

The methods measure symmetrical and antisymmetrical optical aberrations, plus magnification anisotropy, where the image is stretched slightly more in one direction than another. Correcting for these effects raises the resolution of the three-dimensional reconstruction when they are present. The team demonstrates the correction on datasets from two microscope types, including one of the highest resolution structures published at the time. They also show a limitation with phase plate data. The work helps structural biologists squeeze atomic detail from imperfect optics.
europmc-pmc7069073:
Huang and co-authors review interactions between circular RNAs and proteins in Theranostics. Circular RNAs are closed loops of RNA with no caps or tails, produced in patterns specific to tissue, cell type, and developmental stage. Long dismissed as splicing errors, they are now known to act as sponges for microRNAs and proteins, as decoys, scaffolds, and recruiters, and some even serve as templates for making small proteins.

These RNAs bind proteins and drag them to the right compartments, and they tune interactions among proteins and between proteins and other RNAs. Proteins return the favour, governing the circles' birth, working life, and destruction. The exact mechanisms of many pairings remain unknown. The review gathers current knowledge of the interactions and the laboratory methods used to find and characterise them, then summarises fresh ideas about the machinery underneath. The subject matters because these loops participate in many disease processes.
europmc-pmc7128973:
Kim and co-authors test coronavirus vaccines delivered by dissolving microneedle patches instead of syringes, in EBioMedicine. Needle-free skin patches could speed mass vaccination and skip cold-chain and sharps problems. The team built subunit vaccines from the MERS coronavirus spike protein, shaped to mimic the virus's own structure.

In mice, patch delivery produced strong antibody responses, measured by binding tests and virus neutralisation. Versions carrying built-in immune stimulants were also tried. The group then used the same platform to build SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidates quickly during the COVID-19 emergency and tested them in animals. The paper presents the platform as one that can be moved fast when a new coronavirus appears.
europmc-pmc7140973:
Meng, Hua, and Bian set out the challenges COVID-19 poses for dentistry, in the Journal of Dental Research. Dental work brings patients and practitioners face to face, with sprays that can carry virus, so cross-infection risk is high. By 26 February 2020 the disease had reached 34 countries with 80,239 confirmed cases and 2,700 deaths.

Writing from experience in Wuhan, the authors summarise essential facts about the virus and about infection inside dental settings. They give management protocols for practitioners and students in affected areas, covering patient screening, protective equipment, and disinfection. Their own hospital saw nine colleagues infected, and the measures are meant to stop practices becoming spread points while care continues.
europmc-pmc7181373:
Ronzitti and co-authors review how the human immune system responds to AAV vectors. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. These vectors are a leading tool for delivering genes into the body. They are built from a small virus that infects many people in childhood. That early contact leaves lasting immune memory in many adults. Such memory can blunt or block gene transfer.

The review covers both antibody and cell-based responses to the vector. It explains how vector design and dose shape those responses. Animal models often fail to predict human outcomes, the authors note. Trial data offer the best lessons so far. The authors discuss ways to lower immune harm. These include changes to the capsid and to dosing plans. Readers get a clear view of a key barrier to gene therapy and paths around it.
europmc-pmc7218573:
Xue and co-authors combine several omics methods to learn why some dairy cows give more milk protein than others. Their study appeared in Microbiome. Cows raised on the same feed and care still differ in output. The team studied the rumen, the stomach chamber where microbes ferment feed. They profiled rumen microbes, rumen chemicals, and blood chemicals together.

High-producing cows hosted more of several Prevotella species in the rumen. Their microbes made more volatile fatty acids, the cow's main fuel. They also showed weaker methane-making functions. That pattern hints at better feed efficiency. Blood chemistry differed between high and low producers as well. The authors argue that cow performance emerges from microbe and host together. Breeding and feeding programs could use these signals.
europmc-pmc7221473:
Tang and co-authors run a randomized trial of hydroxychloroquine in hospital patients with COVID-19. Their report appeared in The BMJ. The trial enrolled 150 patients at 16 treatment centers in China. Most had mild to moderate illness that had persisted. Half received hydroxychloroquine plus standard care. The other half received standard care alone.

The main measure was whether the virus cleared within 28 days. By that point, most patients in both groups had cleared it. The authors conclude the drug showed no additional benefit for virus elimination. Adverse events and symptom paths were also tracked. The trial was open label, meaning everyone knew who got the drug. Its negative result weighed against early hopes for this repurposed medicine.
europmc-pmc7229173:
Saatci and co-authors show that blocking an enzyme called LOX can restore chemotherapy's power against triple negative breast cancer. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. This is the most aggressive breast cancer subtype, and drug resistance is a major obstacle. The team grew resistant tumors in animals and read their gene activity. A hypoxia-driven tissue remodeler, LOX, stood out.

LOX stiffens the tissue around tumors by crosslinking collagen. Blocking it loosened that scaffold and let more drug penetrate. Key adhesion signals fell, and cancer cells resumed dying under treatment. Blocking the downstream signal gave the same benefit. Tests held in both flat cell cultures and 3D models.
