The authors propose LOX as a lever against resistance. Combining its blockade with standard chemotherapy is the suggested path.
europmc-pmc7230973:
Markowiak-Kopeć and Śliżewska review how probiotics affect the gut microbiome's production of short-chain fatty acids. Their article appeared in Nutrients. Gut microbes ferment food components into these acids. The acids form the main carbon flow from diet to the microbial community. They also feed the gut lining and shape metabolism.

Diet decides which microbes thrive and what they produce. Keeping the intestinal community in balance protects against many diseases. Probiotic products add live microbes meant to restore that balance. Studies reviewed link them to better glucose and lipid control. One nine-strain blend improved cholesterol handling in mice on a high-fat diet. The authors weigh this evidence for metabolic benefits. Their review connects everyday diet choices to microbial chemistry.
europmc-pmc7258473:
Harcourt and co-authors isolate and characterize SARS-CoV-2 taken from the first confirmed COVID-19 patient in the United States. Their report appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. The patient was diagnosed in Washington state on January 20, 2020. Samples came from the patient's nose and throat swabs.

In the lab, the virus grew to high levels in two kinds of Vero cells, even without added trypsin. The team described its genome sequence, growth behavior, and which cell types it could infect. They placed virus stocks in 2 public repositories so other laboratories could obtain the same material. Open access to a shared reference virus, they note, should speed work on tests, drugs, and vaccines.
europmc-pmc7285073:
Simons, Alhanout and Duval review bacteriocins, germ-killing peptides that bacteria make to fight each other. Their review comes as drug resistance spreads and old antibiotics fail more and more. New germ killers are badly needed. Molecules that bacteria use on each other are a strong place to look.

Both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria make these peptides in their ribosomes. Each type attacks its own range of germs. Some are in use in food plants already. The team sums up how the peptides work, what they kill, and how they fare against the pathogens that matter most, above all the strains that shrug off many drugs. The long-term aim is to turn them into medicines for people.
europmc-pmc7296073:
Parker and co-authors review Alistipes, a genus of gut bacteria with puzzling links to inflammation, cancer, and mental health. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. The genus is relatively new to science, with 13 named species in standard taxonomic lists, mostly found in the human gut and clinical samples.

Evidence about these bacteria points both ways. Some studies suggest protection against liver fibrosis, colitis, cardiovascular disease, and poor response to cancer immunotherapy. Others tie Alistipes to colorectal cancer and to signs of depression. Abundance in the gut shifts when the microbial community is disturbed. The authors weigh the conflicting record and note that laboratory identification methods may undercount these species, which could distort the picture further.
europmc-pmc7319273:
Chi and co-authors find a human antibody that neutralizes SARS-CoV-2 by striking a part of the spike most researchers had overlooked. Their study appeared in Science. Antibody hunting had concentrated on the spike's receptor binding domain, the part that grabs human cells. Screening antibodies from 10 convalescent patients, the team found a potent neutralizer that binds somewhere else entirely.

Cryo-electron microscopy located its target: the N-terminal domain, at the other end of the spike's head unit. An antibody attacking there works by a different route than receptor blockers. Pairing it with receptor-binding antibodies in a therapeutic cocktail could make treatment stronger and harder for the virus to escape, since it would need to change two separate sites at once.
europmc-pmc7323373:
Huang and co-authors test the lungs of COVID-19 patients one month after discharge to see what the disease left behind. Their retrospective study appeared in Respiratory Research. Fifty-seven patients at a hospital affiliated with Sun Yat-sen University completed lung volume, breathing, diffusion, muscle strength, walking, and CT assessments at 30 days. Forty cases had been non-severe and 17 severe.

Three quarters, 75.4%, showed some abnormality on lung function tests. Diffusion capacity, the lung's ability to pass gas into the blood, was reduced in 52.6%, and 54.3% still had abnormal CT scans. Breathing muscle strength was also down in many. Severe cases had worse diffusion impairment, lower lung volumes, and shorter walking distances. Recovery, the authors show, is far from complete at one month.
europmc-pmc7360473:
Hou and co-authors examine genes that may shape who gets severe COVID-19, in BMC Medicine. Two host genes, ACE2 and TMPRSS2, control the virus's entry into cells. The team searched DNA variants in both genes across roughly 81,000 human genomes from many populations.

They found variant patterns that differ by ancestry. One ACE2 variant, found in African and African-American genomes, may alter interactions tied to heart and lung conditions. Other variants in both genes were common in some groups and rare in others. The authors present the catalogue as a starting point for explaining why risk varies so sharply between people. Lab and patient studies must test which variants truly change outcomes.
europmc-pmc7400373:
Solomou and Constantinidou survey mental health in Cyprus during the COVID-19 pandemic, in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Strict movement limits reshaped daily life on the island. Their anonymous online survey drew 1,642 adults and measured anxiety, depression, quality of life, and compliance with precautionary measures.

Nearly half reported strong financial worries, and 66.7 percent felt their quality of life had changed significantly. About 41 percent showed mild anxiety symptoms and 23.1 percent moderate to severe ones; for depression, 48 percent were mild and 9.2 percent moderate to severe. Women, younger adults, students, and the unemployed were at higher risk. Following precautions predicted lower depression but, for hygiene measures, higher anxiety. Age and sex, the title notes, matter.
europmc-pmc7409673:
Wu and co-authors review natural killer cells in cancer in Molecular Cancer. NK cells are innate immune killers that destroy target cells without prior training, and they vary widely inside tumors. Most microenvironment therapies harness T cells, with limited success, which the authors take as a cue to stop ignoring NK cells.

Tumors evolve resistance to NK killing too. Counter-strategies include supplementing cytokines, blocking suppressive molecules, and genetically engineering the cells. These approaches promise results in solid and blood cancers alike. The review summarizes NK cell basics and recent advances inside the tumor's metabolic battleground, then weighs the applications and limits of NK-based therapies in the precision medicine era.
europmc-pmc7429473:
Suk and Rousseaux review how TDP-43, a protein, goes astray in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. TDP-43 clumps in the cytoplasm of cells in nearly all ALS cases. Its gene mutations can also cause the disease.

Healthy TDP-43 lives in the cell nucleus. When it slips into the cytoplasm, cells lose its normal work and gain toxic effects. Studies link the move to faulty splicing, stress responses, DNA damage, and wide gene changes. Gene mutations raise baseline cytoplasm levels, so small shifts may start disease early. The authors argue that this wrong placement, not just clumping, is a key early event. Targeting it could lead to earlier treatment and new markers for ALS.
europmc-pmc7486773:
Damas and co-authors predict which vertebrates SARS-CoV-2 can infect by comparing their ACE2 proteins. The virus uses ACE2 to enter cells. Knowing host range can reveal bridge hosts and guard against new outbreaks.

The team joined comparative gene analysis with structural study of ACE2 across species. They found a large number of mammals that could, in theory, host the virus. Species at highest risk include wildlife and endangered animals. Those animals also face spillover from humans. That two-way risk matters for conservation and health alike. The authors urge care in reading the forecasts. Lab proof of infection is thin for most species named. The list is a guide for watch lists, not a verdict on any one animal.
europmc-pmc7492273:
Gupta and co-authors build a Gut Microbiome Health Index from species-level gut profiles. Reading health from a stool sample is a key goal of microbiome work. The index aims to flag disease likelihood without a prior diagnosis.

The formula rests on 50 microbial species tied to healthy gut systems. They came from 4347 human stool metagenomes across 34 published studies and 12 nonhealthy conditions. On the full data set, the index beat diversity scores as a steady predictor of disease. On 679 fresh samples from 9 other studies, it reached a balanced accuracy of 73.7 percent in sorting healthy from nonhealthy groups with sound results. The authors credit shared data for the find. Signatures, they say, can carry real health signal.
europmc-pmc7663773:
Giorgi and co-authors review how COVID-19 affected mental health at work. Lockdowns, distancing, lost income, and fear of illness all pressed on workers. The team searched major databases for studies tied to workplace factors.

The review drew on 35 articles. Anxiety, depression, trauma stress, and poor sleep hit health staff most, above all those on the front line. Migrant workers and staff who face the public also stood out. Job insecurity and long isolation made matters worse. The authors back fixes such as steady protective gear supply and resilience training.
europmc-pmc7724273:
Zuo and co-authors find clot-promoting autoantibodies in patients in hospital with COVID-19. Severe COVID-19 often brings abnormal clotting, in both large and small vessels. The antibodies resemble those in an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks its own fat-protein targets. That disease is known for causing dangerous clots.

The team tested serum from these patients for such antibodies and their effects. Their presence helps explain part of the odd clotting state in severe disease. It differs from the clotting failure seen in classic sepsis. The work points to immune-driven clots as a target for care. It may also guide which patients need the closest watch for clot events.
europmc-pmc7737773:
Rodrigues and co-authors present a web tool that predicts how mutations change protein stability. Missense mutations swap one amino acid for another. Such swaps can loosen a protein's fold and cause disease. Past tools mostly handled single swaps on a still structure. Dynamic tools existed but were slow and costly.

DynaMut2 blends motion analysis with graph-based marks of the local setting. It handles single and multiple swaps at once. Test scores reached a correlation of up to 0.72 for single swaps. It matched rival tools on energy and melting point shifts. The server and its API are free for studies of protein flex and disease variants.
europmc-pmc7782773:
Riggio and co-authors review the open questions around metastatic recurrence in breast cancer. Metastasis causes the most cancer deaths, yet its biology stays poorly understood. Spread often appears after long quiet periods that follow surgery or drug therapy. In breast cancer, relapse can come months to decades after first treatment.

The authors survey the main factors known to shape recurrence. They stress how much remains unknown. Dormant cells, late awakening, and organ spread all lack firm answers. Their goal is to mark the questions that matter most. Answering them, they argue, is what could cut deaths among breast cancer patients.
europmc-pmc7844173:
Kwong and co-authors measure mental health before and during COVID-19 in two UK cohorts. Both cohorts had tracked the same people for years. That design beats one-off surveys for firm claims. The team counted depression and anxiety rates. They also scored general mental well-being.

Pandemic period answers were set against each person's own past. Changes could then be tied to the crisis itself. Age, sex, and prior health all shaped the picture. Young adults drew special focus in the data. The authors stress the worth of long-run data here. Snap polls can mislead about who truly got worse. Such cohorts give policy a firmer base for mental health planning.
europmc-pmc7849173:
Onishi and co-authors review mitophagy, the process that clears worn mitochondria. Cells digest their own mitochondria through this selective route. It is conserved from yeast to humans. The process controls both quality and count of mitochondria.

Signals on the mitochondrial surface start the cleanup. Receptor proteins or ubiquitin tags mark the target. A membrane sac then wraps the mitochondrion for disposal. Mitophagy helps early development and cell change. It also damps inflammation and cell death signals. Steady turnover runs even in healthy cells, the authors note. Faults in the process link to brain decay, heart failure, cancer, and aging.
europmc-pmc7901273:
Li and co-authors report a laboratory study of the SARS-CoV-2 variant known as 501Y.V2. The variant became dominant in South Africa and spread to other countries. It carries many changes in its spike protein. The team asked two questions: does it infect cells more easily, and can it escape antibodies?

They built 18 pseudotyped viruses to test entry into different cell types. Infectivity was not higher in most cells. It rose sharply only in cells engineered to carry the mouse ACE2 receptor. Antibody tests told a different story. The variant resisted 12 of 17 neutralising monoclonal antibodies. Blood from recovered patients and immunised mice also blocked it less well. Two spike changes, E484K and N501Y, caused most of the resistance.
europmc-pmc8004673:
Soares and co-authors report a survey study of factors tied to COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy in Portugal. Tailored plans are needed to raise uptake, the authors argue. They drew on a community survey that ran from September 2020 to January 2021. It tracked plans to take the vaccine, health state, and views of risk. Regression methods sorted which traits went with delay or refusal.

Hesitancy in Portugal was high: 56% would wait, and 9% would refuse. Younger age and income lost in the pandemic went with both stances. So did skipping the flu vaccine and low trust in the COVID-19 vaccine. Doubts about the health service response and mixed public messages also counted. Answers given before safety results came out were more hesitant. The authors urge clear talk that builds trust in the vaccine's safety and power.
europmc-pmc8038573:
Lopes-Coelho and co-authors ask why anti-angiogenic therapy so often falls short against cancer. The strategy, proposed in 1971, starves tumors by blocking new blood vessels. Most approved agents target VEGF, the main driver of vessel growth. These drugs can also lift VEGF's brake on the immune system. Still, in most cases they prove insufficient alone.

The review digs into the molecular machinery of vessel growth and drug failure. Tumors find alternative routes to build their blood supply. The authors propose reviving old drugs that hit those backup mechanisms. Many such drugs act on the tumor microenvironment instead. Combined targeting of several effectors may finally crack resistance. The review maps candidate partners for VEGF drugs. It closes with the trial evidence such combinations still need.
europmc-pmc8100173:
Wu and co-authors profile advanced lung cancer one cell at a time. They ran single-cell RNA sequencing on 42 biopsy samples. All came from patients with stage III or IV non-small cell lung cancer. Bulk sequencing averages every cell in a tumor together. Single-cell work keeps each voice separate. The atlas that results spans cancer cells and their whole neighborhood.

Rare cell types surfaced that earlier studies had missed. Follicular dendritic cells and T helper 17 cells joined the census. Tumors differed hugely from patient to patient. Cell mix, chromosome breaks, growth paths, and cell-to-cell signals all varied. One pattern stood out for follow-up work. Tumor traits tracked with tumor-linked neutrophils in the samples. Their role in this cancer is still murky. Such maps guide more personal treatment choices. They also flag where immune drugs may fail.
europmc-pmc8113373:
Verduci and co-authors review circular RNAs, looped molecules that may serve as disease markers. Most RNA strands have loose ends that enzymes chew. A circular RNA seals into a covalent ring instead. That ring resists decay, so the molecules last. They also appear in tight tissue-specific patterns. Their best-known trick is sponging up microRNAs. Binding proteins and encoding tiny proteins add newer roles.

Disease links now span much of the body. Head and neck, breast, and lung cancers all show altered circles. Diabetes, heart disease, and brain degeneration join the list. The review sorts signal from noise in a noisy field. Claims conflict, and the authors say so plainly. Networks of circles, other RNAs, and binding proteins may set cell balance. Stability plus tissue specificity makes a marker's dream profile. Blood tests built on circles are the goal. Proof in patients is the next hurdle.
europmc-pmc8422873:
Pingali and co-authors report vaccine coverage for United States adolescents aged 13 to 17 years in 2020. Health advisors urge routine shots at age 11 to 12 years. These include Tdap, meningococcal, and HPV vaccines, plus catch-up shots for those behind.

The report draws on a national survey of 20,163 adolescents. HPV vaccine coverage with at least one dose rose from 2019 to 2020. The share fully up to date on HPV also rose. Tdap and meningococcal coverage held close to the prior year. Results are broken out by nation, region, state, and select local areas. The data guide efforts to close coverage gaps.
europmc-pmc8578673:
Li and co-authors review exosomal non-coding RNAs in human health and disease. Exosomes are tiny packets that cells use to talk to each other. Their cargo of small RNAs helps keep body systems in balance. When that cargo shifts, tissues can fail and disease can follow.

The review covers three RNA classes: microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs. It treats cancers and metabolic diseases in depth. Brain, heart, autoimmune, and infectious diseases follow. For each, the authors weigh use as a biomarker. Therapy ideas built on these RNAs are also in view. The piece aims to map a fast field in full.
europmc-pmc8590973:
Haleem and co-authors survey telemedicine for health care, with its tools, limits, and uses. Remote visits can cut travel cost and time for patients and clinics. They grew in value during the COVID-19 pandemic, when in-person contact carried risk. The authors set out what these services can and cannot do.

The review lists traits of remote care and the steps in a remote visit. It names seventeen uses, from follow-up checks to care after a hospital stay. Health apps can help patients keep visits and share their history. The authors also note blocks to wider use, such as access and workflow fit. Readers get a clear guide to where remote care helps most.
europmc-pmc8686573:
Dempster and co-authors introduce Chronos, a model that sharpens gene fitness estimates from CRISPR screens. These screens knock out genes to see which ones cells need. Their results carry biases that can mislead. Chronos models how cell numbers change after each knockout over time.

The team tested it on two large cancer screen datasets. They also used a screen with data across time points. Chronos beat rival methods at separating control genes. Its links to known biomarkers were stronger too. It showed the least bias from copy number and screen quality. The tool is shared as open code for other labs.
europmc-pmc8732273:
Swadling and co-authors show that pre-existing T cells can expand and clear SARS-CoV-2 before antibodies appear. Some exposed people never test positive by PCR or blood antibody tests. The team tracked health workers who were watched closely and stayed negative on all tests. Their T cells were compared with cells from unexposed people.

The exposed workers held stronger, broader memory T cells. Their cells targeted the virus's replication machinery more than its outer proteins. The strongest responders showed an early innate signal that hints at a brief, aborted infection. A viral polymerase was the largest target region. The work suggests cross-reactive T cells can abort infection early.
europmc-pmc8761573:
Kohli, Pillarisetty, and Kim review the key chemokines that direct immune cell migration in solid tumors. Chemokines are signal proteins that guide cells along gradients. Faulty chemokine signals help tumors grow and shut out killer cells. They also draw in cells that suppress immune attack.

The review covers the best-studied chemokine receptors in cancer. It sorts their roles for helpful and harmful immune cells. Animal studies that map each receptor's effect are reviewed. Human and animal trials that block these signals get a look as well. Such drugs are tested alone and with other therapies. The field aims to open tumors to immune attack.
europmc-pmc8879473:
Liu, Chen, and Zhang review liposomes as drug carriers, from approved products to what comes next. Liposomes are tiny fat bubbles that wrap a drug inside. They can target a site and release their load slowly. They also shield drugs from breakdown and clearance. Several liposomal products already serve in clinics. The review builds on those approvals.

The authors list products cleared by US and European regulators. They extract the chemistry behind each approval. Lipid ingredients and manufacturing methods are compared. Drug loading techniques and size control get close attention. Quality attributes that regulators check are spelled out. Current guidance from both agencies is summarized. The authors close with future prospects. The piece is a practical map for developers. It links bench work to plant-scale production.
europmc-pmc9388373:
Isidro and co-authors reconstruct the genomes behind the 2022 multi-country monkeypox outbreak. Shotgun metagenomics gave the first full sequences fast. The virus belongs to clade 3, the former West African grouping. All outbreak strains cluster tightly, pointing to a single origin.

Yet the branch sits apart from the 2018-2019 travel-linked cases. The gap suggests steady, faster-than-expected evolution. Mutation patterns carry the fingerprints of host APOBEC3 enzymes. Signs of ongoing adaptation to humans appear in the changes. Over 2,500 cases had been confirmed by mid-June 2022. The authors say sequencing can track spread even for this slow-changing DNA virus. That gives health teams a map while case links stay unclear.
europmc-pmc9581773:
Förderer and co-authors reveal the structure of a wheat resistosome, an immune receptor complex in plants. Plant NLR receptors spot pathogen effectors inside cells. In Arabidopsis, one such receptor forms a resistosome that acts as a calcium channel. Whether that design is shared across plant receptors was unknown.

The team used cryo-electron microscopy on the wheat receptor Sr35. It was caught in complex with the stem rust effector AvrSr35. The effector binds the receptor's leucine-rich repeats directly. Five units then join into a pentameric resistosome. Its shape closely matches the Arabidopsis ZAR1 complex. Tests showed the complex works as a non-selective cation channel. Shared motifs in the two receptors point to an old design. The team used the shape to retool kin receptors in wheat and barley. The new variants learned to spot AvrSr35 as well.
frus-1861-d173:
Carl Schurz sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 August 1861. It is document 173 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By August, word of the Union defeat had reached Spain. Schurz had to face a court that now doubted Union strength. His report shows a young envoy learning to hold his ground with words when the news ran against him. A young envoy's growth, traced week by week, is one of this file's quiet pleasures. Growth of that kind, seen in real time, is a rare gift of a full record.
frus-1861-d273:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Mr. Brown, dated 17 July 1861. Congress received it as Document 273 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d73:
Frederick W. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 27 August 1861. The younger Seward served as Assistant Secretary of State under his father. The letter is document 73 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

When the Secretary was away or pressed, his son kept the London line open. The note shows the office working as a family shop in a crisis. It also spared Adams any gap in direction from Washington at a tense time. Frederick Seward later wrote the great memoir of his father's years in office. The son's hand kept the father's line unbroken through a crowded autumn.
frus-1862-d173:
On 17 October 1862 Charles Francis Adams sent a report from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 173 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams had held the London post since the spring of 1861.

The son and grandson of presidents, Adams kept a cool style in his official mail even when stakes were high. His reports mixed meeting notes with shrewd reads of British politics. A letter from this date belongs to the weeks when the British cabinet was quietly deciding against stepping into the war. That was the outcome Adams most wanted. The legation's clerks copied each dispatch into bound letter books before the mail sailed.
frus-1862-d273:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 5 May 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 273 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The same day, far away, Mexico's army won at Puebla.

The coincidence of dates is a reminder of how slowly news moved. Seward wrote in ignorance of the battle that would stall France in Mexico for a year. His letter belongs to the Washington-Paris routine of orders and arguments about the war. Read in sequence, such letters show policy being made on partial knowledge, then corrected by the next mail.
frus-1862-d373:
On 13 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to Viscount Treilhard, in a letter printed as Document 373 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The reply followed Treilhard's letter by a single day.

Prompt written answers were the State Department's way of keeping small matters small. In August 1862 that discipline mattered, because any dispute with a foreign representative could feed the larger debate over intervention. The Seward-Treilhard exchange, preserved in quick alternation, shows the method applied steadily through a tense month. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d473:
James E. Harvey, the American minister in Lisbon, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 July 1862. It is Document 473 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Portuguese file.

Portugal was a small power with Atlantic islands and ports that mattered to wartime shipping, and its neutrality had to be exact. Harvey, a Pennsylvania editor turned diplomat, held the Lisbon post through the war. Seward's orders to such outposts dealt in the practical law of neutrality: what belligerent ships could take on, and how long they could stay. The dispatch begins the Portuguese correspondence, a minor file with real stakes for the blockade at sea.
frus-1862-d573:
James Watson Webb in Brazil received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 December 1861. It is Document 573 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

December 1861 was the month of the Trent crisis. Seward's orders to distant posts had to assume their readers knew little of the latest turn. Brazil, an empire with Atlantic ports on the routes to the Pacific, had neutrality duties to define toward belligerent cruisers and prizes. Webb needed Washington's rules in writing. The instruction shows the Department reaching to the far end of its network. A letter there might take two months to arrive. It still had to govern conduct when it did.
frus-1862-d673:
Anson Burlingame wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 March 1862. He was the American minister to China, writing in the second year of the Civil War. The letter is document 673 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

By the spring of 1862 Burlingame had found his feet in the post. His mail reported on the treaty ports, the Qing court's straits, and the acts of the other foreign powers in China. Letters like this one were the State Department's eyes in East Asia. Kept in the printed volume, they still show how much of American policy rested on one envoy's word.
frus-1862-d73:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 29 May 1862. Congress received it as Document 73 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d173:
On 25 April 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 173 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to Seward's first sheet of the day held the next point in line for the British brief. Pairs like this one let Adams take each matter to the foreign office in its own words and time. This letter closes the 25 April pair. It is a near-end piece of the run in this slice of the volume, which closes days later with an Adams report.
frus-1863p1-d273:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 27 August 1863. It is document 273 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d373:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 28 January 1863. It appears as document 373 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d473:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 22 April 1863 letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d573:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 18 June 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d673:
A dispatch dated 23 November 1863 went from Secretary William H. Seward to the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d73:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 73 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams wrote on the eve of a set piece in British public life: the opening of Parliament, set for the next day. His mail that week watched for what the Queen's speech and the houses would say of the war. Reports like this one told Washington how the land lay at the top of British power. It is a short step in the file from this letter to the famous one that follows it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d173: A draft message from the President to Secretary Hull, dated October 30, 1943, is preserved as Document 173 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Drafts earn their place in the official record because they show what was considered, and sometimes changed, before sending. Whether this one went as written, the record here does not say. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the Moscow closing papers, in the section the editors built for them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d273: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers two separate calls on President Roosevelt at Cairo during the forenoon of 26 November 1943. One call was by Admiral Mountbatten, and one by Madame Chiang Kai-shek. The calls are recorded in the President's Log, but no memoranda of either conversation appear to have been made. Elliott Roosevelt's account mentions both calls in passing. The editors presume the main subject of each was Chiang Kai-shek's attitude toward the proposed operations in the China-Burma-India theater.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d373:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the plenary session at Tehran on 30 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, the session at which the Overlord decision was announced to Stalin. Roosevelt opens by expressing his happiness at the decision reached that morning by the British and American staffs.

Brooke reports the agreement: Overlord will be launched during May 1944, with a supporting operation in southern France on as large a scale as landing craft allow. Stalin answers with the pledge he had already given the two leaders privately. Simultaneously with Overlord, the Red Army will launch large offensives at several points to pin German forces down and stop any transfer of troops westward. Roosevelt adds that the Overlord commander will be named within three or four days, and the Western staffs will return to Cairo the next day to work out the details.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d473:
Another message from President Roosevelt went to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 3, 1943, the day before the Second Cairo Conference opened. Roosevelt had finished at Tehran and was preparing to meet Churchill, and Turkey's President İnönü, at Cairo. The State Department kept the message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Two presidential cables to Hull in a single day suggest how much unfinished business followed Roosevelt out of Tehran. Hull, in Washington, was the fixed point of American diplomacy while the President traveled. For the reader, this second message underlines the working partnership between the two men at a peak moment of the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d573:
Patrick J. Hurley, now ambassador to China, wrote to Secretary of State James F. Byrnes on August 11, 1945. Hurley had gone from the President's personal representative in Iran to the hardest embassy in Asia. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

August 11 fell in the war's last days: atomic bombs had fallen, the Soviet Union had entered the Pacific war, and Japan's surrender was days away. Hurley's China was sliding toward civil war even as the world war ended. For readers, his report connects the volume's long China thread, opened at Cairo in 1943, to the moment everything changed in Asia.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d73: Hull wrote to Roosevelt on October 29, 1943, on the last day of the Moscow Conference. His letter is Document 73 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The secretary's Moscow reports were the high point of his long tenure, and this one belongs to the conference's close. The record supplies the date and the two men and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series for its own telling.
frus-1944-quebec-d173:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff opened their Quebec meetings at noon on September 12, 1944, with Sir Alan Brooke in the chair at Admiral Leahy's invitation. Early business was procedural: personnel shipping after Germany's defeat would be studied, and the conference program was approved. The chiefs then took up Eisenhower's appreciation, Scaf 78.

Brooke argued Eisenhower had understressed two points: opening Antwerp and Rotterdam, and a strong attack on the northern flank. He proposed an airborne operation to seize the Schelde islands guarding Antwerp. Marshall countered that German forces massed there, on coverless ground, made bombing more profitable than airborne troops. A draft reply approving Eisenhower's proposals, with the northern emphasis added, was presented for discussion.
frus-1944-quebec-d273:
Redeployment after the European war is the subject of C.C.S. 679, dated September 14, 1944. The United States Chiefs judged the whole problem, including repatriation, too large for the conference to settle. It needed combined study to assure the optimum use of personnel and cargo shipping, and to get forces against Japan to their theater at the earliest date.

They recommended the Combined Administrative Committee study and report on the problem, working with the transportation committee, the shipping authorities, and the staff planners. Questions needing earlier decision would go to the Combined Chiefs. The paper was approved the next day with Brooke's amendment adding the Combined Shipping Authorities to the list of collaborators.
frus-1944-quebec-d73:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on August 28, 1944. His letter sits among the papers gathered for the Quebec Conference. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. Hull led the department that handled the alliance's daily diplomacy.

Letters from Hull to Roosevelt carried the department's view to the top. Two weeks later, the President would meet Churchill in Quebec City. The conference faced Germany's coming defeat and the Pacific war. For readers, the letter shows the State Department stating its position in writing. It did so before the leaders settled questions in person.
frus-1945-50-intel-d173:
A memorandum dated 30 October 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy) and the Assistant Secretary of State for Administration (Russell). The reader was Secretary of State Byrnes. It is document 173 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d273:
On 11 May 1948, Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter sent a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). It stands as document 273 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d373:
The Director of the Executive Secretariat (Humelsine) addressed a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Webb) on 8 March 1949. Readers meet it as document 373 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d73:
The Department of State sent a telegram to the American embassy in London on 12 September 1945. Department telegrams speak in the secretary's name to posts abroad. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A telegram to London in September 1945 belongs to the weeks when embassies were being told how the wartime secret work would change. London was the greatest of the wartime intelligence stations, so word sent there mattered. Readers can place this telegram at the head of the volume's file on the State Department's own intelligence service. It shows the department addressing its posts as it prepared to take in the analysts the president's order was about to give it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d173:
One item survives in this excerpt from the Secretary of State's daily briefing for the President, dated 1 December 1944. The memorandum, “Special Information for the President,” gathers the notable foreign developments of the past few days. The excerpt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The item concerns Yugoslavia and the agreement lately drawn up between Marshal Tito and Premier Subasic, head of the exile government. Brigadier MacLean has told Ambassador Kirk the expected British course. Churchill will press King Peter to accept the agreement. Once it takes effect, Britain will send an ambassador to Belgrade. The short note marks how far Tito's partisans had come toward open allied backing.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d273:
George Kennan cabled from Moscow on 27 November 1944 about American and Soviet prisoners. His report, number 4526, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Note the year: the catalog's earlier summary misdated this cable to 1945. Kennan was chargé in Moscow in Harriman's absence.

At General Deane's request, Kennan had written to Molotov on 6 November about two-way arrangements for prisoners of war. Soviet armies had already overrun one camp known to have held Americans, and were closing on another near Budapest. Molotov's answer of 25 November is quoted in paraphrase. Moscow's first concern is help and homecoming for Soviet prisoners and for citizens deported by the Germans, now freed in the west. In principle, the Soviet government accepts Harriman's proposals of August.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d373:
Bohlen's minutes of February 7, 1945, list four subjects before the plenary: dismemberment, Poland, the world security body, and a French zone. Roosevelt began with Poland. He stressed that he cared less about tracing frontier lines than about the Polish government. He attached no importance, he said, to the continuity or legality of any Polish government.

In truth, he added, there had been no real Polish government for some years. Before going further, he called on Molotov to report the foreign ministers' meeting. The minutes show the President clearing the agenda with a blunt judgment that shocked some Poles for decades after.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d473:
Denmark opens this digest cable from Acting Secretary Grew to Stettinius, written February 2, 1945, while the Secretary was traveling. Washington's lukewarm stand on a three-power statement recognizing the Danes as allies, plus likely Soviet refusal, might send the matter to the Big Three. Meanwhile America was sending its own secret message to the Danish Freedom Council.

The message praised the Danish resistance movement's contributions to the common cause. Further items follow, including a report from Kennan in Moscow: the British chargé had expressed hope to Molotov about arrangements under study. Grew's daily excerpts kept the traveling Secretary briefed on a dozen fronts at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d73:
Six questions left unsettled at Dumbarton Oaks are listed for President Roosevelt in this 15 November 1944 paper. Acting Secretary Stettinius sent it ahead of a meeting at the White House. The memo is one of a set prepared that day and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The six items start with voting in the Security Council and who the first members would be. They go on to the seat of the new body and to trusteeship plans. The court statute and the ending of the League of Nations complete the list. Advice is attached on the first four. On the court, legal experts would draft the statute before the founding talks opened.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d173:
The British Embassy passed on a Foreign Office proposal about population transfers in an extract dated June 28, 1945. The extract is document 173 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message from London, dated June 22, appears later in the volume.

London thinks a full exchange of views with the Americans on transfers of ethnic minority groups in Europe would be valuable. Such talks might lead on to a three-power discussion at the coming Big Three meeting. The embassy is told to sound the State Department on the proposal and report its reaction. Behind the dry wording stood one of the era's harshest subjects: the planned uprooting of millions of ethnic Germans and others from their homes in Eastern Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d273:
A briefing paper argued that Austria should pay no reparations, in a paper dated July 4, 1945. The paper is document 273 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It proposes that the three powers agree on the question before the conference.

The United States opposes exacting reparations from Austria despite her part in the German war effort, the paper says. Such a demand would be economically unrealistic and politically dangerous in Central Europe. It would clash with the Moscow Declaration, which implied creating conditions favorable to Austrian independence. It might turn Austrians against the West and drive Austria back into Germany's arms. Austria's own capacity is doubted. Her World War I obligations were mostly cancelled by 1923. And the country, short of food, will need relief and aid. That aid would make America in effect pay Austria's reparations for her.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d373:
France's lesser request on reparations reached Harriman in a Washington cable of July 11, 1945. The French Embassy's aide-mémoire of June 25 accepted, for now, that France had no seat on the Reparations Commission in Moscow. It asked instead that the chief of the American delegation be told to keep the French ambassador in Moscow closely informed of the Commission's work.

Paris had sent like notes to the British and Soviet governments. Grew instructs Harriman to sound out the proper authorities informally and report their reaction. If asked, he may say Washington is most sympathetic to the French. The cable shows France settling, for the moment, for news instead of a vote.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d473:
Keeping American forces in Italy is urged in a briefing book memorandum for the President dated July 2, 1945. An attached telegram from Caserta indicates what Churchill will do. He will take up at the meeting, it says, the desirability of leaving substantial American forces in Italy. He will raise the same point for Europe as a whole, until major problems are settled. Military needs of redeployment must come first, the memo concedes.

Politically, though, it is most important to keep the Allied character of the forces remaining in Europe, through at least token American participation. Total withdrawal, it warns, would inevitably be read as a sign that the United States is relinquishing direct influence on future settlements. Even limited American numbers inspire confidence.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d573:
Ambassador Kirk reported a firm word from Field Marshal Alexander in an extract sent from Caserta late on June 26, 1945. It is document 573 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The subject was the Yugoslav reservation on article 3 of the Belgrade agreement.

Kirk says he asked Alexander for his view, and Alexander agreed the Allies must stand fast on that point. Alexander added a direct pledge in his own words. The Belgrade agreement, he said, gives him final say on civil rule in the Allied area. He would see to it that the reading of the deal matched the Allied view. The short extract is meant to calm fears in Washington that the commander might give ground.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d673:
Ambassador Winant passed on a British official's doubts about reopening the Tangier talks on July 11, 1945. His secret wire is document 673 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The official was Hoyer Millar of the Foreign Office.

Millar said he did not see how the talks could open unless the Russians were brought in. Yet bringing them in raised at once a harder question. How far would Russia share in any plan for the zone's future administration? That point had to be decided first, and it could not be decided on the minute. Millar's best course was to take the matter up at the Big Three meeting. No start on Tangier should be thought of until after that meeting ended.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d73:
Ambassador John Winant reported from London on June 16, 1945, on the fuss over Attlee's role at the coming conference. His telegram to the Acting Secretary of State is document 73 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. It lays out, step by step, how Churchill's invitation to the Labour leader drew a sharp public statement from party chairman Harold Laski.

Laski had insisted Attlee could attend only as an observer, since Labour could not be bound by deals it had not debated. Winant then quotes the letters Churchill and Attlee exchanged to settle the matter: the government would bear responsibility for decisions, but Attlee would come as a friend and adviser. The report shows election politics shaping Britain's team before Potsdam even opened.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1073: Soviet delegates presented this proposal on liberated Europe to the foreign ministers on July 20, 1945. Only a short extract is printed here. Its other portions appear as separate documents elsewhere in the volume, including the fuller Greece text printed just before this one. The extract charges that the present Greek government is breaking the peace with its neighbors. It threatens Albania and Bulgaria with military action, the paper says. All these circumstances, the Soviets conclude, create the need for urgent measures to end such a situation in Greece.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1173:
Generalissimo Stalin wrote to President Truman on 29 July 1945, nine days after Truman's note to him. The Soviet leader's reply kept the top-level exchange alive as the summit entered its last week. Direct word between these two men was rare and heavy.

Each side read such a message for tone as much as content. A phrase could signal room to deal or a line held firm. This note is Moscow's voice at the very top, set down while the final terms were still fluid. It belongs to the small set of leader-to-leader papers that framed everything the staffs did below.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1273:
The President wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 1 August 1945. The cable went out on the summit's last full day. Truman's word to his China envoy joined the German endgame to the Asian war in one channel.

Hurley's mission needed the president's backing at that hour. China's government was weakening, Japan's defeat was near, and the shape of Asia hung on choices being made in both capitals. A note from the top set the envoy's line for the weeks ahead. This message shows the president closing his Potsdam work with an eye already on the next crisis.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1373:
The United States delegation tabled a formal proposal at Potsdam on 25 July 1945. Unlike a working paper, a proposal was meant for the other delegations to read and answer. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

American proposals show what Washington chose to ask for in the open, in words the British and Soviets could accept or refuse. This one came late in the conference, when the end of the talks was in sight and each side pressed its last claims. Readers can weigh it against the final protocol to see the result of that press. The paper is a fixed point in the bargaining, useful for anyone mapping how the summit closed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-73:
A United States delegation memorandum sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 23, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Four heads of business are reported from the Monday morning session.

Reparations discussion was postponed so the economic subcommittee could study two new Soviet papers. On German economic principles, the Soviet side objected to paragraph 18 of the draft. Each zone, it argued, should as far as practicable draw supplies from the German areas it had drawn on before the war. That question went up to the heads of government. So did a new Soviet paragraph 19, on the priority between reparations and exports to pay for imports. On the Council of Foreign Ministers, by contrast, the revised text won final approval. Trusteeship business was settled by referral: the Italian colonies would be discussed by the new council.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d773:
Field Marshal Alexander, Supreme Allied Commander in the Mediterranean, wrote to the Combined Chiefs of Staff on July 18, 1945. Document 773 brings a theater commander's voice into the Potsdam record. Alexander's command covered Italy and the middle sea. His message reached the joint chiefs as the conference opened.

A theater commander's letter carries the weight of forces in place. Alexander spoke for armies and fleets still in the field. Readers see how field needs reached the summit's military advisers. The document links Potsdam to the war's remaining fronts. Decisions in Germany echoed in commands hundreds of miles away, and this letter is one echo in writing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d873: Soviet delegates offered this revised draft of Article 19 at Potsdam on July 23, 1945, apparently their second draft that day. It repeats that Germans must be left enough to subsist after reparations. It also provides means to pay for imports approved by the Control Council. The change is priority: exports sold to pay for those imports would rank ahead of reparations and home consumption.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d973:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov on August 1, 1945, about art objects held in the American zone. An identical letter went to Britain's Ernest Bevin the same day. Byrnes sorts the works into three classes, from loot seized from public and private owners to property that was truly German.

Orders have gone out, he reports, to return the first two classes to their countries of origin as fast as arrangements allow. For the second class, receipts will record what the Germans claim to have paid. The third class will be shipped to the United States for care and safekeeping. Its final fate awaits future decisions.
frus-1961-63v11-d173: An editorial note in the Cuba volume records a back-channel offer of November 12, 1962. At a Bolshoi Ballet reception, Robert Kennedy told Ambassador Dobrynin the terms by word of mouth. If Moscow ordered the IL-28 bombers out at once and finished within 30 days, Washington would lift the quarantine right away. The note prints both the American typed record and Moscow's version. The Soviet text adds that the timing need not be public. Khrushchev's word alone would serve.
gao-gaoreports-b-295973:
AHNTECH protested the loss of an Army range job in Iraq in GAO decision B-295973, dated May 11, 2005. The job was to run and keep up the Butler Range Complex. The award went to MPRI. The Army rated the firm's work plan as a no-go. Staffing was the core flaw.

GAO denied the protest. The plan leaned on hiring the old crew. The firm showed no proof those staff would join. It also gave no backup hiring plan. GAO found the Army's notes backed its marks. The firm gave no strong reply. The case shows why a staffing plan needs proof, not hope.
gao-gaoreports-b-298573:
Joint Systems, Inc. protested an Army purchase order for 2,550 thumbdrives. The order went to Global Channel Solutions, Inc. The Army's Technology Applications Office ran the buy. GAO decided B-298573 on October 6, 2006.

The request for quotations set a clear proof step. Vendors had to send an image of a drive with a write-protect switch. That image showed the drive met the switch rule. Joint Systems sent no such image. Its claim of a fit, cheaper product did not cure the gap. The agency could fairly reject the quotation as unfit. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299873:
General Dynamics Information Technology protested a Navy award to Raytheon Technical Services Company. The contract covers warfighter field operations customer support services. The work spans training sites at more than 500 sites worldwide. GAO ruled in B-299873 on September 19, 2007.

The flaw lay in the cost math. The terms set a clear rule for clashing rates. The agency had to use the higher rate in each clash. It failed to do so for the winner's bid. That slip shrank the winner's judged price. The pick thus rested on a false cost gap. A source selection built on wrong sums cannot stand. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-308773:
How to count a stopgap budget rate for the Capitol Police is set in this GAO decision, B-308773, dated January 11, 2007. The force ran under the 2007 Continuing Resolution. The rate turns on its fiscal year 2006 General Expenses fund. The force asked which sums count in that base.

GAO drew a careful line. A sum of $4,513,671 moved inside the fund counts in the base. A sum of $5,486,329 moved in from the Salaries fund does not count. Spare no-year and multi-year sums held at year end do not count either. The ruling shows how the math of a stopgap rate works.
gao-gaoreports-b-311273:
Professional Performance Development Group, Inc. lost its protest. That ruling is B-311273, dated June 2, 2008. The Health Department sought work health and clinic services. The bid of this firm was cut from the lead pack. The file shows a bid full of gaps in facts. Key parts of the plan were thin or mute. The firm fought the tech score that drove the cut.

GAO denied the protest. The unfit mark was fair on this file. Talks were not apt to lift the bid to a real shot at the win. A bid with gaps this wide can be cut at the gate. Talk time is not owed to a bid with no fair chance.
gao-gaoreports-b-400173:
Colliers International protested an Army move to buy housing study services under an existing task order contract in Korea. GAO ruled in B-400173 on July 3, 2008. The work would test the U.S. Army Garrison Humphreys Housing Alternative Plan Concept. It sat under a broad program contract tied to the move of U.S. forces from Seoul to Camp Humphreys.

Colliers argued the services fell outside the scope of that contract. GAO found the study fit well within the wide program support work the contract set out. The protest was denied. Readers can see how GAO tests scope claims against the plain terms of the base contract.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-273:
Defense Acquisitions, GAO-05-273 of March 15, 2005, urges the Air Force to rethink a spy plane plan before the build starts. The E-10A would carry many sensors to watch a war zone and guide strikes from the sky. The bill runs to many billions of dollars. The tech is hard and new. A House panel asked GAO to test the plan's base.

GAO weighs how sound the business case for the plane is. It weighs the risks in the buy path as drawn. Shifts in that path are needed first, the title holds. Once the build starts, late shifts cost far more.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-373:
Natural Resources, GAO-05-373 of May 13, 2005, asks if the brush cleared to curb wild fires could earn its keep. Land crews thin woods and range to starve big blazes. The cut leaves piles of small trees, limbs, and brush, called woody biomass. Most of it has no buyer now. It rots or is burned in the open at cost.

GAO lists which federal arms push to find uses for the stuff, from fuel to goods. It tells how they team on the push. It names the blocks the arms see, such as haul cost and thin markets. It checks what steps they take to clear those blocks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-673:
Courthouse building costs outrun estimates in GAO report GAO-05-673 (June 30, 2005). Congress gave about $4.5 billion from fiscal 1993 to 2005 for 78 projects. Final costs beat design-stage estimates by 17 percent on average, and build-stage estimates by 5 percent. The building agency often failed to flag or explain changes between funding rounds. Seven deep looks blame scope growth, much of it from security rules, and late starts, which let inflation bite.

Site troubles and slow funding caused the delays. Cost cutters that helped include value engineering during design and early talks with tenant courts. GAO wants changes reported plainly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-773:
New TRICARE contracts and regions are reviewed in GAO-05-773, a report dated July 27, 2005. TRICARE is the Defense Department's health program. It pairs military clinics with civilian networks run by firms. Big contract and region changes took effect in 2004. Congress told GAO to report on how the rollout went. GAO also covered the new tools used to grade firms and regions.

GAO found a range of rollout problems. They raised costs and strained daily work. Yet the impact on care given to patients was small. Call volume spiked past what firms expected, and hold times grew. Computer flaws added strain. The costliest gap was a referral system, in the works since 2001, that was not ready. GAO made recommendations on the fixes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-873:
Medicare claims contracting reform is graded in GAO-05-873, a report from August 17, 2005. A 2003 law forced open competition for claims work. The work must move to new contractors by October 2011. The health secretary sent Congress a plan for the shift. The law told GAO to judge that plan. GAO tested its framework and its cost and savings math.

GAO found the plan sound in some key areas and thin in others. It lacks a detailed schedule that aligns the shift with other big changes planned at once. Risks in moving claims work are not fully spelled out. Up to nine workload pieces will merge into the first new contractor. The agency sped the shift to 2009, leaving little room to fix problems. Its $666 million cost estimate rests on doubtful assumptions, GAO said, and its savings claims are too uncertain for decisions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-273:
State revenue at stake in the Internet access tax ban is measured in GAO-06-273, dated January 23, 2006. By the end of 2004, some 70 million U.S. adults went online on a typical day. In 1998 Congress froze new state and local taxes on Internet access. Older taxes in some states were allowed to stay. When Congress renewed the ban in 2004, it told GAO to study the revenue effect. GAO read the law's text and history, weighed past studies, and dug into eight case study states.

The impact will vary by state, as the title says. States with older access taxes on the books stand to lose the most if the ban widens. States that never taxed access lose little or nothing. The report gives Congress a state-by-state sense of the stakes. It avoids a single national figure that would hide more than it shows.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-473:
A missile shield built in haste still needs plans to run it and clear cost figures. In GAO-06-473 (May 31, 2006), GAO reviews ballistic missile defense management. The Defense Department has spent about $91 billion since the mid-1980s on the capability. In 2002 the President directed that an initial set of defenses be in place in 2004. The system keeps changing as it is built.

GAO judged progress in planning to operate the system. It checked whether the Future Years Defense Program gives full, clear cost data. Action is needed on both fronts, GAO said. Readers get planning gaps and cost visibility problems in one study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-73:
Charter schools in the District of Columbia are examined in GAO-06-73, a report GAO released on November 17, 2005. The District had a larger share of students in charter schools than any state. Two boards shared oversight duty. The Board of Education ran an Office of Charter Schools, and an independent Public Charter School Board also authorized schools. Congress required GAO to study how the two authorizers worked.

GAO found that the boards differed in revenue and in their use of city services. Yet they spent their funds on similar oversight work. Both gave schools technical aid and gathered academic and financial data. The depth of oversight differed between them, though. GAO also found a wide range of practices when schools closed, and urged a steadier process to ease student transitions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-973:
Ways to fund the Federal Aviation Administration are set out in GAO report GAO-06-973, dated September 29, 2006. The agency lives mainly off a trust fund fed by taxes on airspace users. That fund's free balance fell by more than 70 percent from fiscal year 2001 to fiscal year 2005.

With renewal due at the end of fiscal year 2007, GAO weighed pros and cons of the current tax path. It asked what proof backs the concerns raised. It set out effects of other funding choices. It also weighed debt funding for big projects. The report is a menu, with trade-offs spelled out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-273:
A risky contract type that pays by the hour has quietly doubled at the Pentagon. GAO dug into the trend in GAO-07-273, a report dated June 29, 2007. Time-and-materials deals pay set hourly rates plus costs. Rules say to use them only when nothing else fits. GAO reviewed 82 such contracts and orders. It compared prime and subcontract labor rates on 12 more.

Reported spending rose from almost $5 billion in fiscal year 1996 to about $10 billion in 2005, GAO found. The true sum is higher. Orders on federal schedules went uncounted for years. Over 75 percent of the money sits in three service areas. Files often lacked any written case for the contract type. Little effort went into switching repeat work to fixed prices. Oversight of the work itself was uneven. On one $17 million Army logistics deal, reviewers never checked invoices. GAO urged stronger written justifications.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-373:
Help for struggling nursing homes went mostly to homes already doing better. GAO evaluated the assistance program in GAO-07-373, a report dated May 29, 2007. The Medicare agency paid quality groups $117 million over 3 years from 2002. The groups coach homes on problems like pressure ulcers. Participation was voluntary. GAO surveyed all 51 quality groups. It visited homes and groups in five states.

More homes volunteered than expected, GAO found. The groups picked homes that seemed committed to improve. Guidance told them to skip homes with many violations. Only 2 percent of groups ranked violation counts among their top selection factors. Eight groups shut such homes out entirely. Chosen homes had cleaner inspection records than their peers. The Medicare agency now requires each group to coach up to three poor performers. GAO urged aiming more help at the worst homes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-573:
Applying for food stamps no longer means a trip to the welfare office, and GAO-07-573, dated May 3, 2007, checks the new routes. One in 12 Americans takes part in the Food Stamp Program. States now let people apply or renew by mail, phone center, or web site. GAO asked what methods states use and what proof exists that they work.

All states use mail, and about half run or are building web services and call centers. Five states got deep reviews. States said the new routes ease access, above all for workers and rural homes. They also took steps to guard against fraud without office visits. But hard data on results is thin. No one had sorted out which methods lift access, keep rulings right, or cut costs best. GAO urged the Food and Nutrition Service to study the methods in a planned way and share what works.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-673:
Tax season 2007 gets an interim grade in GAO-07-673, a GAO report dated April 3, 2007. The filing season is the tax agency's public face each year. This one carried extra risk from law changes, among them the telephone excise tax refund. The report also takes up the Internal Revenue Service's fiscal year 2008 budget request and its Business Systems Modernization build.

GAO first scores how the season ran: filings, refunds, phone help, and errors. It then holds the budget ask against past years. Parts aimed at the tax gap get a close look, since the net gap stood at $290 billion for 2001. New spending claims are tested for proof. Chances to shift or save funds are named. The systems build, a long trouble spot, closes the review. The report lands mid-season by design, while fixes can still help the next one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-73:
Safety lapses at the three nuclear weapons labs have worried the public for years. Nearly 60 grave accidents or near misses have hit the labs since 2000, from radiation exposure to toxic fumes. GAO-08-73, dated October 31, 2007, traces the causes and the fixes tried so far.

Loose attitudes toward safety rules, weak follow-up on known flaws, and thin federal oversight recur across some 100 prior probes. Two labs shut sites in 2004 and 2005 after violations. A safety push from 1996 is being revived. GAO urges steady, measured fixes, strong outside watch, and yearly reports to Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-773:
A new pay and grading system for Defense civilians, called the National Security Personnel System, covered about 182,000 staff by May 2008. GAO-08-773, dated September 10, 2008, checks the fairness guards built into the system and what workers think of it, as Congress required.

Many guards are in place: staff input, training, feedback, and a link between pay and performance. Three need quick work. No outside check of ratings happens before they are final, so bias could slip through unseen. Workers voice doubts that leaders must answer. GAO urges a plan to fix the weak guards and address staff concerns head-on.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
On the morning of September 11, 1973, CIA officers briefed President Richard Nixon on the military coup then unfolding in Chile. That top secret President's Daily Brief stayed classified for fifty years. The National Security Archive posted it in August 2023, in a briefing book edited by Peter Kornbluh.

The brief told Nixon that Chilean officers were determined to restore political and economic order. It also warned that they might lack a coordinated plan to use the wide civilian opposition. Reading it shows exactly what the president was told, in the CIA's own words, on the day Salvador Allende fell.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_henry-ki: Kissinger Told Soviet Envoy during 1973 Arab-Israeli War: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
This file holds the chapter of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands covering the campaign of 1600. Motley's contents place the military events of that year at the head of his final volume. Maurice leads an aggressive movement of the Netherlanders into Flanders. The march aims at the Dunkirk pirates who plague Dutch trade.

At Nieuport the invasion meets the Archduke's army on the dunes. The battle, the republic's most famous land victory, saved an army that had marched too far. Motley, in the chapters around this one, weighs its effects on general and statesman alike. Readers should note that this slice presents the year's campaign within his larger narrative. It is the hinge between the war of survival and the war of exhaustion that ended in truce.
hodge-systematic-theology-vol3-1873:
Volume three of Hodge's Systematic Theology, in this 1874 edition, crowns the Princeton system with eschatology, the doctrine of the last things. Hodge had covered God, man, and Christ's work in the earlier volumes. The aged professor writes here with a lifetime of teaching behind him.

He treats death, the soul's state after death, the return of Christ, resurrection, and the final judgment in ordered sequence. His method stays the same: gather the Bible's statements, sort them, and answer rival views with calm reason. Princeton's students received the volume as the completion of the great Calvinist system in America.
human-science-or-phrenology-its-principl:
O S Fowler, a practical phrenologist and lecturer, built this huge system in 1873. Its title promises phrenology's principles, proofs, faculties, and organs. Fowler applies them to nearly everything: health, home, commerce, ethics, and education. God, immortality, intellect, and memory all fall under his map of the head.

Health fills long practical stretches, from acute diseases to wounds and convalescence. Woman needs refinement, Fowler writes, but she needs good health still more. The index alone runs to hundreds of numbered topics. It is the Fowler system entire: skull science stretched into a philosophy of the perfect life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbas-abas-abat: Samuel ben Isaac Abbas was a rabbi at Amsterdam in the latter half of the seventeenth century, and died there about 1693. He translated Baḥya's "Ḥobot ha-Lebabot" into Portuguese, working from the Hebrew version of Ibn Tibbon. The translation came out at Amsterdam in 1670. It won the much-read work a clear gain in reach among the Sephardic groups of western Europe. Abbas also owned a fine library in four languages. A catalogue of it, thirty pages long, was printed the year he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abicht-johann-g:
Johann Georg Abicht was a Christian Hebraist, born in 1672 at Königsee and dead in 1740. He studied at Jena and then at Leipsic. In 1702 he became a teacher of Oriental tongues at Jena. Five years later he moved to Danzig, as head of the gymnasium and pastor of the Church of the Holy Trinity. In 1729 Wittenberg called him to high church and university posts.

Abicht shone in Oriental tongues and in Hebrew antiquities, and cared much for Jewish history and writing. He turned parts of the rabbinic commentaries into Latin, in his "Selecta Rabbinica" of 1703. Rashi, Abravanel, and Ibn Ezra all stand in that book. He also gave a Latin form to a Hebrew work on accents, in 1715. His best known book is a method of the holy tongue, from 1718.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-abi:
Bohemian rabbi Abraham ben Abigdor was born late in the fifteenth century and died at Prague on Oct. 7, 1542. For his last twenty years he served as rabbi of Prague. His pupils included Abraham Jaffe, father of Mordecai Jaffe.

Abraham wrote glosses on Jacob b. Asher's Tur Orah Hayyim, partly printed at Augsburg in 1540. Their clear, plain style stood against the pilpul method then spreading in Poland and Germany. Legend credits him with the seven sciences. A penitential prayer he wrote in 1542, when Bohemia's Jews faced expulsion, still sits in the Polish liturgy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adarsa-called-a: Adarsa, also called Adasa, was a village in Judea. It lay thirty furlongs from Beth-horon. Eusebius puts it near Guphna. There Judas Maccabeus beat the Syrian general Nicanor in a set battle. The fight fell on Adar 13, 160 B.C. Judas had 3,000 men by one count, or 1,000 by Josephus. Nicanor had 9,000, and he fell in the fight. A yearly feast, Nicanor's Day, marked the win. It fell the day before Purim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahaziah-king-of:
Ahaziah was king of Israel and the son and successor of Ahab. His reign lasted less than two years, from 853 to 852 B.C. He kept up his father's military activity.
