He also sought wealth through Red Sea trade with Ophir. Jehoshaphat of Judah was to be his partner in that venture. Jehoshaphat declined, and the plan was given up.

His early death came from a fall. He fell from a window of an upper room in Samaria. Sick from the fall, he sent to ask the oracle of Baal-zebub at Ekron. Elijah denounced this act three times and foretold his death. The entry reads his foreign cults as the mark of the house of Omri.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexandria-loui:
Alexandria, Louisiana, is a city on the south bank of the Red river. It lies 360 miles northwest of New Orleans. Its Jewish community began in 1848, when several Jews settled there. In 1900 the Jewish population was 600. That was about one-fourteenth of the whole city. Jewish citizens worked in banking, brokerage, and cotton-planting. Others were tradesmen, and a few were artisans.

The congregation was probably founded in 1864. A benevolent association followed in 1866, and the first synagogue rose in 1870. A Young Men's Hebrew Association came in 1882. A lodge of B'ne B'rith got its charter in 1884. A Sunday-school and Bible-class opened in 1890. A branch of the National Council of Jewish Women followed in 1896. Seven rabbis served the community in turn, from M. Klein to Alex. Rosenspitz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almalia-joseph-: Joseph Almalia was an Italian rabbi of the early nineteenth century. His responsa came out at Livorno in two parts. The first part came out in 1823. The second part came out in 1855. The book's Hebrew title means the strength of Joseph. The entry adds a note on his name. One index gives his name wrongly as Almagia. That error is flagged so readers are not misled.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amber-1373: Amber turns on a Hebrew word found in Ezekiel alone. The word hashmal shows up three times in that book. Its sense has puzzled readers since Talmud times. The Greek version gives a word of two senses. It can mean amber or a mix of gold and silver. One scholar links it to an Assyrian word for a bright metal mix. The entry holds that Ezekiel meant a shining metal, not true amber.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anapa-1473: Anapa is a town in the province of Kuban in Russia. It stands on the east coast of the Black Sea. Jews are said to have lived there in old times. The entry dates that claim to the first century. It says they had a synagogue in the town. One source in a Russian journal is cited. That source dates to March of the year 1894. The hosted entry gives no more facts for the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aqueducts-in-pa:
Aqueducts in Palestine opens with a contrast: Egypt lived by irrigation, while Palestine was a land of natural waters. Most of its aqueducts, like its roads, were built by the Romans after Jerusalem fell. Four earlier cases stand out, at Tyre, Jericho, Caesarea, and Jerusalem.

Tyre, an island city, once got its water by boat, and an enemy king cut off its mainland spring supply. The remains of an aqueduct nearly four miles long still run from dammed springs held eighty feet above the sea. Most of the stonework is Roman, the entry says, though one stretch shows older false arches. The entry then surveys each city's channels, sources, and ruins in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aristobulus-of-:
Alexandria produced Aristobulus of Paneas, a Peripatetic philosopher placed by the entry in the second century B.C. Scholars cited there argue over his date, but the stronger testimony makes him a contemporary of Ptolemy Philometor. He wrote an exposition of the Law whose exact title is uncertain. Only parts survive, kept by Eusebius and Clement, plus a short passage on the date of Passover.

Those fragments show his method. Human-like words about God in the Bible, such as God's hand or God's rest, are read as signs of power and order, not as literal claims. He argued that Plato and Pythagoras had drawn on an early translation of the Law of Moses. He also read the Sabbath as a birthday of light and wisdom. Greek poetry, some of it forged, is bent to the same point: God's power runs through all things.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asahel-hayyim-1:
Hayyim Asahel, a rabbi and author in Salonica in the first half of the eighteenth century, was a son of Benjamin Asahel, chief rabbi of that city. His Hebrew book Sam Hayyai, Spice of My Life, gathers addresses and legal answers. His son Benjamin published it at Salonica in 1746, after the author's death.

For some years Asahel lived at Jerusalem. He was sent out to gather gifts across Asia Minor for the poor of Palestine. The mission was his last work. He died at Smyrna while traveling on it. The entry keeps his record brief: a Salonica rabbi, a Jerusalem stay, one posthumous book, and a death far from home on an errand of charity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-josep:
Joseph Edels Ashkenazi, a Palestinian commentator and cabalist, lived at the start of the nineteenth century at Jerusalem and Padua. He died at Safed. Sent out from Palestine as a meshullah, an agent gathering money for the Palestinian poor, he stayed a while at Padua in Italy. There he taught Mordecai Samuel Ghirondi.

Ghirondi's record calls him a rich commentator on Bible and Talmud who printed almost nothing. All that appeared was a small commentary on the Sefer Yezirah, the Book of Creation. To it he attached many of his notes on Bible and Talmud. The entry is short and rests on a single source, the Nepi-Ghirondi biographical work. A traveling fundraiser who taught in Italy and died at Safed is the whole outline given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ataroth-2073: Ataroth, in this entry, is a district in Palestine east of the Jordan. Numbers xxxii. 3 names it with Dibon and Jazer as rich land, good for raising cattle. Reuben and Gad both asked for that land. Gad received it, the entry says, and built a city there, as verse 34 of the same chapter reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avignon-2173:
Avignon is the capital of the department of Vaucluse, France. It was once the seat of the papal court. Jews likely settled there in the second century, a few years after Hadrian destroyed Bethar. By 390 they were numerous enough to lead a revolt against Bishop Stephen. They lived in a set quarter, the Carrière des Juifs.

The Carrière ran itself like a small republic under the pope's provost. It held its own assemblies, chose its own officers, and set its own taxes. Its people were split into three classes by wealth, each sending five delegates to its parliament. Schooling was free and required, paid from common funds. Later parts of the entry trace papal laws that choked Jewish trade. In practice those laws were softened, and the Jews lived in a wary, pinched state, with spells of an interested tolerance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baba-or-bab-227:
Baba is a Talmudic term. At root it means gate. In technical use it names a section, part, or clause of a text. A single Mishnah can split into two or three such parts. Their names mean beginning and end, or beginning, middle, and end. Lawyers cited a point as the clause of the first part, the middle part, or the last part of a passage.

The word does its largest work in the order of the Mishnah called Neziḳin, on damages. That order's first section is itself split into three treatises. Their names are simply First Gate, Middle Gate, and Last Gate. The entry notes a like threefold split in the treatise Kelim in the Tosefta. Even the book Seder 'Olam, with its thirty chapters, is grouped into three babas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bailly-jean-syl:
Jean-Sylvain Bailly was an astronomer and public writer born in Paris on Sept. 15, 1736. He was guillotined on Nov. 12, 1793. He joined the Académie des Sciences in 1763 and the Académie Française in 1784. In 1789 Paris sent him to the States General, which made him its president on June 3. The next month he became mayor of Paris.

The entry honors Bailly for his work for the Jews of France. He helped win the decree of Sept. 27, 1791, confirmed Nov. 30, which made Jews French citizens with full rights. It repealed their special taxes and all laws against them. Threats and mockery, the entry says, did not move him. His fall came from other work: using force against crowds at the Champ de Mars cost him his standing, and the Revolutionary tribunal sent him to his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bar-mizwah-lite:
Bar Miẓwah, literally "the son of command," is the term for a boy who has completed his thirteenth year. He has then reached the age of religious duty and answerability. The entry warns that the name in this sense cannot be traced clearly before the fourteenth century. Older rabbinic terms were "gadol" (adult) or "bar 'onshin" (son of punishment), liable for his own misdeeds.

On the first Sabbath of his fourteenth year the boy is called up to read from the weekly portion of the Law. If he cannot read, he at least says the blessings, while the father silently thanks God for taking the child's responsibility from him. A feast marks the day. The entry adds Midrash on Jacob and Esau parting at thirteen, and ties the good desire's arrival to this age. It also notes that Abraham, in one source, cast off idolatry at thirteen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baumgarten-b-ka: Karoly Baumgarten was a Hungarian jurist born at Budapest on Sept. 21, 1853, and a brother of Isidor Baumgarten. He practiced law in Budapest from 1876 to 1892 while editing a journal on criminal law. In 1892 he became a judge of the Court of Commerce and Exchange and head of its appeal council. The entry credits him with strong influence on court practice there. In 1898 he rose to the Supreme Court at Budapest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrend-friedri:
Friedrich Jacob Behrend was a German physician born at Neu-Stettin, in Pomerania, on June 12, 1803. Trained first for trade, he left a clerk's desk in 1821 to study medicine. He took his degree in 1826 and settled in Berlin in 1829.

Behrend served the Berlin police as a medical examiner and rose to chief physician of its morals police in 1876. He edited huge runs of medical journals, some over twenty volumes. His own books picture skin diseases and broken bones and treat public baths and city drainage. He also turned the lectures of famed foreign doctors into German for home readers over many years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-hesed-2873: Ben-Hesed served as a commissariat officer of Solomon, with his residence at Aruboth in Judah. His district, the entry states, covered Hepher and Sochoh. Because several places bore the name Sochoh, the entry weighs which one is meant. It favors the Sochoh near Hebron, citing Joshua xv. 48 and the context of I Kings iv. 10.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-b-matt:
Benjamin ben Mattithiah wrote a large set of responsa and worked in Turkey in the first half of the sixteenth century. By trade he was a merchant, and he also sat in the rabbinical college of Arta. His free hand in legal rulings often gave offense to other rabbis.

His book, printed at Venice in 1539 under the title Benjamin Ze'eb, holds 450 responsa on a wide range of themes. The entry says it throws light on Jewish life in European Turkey and Asia Minor. One ruling against men and women dancing together met strong pushback from the young.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beriah-or-olam-: Beriah, or Olam ha-Beriah, the World of Creation, is a term of the Cabala. It names the second of the four heavenly worlds in that system. It stands between the World of Emanation above it and the World of Formation below it. Angels fill that third realm, the entry notes. A further note treats Beriah's own nature. It is said to be of the purest essence, with no mixture of matter in it at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bertram-corneil:
Corneille Bonaventure Bertram was a Protestant clergyman and Hebraist. He was born at Thouars, France, in 1531. He died at Lausanne in 1594. He fled Cahors to escape a planned massacre. Geneva became his refuge. In 1567 he began teaching Oriental languages there.

The entry lists his works on Hebrew subjects. One compares Hebrew and Aramaic grammar. Another treats Jewish civil and religious institutions. That book passed through many editions. He also wrote a Hebrew and Arabic grammar. In 1588 he published a Bible translation. It followed Munster and Tremelius. It often drew on rabbinic commentaries too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bibliomancy-for:
Bibliomancy is the use of the Bible for magic. Sacred books served divination in many cultures. The Vedas served Hindus that way. Homer served Greeks, and Virgil served Romans. Jews used the Old Testament similarly. Christians used both Testaments. Moslems used the Koran and Hafiz.

Commands to bind God's words gave the practice support. The sixty letters of the Priestly Blessing became a talisman. Psalm xci served as a song against demons. The entry details psalms used against fever and imprisonment. Psalm lxvii was written in a menorah shape. It was claimed to mark David's shield.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blin-d-elbuf-33: Blin d'Elbeuf was a French manufacturer. He introduced woolen cloth for ladies' use into France. His cloth was soon judged Europe's best. It won the prize at Vienna's 1870 exhibition. Presenting a sample to President Carnot, he spoke proudly. The cloth recalled a French industrial victory, he said. It had beaten foreign makers at their own trade. The entry is only a few lines. A single Revue Etudes Juives note is its source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bohm-moses-3473:
Moses Böhm was a German physician who worked in the middle of the eighteenth century. In 1740 the Jewish community of Halberstadt hired him to care for its poor members. His pay, 175 thalers a year, ran till 1747 in the records.

Böhm won trust from nobles and church leaders as well as Jews. Stories of his skill and kindness lived on in Halberstadt. His Hebrew letters attack the use of amulets. They also attack the early and hurried burial of the dead. The letters show strong Hebrew and clear reasoning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borisov-3573:
Borisov is a town and district in the government of Minsk, Russia. It stands on the left bank of the Beresina, about fifty miles from the capital. In 1900 the town held over 10,000 Jews in a total of 18,348.

Its Jewish community dates from the sixteenth century. Merchants traded grain and lumber with Riga by the Düna. In 1812 local Jews built a bridge and a hospital for Russian troops at their own cost. Emperor Alexander I thanked them for that help. Rail building later cut the town's trade, and the community grew poor. Nine houses of prayer served it still.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bregman-eliezer: Eliezer b. Moses Bregman was a Russian financier and giver born in Indura in 1826. He died in Teplitz, Bohemia, on Sept. 3, 1896. A leading business man of Grodno, he farmed the meat tax in many large cities of the empire. The government gave him a gold medal for his work and charities. It also made him a hereditary honorary citizen. He spent more than 100,000 rubles on charitable institutions in his lifetime, the entry reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brunswick-germa:
Brunswick was a German duchy whose capital bore the same name. Jews appear there early: a record from 1241 says the abbess of Quedlinburg owed Jacob, probably the first Jew named, 213 pounds of silver. Jews settled at Helmstedt by 1247. Persecution came with the Black Death in 1349 and again after Luther's polemics.

Relief came slowly in the nineteenth century. Laws of 1821 let Jews enter trades as apprentices, and measures of 1832 made settled Jews native residents with some civic rights. Land buying still needed government leave. The entry describes the rabbinical conference held at Brunswick in 1844, which repealed the special Jews' oath the next year. It ends with two free schools and a population figure of 2,000.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-byeshenkovichi-: Byeshenkovichi appears in a very short entry as a town in the district of Lepelsk, in the government of Vitebsk, Russia. All its facts are figures from 1898. In a total population of 5,000, about 4,000 were Jews. Of those, 576 were artisans. The town had a synagogue and many houses of prayer. It also had three benevolent societies and many religious schools. The entry gives no history of the community and names no people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cansino-isaac-b: Isaac Cansino, son of Hayyim, was a poet and a leading member of the Jewish community of Oran. He died in 1672 and was likely a brother of Jacob Cansino the second. He sang as cantor on the Day of Atonement, a post held as an honor. His chief work was the first part of the Mahzor Oran, which holds many of his poems. He praised a kinsman's poem collection in verse. He also wrote a dirge for Aaron Cansino and a sympathy poem for Samuel, who lost his fortune.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carpzov-johann-:
Johann Gottlob Carpzov, a German Christian scholar of the Old Testament, was born in Dresden on Sept. 26, 1679. He died at Lübeck on April 27, 1767. A nephew of Johann Benedict II, he became the best known biblical scholar of the Carpzov family. He held a chair of Oriental languages at Leipsic from 1719 to 1730.

His Introductio, first issued in 1721, is praised as the first work worthy of that name. His Critica Sacra followed in 1728, and his Apparatus in 1748. The entry sees a mixed record. Carpzov advanced the field in fullness of material and clear order. Yet he held fast to literal inspiration of the Hebrew text. He fought the freer views of Simon, Spinoza, and Clericus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chronologythe-f:
Chronology, the science of computing time and ordering events, anchors this huge survey of Jewish time-reckoning. It splits the field in two: the age of the Bible books and the post-Biblical age. Early pages treat the day, the night-watches, and the dial of Ahaz. The Babylonian week, with a planet set over each day, gets close attention.

Later sections work through months, years, and the eras Jews actually used on documents. The Seleucidan era of contracts, dated from 312 B.C., served into the Middle Ages. Reckoning from the Creation came in later, placed by the entry at 3760 B.C. Maimonides, it notes, could use three eras in a single work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-francis-l:
Francis Lyon Cohen, an English rabbi and expert on Hebrew music, was born at Aldershot on Nov. 14, 1862. He trained at Jews' College and University College, London. He served congregations at South Hackney from 1883 to 1885 and at Dublin from 1885 to 1886. Since 1886 he had ministered at the Borough New Synagogue in London.

Posts followed in teaching and army life. He tutored at Jews' College from 1886 and became acting chaplain to Jewish soldiers in 1892. He first urged the forming of the Jewish Lads' Brigade and served as its staff chaplain from 1896. His Handbook of Synagogue Music appeared in 1889. With D. M. Davis he later issued The Voice of Prayer and Praise in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-community-organ:
Community, Organization of, traces how Jewish communities ran themselves from the start of the common era. At first they stood in Alexandria, Rome, Corinth, and many other cities, while Palestine formed one community centered on Jerusalem. After Jerusalem fell, communal life replaced national life, shaped by Roman forms yet left alone in its inner affairs.

A patriarch led Palestine, an exilarch led Babylonia. Members ranked as full citizens after twelve months, half citizens sooner, and transients under twenty days. A board of at least three, usually seven, governed each place. The huge entry then follows this frame across centuries and lands, down to German laws of 1828 and 1832 that made every Jew a congregation member by duty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-corporation-467:
Corporation, as defined here, joins several persons under a common name into one body that the law treats as a single person. The entry also notes the corporation sole, one office holder who passes rights and duties to successors. Cities of the Holy Land count as public corporations. Jewish communities in the Exile matched them. A shared courtyard in the Mishnah forms a middle case, with set duties and rights.

Private corporations split into charitable and commercial kinds. The chief charitable form was the ḥebra, above all the burial gild. Other groups lodged travelers, visited the sick, and ran hospitals. They held property and kept a lasting life, though the codes say little on the point.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-croneburg-benja: Benjamin ben Solomon Croneburg was a German publicist. He lived at Neuwied, in Prussia, in the eighteenth century. The entry is very brief and names one act of his. In 1758 he founded a Jewish periodical at Neuwied. Its title was Der Grosse Schauplatz, meaning The Great Stage. The periodical was printed in German. No birth or death dates are given. No other writings or posts are mentioned. A history of Jewish literature by Karpeles is the single source cited for the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-demands-5073:
Demands, in law, are the rights a person has to recover money or valuables from others, by contract or for a wrong suffered. The Mishnah treats demands as a kind of property and often names bonds as the most valuable kind. A single demand is often called simply a loan.

The article asks four questions about demands. Can they be transferred to another person, and how? Do they pass to the owner's heirs at his death? Do they survive against the debtor's heirs? And how can they end without payment? Claims from a deposit could be assigned, but claims from a wrong could not. At death, demands pass with the estate to the heirs, who may sue for them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diblah-5173: Diblah is a place name found in Ezekiel chapter 6, verse 14, in the Masorah and the Greek Septuagint, and this entry questions whether such a place ever existed. No site of that name fits the needs of the passage. J. D. Michaelis guessed that Diblah is a misreading for Riblah. He pointed out that in Jeremiah chapter 52 the Septuagint makes the same error, while the Masorah there has the right reading. The short entry sends the reader to the article on Riblah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-donath-leopold-: Leopold Donath was a rabbi born in 1845 at Waag-Neustadtl, Hungary, who died in 1876 at Güstrow, Mecklenburg. A pupil of Israel Hildesheimer, he studied at Berlin University and took his degree at Rostock. He then served as rabbi and preacher at Güstrow. His writings include pieces in Berliner's Magazin and a book on the Alexander legend in Talmud and Midrash, printed at Fulda in 1873. He also wrote a history of the Jews in Mecklenburg, published at Leipsic in 1874.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-duschinsky-wilh:
Wilhelm Duschinsky was an Austrian writer born in Strasnitz, Moravia, on May 6, 1860. He attended the gymnasium in Vienna. He then studied Romanic and Germanic philology at Vienna and Paris. Since 1892 he has taught at the Ober-Realschule in Vienna's seventh district.

Duschinsky's work is a shelf of short studies in language and letters. Early pieces treat the sounds of French speech and the silent e. Others take up Goethe's Hermann und Dorothea and Molière's Misanthrope. Later studies weigh Shakespeare's mark on Schiller's Tell and the sources of Grillparzer's Esther. Textbooks on French syntax from 1901 and 1902 close the entry's list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-enoch-books-of-:
The Books of Enoch are old works laid to Enoch's name. They grow from the verse that says Enoch walked with God. Around that man a whole cycle of legends took shape. Two forms of the work have come down to us. The Ethiopic Enoch is a heap of parts and bits. The Slavonic book sums the tales in one set order.

The entry lists the core tales that both books share. In life Enoch rose to heaven and walked with angels. He saw the hidings of earth and sky laid bare. He saw what became of the angels who fell to earth. Those sons of God had sinned with the daughters of men. Enoch pled their case before the throne on high. The entry sorts the two tale cycles from each other. It shows how the Slavonic book binds them into one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esther-apocryph:
The Apocryphal Book of Esther holds Greek additions to the Bible's Book of Esther, and this long entry studies them closely. The entry states that the Bible book gives the oldest form of the story. In hard times Jews drew comfort from its tale of sudden rescue. Later writers expanded the parts the Bible touches lightly. Those expansions survive in Greek.

Older scholars guessed the additions came from a Hebrew original, but the entry says that guess has been proved wrong. The additions were likely made in Maccabean times. Their chief aim was to supply the religious element missing from the Bible book. The entry dates them no later than 30 B.C. It then works through the additions verse by verse, including Mordecai's dream and Esther's prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-felsenthal-bern:
Bernhard Felsenthal was a German-American rabbi and author born January 2, 1822, at Munchweiler, Germany. He trained at trade and teachers' schools and taught a decade in a small Jewish school. In 1854 he crossed to America and served as rabbi and teacher at Madison, Indiana, for three years. Chicago followed in 1858, where he worked at a bank.

That year he helped found the Judische Reformverein and wrote its 1859 pamphlet on Jewish reform. The group grew into Sinai Congregation, and he became its first rabbi in 1861. In 1864 he took the new Zion Congregation, serving until 1887, then as rabbi emeritus. Chicago University gave him an honorary doctorate in 1886. In later years he stood out as a Zionist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franck-adolphe-:
Adolphe Franck was a French philosopher born at Liocourt on October 9, 1809. He died at Paris on April 11, 1893. He was meant for the rabbinate and was placed at fourteen in a rabbi's care. When no rabbinical scholarship came, he tried medicine, then settled on philosophy. In 1832 he took first place among the new fellows in philosophy. He taught at several colleges before Paris.

Franck's chief work is his dictionary of the philosophical sciences, issued in six volumes. His book on the Cabala won wide fame and was turned into German in 1844. In 1856 he took a chair of natural and civil law, which he held for thirty years. He led the Anti-Atheist League and its paper. He also defended Judaism in lectures and served its central consistory. The Legion of Honor made him chevalier in 1844, officer in 1862, and commander in 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedlander-fri:
Friedrich Friedländer was a painter of everyday scenes, born on January 10, 1825, at Kohljanowitz, Bohemia. He studied at the Vienna Academy and later under Waldmüller. He visited Italy in 1850, Düsseldorf in 1852, and then Paris. At first he painted scenes from history, and one of them made a true stir. Since 1854 he has painted scenes of daily life only. His matter comes chiefly from army life and the street life of Vienna. His Swabian folk scenes are also much praised.

Named among his best works are a crowd pouring out of a public building, of 1859, and a pawnbroker's shop, of 1866. Others show a wine test, a new comrade, and a band of wounded men. He joined the Vienna Academy in 1866 and won orders and a gold medal. He has lately been raised to the nobility. Many of his pictures hang in the imperial gallery at Vienna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gilds-6673:
Gilds were unions that bound each craft and trade to a close body of members. From the twelfth century most west European towns ran on that plan. The bodies set who might work and who might sell. They also served worship and burial needs. In no case might Jews join these brotherhoods.

At Florence none of seventy-three gilds would take a man lacking city freedom, a right denied to Jews. London barred men not born in the liberty. Only one case is known of a Jew in an English merchant gild. Towns passed rules to keep Jews from trade. At Neisse the Jews were expelled in 1468. In Russia, by contrast, Jews might join gilds and gain travel rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldstucker-the:
Theodor Goldstücker was a German Sanskritist. He was born at Königsberg, Prussia, on Jan. 18, 1821. He died in London on March 6, 1872. He took his doctorate at Königsberg in 1840. He studied Sanskrit at Bonn and Paris as well. In 1842 he published a German version of a Sanskrit drama.

In 1850 he moved to England. He helped Professor Wilson revise a Sanskrit-English dictionary. That project swelled out of hand and was dropped at page 480. From 1851 he held the Sanskrit chair at University College, London. He founded the Sanskrit Text Society in 1866. His editions cover mimansa philosophy and Panini's grammar. His essays were gathered as "Literary Remains" in 1879.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ha-asif-the-har:
Ha-Asif, meaning "The Harvest," was a Hebrew year-book edited and published by Nahum Sokolow in Warsaw. Its first volume appeared in 1884, and volumes came out yearly until 1889. A sixth and last volume followed in 1893. Sokolow's later "Sefer ha-Shanah" counts as its continuation.

Better-known Hebrew writers of the day filled its six volumes with literary, historical, and biographical essays. The volumes also hold popular science pieces, poems, sketches, and novels. Yearly reviews and obituaries added record value. A supplement to the fifth volume, "Sefer Zikkaron," gave a biographical dictionary of living Jewish authors. Together the volumes form an important collection of the period's Hebrew writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanan-isaac-717: Isaac Ḥanan was a Turkish rabbi who lived at Salonica about the middle of the eighteenth century. The entry is three lines long and rests on one book. His work "Bene Yiẓḥaḳ" holds homilies and responsa. It was printed at Salonica in 1757. Fürst's bibliography lists the author under the name Honein. No birth date, teachers, post, or other writing is given for him in this brief article.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harrwitz-daniel:
Daniel Harrwitz, born in Breslau in 1823, was a German chess master. He learned much of his game from Anderssen. His career began in Paris in 1845. He beat strong players in England and France, among them Horwitz, Lowenthal, and De Riviere. In 1858 he lost a match to Morphy by 2 games to 5.

Even in that loss, Harrwitz won three games from Morphy, a rare feat. Poor health forced him to give up active play in 1862. The entry calls him perhaps the best of all players at giving odds. He also ran a chess magazine and wrote a chess textbook in 1862.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-b-hanane: Hayyim ben Hananeel ha-Kohen was a French tosafist of the later twelfth century. He studied under Jacob ben Meir, known as Tam, and debated legal points with him. His grandson Moses of Coucy wrote the "Semag," a major book of commandments. Hayyim's views are quoted in the Tosafot at several places. He is also named in notes to the Mordekai. Though a Kohen, he offered to help bury his teacher. His reason was that great men do not pass on impurity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hedyot-i-7473:
Hedyot is a term in the Mishnah, Talmud, and Midrash for a private person or commoner. It stands against kings, priests, and officers. The word can also mean an ignorant man or one of low character. A saying warns that the lowest man rushes to speak first before his betters.

The piece lists paired uses. A common priest is set against a high priest, a Samaritan against an Israelite, an unskilled worker against a trained one. Common speech is split from learned speech. Even a cow of common stock gets the label. Three word books are cited at the end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henry-henry-a-7:
Henry A. Henry, born in London in 1800, was an Anglo-American rabbi and Hebraist. Educated at the Jews' Free School in London, he later became its principal until 1842. He founded a Jewish hospital and orphan asylum. He also resisted groups seeking to convert Jews.

Henry compiled daily prayers in 1836 and wrote books for Jewish youth and on Jewish history. After serving at St. Alban's, he moved to America in 1849. He held posts at Cincinnati, Syracuse, and New York. From 1857 he led Shearith Israel in San Francisco until 1871. He died there on Sept. 4, 1879.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hezekiah-ben-pa: Hezekiah ben Parnak was a Palestinian amora who lived at the end of the third century. The entry says he is mentioned only once, in Berakot. That mention ties him to passing on Johanan bar Nappaḥa's reading of a Bible order. The passage on a faithless wife follows the passage on refusing the priestly tithe, and his name attaches to explaining why. No works, teachers, or other sayings of his are given. Two reference books are cited for this brief record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horonaim-the-tw: Horonaim, meaning the two hollows, was a city of Moab. Isaiah and Jeremiah both mention it. The entry also points to the Mesha inscription, where the name appears in lines thirty-one and thirty-two. Its site is thought by some to lie south of the Arnon river. Josephus speaks of a Moabite city called Oronas or Orone. He says Alexander Jannaeus took it. The article gives no other events from the city's history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hyrcanus-ii-797:
Hyrcanus the Second was high priest from about 79 to 40 before the common era, eldest son of Alexander Jannaeus and Alexandra. His mother set him in office and named him her heir. Within three months his brother Aristobulus rebelled and beat him near Jericho. Hyrcanus gave up throne and priesthood but kept its income.

Antipater then worked on the weak man's fears and sent him to the Nabataean king for help. Rome stepped in. Pompey took Jerusalem, and Hyrcanus went back to the priesthood without power. Caesar made him ethnarch in 47, yet Antipater held real rule. Carried to Babylonia with his ears cut off, he came home at Herod's call and was executed in the year 30.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-illescos-jacob-: Jacob di Illescos was a Bible commentator, probably of Italian origin, who lived in the fourteenth century. His book Imre No'am treats the Pentateuch in allegorical, cabalistic, and grammatical ways. It adds notes on hard passages in Rashi and Ibn Ezra. The book was first printed at Constantinople in 1546. It went through many editions and entered a great rabbinic Bible printed at Amsterdam in 1724 to 1727. Illescos quotes a wide range of earlier commentators, from Rashi to Moses of Coucy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-isaac: Isaac ben Isaac was a French tosafist of the second half of the thirteenth century. Gross and Zunz identified him with Isaac of Chinon, whose glosses appear in the Shittah Mekubbezet on tractate Nazir. In the responsa of Solomon ben Adret he is described as chief of the French yeshibot. Those responsa show him urging Isaac ben Joseph of Marseilles toward moderation in a dispute. He also corresponded with Nathan, with David ben Levi, and with Mordecai ben Isaac Kimhi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jabin-8373:
Jabin is the name of two kings of Hazor in this entry. The first led a great alliance against Joshua in the conquest of Canaan. Amorites, Hittites, and many small kingdoms answered his call. At the waters of Merom the coalition fell, iron chariots and all. Joshua then took Hazor and slew its king.

The second Jabin, king of Canaan reigning at Hazor, pressed Israel for twenty years. His strength lay in nine hundred chariots of iron and in Sisera, his commander. Israel rose under Deborah and Barak; Sisera died in Jael's tent, and God, the text says, subdued Jabin that day, until Israel destroyed him. The entry notes that some take the two accounts as one event. A psalm still names Jabin beside Sisera at the river Kishon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobs-george-8: George Jacobs was an American rabbi of English Sephardic descent, born in Kingston, Jamaica, on Sept. 24, 1834, who died in Philadelphia on July 14, 1884. He came to the United States in 1854 and settled in Richmond, Virginia. There he often officiated for Congregation Beth Shalome while studying for the ministry, and in 1857 he was elected to the rabbinate. In 1869 he followed Isaac Leeser as rabbi of Beth El Emeth in Philadelphia. He helped found the American Jewish Publication Society and published several catechisms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeiteles-jeitte:
Jeiteles, also spelled Jeitteles, is an Austrian family that can be traced to the first half of the eighteenth century. The entry gives lives of many members in turn. First stands Aaron Jeitteles, born at Prague on Nov. 24, 1799, a doctor who taught anatomy at Vienna and later held a surgery chair at Olmütz for more than thirty years.

Aaron also wrote poems, some set by Beethoven, and pled for fairness and freedom under a pen name meaning just and free. Another member, Baruch Jeiteles of Prague, turned from strict Orthodoxy toward the liberal thought of Mendelssohn and ran a study house there. More lives of doctors, rabbis, and writers follow in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jews-walk-8673: Jews' Walk was the name of the southeast corner of the colonnade in the Royal Exchange in London. Jewish brokers used to gather there for business on market days. At the end of the eighteenth century each trade group kept its own spot on the Exchange floor. Dealers in foreign bills still meet in the old Jews' Walk, the entry notes. A second spot of the same name stood by the Guildhall, but that name was taken off the wall in 1838 at the request of Sir Moses Montefiore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonathan-maccab:
Jonathan Maccabeus, a son of Mattathias, led the Jews in the Maccabean wars from 161 to 143 B.C. He is also called Apphus, a name read as the dissembler or the diplomat. He had fought beside his brother Judah against the Syrians, with less dash than Judah but with courage tried again and again. After Judah died, and famine gripped the land, the Jews chose Jonathan as leader.

The Syrian general Bacchides hunted him even into the marsh country east of the Jordan. On a Sabbath Jonathan's men had to fight and swim the river to escape, while Bacchides lost about a thousand men. Jonathan then avenged his brother Johanan, killed by a hostile tribe on a baggage raid, by ambushing a rich bridal party and slaying three hundred.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-asher:
Judah ben Asher was a German Talmudist who later became rabbi of Toledo in Spain. He was born in western Germany on June 30, 1270, and died at Toledo on July 4, 1349. He was a brother of Jacob ben Asher, author of the Turim. At thirteen he set out for Spain, a trip that took him almost two years.

After his father Asher died, the Toledo community chose Judah to follow him as rabbi. When he thought of moving to Seville, the community begged him to stay and doubled his pay. Still, he urged his five sons to go back to Germany. His responsa and part of a commentary on Shabbat were printed as Zikron Yehudah in 1846.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ibn-shabb: Judah ibn Shabbethai, also called Judah Levi ben Isaac, was a Spanish poet of the end of the twelfth century. He may be the doctor Judah b. Isaac of Barcelona whom Al-Harizi praised as a poet. His gift lay in the mosaic style, weaving Bible and Talmud phrases into new verse, with ready humor. In 1214 he wrote a rhymed prose dispute on wisdom and wealth. In 1218 came his sharper work, a comic satire on women cast in the same maqama form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judith-book-of-:
The Book of Judith is an apocryphal book in sixteen chapters, named for its heroine. Judith means Jewess. The entry calls the book a story written for household reading. Its writer cared more for the telling than for the moral, and its early fame, among Jews and Christians alike, rested on its merit as a tale.

It is a historical novel: its scenes are fixed in place and time and tied to great names of history. Its plot turns on an Assyrian army's advance into Palestine and the siege of a Jewish city called Bethulia. Long parts of the entry hunt for that city on the map and settle on Shechem. The false name, the entry argues, hid a Samaritan town under a safer label.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalonymus-ben-k:
Kalonymus ben Kalonymus ben Meïr, called Maestro Calo, was a Provençal thinker and translator. He was born at Arles in 1286. He died some time after 1328. He bore the title Nasi, as his father had before him. He studied at Salonica and read medicine, though he seems not to have worked as a doctor.

About 1314 Kalonymus settled at Avignon. Robert of Anjou sent him on a learned mission to Rome. There the Jewish leaders valued him so much that they fought his recall. His versions from Arabic cover medicine, geometry, and the works of Averroes. His own books include "Eben Boḥan," a survey of human pride and folly. Written in 1322, it ends by listing the woes of Israel. He also wrote a Purim parody in Talmud style.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-katzenellenboge:
Katzenellenbogen is the name of an old and wide-spread family. Many of its members were rabbis. They lived in Italy, Poland, Germany, and Alsace. Some reached America as well. The name comes from a town in Hesse-Nassau. In 1312 an emperor let a local count keep twelve Jews there. In 1330 the count's house gained leave for twenty-four.

The long entry gives lives of the family's rabbis one by one. Meïr of Padua, born about 1482, stands as the family's founder. Ezekiel of Altona drew a harsh sketch from Jacob Emden. Saul of Wilna was a pupil of the Vilna Gaon. The family's men served towns from Brest-Litovsk to Venice. Their books cover responsa, Talmud notes, and prayers for the Jahrzeit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kempner-max-pse:
Max Kempner was a German author born at Breslau on March 5, 1863. He wrote under the names Max Hochstädt and Eckart. He began his writing life at twenty-five. His first book, a set of poems called "Buch der Liebe," came out in 1888. A tragedy, "Warbeck," followed in 1891.

The entry lists Kempner's books year by year through the 1890s. Plays make up most of the list. There are dramas, a farce, a comedy, and an operetta. Titles range from "Sünden Unserer Gesellschaft" to "König Rhampsinit." At the time of the entry he edited a fashion paper. He also published a home magazine, "Mode und Haus."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klein-felix-937: Felix Klein was a German mathematician. He was born at Düsseldorf on April 24, 1849. He studied at Bonn and took his Ph.D. in 1868. He became professor of mathematics at Erlangen in 1872. He later held chairs at Munich, at Leipsic, and at Göttingen. Since 1875 he has been coeditor of "Die Mathematischen Annalen." His works include lectures on the icosahedron. He also wrote on Riemann's theory of algebraic functions. In 1893 he represented Germany at the Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kornfeld-aaron-: Aaron Kornfeld, an Austrian Talmudist born on Aug. 2, 1795, at Goltsch-Jenikau in Bohemia, died there on Oct. 26, 1881. His father, who ran a yeshibah, was his only teacher. At eighteen Kornfeld took over the school on his father's death. Its fame drew as many as eighty pupils at times. Sir Moses Montefiore made a hard side trip on his way back from Damascus just to meet him. In 1864, barred from reading by an eye illness, Kornfeld composed from memory a list of 300 commandments, printed in 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leon-ha-levi-95: Leon ha-Levi was a Provençal Jew who wrote a Purim parody under the pen name Labi ha-Levi. He hid his name, the entry says, because he feared Orthodox Jews would condemn the work. His treatise "Megillat Setarim" came out at Venice in 1552. It copies the plan of a Talmud tract, with mock Rashi and Tosafot notes. A second work, "Sefer Habakbuk," parodies the Pentateuch and the prophetic style. It stages a contest between wine and water.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leopard-heb-nam:
Namer, the leopard, is a fierce meat-eating mammal named in the Old Testament and the Talmud. The Bible cites its fierceness in Isaiah, its speed in Habakkuk, and its cunning in Jeremiah and Hosea. Its fixed spots serve in Jeremiah as a picture of what cannot change. In Daniel it stands as a sign of one of the great monarchies.

The animal still lived in the forest of Gilead, round the Dead Sea, and in the hills, the entry says. Place names like Beth-nimrah and Nimrim may keep its old range. In the Talmud the namer ranks with the wolf and lion for danger. Some rabbis took it as a cross of pard and lioness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-hirschel-:
Hirschel Levin, also called Hirschel Löbel and Hart Lyon, was a German rabbi. He was born at Rzeszow, Galicia, in 1721 and died at Berlin on Aug. 26, 1800. His father was rabbi at Amsterdam. Hirschel was a nephew of Jacob Emden and a strong Talmudist.

In 1751 Levin joined the fight between Emden and Eybeschütz, on Emden's side. His letters made such a mark that London's German and Polish Jews chose him as chief rabbi in 1756. A clash over his wish to defend London's butchers in print led him to resign in 1763. He later served at Halberstadt and Mannheim. In 1772 he became chief rabbi of Berlin, where he was a close friend of Mendelssohn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-alphonse-9: Alphonse Lévy, a French painter, was born at Marmoutier, Alsace, in 1843. At seventeen he went to Paris and studied under Gérôme. As an illustrator he drew for all the great Paris journals. He gave himself almost wholly to scenes of Jewish life. His drawings for the Jewish tales of Sacher-Masoch stand out, the entry says. So does his set of thirty drawings, lithographed by his own hand. In 1904 he was at work on sketches of Jewish life in Algiers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-liebreich-richa:
Richard Liebreich, an English ophthalmologist, was born at Königsberg on June 30, 1830. He was a brother of Oskar Liebreich. He took his medical degree in 1853 after study at Königsberg, Berlin, and Halle. He trained further at Utrecht and Berlin, then worked at Berlin University's eye institute from 1854 to 1862.

Liebreich set up as an eye doctor in Paris in 1862 and moved to London in 1870. There he taught at St. Thomas' Hospital. He built two ophthalmoscopes that came into wide use. The small portable one filled a long-felt want, the entry says. His atlas of ophthalmoscopy first came out in 1863. Since about 1895 he has spent most of his time on art research.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucas-louis-art:
Louis Arthur Lucas (1851–1876) was an African explorer born in London, profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind. After travel in the United States and Egypt, he organized an expedition to explore the Kongo. He reached Khartum in January 1876 and died at sea that November, aged twenty-five.

At the Albert Nyanza, Lucas navigated the lake’s northern part in the first steamboat ever launched on it, working alongside Colonel Gordon. He also compiled a vocabulary of Bisharin words, later published by the Anthropological Institute. Against Gordon’s advice he then tried to cross Africa, fell sick and paralyzed, and died on a steamboat between Suakim and Suez. He was buried at Jiddah. The entry tells a short, stark story of ambition, illness, and an early death in the age of exploration.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-lady-kat:
Lady Katie Magnus, an English author and communal worker, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Portsmouth on May 2, 1844, she was the daughter of E. Emanuel. She married Sir Philip Magnus. Her public life joined writing to service in London's Jewish community.

The article lists her books and her posts together. She served on committees of the Berkeley Street Synagogue and backed the Jews' Deaf and Dumb Home. As treasurer of the Jewish Girls' Club she worked for young women. Her writing began with Bible stories and holiday tales for children. Two sketches of Jewish history followed, one reaching three editions. Her Outlines of Jewish History was reprinted in America by the Jewish Publication Society. A second edition of her Jewish Portraits appeared in 1901. The entry shows a writer who taught her community its own past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manoah-b-jacob-:
Manoah ben Jacob, a French Talmudist of Lunel, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He lived in the second half of the thirteenth century. After a short stay at Narbonne, where he studied with Meir ben Simon and Reuben ben Hayyim, he returned to Lunel. He often cites rulings in his father's name.

The article centers on his one known work. Like several of his contemporaries, Manoah studied Maimonides closely. He wrote a commentary on the Yad ha-Hazakah, Maimonides' great code. Later writers quote it under the title Sefer ha-Manoah, or Sefer ha-Menuhah. It was printed at Constantinople in 1518, centuries after his death. The entry rests on the standard name-books of Azulai and Conforte and on Gross's Gallia Judaica. It preserves a Provençal scholar who helped France read Maimonides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matah-mehasya-m:
Matah Mehasya was a town in southern Babylonia. Solomon Schechter and Wilhelm Bacher untangle it from its neighbor Sura in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Sherira Gaon used the two names as if they were one place, since both named the seat of the great academy founded by Rab. The article argues from Talmudic passages, including one that contrasts the two towns' ways of speaking, that they were really separate towns. The school likely sat between them.

Most of the entry belongs to the age of Ashi, in the later fourth century. The academy then sat at Matah Mehasya, and Ashi himself lived there. He protected the town by forbidding houses taller than its synagogue. He also complained that its non-Jewish residents stayed hard-hearted. They saw the splendor of the Torah at the great Kallah gatherings twice a year, and still stayed unmoved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-isaac-:
Meir ben Isaac of Orleans, a French liturgical poet of the end of the eleventh century, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn. He and his son Eleazar are quoted in a commentary on Chronicles that was wrongly ascribed to Rashi, and the entry floats the possibility that Meir himself wrote biblical commentary. His certain work is poetry for the synagogue, signed in acrostics that spell the name Eleazar, apparently for his son.

Two poems are singled out. "Torah ha-Temimah" is a supplication woven with Aramaic and Talmudic phrases, expressing his horror of apostasy. "Almanot Hayyot" is a penitential prayer for the Day of Atonement, which Zunz translated into German. A third penitential poem, on a Crusader massacre of three thousand Jews, carries the same signature, but Zunz judged it a work of a century later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-nasi-fra:
Francisco Mendes-Nasi, head of a great Lisbon banking house and husband of the famous Gracia, is noticed in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling. One of the richest and most respected Portuguese Marranos, he died about 1536; his bank, with branches in Flanders and France, advanced money to Charles V and other rulers. His brother Diogo, who ran the Antwerp branch, succeeded him as the richest Portuguese Marrano, and with his sister-in-law spent great sums trying to keep the Inquisition out of Portugal.

The entry ends with a kinsman's repartee. Hector Mendes, a very rich man, was asked by the King of Portugal what he called his own, and answered: "The alms which I have given." The notice is short, but it sketches the banking dynasty into which Beatrice de Luna married and which she would soon lead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mezey-franz-107:
Franz Mezey, born at Acsad in Hungary on February 5, 1860, was a jurist who became the organizational backbone of Hungarian Jewry. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Destined by his parents for the rabbinate, he mastered Hebrew, then chose law and was admitted to the Budapest bar.

In 1883 Mezey was a mainstay of the defense in the Tisza-Eszlár blood accusation case, acting for Hungary's Jews. As secretary of the national Jewish chancery for twenty years, he drove progress in religious and school affairs. He co-founded the Hungarian Jewish Literary Society, edited journals with Bacher and Blau, and ran Budapest's burial society, grown to 10,000 members under him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mires-jules-isa:
Jules Isaac Mirès, born at Bordeaux on December 9, 1809, was the French financier who built a railway-and-press empire and twice stood convicted. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. A broker in 1848, he took over the Arles gas company after the February Revolution and moved into newspapers.

With Millaud he ran the Journal des Chemins de Fer and organized its investment fund, and by 1851 he owned Le Pays and Le Constitutionnel as well. At Marseilles he built a harbor, a new quarter, and gas lighting, and in 1860 he won the Roman railways concession. A five-year prison sentence in 1861 was overturned on appeal, though a pamphlet attacking his judges earned him six months in 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monzon-abraham-:
Abraham Monzon the Elder, a rabbi of the later sixteenth century who died at Constantinople, was called by his contemporaries Sinai we-Oḳer Harim — an encyclopedia, and an uprooter of mountains. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Meyer Kayserling give him his Jewish Encyclopedia notice in 1906. A pupil of Bezaleel Ashkenazi, he served first as rabbi in Egypt.

He was also a fine scribe whose Torah scrolls were still extant in Egypt centuries later. His decisions and responsa survive scattered through the great collections — Samuel of Medina's, Solomon Cohen's, Abraham de Boton's, Joseph di Trani's. Still in manuscript when the entry was written were more responsa, novellae, sermons, and a defense of Ḥayyim Vital against Menahem di Lonsano.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ha-darsha:
Moses ha-Darshan was a French Bible exegete who headed the yeshiva of Narbonne in the middle eleventh century. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He came from a Narbonne family long distinguished for learning. His name means Moses the expounder of Scripture.

With Tobiah ben Eliezer, Moses was the leading voice of midrashic, symbolic reading of the Bible in his century. His book, perhaps called Yesod, is lost and known mainly from quotations in Rashi. It mixed older haggadah with ideas of his own, some touched by Christian thought, which may be why it perished. Its echoes live on in later midrashim, and his pupils included Nathan ben Jehiel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosse-benjamin-:
Benjamin Mosse was rabbi of Avignon, born at Nimes on December 8, 1832. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He founded the monthly periodical La Famille de Jacob. He died at Marseilles on July 24, 1892, after a life of writing for French Jews.

His books range wide: poems, a work on the rights and duties of man that ran through fourteen editions, and a civic instruction manual. He wrote on the women of Jewish antiquity and on Dom Pedro the Second of Brazil. He also made a literal, line-by-line translation of the Psalms, with a grammar before it. In 1884 he translated Abravanel's Rosh Amanah into French.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-salomon:
Salomon Neumann was a German doctor and maker of statistics. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Pyritz, Pomerania, on Oct. 22, 1819. He studied medicine at Berlin and at Halle. He took his degree in 1842.

Neumann practiced as a doctor in Berlin from 1845. In 1875 he received the title Sanitätsrat. His essays filled many medical journals of the day. His first book treated public health care and property. He wrote on the Berlin census of 1861. He wrote, too, on Berlin's syphilis question. His fame rests most on his use of numbers. He aimed statistics at the claims of anti-Semitic writers. His 1880 book attacked the mass-immigration fable directly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-noah-mordecai-m:
Mordecai Manuel Noah was an American Jewish public man. Cyrus Adler and Max Raisin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Philadelphia in 1785. He died in New York city in 1851. Orphaned early, he was apprenticed to a carver.

Schooling came to him a few hours each day. Evenings went to the theater and the Franklin Library. Law study took him to Charleston as an editor. War articles under a pen name made him enemies. In 1813 he became consul to Tunis. He freed twelve enslaved American sailors there credibly. Overspending his allowance let opponents force his recall. Monroe's letter blamed his Jewish faith for it. Sheriff, judge, and port surveyor followed at home. His plays made him America's most popular playwright then. In 1825 he planned a Jewish city, Ararat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ohalot-tents-11:
Ohalot, which means Tents, is a tract of the Mishnah. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It deals with uncleanness from a dead human body. It also deals with dead beasts and with sick touch. Its base text is a passage in the book of Numbers.

Ohalot is the second tract in the order called Tohorot. That order treats rules of clean and unclean things. The tract holds eighteen chapters in all. It holds one hundred and thirty-three parts as well. The first part lists kinds of uncleanness from the dead. It counts the parts of the human body at 248. Later parts treat flesh, bones, blood, and ash. They ask how much of each can make a man unclean.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornstein-abraha:
Abraham Philip Ornstein was an English rabbi and school man. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in the year 1836. He died at Cape Town on December 6, 1895. At first he taught at the Jews' Free School, London.

At eighteen Abraham became minister to the flock at Portsea. In 1860 he moved to Birmingham as a school head. He ran the Hebrew National Schools there for six years. He then took a call to Melbourne, in Australia. He held that post for ten full years there. In Melbourne he ran a paper called Australian Israel. He helped found and run the almshouses of that town. In 1882 he went to Cape Town for good. He led the flock there till the year 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palm-phnix-dact:
The palm is a tree that stays green in hot, dry lands. Emil G. Hirsch and Gerson B. Levi wrote on it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its word, tamar, is shared by three old tongues. Those tongues are Aramaic, Ethiopic, and Hebrew as well. The Arabic word tamr names the fruit more than the tree.

The date palm has a slim stem that bends in storms. It sways back and forth but does not break apart. Rings on its stem mark where old leaves fell off. A crown of fronds, forty to eighty in count, tops it. The fruit grows in that crown of green fronds. Some trees are male and some are female in kind. So men must spread the dust of one to the next. Its fruit turns from green to gold, then to dark.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pecs-funfkirche:
Pecs, also called Fünfkirchen, is a royal free city in Hungary. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its first Jewish families came late in the eighteenth century. They held services in a rented room at first.

By 1835 some twenty families had formed a congregation. Growth led to a large new synagogue, dedicated in 1869. The congregation was Reform in style from early on. It used an organ and sermons in Hungarian. A school for its children opened in 1840. About two thousand Jews lived in the city then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinsk-12173:
Pinsk is a Russian city in the Minsk government. Three scholars shared its entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were J. G. Lipman, Herman Rosenthal, and Benzion Eisenstadt. Jews lived in Pinsk before the year 1500. Its archive record runs long and detailed.

In 1506 the prince granted land for a synagogue. The same grant gave land for a cemetery too. It confirmed the Jews in their Lithuanian privileges. Queen Bona confirmed the grant again in 1533. Pinsk Jews traded in the market by the castle. Some owned land, farmed taxes, and held leases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-rabbath-:
Rabbah, also called Rabbath, was the capital of the Ammonites. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. There the bed of the giant Og was shown to men. Deuteronomy tells of that vast iron bed. David laid siege to the city and took it. The tale stands in the second book of Samuel.

Under Solomon the city passed from Israel's hand again. Ammon won back its freedom at the kingdom's split. Rabbah grew great and rich once more in that age. Fine palaces rose inside its walls. The prophets spoke doom on it more than once. Amos and Jeremiah both name it as a hated foe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raphael-ben-jek:
Raphael ben Jekuthiel Süsskind ha-Kohen was a Talmudist born on November 4, 1722. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Bernhard Friedberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Livonia. He died at Altona on November 26, 1803.

The article lists rabbinates at Rakov, Vilkomir, Minsk, and Pinsk. In 1772 he became rabbi of Posen. Four years later he led the Three Communities near Hamburg. He served them for twenty three years before retiring. The King of Denmark thanked him in a letter. Raphael also fought hard against Mendelssohn and modern culture. The entry shows a strict leader held in high honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reuchlin-johann:
Johann Reuchlin was a German humanist born on February 22, 1455. Gotthard Deutsch and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Pforzheim and died in 1522. He studied at Freiburg, Paris, and Basel.

The article credits him with bringing Greek and Hebrew study westward. He served dukes as companion, judge, and ambassador. Later he taught Greek and Hebrew at Ingolstadt and Tübingen. Pico di Mirandola first sparked his interest in Cabala. Jacob Loans taught him Hebrew from 1492. Obadiah of Sforno later taught him in Rome. His Bible work led him into Talmud study. The entry then turns to his fight with Pfefferkorn. That fight concerned the planned destruction of Hebrew books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rittangel-johan:
Johann Stephanus Rittangel was a German controversial writer who died in 1652. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Forscheim near Bamberg. He died at Königsberg.

The article reports a shifting religious path for him. He was born a Jew, it is stated. He then became Catholic, then Calvinist, then Lutheran. He taught Oriental languages at Königsberg. He translated the Sefer Yezirah in 1642. He translated the Passover Haggadah in 1644. One of the earliest translations of Jewish prayers was his. A posthumous work argues the Targums prove the Trinity. That claim was also the theme of another book. The entry follows a convert who argued from Jewish texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rozsavolgyi-ros:
Markus Rózsavölgyi, born Rosenthal, was a Hungarian composer born at Balassa-Gyarmath in 1787. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. At eleven he went to Vienna to study music, drawn to Magyar song.

Rózsavölgyi built his works on Hungary's national music and themes. He became the most popular violinist of the century's first decade there. In 1812 he conducted the orchestra at Pesth's German Theater. His surname was publicly Magyarized to Rózsavölgyi in 1824. Famous Gypsy musicians of the age had been his pupils at Vienna and Pesth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabsovich-hirsc:
Hirsch Leib Sabsovich was mayor of Woodbine, New Jersey, a Jewish farm colony. Cyrus Adler and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born at Berdyansk, Russia, on February 25, 1860.

Sabsovich studied agriculture and farm chemistry at Odessa and at Zurich. In 1888 he emigrated to the United States for good. He worked as chemist at Colorado's experiment station for two years. From 1891 he advised the new Woodbine colony on its farming. He also ran its Baron de Hirsch school and served as borough mayor. He also served as secretary of the Cape May county board of agriculture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-abra:
Samson ben Abraham of Sens was a French tosafist born about 1150. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Called the Prince of Sens, he studied under Rabbenu Tam at Troyes.

For ten years Samson attended Isaac ben Samuel's school at Dampierre. On that master's death he took charge of the school of Sens himself. Asheri ranks his influence on Talmud study next after Tam and Isaac. His tosafot, cut down by Eliezer of Touques, remain principal sources for reading the Talmud. He told questioners to reject his view if theirs differed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sandals-hebrew-:
Joseph Jacobs, Immanuel Benzinger, Wilhelm Bacher, and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on sandals. In the warm East, shoes matter less than in cold northern lands. Still, people in hilly Palestine did not go barefoot as often as Egyptians did. Bible verses suggest even the poor usually owned shoes. Many went barefoot at home and wore sandals for travel.

The Hebrew sandal was a simple sole tied on with straps. Sandals were made of leather, woven work, papyrus, or linen. Some had a bent-up front or a heel piece. Two straps crossed over the instep. A third, thinner strap passed between the great toe and the second toe. Men and women wore the same style. No shoes were worn indoors. The sanctuary was always entered barefoot. The article ends with rabbinic rules on sandal shapes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiller-szines:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Solomon Mayer Schiller-Szinessy. He was reader in rabbinic at Cambridge University. Schiller-Szinessy was born at Alt-Ofen, in Hungary, in 1820. He died at Cambridge on March 11, 1890. He took his doctorate at Jena and was ordained a rabbi. He taught at the Lutheran College of Eperies.

In 1848 Schiller-Szinessy backed Hungary's revolution against Austria. He carried out the order to blow up the bridge at Szegedin. That blast checked the Austrian advance. Wounded and captured, he escaped the night before his execution. He reached Ireland, then London, then a pulpit at Manchester. In 1863 he moved to Cambridge. He catalogued the university's Hebrew manuscripts in 1876. The university made him its teacher of Talmud in 1866. It granted him a master's degree in 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shibboleth-1357:
Shibboleth is a Hebrew word meaning flood, ear of corn, or branch. Emil G. Hirsch and S. Hecht wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The word appears in several Bible passages with those senses. Its fame comes from one grim scene in Judges.

After beating Ephraim, the Gileadites held the Jordan fords. They stopped fleeing men and asked if they were Ephraimites. A man who said no faced one spoken test. Say Shibboleth, they demanded at the crossing. Ephraimites pronounced the first sound differently, as Sibboleth. That slip betrayed them to their deaths. The entry explains how a word for corn became history's best-known password test.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shma-asmodeus-a:
Aeshma, known in Jewish sources as Asmodeus or Ashmedai, was chief of the demons in the Mazdian faith. Erik Stave wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the figure. In the oldest Avesta texts he seems mostly an abstract idea. Later Avesta passages present him as a personal evil being.

Aeshma serves Angro-mainyush, the great spirit of evil. His foe is Sraoscha, one of the good angels of Ahuramazda. His special work is filling human hearts with anger and revenge. All evil in the world runs through his agency, believers held. He hardens men in evil and blocks the path of right. Whether lust defined him, as with Tobit's Asmodeus, stays undecided. The entry compares Persian and Jewish demon lore with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silveyra-miguel:
Miguel de Silveyra was a Spanish poet born at Celorico, Portugal, in the late sixteenth century. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied philosophy at Coimbra University in Portugal. Salamanca added law, medicine, and mathematics to his learning.

For twenty years Silveyra lectured at the Spanish court. He taught different sciences there, and poetry as well. Late in life he followed his patron to Naples. The duke of Medina de las Torres was that patron. At Naples his great heroic poem El Macabeo appeared in 1638. The poem celebrates the Maccabees in octave stanzas. Barrios counted Silveyra among the Jewish poets of Spain. Other critics doubt he ever professed Judaism at all. He died at Naples in 1638, the year his poem appeared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-isidore-:
Isidore Singer was an Austrian author and editor born in Moravia in 1859. Cyrus Adler and Frank H Vizetelly wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He founded the Jewish Encyclopedia itself. He studied at Vienna and Berlin, taking his degree in 1884. He then edited a literary journal in Vienna.

Singer later served a French ambassador and worked in Paris. There he founded La Vraie Parole to answer an anti-Semitic paper. In 1895 he went to New York to publish his encyclopedia. It first bore a longer title about Jewish history and thought. His many books dealt with antisemitism and the Jewish question in Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitz-yom-tob-b:
Yom-Tob ben Isaac Spitz taught Hebrew and German at Prague. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He taught in the Jewish school of Prague for years. His time was the first half of the nineteenth century. His grandfather was Rabbi Eleazar Fleckeles of Prague.

He wrote Alon Bakut on his grandfather's death in 1826. His Zikron Eliezer gave a biography of Fleckeles in 1827. He also wrote a biography of his father, Isaac Spitz. He contributed sixteen scientific essays to Bikkure ha-Ittim, a Hebrew journal. Those essays appeared in volumes six and seven of that journal. The entry preserves a teacher's quiet literary career in brief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-straus-ludwig-1:
Ludwig Straus was a Hungarian violinist born at Presburg on March 28, 1835. Isidore Singer and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied violin under Hellmesberger and Joseph Böhm. He also studied composition with Preyer and Nottebohm. His first public performance came at Vienna in 1850.

Straus toured widely and met the cellist Piatti in 1857. They concertized together through Germany and Sweden. In 1859 he led the opera orchestra at Frankfort. He settled in England in 1864 for good. There he played solo violin in the court orchestra. He conducted Philharmonic concerts in London and Manchester. He taught violin at the London Academy of Music until 1894. The entry charts a touring virtuoso turned London fixture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-suretyship-1337:
Suretyship is the pledge to answer for another person's debt. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Pentateuch names a surety only once. In Genesis, Judah pledges himself for Benjamin's safe return. Proverbs returns to the theme again and again.

Proverbs warns often against standing surety for others. It also urges sureties to keep their word once given. The Hebrew word for pledge passed into Latin as arrabo. Talmud law splits sureties into two kinds. One joins the loan from the start as a party. The other, the kabbelan, takes the debt as his own. Modern law calls that figure an accommodation maker. The entry maps an old contract idea onto modern terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szanto-emil-141:
Emil Szanto was an Austrian philologist born at Vienna in 1857. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on November 22, son of Simon Szanto. He studied at the University of Vienna. He died there on December 14, 1904.

Szanto became a lecturer at Vienna in 1884. He rose to professor of Greek history and archaeology in 1898. Greek inscriptions were his ruling specialty. His books study Athenian citizenship rights in depth. Others treat Greek state loans and mortgage law. A travel volume reports his journey in Caria. He also revised a handbook of Greek antiquities. The entry records a short life spent on Greek stones and laws.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tax-gatherers-1:
Tax-gatherers farmed the revenues of cities under foreign rule. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Under Egypt, each city's taxes went to the highest bidder yearly. The farmer paid the treasury a fixed sum. Any surplus above it was his own gain.

Under Ptolemy the Fourth, Joseph ben Tobiah leased whole regions. Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, and Judea all fell under his lease. He held the collector's office for twenty-two years. His son Hyrcanus succeeded him in the post. Rents doubled from 8,000 to 16,000 talents meanwhile. Both men still amassed immense riches. Joseph beheaded twenty citizens who refused their taxes. Toward fellow Jews, though, father and son showed leniency. The entry shows tax farming as power and peril.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thomas-emile-em:
Emile Thomas, born Emil Tobias, was a German actor born at Berlin in 1836. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He debuted in 1852 with a touring company in Saxony. For three years the troupe paid him in food alone.

Engagements followed at Görlitz, Leipsic, Cologne, and Breslau. A Berlin director spotted him and made him stage-manager. He staged Offenbach and led Hamburg's Thalia Theater for nine years. Later he managed theaters in Berlin and toured as a star. An American tour in 1886 brought money and praise. His own Thomas-Theater venture failed, though. He kept acting in Germany and Austria afterward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-traditions-1447: Traditions are doctrines and sayings passed by word of mouth from father to son. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Such traditions form a large part of Jewish oral teaching. Many legal doctrines trace their line back to Moses at Sinai. Other traditions concern national and historical events instead. One holds that Amoz, Isaiah's father, and King Amaziah were brothers. Another says the Holy of Holies stood outside the Temple's set measure. Hebrew calls tradition Masoret or Kabbalah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ulmann-albert-1:
Albert Ulmann was an American banker and author born in New York in 1861. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Public schools and City College gave him his education. In 1900 he joined a New York Stock Exchange firm. He helped found the Judaeans society and served as governor.

New York history and its Jews drew his keen interest. He wrote for the New York Times Saturday Review. The Saturday Evening Post also carried his work. His first book, Frederick Struther's Romance, appeared in 1889. Chaperoned followed in 1894 as a second novel. A Landmark History of New York came in 1901. Another volume cataloged the city's historical sites and tablets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verblovski-greg:
Gregori Leontyevich Verblovski was a Russian jurist. Herman Rosenthal and Vasili Rosenthal wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Verblovski died at Moscow in 1900. He studied law at the University of St. Petersburg. He graduated from there in 1866. He then served as a court secretary and judge.

His books collect and explain Russian court rulings. His first set covers civil court decisions from 1866 to 1875. Later sets carry the series through 1888. He also wrote on how a Russian civil lawsuit proceeds. Other works treat tax law and railway rules. The entry lists a long shelf of practical legal guides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wandering-jew-1:
The Wandering Jew is a figure from Christian legend. Joseph Jacobs wrote this long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The tale tells of a Jerusalem shoemaker. He taunted Jesus on the way to the cross. Jesus told him to go on forever until his return. The legend first appeared in print in 1602.

The first pamphlet named the wanderer Ahasverus. Eight editions appeared in Germany in that first year. Forty more followed by 1800. The story spread to France, England, Denmark, and Sweden. Reports claimed sightings from Hamburg to Paris. Claims of a living witness to the crucifixion fed the tale. The entry tracks each version and appearance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wessely-moritz-:
Moritz August Wessely was a German doctor. He was born at Bleicherode on October 15, 1800. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Nordhausen on March 7, 1850. He was a nephew of Naphtali Hirz Wessely. He studied at Halle and Göttingen.

Wessely took his medical degree in 1823. He then studied in Paris for five years. In 1828 he settled at Nordhausen to practice. He practiced there until his death. The Duke of Nassau gave him a privy title. Prussia's king named him a health councilor. In 1849 he founded two medical journals. He edited both journals until he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-adolph-gra:
Adolph Grant Wolf (born 1869) was an American lawyer who rose to a high court post. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Washington, he took degrees at Johns Hopkins. He then earned law degrees at a Washington law school.

He joined the bar in 1893. Next he took more study at the University of Berlin. Back in Washington, he worked for the United Hebrew Charities. He served there as financial secretary from 1895. In 1902 he won a seat as a judge. The post was on the Supreme Court of Porto Rico. The short entry traces a fast rise in law. It links city charity work with a federal court role.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yehudai-ben-nah:
Yehudai ben Nahman, known as Yehudai Gaon, led the Sura school for four years. Isidore Singer and Max Schloessinger wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held that post from 760 to 764 of this era. His rise broke with the old way of choice.

The exilarch passed over the men of Sura at that time. He chose a man of the Pumbedita school in his place. Soon after, the man's brother took the Pumbedita chair. Yehudai was blind in both of his eyes then. Some hold he was blind when he won the post. That fact cuts against a Talmud rule on blind judges. Yet Yehudai held that a blind man could lead prayer. His word on the law was held in high awe for ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarfati-15173:
Zarfati names an east Jewish family traced back to France. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A book man traced the line to the kin of Rashi. That line runs through his grandson Rabbenu Tam of France.
