The entry names five men of the line in brief. Elijah Zarfati was chief rabbi of Fez near 1770. Joseph Zarfati was a Turk scholar of the early 1600s. His book of sermons bears the name Yad Yosef in print. Samuel Zarfati was chief rabbi of Fez in the 1700s. He wrote a work in defense of the views of Maimonides. Two men named Vidal held the Fez post in past years. One wrote a work on the Talmud with a sweet name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zirndorf-heinri:
Heinrich Zirndorf was a German poet and rabbinical scholar who ended his career in America. Isidore Singer and M. Zametkin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Fürth, Bavaria, on May 7, 1829, he died in Cincinnati on December 17, 1893. His parents planned a business career for him, but poetry pulled him toward study.

After years in Munich, Vienna, Hungary, and London, Zirndorf taught in Münster and then took a pulpit in Detroit. In 1884 he became professor of history at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati. His works include the tragedy Kassandra, a volume of poems, and a book on Isaac Marcus Jost and his friends. A set of his sketches appeared in English as Some Jewish Women.
junctinus-speculum-astrologiae-1573:
Francesco Giuntini, known in Latin as Junctinus, was a Florentine Carmelite and astrologer to great houses. His Speculum Astrologiae, Mirror of Astrology, appeared in 1573. The massive commentary treats the casting and judgment of nativities, the birth charts on which the art staked its fame.

Junctinus gathers the rules of Ptolemy, the Arab masters, and the Latin tradition into one vast storehouse for the working astrologer. Kings and courtiers of his age kept such men close, and his book shows the learning their favor bought. Scholars of Renaissance astrology still quarry the Speculum for the tradition it preserves entire. The sheer size of the work is part of its claim on the reader.
kant-critique-practical-reason-abbott-18:
Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Practical Reason in 1788, his main work on moral philosophy. The English text here is T. K. Abbott's translation of 1873. Kant argues that moral law comes from reason itself, not from desire or reward. His categorical imperative bids us act only on rules we could will for all.

Persons, for Kant, must always be treated as ends, never merely as means. He links morality to freedom and to belief in God and immortality as hopes of reason. The book founded a major school of ethics centered on duty. Its claims still anchor debates in moral philosophy today.
kant-groundwork-abbott-1873:
Immanuel Kant published his Groundwork on morals in 1785, here under the title Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals. The English text is T. K. Abbott's translation of 1873. Kant seeks the supreme rule of morality in reason alone. Good will, he says, is the only thing good without limit.

He states the categorical imperative in several forms for clarity. Act only on maxims fit to be universal law, and treat humanity always as an end. Shorter and clearer than the Critiques, the Groundwork is widely taught. It is the classic statement of duty-based ethics. Students of philosophy still meet Kant first through these pages.
maxwell-treatise-electricity-magnetism-v:
James Clerk Maxwell published Volume 1 of A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism in 1873. Maxwell, a Scottish physicist at Cambridge, set out to present the whole science in mathematical form. Volume 1 treats electrostatics and electrokinematics, the study of steady currents.

Maxwell defined electric charge, potential, and capacitance with care and built the math his theory needed. He wrote for students who would work problems, not just admire results. The famous equations take their full form in the second volume, but the first lays every tool they use. The Treatise began the mathematical unification of electricity and magnetism that changed physics and, in time, radio and all electrical technology.

Volume 2 of Maxwell's Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism appeared in 1873, completing the work. The second volume treats magnetism and electromagnetism, where Maxwell's own discoveries stand. It is here that his theory reaches the speed of light and names light itself an electromagnetic wave.

Maxwell showed that electric and magnetic disturbances travel at a fixed speed matching the measured speed of light. From that match he concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave, a claim Hertz later proved by experiment. The equations appear here in their original form, in components rather than modern vector shorthand. The volume is one of the great achievements of nineteenth-century science.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume fourteen of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter one hundred five. A long war of words splits the King of England and his son. George has driven the Prince of Wales from the palace.

The King cut his son's income till he could barely subsist. Saint-Simon says the King did not believe the prince was his own. The Princess of Wales, full of sense and grace, softens the breach. Her court draws the most famed and trusted folk in England. Ministers feared her credit with the public and with Parliament. A royal family feud becomes state business in this telling.
mill-autobiography-1873:
John Stuart Mill's Autobiography appeared in 1873, the year of his death. Mill tells the story of his remarkable education under his father, James Mill. Greek at three and logic in childhood formed a mind of rare power. The book then recounts his mental crisis in his twenties, when dry analysis failed him.

Poetry, above all Wordsworth, restored his feelings and saved his life. Mill describes his growth toward a softer, wider utilitarianism. He also honors Harriet Taylor, his wife and intellectual partner. The book is the classic intellectual autobiography in English. It shows both the cost and the glory of a life of thought.
northern-nut-growers-association-report-:
Battle Creek, Michigan, hosted the tenth annual meeting of the Northern Nut Growers Association on December 9 and 10, 1919. This book reports the proceedings of that meeting. Like the sixth meeting's report, it opens with a long modern disclaimer. Member papers form the body of the book.

The disclaimer stresses that articles voice their authors alone. No product named is backed by the group, and none unnamed is slighted. Pesticide rules, it warns, have shifted since these talks were given. Growers must follow current label directions by law. Named nut kinds and growing methods may fail in other soils. The report preserves early American nut growing in detail.
openalex-w1794342673:
Albert Auguste, Scott Weaver, and co-authors studied this outbreak. Their paper appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2015. Fever with joint pain struck a Venezuelan village in 2010. The cause was Mayaro virus, a mosquito-borne alphavirus. Seventy-seven cases were reported in the outbreak.

Nineteen cases were confirmed by blood tests, they report. The virus was isolated from six sick patients. The team sequenced twenty-seven full virus genomes. Local strains belonged to genotype D, they found. A new genotype, called N, was also detected. The virus proved highly conserved across its range.
openalex-w2024037973:
Beverley Shea, Lex Bouter, Joan Peterson and colleagues tested a tool for judging systematic reviews. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2007. Thousands of health reviews have been published. Their quality varies a lot. The AMSTAR tool was built to appraise them. This study checked whether AMSTAR itself works well.

Two assessors applied AMSTAR to forty-two reviews. The reviews covered stomach acid related diseases. Other assessors gave each review a global quality rating. AMSTAR scores spread across a wide range. Different assessors mostly agreed on AMSTAR items. Total scores showed excellent agreement between assessors. AMSTAR results also matched the global ratings well. The authors concluded the tool is reliable for appraisal.
openalex-w2025773173:
Gary Weil, Will Kastens, Melinda Susapu and colleagues measured mass drug treatment for filariasis in Papua New Guinea. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2008. The Pacific's worst filariasis burden sits in that country. The disease comes from worms spread by mosquitoes.

Villages near Madang were studied before and after treatment rounds. Everyone was offered two drugs together, once a year. Three rounds were given under world health guidelines. Infection rates in blood fell sharply after three rounds. Signs of adult worms and worm antibodies also fell. Children showed the fastest drops of all. Worm DNA in local mosquitoes fell steeply too. The authors say follow-up must check if low levels rebound.
openalex-w2054711773:
Paul Martin and Estelle Martin-Granel traced the history of the word epidemic over twenty-five centuries. Their review appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2006. Homer first used the Greek word in a general sense. Hippocrates later gave it a medical meaning. Its sense has shifted many times since.

For Hippocrates, the word named a set of syndromes in one place. Medieval plagues narrowed the meaning. An epidemic became the spread of one clear disease. Germ science reshaped the term again in the nineteenth century. Its meaning shifted once more in recent decades. The authors expect further change ahead. Word history shows how medicine itself has changed.
openalex-w2162510673:
Evelyn Bromet, Laura Andrade, Irving Hwang, and colleagues published this study in BMC Medicine in 2011. They report the cross-national epidemiology of major depressive episodes from the World Mental Health Surveys. Depression ranks among the top causes of disability, yet basic data were missing for many countries, above all poorer ones.

Face-to-face interviews covered over eighty-nine thousand adults in eighteen countries. Lifetime rates ran higher in rich countries than in low- and middle-income ones, while recent rates were similar. Onset came in the mid-twenties on average, and women were affected about twice as often as men. Broken partnerships were the strongest social correlate. The authors tie depression firmly to social conditions everywhere.
openalex-w2168717473:
Luíz Trabulsi, Rogéria Keller, and Tânia Gomes published this synopsis in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2002. They contrast typical and atypical enteropathogenic Escherichia coli, gut bacteria that cause diarrhea. Typical strains lead infant diarrhea cases in developing countries but stay rare in rich nations, where atypical strains matter more.

The two types differ in several ways. Typical strains live only in humans, while atypical strains also live in animals. They differ in genes, surface types, and harm-causing traits as well. Atypical strains sit closer to the Shiga toxin producers, a dangerous E. coli group. The authors present atypical strains as emerging pathogens that health systems should watch more closely.
openalex-w2523258773:
Renata Nunes Oliveira, Maurício Cordeiro Mancini, and Fernando Cabral Salles de Oliveira studied natural wound-healing products in this 2016 paper. They tested five plant extracts sold in shops, including Brazilian and British propolis, pomegranate, dragon's blood, and sage. Such products are used on wounds partly to stop infection. The team measured their phenols and flavonoids, plant compounds tied to germ-killing and antioxidant action.

Infrared analysis, called FTIR, confirmed active compounds in every sample. Brazilian propolis held the most phenols, followed by pomegranate and the British kind. British propolis was richest in flavonoids, which the authors link to its origin. Pomegranate, British propolis, and dragon's blood showed the strongest antioxidant action. Every sample scored above eighty-two percent on that test. The results show which natural extracts carry the chemistry wanted for wound-care materials.
openalex-w2533504273:
G. Sybren de Hoog, Karolina Dukik, and Michel Monod led this taxonomy paper in Mycopathologia, published online in 2016. It proposes a new classification for dermatophytes, the fungi that infect skin, hair, and nails. The naming of these fungi had grown tangled over time. DNA family trees now offer a firmer basis for sorting them.

The team sequenced several genes from type and reference strains of the family Arthrodermataceae. The resulting trees largely agreed with each other and with earlier published trees. They showed the big genus Trichophyton was not one natural group. The paper therefore narrows Trichophyton and Microsporum and moves other species into Arthroderma, Lophophyton, and Nannizzia. It proposes one new genus and thirteen new name combinations. The scheme aims to give doctors and researchers stable, accurate fungal names.
openalex-w2802172273:
Francisco Tomás Gallo, Cynthia Katche, and Juan Facundo Morici, with colleagues, reviewed immediate early genes in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience in 2018. These genes switch on within minutes when neurons fire during learning. Three of them, c-Fos, Egr1, and Arc, star in this review. Psychiatric disorders, despite their differences, share memory and thinking deficits.

Memory problems may be a shared trait running underneath many diagnoses, the authors note. Episodic and fear memories suffer in schizophrenia, depression, PTSD, and other conditions. Immediate early genes mark the neurons engaged as memories form and later reconsolidate. Tracking them reveals which circuits store which memories. Their dysregulation could link molecular events to psychiatric symptoms. The review connects gene-level neuroscience with the clinic. It argues memory machinery deserves more attention in how mental illness is understood.
openalex-w2910993873:
Kaustubh Adhikari, Javier Mendoza-Revilla, and Anood Sohail lead this genome-wide association study of pigmentation, in Nature Communications in 2019. Skin color lightens with distance from the equator, an adaptation to weaker sunlight. Europeans and East Asians lightened partly through different genes, suggesting convergent evolution. Latin Americans, with mixed ancestries, offer fresh ground for finding pigmentation loci.

The team scanned genomes of over six thousand Latin Americans for skin and eye pigmentation. They found eighteen association signals across twelve genomic regions. One locus, on chromosome ten, was new for skin pigmentation. Three more were new for eye pigmentation. Known regions near the TYR and OCA2 genes held multiple independent signals, plus interactions between loci. The results confirm that lighter skin evolved convergently in western and eastern Eurasia. Latin American genomes, the study shows, still hold undiscovered human variation.
openalex-w3080673473:
Andrey Chaves, Javad Azadani, Hussain Alsalman, and colleagues wrote this review in npj 2D Materials and Applications in 2020. It covers bandgap engineering in two-dimensional semiconductors, sheets of material a few atoms thick. The bandgap sets the colors of light a material absorbs and the voltages at which devices switch.

In these thin sheets, the bandgap changes with the number of layers in ways that break the usual textbook model. Stacking unlike sheets opens still more freedom, since no lattice matching is needed as in older layered devices. Twist angle and coupling between layers become design knobs of their own. The review gathers the physics and the experiments, showing how engineers can tune tomorrow's electronics and light sensors sheet by sheet.
openalex-w3155263273:
Wayne Holmes, Kaśka Porayska-Pomsta, Ken Holstein, and colleagues wrote this article for the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, published online in 2021. It asks how researchers who build AI tools for learning should handle ethics. The authors argue that good intentions alone do not make a system fair or safe for students.

The team invited sixty leading researchers in the field to answer survey questions about ethics in education technology. Seventeen replied, and the paper sums up what they raised. Most had no training for the ethical questions now appearing. The authors call for a shared framework that joins expert guidelines with views from many fields. Such a framework, they argue, would help the field act with care.
openalex-w3202964273:
Laura Evans, Andrew Rhodes, Waleed Alhazzani, and colleagues present the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines in Intensive Care Medicine. Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to infection, and septic shock is its most severe form. Hospitals worldwide need shared, current rules for spotting and treating both fast. These guidelines update earlier campaign advice for adult patients.

The panel recommends that hospitals run formal sepsis improvement programmes. These include screening acutely ill, high-risk patients and standard procedures for treatment. Each recommendation carries a strength rating and a note on the quality of its evidence. The aim is faster, more even care, so fewer patients die of a condition where hours matter.
openalex-w4213422773:
James Ratter, Samuel Bridgewater, and José Ribeiro compared the woody plants of Brazil's cerrado across hundreds of sites. Their paper appeared in the Edinburgh Journal of Botany in 2003. The cerrado is a vast savanna of trees and shrubs in central Brazil. This paper is the third in a series on its plant makeup. Knowing which species grow where underpins conservation of a fast-shrinking landscape.

The team analysed three hundred seventy-six areas of cerrado and Amazonian savanna. They recorded nine hundred fifty-one tree and large shrub species in total. About a third of those species appeared at only one site, showing strong local character. Computer clustering sorted the sites into regional groups, from the core cerrado to distinct Amazonian outliers.
openalex-w4220965973:
The LHCb collaboration reports a test of lepton universality in beauty-quark decays, in Nature Physics in 2022. The standard model of particle physics says electrons, muons, and taus should interact with identical strength. That sameness is called lepton universality. Earlier checks had mostly agreed with it, so any crack would be major news.

Using proton collision data from CERN's Large Hadron Collider, the team measured beauty mesons decaying to strange mesons plus electron or muon pairs. The rates did not match the predicted sameness. The mismatch reached a significance of just over three standard deviations. If later data confirm it, the result points to new physics, perhaps a new force between quarks and leptons.
openalex-w4283319873:
The One Health High-Level Expert Panel offers a new definition of One Health in PLOS Pathogens in 2022. One Health is the idea that human, animal, and environmental health form one linked system. The panel, shortened to OHHLEP, brings together experts advising world health and agriculture bodies. An opinion piece like this one carries weight because so many authorities stand behind it.

The panel argues that a clear, shared definition is needed for a sustainable and healthy future. Vague wording has let agencies pull in different directions during crises. A common definition should guide joint action on threats such as pandemics and food safety. The piece sets the wording that governments and agencies are urged to adopt.
openalex-w7202285173:
Ria Goyal, of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in Rishikesh, led a 2026 cross-sectional study of resilience among medical undergraduates at a tertiary institute in North India. Medical training brings heavy academic and personal stress, and resilience may buffer its mental health effects. The team surveyed students online with a validated sixteen-item resilience measure and analyzed 324 valid responses from five hundred invited students.

Most students, just over two thirds, showed moderate resilience, with smaller shares at low and high levels. Higher resilience was linked to being further along in training, having more siblings, and taking part in extracurricular activities. The authors recommend that institutions build structured resilience programs rather than leaving students to cope alone.
openalex-w7204938173:
Leandro Soares Machado led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on neuroscience and childhood learning problems. Understanding how the child's brain develops helps explain the mechanisms behind learning problems and their effects at school. Searching four sources for 2020 to 2026 publications in Portuguese and English, the team selected fourteen studies covering neurobiological, cognitive, and environmental aspects.

Learning problems are multifactorial, the review finds, involving altered brain growth, perinatal factors, environmental influences, and school processes. Childhood brain plasticity stands out as central to acquiring cognitive skills, and cognition and school results influence each other in both directions. Learning is a dynamic process shaped by many interactions across growth, and joining neuroscience with schooling, the authors argue, is the way forward.
openalex-w7206174973:
Jose Nicolau Martins Ferreira and five colleagues reflect on how the nursing process works inside a hospital hemodynamics service, where heart and vessel procedures are done. Their 2026 article, set in a Brazilian university hospital, reads scientific and official sources, including a 2024 national nursing council resolution. It is organized around five themes, from core concepts of nursing care to the five steps of the process in practice.

Rules have advanced, the authors note, but full use of the process still runs into fast patient turnover, a wide mix of procedures, and urgent interventions. They argue for ongoing staff education, faster and simpler record tools, and a stronger safety culture. Done well, they conclude, the nursing process supports care that is safer, better quality, and continuous across a patient's stay.
openalex-w7212161373:
Valdineia Barreto Coelho leads a team on how sixth graders learn to write fables in school. A fable is a short tale, most often with beasts that talk, and a moral at the end. The team treats writing as a path with clear steps. Pupils read fables, plan a text, draft it, take the teacher's notes, and then rewrite. The study sets one pupil's first draft by the rewrite to show the shift.

The rewrite, they find, is where the growth sits. Guided by the teacher's notes, the pupil reshaped the plot. The clash, the peak, and the end of the tale fell into place. Marks on a page, the authors argue, should not end the work. They should feed a fresh pass at the text. That loop of draft, note, and rewrite is what turns young writers into authors.
openalex-w7213510673:
João Acyr Chueiry Filho and colleagues mount a psychiatric and cognitive critique of form in philosophy. Their 2026 essay engages Kant, Husserl, Heidegger, and Wittgenstein. It questions the split in method between philosophy and psychology, and the treatment of form as if it grounded the world.

Kant held that the mind actively unifies sensory material under prior forms, the authors recall. Yet how that unity is achieved, and where its force comes from, stays unclear in that account. The essay proposes a third way joining formal analysis with development, practice, and clinical evidence. Its central claim is plain: form bears witness to the world rather than grounding it.
openalex-w7213520773:
Juarez Clementino da Silva Junior examines authorship in work assisted by artificial intelligence. His 2026 article reviews published work, official guidance, and rules on academic ethics, with a Brazil focus. It separates simple chat tools from intelligent agents that can plan and carry out complex tasks.

Human-machine collaboration can be assisted, autonomous, or agent-led, the article finds. Working autonomy in a system does not remove human duty for the result. A task-executing tool, Manus AI, is used as a reference case. Integrity, Silva argues, needs human review, documented process, checked sources, and honest declaration of the technology's share. Editorial policy and authorship criteria should follow that distinction.
openalex-w7213547973:
Willrobson Franco Toledo and co-workers review digital tools for formative assessment. Their 2026 undergraduate thesis work is a literature review based on articles from the CAPES journals portal. Formative assessment is presented as a continuing process that improves learning and adjusts teaching to student needs.

Tools named include Moodle, Kahoot, Mentimeter, Google Forms, Google Meet, and Google Classroom. They can raise engagement, give instant feedback, and support self-assessment and progress tracking. Weak infrastructure, poor connectivity, and limited teacher training hold back use. Even so, the authors judge the opportunities larger than the obstacles. Strategic joining of formative assessment with digital tools is presented as vital for current education quality.
openalex-w7213983473:
Marcelo Paulino de Souza and co-workers analyse Manaus's intelligent video monitoring system, nicknamed Paredão, and vehicle crime. Their 2026 mixed-methods article uses official secondary data and specialist published work. The system was implemented in 2021 in the Amazonas capital.

Vehicle robbery fell by more than seventy percent after implementation, the results indicate. Vehicle healing rose expressively, and security forces worked more efficiently. Situational crime prevention and intelligence-led policing frame the reading. Limits are also discussed: data governance, operating costs, and legal questions around technology-based surveillance. The system is judged strong against property crime, with those cautions attached.
openalex-w7214593473:
Meika Danielle dos Santos Silva wrote a 2026 Brazilian legal article on digital inheritance: what happens to a person's online assets after death. Heirs may expect to inherit accounts, files, and other digital goods, but many are locked behind passwords and hold private content. Her study centers on a Superior Court of Justice case from São Paulo and sorts digital goods into property-like, deeply personal, and mixed kinds.

Inheritance rights, she finds, do not grant heirs automatic and unlimited access to everything the deceased left online. Courts can instead use a procedure to identify, classify, and value digital assets without exposing private life indiscriminately. The conclusion balances two duties: making inheritance effective, and protecting personality rights and third parties' privacy. Clearer specific rules, she argues, are still needed for legal certainty.
openalex-w7216400073:
Annalice Gomes Ferreira Castro led an eleven-author 2026 article on dialogue between constitutional courts across countries. Globalization, states' deep links, and the intense flow of arguments and precedents mean fundamental rights questions no longer stop at national borders. Their documentary study weighs transconstitutionalism against the risks of taking in foreign legal models without critique and copying asymmetries between legal orders.

Foreign cases can make decisions argue better and help protect basic rights, the authors find, if courts fit them to local ground, stay transparent in method, and respect each state's constitutional identity. This exchange can work as horizontal cooperation between distinct legal orders, they conclude, without implying uniformity or surrender of national autonomy in reading the law. The piece maps both the promise and the discipline that cross-border court conversation requires.
openalex-w7221122473:
Thaysa Amuy da Silva, Eduarda Cunha Pinheiro, and Geraldo Gonçalves de Lima wrote a 2026 article on the conversation circle as philosophy in basic education. In a roda de conversa, pupils sit together and build knowledge through dialogue, and the authors ask what digital tools add to that old practice.

Their sources run from Socratic questioning in Plato and Paulo Freire's dialogical teaching to Matthew Lipman's community of inquiry. Walter Kohan's point that children have historically been silenced as thinkers gives the argument its edge. Digital mediation, read through Pierre Lévy's collective intelligence, can widen who speaks. The authors conclude that the circle, so supported, strengthens critical, democratic schooling.
pare-deux-livres-chirurgie-1573:
Ambroise Pare, the great French surgeon of kings, brought out the first print of these two books of surgery in 1573. The text is in French, the tongue of his court and craft. Pare rose from a barber's shop to the chief surgeon's post of France.

The second book is his famed work on freaks and portents, Des monstres et prodiges. In it he sorts births of strange form, beasts of the land, and freaks of the sea. One part deals with sea freaks and the siren, and the book founds the learned study of such births.
plos-pbio-0020173:
David R. Halpin and Pehr B. Harbury launched a three-part methods series in PLOS Biology in 2004. The first paper sets out DNA display, a way to route large mixed pools of DNA based on their sequences. Each DNA strand acts as a label that directs where its attached cargo goes.

Sorting molecules by sequence could let chemists run many reactions in one pot and still keep track of each product. That is the base idea behind DNA-encoded libraries, now a major tool in drug hunting. Part one lays the routing rules. Later parts build genetic handling and synthesis on top of them. The series is a blueprint, best read as one project in three steps.
plos-pbio-0020273:
Miria Ricchetti, Fredj Tekaia, and Bernard Dujon traced stray DNA in the human genome in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, have their own small genome. Over time, chunks of that DNA have leaked into the main genome in the nucleus, and the authors show the process has not stopped.

Fresh insertions can still be told apart from ancient ones by their condition. Recent arrivals look nearly intact, while old ones have decayed. That ongoing traffic means our genome is still being edited by its own power plants. It also creates a trap for researchers. A test for mitochondrial DNA may pick up a nuclear copy by mistake. That is a real concern in disease and ancestry studies.
plos-pone-0000073:
Esther Clarke, Ulrich H. Reichard, and Klaus Zuberbühler analyzed wild gibbon songs in PLOS ONE in 2006. Gibbons sing long, patterned duets at dawn. The authors broke those songs into units and asked whether the units combine by rules, like a simple syntax, and carry meaning for listeners.

Certain unit orders appeared again and again, and songs changed with context, such as the presence of a predator. Patterned rules plus context-linked change are two marks of a language-like system. Gibbon song will not be mistaken for speech, but it shows building blocks of it in our ape kin. That makes these songs a useful test case for how language could have evolved.
plos-pone-0000173:
Pedram Sendi, Huldrych F. Günthard, Mathew Simcock, and colleagues published this health economics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. When HIV treatment fails, doctors can order genotypic resistance testing, a lab test that reads the virus's genes to find drugs it still fears. The authors weigh whether that testing is cost-effective for patients whose therapy has failed.

Resistance tests cost money up front but can steer patients to drugs that work. The authors model the balance of cost and benefit. Their analysis helps clinics and insurers decide when testing pays for itself, a practical question in HIV care where second-line drugs are far more expensive.
plos-pone-0000273:
Aswin Sai Narain Seshasayee published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA adenine methyltransferase, Dam for short, stamps chemical marks on E. coli DNA. The author assesses the enzyme's role in regulating gene expression, testing how much of the bacterium's gene control actually runs through this one methylating enzyme.

Dam methylation was known to affect a handful of E. coli processes, from DNA copying to virulence in relatives. A genome-wide assessment separates its broad effects from its minor ones. The paper helps settle how central this chemical marking system is to a model bacterium's daily life.
plos-pone-0000373:
Carmen Capone and co-authors investigated cell therapy for stroke damage in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They worked with cells grown from neurospheres, small balls of neural stem-like cells raised in the lab. The question was whether these cells can protect the brain after blood flow is blocked, the event known as ischemia.

Rather than replacing lost brain cells, the transplanted cells appear to protect by changing the damaged tissue around them, the ischemic microenvironment. That shift in thinking matters for therapy design: a cell treatment might help mainly by calming harmful conditions near the injury. The study adds to efforts to turn stem cell science into stroke treatments.
plos-pone-0000473:
Claudio Lunardi and colleagues linked antibodies against a common virus to blood vessel damage, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human cytomegalovirus infects most adults quietly and stays for life. The team found that a subset of antibodies against it can activate endothelial cells. These cells line the blood vessels. The antibodies can also push them toward apoptosis, programmed death.

Injured vessel lining is an early step in atherosclerosis, the artery disease behind heart attacks and strokes. If antiviral antibodies cross-react with the vessel wall, a lifelong infection could quietly raise cardiovascular risk. The authors draw that relevance explicitly, proposing one route by which chronic infection may feed chronic disease.
plos-pone-0000573:
Melissa A. Fowler and colleagues mapped two channels' presence across the rodent brain's emotion circuits, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The channels are TRPC4 and TRPC5, which let ions into neurons and shape their firing. The team charted corticolimbic expression of both channels, in cortex and limbic areas that process emotion and memory.

An expression map tells researchers which circuits a channel could influence, from fear to reward. TRPC channels have been tied to anxiety-like behavior in animals, making their addresses relevant to drug hunting. Mapping studies like this precede any claim that blocking a channel would help the brain rather than harm it.
plos-pone-0000673:
Dominique Lévesque, Francis P. Brière and Jean-Pierre Perreault described a modern way of switching on nucleic acid enzymes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Enzymes evolved subtle activation modes to keep their targeting precise, as modern cell metabolism demands. One mode uses a target-dependent module, a docking domain that engages only when the right target appears. Such modules appear in small interfering RNAs and other systems.

Nucleic acid enzymes, made of DNA or RNA themselves, cut or join other nucleic acids. A docking-based switch keeps them off until their target is present. Understanding that design helps researchers build precise molecular tools, and it explains how cells avoid costly targeting mistakes.
plos-pone-0000773:
Ken Dawson-Scully, Gary A. B. Armstrong, Clement Kent and colleagues linked heat tolerance in nerves to one signaling enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genetic variation is known to contribute to individual differences in thermotolerance, the ability to withstand heat. The specific genes and pathways involved, and how the environment modulates them, remained poorly understood. The team connects natural variation in neural function and behavior under heat to a cGMP-dependent protein kinase.

An enzyme best known from learning and feeding studies thus also helps set heat limits. As climates warm, the genes behind thermal tolerance move from academic to urgent. Model animals reveal which pathways might help or fail first.
plos-pone-0000873:
Thomas Hansen, Line Olsen, Morten Lindow and colleagues searched for brain microRNAs tied to schizophrenia, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genes that code for proteins have long been the main target in schizophrenia genetics. MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that tune how genes are used, and they play a real part in brain growth and function.

That made microRNA genes fresh candidates for the search. The team focused on ones active in the brain and checked them for links to the illness. Work like this widens the hunt beyond protein genes alone. It also fits a view of schizophrenia as a disorder of how brain circuits are built and tuned.
plos-pone-0000973:
Kevin Langergraber, Heike Siedel, John Mitani and colleagues read the genetic signature of sex biased migration, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In many societies one sex leaves home to breed while the other stays. Patrilocal groups, where females move, include both chimpanzees and many human cultures.

The team compare DNA passed only through mothers with DNA passed only through fathers. Different migration by sex leaves opposite marks on those two records. Their study tests how clearly that signature shows in chimps and humans. A clear signature lets researchers read past social structure straight from present day genes.
plos-pone-0001073:
L. Niels Cornelisse, Ronald van Elburg, Rhiannon Meredith and colleagues filmed calcium surges in dendritic spines at high speed, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fast calcium changes in postsynaptic structures are crucial for synaptic plasticity, the tuning of connections that underlies learning. Most work had studied how calcium falls after a surge, not how it rises.

Using high speed two photon imaging, the team follow the rise in tiny dendritic spines. Rise speed sets how much calcium a spine's buffers must absorb, and how strong the signal becomes. Their work links the kinetics in a spine, a structure a micron wide, to the capacity of the whole synapse to change.
plos-pone-0001173:
Tuberculous meningitis, TB infection of the membranes around the brain, is a devastating condition that demands fast treatment. Maxine Caws and colleagues evaluated a diagnostic technique called MODS culture for the disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rapid diagnosis remains elusive, since the standard smear test on spinal fluid misses most cases.

The MODS technique grows TB bacteria in liquid and watches for their distinctive growth under a microscope. The authors tested how well it identifies tuberculous meningitis. A faster, more sensitive test matters because every day of delay in starting chemotherapy raises the risk of death or lasting damage.
plos-pone-0001273:
Nerve cells release their chemical signals when an electrical signal opens calcium channels at the cell's ending. Roy Cohen, Merav Marom, and Daphne Atlas studied one protein in that release setup, syntaxin 1A, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Syntaxin works with the calcium channel and with other release proteins to couple excitation to secretion.

The authors report that depolarization-evoked secretion requires two neighboring cysteines in the part of syntaxin that spans the membrane, at positions 271 and 272. Two atoms' worth of chemistry decides whether secretion proceeds as it should. The finding pinpoints a vulnerable spot in the release mechanism.
plos-pone-0001373:
Carey Anders and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on breast cancer in young women. Breast tumors in women under age 45 tend to act more harshly than those in older women. The team wanted to learn what sets these young cases apart. They drew on records from 784 women with early stage disease.

From that group, 411 women met the study rules, split into a young group and an older group. The authors compared which cancer pathways were off track in each group. Their work maps how tumor biology shifts with age. Those maps may help doctors match care to the age and type of each case.
plos-pone-0001473:
Matthew Lohse and Alexander Johnson wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two forms of a yeast that infects people. The yeast, Candida albicans, lives in the gut of most healthy people. It can switch at random between a white form and a dull opaque form. The team asked whether immune eater cells treat the two forms alike.

Using both fly and mouse eater cells, they found the forms are eaten at unlike rates. That gap may help the yeast hide or spread in the host. The work shows a shape shift can change how the immune system sees a germ. It adds a twist to how this common yeast causes grave ills.
plos-pone-0001573:
Jennifer Hayden and Sarah Ades published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a stress factor that keeps the E. coli cell skin sound. A class of backup gene switches sense stress in the cell's outer skin. One such switch is vital for the skin to hold in many germs. The team tested its role in the lab germ E. coli.

They show the factor is a must for keeping the cell skin intact in this germ too. Without it, the skin leaks and the cell fares poorly. Skin stress paths are drug targets, since our own cells lack them. Each firm fact here aids the hunt for new germ drugs.
plos-pone-0001673:
James P. Stewart, Anja Kipar, Helen Cox, and their co-authors studied airway responses to virus infection in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The focus is a family of messenger molecules called tachykinins. One of them, substance P, is a known driver of inflammation linked to nerve signals in the airways.

Earlier work on tachykinins in lung defense had centered on nerves. Stewart's team instead asked whether the airway lining itself, the epithelium, starts making tachykinins when a virus infects it. The full text gives the infection model, the molecule levels they measured, and where production rose. If the lining joins in, then airway inflammation has a local source that treatments for asthma and chest infections may need to address.
plos-pone-0001773:
Gerard A. J. Morris, Usman N. Ikumapayi, Martin Antonio, and their co-authors identified a new bacterial type from a sick baby in The Gambia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Molecular diagnostic methods matter greatly in poor settings, where culture-based labs miss many infections and the true causes of illness stay murky.

A blood sample from a seven-month-old patient diagnosed with malaria in 2001 had grown nothing in culture. Molecular tests instead revealed a novel Campylobacter jejuni sequence type, a food-poisoning germ not previously recorded there. The full text gives the typing method and the sequence. One found case shows how much infection hides behind malaria diagnoses in West African clinics.
plos-pone-0001873:
Shiva Akbarzadeh and co-authors studied a cell-surface protein named ROR2 in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. ROR2 looks like a member of a known family of signal proteins, yet how it sends its signal was still unclear. The question counts because faults in ROR2 cause two human growth disorders, one of which shortens the fingers.

The team focused on one part of the protein, the part lost in the short-finger disorder, and tested what that part does. They report that the part is needed to switch ROR2 on, and that it works by drawing in a second protein, Src. That gives a concrete step in a pathway that shapes bone growth.
plos-pone-0001973:
Ruth Stavrum and co-authors compared the genomes of tuberculosis strains from Myanmar, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. One family of the TB bacterium, the Beijing family, dominates in East Asia and may spread or harm in unlike ways. Variety inside the TB genome may explain why strains differ in virulence.

No study of this kind had been done in Myanmar. The team set Beijing strains beside non-Beijing ones from the same country and charted their genomic diversity. A first map for a country fills a gap in the world picture of TB, and helps local labs track which strains drive their epidemic.
plos-pone-0002073:
Thimmaraju Rudrappa and co-authors studied poison-making bacteria around plant roots, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The rhizosphere, the thin soil zone around roots, is crowded: roots must cope with both harmful and helpful bacteria there. Some bacteria release their own chemical products that can steer root growth and the other microbe ties around them.

The team clarified the role of cyanide production by these pseudomonad bacteria. A poison made by one microbe can shape a whole web of interactions among plant, pathogen, and ally, a chain called multitrophic. Knowing the chain helps farmers use root bacteria to guard crops.
plos-pone-0002173:
Olivier Faivre and Mikko Juusola recorded how locust eyes turn light into signals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Photoreceptor cells capture the light that all later vision depends on, so their limits set the quality of everything the brain can see. The team placed fine electrodes in locust photoreceptors inside the living animal.

They showed the cells random flicker and natural-style patterns of light, then measured how faithfully the cells encoded each one. Comparing the two kinds of input shows how well the eye handles the scenes a locust actually meets in flight. Work like this links the physics of light to the design of an eye.
plos-pone-0002273:
Zhiyong Li, Yongzhu Yi, Xiangping Yin, and co-authors made foot-and-mouth disease vaccine proteins in silkworms, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Foot-and-mouth disease is a highly contagious illness of cattle, pigs, and other cloven-hoofed animals, and outbreaks cause severe farm losses. The traditional vaccine, made from killed virus, works, but making it carries a risk of accidental virus escape.

The team used a baculovirus system in silkworms to produce the virus's capsid proteins instead. Such subunit vaccines hold only pieces of the virus, so they cannot start an outbreak. The approach could make vaccination safer for the farms it is meant to protect.
plos-pone-0002373:
Gee, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Elaine P. S. Gee, Donald E. Ingber, Collin M. Stultz, among others. Its subject is fibronectin Unfolding Revisited: Modeling Cell Traction-Mediated Unfolding of the Tenth Type-III Repeat. Fibronectin polymerization is key for the development and repair of the extracellular matrix.

so, deciphering the mechanism of fibronectin fibril formation is of immense interest. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002473:
Nosten-Bertrand and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Marika Nosten-Bertrand, Caroline Kappeler, Céline Dinocourt, among others. Its subject is epilepsy in Dcx Knockout Mice Associated with Discrete Lamination Defects and Enhanced Excitability in the Hippocampus. Patients with Doublecortin (DCX) mutations have severe cortical malformations linked to mental retardation and epilepsy.

Dcx knockout (KO) mice show no major isocortical abnormalities, but have discrete hippocampal defects. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002573:
Ngo and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Yen Ngo, Yves Benhamou, Vincent Thibault, among others. Its subject is an Accurate Definition of the Status of Inactive Hepatitis B Virus Carrier by a Combination. The rest of the title points to Biomarkers (FibroTest-ActiTest) and Viral Load. The combination of transaminases (ALT), biopsy, HBeAg and viral load have classically defined the inactive status of carriers of chronic hepatitis B.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002673:
In 2008, David Eriksson and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Non-Linear population firing rates and voltage sensitive dye signals in visual areas 17 and 18 to short duration stimuli. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David Eriksson, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Visual stimuli of short duration seem to persist longer after the stimulus offset than stimuli of longer duration. A further point appears in the abstract. This visual persistence must have a physiological explanation. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002773:
In 2008, Karine Toupet and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about effective gene therapy in a mouse model of prion diseases. The catalog record names Karine Toupet first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Classical drug therapies against prion diseases have encountered serious difficulties. A further point appears in the abstract. It has become urgent to develop radically different therapeutic strategies. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002873:
Alison E. Coluccio, Rachael K. Rodriguez, Maurice J. Kernan and co-authors asked in 2008 whether yeast spores can live through a fruit fly gut. In nature, flies of the genus Drosophila eat yeast. When food runs short, the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae forms a dormant spore that resists heat and other stress.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study centers on the spore wall as the part that makes survival possible. It follows what happens when spores pass through the fly digestive tract. The work helps explain how yeast may spread from place to place by hitchhiking inside the flies that eat it.
plos-pone-0002973:
Shihui Yang, Quan Peng, Michael San Francisco and co-authors studied how plant chemicals switch on a bacterial secretion system in 2008. Dickeya dadantii infects a broad range of plant hosts. Its type III secretion system, a major virulence device, is governed by two main regulators.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team reports that phenolic acids from plants induce the system's genes. In other words, the pathogen senses plant chemistry and arms itself. Knowing the trigger helps plant pathologists think about blocking the signal before infection takes hold. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003073:
Manfred Gahr, Reinhold Metzdorf, Dieter Schmidl and co-authors measured the song nucleus HVC in a duetting songbird in 2008. Sex differences in brain area size are thought to link causally to sex differences in behavior and cognition. Which sex has the size advantage differs between areas and species.

In this species, pairs sing in unison, and both sexes sing. The team reports bi-directional sexual dimorphisms of HVC, meaning parts differ in opposite directions by sex. Published in PLOS ONE, unison song offers a rare check on simple male-larger stories of songbird brains. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003173:
Philly O'Riordan, Uli Schwab, Sarah Logan and colleagues report on fast drug resistance testing for tuberculosis in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Multi-drug resistant tuberculosis is a major public health concern because diagnosis is often delayed, raising spread to the community and health workers. Treatment is prolonged, and the total cost of a single case is high. Diagnosis had traditionally been slow.

Their case-control study tests whether rapid molecular detection of rifampicin resistance speeds early diagnosis and treatment of resistant disease. Readers get a practical check on a faster test where time matters. Quicker results can mean earlier correct therapy and less transmission.
plos-pone-0003273:
Jessica L. Dermody, Jonathan M. Dreyfuss, Judit Villén and colleagues study a yeast RNA-binding protein in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Production of a functional messenger RNA is regulated at every step of transcription. An area not well understood is the transition of RNA polymerase II from elongation to termination. The yeast SR-like protein Npl3 functions to negatively regulate transcription termination.

The title reports that unphosphorylated Npl3 stimulates RNA polymerase II elongation. Readers learn how one protein's phosphate state can switch its effect on the transcription machine. Such details explain how cells tune the length and amount of their messages.
plos-pone-0003373:
Daniel C. Richter and colleagues built a software tool called MetaSim, described here in 2008. Their field, metagenomics, reads DNA from whole habitats like soil or sea water. New sequencing machines were pouring out data faster than labs could check their methods. MetaSim makes fake sequencing data that acts like the real thing.

With fake data, scientists know the right answer before they start. They can test new analysis programs and see where the programs go wrong. The paper explains how the tool builds its test sets and what it can mimic. Such test data helps labs trust their results on real samples later.
plos-pone-0003473:
P. Christiaan Klink, Raymond van Ee, and Richard J. A. van Wezel tested old laws of vision in this 2008 paper. When each eye sees a unlike image, perception flips between them. Laws from Levelt describe how those flips behave. A second kind, perceptual rivalry, poses like puzzles.

It was unclear whether both kinds of rivalry share the same rules. The team found Levelt's propositions hold broadly across both. That shared behavior points to common computing steps in the brain. The work unites two classic windows onto conscious seeing. Rivalry tests are cheap and safe, which makes them a favorite probe of consciousness.
plos-pone-0003573:
Christian Mulder, Henri A. Den Hollander, and A. Jan Hendriks studied life in soil in this 2008 paper. Soil invertebrates reflect their habitat and most changes within it. They can serve as a universal currency for ecosystem quality. The team's goal was to find reference states for such living gauges.

Aboveground herbivory reshaped biomass distribution below ground. Grazing also altered the flux of soil invertebrates. Hungry mouths above thus quietly engineer the economy beneath. Soil checks must account for what happens on the surface. Soil life drives decay and soil carbon, both key to farm yields.
plos-pone-0003673:
Mikaël Lucas, Yann Guédon, Christian Jay-Allemand, and colleagues published this plant modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A plant's root system takes shape mainly through branching, which lets it search patchy soil. The team modeled branching in Arabidopsis thaliana, a standard lab plant.

Their model runs on the transport of auxin, a growth hormone that flows through root tissues. It covers both steps of branch formation: where a side root starts and how it emerges. The math gives growers and biologists a way to predict root shape, a key part of how plants find water and food.
plos-pone-0003773:
Matthew R. Skerritt and Donald L. Campbell published this channel study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Potassium channels open and close in response to voltage, and a domain called S4 carries most of the charge that senses it. In Kv4 channels, one key position in S4 holds a neutral valine instead of a charged arginine.

The authors put a non-native arginine back at that R1 position in the Kv4.3 channel. The single swap uniquely altered how the channel gates. The change shows how precisely evolution tuned these electrical gates in different channel families.
plos-pone-0003873:
Matilde Marchi, Angela D'Antoni, Ivan Formentini, and co-authors compared two closely linked cell signals in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns ERK1 and ERK2, two kinases that carry signals into cells. Both respond to outside cues and help control growth, cell change, and memory links in the brain. Once switched on, both move into the cell nucleus.

The authors asked why two such alike kinases still act in distinct ways. They traced the split to the front end of ERK1, called its N-terminal domain. Swapping that part changed how the kinase behaved. The result shows how a small part of a protein can set its job apart.
plos-pone-0003973:
Frédéric Coutant, Marie-Pascale Frenkiel, Philippe Despres, and co-authors tested a safer viral vaccine carrier in 2008. Lentiviral vectors can start strong, lasting immune responses. That makes them attractive carriers for vaccines against tumors and tough germs. Safety worries have slowed their move into clinics.

Their PLOS ONE article uses a vector that does not integrate into cell DNA. Integration is the step feared to cause harm over time. The nonintegrative vaccine still conferred protective antiviral immunity in their tests. A safer carrier could widen use of this vaccine platform. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004073:
Mariantonietta Di Stefano, Maria Luisa Calabrò, Iole Maria Di Gangi, and co-authors tested herpesvirus infection of placenta in 2008. Placental herpes infection can harm pregnancy in several ways. It may cause growth problems, early delivery, or miscarriage. Human herpesvirus 8 had been linked to abortion and low birth weight.

Their PLOS ONE article studied HHV-8 infection in lab and pregnancy samples. Direct evidence in placental tissue tests those earlier links. Knowing whether the virus reaches the placenta guides screening debates. It also informs care for infected mothers in endemic regions. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004173:
Guillaume Mabilleau and Afsie Sabokbar published this bone study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interleukin-32 is a recently described cytokine, a small immune signal made after stimulation by other signals such as IL-2, IL-18, and interferon gamma. It acts like a typical driver of inflammation, and a role in rheumatoid arthritis had recently been reported. IL-32 is one of the newer signals of its kind to be described.

The authors tested what IL-32 does to osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. They report that it promotes the formation of new osteoclasts but does not switch on their bone-eating activity. That split matters for arthritis, where inflammation and bone loss do not always move together.
plos-pone-0004273:
Natalia Meani and colleagues published this zebrafish development study in PLOS ONE in 2009. PRDM genes form a family of transcriptional regulators that modulate cell differentiation, growth, and death. Some family members help tissues and organs mature, and they switch on and off at specific phases of embryonic development.

The team studied PRDM5, a family member known as a tumour suppressor. They report that PRDM5 regulates Wnt signalling at early stages of zebrafish development. Wnt is one of the master signalling systems of the embryo, so an early regulator of it shapes much that follows.
plos-pone-0004373:
When blood flow to the brain is cut off, as in a stroke, many cells in the cortex die. Thai Bui, Judith Sequeira, Tong Chun Wen, and co-authors published a 2009 PLOS ONE study on how some brain cells fight back. Their focus was a fast survival pathway switched on after cortical ischemia, the loss of blood flow to the cortex.

The authors report that a protein called ZEB1 links two related proteins, p63 and p73. That link forms a survival pathway inside neurons. The pathway switches on fast after injury. Work like this matters because stroke damage grows minute by minute. A built-in rescue route, once mapped, could point drug research toward helping cells hold on.
plos-pone-0004473:
Patterns where proteins grip small molecules are charted atom by atom by Ke Chen and Lukasz Kurgan in PLOS ONE in 2009. Shape fit and weak chemical forces are thought to drive how proteins bind small partner molecules, called ligands. Protein contacts with other proteins, DNA, and RNA had been studied in a systematic way, but contacts with small ligands had not.

The authors examined the atomic-level patterns in these binding sites across many known structures. They looked at which atoms meet, and what forces hold them together. A clear map of the rules helps computers predict where a drug molecule will sit on a protein. It also helps chemists design small molecules that grip their targets more firmly and cleanly.
plos-pone-0004573:
What people in Kisumu, Kenya believe about HIV treatment tracks with how common HIV is there, report Craig Cohen, Michele Montandon, Adam Carrico, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. When antiretroviral therapy became available in wealthy countries, unprotected sex and sexually transmitted infections rose, perhaps because fear of HIV fell. The team hypothesized a similar phenomenon might occur in sub-Saharan Africa.

They measured attitudes and beliefs toward antiretroviral therapy in the general population of Kisumu. They then set those attitudes beside HIV seroprevalence, the share of people testing positive. Linking beliefs to prevalence helps health programs judge whether treatment optimism is changing behavior. That knowledge shapes prevention campaigns in the treatment era.
plos-pone-0004673:
Byungchan Ahn and colleagues studied how the WRN protein unwinds DNA for a PLOS ONE paper in 2009. WRN belongs to a family of enzymes that help copy, repair, and protect DNA. It also helps care for the ends of chromosomes and fix some kinds of DNA damage.

The team showed that WRN can unwind DNA even when a small gap sits in the strand it moves along. Two partner proteins, POT1 and RPA, boost that action. The finding helps explain how cells keep copying past flaws. It also adds detail on a protein lost in a rare early aging illness.
plos-pone-0004773:
Dimitrios Koutsonanos and colleagues tested flu vaccination through the skin with vaccine coated microneedle arrays, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Flu causes outbreaks each year with thousands of hospital stays and deaths worldwide. Because the virus changes and immunity fades, vaccination is needed each year, yet coverage stays incomplete in many places.

Needle arrays offer a painless patch like route that could widen uptake. The team coated tiny needles with flu vaccine and applied them to skin. Skin delivery targets rich immune zones. If it works well, patches could simplify flu campaigns. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004873:
Aashir Awan, Aaron Bell, and Peter Satir showed Kin5 knockdown in Tetrahymena blocks cargo transport of Gef1 using RNA interference, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Intraflagellar transport builds and maintains the eukaryotic cilium. It utilizes kinesin superfamily members to transport cargo into the cilium and a dynein motor for retrograde traffic. A novel knockdown approach targeted the Kin5 kinesin in the ciliate model Tetrahymena thermophila.

Blocking anterograde transport strands specific cargo. Cilia defects underlie many human diseases called ciliopathies. Model ciliates allow fast genetic dissection. Gef1 delivery requires Kin5 specifically. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004973:
Muscle wasting follows bed rest, illness and starvation. A protein-shredding enzyme called Atrogin-1 drives much of that loss. Its substrates during wasting were poorly known. Julie Lagirand-Cantaloube and colleagues studied one target in PLOS ONE in 2009. The target is MyoD. MyoD controls muscle stem cell function and specialization.

Atrogin-1 tags MyoD for destruction by the proteasome. Blocking Atrogin-1 protected MyoD in living mice. With MyoD spared, skeletal muscle atrophy was prevented. The study flags the shredder as a drug target. Stopping it might protect patients whose muscles waste away during illness or immobility.
plos-pone-0005073:
Atherosclerosis is inflamed arteries slowly narrowing. Diet, blood pressure and blood lipids all feed it. Janet Chamberlain and colleagues studied one inflammatory driver in PLOS ONE in 2009. The driver is interleukin-1, an immune signal. They fed animals a fatty diet. Then they tracked several atherogenic mechanisms at once.

Interleukin-1 regulated multiple mechanisms in response to fat feeding. One signal coordinates much of the artery-clogging program. Blocking it could cool several pathways together. The finding ties diet, inflammation and vascular risk into one chain. It supports a focused treatment idea. Rather than chasing each mechanism separately, aim at their common conductor. The study gives that idea experimental weight.
plos-pone-0005173:
Limbs grow under the control of signal families that tell young cells where to form and what to become. Two proteins, Smad6 and Smad7, act as brakes on those signals. Vargesson and Laufer reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the chick versions of these brake genes.

The pair cloned one chick Smad6 gene and two forms of Smad7, then mapped where each is switched on in the growing limb. The maps show where growth signals are likely held in check during development. For biologists, the work fills in the control wiring that shapes arms, legs, and wings.
plos-pone-0005273:
Lupus is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. A peptide called P140, taken from a spliceosome protein, can calm lupus in mice. Page and colleagues explained how P140 works in PLOS ONE in 2009.

P140 is recognized by lupus T cells and briefly quiets their response to other targets. The team showed it interacts with the HSC70 protein and acts through a mechanism involving gamma-delta T cells. A defined mechanism strengthens the case for P140 as a lupus treatment. Lupus can harm the skin, joints, and kidneys at once, so a shot or pill form of this peptide could help many parts of the body with one line of attack.
plos-pone-0005373:
A human antibody called B7-DC XAb protects mice from tumors, both before and after tumors appear. It works by binding a molecule on dendritic cells, the immune system's sentries. Radhakrishnan and colleagues traced its downstream signaling in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Binding gathers a multi-protein cap on the dendritic cell and switches on signaling. The CD40 pathway is recruited indirectly, and T cell functions change as a result. Explaining the antibody's hidden wiring helps designers build better immune therapies against tumors. Tumors learn to hide from T cells, so a drug that wakes the sentry cells and. Through them, the T cells, takes a path that pure tumor poisons do not use at all.
plos-pone-0005473:
Takahito Kashiwagi and co-authors studied a flu virus enzyme part in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The flu virus copies its genome with an enzyme made of three parts. One part, called PA, helps the enzyme grip the start of a gene so copying can begin.

The team focused on the front end of PA from a bird flu strain found in Hong Kong. They tested how that end changes the enzyme's grip. Small differences there may help explain why some flu strains copy better in new hosts, a key step in how flu jumps between species.
plos-pone-0005573:
Iris Böselt and co-authors studied water saving in mammals in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Mammals live in habitats that range from lush to very dry. Along with kidney changes, hormone systems help them cope when water is scarce.

The team focused on the receptor for vasopressin in the kidney, which tells the body to hold on to water. They examined how that receptor is involved in adapting to a limited water supply. The work links one receptor to the wider story of how mammals colonised dry lands. Desert mammals push this system to its limits, and their versions of the receptor may hold extra lessons.
plos-pone-0005673:
Vijaya Musini and James Wright looked back at two large reviews of blood pressure trials in 2009, hunting for lessons the first reports missed. Their focus was blood pressure variability, the way readings swing up and down in one person. They asked how entry rules for a trial shape the numbers it reports.

The authors pose three plain questions about starting levels, swings, and trial design. Reviews built for one goal can still reveal facts about another, they argue. Their checks matter because doctors set drug doses from trial data. If entry rules skew the spread of readings, treatment advice built on them can mislead.
plos-pone-0005773:
Jean Lehmann, Michel Cibils, and Albert Libchaber explored in 2009 how a code could emerge as amino acids chained along RNA strands. The origin of the genetic code in an RNA world is a core puzzle of early life. Their setup lets amino acids polymerize on RNA templates and watches how the template steers the chain.

Both partners' traits shape the result: the RNA's sequence and the amino acids' chemistry. Order in the chains hints at how a code might start without any designer. Such lab models cannot replay history, but they can show which paths were possible. This one links chemistry to coding in plain steps.
plos-pone-0005873:
Branislava Janic and co-authors streamlined in 2009 a method for tagging cells with magnetic particles so they can be tracked by MRI. The standard FePro method mixes iron oxide with protamine and soaks cells overnight. That long process limits clinical and lab use.

The team optimized and validated a faster labeling protocol. Well-labeled cells can be followed after transplant to see where they go and how long they stay. That visibility is crucial for cell therapies, from stem cells to immune cells. A quicker, reliable label removes one bottleneck from imaging-guided treatment studies.
plos-pone-0005973:
A germ that lives in pigs can cause harsh meningitis in people who handle or eat pork. Heiman Wertheim, Huyen Nguyen, Walter Taylor and colleagues reported the scale of that risk in northern Vietnam in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents the first fifty cases of Streptococcus suis infection found there.

The germ is often missed, the authors note, because doctors do not expect it and tests can confuse it with other bacteria. A clear case series puts the disease on the map for clinics in the region. It also warns people who work with pigs, or who eat undercooked pork, that a rare germ can turn grave fast.
plos-pone-0006073:
A chemical colitis model is a workhorse of bowel disease research, yet its course is often loosely known. Yutao Yan, Vasantha Kolachala, Guillaume Dalmasso and colleagues charted that course in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper maps clinical signs and molecular changes over time and across gut regions in mice given dextran sodium sulfate, a compound that inflames the colon.

Bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's arise from genes and environment together, so a model's stages must be known to read drug tests fairly. A time-and-place map lets teams dose at the right stage and sample the right region. The work makes a common model more honest and more useful.
plos-pone-0006173:
Predators can shape the bodies of the animals they hunt, sometimes very fast. Fabrice Eroukhmanoff and Erik Svensson studied a small water isopod, a shrimp-like animal, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They looked at how defences against predators arose in parallel in separate groups, and how many traits changed together as one package.

Groups facing different hunters developed matching sets of defences over short spans of time. Body traits moved together rather than one by one, which the authors call integration of traits. The study shows that splits between groups can begin quickly when hunters differ. It gives students of evolution a neat case of change happening in the present day.
plos-pone-0006273:
Predicting whether a new protein will trigger allergies is a safety problem for food and medicine. Suchita Singh and colleagues tested whether whole-protein physical traits can forecast allergenicity in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Traits that change uptake by antigen presenting cells may tip a protein toward allergy.

The authors evaluate such properties as added predictors in computer screening. Catching likely allergens early saves costly lab work and protects trial volunteers. The approach complements sequence-based methods that miss physical behaviour. It is a step toward safer engineered proteins and novel foods.
plos-pone-0006373:
Orange pigments in roots store the raw material for vitamin A. Dirk Maass and colleagues raised levels of phytoene synthase in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. That enzyme starts carotenoid production, and the team raised it in Arabidopsis and carrot roots. The enzyme is a prime regulatory target, and boosting it had raised carotenoids in several crops.

Increased enzyme levels caused carotenoid crystals to form in the roots. Crystals show pigment packed beyond normal storage limits. Understanding that packing helps biofortification efforts for vitamin-poor diets. Carrot and the model plant Arabidopsis tell the same story here.
plos-pone-0006473:
Thorsten Schmidt, Hans-Werner Mewes, and Volker Stümpflen proposed a new signal for microRNA targets in PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that tune gene activity by binding target messages. Their target sites are very short, so binding alone looks unspecific. Recent experiments suggested extra context around the site shapes whether binding works.

The authors describe a putative enhancer signal that may strengthen target recognition. A better signal would improve computer predictions of which genes a microRNA controls. Prediction is a bottleneck in the field, since lab testing every candidate is slow. The proposal gives experimentalists a sharper place to look.
plos-pone-0006573:
Elise Nowbahari, Alexandra Scohier, Jean-Luc Durand, and colleagues documented rescue behavior in ants in PLOS ONE in 2009. Although helping behavior is ubiquitous throughout the animal kingdom, actual rescue activity is particularly rare. The team report the first experimental evidence of precise rescue in the ant Cataglyphis cursor. Ants freed entrapped relatives in their tests.

The rescuers directed their efforts precisely, digging and pulling where it mattered. Such targeted rescue goes beyond simple attraction to a nestmate in trouble. It suggests ants assess the situation and act accordingly. The study expands what social insects are known to do for each other.
plos-pone-0006673:
Dejia Li and colleagues tested a gene therapy idea in mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. Their target was oxidative stress, which is thought to weaken muscle contraction. Ordinary antioxidant supplements have failed to improve performance in tiring exercise. One problem may be that swallowed antioxidants never reach the right place inside muscle cells.

The team used an adeno-associated virus to place extra catalase inside mitochondria. Catalase is an enzyme that breaks down harmful oxygen compounds. Mice receiving the treatment were then tested for exercise performance. The approach asks whether protecting mitochondria directly can succeed where general antioxidants did not. It points toward more precise ways of protecting muscle during hard effort.
plos-pone-0006773:
Gregory S. Berns, Sara Moore, and C. Monica Capra scanned teen brains and asked about risky acts in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brain's white matter keeps growing through the teen years. It is not done until early adult life. That half-done state is often blamed for wild teen acts. The team tested that claim head-on in healthy teens.

Scans gauged how grown the white matter was in the front of the brain. Teens who did more risky acts had more grown white matter, not less. The result cuts against the simple blame-the-brain story. Taking risks rose as the front brain matured. The find forces a fresh look at why teens seek thrills.
plos-pone-0006873:
Jennifer Evertsen, Ramin Alemzadeh, and Xujing Wang tracked childhood type 1 diabetes in southeastern Wisconsin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Several studies confirm rising rates of the disease in children. Rising body weight at diagnosis has been linked to the trend. That link is called the accelerator hypothesis. Heavier children may stress insulin-producing cells faster.

The authors assessed whether regional incidence was truly changing. They related the change to body weight at diagnosis. Local data test whether national patterns hold in one community. If weight drives earlier onset, prevention gains a clearer target. The study adds a regional chapter to a global increase.
plos-pone-0006973:
Wei Wang, Wen Wang, Xiaopeng Mei, and colleagues studied nerve pain signals in the spinal cord in PLOS ONE in 2009. Nerve injury can leave lasting neuropathic pain. Both neurons and support cells called astrocytes in the spinal dorsal horn take part. How the two cell types talk to each other was not clear.

The team used rats with a tied spinal nerve, a standard pain model. They tracked signals passing between astrocytes and neurons after the injury. Mapping that crosstalk matters for treatment. Drugs that quiet the astrocyte side of the conversation might ease pain that painkillers barely touch.
plos-pone-0007073:
Bang-Ce Ye, Yan Zhang, Hui Yu, and colleagues recorded a bacterium's response to food signals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microbes rebuild their gene activity to fit their surroundings. They sense the pools of nutrients inside themselves. The team used Bacillus subtilis, a well-studied soil bacterium.

A custom microarray covering more than four thousand genes tracked the response over time. The bacteria were fed three amino acids: valine, glutamate, and glutamine. Time-resolved profiles show which genes answer first and which follow. Such maps help engineers use this bacterium as a factory for useful products.
plos-pone-0007173:
Mayank Bhagat, Chitresh Bhushan, Goutam Saha, and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on brain responses to colored flicker. Flickering light can trigger seizures in photosensitive epilepsy. Yet brain responses to different color combinations were still poorly studied when they began.

The authors record neuromagnetic signals while people see chromatic flickering stimuli. They analyze those signals with wavelet entropy, a math tool for measuring disorder in a signal over time. Their paper helps explain how the brain reacts to the colorful displays that surround daily life. It also offers a method other researchers can reuse for studying visual stimulation and seizure risk in the brain.
plos-pone-0007273:
Yixuan Gong, Evelyn Yao, Ronglai Shen, and colleagues tested a lung cancer drug target in PLOS ONE in 2009. The IGF-1 receptor pathway often goes wrong in human tumors. It had become an attractive target for anti-cancer therapy, including a fully human antibody called R1507.

The authors use a panel of non-small cell lung cancer cell lines. They ask which tumors are sensitive to the antibody in lab tests. They report that high total IGF-1 receptor levels track with sensitivity. Their biomarker work could help select patients most likely to benefit.
plos-pone-0007373:
Rosa H. Jimenez, Joan M. Boylan, Ju-Seog Lee, and colleagues compared drug responses in liver cell lines in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rapamycin blocks the mTOR pathway and shows anti-tumor activity in many cancers. Those cancers include hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer in adults worldwide today.

Resistance to rapamycin's growth-blocking effects is common, however. The authors hypothesize that tumorigenic and non-tumorigenic hepatic cell lines differ in response programs. They compare responsive and resistant lines to find shared patterns. Understanding resistance could guide combinations that make mTOR inhibitors work better in liver tumors.
plos-pone-0007473:
