Dozens of species had never before been reported for this use, and several were new medicinal records for the country. The inventory gives pharmacologists a starting list for safety and effect testing.
plos-pone-0355473:
Na Li and colleagues study a small helper protein in eye cells damaged by high sugar, a lab model of diabetic eye disease. Diabetes can harm the retina over time, and earlier work had linked this protein to several illnesses but not to this one. The team grew human retinal cells in very sweet conditions, then switched the protein down and read which genes changed activity or changed how their messages were cut and rejoined.

High sugar lowered both cell growth and the protein's level. Switching it down shifted hundreds of genes, mostly ones that run the cell division cycle, and altered the cutting of many more. Li and colleagues suggest the protein helps coordinate growth control in retinal cells, making it a candidate lead for protecting sight in diabetes.
plos-pone-0355673:
Matt Vogel and three colleagues question a growing habit in violence research in this 2026 paper. A federal index built to gauge how well communities withstand natural disasters, called the Social Vulnerability Index, is now often used to flag places at risk of gun violence. The authors ask whether a disaster tool really fits that job.

They compared the index head-to-head with a long-standing measure of concentrated disadvantage across census tracts in more than eighty American cities. The disaster index consistently explained firearm violence less well, and what power it had came almost entirely from its economic component. The authors argue that borrowing the index amounts to conceptual drift. It measures how a community absorbs outside shocks, not the local conditions that breed violence. Using it could steer prevention money to the wrong places.
plos-pone-0355873:
Anjali Saini and Shalini Rai present a plan to map laboratory evidence on traditional Indian mineral and herb mixtures used against cancer. The formulations come from the Ayurveda and Siddha systems of medicine. Their 2026 protocol asks what cell and animal studies actually show about these mixtures, since that evidence is scattered.

The paper reports a method, not finished findings. Two reviewers will search selected databases and sort studies using set eligibility rules. Results will be shown in tables and summary text, following standard reporting guidance for scoping reviews. Saini and Rai hope the map will help researchers pick the most promising formulations for closer study.
plos-pone-0355973:
Gabriel Haddad and three colleagues sort out which forms of an invasive malaria mosquito are living in Djibouti City, in this 2026 entomology study. Anopheles stephensi, an Asian species first found in Djibouti in 2012, has been linked to rising urban malaria across the Horn of Africa. It exists in three biological forms with different habitats and different abilities to transmit malaria, distinguishable by ridges on their eggs and, supposedly, by a scent-related gene.

Six hundred eggs collected at six city sites in April 2023 covered all three forms living side by side. Surprisingly, the form thought rural and a weak transmitter dominated even in high-malaria urban districts. The gene test did not match the egg-based identification, so the authors judge it unsuitable for telling the forms apart. They say the forms' actual roles in city transmission must be pinned down before control policy can be well aimed.
plos-pone-0356073:
Yang Wang, Asif Ali Safeer, and Yewang Zhou ask what makes travelers bond with artificial intelligence chatbots, in this 2026 survey study. Their respondents were Chinese tourists who use chatbots to plan and manage trips. Nearly seven hundred responses were analyzed with two statistical approaches, one tracing average pathways and one hunting for winning combinations of traits. The model connects chatbot features, through trust, to engagement and emotional connection, with the bot's social presence as a booster.

Personalization, interactivity, and ease of use each built trust, and trust in turn raised engagement and emotional connection; engagement itself deepened the emotional bond. A stronger sense of social presence further amplified engagement. The combination analysis singled out a personal touch, ease of use, and engagement as the key ingredients of emotional connection. The authors advise travel firms to design chatbots as relationship partners, not transaction machines.
plos-pone-0356173:
Chiel van der Laan and Alessandro Corbetta published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how pairs of pedestrians move through crowds. Most people in public spaces walk with a companion, side by side to talk, but crowds force pairs to adjust. The authors mined a huge dataset from Eindhoven Central Station, millions of walking pairs tracked over years, modeling how pair speed and formation respond to crowd density and flow.

Pairs slowed and reshaped themselves predictably as crowds thickened. Walking abreast favors conversation, while falling into single file favors pushing through, and pairs traded between the two as conditions changed. They built diagrams linking pair behavior to crowd state and introduced a number for how strongly a pair prefers side-by-side over in-file walking in a given situation. That measure breaks into two standard crowd diagrams, giving engineers a grounded way to include social groups in simulations.
plos-pone-0356373:
Petko Karagyozov, Inna Dobreva, and Ivelina Zhecheva report a Bulgarian tertiary center's experience with liver biopsy performed through an endoscope, in this 2026 study. Using ultrasound guidance from inside the stomach, doctors can sample the liver while watching in real time, avoiding some drawbacks of needle-through-skin and vein-based routes. The team reviewed three years of consecutive cases done with a fine 22-gauge Franseen-tip needle and a gentle slow-pull technique, for both widespread liver disease and focal lesions.

All seventy-two patients yielded tissue that pathologists judged adequate for diagnosis. About three quarters proved to have malignant disease and the rest benign conditions. No complications appeared in the first two days or over a month of follow-up. The authors present the technique as safe and effective, with shorter recovery than conventional biopsy routes, aided by live imaging that helps the needle steer clear of blood vessels.
plos-pone-0356473:
Lidong Hou and five colleagues explain why water quietly destroys mudstone from the inside, in this 2026 multi-scale study motivated by oil drilling. Mudstone formations that drink water make boreholes unstable, and the chief suspect is a swelling clay mineral, montmorillonite. The team combined mineral analysis, mechanical tests on soaked rock cores, and molecular dynamics simulations that watch individual water molecules at work.

Soaking cut the rock's compressive strength by more than half. The simulations show why: water slips between the clay's layers in stages, forming one, then two, then three molecular films, prising the layers apart unevenly while sodium ions shuffle among the water. That staged swelling explains why real cores first flake, then fragment, the longer they sit in water. The authors say blocking this interlayer hydration is the key to stable boreholes.
plos-pone-0356773:
Tae-Eun Kim and colleagues link an eye condition of early birth with later development using nationwide Korean health screening records. The eye condition scars the retina of premature babies. Records covered more than eight hundred thousand children screened near age five, including several thousand with a history of the condition, and tested six areas of development from language to movement.

Children with the eye history faced higher odds of delay in every area tested, with the largest gap in large-muscle skills. Risk ran higher still when eyesight at screening was also weak. Kim and colleagues propose the eye history as an easy flag in records, marking children who deserve close developmental watch and joined eye and development care.
plos-pone-0356873:
Nobuo Nagano and colleagues pool three Japanese clinical trials of tenapanor, a newer drug for the phosphate build-up that plagues dialysis patients. Failing kidneys cannot clear phosphate, which drives bone and heart harm; older binder pills work but pile up daily doses that patients skip. Tenapanor instead blocks phosphate absorption in the gut, and its dose is raised step by step until blood levels respond, though stomach side effects make some patients resist higher doses.

The pooled analysis asks which patient traits mark those who end up needing the high end of the dose range. Knowing the profile in advance could help doctors counsel patients and set expectations before titration begins. Nagano and colleagues draw on the three registered trials' combined records for this prescribing question.
plos-pone-0357173:
Abdul Mannan and co-authors model hepatitis C spread with a twist. Alcohol use deepens liver damage in infected people. Here it enters the transmission equations as its own factor. The virus drives much chronic liver disease worldwide. Their six-group model tracks people through stages of infection and drinking. Classic numerics can solve the stiff equations, but slowly. So the team also trained a deep learning solver. They compared its answers against trusted methods.

The learning solver matched the classic results with strong stability and convergence in their tests. Stability analysis located the thresholds where infection dies out or settles in, and sensitivity checks named the parameters that matter most. Mannan and colleagues present machine solving as a practical extra tool for epidemic forecasting.
plos-pone-0357273:
Hyeon Ah Kim and colleagues describe, organ by organ, what healthy tissue looks like under a microscope in baby common marmosets. Marmosets serve widely as lab primates, yet reference detail for the first weeks of life is thin. The team compared five major organs from infants in their first three weeks with the same organs from adults, using several standard stains and a marker of dividing cells.

Infant livers still made blood cells and held loosely layered tissue, while adult livers showed tidy plates. Infant kidneys were still building their filtering units, spleens held small pale zones, lungs had thick walls between air sacs, and hearts packed muscle loosely. Adult organs looked mature on every count. Kim and colleagues offer the atlas for judging normal growth against disease.
plos-pone-0357473:
Tancredo José Carlos and colleagues run field trials in Mozambique on feeding cowpea plants extra zinc and iron. Cowpea is a staple bean, and enriching it in the field could fight hidden hunger while raising yields. Their 2026 trial crossed three ways of applying the minerals, on soil, on leaves, or both, with several dose levels of each mineral in blocked field plots.

Combined soil and leaf feeding gave the best yields, and a growth curve pointed to one dose pair for the largest harvest. The profit peak, however, sat at lower doses, especially for iron, which could be cut nearly in half while keeping almost all of the yield gain. Risk checks stayed positive across treatments. The authors advise farmers to aim for the profit point, not the biggest harvest.
plos-pone-0357573:
Simon Alexander Berry and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for PAINLESS, a trial asking whether smoothing blood sugar can ease the burning pain of diabetic neuropathy. Painful neuropathy is common and hard to treat, and hints link flare-ups to glucose swings rather than average levels. Hybrid closed loop pumps, automating insulin delivery from continuous glucose readings, flatten those swings. The two-center crossover trial will recruit just under fifty adults with type 1 diabetes and painful neuropathy.

Each participant spends twelve weeks on the closed loop and twelve on standard care with glucose monitoring, in random order, keeping daily pain diaries. The main comparison is change in average daily pain. Secondary measures cover responder rates, quality of life, mood, and global change, while exploratory tests probe nerve function, sleep, and activity. If pumps relieve pain as a side benefit, the funding case widens beyond glucose numbers.
plos-pone-0357673:
Belal Elmarhoumy leads a lab study of the soft silicone used to rebuild faces after surgery or injury, asking how tiny added particles change its strength over time. Some samples sat outdoors in a hot, humid climate for two full years, while matching samples stayed indoors. The fillers were two common mineral powders mixed at low and higher shares into a medical silicone.

Fresh samples with a low share of silica powder tore and stretched far better than plain silicone. After two years outside, every mix lost stretch, but filled samples kept far more of theirs than the plain control, which lost about half. Elmarhoumy and colleagues conclude that a small silica dose helps prosthetic material survive harsh weather, a practical point for clinics in tropical regions.
plos-pone-0357773:
Yi Luo led a team of eight authors tracing air pollution damage in rats, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Breathing fine particles, PM2.5, harms the lungs first, but this team found effects far beyond them. Nasal exposure to the particles caused testicular injury and switched on a form of inflammatory cell death called pyroptosis.

Luo's group also tested inhibitors of that pathway and checked public gene data to support the chain. Their work suggests pollution's reach may extend to male fertility. If the damage route can be blocked, a future treatment path opens, though human evidence is still needed. The study adds weight to clean-air arguments by showing harm in organs people rarely connect with breathing.
plos-pone-0357973:
Rosella Muresu, Monica Rodriguez, and Andrea Squartini published a 2026 analysis in PLOS ONE questioning how well a standard bacterial barcode identifies Rhizobium, the root bacteria that help legume plants capture nitrogen. Identification usually rests on one gene, called 16S, assumed to match species, host plant, and origin. The team pulled thousands of Rhizobium sequences for that gene from the GenBank database and compared every pair that matched perfectly.

Among identical sequences with full records, about two-thirds disagreed on all three labels: species name, host plant, and country. Only a tiny share agreed on everything, and the single most common sequence appeared under dozens of host plants, many countries, and several species names. The gene, they argue, changes too slowly, while key traits move between bacteria on mobile DNA. Naming species needs genome, trait, and ecology data together.
plos-pone-0358073: Sowińska and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on bedsores as a safety problem in hospital care. Pressure injuries form when patients lie or sit too long without moving. The team reviewed cases at a specialist hospital from 2013 to 2020, treating each injury as an adverse event. Tracking these wounds over years shows whether prevention efforts are working.
plos-pone-0358773: Entwistle and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on why promising animal results often fail in people. They traced therapies for acute injury that began in small rodents. The trail runs from early promise through human testing to approval and safety results. As a systematic review, it gathers the full record. Seeing where the trail breaks can save money and spare patients false hope.
plos-pone-0358873:
Daniel Y Tsybulnik, Justin J Gillette, and Thomas F Heston ask whether language models agree with each other when grading clinical trial reports, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Journals expect trials to follow the CONSORT reporting checklist, and automated checking would help editors, if the checkers were consistent. The team had three leading models independently score twenty randomized trials from immunology journals against thirty-seven checklist points.

The models diverged sharply. One awarded an average compliance score of about eighty-one percent, a second about sixty-four, and the third about fifty-five. Against a strict ninety percent quality bar, the most generous model passed five papers while the other two passed none at all. Agreement between models was too weak for interchangeable use. The authors warn that swapping one model for another silently changes the verdict, so any editorial workflow needs a fixed, validated checker.
plos-pone-0358973: Hwang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on drug-resistant gut germs in long-term care hospitals. Some patients carry carbapenem-resistant bacteria without being sick, yet can spread them. The team actively checked patients over time to measure how common carriage is and how people pick it up. They also hunted risk factors. Quiet carriers are a hidden route for outbreaks in care homes.
plos-pone-0359573:
Muna Elsadig, Shamsa Kanwal, Rab Nawaz, and Qazi Muhammad Zaigham Zia wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in applied mathematics. It studies beam-foundation systems, structures where a beam rests on a supporting base, with viscoelastic constraints, materials that behave partly like solids and partly like thick fluids. The authors model the system's computational dynamics.

Their focus includes damping-induced transitions, moments when energy loss shifts the system from one pattern of motion to another. Bridges, rails, and building foundations all involve beams on elastic supports, so these transitions matter for safety. Structural engineers and mathematicians share this ground where equations predict how real structures vibrate and settle.
plos-pone-0359773:
Orarat Karnjanawanichkul and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a prospective observational study of Thai adults under general anesthesia. The authors hunt for predictors of needing airway adjuncts, extra devices that keep the airway open, during mask ventilation.

Predicting who will be hard to ventilate lets anesthetists prepare equipment and help before trouble starts. Observing patients prospectively, as care unfolds, captures real practice rather than records alone. Anesthesia teams are the readers, since failed mask ventilation is one of the emergencies their specialty trains hardest to prevent.
pmc-10654273:
Philipp Schadte and twelve co-authors printed a wound dressing that can carry healing proteins, in a study published in 2023. Good dressings must keep the wound moist, guard against germs, let it breathe, and deliver treatment. Their ink blends a seaweed-based gel with four-armed zinc oxide particles, which kill germs on their own. The ink prints with a high load of the particles, in open or closed cell pads.

Open pads let the arms of the particles stick out and proved to kill germs. The particles also hold proteins well, which marks them as drug carriers. Skin tests on removed skin showed no harm from the gel pads. The team sees the pad as a platform: swap the protein, test the treatment. Each print can be shaped to the patient. The work joins printing craft with wound care needs.
pmc-10655373:
Yasuyuki Suzuki and his four co-authors lay out, in a 2023 protocol paper, a trial testing whether lighter anesthesia can stop a common childhood side effect. About thirty percent of young children wake from anesthesia agitated or delirious, thrashing and inconsolable. The cause is unclear, but total exposure to the anesthetic gas is a suspect. Brain-wave monitors can show how deep a child is, moment to moment.

The trial will randomize 180 children aged one to six, all having low-pain surgery, into two arms. One gets the standard fixed dose of sevoflurane gas. The other gets the minimum the brain monitor says is enough. Blinded observers will score delirium in the recovery room over the first half hour. The authors reason that routinely giving a standard dose may simply be giving too much, and that the monitor can prove it.
pmc-10656773:
Husain Shakil and co-authors (2023) studied when life support is withdrawn after severe neck spinal cord injury. The decision is grave and lacks clear guidelines. The team used a North American trauma database covering 2017 to 2020. It held 5,070 adults with complete cervical cord injury at 477 hospitals. About nineteen percent had life support withdrawn during admission. A statistical model weighed patient, injury, and hospital factors together.

Older age, male sex, prior dementia, deep coma, and cardiac arrest before arrival all raised the odds. So did very high injury levels and severe head or chest injuries. Black and Asian patients were less likely to have support withdrawn than white patients. Even after accounting for case mix, hospitals differed a lot in their rates. The authors call for shared guidelines, hoping to make these decisions more consistent and more fair across centers.
pmc-10657373:
Kenji Shibata and co-authors published a 2023 study on transistors built from a single speck of semiconductor. The specks, colloidal quantum dots of lead sulfide, are under ten nanometers wide and made by liquid chemistry. In principle they could switch single electrons even at room heat, a prized trick for future devices. Building such a transistor, though, is hard, and few groups had managed it.

The team coupled one dot, coated in oleic acid, to metal contacts separated by a nanoscale gap. They watched single electrons tunnel through one by one. The behavior changed with dot size: charging energy and conductance depended on which internal level the electron used. An electric field could reshape the dot's grip on electrons, and a magnetic resonance effect known from metals appeared too. Small dots held charge so strongly that single-electron switching worked at room temperature.
pmc-10673473:
Valentina Orlandi and seven colleagues published a food science study in two thousand twenty-three on turning unwanted fish into collagen peptides. Small or unwanted catches are often discarded. Their collagen could instead become a health ingredient if extracted cleanly.

The team used ultrasound and enzymes to extract peptides from grey mullet, both from mixed scraps and from whole fish. Small peptide fractions dominated the yield. The process also recovered oils and other proteins, adding value. Lab checks confirmed the collagen content of each fraction. On human vessel cells, the smallest fraction showed clear effects at a low dose. A scratch test suggested support for wound closing. The authors pitch a green use for fishery side streams.
pmc-10674773:
Lunin, Andreyanov, Makarov, and Bermeshev polymerized a class of monomers in this study from twenty twenty-three. Norbornenes carrying bromine-tipped chains are prized starting points for membrane materials. Their stiff backbones give heat and chemical resistance. Yet making long homopolymers from them is often hard.

The team varied the chain length between the ring and the bromine, from one to four carbon links. Palladium catalysts with carbene ligands drove the additions. The closer the bromine sat to the reactive bond, the slower the monomer reacted. The longest-linker monomer reacted fastest of the three. With tuned catalysts and conditions, chain weights reached very high values. The authors also mapped the basic physical traits of the new polymers.
pmc-10675273:
Jiayue Xu and co-authors present a light network that guesses depth from one panoramic image, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Wide views help robots and self-driving cars, but warp and wide context strain depth tools. Their design joins a warp-aware attention block with a global scene block.

The attention block flexes its view window by place to handle warp. The scene block folds whole-view context into the feature maps. Tests on three sets, fake and real, matched top rivals on scores. The net is small and bends to new uses with ease. Readers in mobile AR get a depth tool built for tight hardware.
pmc-10686373:
Sneha Datwani and co-authors track the T cell arm of immunity in older adults through COVID-19 vaccination and later infection. Older people often make weaker antibody responses, but their T cells were less charted. The team measured spike-reactive T cells in 40 older adults and 50 younger health workers after two and three vaccine doses, and in a subgroup after a first breakthrough infection.

A third dose lifted both helper and killer T cell counts above the two-dose levels in both age groups. After either dose, older and younger adults did not differ meaningfully, and age itself did not predict weaker cellular responses once other factors were counted. A person's post-second-dose count was the best predictor of their later one. Breakthrough infection raised counts again, equally in both groups. The authors conclude that older adults mount robust T cell defenses.
pmc-10688873:
Huan Shu and Jingyi Duan study social responsibility in China's construction industry in a 2023 paper. They ask whether meeting duties to shareholders and employees helps or hurts the industry's competitiveness, and whether day-to-day operations management carries that effect. Their data cover the construction industry in twelve provinces from 2015 to 2020.

They found a curved pattern: overall responsibility first raised competitiveness, then lowered it past a point. Duties to shareholders followed the same curve, while duties to employees showed the reverse curve. Responsibility also shaped operations management, which itself raised competitiveness and carried part of the link. The findings give managers a more nuanced view than a simple claim that doing good always pays.
pmc-10689373: Qi Ting Tan, Tania Morgan, and James Patrick Scurry describe a benign vulval tumor with an unusual inflammatory rim in this 2023 case report. A woman in her late twenties noticed a cyst-like lump during pregnancy that hurt and kept growing. Lab study identified it as a superficial myofibroblastoma, a soft-tissue growth with well-known features under the microscope.
pmc-10691173:
Monica Carolina Nery Wittmaack and co-authors compare three ways of removing the gallbladder with keyhole surgery, using rabbits as the test model, in a 2023 paper. Gallbladder removal is common in people and animals, and surgeons differ in how they dissect and seal the duct. The team randomised thirty rabbits among three techniques, mixing two dissection styles with two duct-sealing methods. Outcomes covered complications, liver blood tests, scar tissue, and liver-bed tissue changes.

One approach, dissecting from the top down with a hook tool and a slipknot seal, took longer to free the gallbladder. Bleeding and accidental punctures were similar across all three groups. Two liver enzymes rose more after the first technique by day three. Later checks compared internal adhesions and healing. The study helps veterinary and training surgeons weigh speed, safety, and tissue cost.
pmc-10691773:
Paul Sands leads an eight-author team measuring dopamine flickers in the human brain during learning, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Work in animals long hinted that dopamine encodes reward prediction errors. Those are the gaps between what was expected and what was received. Direct proof in humans was thin on the ground till now.

The volunteers were patients in the midst of deep brain stimulation surgery. Electrodes recorded dopamine release in the striatum at subsecond speed. At the same time, the patients played a probabilistic reward and punishment game. Dopamine was found to encode both reward and punishment prediction errors at once. The two signals showed up in distinct time intervals, through separate mechanisms. The results give the classic learning hypothesis its first direct subsecond support in humans. They add a twist for punishment that the old view did not have.
pmc-10693573:
Yuval Or and co-authors introduce, in 2023, a computer-based method for dating the lining of the womb within the menstrual cycle. Knowing the cycle day guides fertility care, yet current dating methods are disputed and often wrong. Their approach photographs fresh tissue at high magnification and analyzes the images statistically.

In a clinical trial, image features were compared with patient reports, blood hormone levels, and the standard microscope method. The new method agreed strongly with the standard in the post-ovulation phase. Because it works on living tissue without cutting samples, it can be repeated, and the authors suggest timing embryo transfer in fertility treatment as a first use.
pmc-10694573:
Teresa Smith and colleagues compared immune responses to natural Zika infection and to a DNA vaccine in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. Zika can cause severe birth outcomes, so vaccines are urgently needed, along with better blood tests for past infection. They built a test around two lab-made antibodies that block the virus strongly.

Blood from naturally infected people reliably competed with both antibodies, while vaccine samples did not do so consistently. The test proved accurate and did not confuse Zika with dengue. Vaccine scientists learn that natural and vaccine-made immunity differ in a measurable way, which matters for judging future vaccines.
pmc-10694873:
Li and five co-authors studied in twenty twenty-three whether a simple ratio predicts diabetes in Chinese adults with pre-diabetes. The ratio divides creatinine, a waste product tied to muscle, by body weight. Little evidence existed on whether it forecasts who will progress to full diabetes.

The study followed twenty-four thousand five hundred six adults who had health checks between twenty ten and twenty sixteen. About ten percent developed diabetes during follow-up. Higher ratios meant lower risk: each unit rise cut risk by over half in adjusted models. The link was curved, with a turning point the authors identify. The protective link was strongest in younger adults and those with lower blood pressure or blood fats.
pmc-10694973:
Buda and four co-authors study silver stress in a salt loving archaeon, in work from twenty twenty-three. The microbe Haloferax alexandrinus lives in extreme salt and can make silver nanoparticles. How it tolerates silver at the gene level had been overlooked.

Growth tests confirmed the microbe survives silver exposure. Microscopy showed silver nanoparticles in cultures at the highest dose. Gene activity profiling at three silver levels revealed many changed genes. The pattern points to the molecular tools behind heavy metal tolerance. Such salt hardy microbes could serve in metal recovery or sensing in harsh brines.
pmc-10696673:
Harring and eight co-authors argue for a new medical subject heading, in work from twenty twenty-three. Subject headings organize the medical literature for searching. The heading Call Center covers everything from sales desks to emergency dispatch, which blurs a critical function.

Emergency medical communication centers handle urgent calls and dispatch ambulances under time pressure. The authors recommend the precise heading Emergency Medical Communication Center. A sharper term would let researchers find studies on emergency dispatch without wading through general call center literature. The short piece is a terminology proposal to the indexing community.
pmc-10696873:
Ricardo Blázquez-Encinas and co-authors study the RNA splicing machinery in lung carcinoids, a rare and slow-growing lung tumor type, in a 2023 study. Splicing cuts and rejoins RNA messages, and faults in that machinery are a growing theme in cancer research. The team measured splicing parts in twenty-five tumors and checked the results in a second set of samples. They then tested three altered factors in tumor cells grown in the lab.

The splicing machinery was widely out of tune in the tumors. Three factors, named NOVA1, PRPF8, and SRSF10, stood out between tumor and healthy tissue. Each factor linked to its own set of splicing changes and cell pathways. Turning the factors up or down in lab cells shifted growth and colony counts as expected. The authors propose the trio as markers and possible drug targets for these tumors.
pmc-10700573:
Wenlu Li, Steffen Tiedt, and Eng Lo wrote this 2023 commentary on a protein best known from brain disease turning up in the pancreas. The protein, called tau, helps hold cell scaffolding in place. A recent study proposed that too much tau in the pancreas's insulin making cells could choke off insulin release.

That study mixed cell tests, animal models, and patient tissue. It confirmed tau sits in the insulin cells of both healthy people and patients with type 2 diabetes, and that its levels run higher in the patients. The commentary weighs what this brain and pancreas link could mean for both diabetes and Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-10705673:
Xiaoqi Xu and co-authors run, in 2023, a tank experiment on how combined stressors reshape lake-bottom animal communities. Forty-eight large outdoor tanks mimicked shallow lakes under crossed treatments: added nutrients, sustained warming, and a common pesticide. These bottom animals drive nutrient cycling and sediment breakdown, and they are declining in real lakes.

Warming stood out as the strongest force, raising species richness and diversity by speeding metabolism, growth, and reproduction. Nutrient enrichment and the pesticide each left marks, and their interactions with heat were the understudied piece this design targeted. The authors warn single-stressor studies misjudge how lakes will respond when stressors arrive together.
pmc-10706373:
Shotaro Teruya leads a team screening young baseball players for a serious elbow condition, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. Osteochondritis dissecans of the elbow can end a young pitcher's development if caught late. Many cases produce no symptoms at first.

Screening ran for two years across Ibaraki Prefecture in Japan, with the local high school baseball federation's help. One hundred sixty elementary students were invited; one hundred thirty-five were successfully screened. Pitchers, catchers, and symptomatic players received physical exams and ultrasound. Ten students had the condition, and seven of them felt nothing wrong. Limited extension range and pain on extending the elbow emerged as significant risk factors. The authors advocate field screening to catch silent cases.
pmc-10707273:
A rare disease that blends traits of several immune illnesses often scars the lungs, and that scarring is a main cause of death in these patients. Manuel Silvério-António and co-authors hunt for warning signs of the scarring in a 2023 study of patients across Portugal. All patients in the study had chest scans on record, so lung state could be checked directly.

Nearly half the group had lung scarring, and about half of those had no symptoms at all. Most showed a pinched breathing pattern and one common scan pattern. Swollen glands at the start of illness and older age at diagnosis each predicted scarring on their own. Gut involvement also tracked with scarring in simpler tests. The authors say a scan is worth doing even when a patient feels fine.
pmc-10707673:
Ksenia Baranova, Natalia Nalivaeva, and Elena Rybnikova review how brief remote ischemia can shield the brain. In this method, short blood flow cuts in a limb trigger body-wide protection. The review sums up the biochemical paths that carry that shield. A nerve-immune-hormone route passes the signal from limb to brain.

Early and late phases of protection rest on distinct molecule sets. Parts block cell death, curb oxidation harm, and calm swelling. A brain hub for memory, the hippocampus, gains cover against later damage. Hormone stress systems join the story through hypoxia-linked factors. The authors tie those links into one adaptive picture of the method.
pmc-10708673:
Nam-Kyung Lee and a team of co-authors tour the physics of charged polymers, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. The tour starts from a landmark nineteen seventy-six paper and the early work that treated charge as spread evenly. Newer study shifts focus to the exact order of charges along the chain.

The authors revisit how such chains pair up and mix. A random charged chain in poor solvent forms pearl-necklace shapes, their worked example. The pearls split mass and charge unevenly and keep reshaping over time. Single chains often break the group averages, giving rich varied behavior.
pmc-10708973:
Sebastião Vieira de Morais and co-authors track blood loss in spine fusion for curved spines, in work from 2023. Thirty patients with idiopathic scoliosis had back fusion with screw systems at a university hospital. The team logged loss during and after surgery and hunted traits that predict heavy bleeding.

Loss during surgery ran near a quarter of blood volume on average. Nine patients lost a massive share. Older age, a wider curve angle, more fused levels, and more screws all tied to more loss. After surgery, stay length and bag count joined that list. The authors say younger repair with a smaller curve may cut the risk.
pmc-10709073:
Ruowen Liu, Pengyan Li, Zejun Li, Zhenghui Liu, Yanfeng Ding, Wenjuan Li, and Shouyang Liu build Bio-Master, a fast profiler for crop canopies in two thousand twenty-three. Knowing a crop's chemistry shows its health, but lab assays are slow and destructive. Field scans are quick but lose accuracy to canopy shape and light.

Bio-Master splits the difference: fresh plants are cut and chopped into even bits, then weighed and scanned in a dark box with its own light. A built-in model reads the scan and reports four traits at once: dry matter, water, chlorophyll, and nitrogen. The training set spans many rice types, nitrogen levels, and growth stages. A Gaussian process model does the final reading.
pmc-10709573:
Ahmed and co-authors review microgrid design and monitoring for greener energy networks. Microgrids are local power systems that can run linked to the main grid or alone as islands. They draw on local sources such as solar and wind, plus batteries, to match local demand more flexibly.

Wide use of inverter-based gear brings fresh technical challenges for control and protection. Central monitoring and smart design are needed to keep these small grids stable. The review surveys design approaches and monitoring methods in the field. It weighs what sustainable microgrids need to run safely at scale in cities and remote areas.
pmc-10710573:
Taketo Ezaki and eleven co-authors published a 2023 study of why brain tumours resist a drug that starves them of blood vessels. Glioblastoma patients often receive bevacizumab, which blocks one growth signal for vessels. Tumours adapt by turning up other signals, and this team measured those backups in human tissue.

They examined 54 tumours taken before treatment, during response, and after relapse, including paired samples from the same patients. One vessel factor rose while the drug worked, and two others rose at relapse. In paired samples, the first factor was higher after relapse than before treatment. The findings are early clinic evidence that escape routes shift over time. Knowing the sequence may help doctors time combination treatments.
pmc-10716373:
Yuhei Iga and seven co-authors track the progress of an inherited eye disease in a 2023 study. The disease kills light sensing cells over time, shrinking the visual field. New treatments are in trials, and trials need measures that detect change early and reliably.

The team followed seventy six patients using three measures: a visual field test, a scan measure of surviving light sensing tissue, and a ring pattern seen in eye images. The scan and ring measures shrank at steady rates and moved closely together. Faster ring shrinkage also matched faster visual field loss. The authors support scan and ring measures as sensitive outcomes for future treatment trials.
pmc-10716673:
Joseph Tardanico and Thomas Hovestadt use a computer model to ask how the layout of a landscape shapes the variety of life in it. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. Real landscapes mix patches of different quality, and how those patches cluster may steer which species settle where.

The model follows single organisms that live, breed, spread, and compete on grid landscapes built with fractal patterns. The landscapes vary in how much their conditions differ from place to place and how smoothly those changes run. Long-term community building is then tracked at the whole landscape scale and within single patches. Time-based shifts in conditions add realism. The work seeks rules for how mixture and pattern, not just habitat amount, drive diversity.
pmc-10717973:
Suh and co-authors extend a cord blood trial in children with cerebral palsy. The first trial paired cord blood cells with erythropoietin. This open follow-up ran one more year with 69 children. All children got one extra cord blood infusion at the start. Rehab care continued for every group in the study.

Motor and infant development scores were tracked at 3, 6, and 12 months. Groups kept their first trial labels for comparison. The team tested if paired gains held past the first year. Mean age was 4.29 years, with sexes near even. Results weigh whether one more infusion sustains the early synergy.
pmc-10728873:
Ting Fang and co-authors test in 2023 whether underactive thyroid function causes diabetes and its small-vessel complications, using genetic instruments. Observational studies had linked the two, but cause and effect were unclear. They ran a two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis, drawing thyroid data from UK Biobank and diabetes data from large genome studies, with several methods and sensitivity checks.

Estimates linked hypothyroidism to type 1 diabetes and to type 1 diabetes with kidney complications. No link appeared for type 2 diabetes or its kidney complications. The thyroid condition also raised risk of severe and proliferative diabetic eye disease. The authors report causal roles for the thyroid condition.
pmc-10730373: Xin Yang and co-authors lay out a protocol for genome-wide screens that find the regulators of ferroptosis, in work from 2023. Ferroptosis is an iron-driven form of cell death set off by fat damage, and it holds promise as a therapy lever. The protocol uses CRISPR knockout screens: cells lose one gene at a time, then face a death trigger. Steps cover library growth, drug dosing, sequencing prep, and a named analysis pipeline. A follow-up method checks the candidate regulators fast.
pmc-10732073:
Barbara Clough and five co-authors find a host protein crew that tags a parasite's home bubble for doom in human cells, in a 2023 journal article. The parasite, Toxoplasma, lives in a third of all people and is held in check by means still not fully known. An alarm cytokine wakes the cell's inner guards.

In woken human vessel cells, three host proteins home to the parasite's bubble once it is tagged. One, an energy driven sorter called p97, works in many tag based cell jobs. With the crew set, the bubble is steered to an acid bath that kills its guest. The sorter hunts bubbles in many human cell kinds, not just vessel cells. The authors name new hands in the inner guard.
pmc-10733073:
Byeong Geun Park and three co-authors try a tight beam light cure on mid eczema in Korean grown folks. Their first study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Cure picks for mid forms of this skin ill are thin. Twenty-five folks with twin-side like sores had one side lit twice a week for four weeks and the mate side left as mate.

Twenty-three folks made the end. The lit side eased in ill grade far past the mate side. Skin wall work, read by water loss and hold, rose too on the lit side. The team call the beam a fit pick for set mid sores.
pmc-10736273:
Brianna Morgan, Rita Hu, and Jacqui Smith present the abstract for a presidential symposium held in two thousand twenty-three on new careers in aging research. The session honors four early-career professionals who build links across fields, push research forward, and support people of all ages.

Cal Halvorsen speaks on roots in policy and advocacy work and on sharing scholarship with the public. Lindsay Kobayashi speaks on joining cohorts from many countries to study health risks in old age. Jamie Justice presents a framework for trials of aging treatments. Glenna Brewster Glasgow shares methods for research with families facing memory loss in the United States and the Caribbean. Jacqui Smith closes by drawing the talks together.
pmc-10736773:
Kate Perepezko and Pamela Toto report on goal setting in the CAPABLE program for older adults. Their 2023 report compares how care partners and older adults take part. CAPABLE helps elders age in place by improving daily function. It is built to be person-centered, yet family helpers often join decisions.

The study sits inside a trial aiming for one hundred participants, with recruiting still open. Older adults set goals like safer showering, better mobility, and easier dressing. Care partners aimed at respite and preventing injury. Everyone who finished the program reached their goals, the team reports. The findings back care partner involvement in setting and backing goals.
pmc-10736873:
Bas Dikmans and co-authors describe a 2023 study of older adults who feel shut out of civic life in Brussels. Past work on civic activity in old age often missed how place and life history shape who takes part. The team focused on two poor districts of the city.

They held forty long talks with older residents, aided by life diagrams that mapped change over time. The talks covered paid style help, unpaid aid, group membership, voting acts, and online civic acts. Life stories were read for themes and plot. Results stress that a life course view is key to grasp why some join in and others do not. The findings will guide city policy to widen access.
pmc-10737173:
Age brings calmer feelings in many lands, and calm attention may be the bridge. Peace Amanambu, JohnBosco Chukwuorji, and Eric Allard tested that chain in 2023 on two hundred forty-two Nigerian adults aged eighteen to seventy-five. Past work had built the chain on Western folk alone. Each person scored their good and bad moods, their bounce-back strength, and how mindfully they live.

Older folk did report more mindfulness. For bad moods, the age link ran through mindfulness: once attention was counted, age alone no longer spoke. For good moods the chain stayed thin, with only the age-to-mindfulness step firm. Bounce-back strength changed neither tale. The team suggest attention training as a lever for the well-being of older folk, in this setting new to the claim.
pmc-10737273:
Lindsay Ryan studies how a spouse who gives care shapes the well-being of an older partner. Her paper, from twenty twenty-three, uses a part of the Health and Retirement Study. She looks at life satisfaction and signs of low mood. The partners differ in thinking skill, from normal to dementia.

The sample holds one hundred ninety pairs where the spouse in the study also gave care. Ryan groups the caregivers by their sense of purpose and feelings. She also uses their reports of support from spouse, children, and friends. The aim is to see which care patterns pair with better or worse days for the partner.
pmc-10737773:
Alison Huang, Roger O'Sullivan, and James Lubben wrote this conference paper, published in 2023. It frames a session on hearing and vision loss in older adults, and how these losses tie to isolation, loneliness, and mood disorders.

Two-thirds of older adults have hearing loss, and over a quarter have vision problems. The session looks at links between measured hearing, vision, and combined loss and social and mental health in a national sample. It also weighs causes such as fatigue and clinics that shut out people with sensory loss. A final talk shares results from a trial testing whether hearing aids and related support improve social and mental health. The authors treat both losses as risks that can be acted on.
pmc-10737873:
Hongting Ning, Hui Feng, and Junxin Li study cognitive frailty in China in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. The condition pairs physical frailty with cognitive decline short of dementia. Its spread and death risk in middle-aged adults were little known.

Nearly eight thousand adults from a national aging study were followed for seven years. Overall prevalence was twelve percent, and the middle-aged rate matched the old group. Rural living, long sleep, low social participation, depression, and multiple illnesses all raised risk. People with cognitive frailty died at roughly seventy percent higher rates than robust peers in each age band. An early stage of the condition raised risk only in the middle-aged. The authors urge prevention that starts before old age.
pmc-10740473:
Ishihara and co-authors stress-test three vision models on shifted eye images. Diabetic retinopathy is a top cause of vision loss. Models must hold up when clinic images differ from training sets. The team added fundus-specific noise to the EyePACS data set. ResNet, Swin-Transformer, and MLP-Mixer were compared head to head.

Swin-Transformer held the highest accuracy score under every noise type. Its score also fell least as noise grew. Calibration error showed no steady pattern across the models. The authors favor transformer designs for robust eye screening. Safety-critical use, they note, demands this kind of shift testing.
pmc-10741873:
A large team of co-authors presents a proof-of-concept study in two thousand twenty-three on a lab test for allergic reactions to a chemotherapy drug. Paclitaxel triggers immediate hypersensitivity in a notable share of breast and gynecologic cancer patients. The only workaround is slow desensitization, since no equal alternative drug exists.

The new test measures activation of basophils, a white blood cell type involved in allergy. Thirty-one patients on the drug took part, seventeen of whom had reacted to it. The aim is a blood test that reveals the reaction's mechanism and helps clinicians manage or prevent it, where skin tests have given mixed signals.
pmc-10742573:
Smita George Thoduka and co-authors track use of a targeted radiation therapy for liver tumors across Germany, in a population study from 2023. The therapy, called SIRT, sends radioactive beads through the liver's blood supply to the tumor. Billing and hospital reports cover the years 2006 to 2021.

A total of 14,165 procedures were counted. Yearly cases leapt from 99 in 2006 to 1,605 in 2015, then eased to 1,175 in 2019. Hospitals offering the therapy grew from 21 in 2008 to 53 in 2021. Liver spread stayed the top reason, but shares for primary liver cancer and bile duct cancer rose steeply. Death in hospital after the procedure was just 0.2 percent.
pmc-10743473:
Xu Yang and six co-authors test peony pollen as a treatment for painful periods in mice. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. Peony pollen has long use in Chinese medicine and holds many nutrients. Its effect on this kind of pain, called primary dysmenorrhea, was not yet clear.

In lab and animal tests, the pollen calmed womb tightening and cut pain signs in mice. It eased harm to womb tissue and lowered the rush of immune cells. Levels of key swelling signals fell. A pathway tied to pain compounds was also held down. Stress and cell death in the womb improved as well. The work gives a base for more study of this old remedy.
pmc-10747473:
Changming Dou and co-authors study how pokeweed sheds excess manganese at its roots in two thousand twenty-three. Pokeweed is a plant that soaks up huge amounts of the metal without dying. How it keeps that load from harming it was the open question.

Water-grown plants dosed with high manganese grew white crystals first on root hairs, then across the root surface. X-ray and element tests named the crystals as a manganese phosphate salt. The fluid's acidity eased before the crystals showed, and they came faster without iron or not at all without phosphate. Plants denied phosphate took far more manganese into their leaves. The root shield thus works by locking the metal outside.
pmc-10748373:
Blending two common plastics could toughen products and recycle waste, if only the pair would mix. Wenjun Shao and co-authors study a block copolymer designed to marry them in a 2023 paper on polypropylene blends.

During cooling, X-ray and heat measurements watched crystals form in real time. The copolymer's polypropylene blocks crystallized early, following the partner resin and forming a shared eutectic structure. A stable crystal form with strong performance appeared in the blend. Polyethylene crystals ended up dispersed inside the polypropylene ones, stitching the phases together. Impact strength improved at room temperature and at five below zero. The findings matter both for recycling mixed plastic waste and for pipes that must not crack in the cold.
pmc-10772673:
Liang Li and six co-authors build a prediction tool for stomach cancer care, in a 2023 paper. Patients with locally advanced stomach cancer often receive chemotherapy plus immune therapy drugs before surgery. Those whose tumors vanish completely by surgery tend to fare best, but only some reach that point. A tool that forecasts who will respond could spare others needless treatment and guide personal plans.

The team gathered clinical and tissue data from patients treated with chemotherapy plus a PD-1 antibody drug. From these data they built a nomogram, a chart that turns patient features into a response probability, and checked how well it worked. The paper reports the tool's accuracy and which features mattered most. Such a chart could help doctors discuss likely outcomes before treatment begins.
pmc-10808373:
Marco Garegnani and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three study growing radish microgreens under different LED light mixes, aimed at space farming. Astronauts need fresh, nutrient-rich food that grows fast. Microgreens fit, but light recipes shape their chemistry.

Two radish varieties grew without soil under three red, green, and blue blends. Plants were harvested eight days after sowing. A fluorescence method tracked metabolism live without destroying the plants. Light colour balance shifted nutrient build-up between the varieties. The work helps design compact growing systems for long missions where every bite should count.
pmc-10838173:
Pedro Penaherrera-R and Roberto Leon-E describe two new tarantula species from Ecuador and weigh threats to their survival, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. The spiders belong to the genus Psalmopoeus. Both live on the west-facing slopes of the Andes, one in the north-west and one in the central-west. Each can be told from its kin by the shape of key breeding organs.

The team also updated the naming marks for a third, older species of the group, based on fresh specimens. They then rated the new species for conservation risk, weighing harm to the forests and lands where they live. The paper closes by urging more care for Ecuador's tarantulas, whose homes face growing strain.
pmc-10880573:
Jing Wang and six co-authors studied a hard form of blood cancer spread in a 2023 paper. Multiple myeloma sometimes grows outside the bone marrow, a pattern called extramedullary disease. The team followed 518 newly diagnosed patients, 121 of whom had this spread at diagnosis.

Patients whose spread reached soft tissue fared worst, with shorter times before the disease advanced and shorter survival. Spread to many sites, or fast-growing tumor cells, also spelled a poor outlook. Stem cell transplant clearly improved survival for these patients. The authors built a risk score from four factors, including blood markers and a gene deletion. The score aims to give each patient a more personal survival estimate.
pmc-11524073:
Akira Saito and co-authors published a study in 2023 on a diabetes drug and colon cancer. The drug lowers blood sugar and has been tied to lower cancer deaths in patients with diabetes. The team asked if it helps colon cancer patients by calming a web that white blood cells spin.

Those webs, meant to trap germs, can block killer T cells from reaching tumors. In charts of 289 diabetic patients who had colon surgery, prior use of the drug tied to longer survival, near the level of non-diabetic patients. Lab tests showed the drug cut web output to about sixty percent of normal. Tumor samples from users held fewer web-spinning cells and more killer T cells at the invasion front. The authors credit part of the benefit to web suppression.
pmc-11532473:
Ghelichi-Ghojogh, Fararouei, Seif, and Pakfetrat study links between the world around people and chronic kidney disease in Iran. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The study is a case-control design, with kidney cases matched to controls of like age and sex from a hospital base.

They find higher odds of disease for those who live near mines or phone masts, and for those exposed to chemicals at work or at home. Heat at work is also flagged, since loss of body water can harm the kidneys. The authors urge plain steps in hot jobs: drink more, work shorter shifts, and improve air flow and clothing.
pmc-11536373:
Lisa Stagi and co-authors survey drug safety teams in Italian drug firms, in a 2024 national study. These teams track harm from medicines and vaccines and act to prevent it. Their work has grown from simple case handling in the 1960s into a complex, rule bound system.

The survey went to members of a national society for drug medicine, at both local and head office firms. It asked how safety work is staffed and run now, and what change staff expect next. New science, a complex industry, and digital tools all press on these teams. The results give firms and trainers a snapshot of where the field stands in Italy.
pmc-11536973:
Anja Botngard and four co-authors survey staff in Norwegian nursing homes on abuse of residents by their own kin. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Most past work on home abuse looks at staff or fellow residents as the source. Yet kin keep giving care after a move to a home, and strain can raise the risk of harm.

Near four thousand staff from one hundred homes took part. Close to half had seen at least one case of kin-to-resident abuse in the past year. Mind abuse was by far the most seen kind, with body abuse next and money abuse rare. The team calls for more focus on this source of harm and for checks that go past staff views alone.
pmc-11539773:
Karl Aharonian and colleagues ask if students teaching students lifts exam scores in medical school, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Peer-led sessions, where senior or fellow students run review classes, are common add-ons to lectures. They are known to help the student teachers; whether the audience gains was less clear.

The team tracked 67 first-year students at one medical school through two board-style exams. Students who attended at least five sessions formed the study group. On the first exam, on basic science, attendees scored higher than non-attendees, by about four percent. On the second exam, on organ system physiology, the gap vanished. Entry scores and backgrounds were alike in both groups, so the gap is hard to blame on talent. The authors conclude that peer teaching pays early, when the science is new, and matters less as students find their own methods.
pmc-11542473:
Hidig and coauthors report a rare first sign of a nerve illness. Guillain-Barre illness causes fast limb weakness and loss of reflexes. Up to two in three patients also have gut and heart control loss. In this case, a blocked gut was the first sign.

A 55-year-old man came in with a gut that had stopped moving. Gut drugs and vein feeding gave no real relief. Weakness then rose from his legs to all four limbs. Breath muscles failed, and a machine had to breathe for him. The case warns teams to weigh nerve causes in gut block.
pmc-11563173:
Antonio Migliore, Debjani Mueller, and Wija Oortwijn gather learning resources for newcomers to health technology assessment, in a 2024 guide. That field judges the value of drugs, devices, and other health tools to guide policy. Training people for it is a stated goal of the field's global society, since the work blends medicine, economics, and policy skills that few single degrees cover.

New programs exist but stay few and unevenly spread, so self-study materials carry much of the load. The guide collects resources that build the core skills the field has named, from judging evidence to weighing costs and ethics. It also explains how skill building serves the wider system around the work, including public support. The authors aim the collection at early-career readers worldwide.
pmc-11569173:
Alberto Iannuzzo and colleagues explain how certain gene variants trapped in the cell's shipping hub cause autoinflammatory disease through trafficking defects. Their 2024 study examines variants of a signalling protein linked to newborn-onset inflammation syndromes.

The recurrent variant sits stuck in the Golgi apparatus and blocks transport in both directions through it. That blockage makes an immune sensor accumulate in the Golgi, overactivating its pathway and the type one interferon response. The trapped variants also stressed the cell's protein-folding compartment. Variants that did not accumulate in the Golgi showed none of these effects. Patients carrying trapped variants had very high circulating interferon levels at disease onset, matching the laboratory picture.
pmc-11571773:
Weichao Wang and co-authors probe, in a 2024 study, whether diabetes raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease. Past work on the link has been mixed. The team used Mendelian randomization, a genetic method that mimics a trial, comparing people who inherit markers for a trait with those who do not. That design cuts the effect of lifestyle habits.

They pulled genetic markers for six diabetic traits, eight metabolic risk factors, and seven diabetic genes from large European cohorts. High fasting insulin and high total cholesterol each tracked with higher risk of Alzheimer's disease. High blood pressure, by contrast, tracked with lower risk. Diabetes itself, of either main type, showed no clear effect, and neither did the named genes. The authors conclude that metabolic traits tied to diabetes, rather than the disease itself, may drive the risk.
pmc-11573973:
Min Yan and five co-authors issue an author correction to a review on reservoir computing, a way of training simple networks for hard tasks. The correction is from two thousand twenty-four.

The first text had wrong reference numbers in the labels of a box and two charts. The note lists, one by one, which old numbers stand in error and which new numbers take their place. It also fixes a wrong reference number in a line about a word error rate in a part on test tasks. No claims or results change. The note keeps links from text to sources sound, so later readers can trace each cited work.
pmc-11585273:
Xiuwen Ling and co-authors compare two ways to build a rat model of a heart rhythm problem in sepsis in 2024. Sepsis is a severe whole-body response to infection, and a fast, uneven heartbeat often starts during it. That rhythm problem raises the risk of harm and death for patients. An animal model is needed to study how it starts. The team tried gut surgery that mimics infection and injections of a bacterial toxin at four doses.

Forty-seven rats were split across the method and dose groups. The toxin dose in the middle range gave the most stable model of the rhythm problem. Those rats showed a wider upper heart chamber, more scarring, and weaker pumping. Their hearts were easier to push into the uneven rhythm. Levels of swelling-linked proteins rose in the heart tissue. The authors name the pathways they think drive the problem.
pmc-11589873:
Kenji Shimazoe and nine co-authors design an X-ray detector that counts photons and sorts them by energy. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Such counting scans give fine images at low dose and can tell materials apart. Trade detectors use rare crystals, which limits the choice of build.

Their design is indirect: a fast glow crystal turns X-rays to light, and a tiny silicon light sensor counts it. The pixels are very small, far finer than past indirect builds. The test array splits photon energies with a fair spread, keeps sharp detail, and blocks charge leakage between pixels. It may ground a new line of low-dose scan machines.
pmc-11590573:
Chen and seven co-authors apply Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle management to speed medical record documentation by residents, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Late or incomplete electronic records harm care continuity and compliance. Residents rotating through a head and neck oncology unit form two cohorts. Earlier rotators serve as controls, while later ones receive cycle management.

Late records and unqualified records both fall sharply under management. Adjusted odds drop to a fraction of control levels for both outcomes. Two hundred forty-five residents are included across both cohorts. The management cycle adds training, checks, and feedback loops for documentation timeliness. Authors recommend wider rollout of the approach in teaching hospitals.
pmc-11591873:
Maha Khalaf and colleagues use stem anatomy to tell apart Ephedra species and sexes in Egypt. Their study from twenty twenty-four addresses a tricky identification problem. These desert shrubs supply pharmacologically valued compounds. Leafless, cone-less fragments defeat ordinary identification keys.

Five species, each in both sexes, were sectioned and examined. Stomata types and tissue features varied diagnostically. Growth rings and stem outlines added further characters. Ten sex forms from South Sinai supplied the material. Anatomy works when flowers and cones are absent. Pharmaceutical sourcing needs exactly this fragment-level certainty. The key helps verify raw drug plant material.
pmc-11593573:
Sabina Otarbayeva and Dmitriy Berillo build a gel that holds and slowly frees drugs, in this twenty twenty-four study. Better drug delivery could help wounds heal and allow patches that dose medicine over time. Their gel uses a common plastic-like polymer mixed with a solvent that carries drugs into tissue.

The team loaded the gel with two germ-killing drugs and tuned the mix for steady release. The gels swelled modestly, taking up some fluid. One drug came out nearly twice as slowly as the other, giving a longer, more even dose. The work shows the gel can serve as a base for wound dressings and slow-dose patches.
pmc-11596973:
Serio and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on the chemistry of two Tunisian chili pepper powders. The peppers, Baklouti and paprika types, are dried for use as spice. Two scent-profiling tools map their volatile compounds in depth. Major scent parts include several terpene family members. Extracts also prove rich in sulfur compounds, fatty acids, and sugars. Eleven bacterial strains face the extracts in lab tests. Effects vary by strain, with lab strains more sensitive than wild ones.

Gram-positive bacteria, including two food-poisoning types, respond best. The work is the first such profile for these Tunisian peppers. Results support food and preservation uses for the powders.
pmc-11598373:
Malina Flessner and co-authors test a pocket-sized climate logger meant for use inside cattle barns. Their evaluation study was published in twenty twenty-four. Heat stress cuts cow health and farm income, and acting in time needs exact, nonstop records of barn air.

The team set the logger beside several rival devices in varied barn spots and recorded for over a year in total. Readings for temperature and humidity matched the rivals very closely. Judged against a common heat stress threshold, the logger scored near perfectly at flagging hot spells. The authors conclude it performs as well as the established tools. For farm use, it is a fit and simpler choice.
pmc-11603073:
Shi and co-authors compare three ways to draw the edge zones of a city, called peri-urban areas. As cities spread, methods to spot these fringe zones have multiplied, and they do not always agree. The team tested methods on the same city to see how results and spatial patterns differ.

Zhengzhou City in China served as the test case, judged by a shared multi-indicator system. The threshold method found the most fringe land but with the lowest accuracy. Breakpoint clustering scored slightly below the multilayer perceptron method. The comparison helps planners pick a method that fits their data and goals.
pmc-11603173:
Xu and co-authors profile the chemistry and gene activity of three Paris plant species used in Chinese medicine. The plants' value rests on compounds called polyphyllins, which vary by species. The team measured these compounds in 206 samples from 16 growing areas. Based on the results, they picked samples from three species for deep analysis. The species were a yunnanensis variety, P. fargesii, and P. forrestii.

Chemical profiling found 1,243 metabolites across the samples. Gene reads produced over 92 Gb of full-length transcript data. Joining the two layers flagged genes that may build polyphyllins. The work aims to support lab production of these compounds. It also helps sort which species suit which medicinal use.
pmc-11603873:
Ming-Yang Lee, Jun-Ding Zhu, Hsin-Jung Tsai, Shih-Jen Tsai, and Albert Yang scan brains to find where sex and a bipolar diagnosis interact, in work from 2024. Bipolar I disorder reshapes brain structure and function, and its course differs between men and women. No study had mapped the interplay directly.

The team gathered structure and function scans from 105 patients and 210 healthy peers. Models weighed age, sex, diagnosis, and their interaction at every point in the brain. Six regions, including deep movement and relay hubs, showed clear sex-by-diagnosis effects on gray matter size. Links between regions shifted too. The results argue for sex-aware reads of bipolar brain changes.
pmc-11604773:
Hedlund and four co-authors update drug picks to calm the pee tube's smooth wall in this twenty twenty-four review. Stones in that tube cause sharp pain and are on the rise in rich lands. Drugs that relax the tube wall could speed a stone's pass and ease its pain.

Inside, the review walks drug clans tried in dish, beast, and ward work for years. Block drugs for one scent lock and two ring-path brakes look most strong. Pair runs of those picks may beat one drug lone in stone pass tests. Gas donor and flow drugs face wide body side acts that cap their use. One rock-path brake clan is flagged for more work as a fresh route.
pmc-11604973:
Miyuki Takashima and four co-authors trace how a garlic compound calms udder inflammation by nudging a gene-splicing choice inside mammary cells. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Mastitis, infection-driven inflammation of the mammary gland, cuts milk quality and yield. The compound, from aged garlic extract, was known to damp such inflammation without a clear mechanism.

In mice and in cultured mammary cells, the compound curbed a bacterial toxin's inflammatory push. A phosphoprotein sweep showed most toxin-raised signals falling under the compound. Splicing machinery proteins were among those dialed down. The key result: more of a short, inhibitory form of a signaling adaptor was produced. That short form brakes the very pathway the toxin fires. The authors suggest the compound could ease several inflammatory diseases through splicing control.
pmc-11605073:
Bianca Myers and co-authors report brain tumor research from two thousand twenty-four on two gene switches that drive glioblastoma. This cancer is fast-growing, invasive, and mixed in cell types. The two switches, called ASCL1 and OLIG2, appear together in the tumors, but how they jointly shape cell variety and spread was unclear.

In a mouse model, mutations in progenitor cells disturbed both switches, and tumors needed both to form. The switches bind each other's genes and shared targets, which sets the cell types in the tumor and how far cells migrate. Single-cell sequencing showed high levels of one switch mark highly migratory, stem-like tumor cells. Those cells also switch on genes tied to spread and drug resistance.
pmc-11606273:
Megha Bhargava and five co-authors published a clinical trial in twenty twenty-four comparing two ways of blocking the genicular nerves to ease chronic knee osteoarthritis pain. Blocking more nerves might relieve pain better, but the benefit was unproven. The double-blinded randomized trial ran at a hospital department in Jodhpur, India.

Patients received an ultrasound-guided block at either three points or five points around the knee. Both groups got the same mix of lidocaine and a steroid. The researchers then tracked pain and quality of life in each group. The comparison tests whether targeting extra nerves is worth the added injections for people whose knees hurt every day.
pmc-11610473:
Chao Mei and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-four genome study of a gene family in potato. Trihelix transcription factors respond to light and steer plant growth and stress defence. Their potato members were uncharted until now.

The team found forty-three family genes spread unevenly across the potato chromosomes. Shared building blocks suggested which parts do the core work. Family trees split the genes into six groups, including a rarely seen one. Duplicated gene pairs hint at how the family expanded. Expression data covered most genes across tissues. Breeders get a parts list for future crop improvement work.
pmc-11612173:
Bin Fang and co-authors create, in 2024, gene-edited pigs whose red blood cells might one day be transfused into people. Pig cells could ease blood shortages, but the human immune system attacks them. Using gene editing, the team knocked out three pig genes that trigger attack and added two human shield genes.

Cells from the edited pigs bound far fewer human antibodies than normal pig cells. In monkeys, edited cells stayed detectable for two hours after transfusion, while normal pig cells vanished within twenty minutes. The window is still short, yet the jump shows multi-gene editing can buy real survival time for cross-species blood.
pmc-11613373:
Sawsan Mohammed Alblewi presents a 2024 review comparing daily and intermittent iron dosing for children with iron deficiency anemia. Giving iron once or twice a week is easier for families, but it may raise blood levels less than daily dosing. The author pooled randomized trials to settle the comparison.

The search covered major databases for trials from 2012 to late 2023, spanning ages two months to 18 years. From 735 records, ten studies made the final cut. Daily iron raised hemoglobin more than weekly or twice-weekly schedules. The pooled edge was clear and highly significant in both arms of the analysis. The author calls for larger trials that also track side effects and how well families stick to each plan.
pmc-11613473:
Elisabeth Klæbo Reitan and co-authors explored how patients experienced a Norwegian hospital ward that offers treatment without medication for severe mental illness. The ward opened in Tromsø in 2017 after a government decision to give patients a drug-free option. The team interviewed nineteen people who had stayed there between 2017 and 2021 and sorted their accounts into themes.

Patients valued the chance to talk openly about living without medication, and praised the ward's focus on empowerment, activity, and flexibility. Not everyone managed to taper off, and some described mixed feelings or fear. The analysis points to three core themes, tapering, relationships, and the ward's frames, and argues that medication-free care means far more than simply stopping pills.
pmc-11615373:
Some pregnancies and deliveries turn life-threatening, and Ethiopia carries one of the world's heaviest burdens of such cases. Fitiwi Tinsae Baykemagn and co-authors hunt for the drivers in Tigray, in the north. They compare 341 women who suffered a life-threatening condition with 686 who did not, using interviews and medical cards from 2024.

Chronic high blood pressure stood out, multiplying the odds more than tenfold. Induced labor, a past stillbirth, alcohol in pregnancy, and missing folate tablets all raised the risk several-fold. Having no schooling and carrying twins added danger too. One factor protected: completing the recommended prenatal visits cut the odds clearly. The authors address their list to health planners and frontline providers alike.
pmc-11616273:
Faeghe Deljoo Ghamgosar, Muhammad Sadra, Hassan Yari, and Mina Honarbakhsh ask Iranian mothers what helped them handle labor pain, in a 2024 study. Caesarean rates in Iran have risen sharply. Fear of labor pain is the main reason mothers give. Pain in childbirth carries different meanings in different settings. The team interviewed twenty-five mothers who gave birth in four large hospitals. The talks were open and in depth.

Two settings shaped the pain experience. The inner setting covered personal beliefs and self-confidence without fear. The outer setting covered the room itself, the people present, and how staff interacted. Together these factors set what the pain meant to each mother. Meaning, in turn, set how well she coped. Self-confidence and a positive outlook stood out as aids. The authors say support should fit each mother's needs. Room design and partner involvement may cut unneeded surgery.
pmc-11617473:
Min-Che Tung and five co-authors study a long noncoding RNA, a gene-like molecule that does not build proteins, and its link to prostate cancer risk and progression. Their study came out in 2024. Variants of this RNA have been tied to several cancers, but its role in prostate cancer was unclear.

The team compared nearly seven hundred patients with the same number of healthy controls, testing five variants. One variant stood out. Patients carrying its minor form were more likely to develop tumors with high Gleason grades, a score of how aggressive the cancer looks. Tissue data showed that carriers also produced more of the RNA in the prostate. Cancer atlas data linked higher RNA levels to larger tumors, spread to lymph nodes, and shorter time without progression.
pmc-11619273:
Haiyang Chen and co-authors improve heart muscle tracking in MRI movies in two thousand twenty-four. Standard tracking tools follow points frame by frame, and small errors pile up into drift. Drift blurs the strain measures that show how the heart wall deforms.

Their method aligns all frames at once rather than in pairs. A local rank-based score judges how well each patch lines up across the full cycle. Tests ran on a simulated set, a public movie set, and scans from patients at their center. The new method gave the lowest tracking errors in most checks and lower strain error than rivals. Two general group methods were also beaten in most tests.
pmc-11619673:
Pere Rehues and co-authors published a 2024 study of seven forms, called proteoforms, of apolipoprotein C-III, a blood protein in fat metabolism, and how each form tracks health markers. The protein is known to raise blood fats, promote inflammation, and worsen insulin resistance. Most previous work measured only its total amount, or a few of its forms.

The team measured all seven forms in 875 adults from a Spanish health study of diabetes.
