Lipid profiles were measured with a laboratory test, and inflammatory markers came from a scan of blood proteins. Three proportions of the forms, each measured against the most common form, tracked with better markers across the board. They were linked to lower blood fats, lower inflammation, and healthier glucose handling. Those links held independently of the protein's total amount. The work suggests that the individual forms, not the total, may be the true markers of risk.
pmc-11622573:
Rena Hidaka and four co-authors report a pilot study from Japan, published in twenty twenty-four, on weak mouth function in adults. Poor mouth function has been linked to poor nutrition and frailty. The team checked how common it is across age groups and between men and women.

The study tested one hundred fifty-five healthy adults, from young adults to people near ninety. Staff scored seven measures, such as mouth dryness, bite force, tongue pressure, chewing, and swallowing. Hand grip strength was also taken. Weak mouth function was far more common in the oldest group than in younger adults. Some scores, such as tongue pressure, also tracked with grip strength in both sexes.
pmc-11624673:
Ding-Chao Xu and colleagues determine the optimal timing for programmed intermittent epidural boluses during labor pain relief. In this technique, the epidural pump delivers scheduled boluses, and the interval over which one bolus keeps pain controlled without rescue doses is a key design parameter. Patient-controlled top-ups offer flexibility but risk overuse; a well-chosen interval minimizes both pain breakthrough and total drug.

Participants were randomized to five groups with bolus intervals ranging from thirty-five to fifty-five minutes, using a standard ropivacaine and sufentanil mixture. Analgesia counted as effective if, during the first stage of labor, the patient needed at most one patient-controlled bolus per interval and no manual rescue. Probit regression estimated the intervals achieving fifty and ninety percent success rates, the field's standard way of defining an optimal dose interval. Its output guides pump programming with an evidence-based default interval.
pmc-11626473:
Urena and Stark study the hand gestures people use while telling stories after traumatic brain injury. Gestures that picture meaning often grow when speech is impaired, as in stroke-related aphasia. Brain injury brings both word-finding trouble and thinking problems, a useful test case. The team filmed 54 adults with moderate to severe injury. At three months post-injury, each told how to make a sandwich. The team counted and classified their iconic gestures.

Three questions guided the work: how much gesturing occurs, how it links to language loss, and how it changes over recovery. Answers could shape therapy that builds on gesture. Spontaneous speech, not lab tasks, was the setting throughout.
pmc-11627173:
Wan Fadzleen Ezyani and co-authors report a pregnancy case where early care spotted signs of achondroplasia. This genetic disorder shortens the limbs and is the most common cause of disproportionate dwarfism. More cases are now found before birth, as ultrasound scans are routine in primary care.

The mother was a healthy 26-year-old in her first pregnancy. Scan findings raised concern, and soft markers guided the diagnosis before birth. The case shows which scan signs primary care staff should watch for. Early spotting lets families plan care and support around the birth.
pmc-11628973:
Pamela Mathura and colleagues offer a blueprint for growing a hospital that exists inside patients' homes, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Edmonton built its virtual home hospital in twenty eighteen through an innovation lab, designing with stakeholders and iterating rather than following a rigid research script. Acute, hospital-level care went to the home through technology and shared staff.

Five years on, the growth is the result: staff from two to fifteen, physicians from fourteen to twenty-five. Patients served rose from forty-five to eight hundred seventy, capacity from ten to seventy-five, and one hospital served became six plus a health center. Along the way came remote monitoring in place of plain telehealth, more community partners, longer hours, and wider referral doors. The authors present the model as a permanent bridge between hospital and community care.
pmc-11629673:
Haitao Li and co-authors report a 2024 study of patients with fatty liver disease. They test a combined score built from blood fat, blood sugar, and body weight. The question is whether a high score is linked to high uric acid in the blood. The study drew on patients seen at one hospital in late 2023.

Patients with high uric acid were compared with those without it. The team split scores into four groups and used models that adjust for other factors. They also tested how well the score could pick out patients with high uric acid, next to a simpler score. The findings suggest the combined score may help flag risk in clinic. The design looks back at one point in time, so it shows links rather than causes.
pmc-11634073:
Vimalraj Selvaraj and co-authors write a letter to the editor in a 2024 piece on nanotechnology in cancer surgery. Cutting out a tumor is a core cancer treatment, yet surgeons struggle to take all of it while sparing healthy tissue. Tiny engineered particles, the letter argues, are starting to change that balance.

Gold particles tied to tumor-seeking tags can sharpen scans so small growths stand out. Magnetic particles can boost MRI views during the operation itself. Glowing probes built from particles are brighter and last longer than plain dyes, which helps fluorescence-guided surgery. The letter also covers drug delivery and light-based therapies used in the wound. The authors present these tools as aids to cleaner removal and faster healing, while the field is still young.
pmc-11634173:
Ashokkumar Singaravelu and co-authors tested an AI system that mimics expert judgment during bowel surgery in a 2024 study. Surgeons use a glowing dye to judge blood flow in the bowel before choosing where to cut and rejoin. Reading that glow is a skill learned over years, and poor choices risk leaks after surgery.

The AI displays, in real time, how expert surgeons would read the dye signal. The team evaluated it live during colorectal resections. A faithful digital expert could steady less experienced surgeons and standardize decisions across hospitals. The study moves such AI from lab videos into the operating room, where lighting, smoke, and movement test it honestly.
pmc-11634673:
Yuji Fujita, Takashi Matsushita, Megumi Sato, and Shigemi Yoshihara present a 2024 case report, in letter form, on a blood test that briefly misled doctors treating a young patient. The child had juvenile dermatomyositis, a rare disease in which the immune system attacks muscle and skin. Antibodies in the blood can aid diagnosis, and one key antibody is known as anti-TIF1γ.

The patient was a seven-year-old girl whose first test for the antibody sat just above the cutoff. Seventeen days later, before any treatment, the same test read below the cutoff, which suggested a false negative. A second, more direct test on stored serum showed the antibody was present all along, and repeat measures stayed high. Levels then fell once steroid treatment began. The authors warn that a single test method can miss this antibody.
pmc-11638673:
Timothée Gérard leads a team feeding captive common hamsters varied crop diets to find what the endangered rodent needs to hibernate and breed well. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Modern monoculture farming starves hamsters of dietary variety. They emerge from hibernation lighter and breed less than before.

Eight diets were tested under controlled conditions, chosen with farmers' input. Fat-rich mixes left hamsters in better shape after hibernation. Breeding success stayed low across all groups, though. Mothers who ate more protein before mating were likelier to give birth. Pups survived to weaning more often when mothers were in good condition. The authors conclude hamsters need balance, not just calories. Protein shortfalls in modern fields emerge as a key threat. Diet diversity on farmland becomes a conservation lever.
pmc-11638773:
Aging well is not a fixed state but a daily one, argues a study published in 2024 by Dwight Tse and co-authors. Eight day diaries from 716 older Americans in a national sample tracked symptoms, functioning, and engagement alongside the day's stressors and bright spots.

The measures swung widely within each person from day to day. Bad days for stress dragged them down, and good events lifted them. People whose averages ran high also scored better on one time health measures, though day to day swing size linked less neatly. The authors urge programs that help older adults stack good days, not just pass a yearly check.
pmc-11639773:
Ryo Masuda and co-authors use a yeast trick to find new jobs for ubiquitin, a small protein that tags other proteins for handling. Their 2024 paper searches for mutants whose heat weakness is rescued when ubiquitin is produced in excess. That rescue hints at a link worth chasing.

The screen turned up a gene for a part of a complex that clips signal tags off new proteins in the cell's folding compartment. Extra ubiquitin covered for the missing part at high heat. Pairing the missing part with a missing ubiquitin ligase made growth far worse, which supports a real link. A further pairing with a known handling gene also interacted weakly. The authors offer the approach as a general way to find ubiquitin-linked processes.
pmc-11640173:
Dong Yang and co-authors study a fish disease from skin mucus in this 2024 paper. Hybrid grouper are valuable farmed fish in Asia. A bacterium causes white spot disease inside their organs and heavy farm losses. The team sampled tiny parcels called exosomes from the mucus of infected and healthy fish.

Infected fish parcels carried more immune and cell-cleaning proteins. Metal-grabbing proteins also rose, which fits a defense that starves germs of iron. One protein sat at the hub of the response network. Several proteins jumped sharply after infection and could serve as warning markers. A mucus test would let farmers spot disease without killing fish.
pmc-11640473:
Chen and colleagues report a study from twenty twenty-four on keeping guavas fresh after harvest. Guavas spoil fast, which holds back the guava trade in China. The team soaked fresh guavas for ten minutes in plain water or in a mild acidic water made by electric treatment. They then stored the fruit for fifteen days in warm, damp air. They tracked rot, firmness, and taste-linked traits over that time.

Fruit soaked in the treated water rotted less and stayed firmer than plain-soaked fruit. It kept more acid, sugar, and vitamin C, and more fruit stayed fit to sell. The soak also raised levels of natural defense compounds in the fruit. The authors link the gain to stronger fruit defenses that slow rot.
pmc-11640973:
Marten Beeg and a team of co-authors use a light-based sensor method to detect broken fragments of the amyloid fibrils tied to Alzheimer's disease. Their study came out in 2024. The amyloid protein forms stable fibers that pile into plaques, but smaller pieces may drive much of the damage.

Their assay uses surface plasmon resonance, which senses molecules binding to a metal film, paired with antibodies that select the target. Earlier work showed it could separate small aggregates from whole fibrils without altering the sample. Here the team used it to reveal fragments created when fibrils are mechanically broken, something other methods measure poorly. Those fragments proved more toxic to cells than the intact fibrils. The finding strengthens the case for fragment-aware tests in Alzheimer's research.
pmc-11641773:
Syuykum Shumilova and colleagues sequence seventy-eight DNA repair genes in women from Central Russia to draw the region's breast cancer risk map, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Eight hundred sixty patients and five hundred twenty matched controls were tested. Two thirds of the patients were fifty or younger at diagnosis.

Twenty-two percent of patients carried a harmful variant, across thirty genes, against six percent of controls. The famous genes dominated the risk: BRCA1 carriers had about sixteen times the odds, BRCA2 about twelve, and ATM about seven. The team also found variants never described before, including in BRCA1, BRCA2, and PALB2, plus fresh evidence for several lesser genes. Three suspected genes showed no link at all. For patients, a find changes management; for healthy carriers, it opens prevention. The authors supply the missing Central Russian numbers for panel testing.
pmc-11642673:
Kozub and co-authors test how oils change the traits of foamed building materials made from fly ash, in a study from 2024. The materials, called geopolymers, can turn industrial waste into a greener building stock. The team added new and used oils at 5, 10, and 15 percent by weight.

Samples were made from class F fly ash with a strong alkaline mix. The team measured density, heat flow, bending and crushing strength, and pore structure. Oils reshaped the pores and shifted the strength of the foam in clear ways. Which oil was used, and whether it was fresh or spent, mattered for the final strength. The authors see oils as a way to improve the foam while recycling waste oil.
pmc-11643573:
Igor Shtrom and co-authors grow gallium arsenide nanowires using lead as the catalyst. Their study appeared in 2024. Nanowires usually grow when a droplet of catalyst gathers material and deposits it as a crystal thread. Gold is the usual catalyst, but lead is unusual: it dissolves arsenic well, while gallium and lead refuse to mix. The team grew wires on silicon with molecular beams at varied temperatures.

The wires formed as hoped, and the lead droplet survived the growth. Traces of both lead and silicon ended up inside the wires, doping them without being asked. The authors say the case stretches the standard picture of droplet-led growth. It also matters for work that dopes such wires on purpose for electronic devices.
pmc-11643873:
Yongqiang Niu and co-authors report a better way to make oxygen separation membranes in a 2024 paper. The membranes are hollow fibers made of a ceramic like material that lets oxygen pass. During making, soaking in pure water washes out key elements, in particular the added fluorine, which harms performance.

Their improved method uses saturated solutions instead of pure water as the setting baths, holding the element mix steady. Oxygen flow through the membrane rose by about a fifth at high temperature compared with the water method. The membrane met commercial flow standards even at a lower temperature. The authors say doping plus stability tricks can push these membranes toward real use.
pmc-11643973:
Xinxin Cheng and her co-authors study diet, oxidative stress, and thinking problems in lung cancer patients. Their twenty twenty-four cross-sectional study deals with cancer-related cognitive impairment, the fog that many patients report. The team scored each patient's oxidative balance, a tally of pro-oxidant and antioxidant habits and foods.

Three hundred fifteen patients took part, and a third showed impairment on a standard test. Those patients had lower balance scores and lower activity of two protective enzymes in blood. Each added point of balance cut the odds of impairment by about a tenth. Fiber and vitamin E intake were also protective. The enzyme levels carried part of the diet effect, a mediation the tests support.
pmc-11644173:
A ketogenic diet slashes carbohydrates so the body burns fat, and Grzegorz Klonek and co-authors test it in women whose sugar and lipid readings were already disturbed. For twelve weeks, obese, overweight, and healthy-weight women ate fewer than thirty grams of carbohydrates a day, with about sixty grams of protein and one hundred forty grams of fat. Blood tests and body measures were taken before and after.

Every group improved. Blood sugar, insulin, glycated hemoglobin, and insulin resistance fell, triglycerides dropped, and protective HDL cholesterol rose. Body mass, waist, hip, and thigh measures all shrank. The obese women gained the most on nearly every measure. The authors conclude that a twelve-week ketogenic diet can help women with disturbed glucose and lipid metabolism, with the largest payoff in obesity.
pmc-11644773:
Ya Chen and co-authors build glowing beads that sniff out an antibiotic hiding in food, in a 2024 study. Norfloxacin residues in meat and milk threaten health and breed resistant bacteria, so inspectors need fast tests. The team's sensor is a tiny sphere with a metal-framework core, wrapped in a polymer stamped with the drug's molecular shape, like a lock cut for one key. Two quantum dots inside glow green and red.

When the drug binds, the red glow dims while the green stays constant, so the colour ratio reports the dose. The response stayed linear across a wide range, with spiked recoveries near one hundred percent in chicken, pork, fish, and milk, and a detection limit of two micrograms per litre. A two-colour readout guards against the false alarms that plague single-signal tests.
pmc-11644973:
Jiali Zheng, Huagui Huang, and Qiwei Hu present a portable device that measures the crosswise profile of metal rolls used in rolling mills, in this 2024 paper. Knowing a roll's exact curve matters for making flat, even sheet metal. Their design improves on a classic saddle shaped gauge by adding a contact sensor and a camera based positioning module that finds measuring points on its own.

The device resolves down to one micrometer. The authors analyze errors that creep in during setup and state how the gauge must be installed to avoid them. Field tests on real rolls showed an error of two hundredths of a millimeter on a flat roll. A new compensation method cut crown measurement error by about sixty-nine percent. Results met industrial needs.
pmc-11646373:
Jiaxin Bei and co-authors study a gene called PPIH in liver cancer, in a research paper from 2024. The cancer has complex roots and an immune setting that blunts treatment, so outcomes stay poor. The gene helps fold proteins, and its level in tumors may track how aggressive the cancer is and how immunity behaves.

Data from large cancer and healthy tissue sets show the gene is raised in many cancers. High levels track with poor survival in liver cancer. The team also checks gene silencing marks, mutations, and immune cell entry. Lab and animal tests probe what the gene does in tumor cells. The work marks it as a risk signal.
pmc-11647073:
Malissa Bentham and co-authors present a 2024 case report on a rare, treatable cause of high blood pressure after a kidney transplant biopsy. Bleeding inside the organ squeezed it and set off a hormone chain that drove pressure up.

The patient, a man in his seventies, had a biopsy of his transplanted kidney. A growing blood collection then compressed the organ. His blood pressure rose and kidney function fell. Surgery relieved the pressure and saved the transplant. The authors say this is the first such case in a transplanted kidney reported from the Caribbean region. They stress early recognition, since prompt action can rescue the organ.
pmc-11648973:
Erdman and seven co-authors used DNA data in twenty twenty-four to ask how much hatchery fish have mixed into wild brook trout in Wisconsin's Driftless Area. Stocking has propped up trout for over a century, so many streams may hold native fish, mixed fish, or planted fish with no easy way to tell.

The team sampled six hundred forty-three trout from thirteen wild populations and one hatchery strain. The wild groups looked sharply distinct from each other, even between near neighbors, and showed little sign of hatchery mixing. That sounds like good news for native fish. But computer simulations told a cautionary tale: a population founded by stocking could drift apart this fast on its own. If so, the standard clustering tests would undercount hatchery influence. The authors warn managers not to read clean test results as proof of a pure native past.
pmc-11650773:
An eleven-author team watched silicon anodes crack inside solid-state batteries, using X-ray tomography during operation. Silicon stores far more lithium than graphite but swells enormously when charged. In liquid cells that swelling is partly cushioned; in solid-state cells it fights rigid materials. Imaging revealed mud-like channel cracks spreading across the electrode as lithium left. Separate cracks opened at the silicon-electrolyte interface.

The interfacial damage came from neighboring domains of different sizes reacting at different rates, straining their shared boundary. Phase-field modeling quantified the cracking and showed the lithiated silicon's stress state decides how far interface fractures run. The twenty twenty-four study hands battery engineers design rules: manage silicon's stress, or high-energy solid-state cells will tear themselves apart from inside.
pmc-11652373:
Haiping Zhao and co-authors present a 2024 study on how a tumor suppressor protein shapes the editing of gene messages. Cells cut and rejoin RNA in varied patterns, called alternative splicing, and errors in that editing feed cancer. The protein TSSC4 sits inside the splicing machinery, but its exact role was unclear.

The team sequenced RNA from cervical cancer cells with and without TSSC4. Losing the protein scrambled splicing patterns widely and disturbed many tumor-linked genes, including known cancer drivers. The same pattern appeared in lung, pancreatic, and breast cancer cell lines after the protein was removed or reduced. The work ties message editing directly to how this suppressor holds tumors back.
pmc-11655273:
Ann Wilson and Clive Phillips wrote a study from 2024 on why tourists seek out lion cub petting and what they expect from it. Such encounters are popular at South African facilities, though critics say the cubs' welfare suffers. The team surveyed three hundred visitors at three interaction sites about their motives, awareness, and reflections. The answers complicate the usual picture of the trade.

About a third knew of the controversy before they came, and more than two thirds wanted the encounter anyway. Yet three quarters said they would still have visited the site without cubs on offer, so the cubs were not the main draw. Most came for their children. Expectations were met for most, but three in five said the encounter left no mark on them. A third had a favorite among several species: the animals that chose to engage back. Almost none learned about wild lions' plight.
pmc-11655873:
Conway and colleagues published a global review in twenty twenty-five on unequal access to diabetes technology for young people with type 1 diabetes. Nearly nine million people live with this condition, and wearable glucose sensors plus automatic insulin pumps are now the best standard of care.

The reviewers surveyed device makers and doctors across many regions and searched the medical literature. Money stood out as the biggest barrier almost everywhere, either keeping devices out of a country or pricing families out. Strict insurance rules on who qualifies blocked many others, whether the coverage was public or private. Habits and knowledge among doctors and families added further friction. The authors call for governments, insurers, makers, and clinicians to act together. Without that joint push, they warn, the best care will keep flowing to the already advantaged.
pmc-11655973:
Emily Alefeld and co-authors build, in 2024, a lab model of a child eye tumor and the tissue around it. Treatment has shifted toward saving the eye, so how tumor cells interact with nearby support cells matters more. The team grew tumor cells and support cells taken from real tumors and compared their gene activity.

Tumor cells grown with serum looked more mature, while those grown without it looked more like stem cells. The team also created long-lived versions of both cell types and described their traits. The tumor line formed growths in a chick membrane test. The model gives researchers a fuller way to study this cancer.
pmc-11657473:
Huijing He and co-authors link routine blood counts to heart risk factors in a 2024 study of the China National Health Survey. Red blood cell measures are cheap to test, and if they track risks such as diabetes and abnormal lipids, they could flag people for early checks. The team analyzed nearly thirty-two thousand survey participants from 2012 to 2017.

Three measures, hemoglobin, red cell count, and hematocrit, each rose in a straight-line pattern with every risk factor studied. People in the highest group for hemoglobin faced notably higher odds of high uric acid, diabetes, and poor lipid readings, though one good cholesterol measure fell. Most links bent rather than ran straight at the extremes, and the patterns differed between men and women.
pmc-11662173:
Devalla Venu Babu and four co-authors tested tiny particles that rebuild mineral in etched tooth dentin. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, starts from a flaw in tooth bonding. Acid etch strips mineral from the top layer of dentin to make room for glue. Water in the tooth keeps some spots free of glue, which leaves bare fiber open to decay by enzymes. The bond then ages fast and fails.

The team made three kinds of mineral building particles and charted their shape, size, and makeup. Forty-eight pulled teeth with no decay were used to test the effect at the bond face. Readers who fix teeth get a route to bonds that heal their own weak spots.
pmc-11663773:
An editorial in eBioMedicine in 2024 discusses inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD. The term covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. These are long-term bowel conditions that are related but distinct. Many patients describe the illness as invisible yet life changing. Other people often doubt how sick they really are.

Inside, the editorial stresses embarrassment, silence, and hard daily choices. Symptoms come and go, so life feels unpredictable. Many patients wait years for a diagnosis or for newer treatments. Insurance rules can make delays worse in some countries. The piece also notes new genetic research on causes. It calls for urgent work on causes, diagnosis, and care. Better understanding could shorten waits and improve daily life.
pmc-11664173:
Miguel Robles-Garcia and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on growing notochord progenitor cells from human stem cells. These rare embryo cells help pattern the body and later maintain the discs between vertebrae, but how they arise was unclear. The team used micropatterned dishes plus growth signals to steer stem cells through the earliest patterning stage in a controlled way.

A WNT pathway activator set the dose, which in turn steered the cells' own TGF-beta family signaling. Lasting NODAL signal made gut-type cells, blocking it made nerve-muscle types, and blocking it late inside tight patterns raised WNT activity. That recipe produced the notochord progenitors efficiently.
pmc-11664273:
Rungnapha Khiewwijit and colleagues grow microalgae on chicken farm waste and tally what the partnership could do for Thailand, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Anaerobic digestion of poultry waste leaves a nutrient-rich effluent. Three outdoor systems were compared: free-floating algae, algae as a biofilm on supports, and a no-algae control.

The biofilm won on nearly everything. In fourteen days it stripped ninety-seven percent of ammonium nitrogen, ninety-three percent of phosphate, and seventy-five percent of dissolved organics, beating the suspended culture, and its mat was easier to harvest. The national arithmetic is the headline: scaled to Thailand's laying hen farms, the biomass could generate seventy-two gigawatt-hours yearly and cut ninety-nine thousand tonnes of carbon dioxide. Its emissions run at least twenty-nine percent below conventional fuels. Waste treatment that pays for itself, the authors argue.
pmc-11665373:
David Larbi Simpong and seven co-authors pilot a survey of mild cognitive impairment in Cape Coast, Ghana, in this 2024 study. Dementia is rising fastest in poorer countries, and the mild stage before it is a chance to intervene, yet Ghanaian data were nearly absent. One hundred adults took the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, a standard screening test.

About two in five men and women scored in the impaired range. Surprisingly, the forty to forty-nine age band carried the highest share, about sixty-five percent of that group. Schooling tracked scores closely: more education, higher results. Those flagged as impaired performed worse across nearly every test domain, from spatial tasks to delayed recall. The authors validate the tool for Ghanaians with at least seven years of schooling and call for larger studies of the young onset pattern.
pmc-11666373:
Fischer and five co-authors tested in twenty twenty-four wheth-er the fruit fly can screen drugs for seiz-ure con-trol. Drug proofness is a big block in epilepsy care and has not eased with new drugs. Two fly strains that seize when shook give a cheap test bed.

Sev-en wide-used drugs were fed to the flies for two days, then the flies were shook. In one strain, two salt-path block-ers and val-pro-ate cut seiz-ure chance or length well. The sec-ond strain shook off all drugs, like hard hu-man cases. The fly thus works as a fast first screen, they find.
pmc-11668773:
Yoonhoi Koo and co-authors track inflammation markers after induced seizures in dogs, in a research paper from 2024. Seizures can both stem from and cause brain inflammation. Blood markers that shift after a single seizure could aid diagnosis and care, but their time course in a controlled model was unmapped.

Five healthy beagle dogs received a drug infusion until a full convulsion occurred. Blood was sampled over two windows, from minutes to two days after the seizure. Ratios built from white cell and protein counts shifted at set times. Two lipid mediators were also measured by lab assay. The pattern shows which markers move early and which move late after a seizure.
pmc-11669373:
Chetna Malhotra and co-authors build and test a website that helps heart failure patients plan future care, in a study from 2024. Advance care planning lets patients state their values and choices before they become too ill to speak. Web tools can help, but none had been designed for heart failure patients and their caregivers.

The site, called My Voice, has separate parts for patients and caregivers. It was built with an advisory board and tested in rounds. Thirty people took part: patients, caregivers, and health staff. They found the site easy to use, with clear content that helped talks about goals. Users liked that they could revisit their choices over time. Scores rated usability as good, and most patients and caregivers rated it highly.
pmc-11669973:
Yen-Po Lin and co-authors published a 2024 study on how night guard duty affects the heart and metabolism of soldiers. Standing sentry at night cuts into sleep, and lost sleep is known to raise weight and blood pressure. Whether occasional night duties shift these measures over a few months was unclear.

The study covered 867 service members in Taiwan, aged eighteen to thirty-nine, none on blood pressure medicine. Each reported how many night sentry shifts they had worked per month over the past three months. Resting blood pressure and pulse were measured, along with the standard markers of metabolic syndrome. The team adjusted for age, sex, habits, body weight, and fitness. They then tested whether more frequent night duty tracked with worse readings. The work speaks to how armies schedule night work, and to the hidden health costs of broken sleep in young, fit adults.
pmc-11671473:
Dominik Stursa, Pavel Rozsival, and Petr Dolezel use generative networks to grow training data for spotting coating damage. Their task is semantic segmentation of corrosion round a scribe line on coil-coated steel. Deep models need many labeled images, and labeling is slow hand work. The team trained a deep convolutional GAN to forge synthetic image-and-label pairs that look like real ones.

The forged pairs were mixed with real data to train two leading segmentation models, U-Net and DeepLabV3. Adding synthetic data improved detection accuracy and F1 score. The sweet spot sat at a synthetic-to-real ratio between 0.2 and 0.5: enough new variety to help, not so much that fake patterns swamp real ones. A model that grades coating damage can thus be trained well even when real defect photos are scarce.
pmc-11671973:
Xiaoqing Fan and colleagues find a fatty tag on a spinal cord protein that stokes cancer pain, and a peptide that strips it, in this study from twenty twenty-four. In their mouse model, tumor cells planted by the sciatic nerve bring growing pain. Star-shaped support cells in the spinal cord switch on, and an enzyme in them, ZDHHC23, rises.

That enzyme tags the scaffold protein GFAP with a fat anchor, palmitoylation. Tagged GFAP goes with a surge of inflammatory factors, which re-excite the support cells through a known signal loop, locking in pain. A designer peptide that competes for the tagging site calmed pain signaling and factor release. It also eased the tolerance that blunts morphine in cancer care. The authors propose aiming at astrocyte GFAP tagging as a precise way to treat cancer pain, pending human work.
pmc-11672673:
Simulating molecules in water is slow because the water itself forces tiny time steps. The head byline names Rosas Jiménez and co-authors for a 2024 paper that builds a faster water model by rebalancing atomic masses.

Their trick shifts mass and rescales the model so steps stay stable while the water's structure and heat behavior stay faithful. The lighter-feeling water diffuses faster, so proteins and solvent explore their shapes sooner. Built on the widely used TIP3P model, the fast version roughly doubled sampling efficiency at little cost in accuracy. The authors note the recipe transfers to other water models and solvents. Faster sampling also trims the energy bill of big simulations.
pmc-11672973:
Hong-Ren Yu and co-authors study the lungs of rat pups whose mothers were exposed to polystyrene microplastics before birth. Plastic particles reaching the womb may disturb oxidative balance and metabolism in the developing lung. Their 2024 study runs metabolomic scans on lung tissue from seven-day-old pups born to exposed mothers. Oxidative stress ran high in those lungs, with nucleic acid metabolism out of balance and amino acid profiles skewed.

The team then tested melatonin over a longer span. At 120 days old, exposed pups treated with melatonin breathed better and showed healthier lung structure than exposed pups without treatment. The scans name the pathways that the plastic exposure harmed. The authors call for proof in humans, for study of other treatment routes, and for a clinical plan.
pmc-11673273:
Seo Jung Shin and her co-authors present a 2024 study on how young South Korean adults see romantic love. The team used Q methodology, a technique for sorting people's viewpoints, with twenty-three participants in their twenties and thirties. Each sorted forty statements about love, and the patterns revealed shared stances. Four types of lover emerged from the sorts.

One type finds healing and well-being in love. A second longs for true love yet feels anxious. A third puts self-knowledge first, hoping healthy love follows. A fourth seeks a partner bond while guarding independence. The authors compare these types with known attachment and love styles. They suggest counselors tailor support to each stance. The study offers a base for coaching services that help young adults build mature, healthy relationships.
pmc-11673773:
Basheer Abdullah Marzoog and co-authors report a 2024 study on a breath test, read by a learning model, to spot heart disease from poor blood flow. The disease is a top cause of illness and death round the world, and early finds are often missed. Breath holds a mix of gases that shift with body state, which may give a painless clue.

The study drew 80 adults aged 40 and up at one centre. Each gave breath reads at rest and around a bike test, plus heart scans and a stress imaging test that set the true label. A sparse regression model picked the breath gases that track the imaging result. The breath model sorted cases with about 84 in 100 on a joint score, far above the bike test alone at about 51.
pmc-11675373:
Xin Wang and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on an injectable gel that coaxes stem cells to build bone and repairs skull defects in rats. Collagen gels mimic the cell's natural scaffolding and deliver cargo well, but they are mechanically weak. Adding glycerol and a plant-derived sugar polymer made the gel stronger, stickier, moldable, and still injectable.

The team characterized the gel's structure and chemistry, then tested bone-forming power in dishes and animals. Compared with plain collagen, the blend adapted better to irregular defects and supported the stem cells' turn toward bone. Defects filled more convincingly. The authors present the gel as a practical implant candidate for complex bone injuries that resist standard grafts.
pmc-11675873:
María Guadalupe Nieves-Hernandez and co-authors study, in a 2024 paper, a way to add nutrients to Mexican tortillas without changing how they are made. Tortillas are a daily staple, yet many people in Mexico lack key minerals and vitamins. The team mixed traditional lime-treated corn dough with a commercial lime-treated flour that is fortified with zinc, iron, vitamins, and folic acid.

They measured the chemistry, minerals, protein quality, and starch of tortillas made from each source and from blends of the two. The flour-based tortillas carried more iron, zinc, and folic acid, while the traditional ones held more calcium. A half-and-half blend supplied large shares of the daily needs for calcium, iron, zinc, and folic acid across age groups. The authors suggest blends as a practical path against nutrient gaps.
pmc-11676373:
Sebastian Boehler and colleagues compared four pain plans after minimally invasive removal of the esophagus at a center with a high case load. This surgery is a key part of esophageal cancer care, and pain control shapes how patients heal. The review looked back at 110 patients treated between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty-three. The plans ranged from continuous thoracic epidural to patient-controlled intravenous analgesia alone. Two catheter-based regional techniques, each combined with intravenous control, completed the set.

The main outcome was pain over the first seventy-two hours, scored on a numeric scale. Moderate-to-severe pain during moving hit roughly half to sixty percent of patients, varying by group. Complications, satisfaction, and anesthesia times were also compared. Data from a busy center show what each method gives outside trial settings. This twenty twenty-four study helps teams pick an analgesia plan with open eyes.
pmc-11676973:
Viorel-Dragos Radu and eight co-authors weigh twin-J urine tubes in birth and women's care: prime tool or problem. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-four. Works past nineteen ninety-five in three bases were read, and sixty-nine made the cut. In birth care, the tubes treat swell, stones, and harm at big cuts. In women's care, they shield the tube in hip cuts and fix harm, plus treat blocks past ray care.

Harms span more pee ills, low tract signs, crust, and off place sets. None read as a bar to use. The team call the tubes fit and safe in whole.
pmc-11677173:
Fouad Oumassi and a large team profile a brown seaweed extract for health uses. Their study from twenty twenty-four examines Dictyota dichotoma from marine waters. Seaweeds carry compounds with antioxidant and antimicrobial promise. The team combined lab tests with computer modelling.

Chemical analysis found the alcohol extract rich in phenolic compounds. Twenty-two distinct compounds were identified in total. Standard assays measured its power against free radicals. Bacteria tests checked growth inhibition zones as well. Computer docking explored how compounds might bind targets. The extract showed real antioxidant strength in the assays reported. The authors present the seaweed as a candidate source for natural protective products.
pmc-11677373:
Altaf Farraj and co-authors review the literature on coffee and cardiovascular health, in work from twenty twenty-four. Heart and vessel disease is the top cause of death worldwide and is rising. Diet is a key factor people can change, yet coffee's place in a heart safe diet stays debated.

The review weighs data from observational studies and controlled trials. It looks at active compounds in coffee that may help or harm the heart and vessels. Possible pathways for those effects get a close pass. The authors also set out where research should go next. Readers get a balanced map of a popular drink and a major disease burden.
pmc-11677873:
Tumors starved of oxygen resist drugs, but that low-oxygen state can arm a sleeping prodrug. Tan Ba Tran and co-authors build candidate prodrugs that pair two metals, cobalt and ruthenium, on a single iron-grabbing carrier molecule derived from deferiprone. The carrier can hold metals at two grips. The team attached cobalt units in two styles, added a ruthenium cap at the free grip, and checked products with methods including X-ray structures.

Electrical measurements showed the ruthenium-bearing versions with one cobalt style reduce more easily, hinting they can wake in low-oxygen tissue. Tests on human breast cancer cells confirmed two compounds activate under hypoxia. The freed carrier acted like an iron-stealing drug, raising the cell's iron-hunger signals and a brake gene. Gene readings after three days in low oxygen proved the cobalt compound was reduced and released its partner.
pmc-11678473:
Ji Su Hwang and co-authors analyzed small RNAs and proteins in spinal fluid from Parkinson's patients in a 2024 study. Parkinson's is a progressive brain disorder marked by clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein in neurons. Spinal fluid bathes the brain, so it is the best source for clues about the disease process and for biomarkers.

 Tiny RNAs in the fluid help control gene activity after genes are read. The team profiled those RNAs alongside proteins and mapped the biological jobs they touch. Shifts in these molecules may reveal pathways that drive neuron loss. The analysis also nominates fluid markers that could aid diagnosis or track progression, a standing need in Parkinson's care.
pmc-11678873:
Ioana Baldea and eleven colleagues build a cocrystal of the antifungal drug ketoconazole with fumaric acid. Like many drugs, ketoconazole dissolves poorly in water, which limits how much of it the body can take up. Joining a drug with a second molecule in one shared crystal is a known way to fix that flaw while keeping the solid form stable. The team set up a controlled process to grow this cocrystal.

The work runs from design through testing. The aim was to improve how well the drug is taken up in the body. The team also tested how well the cocrystal agrees with living tissue, and how well it still fights fungi. The study presents cocrystal design as a workable route to better forms of a drug that dissolves poorly.
pmc-11679173:
Livio Tenze and colleagues presented a fingernail health tool called NAILS in 2024. Looking at nails can hint at health problems, since nutrition problems and skin diseases can change colour around the nail plate. The system aims to let people capture those early signs themselves, without a clinic visit.

A pre-trained neural network finds and labels fingernail regions in images, then normalises colour values so tiny changes can be tracked over time. Results appear through a simple interface fed by a high-definition webcam in real time. The authors suggest the tool could help people record and store early disease signs, especially in rural areas where other testing is hard to reach.
pmc-11679573:
Surfaces that mix mirror shine and matte patches defeat standard 3D scanners, and a 2024 paper by Chung-Hsuan Huang and co-authors merges two optical methods to profile them. Fringe projection handles matte areas well but stumbles on shine, so the team adds digital holography along the same light path.

One setup now catches both kinds of reflection at once, across the whole field of view. Tests on circuit boards carrying chips, a classic mixed surface, recovered accurate profiles of both parts. The authors present the hybrid as a practical tool for inspecting electronics, where shine and matte sit side by side.
pmc-11679673:
Amir Sayadi and colleagues described an engineering study in 2024 on making epidural injections safer with robots and augmented reality. Epidural injections deliver medicine near the spinal cord for pain control. A misplaced needle can cause lasting nerve damage, so accuracy matters a great deal. The team built a system meant to guide the physician's hands and eyes.

Their setup pairs a leader and follower robot so the doctor works remotely with steady force feedback, using a new method to keep that feedback stable. Augmented reality projects a three-dimensional model onto the patient's body in real time, tracked magnetically. Early results suggest the system may lower mental workload and improve needle accuracy, though the authors say larger studies in varied clinical settings are still needed.
pmc-11679873:
Liu and a large team make a new glass like layer for thin film transistors in twenty twenty-four. A transistor is a tiny switch used in screens and other devices. The layer must block current well yet let the switch work at low voltage. The team mixed five metal oxides into one layer by a simple liquid method.

One mix of the five metals gave low leakage and let light pass through well. Adding more of one metal raised a key score while keeping the layer clear. Switches built with the layer moved charge fast and turned on near zero volts. The cheap, low heat method could suit bendy and see through devices.
pmc-11680273:
A team of veterinarians reviews vaccination against cattle respiratory disease in a paper from 2024. The disease complex harms beef and dairy herds across North America. Vaccines are routine, but studies report health and growth outcomes in uneven ways. The team searched five databases for studies from the United States and Canada over forty years.

Of more than three thousand records, one hundred one studies entered the final review. Most covered beef cattle rather than dairy cattle. Each study had to report antibody levels plus health or growth outcomes. Methods varied so much that direct comparison was hard. The authors call for consistent reporting so vaccine value can be judged fairly.
pmc-11681873:
Mohammad Mobarak Hossain and co-authors review how heat shock harms rice, and how growers might cut that harm. Their full 2024 review deals with rice grown in a way that can last, in a world where the climate is in flux.

Heat shock is a brief spell of high heat. It upsets rice growth and cuts both grain yield and grain quality. The review sets out its effects on panicle growth, pollen viability, fertilization, and grain filling. Steps put forth include new sowing dates, heat-tolerant cultivars, changed irrigation and fertilization, and growth regulators. Breeding and gene change for heat tolerance are also covered. The piece gives a broad look at ways to guard a staple crop that billions of people eat.
pmc-11683573:
Lars Lindgren and Karla Fredricks wrote a viewpoint piece in 2024 on the health rights of immigrant children in the United States. They start from world agreements that say all children have a right to health care. The United States is the one country that has not signed the main treaty on child rights.

The authors argue that help does not have to wait for the national government. They review steps taken at the state and local level as well as the national level. Some places have found ways to give immigrant children care even when national rules fall short. The piece shows how action at many levels can add up to real access for these children.
pmc-11688373:
Pengfei Pan and colleagues searched for genes shared by two diseases in 2024. Systemic sclerosis raises lung cancer risk. Shared genes might explain that link. Gene datasets for both diseases were mined. Overlapping active genes were then tested. Protein interaction maps guided the search.

One shared gene stood out strongly. Its levels ran low in patients. Lung patients with higher levels lived longer. Disease-free time was also longer there. Lab tests confirmed its restraining effect. Cancer cells grew and invaded less. The gene may guide prognosis work. Further validation is still needed.
pmc-11688973:
Sato Ashida, Freda Lynn, Maria Donohoe, and Emily Killian survey the support networks of families caring for a person with dementia, focusing on disaster readiness. Their study came out in 2024. Dementia caregivers and their relatives are especially vulnerable when emergencies strike.

Fifty-nine caregivers named more than six hundred support members in total, about ten each. Under half of those members were expected to actually help in an emergency. Yet caregivers had shared preparedness information with only about one member in eleven, and discussed disaster plans with few more. Caregivers felt readier for everyday care than for emergencies. Bigger helper networks did predict feeling readier for disasters. The authors urge families to talk through disaster plans with their networks before a crisis.
pmc-11689573:
Pamela Teaster, in a talk from two thousand twenty-four, tells how a year as a health and aging policy fellow let her work on the rights of older adults. She was placed with a large United States office for town living.

Teaster first sets out what that office does. She then turns to three areas of her work: a service that guards adults from harm, a program that speaks for people in long-term care sites, and the court role of guardians. She closes by showing how the year shaped her study, teaching, and outreach. The talk gives a plain view of how policy work on elder rights is done day to day.
pmc-11689873:
Traci Wilson, Marisa Sheldon, and Heather Menne present a 2024 symposium paper on how local aging agencies use national data to improve services. These agencies plan and run support for older adults in their home areas. Many older people rely on meals and in home help funded by a federal aging law.

Demand now stretches past those core services into housing and emergency readiness. Each speaker brought a view from a different level of the aging network. The talks share data based ways to adapt services and to pair agencies with researchers. The aim is fresh ideas that help older adults live at home in good health.
pmc-11690073:
Dolores Majon Valpuesta and Melanie Levasseur report what helps baby boomers take part in social life in Canada and Spain in this 2024 study. Boomers made up more than a quarter of both populations in 2021. Social participation is a key driver of healthy, active aging. Their generation is committed to taking part, yet little was known about what helps them. Two qualitative studies, one in each setting, gathered their views. Interviews were held with more than one hundred boomers and dozens of community staff.

The title quotes a shared demand: they insist on being heard. Helpers for participation are the paper's focus, drawn from those voices. Health and social services are being reshaped for this large cohort. Knowing what boomers say they need can guide that redesign. The studies ran in Quebec and in Spain in parallel. The piece is a conference-style report of both studies.
pmc-11690273:
Philip Taylor and Kezia Scales set out a research and policy agenda for the direct care workforce in long-term services and supports, in this 2024 article. Demand for care is rising while the jobs themselves stay poor in pay and quality, falling hardest on a workforce that is mostly women and people of color. The authors review worldwide evidence linking job quality with worker well-being and care quality.

The pattern is consistent: bad jobs hurt workers, good jobs support good care. Big gaps remain in how job quality can be built into daily practice, dimension by dimension. The article, shaped with worker and union voices, argues for reframing reform around job quality, and floats a national taskforce or an international agreement on the care workforce.
pmc-11690473:
Alisha Thompson, Barbara Mendez Campos, and Laneshia Conner presented this symposium overview in 2024 on diversity and aging. The piece compares the parts of diversity to ingredients in a favorite recipe: each person's mix shapes how they age and how healthy they stay. The symposium gathered talks and discussion on how these factors play out in later life, with race and ethnicity as the starting point.

Sessions covered end-of-life care choices during serious illness and the duty to give culturally sensitive care. Another session took up partner violence among older immigrants, an often-hidden problem with its own patterns. Later talks widened the lens to thinking, hearing, and vision differences, linking sensory loss to pain and to gaps in telehealth use. The authors aim to equip providers, policymakers, and advocates to build fairer care for older adults.
pmc-11690673:
Cindy Vang, Yeonjung Lee, and Youhung Her-Xiong explore hardship and bias among Asian and Asian American older adults in a 2024 study. This group is among the fastest growing older minority populations in the United States, yet often left out of bias research. The pandemic deepened old and new vulnerabilities for them. Thirty adults aged fifty and older took part in open interviews about their experiences.

Using grounded theory, the team mapped how people overcame pandemic hardship and discrimination. Staying vigilant against both virus and bias sat at the center, shaped by background and support factors. Resilience and mental, emotional, and social effects followed. Readers learn what support policies might strengthen well being for this growing group.
pmc-11692273:
Hyunjin Noh and co-authors shared a 2024 pilot study of what shapes the views of older adults on deprescribing, the cutting back of their drug lists. To deprescribe is to stop a drug that no longer helps, or that harms. Evidence of the risks of clashing drugs is ample. Yet how older adults view the cut, and what sways that view, was thin in past work.

Over a hundred older adults were surveyed by phone. All lived at home, were over sixty-five, and bore two or more chronic illnesses plus chronic pain. All took drugs for those illnesses. A known questionnaire read their views on five marks: burden, fit, fear of stopping, say in the decision, and willingness to stop. More drugs in hand tied to more felt burden. Pain scores tied to belief that drugs cause side effects. Age and race tied to less say.
pmc-11692573:
Fat tissue fills with immune cells as the body ages, and that shift disturbs how fat is stored and burned. Bhaswati Ghosh studies one protein, Siah2, that tags other proteins for disposal. Her team bred mice whose fat immune cells lack the protein. Those cells were grown beside fat tissue to mimic the real setting. Cells without the protein took in more fat and grew larger droplets.

The same cells also failed to send fat droplets to their recycling centers, which swelled. They leaned toward inflammation and burned less oxygen. The results suggest the protein helps fat immune cells clear lipids with age. Losing it may feed the inflammation that comes with aging and weight gain.
pmc-11692773:
Andrew Pickering argues in a 2024 study that a broken protein-disposal system sits at the heart of Alzheimer's disease. The disease is the top cause of dementia, and many drug trials aimed at the amyloid protein have failed. Pickering's team tested whether amyloid harms the proteasome, the cell machine that chews up worn-out proteins.

In lab cells, clumps of amyloid slowed one form of the proteasome and broke apart the larger form. Drugs that boost the machine cut the harm. In fruit flies and mice that make amyloid, the same drugs delayed death, protected memory, and improved learning. The findings suggest that raising proteasome activity could become a new way to treat the disease.
pmc-11693073:
Lourdes Romanach Alvarez, Mateo Farina, and Elizabeth Munoz ask whether the neighborhood an older Brazilian lives in shows up in their cognitive test scores. Their study came out in 2024, using a nationally representative aging survey of more than nine thousand adults.

Two neighborhood qualities mattered. People who judged their neighborhood a good place to live, and who trusted most of their neighbors, scored higher on cognition. So did people who reported fresh fruit and vegetables readily available nearby. The links survived adjustment for personal characteristics. In a middle-income country with sharp inequality, the authors argue, social cohesion and food access may protect the aging brain. They call for work on the mechanisms behind the pattern.
pmc-11693173:
Liyat Kebbede, Brandy Weathers, and Tripti Nair explore how serotonin shapes aging and immunity in this 2024 paper. Serotonin is a brain signal chemical that also steers swelling and immune defense. As people age, that signal weakens and immune response fades. The authors study the link in a tiny worm, Caenorhabditis elegans, whose defenses resemble the built-in human system.

Worms bred with low serotonin signaling fail to sense a deadly germ. They stay on the germ far longer than normal worms instead of crawling away. The worm's short life and clear body let the team trace signals across its whole lifespan. Findings in the worm may point to ways serotonin loss weakens human immunity with age. The paper ties a mood chemical to the daily work of staying healthy.
pmc-11693373:
Seven authors present early findings in two thousand twenty-four from a long-term study of aging in Vietnam. The study follows more than two thousand four hundred adults aged sixty and older. Many lived through the American War, and the team asks how stress and trauma from those years shape health in old age.

Using blood markers and body measures gathered in two thousand twenty-one and twenty-two, the team looked for links with age, sex, home district, and military service. Early results varied by measure. Risk tied to high blood pressure ran higher in men. The authors stress that most aging research comes from rich countries, leaving war's long shadow understudied elsewhere.
pmc-11695073:
Fuminori Kamakura and five colleagues published a case report in two thousand twenty-four on a rare neck joint lock in an adult. The top two neck bones can fix in a rotated position, a condition usually tied to injury or seen in children. This patient woke with the problem and no injury at all.

The twenty-five-year-old woman had neck pain, stiff movement, and the tilted head pose typical of the condition. A CT scan confirmed the first neck bone was rotated on the second. She had no nerve damage. A soft collar held her neck still for four weeks, after which all symptoms cleared. The authors warn that delay can force surgery, so early spotting matters.
pmc-11696773:
A team including Tringale and colleagues published a large chart review in twenty twenty-four on how treatment patterns changed for primary central nervous system lymphoma. This rare cancer grows in the brain or spinal cord, and after a first round of drug treatment doctors add a follow-up step, called consolidation, to hold the gains.

The review covers five hundred fifty-nine patients treated from nineteen eighty-three to twenty twenty. Of them, three hundred eighty-five received some form of consolidation. Whole-brain radiation fell from sixty-one percent of cases in the nineteen nineties to twelve percent in the twenty tens. Stem cell transplant and gentler drug courses rose over the same span. After adjusting for patient differences, no option clearly beat the others on survival. The authors note that lower-dose radiation still deserves a place for patients who cannot have a transplant.
pmc-11704573:
Xiaohui Wang and co-authors pool trials of psychodrama for mental health in China, in work from 2024. Psychodrama is a therapy where people act out scenes to work through feelings. The team searched for randomized trials run in mainland China from 1982 to 2023 and kept seven studies with just over three hundred people.

Across ages and settings, the therapy helped by a clear margin. Gains split into two kinds: easing illness signs and lifting general health. Both kinds showed strong effects. The authors call psychodrama a tool for cure and for prevention alike. They urge more trials run to a shared standard in China.
pmc-11709373:
Sofia Moura and a large team of co-authors study Alzheimer's disease in 2025 using lab-grown immune cells of the brain. In the United States, Black and Hispanic groups face higher rates of the disease than non-Hispanic White groups. Most past work focused on the last group.

The team grew microglia from stem cells of donors with African, Amerindian, and European ancestry. They measured gene activity and gene access in the cells. More than a thousand genes differed in activity across groups. The work aims to reveal ancestry-linked paths that may shape disease risk.
pmc-11709673:
Cory C Funk and co-authors present a 2025 mouse study of how repeated flare-ups of herpes simplex virus in the brain may echo early Alzheimer disease. Herpes viruses hide in nerve clusters and reactivate across a lifetime, and their role in dementia is an open, heated question. The team infected young mice carrying human versions of two Alzheimer risk genes.

After infection, they reactivated the virus repeatedly and traced its spread outward from the trigeminal ganglion, the nerve hub where it sleeps. Gene activity in the brain shifted in synaptic and immune genes, in patterns resembling early Alzheimer changes. The model offers a way to test whether decades of quiet flare-ups can nudge the brain toward disease.
pmc-11709773:
Julio F Jiménez-Bonilla and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on brain scans of amyloid clearance in healthy adults. Slow clearance of amyloid may set the stage for Alzheimer's disease long before symptoms. The team used dynamic PET scans with a tracer that binds amyloid, and compared the results with spinal fluid measures.

Only eight volunteers took part, with a mean age near 64 years. Four already showed an abnormal spinal fluid amyloid ratio. Scan values in several brain regions tracked that ratio closely, most strongly in parietal and temporal areas. Clearance slopes in some regions also lined up with the fluid measure.
pmc-11709873:
Cynthia Nyen Tangban tests whether omega-3 oil can shield the rat brain, in work published in 2025, from harm caused by aluminium chloride. Aluminium can build up in the brain and drive oxidative stress, a chemical strain that damages cells. The cerebellum, which helps control movement, is one target. Natural oils rich in protective compounds might blunt that harm.

Forty adult rats were split into four groups: plain water, the aluminium salt, the oil alone, or both. Dosing ran for twenty-eight days. Rats given aluminium alone grew weak, ate and drank less, and lost weight. Their movement and exploration also suffered. Their cerebellum tissue showed more cell damage, more signs of stress, and loss of a key cell type. Rats given the oil with aluminium stayed close to normal. The author concludes the oil lowered the stress the salt caused in the cerebellum.
pmc-11709973:
Ricardo D'Oliveira Albanus and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on blood vessel cells in Alzheimer's disease. Vessel trouble raises the risk of brain degeneration, yet its details are murky. The team built a method to pull more vessel cells from human brains and profiled their gene activity cell by cell.

The study spanned 72 donated brains richly scored for vessel disease, including amyloid in vessel walls. The resulting atlas held about 133,000 vessel-related cells across five cell types. Disease brains showed strained vessel cell programs, and one gene, ANKRD36, fell sharply in muscle cells of early-onset cases. Signatures tied to vessel amyloid also emerged.
pmc-11710173:
Perminder S Sachdev, Adam C Bentvelzen, and the VasCog-2 group present a 2025 conference abstract on updated rules for diagnosing vascular cognitive disorders. These disorders cover thinking problems caused by blood vessel damage in the brain. Expert rules were last set in 2014, and the field has moved on since then.

An international panel used a structured Delphi process, with rounds of anonymous surveys and feedback, to rebuild the rules. Seventy experts joined, and 54 finished the first round. The group also planned a matching set of rules for research use. The final criteria await formal approval by all participants.
pmc-11710373:
Asma Naseer Cheema and co-authors describe a 2025 search for a rare form of a well known risk gene. The gene has three common forms that shape Alzheimer disease risk. Gene logic says a fourth form should be possible, yet it has been seen only a few times by chance.

The team looked through gene records for more than fourteen thousand people, ill and well. They found hundreds of people who carry two linked changes, then cloned and read their gene copies one by one. In each case so far, the two changes sat on opposed copies, not the same one. No fourth form appeared. The authors say it likely has little or no effect on risk.
pmc-11710673:
Andre Fischer and co-authors present a 2025 study of small gene control molecules in blood and their link to decline. These molecules tune gene activity and can shift with disease. Blood tests for Alzheimer disease have grown strong, yet gene and life factors still blur the picture.

The team read these small molecules in blood from two large aging groups, each with near a thousand adults. Groups held healthy adults and people with felt decline, mild loss, or dementia. They used pattern tests and learning tools to find molecule sets that mark disease stage. They also matched the sets to thinking scores and disease markers. The authors propose a frame for tests based on these molecules at the point of care.
pmc-11712173:
Saket Saxena and ten co-authors build a thinking risk score that runs in the back of the health record, in a 2025 conference paper. Sorting who will lose ground is hard in first line care, where fancy brain tests are rare. A score that feeds on facts already in the chart could help, if its ground truth is sound.

The team gave 338 first care patients aged sixty and up short thinking tests to set a firm base. They then mined five years of each chart for body measures, ills, drugs, and life facts. A step down model kept the marks that best sorted the test results. Past scores built on chart notes alone were shaky, since notes miss loss. This one is checked by test scores, and it runs with no new work for staff.
pmc-11712373:
Jennifer A Frontera and co-authors link blood markers to brain shrinkage two years after COVID-19 in a 2025 study. Thinking problems are a common long-term complaint after the infection, but their cause is unknown. The team scanned ninety people, seventy-five of whom had confirmed past infection, at a median of about two years after illness.

Blood markers of nerve damage, barrier leak, and inflammation ran high in many post-COVID patients. Higher marker levels tracked smaller volumes in limbic and hippocampal regions on MRI. That pattern did not appear in the fifteen controls who had never been infected. Among infected patients with thinking problems, the links were also present. The authors say lasting brain injury signals may underlie post-COVID thinking complaints.
pmc-11712473:
Shveta Bathla published a research paper in 2025 on tau marks that show up across species, from mice to monkeys to humans, in Alzheimer's disease. Shared marks could serve as test targets and drug targets alike. Bathla compared the chemical tags placed on tau in each species' brain.

Dozens of tag sites were counted in human and mouse tissue, and several rose in the disease model mice. Aged monkeys, which grow amyloid and tau changes on their own, showed matching shifts. A drug that blocks a certain enzyme was also tested for whether it trims the tags in monkeys. Blood and spinal fluid tests backed the tissue findings in patients.
pmc-11712573:
Tobi Nifemi Olajide and co-authors published a review paper in 2025 on dementia and lifestyle risk factors in Sub-Saharan Africa. The region's older population is growing fast, yet recorded dementia rates sit lower than many expect. The team gathered studies from the past decade to map what is known and what is missing.

Sixty-nine papers passed their checks. Rates and risks varied widely across the region's many settings. Habits such as smoking and drinking, along with heart health, shaped risk, while schooling and social life seemed to guard some groups. Culture also shaped how families name and handle the illness. The authors call for local studies and policies built for the region, not borrowed whole.
pmc-11712873:
A 2025 methods paper by yun Jiao sets out a way to read the full protein content of a single amyloid plaque cut from brain tissue. Plaques are a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and knowing which proteins sit inside one plaque could explain how it forms and harms nearby cells. A single plaque holds only a tiny amount of protein, so the task is hard.

Jiao used a laser tool to cut one plaque, about fifty micrometres wide, from a stained slice of mouse or human brain. A tuned chemical method then freed the proteins without a loss-prone cleaning step. The setup read about twenty thousand protein fragments from one plaque.
pmc-11713173:
Geert Molenberghs gives an overview of stand-in endpoints in drug trials in this 2025 paper. A stand-in endpoint is an early measure, such as a scan result, used in place of a slower clinical outcome. Judging whether such a stand-in is trustworthy is the core problem he reviews.

The paper traces the main ways experts have judged stand-ins, from early rules to pooled trial analysis and cause-based views. Molenberghs then applies the pooled approach to tau scans as a likely stand-in in Alzheimer's disease. The plan joins trial data with real-world data, with each site first working on its own data before a central team merges the results.
pmc-11713373:
Petrovsky and co-authors interview patients and caregivers to shape a music app for better sleep in dementia, in this 2025 paper. Most people with dementia face sleep trouble at some point. Memory for music often lasts, so songs may calm patients and ease them toward rest.

The team held thirteen online interviews with twenty people, seven patients and thirteen caregivers. Some talks paired patients with their caregivers. A mobile health framework guided how the answers were sorted. Users were asked what content, features, and layout the app should have. Their input will guide the first working version of the app, called CoMPoSER.
pmc-11713973:
Sara Zsadanyi and co-authors measure the memory zone of the brain in adults with Down syndrome across the span of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. Nearly all adults with Down syndrome develop the disease in time. Spotting early change is hard because learning disability masks the first signs.

The team scanned 253 adults with Down syndrome and 190 controls with a strong scanner in Barcelona. A program split the memory zone into small parts, from the hippocampus to nearby rims. Scores were scaled so age and head size would not bend the results. Spinal fluid tests gave disease marks for match up. The authors seek a scan sign that can flag the disease early in this group.
pmc-11715673:
Chirag Vyas and co-authors report a 2025 trial study on two common supplements and blood signs of brain disease. Vitamin D and fish oil fats are cheap and easy to take, and both hint at guarding thinking skill. No large trial had yet tested if they move the blood signs that track Alzheimer's disease and kin forms.

The work sat inside a large US trial and drew 929 adults who gave blood over four years. Five blood signs were read, covering plaque parts, nerve harm, and brain support cell stress. Neither supplement cut the signs overall, though vitamin D showed a trend on one ratio. Split by sex and race, some groups did show drops, but those splits were not checked for false hits and need care.
pmc-11716673:
Sakshi Arora, Raghav Prasad, Jonas S. Sundarakumar, and Pooja Rai published a study in 2025 on frailty and daily life in older adults in India. Frailty is often judged on the body alone, through grip strength, walking speed, and weight loss. The authors argue that low mood and worry should count too, and they test how each type of frailty links to trouble with daily tasks.

Using data from nearly four thousand older adults, they sorted people into four groups, from not frail to frail in body and mind. Those frail in both ways faced far higher odds of trouble with daily tasks. The work supports a wider view of frailty in aging care.
pmc-11716873:
Laura M Rueda-Delgado and four co-authors published a study in 2025 on spotting dementia from data gathered at home. Standard tests need a trained examiner in the room and can be skewed by nerves or bias. A tablet platform that people use on their own, again and again, could give a steadier picture of daily function.

One hundred one people, about half with mild Alzheimer's dementia, used the platform at home for two weeks. It mixed tablet tasks with brain wave recordings during waking and sleep. Machine learning sorted patients from controls about as well as a traditional combined scale. Home data, gathered often and without a clinic visit, may serve trials that need exact staging.
pmc-11728473:
Min Li and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on finding the cell targets of L-shikonin, a plant compound that fights melanoma. The compound's anti-tumor effects are known, but its direct targets were not. The team attached the compound to magnetic particles with a light-activated linker, then fished for the proteins it grabs in melanoma cell extract.

Mass spectrometry named three target proteins: RPN1, CPEB4, and HNRNPUL1. Docking software supported the matches. When melanoma cells were treated with the compound for two days, CPEB4 levels fell at the high dose and HNRNPUL1 fell at medium and high doses. The authors link the compound to melanoma markers and pigment cell structures.
pmc-11731673:
Widaja and Pawitan review a paired plan for Alzheimer care that joins gene-switch tweaks and stem cells in this twenty twenty-four paper. The disease is the top cause of dementia, and current drugs ease signs for a time but cure no one. Gene switches that can flip back give a fresh route to fix faulty gene use.

Inside, the review maps how gene-switch shifts feed the known harms of the disease, from clumps to cell death. It then weighs stem cell care that could swap lost brain cells and calm swelling. Joined, the two routes might slow the disease and rebuild lost paths. Cost, ethics, and weak methods still block the path to real care.
pmc-11739173:
Hans Theodor Eich and co-authors wrote a memorial in 2024 for Normann Willich, who lived from 1946 to 2024. Willich led the radiation oncology unit at Muenster University Hospital for twenty years. He died in September 2024 at age seventy-eight.

The memorial traces his training in Kiel, Berlin, and Munich, and his later work in Augsburg. His thesis work dealt with heat treatment for tumors. From 1991 he shaped the Muenster unit until he retired in 2011. He wrote more than 250 papers and more than 100 book chapters in his long career. Colleagues present him as a key figure in German radiation care for cancer.
pmc-11755773:
Maria-Ioanna Stefanou and a large team published a narrative review in twenty twenty-four on the neurological face of long COVID, frankly subtitled as more questions than answers. About a third of COVID survivors report neurological symptoms lasting a year or more. The review synthesizes what those symptoms are and what might cause them.

Core complaints include fatigue, post-exertional malaise, thinking problems, headache, brain fog, sleep disturbance, smell and taste disorders, and mood symptoms. The picture overlaps heavily with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, and post-intensive-care syndromes. The authors review diagnostic and treatment approaches and the new electronic-record studies using machine learning. Their verdict: phenotypes are clear, mechanisms and therapies are not.
pmc-11788273:
Zhiqin Du, Xiao Ma, Jianhua Li, Fang Yang, and Yangfan Guo report a rare heart picture in a genetic disorder, in a case report whose journal record is dated 2024. The disorder, tuberous sclerosis complex, grows harmless tumors in many organs. The heart is usually spared or shows soft muscle tumors in infancy. This patient, a 26-year-old woman, carried something far rarer: a two-leaflet aortic valve, where three leaflets are normal, alongside severe leakage of that valve.

Testing found a new disease-causing variant in the TSC2 gene, confirming the diagnosis. Her illness touched skin, brain, lung, kidney, and bone as well. Surgeons replaced the leaking valve, but fluid gathered around her heart and lungs afterward, needing drainage and then a further operation on a lymph duct. The authors say the case widens the known heart spectrum of the disorder and shows why genetic testing matters.
pmc-11798973:
Monisha Chawla, Jennalyn Vandenheuvel, and Shannon Sibbald survey in 2025 how Asian Americans view help for ADHD. The condition is often diagnosed in children worldwide. Yet Asian children show the lowest recorded rates across ethnic groups in past reviews.

The authors ask if culture and symptom views explain part of that gap. Asian Americans form a fast-growing group, but health policy often overlooks them. Prior work suggests Asian children with ADHD may get less treatment than peers. The paper reviews social and cultural factors that shape whether families seek help at all.
pmc-11799273:
Huaqu Zeng and co-authors present a study whose head gives the year as 2024. The catalog lists it under 2025. The setting is radiation therapy for brain metastases. Whole-brain treatment now spares the hippocampus to protect memory, while boosting dose to visible tumors at the same time. Two delivery styles are compared: arc therapy that moves the beam, and fixed-field intensity-modulated therapy. Both use off-plane beam angles. Twenty-two patients each receive both plans on a commercial planning system.

Dose to targets and to organs at risk is compared plan against plan. Machine output units and pre-treatment checks join the comparison. Radiation physicists get a head-to-head for a complex, memory-sparing technique. The hippocampus sits close to likely tumor sites, so delivery style decides the sparing quality. Plan studies like this one set department defaults before patients are treated.
pmc-11841473:
