Liang Mao and co-authors build a fruit-spotting system for orchards in a study published in 2024. Their target is litchi fruit in real groves, where bunches hide behind leaves and the fruits are small. The method, YOLOv5-Litchi, adapts a popular real-time detection network to that hard scene.

The team slimmed the network's neck, added detection heads until there were five, and swapped two heads for a design that catches small targets better. Two of the training losses were replaced with sharper versions to tighten the boxes and cut missed fruit. A sliding slice tactic then scans big images in tiles so tiny fruits are not lost in the shrink. The goal is a detector that robotic and survey systems can trust in messy, moving orchard light.
pmc-11914873:
Walaa Mousa and a team of co-authors survey fungi living on desert plants and soils of the Arabian Peninsula, in two thousand twenty-four. Microbes in harsh places evolve special chemistry to compete and defend themselves. Those chemicals can seed new drugs and industrial products, yet desert fungi are little explored.

Twelve fungal species were grown from four desert plants and their soils, with each plant hosting a distinct set. Extracts from all of them showed some useful activity in lab assays. One genus stood out for antioxidant strength and rich chemical content. Extracts from one host plant's fungi fought a common bacterial pathogen well. The authors argue deserts are a rich, untapped source for discovery.
pmc-11935073:
Shaolan Guo and co-authors present a 2023 review on dual-energy CT scanning in breast cancer care. Breast cancer care is moving from one-size-fits-all treatment to plans matched to each tumor's biology. Better tissue reading could spare women needless biopsies of harmless lumps and speed the whole process.

Dual-energy CT scans a patient at two energy levels, blending anatomical pictures with functional and molecular hints. Over the past decade it has gained ground in cancer radiology. The review sums up where the method stands in breast cancer: choosing treatment strategy and predicting outcomes. Open challenges include forecasting which patients will respond to drug therapy given before or after surgery.
pmc-12082673:
Castano and colleagues present a case report on a rare, harmless growth of cartilage in the tongue of a boy of seven. Such growths, called cartilaginous choristomas, are made of mature cartilage in a place it does not belong. The boy's swelling sat on top of the tongue and had grown slowly for three years without pain.

Surgeons removed the lump while the boy was asleep under full anesthesia. Tissue study under the microscope, plus special stain tests, confirmed the diagnosis. The authors address doctors at smaller hospitals. They urge full tissue checks on all mouth swellings, since this rare growth can be mistaken for something else on sight alone.
pmc-12118273:
Yong Qi and Shufen Zhang review color-changing sensor materials in a 2023 paper. The sensors pair tiny crystal patterns with plastics that barely swell in liquid. When the crystal spacing or order shifts, the color shifts too. That color change can report a chemical or force signal with no wires or power.

The review covers how swelling works, how color signals are tuned, and how the sensors are built. It also walks through uses in chemical plants, medicine, and the environment. Pairing the right crystal pattern with the right plastic is the core design problem. A clear map of what has been tried helps engineers build sensors that report quickly and hold up in real use.
pmc-12539873:
Yolanda Monserrath Jacobo-Delgado and co-authors trace the long history of tuberculosis and its drug resistance, in work from 2024. The disease has walked with humans for three thousand years, shown in mummies from Egypt and the Andes. Old texts blamed social causes before germs were suspected. Wild early cures did more harm than good.

Antibiotics in the last century raised hopes of wiping the disease out. Instead, selection bred strains proof against many drugs. The review ends with fresh hope from computing and AI for new drugs and immune aids. The authors warn that forgetting this past invites its repeat.
pmc-12689473:
Waad Bin Khanin and co-authors present a 2025 case series on Heck's disease, a rare benign growth condition of the mouth lining. Linked to human papillomavirus, it forms soft, skin-colored bumps inside the mouth. It mostly affects children and was first described in Native American, Inuit, and African groups, though cases now appear worldwide.

The report details three Saudi women, aged 70, 39, and 49. Their lesions sat on the lips and tongue, ranging from one dome-shaped nodule to four smooth white bumps. A literature review places these adult cases against the usual childhood pattern. A gene locus tied to immune typing has been floated as a risk factor. The authors add Middle Eastern cases to a thin record.
pmc-12692573:
Patcharaporn Boonroumkaew and co-authors chart the bacteria in a traditional Thai fermented fish sauce, in a study from 2025. The sauce, called tai-pla, is made from salted fish entrails and comes from five provinces. Samples used seven fish species, three from fresh water and four from the sea.

The team read a marker gene from the microbes in three subsamples of each sauce. Salt levels ran from 3 to 13 percent, and acidity varied widely. Lactic acid bacteria, the kind that drive many ferments, were rich in several samples, as were salt-loving bacteria. Each fish species gave a distinct microbe mix, shaped by raw materials, salt, recipe, and ferment time. The authors offer the survey as a base for starter cultures and quality control.
pmc-12696073:
Juan Wang and co-authors survey patients who had surgery for cancer of the food pipe, asking how well they follow healthy daily habits. Their study, published in 2025, drew 438 patients from 14 cancer centres. Patients filled in forms on their habits, social support, and belief in their own ability to cope.

The team sorted patients into three groups by habit level: low, middle, and high. Most fell in the middle group, and only a small share reached the high group. Age, schooling, place of residence, and prior treatment all shaped which group a patient fell into. So did support from others and self-belief. The authors say care teams should spot patients with weak habits early and offer tailored help.
pmc-12697273:
Luyao Xu and co-authors study older dialysis patients in this 2025 paper. Peritoneal dialysis cleans the blood through the belly lining, and many older patients also have diabetes. Doctors have worried that diabetes makes outcomes worse for this group. The team reviewed 210 patients aged seventy or older who started the treatment over a decade.

About two in five had diabetes. Death rates per year were nearly the same with or without diabetes. Survival, infection-free time, and treatment durability also matched between the groups. Female sex raised death risk, while better nutrition and remaining kidney function lowered it. The findings suggest diabetes alone should not bar older patients from this dialysis choice.
pmc-12700373:
Lian Trapman and four co-authors ask health workers what blocks talks about end-of-life wishes. Their 2025 study concerns patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis, a lung disease that kills within years. Planning care ahead matters, yet such talks remain rare in practice. The team gathered workers' views in group and solo interviews.

Three themes emerged from the talks. First, clinics lack a shared vision of palliative care, so approaches clash within one team. Second, a learning-friendly setting would help workers build skill and confidence. Third, progress rests on each worker's own growth. The authors argue that structure and training must support these delicate conversations.
pmc-12701873:
Gabriel Bsteh, Luisa Velez Escola, and Harald Hegen lead an Austrian expert network issuing shared recommendations for eye scans in multiple sclerosis care. Their consensus paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Optical coherence tomography measures the retina's layers quickly and without contact. The scan has entered the formal diagnostic criteria for MS in their latest revision.

The network's guidance covers when to scan, what to measure, and how to read the results. Retinal thinning tracks the disease's damage to nerves elsewhere. That makes the eye a window for prognosis as well as diagnosis. Standard practice varied between centers before this consensus. The paper aims to harmonize Austrian MS care around the technique. It reflects the field's shift toward measurable nerve loss. Clinicians get one agreed playbook instead of local habits.
pmc-12708773:
An and a large team hunted in twenty twenty-five plant compounds that block an enzyme tied to gout, in two rare Balanophora plants. Past tests showed brews of these plants block that enzyme, but the parts at work were not known. They read the brews with fine lab tools to name their parts.

Smart models trained on known blockers then screened the named parts for likely hits. A dock test checked how each part fits the enzyme's grip site. One part, taxifolin, stood out as the top new hit, past a known gout drug in their tests. The work may aid new gout care from plants.
pmc-12708873:
Takuya Takahashi and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 study comparing the value of two treatments for a slipped lumbar disc in Japan. One option injects an enzyme, condoliase, into the disc to shrink it; the other is keyhole surgery to remove the bulge. The injection costs far less up front, but value over time needed proof.

Nine centers contributed 229 injection patients and 98 surgery patients, all with the same herniation type on scans. A Markov model rolled costs and quality-adjusted life years forward. The injection matched surgery on health outcomes at clearly lower direct cost, a pattern that held under stress tests of the assumptions. The authors present the injection as the better buy for suitable patients.
pmc-12715073:
Hiroyuki Ogawa, Masateru Ohta, and Mitsunori Ikeguchi set out a computer-driven protocol for hit-to-lead optimization, an early stage of drug discovery. In that stage, chemists start from a weak screening hit and hunt for a strong lead. Bench work is slow and can test only a few chemical forms. Their 2025 study uses PDE9A, a brain enzyme target, as the case.

The protocol generates vast sets of variant compounds in the computer, then scores them three ways. A precise physics method ranks how tightly each form binds the target. Machine learning tools then predict traits such as solubility, metabolic stability, and membrane permeability. The team worked site by site across the hit's structure. A known lead from past bench work sat near the top of their list. The result backs the protocol as a way to search far more forms than bench work allows.
pmc-12715773:
Joke van Vugt and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on short repeated stretches of DNA and a disease called ALS. In ALS, the nerves that control muscles die off, and patients grow weak. Repeated DNA stretches that expand too far cause several brain diseases, and some have been linked to ALS with mixed proof.

The team read a panel of thirty-nine such repeats in more than six thousand patients and about twenty-four hundred controls. They used a large shared project that gathers DNA from ALS patients worldwide. Repeat sizes were compared with a huge public database of genomes as well. The aim was to judge which repeats truly raise the risk of ALS or change its course. Firm answers help doctors read a patient's DNA with more confidence.
pmc-12717873:
Cancer drugs that release the immune system's brakes can, in rare cases, turn it against the nerves, and one such case ended in death. Ivan Bivolarski reports that case in a 2025 paper and draws a timing hypothesis from it. The patient, treated for melanoma, grew worse in step with infusions given at irregular, late hours.

Scans and labs ruled out spread of the cancer and other causes. Blood inflammation markers peaked soon after late-afternoon infusions, while earlier infusions had passed more quietly. One case cannot prove a cause, and the author says so. Still, the pattern raises a fair question: does the body's daily clock change how hard these drugs strike? The report urges steady, clock-aware scheduling and study of the idea.
pmc-12718273:
Eyasu Elias and co-authors measure, in a 2025 study, what twenty years of land restoration have actually achieved in the Ethiopian highlands. These hills are a textbook case of severe land degradation in Africa, driving food shortages, and vast conservation work has been poured into them since a landmark national study.

The team mined the national watershed database and checked fifty-six sample watersheds in the field. Satellite greenness and land cover maps from 2002 to 2022 tracked vegetation recovery and forest change. Their aim was to replace effort counts with outcome evidence: how much soil and water work exists on the ground, and whether the land is truly healing.
pmc-12722773:
Md Entaz Bahar and three co-authors pair laboratory work with machine learning and artificial neural networks to sharpen metabolic phenotyping of intervertebral disc cells. A bench analyzer tracks oxygen consumption and acid output in living cells, showing how cells produce energy. Accurate readings need a uniform cell layer and carefully titrated doses of key reagents. Their 2025 study asks which mathematical tools best predict the readings and cut wasted experimental runs.

Tree-based models won the prediction tasks for both continuous scores and class labels. One classification tool using straight and curved cuts also did well. The team then built a strict workflow joining blinded grouping with a trained neural network, and its output sat close to the real laboratory readings. They offer the workflow as a fair, data-driven way to read cell energy use at fine scale. It may serve both basic research and drug screening.
pmc-12727173:
Wagner Hummig and co-authors test a shell ginger essential oil against face pain in rats and inflammation in cells, in a 2025 study. Drugs for acute orofacial pain carry limits and side effects, pushing interest toward plant-based alternatives. The oil, from Alpinia zerumbet, has folk uses against pain and swelling but thin scientific backing. The team applied the oil, and a cream built on it, to rats after a small incision inside the mouth.

Treated rats flinched less from heat and pressure around the wound over three days of applications. Movement tests confirmed the animals were not merely sedated. Cell experiments probed the anti-inflammatory side in parallel. The authors present the formulation as a candidate topical treatment for post-surgical mouth pain, pending the usual climb from animal evidence toward human trials.
pmc-12727773:
Wiktor Więcławski and Jakub Paszulewicz published a 2025 brainwave study testing a famous claim about attention and eye movement. The premotor theory says attention benefits exist only where the eyes can move, since attention is just movement preparation. An earlier study seemed to confirm this: orienting shrank in the far temporal field when the eye was turned outward. The present team reran the setup while recording EEG, expecting a smaller attention-linked brain signal there.

No such reduction appeared. The signal stayed full size in the hard-to-reach field under eye abduction. The authors read this as support for the view that attention is its own process, not chained to the oculomotor range. Their result adds brain evidence to a behavioral debate.
pmc-12729173:
Taoyun Chen and seven co-authors present a 2025 study of a two in one vaccine for calves against two gut viruses. Both viruses are rising causes of severe diarrhea in young cattle around the world. A single shot that covers both could ease farm losses.

The team built the vaccine inside a weakened carrier virus. The carrier was fitted with a surface protein gene from each target virus. They gave the vaccine to mice and calves by muscle shot and by mouth. Blood tests showed strong antibody rises within two weeks of the shot. Levels peaked at high values in both routes, the authors report.
pmc-12731073:
Galant and a large team present a review from twenty twenty-five on skin-applied drugs for jaw joint disorders. Jaw pain is common, and creams offer a gentler route than pills or needles. The team search six databases for randomized trials on the topic. Nine trials with near four hundred patients qualify. Most carry low bias risk by standard scoring. Certain active creams cut pain scores significantly. A cannabidiol cream gives the largest pain drop.

Jaw opening effects look equal to placebo, likely from the rubbing itself. The authors call the evidence promising but thin. More trials are needed before firm advice. Safety and efficacy both need larger samples.
pmc-12731773:
Luis Chauca-Bajaña and colleagues pooled data on whether gum disease and mouth bacteria raise colorectal cancer risk. Periodontitis drives inflammation through the body, and two oral species are plausible cancer drivers. The review followed PRISMA guidance. It searched three databases through December twenty twenty-four. Included studies measured gum disease or oral bacteria against colorectal cancer cases or survival. Random-effects models pooled the risk estimates.

Trial sequential analysis, a further check, tested whether the data so far are even enough for firm claims. The team also measured how much the studies differed from one another. The analysis sorts a real link from a pile of small, inconsistent studies. For dentists and oncologists alike, the mouth-gut axis is a live hypothesis. This twenty twenty-five paper tests how much of it survives careful pooling.
pmc-12732273:
Faezeh Parastesh, Behnam Asgari Lajayer, and Bernard Dell present a 2025 review on teaming helpful root bacteria with biochar to defend crops against drought. Drought, worsened by climate change, threatens harvests worldwide. Biochar, charcoal worked into soil, forms a porous shelter where the bacteria colonize and survive better. Protected, the microbes then help the plant on several fronts at once.

They tune the plant's hormone balance, free up nutrients, and switch on antioxidant defenses. Gene activity shifts wholesale from a stressed profile toward a resilient one. The authors argue the pairing beats either partner alone. They call for field trials of custom combinations, long-term validation on farms, and deeper work on the molecular conversation between microbe, char, and plant. The review maps a route toward climate-ready farming.
pmc-12732773:
Brian Farley leads a team that backs low cost digital care plus metformin. Their paper from twenty twenty-five deals with diabetes and heart disease prevention. These ills kill more than a million folks in the US each year.

New weight drugs are costly and can drive health spend up. Metformin is cheap and proven to block diabetes onset. Digital tools can guide life change at large scale. A drug plus digital mix is put forth for first prevention. Rules for drug linked software open a path for it. The aim is care folks can afford.
pmc-12732973:
Robert Sattarov and co-authors test in 2025 a template-jumping gene editing approach for hemophilia B, a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by mutations in one gene. Current gene therapy uses viral vectors with limits, and factor infusions require frequent dosing. Some patients also develop antibodies against the replacement factor.

Their prime-editing method targets a gene region covering about nine percent of patients. It could address about seven percent of mutation types, they estimate. The design needs no change in key guide parts from lab to clinic. Added gain-of-function edits may offset low editing rates in the body.
pmc-12733373:
Florent Kouamé Amien and colleagues tested whether shade-tree agroforestry changes the flavor of Ivorian cocoa and chocolate. Beans of a common hybrid cultivar came from agroforestry and full-sun plantations in five producing regions. Pods were opened after a delay, fermented six days in wooden boxes, and sun-dried. The beans were processed into chocolate. Volatile aroma compounds were measured by mass spectrometry, and twelve professional judges scored the chocolates.

Aroma families like esters, aldehydes, and ketones varied widely across samples regardless of system. Some families, including alcohols, acids, and pyrazines, behaved similarly between systems. Geography and farming system interacted in the sensory results. The twenty twenty-five study matters as climate pressure pushes cocoa toward agroforestry; knowing the flavor cost or benefit guides that transition.
pmc-12734573:
Roberto Giurazza and co-authors reviewed airway care for throat and windpipe surgery in a 2025 paper. Surgeon and anesthesiologist must share one narrow airway through the whole case. Keeping oxygen up while the field stays clear is among the hardest tasks in anesthesia.

The review searched four databases for all work up to the end of June 2025. It sorts current tricks, from jet ventilation to tube-free spans, by their gains and risks. Each choice trades view, safety, and carbon dioxide control in its own way. The map helps teams pick a plan before a hard case starts.
pmc-12734973:
Wang and seven co-authors test how iron-bearing dust additions affect ferro-coke reactivity and hot strength, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Ferro-coke feeds blast furnaces, where strength at heat matters greatly. Dust additions from five to twenty percent and varied gasification temperatures are tested. Microscopy and CT imaging examine fracture patterns.

More dust raises reactivity from about fifty-nine to seventy-six percent. Hot strength falls from about thirty-two hundred to nineteen hundred newtons. Catalytic iron and zinc in dust speed gasification and porosity. Higher gasification temperature shows the same weakening trend. Raw material strategy must balance reactivity against strength loss.
pmc-12735973:
Chongyang Hu and co-authors compare how three fertilizers reshape soil microbe communities, in a 2025 study. Castor bean cake, a plant based by-product rich in carbon and nitrogen, is gaining use as a soil booster. Its effect on soil life was still unclear.

The team set castor cake against a chemical blend and a manure based product, each at several doses. Castor cake raised the range of bacteria and built denser, tougher webs of microbe links as dose rose. The manure product lost richness at high dose. Chance events drove most community change in all plots. The results favor castor cake for lively soil, with dose kept in a sound range.
pmc-12736273:
He Sang and co-authors present a 2025 lab study of propolis, a resin bees make, against a drug-resistant staph germ known as MRSA. The germ resists many drugs and often infects patients in care settings. It also builds biofilms, slimy layers that shield it from treatment, so new anti-biofilm options are in demand.

An alcohol extract of propolis stopped both test strains at the same dose. Staining and cell tests showed the extract blocked new biofilm growth and shrank films already formed, and microscope images showed fewer germs sticking to surfaces. Gene tests showed the extract turned down genes the germ uses to attach and build its film.
pmc-12738073:
Campos-Magaña, Martins dos Santos, and Garcia-Morales present a protocol from twenty twenty-five for mining bacterial genomes for product-making gene clusters. Soil bacteria hold vast untapped chemical variety in such clusters. Their pipeline starts with long-read sequencing of draft genomes. A search tool then flags clusters that may encode new natural products. A recombination method clones those clusters into an engineering-ready carrier. The whole route runs fast and at low cost in-house. Overnight sequencing on a small device allows many samples at once.

The protocol suits diverse bacteria if clean, long DNA can be drawn. It targets several product classes, from peptides to complex chains. Cloned clusters can then be studied or engineered further. The authors frame it as a prospecting tool for biotechnology.
pmc-12738673:
Shaya Alshaya builds a privacy-preserving system that identifies smart devices on a network in a paper from 2025. Connected devices ease daily life but widen the attack surface. Knowing which device is which helps secure a network, yet training data is sensitive. The proposed framework trains models across sites without moving raw data. A memory network reads the timing patterns in device traffic.

Error-correcting codes turn the multi-class problem into robust binary votes. Differential privacy noise guards the shared updates against inference attacks. Tests reached about ninety-six percent accuracy while cutting communication rounds by a quarter. The author argues the design scales to mixed, real-world device fleets.
pmc-12739173:
Dinesh Komarasamy, Rajkumar Rajavel, Karthikeyan Harimoorthy, and Aravind Pitchai present a scheduling framework for cloud business software in a 2025 paper. Cloud customers rent computing power on demand, but surges in job arrivals stretch queues and drag down service. Standard schedulers handle jobs well yet often miss the joint problem of queue delay and flexible supply.

Their algorithm pairs two parts. A tree-based scheduler maps each incoming job to the best virtual machine at once, trimming waits. A scaling part grows or shrinks capacity as load and provider rules dictate. In experiments the pair lifted resource use by roughly five to ten percent and finished jobs faster through early scaling. The authors aim it at business tools that cannot afford stalls.
pmc-12739473:
Elena Maryukhnich and a large team of co-authors give a protocol for an ex vivo lung tissue culture model to study lung infection and immune response, with SARS-CoV-2 as the test virus. Kept tissue holds the full build of the organ, unlike flat or organoid cultures. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Explants keep the matrix and the mixed cell sets, resident immune cells among them. Human samples from biopsy or autopsy dodge the leap from animal results to people, under proper ethics. Short tissue life is the main flaw, though tricks stretch it long enough to watch infection start and grow. The protocol lays out the full method.
pmc-12745773:
The deadliest heat waves may kill in ways that standard risk curves miss. Christopher Callahan and co-authors revisited the August two thousand three heat wave in France. Standard curves undercounted its deaths by fifty-five percent. Adding the piling effect of many hot days in a row matched the record far better. A machine learning method then split the blame between natural and human-caused warming.

About six thousand seventy-nine deaths were assigned to climate change in that one event. Since then, France has adapted strongly to heat. A repeat event today would kill over seventy-five percent fewer people, the team projects. The study shows both the rising risk and the payoff of adaptation.
pmc-12747673:
Zhiyang Tian and Changhui Li wrote a 2025 review on the gut's microbes and sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection. Sepsis kills many critically ill patients worldwide. The review argues that a disturbed gut community is not just a bystander but a driver of the downward spiral.

When gut balance breaks, the bowel wall leaks, bacteria and their toxins slip into the blood, and inflammation spreads to distant organs, which then harm the gut again. The authors survey fixes that aim at the gut, such as helpful bacteria and stool transplants. Those ideas show promise but lack standard protocols and strong trial proof. The paper maps what must be settled before gut therapy joins sepsis care.
pmc-12748873:
Adhithi Ravikumar and co-authors build an ensemble model to predict crop yields in a 2025 study. Accurate yield forecasts guide farm planning, food distribution, and policy. Standard statistical models often miss the nonlinear and time based patterns in yield data. Their model blends three learning methods: a memory network, a support vector method, and a boosting method.

Weights for each method shift based on recent error, giving more say to the model that validates best. Training used decades of data from a Tamil Nadu government crop report on food grains. The blend beat single models and other pairs on all error measures, with a very high fit score. Readers see dynamic weighting as the key to the gain.
pmc-12749473:
Oberndorfer and a large team showed the parents of pandemic-born babies differed socially from earlier cohorts in twenty twenty-five. Babies born during COVID-19 will be studied for years for early-life effects. But if their parents differ from past parents, comparisons can mislead.

The team analyzed over seventy-seven point nine million live births across fifteen countries. They compared the social makeup of the December twenty twenty to December twenty twenty-one cohort against what trends predicted. In Austria, England, Finland, the Netherlands, Scotland, Spain, Wales, and the United States, advantaged parents formed a larger share. In Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, and Mexico, the shift ran the other way. The authors warn that later outcome gaps may reflect this changed mix rather than the pandemic itself.
pmc-12749673:
Aparna Shil, Owura Amoakohene, and Havovi Chichger report a two thousand twenty-five cell study of natural sweeteners and the gut barrier. A leaky intestinal lining can precede metabolic disease. Artificial sweeteners were already known to disturb that barrier.

Three plant-based sweeteners were tested on a standard gut cell layer. Two of them, miraculin and a monk fruit compound, cut cell survival and raised damaging oxygen species. Barrier tightness fell and leakiness rose with both. Stevia caused none of these effects at any tested dose. Silencing the sweet taste receptor changed the response, naming a mechanism.
pmc-12750073:
Lele Wang and colleagues published a 2025 study of daily rest rhythms and heart disease. Wrist sensors measured how strongly activity rises and falls each day. A weak daily rhythm may signal poor health. The team used UK Biobank data. Participants had no heart disease when tracking began.

People with the weakest rhythms faced higher risk. Genetic risk scores were added to the picture. A genetics-based analysis tested whether the link is causal. Combining both approaches strengthens the conclusion. Daily rhythm strength could become a simple risk marker. It may also interact with inherited risk.
pmc-12750573:
Rebecca Aslakson and co-authors report, in a 2025 mixed-methods study, how cancer patients, families, and care teams shared treatment choices during the COVID-19 pandemic. The team guessed that stress and changes to care ran high for all three groups and set out to map what drove them.

Patients were facing surgery meant to cure upper digestive tract cancers. Between late 2020 and mid 2021, the team collected hundreds of surveys and dozens of deep interviews. Patients and families mostly trusted their teams and barely noticed pandemic changes. Staff, by contrast, reported large shifts in daily care. Quality of life scores did not track the waves of the virus.
pmc-12750873:
Hassan Daneshmandi and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2025 on a band-wrapping method meant to loosen stiff ankles in athletes. Limited upward bending of the ankle is common in sport and is linked to worse performance and higher injury risk. Half of the male athletes in the trial had their ankles wrapped tightly and then did pumps, squats, and lunges. The other half did standard calf stretching instead. Movement was measured before, right after, and one hour later.

The wrapped group gained more upward ankle movement right away than the stretching group, on both legs. A small part of that gain was still present an hour later. Bending in the opposite direction also improved more with wrapping on the stronger leg. Because the wrapping session combined several exercises and lasted longer, the authors say more work is needed to confirm the result and isolate what caused it.
pmc-12752073:
Fanxu Zeng, Shuishi Li, and Pengbo Deng weigh, in a 2025 analysis, whether a costly new lung cancer drug earns its price. The drug pairs an antibody with a cell-killing payload. The authors model the trade from the view of American payers.

Their twenty-year model found the new drug added over two hundred thousand dollars in cost for about a tenth of a quality-adjusted life year. The cost per unit of benefit landed in the millions, far past the usual threshold. In the squamous subtype it cost more and did worse outright. Body weight and the drug's price drove the results most. The authors conclude the drug is poor value for this use in the United States.
pmc-12753773:
Zhipeng Liu, Sa-Hoe Lim, and Shin Jung combined radiation with a metabolism drug in 2025. Radiation kills cancer by damaging DNA. Tumours often resist that damage, though. Low oxygen inside tumours also helps resistance. Cancer cells switch energy pathways to survive. Blocking one energy pathway was tested.

Mice carried sarcoma tumours inside the skull. One group got radiation plus the blocker. Scans showed the greatest tumour shrinkage there. Survival also improved in that group. Cancer cells piled up harmful oxygen radicals. DNA repair faltered and cell death rose. Stem-like traits in tumours also fell.
pmc-12753973:
Meiting Jiang and co-authors surveyed nurses about night shift work and low mood in two thousand twenty-five. Nurses at a large hospital in Haikou, China, took part. The authors asked how heavy night work links to signs of depression, and what steps lie in between.

Of six hundred fourteen nurses, about half screened positive for depressive signs. Heavier night work was linked to higher scores. Poor sleep was the strongest middle step, with social avoidance and fear of missing out also playing a part. The authors call for broad steps that ease night load and protect sleep, social life, and mental health for nurses on night shifts.
pmc-12757373:
Ya-ping Li and co-authors present a 2025 study of an old alcohol treatment drug as a block on a fiery form of cell death. In mouse immune cells, the drug stopped the joint death mode and kept cell membranes whole. It blocked death proteins from binding the cells' power units, which cut leaks and toxic oxygen bursts. It also stopped the death complex from forming. In mice with a blood cell swelling disease, the drug eased body wide swelling and organ harm. The authors pitch it for reuse.
pmc-12764173:
Ahmed Shamakhi and seven co-authors report two boy cases of Bruton's disease, a rare gene flaw that leaves kids with near no germ shields. Their case set appeared in twenty twenty-five. The flaw sits in a gene for B cell growth, so boys face repeat grave chest germs. Early gene tests and set shield drips are key to care.

One boy, at fourteen months, had repeat chest ills and slow growth, and died when drips were missed. A boy of three, with repeat chest ills and low white cells, had the gene flaw proved by tests. Set drips and close watch steadied him. The team stresses fast gene checks and strict drip care.
pmc-12766773:
Matthew Asare and co-authors adapt a talk-plus-self-test plan to lift cervical screening among women living with HIV in Ghana, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. A thirty-six-member board of patients, providers, and neighbors reshaped the plan. Forty-five users then graded the result.

Core parts stayed: self-sampling plus a three-step message frame. Hospitals and pharmacies were the top sampling spots, picked by near all. Voice notes in English and local tongues won as the delivery mode. Scores for fit, ease, and uptake ran high. Ease, privacy, and pride cut fear and raised engagement. Readers get a culture-tuned path to a lifesaving test.
pmc-12768373:
Tuberculosis bacteria survive inside macrophages, the very cells meant to kill them. Yuzhong Xu and co-authors identify a long noncoding RNA, LINC02528, that the pathogen exploits. Deleting it with gene editing cut bacterial survival and raised a key immune signal. Blocking that signal erased the benefit.

pmc-12772573:
Rachel Nelan leads a fifteen-author team shaking cancer cells off biopsy surfaces to feed genome sequencing without consuming the tissue, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Whole-genome sequencing wants abundant, high-quality tumor DNA. Diagnosis wants the same tissue intact under the microscope. Both claims collide in small biopsies.

Cells shaken from fresh biopsy surfaces yielded DNA for sequencing, benchmarked against the frozen-tissue gold standard. The tissue itself remained for histology and staining. The workflow was piloted on real breast cancer samples. If shaken cells sequence faithfully, pathology departments can serve molecular and microscopic masters from one specimen. The trick is humble, a shake, but it resolves a daily logistics fight in cancer genomics.
pmc-12772973:
Umberto Pensato, Andrew Demchuk, and a large team compare scores that predict brain bleed growth. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, works with patients in southern Alberta, Canada. A bleed inside the brain can swell in the first hours, which worsens outcomes. Many scores claim to flag who will swell, using scans of three kinds.

Sixteen scores enter the test on two hundred seventeen patients. Plain scans give eight scores, and dye-based scans give the rest. Growth is counted at two levels, standard and severe. Fancy scans do add power step by step, as the title says. The best score of each kind is compared head to head. The work guides which score a hospital should trust.
pmc-12781373:
Zoran Golušin and co-authors track syphilis trends in the Vojvodina province of Serbia and survey medical students on the infection, in a paper from 2025. Syphilis is rising in many countries. Future health workers will play a key part in prevention, early detection, and teaching the public.

Case records from 1997 to 2024 held just over one thousand reported cases, most in people aged twenty-five to thirty-four. Rates were recalculated in standard forms to allow fair comparison across years. The team also surveyed more than three hundred and fifty medical students in late 2024. The survey tested facts about the infection and views on prevention, stigma, and training. Results point to where student teaching can be improved.
pmc-12785973:
Sihle Mabhida and ten co-authors review inflammation as a warning signal in a combined heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome in a 2025 article. The syndrome, formally recognized only recently, links cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic disorders, and body wide inflammation is thought to drive both its course and its outcomes.

The team searched five databases for studies from the syndrome's first eighteen months of formal existence. Eligible work measured inflammation markers in adults and tracked death or disease progression. Studies varied too much in markers and follow up for pooled statistics, so the authors summarized narratively. Bias was checked with a standard tool. Their verdict: inflammation markers look prognostic, but the young field needs standardized markers and validation before clinical use.
pmc-12786473:
Jed Bailey and co-authors review hybrid fixation for ankle syndesmosis injuries in a 2025 paper. The syndesmosis is the tight joint that binds the two shin bones above the ankle. It can tear alone or with a fracture. Hybrid fixation joins a stiff screw with a flexible dynamic implant, either as two parts or in one device.

The search found six studies, four in patients and two on cadavers. Ninety-three patients got the hybrid method, and their mean ankle function scores at last check were high. X-rays showed the joint mostly stayed in place. A small share had poor alignment, removal of implants, or implant failure, and all failures were silent ones in a single study. Cadaver tests showed the joint moved much as a healthy one does. The authors back the method but note thin, uneven evidence.
pmc-12787673:
Naluemol Sriprasert and colleagues measure fracture resistance of ceramic-reinforced polymer tooth crowns glued with cements of different stiffness. Their 2025 laboratory study compares two commercial crowns and one newly developed printed crown.

Ninety-nine lower molar models each received a crown of one type, fixed with one of three cements. Micro scanning examined the cement layer shape before load testing. Crowns on two resin cements withstood very high forces without visible failure. Glass-ionomer cement crowns were weaker and cracked or fractured. The commercial printed crown sometimes broke fully, while the new material only cracked superficially. All combinations withstood forces above typical chewing loads, supporting the new crown's promise.
pmc-12787873:
Weihua Zhang and co-authors study, in a 2025 plant paper, the switch that controls a small RNA in a eucalyptus tree tied to cold defense. The RNA rises in roots under cold and helps tune a known cold pathway. The team asked where the RNA is made most and what DNA switch drives it.

The RNA gathered mainly in roots, rising there under cold while falling in shoots. Its switch region, nearly two thousand letters long, carried many stress and hormone response sites. In test plants, the switch drove strong root-focused activity and answered to cold and a defense hormone. Cutting the switch into pieces mapped which parts do the work.
pmc-12788073:
Domaradzki studies diet, activity, and sleep quality in university students in twenty twenty-five. Diet and movement are key lifestyle factors tied to sleep. Their joint and sex specific links were not well understood. The study surveyed four hundred eighteen students at a Polish health and sport university.

A feature selection step found nine eating behaviours tied to sleep quality. Fast food, fried meals, and sweet or energy drinks linked to poorer sleep. Vegetables, curd cheese, and wholegrain bread linked to better sleep. Poor sleep was far more common in women than in men. Physical activity formed part of a modest indirect path from diet to sleep. That indirect path was stronger among women. The author supports integrated, sex sensitive lifestyle programs.
pmc-12793073:
Liu and Bian present a study from twenty twenty-five on RNA oxidation in heart cell enlargement. A hormone-driven cell model mimics high blood pressure heart strain. Key markers of enlargement are tracked by gene tests. An oxidation product in RNA climbs as cells enlarge. A guardian enzyme that clears that product also rises. A signaling pathway switches on alongside the damage. Flooding cells with extra guardian enzyme cuts the oxidation product. Pathway activity and cell enlargement then fall as well.

The authors conclude oxidation damage helps drive the enlargement. The damage product may act by switching on that pathway. The work opens a fresh angle on heart failure origins. Age-linked diseases may share the mechanism, they suggest.
pmc-12796073:
Mingzhe Shi, Shounan Qi, Chenming Wang, and Chenguang Wang report a severe eye injury from caterpillar hairs in this 2025 case paper. Their patient, a fifty-five-year-old man, brushed against a pine processionary caterpillar and felt pain and blurred sight in his left eye. The illness is the rarest form of nodular ophthalmia, an inflammation driven by hairs lodged in the eye.

Doctors removed the hairs they could see and started anti-inflammatory drops, but the inflammation ran out of control. At the authors' hospital, sight in the eye had fallen to sensing hand motion. Two hairs remained, one under the surface and one inside the front chamber. Surgery removed them, and drugs calmed the eye. Four years on, mild inflammation, swelling at the back of the eye, and a cataract persisted, with vision settled low. The authors urge searches for hidden hairs and follow-up.
pmc-12797473:
Jiao Yu and co-authors read the gene activity of a rare cycad under freezing stress in a 2025 study. Cycas panzhihuaensis is a subtropical plant with conservation value, and cold blocks its spread to higher, cooler ground. Plant hormones run the cold response through tangled signaling webs, but in this species the wiring was largely unknown.

The team chilled plants at minus five degrees for two set times and measured hormone levels in the leaves. In parallel, transcriptome sequencing listed which genes switched on or off. Joining the two views shows which hormone paths carry the freezing signal in this cycad. That map guides both conservation planting and any attempt to breed or engineer hardier stock. The work is a first molecular pass at an ancient plant lineage.
pmc-12798773:
Canada tracks accidents in labs that work with human pathogens and toxins, and Emily Tran, Audrey Gauthier, Antoinette Davis, Christine Abalos, and Samuel Bonti-Ankomah report the twenty twenty-four tally. A national system logged seventy-one confirmed exposure incidents that year, affecting one hundred and thirty-two people. That works out to about sixty-eight incidents per thousand active licences, a rate above the year before.

Bacteria caused nearly two thirds of the events, and routine microbiology work was the setting for most. Public health labs had the highest rate, and technicians were the most often affected group. Slips in procedure and human factors led the causes, with a median five days before reports came in. Working outside safety cabinets recurred in the stories.
pmc-12799873:
Elwakkad and three co-authors published an animal study in twenty twenty-five testing carvacrol, a compound from herbs such as oregano, against breast cancer in rats. Earlier lab work hinted the compound can push cancer cells to self-destruct, so the team tested it in living animals.

The compound switched on genes that guard against tumors and raised signals that drive cell death, while lowering a protein that blocks it. It also cut chemical damage from oxygen stress and helped the liver and kidneys recover. Injection worked best of the three routes. The authors read the results as support for carvacrol as a helper treatment, while noting that dose and delivery need more work before human use.
pmc-12801573:
Leili Mosalanejad and co-authors explore, in a 2025 interview study, why medical students at an Iranian university put work off and lose pleasure in it. Procrastination and anhedonia, the fading of enjoyment, feed on the heavy pressure of medical training and drag down both grades and well-being.

Thirty-two students across preclinical and clinical years and several health programs gave deep interviews. Five themes emerged: fading motivation tied to job insecurity, a curriculum felt as too theoretical, weak teaching contact, structural flaws in planning and training, and personal struggles with time and emotion. The map of causes points to fixes beyond telling students to try harder.
pmc-12801873:
Borja Herraiz-Ahijado and colleagues report the Active Legs trial on exercise for venous leg ulcers, published in two thousand twenty-five. Venous ulcers burden patients' quality of life and health budgets. Physical activity might speed healing, but earlier evidence was patchy.

The pragmatic randomized trial ran in thirteen Madrid health centers. Forty-four patients with venous ulcers received standard care. Half also joined a structured educational exercise program. Follow-up lasted six months, with healing checked at three and six months. Recruitment ran from two thousand twenty-one to two thousand twenty-three. The paper evaluates whether the activity program raised complete healing rates. Primary care delivery makes the intervention cheap to scale if it works.
pmc-12802273:
Feifei Li and three co-authors study why feeling worse off than others can make students less forgiving, in a paper published in twenty twenty-five. Forgiveness supports mental health, yet most past work looked at personal hurts rather than social pressures. The team tested a chain: feeling deprived drains mental energy, and that drain blocks forgiveness.

Over eight hundred college students in Shandong Province, China, filled in surveys on site. The measures covered felt deprivation, forgiveness, drained energy, and psychological resources such as hope and resilience. As predicted, stronger deprivation tied to less forgiveness. Drained energy carried part of that link. Students rich in psychological resources felt the drain less, which softened the chain. The model points to ways schools might protect forgiveness.
pmc-12804773:
Ruizong Xu, Liangfu Xie, and Yongshou Zhang study blasting in layered rock in a 2025 paper. Most prior work assumed rock with uniform traits, but real sites often have layers of hard and soft rock stacked together. The team used a particle based simulation method to track stress, cracks, and contact forces during blasting.

They found that the surrounding rock type and the layer thickness strongly shaped blasting results, while the angle between layers mattered little. In hard rock, reflected stress first rose and then fell as layers grew thicker. In soft rock, stress changed little, but crack patterns shifted even with thin layers. The simulation matched real blasting tests, which supports its use in planning.
pmc-12815873:
Aswathi Ramesh and co-authors present a study whose head gives the year as 2025. The catalog lists it under 2026. The topic is a yeast that causes brain infection, worst in people with weak defense systems. After entering through the airway, the yeast crosses into the brain. There it sheds a sugar coat that drives much of the harm. The team asks how host membrane fats steer where that coat strikes.

The team purified the sugar coat from a standard yeast strain. Human stem-cell models of brain tissue served as test beds. The models include nerve cells and organ-like brain balls that lack one defense cell type. Stains, blots, and tissue slices track the coat's targets. Brain researchers get a map of which cells the coat hits and how membrane fat mix changes the hit list. That map may point to new ways to block brain harm.
pmc-12816373:
Pengfei Zhao and co-authors review progress, in a paper whose journal version is dated 2025, on using a natural body chemical to flag harmful drug interactions. When two drugs are taken together, carrier proteins that move drugs through the liver can be blocked, changing how a drug behaves. Lab and animal tests for this effect have limits, so researchers seek markers already present in the body.

The marker in focus is coproporphyrin, in two forms made by the body itself. Its blood levels rise when a key liver carrier, OATP1B, is blocked, which makes it a promising sign of such interactions. The review covers the evidence so far and how models can pair with the marker to predict interaction size. Open gaps include clear cutoff values and the effect of disease.
pmc-12817673:
Steven Patrick Ahumada Prado, Shayne Mason, Robin Wood, and Laneke Luies read the chemical fingerprints in urine to see how HIV and tuberculosis together disturb the body's metabolism, in a 2025 paper. Each infection strains the immune system and the body's chemistry, and together they hit harder. The team used a magnetic resonance method to profile urine from three groups: healthy people, untreated people carrying both infections, and coinfected people on standard HIV therapy.

Coinfection shifted chemicals tied to gut microbes, energy production, and sugar handling. The pattern pointed to strained cell powerhouses, signs of insulin resistance, and an unbalanced gut. Therapy partly repaired the picture: cell energy markers steadied, gut signals calmed, and stress chemicals fell. Sugar control, though, stayed off track. Two chemicals stood out as possible markers for telling coinfection apart and tracking response to treatment, and the authors call for larger studies to confirm them.
pmc-12817773:
Napolitano and three co-authors measure how strong the working bond is between nurses and patients with inflammatory bowel disease. The study ran in several Italian centers with 453 adult outpatients. Patients filled in a 20-item scale covering trust, shared decisions, and the nurse as a point of reference.

Scores came out high overall, and patients with ulcerative colitis scored higher than those with Crohn's disease. Privacy and attention to well-being earned the best marks. Emotional sharing and clarifying information from other professionals scored lower. The authors say nurses hold a central place in long-term bowel care. They suggest better emotional communication could strengthen the bond further.
pmc-12819673:
Feng and five co-authors probe how a surface protein helps melanoma dodge the immune system. The text is dated 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. The protein, podoplanin, is common on tumor cells. It is known to aid spread, but its part in immune escape was less clear.

Stains and data checks tied high podoplanin to more PD-L1 and fewer killer T cells. A peptide that blocks the protein cut PD-L1 through the beta-catenin path. Mouse tests showed the blocker restored immune attack on tumors. The team offers the protein as a drug target. Blocking it may sharpen immune therapy for melanoma.
pmc-12820273:
Xie and co-authors present MVPHI, a learning framework that predicts microbe interactions of two kinds. It targets links between phages and bacteria, and between bacteria themselves. Phages, viruses that infect bacteria, steer microbe communities and their turnover, so these links matter for microbiome science.

Wet-lab tests of such links are costly and risky, pushing the field toward computation. Older predictors suffer from low accuracy and slow speed, the authors note. MVPHI uses multi-view learning, joining several data views of each microbe. The aim is faster, sharper forecasts of complex microbial interactions for research use.
pmc-12821973:
Xiaoling Li and six colleagues compare anesthesia strategies for keyhole lung surgery within an enhanced recovery protocol. One hundred twenty patients having video-assisted wedge resections were randomized to a double-lumen breathing tube, or to a laryngeal mask combined with either an intercostal nerve block or a paravertebral block. The tubeless options avoid full intubation.

The mask plus paravertebral block group left hospital sooner, walked and ate earlier, and reported less pain for the first day. Inflammatory markers were lower in both mask groups. The tube gave surgeons a better view but brought more sore throats, hoarseness, and higher costs. The authors recommend the paravertebral combination for suitable patients.
pmc-12822173:
Hanrahan and a large team study gene balance in a skink that can reverse its sex in twenty twenty-five. Most animals with two unlike sex chromosomes must even out gene output between the sexes. This skink has an XY system, but cold nests can turn a female into a male. That gives a rare chance to split the roles of genes and body type.

The team built a draft genome for the skink and read gene use in brain and heart tissue. Males made somewhat less from their single X than females from two. In sex reversed males, X output matched females, not normal males. Gene balance thus follows the gene set, not the body type.
pmc-12827773:
Nakia Best and six colleagues published a brief report in two thousand twenty-five on burnout among school nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic. School nurses carried heavy new loads: testing, tracing, shifting rules, and exposure risk. The strain threatened to push them out of the workforce.

Those burned out scored much higher on moral distress, and the two rose together. Being blocked from giving preventive care tied most strongly to burnout. Written answers blamed crushing workloads and system barriers. Peer support stood out as the main source of hope.
pmc-12829273:
Minghui Deng and four co-authors mapped how community programs fight youth substance use in the northeast of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in this 2025 study. Five training centers teach young adults job skills as a shield against drug use, backed by churches, community workers, and aid groups. Four groups carry the work: the youths, a leadership team, teachers, and youth leaders. The map shows how they hand tasks and trust to each other. The authors stress that local engagement is the engine, and they point to technology as the next lever for making the centers run better and reach further.
pmc-12830873:
Mona Hamelian and co-authors made magnetic particles that pull an antibiotic out of water, in a 2025 study. The drug, ciprofloxacin, escapes into water systems and feeds resistance risks. Their particles are magnetite coated with tannic acid, a plant compound rich in sticky groups. A magnet can then lift the loaded particles out of cleaned water for reuse.

The team tuned acidity, dose, contact time, and drug level with a response surface method. At the best settings, removal topped eighty-seven percent. The uptake pattern fit a single-layer model, and the speed pattern pointed to mixed physical and chemical binding. After five reuse cycles, performance fell by only eight percent. The authors present the particles as a cheap, green option for antibiotic cleanup.
pmc-12835273:
Human milk holds live cells from the breast, a rare painless way to study the gland at work. Marion Salmon-Legagneur and fifteen co-authors read one hundred twenty-seven milk samples in 2025 to see how stage of feeding, mother's age, and past births shape those cells. They sorted the cells by type, read their gene use, and grew them for three weeks to test how well they thrive.

As feeding went on, total cell counts fell while the share of lining cells and milk-gene use rose. Older mothers gave fewer lining cells, with weaker growth in the dish. Milk from mothers with past births held more of the milk-making type than the base type. The team say milk can serve as a live model of the breast, with links to long-term breast change and cancer risk.
pmc-12836773:
Yazdani and co-authors test whether two high-risk virus types show up more often in bladder tumors. Human papillomavirus types 16 and 18 are known cancer drivers at other body sites. Their role in bladder cancer is less settled. The team took tissue from patients with bladder tumors and from a control group without tumors. Both virus types appeared more often in tumor samples than in controls. That gap, though, was not strong enough to rule out chance. Viral load told a clearer story: type 16 load was far higher in patients, and type 18 load was higher too. The authors weigh what the load gap may mean.
pmc-12839273:
Rachel Herz argues that smell and emotion are, at their core, the same thing, in a 2025 perspective essay. It draws on theory and lab findings to show that a smell's emotional tone is the experience, rather than an extra layer. Herz hopes the argument will widen how feeling science defines its terms and guide new work on smell, emotion, and care.
pmc-12840273:
Vania Hungria and co-authors present a 2025 study of real-world care for multiple myeloma, a cancer of the blood, in Argentina and Brazil. pmc-12845073:
Rousou and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a methods comparison for judging Salmonella test accuracy. Salmonella from food is a major cause of illness worldwide. All models found the DNA tests highly specific, above ninety-eight percent. Sensitivity estimates ranged from about eighty-six to ninety-five percent by model. Models robust to threshold differences gave more cautious estimates. Culture itself looked highly accurate but with wide uncertainty ranges. pmc-12847573:
Xiujie Liu, Donghai Cheng, and Fangyan Wang report a single case in which gut treatment seemed to strengthen lymphoma therapy, in a 2025 case report. Their patient had high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, an aggressive blood cancer, treated with the standard drug mix called R-CHOP. The hope was that a healthier gut would support the immune side of treatment.

The tumor shrank markedly while blood counts stayed stable. Gut analysis showed more of several helpful bacterial genera after treatment. pmc-12849373:
Tizita Mesfin and colleagues measured undernutrition in Ethiopian cancer patients in 2025. Poor nutrition drives many cancer deaths. Past Ethiopian estimates varied very widely. A standard global method was used here. It mixes body signs with causes.

pmc-12852173:
Yanyao Zhang and a large team of co-authors squeeze an iron mineral to pressures found inside large planets, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. pmc-12855673:

Many sites had set their own ways to run the scan. That made joint work and shared data hard to build. Teams from seven sites met online to align their steps. They used test objects and expert views to set values. Each gear type gets its own clear scan plan. Shared rules should help care and research alike.
pmc-12857773:
Hernandez-Mancillas and three co-authors report surgery that restored transplant hope, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their patient was a man on dialysis with severe obesity. A huge hanging fold of belly tissue blocked access to the spot used for a kidney transplant.

That tissue problem kept him out of the transplant protocol. Checks showed stable blood tests and clearance from several teams for major surgery. Surgeons removed the massive fold in one block in an extended panniculectomy. The goal was to clear the anatomy so transplant steps could resume. The case shows a practical bridge step for select patients shut out by body shape alone.
pmc-12885173:

pmc-12929373:
Misato Ota and Toshiaki Makino trace the history of rhubarb medicine in Japan in a paper whose text is dated 2025. Rhubarb root has served as a drug in Asia and Europe for ages. Which plant truly supplied the drug was long confused. The pair set out to settle the Japanese record.

Later, a Chinese rhubarb species was imported and grown as the true source. That species is a weak laxative, so strong effects were likely not expected. A stronger Russian type arrived with Dutch medicine late in the Edo era. The study untangles names that shifted across centuries.
pmc-13100273:

Earliest steps involve the tissue lining, alarm signals, and innate immune cells. Those steps not only start the classic allergic response. They also keep chronic inflammation burning on their own. Allergy antibodies and helper cells then direct which triggers cause harm. Grains of detail extend to the cells that flood inflamed tissue. Control ideally means removing the trigger, but that is rarely full in asthma. Genes and gene regulation help explain why most exposed people stay healthy.
pmc-13101773:
Xiang Lin and co-authors build a skin treatment in a 2026 paper on sun-aged skin. pmc-13134973:
Ayşe Kubat Üzüm and co-authors study life quality in people treated for an underactive thyroid, in work from 2026. Patients take a daily hormone pill, and doctors track a blood marker to judge dose. Whether hitting the target range for that marker tracks with feeling well was unclear.

The study drew records from twenty-six centers and 1,750 patients, most of them women. About one in ten had never reached their target in three years of follow-up. Patients who hit the target least often reported worse thyroid-linked life quality on many fronts, from tiredness to mood and daily function. Their general health scores were also lower. The authors urge personal targets and steady follow-through.
pmc-13138273:
Truc Tam Vu, Thai Duc Hoang, and Hanh The Nguyen present a surgical study dated two thousand twenty-six on severe adult spinal deformity. The condition bends the spine out of line and can squeeze nerves, cutting quality of life for older patients. When gentler care fails, surgery is the remaining route.

The team used a modified fusion method that joins vertebrae through the side of the disc space. Their version adds four changes, including reshaping the back of the spine and placing the spacer toward the front. Seventy-two patients, with an average age near sixty-five, were treated at one center. The study reports both X-ray measures and patient outcomes.
pmc-13138773:

They scored each scan for ossification using published criteria. Comparing its frequency between the groups tests whether bone specks separate true disease from mimics. pmc-13141373:
Naglaa Bahr and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six rat study pairing purslane extract with metformin against diabetes-related memory loss. Diabetes often dulls thinking over time. Purslane, an edible plant, carries many protective compounds.

Groups received purslane extract, metformin, or a half-dose combination for four weeks. Memory was tested in a water maze. Brain tissue was checked for oxidative stress, inflammation, and transmitter changes. The combination aimed to match full-dose benefits more gently.
pmc-13148873:
A replacement kneecap's thickness is a surgical judgment call with mechanical consequences no one had mapped fully. Ning Guo and co-authors run the numbers in a 2026 simulation study of total knee replacement.

Computer models varied the kneecap thickness and watched walking and squatting change. A thicker kneecap strengthened the extensor mechanism, the lever that straightens the knee, and eased loading between thigh and shin bones at deep bends. A thinner one cut contact forces on the kneecap itself and may allow a wider range of motion. Surgeons' caution cuts both ways, the authors show: each choice buys one benefit with another's coin. The map should help tailor the call to the patient.
pmc-13152873:
Lei and four co-authors test a wearable laser device that treats head pain through acupuncture points. Forty-eight volunteers with right-sided temple pain were split evenly between the real device and a sham.

Pain was scored on a standard scale and probed with a pressure filament. After treatment, the laser group's pain scores fell clearly more than the sham group's. Deep pressure pain eased as well. The authors conclude the wearable therapy works for this kind of head pain. They note the trial was triple-blinded, so neither patients nor testers knew the assignments.
pmc-13154473:
Kajsa Söderhielm and co-authors evaluate how a digital stroke rehabilitation program landed in real clinics. F@ce 2.0 pairs person-centred goal setting with phone-based support for survivors at home. Pandemic strain and thin rollout planning dogged the launch. Reach among survivors stayed low, and teams were not ready to deliver the program as drawn. pmc-13155173:
Milani and colleagues screened blood donations in Manaus, Brazil in 2026 for Oropouche virus during the 2023 to 2024 outbreak. The authors say the findings raise real blood safety questions and demand continued donor and recipient watch.
pmc-13156073:

Many failed programs, they say, died of recruitment strain, not weak drugs. They urge regulators to formalize such designs.
pmc-13156973:

The authors argue that joint cells, starved of proper fuel and under chemical stress, may be prone to this death. Dying cells could then feed more swelling, locking the joint into a harmful cycle. They list candidate treatments, from plant compounds to targeted blockers and gel-based drug delivery. Direct proof in this disease, they note, is still missing.
pmc-13161573:

The authors urge narrow use of the test and strict reading of results, to avoid wrong labels and wrong care.
pmc-13166273:
Five authors present a survey, published in two thousand twenty-five, on limiting futile treatment in Polish intensive care units. The team handed an anonymous questionnaire to staff at a national intensive care conference. Three hundred fifty-four people answered. Nearly all said talking with patients about end-of-life care matters. The authors compared junior and senior staff to see how experience shapes views on when treatment should stop.
pmc-13167373:

Burden rose as unmanaged symptoms grew. The team used layered models to weigh the link over time. The findings argue for symptom control as carer support, not just patient care.
pmc-13171373:

One group had mixed sense-and-movement damage, one sense-only, one none.

Clinical features and blood markers were compared across groups. The aim was a clearer basis for diagnosis and care. Nerve involvement changes how the disease is graded and treated.
