pmc-13178473:
Kegya and four co-authors studied diet and cognition in young people with sickle cell disease in Kumasi, Ghana, in twenty twenty-six. Sickle cell disease alters red blood cells and often comes with thinking difficulties. Micronutrients, the vitamins and minerals in food, might affect cognition, but evidence in this group was thin.

The study compared sixty-four stable patients with sixty-four community controls, all aged thirteen to twenty-four. Food intake came from a one-day recall, and cognition from a digit span memory test. Surprisingly, patients scored higher overall, driven by one genotype group and offset by another. After strict correction for many tests, no nutrient was clearly linked to cognition. Niacin and selenium showed plausible trends worth further study, the authors say.
pmc-13179273: Naoko Fujita, Spyros Lytras, and Yuka Hagiwara-Komoda report a new plant virus found in a persimmon cultivar in a paper from 2026. The virus came from a male tree of the cultivar Kumemaru. Its complete genome runs about six thousand four hundred nucleotides and encodes one large polyprotein. The protein carries the conserved domains typical of its genus, Marafivirus. Family tree and sequence comparisons place it as a distinct species in the family Tymoviridae. The authors propose the name persimmon marafivirus for the newcomer.
pmc-13180573:
Yujia Lin, Yue Zou, and Xin Wang published this consumer psychology study in 2026. Live-streaming commerce increasingly uses AI anchors, digital hosts that sell products on camera around the clock. Whether they can replace human hosts is an open question. The team ran an experiment with 439 people, each randomly shown a sales stream hosted by a human or by an AI anchor, then surveyed on trust and buying intent.

Human anchors won more trust and stronger buying intent overall. The path to trust differed, though. A feeling of closeness carried the human advantage, above all for viewers shopping for pleasure. A feeling of responsiveness helped the AI anchor only among viewers focused on efficiency, and it backfired when that focus was weak. The authors conclude that AI anchors will not broadly replace humans, but can work when matched to goal-driven shoppers.
pmc-13183073:
Yu Zhao and co-authors build a tool to spot frailty in older patients on long term dialysis, in a 2026 study from China. Frailty in this group links to worse daily life, hospital stays, falls, and death. A clear early check can help nurses act in time.

The team studied close to three hundred patients aged sixty and over at two large hospitals in Hohhot. They used standard scales for illness load, daily function, food risk, sleep, and mood. About two thirds of the patients proved frail. The authors used the strongest factors to build a scoring model and tested how well it sorted frail from non-frail patients.
pmc-13184173:
Elzana Odzakovic and four co-authors shadow nurses to see how home care work is changing in Sweden. Their 2026 study follows registered and specialist nurses in municipal home care. Roles, duties, and skill needs are shifting as more older people live at home. The team watched whole shifts to catch the changes as they happen.

They shadowed eighteen nurses, twelve registered and six specialists, from shift start to end. Notes grouped into four themes, from hidden work in the system to tasks moving toward neighborhoods. Nurses were seen working around gaps with limited support. The authors urge that nurses' coordinating role be made visible and valued. Home care planning, they argue, must reckon with the load these nurses quietly carry.
pmc-13186573:
Arreola-Calderon and three co-authors mapped in twenty twenty-six a germ path that breaks down a plant-scent acid across the germ world. That path is a core route to clear scent waste, yet its spread was not well known. They read more than six thousand germ and archaea genomes for its parts.

They found high-trust signs of a key start part in more than eight hundred genomes, near one in eight. Core build traits of that part were kept, which backs the name calls. The path's gene layout shifts a lot by line, but a small set of rule genes stays. Old germ lines hold just bits of the path.
pmc-13187873:
Ioana Popescu and co-authors report a 2026 study on why rates of major leg removal after diabetic foot wounds vary by US region. Such wounds are common in older adults with diabetes, and loss of a leg is a grave outcome. Knowing which local traits track with high rates can guide policy to cut them.

The study pooled Medicare cases from 2017 to 2019 for people aged 66 and up, grouped by hospital referral region. In all, close to 708,000 wounds were counted across 306 regions. Local traits in view were racial mix, a poverty index, counts of doctors by type, and whether hospitals ran wound care programs. Rates and local traits varied widely across regions. A space-and-time model weighed how each trait links to the share of wounds that end in major removal.
pmc-13190873:
Aiman Fatima and co-authors present a 2026 report on a screening program for pregnant patients in rural Missouri. The program asks about adverse childhood experiences, meaning trauma faced before age 18. Such experiences are linked to later illness, and in pregnancy they raise the risk of depression, anxiety, and substance use.

The clinic began screening in 2019 so patients with high scores could get referrals and support. The team reviewed charts from early 2021 and early 2022 to judge how well the program worked. Of 144 patients, 50 had a score of three or more. Scores did not differ much between the two periods. The report shows both the reach of screening and the need it reveals.
pmc-13195673:
Thomas Whittemore and co-authors build an iron-based dye for solar cells in a 2026 chemistry paper. Dyes that harvest light usually rely on rare metals like ruthenium. Iron is cheap and plentiful, but its excited states usually die too fast to use. Their iron compound pairs a strong donor part with a greedy acceptor part to hold the excited state longer.

Anchored on titanium dioxide, the dye fired its energized electrons into the solid in a hot, fast step. The separated charge then lasted for thousandths of a second, an age in this field. Careful spectra and computer models explained why the state survived. Iron dyes that behave could cut the cost of solar fuel devices sharply.
pmc-13196673:
Pan and eight co-authors studied soils under salt-tolerant plants in dry salt marshes in twenty twenty-six. Such plants, called halophytes, drop litter that changes the soil beneath them, creating salt island effects. The team compared four species forming a natural sequence in an arid region.

Moving along the sequence, soil water, acidity, and salt ion levels fell step by step. Leaf carbon in the plants fell as soil salt rose, while leaf nitrogen and phosphorus rose with salinity. The last species in the sequence held the richest soil carbon and the most diverse, complex microbe networks. Statistical models showed soil properties and plant traits jointly set the soil's element ratios. The authors map how plants, soil, and microbes shape these dry saline ecosystems together.
pmc-13197273:
Shuo Yang and a team of co-authors hunt for warning signs that trauma-related flesh-eating infection will cost a limb. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Necrotizing fasciitis races through soft tissue, and amputation is its bleakest outcome short of death.

Ten years of records at a Hebei hospital covered one hundred thirty-four patients. Twenty-two, about one in six, lost a limb. Amputees arrived far later, a median of two hundred forty-two hours against sixty-five. They more often had multiple injuries and diabetes. A blood enzyme, lactate dehydrogenase, was triple the level in others and predicted amputation superbly. Delay itself predicted well too. The authors urge faster arrival and enzyme checks at the door.
pmc-13199673:
Jun P Hong and Michel C Nussenzweig present a 2026 protocol for a gene screen in mouse immune cells. Germinal center B cells mature antibodies inside lymph nodes, but no lab dish copies their biology well. Genetic screens must run in living mice, so the protocol adapts CRISPR tools, which cut or silence genes, for that setting.

Steps cover building a guide RNA library, delivering guides with a mouse-only retrovirus, and running the screen in an immunization model. Sequencing and analysis steps close the workflow. Tweaks include a refined guide scaffold and matched primers. Animal and biosafety approvals are stressed throughout. As a protocol, it reports no results; it gives labs a tested recipe for in vivo screens.
pmc-13200373:
Anett Mau-Moeller and colleagues compared inpatient versus outpatient rehabilitation after knee replacement in Germany in a 2026 trial. German care usually adds a three-week rehab stay after knee joint replacement surgery. Whether patients must stay in a facility or can attend daily was little tested, so the team ran a blinded comparison.

Patients chose their setting: twenty-six went inpatient and sixteen outpatient. Tests ran before rehab and three months after surgery. Outpatients logged far more daily steps in the first rehab week. At three months, outpatients also showed better joint position sense, the feel for where the knee sits. Other measures covered pain, swelling, motion, and timed walking tasks.
pmc-13200473:
Ayman Shaban and colleagues tested nano fertilizer sprays on olive trees in a 2026 field study. Olive trees often bear heavily one year and lightly the next, a pattern called alternate bearing. Spray feeding in the off-year might even out yields, so the team sprayed nano NPK and calcium-boron mixes on fifteen-year-old Picual trees.

Trials ran across the 2023 and 2024 seasons. The best blend raised flower counts, perfect flower share, and fruit set above controls. Off-year yield peaked under that blend, while fruit drop fell by about half versus controls. Leaf and fruit mineral levels rose. Oil kept its extra virgin grade with a richer share of oleic acid, its main healthy fat. Alternate bearing severity fell sharply.
pmc-13200673:
Jiasheng Du and four co-authors present a 2026 study on fear of cancer recurrence in patients with primary liver cancer. This fear is a common and heavy burden for people who have faced cancer. The team measured it in 175 patients at one hospital and looked for factors that raise or lower it. They then built a nomogram, a chart-based tool that turns risk factors into a personal risk estimate.

Just over half the patients showed high fear on a standard short questionnaire. Being female and having a more advanced tumor raised the odds of high fear. Middle income, longer time since diagnosis, and stronger social support lowered it. The tool sorted patients with fair accuracy and matched real outcomes well. The authors say it may help clinics spot patients who need support, once tested in other hospitals.
pmc-13202173:
Zhiyun Yang and Zongchao Jia show an ancient molecule quietly loosening the cell's loudest gene switches in this 2026 paper. Inorganic polyphosphate is a simple chain of phosphates found in nearly every living thing. Its grip on gene control in mammals was unexplored until now.

The team found the chains attach to three core parts of the super-enhancer complex, the machinery that drives high-output genes. The attachment breaks the parts' ability to gather into droplets, a step their teamwork needs. It also lowers the amounts of two parts and keeps a third out of the nucleus. That third part can no longer pair up or loop DNA to its targets. Gene output falls across the board. The authors cast polyphosphate as a new layer of gene regulation with reach into how cells set their identity.
pmc-13203873:
Saimi Yamamoto and seven co-authors study internet addiction and problem gambling among Japanese university students in a 2026 paper. Both problems affect many young people, and the pair may travel together. Few studies had mapped their overlap and lifestyle links in this group.

Over five thousand students completed standard tests for both conditions plus questions on daily habits. Internet addiction was strongly tied to problem gambling, and gambling risk rose with addiction scores. Addiction also linked to being male, earlier study years, poor sleep, low activity, and unhealthy eating. The results suggest campus programs should screen for both problems at once. Sleep and activity support may form part of prevention as well.
pmc-13204773:
Minchae Kang, Suyeon Seo, Eunsol Park, and Min-Woo Han published a 2026 paper on a soft underwater robot that grips objects and controls its own floating. Rigid robots can harm delicate sea life and struggle in tight spots. Soft robots bend and adapt, making them safer for exploring reefs and wrecks. This design adds a trick: it manages buoyancy without any outside mechanism.

The robot's gripper holds a reservoir of fluid. Pumping fluid in or out changes both its grip and its buoyancy. With little fluid, buoyancy drops and the arms close firmly on an object. With more fluid, the robot rises and can set the object down gently. In tests, the gripper picked up and released several objects. An added channel even let it crawl. The authors present the system as a versatile, gentle tool for underwater research. It works without harming the marine environment it explores.
pmc-13205773:
Andreas Tsipourlianos, Nikolaos Veliotis, Rafael Angelakopoulos, Themistoklis Giannoulis, and Katerina Moutou chart when eye lens genes switch on in fish embryos in this two thousand twenty-six study. The lens is key to sight, but the timing of its gene activity in European seabass was not mapped. The team reused public gene data from embryos at three stages, from early body plan to hatching, and focused on genes that build the lens.

The lens genes moved in clear stage-linked waves. A broad shift in the data split samples by stage, with the first two axes holding most of the spread. The biggest change came between the early stage and the stage when body segments form. Genes for crystallins, the clear proteins of the lens, rose sharply. So did genes for lens fiber shape, membranes, and cell scaffolding. The map ties gene timing to the classic stages of fish development.
pmc-13206973:
Yunjin Nam, Jae Hyuk Yang, Dong-Gune Chang, and Seung Woo Suh checked whether MRI scans and electrical tests agree on which nerve root is hurting, in this 2026 study. The patients had an anatomical variant at the spine's base. These transitional vertebrae blur the numbering of spinal levels, so scan findings and symptoms can point to different roots.

The team reviewed twenty-nine patients who had both scans and needle electrical tests for single-level nerve pain. The two methods named the same level in only about twenty-eight percent of cases. Patients whose variant joined the spine fully showed even more disagreement than those with partial forms. The authors say the two tests give complementary information and both deserve weight in this group.
pmc-13207473:
Eirini Maliagkani and co-authors build a clinician-centered way to judge explanation heatmaps from retinal AI. Their 2026 paper concerns models that classify eye scans by disease and highlight the regions behind each call. A heatmap that looks right to engineers may still mislead the doctors who act on it.

Their framework runs in two phases. First, one eye specialist and one AI specialist screened a hundred heatmaps per method for quality and anatomical sense, cutting the field to three methods. Then a panel of specialists rated the finalists across cases for agreement with the diagnosis. The team's own contrast-based map scored highest, a popular gradient method followed, and a fusion map trailed. Ratings reflect clinical plausibility, guiding which explanations deserve trust.
pmc-13207773:
Corina Cinezan and Maria Luiza Hiceag study how daily activity before a heart attack links to how wide the heart's artery disease is. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The spread of blocked arteries is a strong guide to a patient's outlook after such an attack. Drills in a gym are known to guard the heart, but plain daily effort was less clear.

Patients in hospital for a heart attack rate their usual effort over the past month, then have their arteries scanned. Effort scores fall step by step as disease goes from one vessel to three. The link holds when age, smoking, pressure, sugar, and fats are held in check. The authors urge care in reading self-reports.
pmc-13208973:
Carbon fiber sheds heat too well to serve as a blanket, so a heat-proof coat is asked to slow it. Xiaohui Zhang and Guangsheng Huang wrap the fibers in a stiff ring polymer in 2026. They wake the fiber skin with plasma first so the coat grips. Then they bake the wrap to charcoal at heats up to a fierce grade. The bake cleans the coat and stacks its carbon in neat radial sheets.

Felt mats woven from the wrapped fibers bore crush loads a tenth to a quarter better than plain mats, and sprang back through ten hard cycles. Their heat leak fell to near half or less of the plain mats', from room heat to furnace heat. The pair pitch the wrap for blankets that must also bear weight.
pmc-13211873: A correction notice from Si-Ting Chen and co-authors, published in 2026, fixes figure errors in their 2023 eLife paper on embryo-derived TNF and uterine decidualization. Assembly mistakes had duplicated a loading-control band across two figures, copied immunoprecipitation bands into a later figure, and repeated one histogram in place of another. The authors replaced the affected panels, updated the source data, and apologized for the inadvertent errors. Only the correction notice itself survives here, so the study's data are not re-presented.
pmc-13212173:
Jiezhi Lin and co-authors review, in 2026, what regulatory T cells do in the slow healing of wounds among people with diabetes. These immune cells normally calm inflammation and help tissue rebuild, so their failure may help explain why diabetic foot ulcers linger.

The narrative review pulls together work on inflammation, new blood vessel growth, and cell regeneration in diabetic wounds. It also surveys therapies that aim to boost or guide these cells, including new biomaterials and molecular approaches. Problems remain, from obtaining good-quality cells to risks of infection and over-suppressed immunity. Still, the authors see cell-based care as a promising direction worth careful trials.
pmc-13212673:
Tatiana Palotta Minari reviews in 2026 how population surveys should measure nutritional status in a digital age. No single method captures the full picture: body measurements are cheap but blunt, while laboratory markers are sensitive yet hard to collect at scale.

The review weighs body measurements, body composition tools, and biochemical indicators side by side. Composition methods reveal tissue distribution but need costly equipment, and blood tests face logistical and ethical hurdles in large surveys. The pandemic exposed fragile data systems, while digital tools now offer new ways to combine sources. Minari argues surveys must blend methods and invest in staff, infrastructure, and fair data governance.
pmc-13213173:
Xueyuan Li, Ming Hu, and Yi Shen compare in 2026 two drug regimens for bone loss in women after menopause. One group received an active vitamin D compound alone with calcium, while the other added denosumab, an injected antibody that slows bone breakdown.

Records for 306 women treated over twelve months showed the combined group gained more bone density at spine, hip neck, and total hip. Bone turnover markers fell further, calcium balance measures improved, and pain, disability, and daily function scores all improved more. Side effects stayed low and similar in both groups, with none judged serious. The pairing looks promising, though the retrospective design invites a confirming trial.
pmc-13213473:
Daniela Tres and co-authors published a study in 2025 evaluating an electrospun fiber loaded with ozonated oil. The fibers treat lesions caused by leishmaniasis, a parasitic disease. The disease is neglected, yet its lesions can cause scarring and psychosocial harm. Treatments suffer from poor adherence because of side effects and dosing demands.

The team produced fibers carrying ozonated sunflower oil, a low-cost bioactive material. Mice infected with the parasite were divided into groups. One received a drug alone, one the drug plus a fiber with ozonated oil, and one the drug plus a fiber with plain oil. The fourth was an untreated control. After thirty days, all lesions had grown, least in the drug-only group. In the drug plus ozonated fiber group, no live parasites could be cultured from paw samples. All other groups showed live parasites. Both drug groups showed healing of the skin.
pmc-13214273:
Zuyun Yan and colleagues engineer in 2026 an implantable scaffold meant to finish off bone cancer after surgery while rebuilding the bone it leaves behind. Drug-resistant osteosarcoma poses all three problems at once: leftover tumour, weak immune attack, and a large defect.

Their scaffold releases two agents in response to tumour acidity and a light trigger. One agent blocks DNA repair so the other's platinum damage lands harder, reversing resistance, while together they provoke an immune-visible form of cell death. Silicon released from the scaffold plus the second agent encourage blood vessels and new bone. Animal tests showed tumour suppression first, then substantial bone bridging, without obvious whole-body toxicity.
pmc-13214373:
Mingze Zheng and co-authors reviewed RNA-binding proteins in a 2026 paper on brain swelling. Lasting swelling in the brain and nerves shows up in many nerve diseases, and its control web is deep and wide. The proteins in the title grab RNA and shape what cells do with it after the RNA is made.

The review pulls together proof that these proteins do far more than sense RNA and spark defense. They shape signal flow, cell death, fuel use, gene marks, and cross-talk with short RNA strands. Shifts in where they sit in the cell add more reach. The authors map how faults in these proteins may drive nerve disease and where new drugs might act.
pmc-13214573:
Esteban Villar-Rodríguez and colleagues examine in 2026 whether the brain sides used for speaking, listening, and reading agree with each other in left-handers. This group includes more people with right-sided or split language organisation, which makes it ideal for testing independence among components.

Brain scans of sixty-nine selected left-handers showed speaking and listening lateralised together strongly, while reading aligned more loosely with both. Forty-four people were consistent across all three tasks, and twenty-five had one component straying, usually reading, most often within overall rightward dominance. Inconsistent organisation, especially between speaking and reading, came with slightly slower reading speed. Language sides, the authors conclude, are coordinated but not locked together.
pmc-13215373:
Yuya Nakajima and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study on cognitive testing and driving among older adults living in the community in Japan. The team asked which tasks within the Japanese-language version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment relate to driving as a person's main way of getting around.

The study covered 199 participants in a long-term preventive care program, of whom 156 mainly drove themselves and 43 used other transport. Drivers scored higher on trail-making, digit span, and verbal fluency tasks, yet only trail-making stayed linked to driving after regression adjustment, with an odds ratio of 2.82 in the model. The authors suggest this single task could help clinicians guide older patients on driving decisions.
pmc-13216373:
Mugahid Ali and Fumin Huang present a 2026 optics paper giving simple formulas for how layered, stretched nanoparticles interact with light. Such particles, treated as stacked spheroids, are workhorses in plasmonics, sensing, and Raman spectroscopy.

With the particle far smaller than the wavelength, the authors solve Laplace's equation layer by layer with the light polarized along the long axis. The key surface factor falls out as a ratio of two matrix determinants, and from it they derive one general expression for the particle's polarizability, which drives scattering and absorption. Worked examples with two, three, and five layers check the formulas' accuracy and speed against heavier number-crunching approaches.
pmc-13218173:
Ayuba Issaka and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of voice-assisted AI in cardiovascular care. Heart and vessel diseases remain a leading cause of illness and death, and how patients manage their condition affects outcomes. Voice assistants and apps are a hands-free way to support self-management, but their value for heart patients is unproven.

The review will search MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane register for studies from 2010 to 2025. Eligible work includes randomized trials, non-randomized studies, and observational work on voice-based tools for heart self-management. The primary outcome is cardiovascular death. Secondary outcomes are quality of life, blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose measures, diet, and physical activity. Quality will be judged with Cochrane and Newcastle-Ottawa tools, and results will be pooled with random-effects models, using subgroup analyses and meta-regression to explain differences.
pmc-13219673:
Nolan and O'Connor, two authors listed by surname, review in 2026 treatments for infantile haemangiomas, the most common growths of infancy. These red marks grow fast, then shrink slowly on their own over years. Most cause no harm, but some ulcerate, block function, or leave lasting marks.

Care changed in 2008, when a heart drug called propranolol was found to shrink them fast. It is now the first-choice treatment, with strong trial backing. The main risk is low blood sugar, so parents learn feeding rules for sick days. Other beta-blockers and skin gels help in narrow cases, and older harsh drugs are now last resorts. The review also covers family burden and photo-based check-ins.
pmc-13219873:
Takanori Komada and colleagues report organized lymphocyte clusters inside kidneys damaged by potassium deficiency in a 2026 research letter. Hypokalaemic nephropathy, kidney injury from long low potassium, is usually treated by replacing potassium, and its long-term course was assumed benign. Inflammation's role in the condition, however, had drawn the team's earlier interest.

Five kidney biopsies from patients all showed T-cell infiltration, and three contained clusters of T and B lymphocytes resembling tertiary lymphoid structures, the outposts familiar from chronic inflammation and cancer. None of the patients progressed to kidney failure over an average of eight years of supplementation. In a mouse version of the disease, potassium and kidney function recovered on a normal diet, yet scarring and the same lymphoid clusters developed anyway, and both amounts rose. The authors suggest these structures may flag kidneys at risk of chronic decline and keep inflammation smoldering after the deficiency is fixed.
pmc-13220073:
Dmytro Kobzev and colleagues wrote this 2026 review of medicines that switch on only when triggered by a signal, such as light, heat, sound, or body chemistry. Such control could let a drug act at the right place and time instead of spreading through the whole body.

The authors mapped research from 2014 to 2024, covering over 90,000 papers and 1,000 clinical trials. Light was the most used outside trigger, while internal triggers like acidity and enzymes made up nearly half the work. They also list six barriers slowing use in patients, from complex designs to cost, and offer practical fixes for each.
pmc-13222073:
Hassanien and four co-authors trace a babe's brain hurt to a rare clot gene form in this twenty twenty-six case report. Early strokes can lame a child for life with no clear cause. Clot-tilt genes may join small traits to drop the clot line in babes.

Inside, the boy showed right-side weak acts at nine months of age. Scans showed old loss in left brain zones from a past clot hit. Blood checks found a sickle trait in the boy as well. Gene reads found a rare clot gene form of dim weight in him. The team reads both traits as a joint tilt to the clot.
pmc-13222273:
Ligang Xing and a large team report real-world lung cancer care in China in a 2026 paper. The MOOREA study followed patients with stage III non-small cell lung cancer, a mixed group with fast-changing treatment options. Twenty-eight hospitals enrolled untreated patients from 2019 to 2022.

In total, 486 patients were analyzed, split between unresectable and resectable disease. Testing rates for key gene markers were low, near one in five at best. Under half of the unresectable group received combined chemo-radiation. About half of those got follow-on consolidation therapy, some with immunotherapy. The study maps gaps between guidelines and practice.
pmc-13222773:
Hanyi Wang and co-authors test the enzyme PepO against ulcerative colitis in mice, in a 2026 study. It was given to mice with drug-induced colon inflammation. Disease scores, colon length, tissue damage, and tissue signals measured the effect, while cell and gut tests traced the mechanism.

Treated mice showed milder disease, longer colons, and less tissue damage. The enzyme directly cut output of CCL2, a macrophage-attracting signal, reducing immune cell invasion of the colon. Gut microbe mixes also shifted toward helpful species such as Lactobacillus and Akkermansia. Wiping out gut microbes erased the protection, and transplanting treated gut contents reproduced it.
pmc-13223173:
Chen and three co-authors studied in twenty twenty-six why many elderly stomach cancer patients cannot tolerate early tube feeding after surgery, and built a model to predict who will struggle. Feeding the gut early aids recovery, yet intolerance blunts the benefit.

The team reviewed three hundred forty-six elderly patients who had keyhole stomach cancer surgery. More than half, fifty-six percent, developed feeding intolerance. Five factors independently raised the risk: age seventy-five or more, advanced cancer stage, diabetes, radical surgery, and heavier blood loss during the operation. A scoring model built from those five factors sorted patients well. The authors suggest nurses use the score to tailor care before trouble starts. Closer watching and gentler feeding plans for high-risk patients could improve nutrition outcomes in this fragile group.
pmc-13223373:
Jingjing Li and her four co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, whether plant and natural compounds can blunt the organ damage of sepsis by steering a particular form of cell death. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, often wrecks lungs and liver. One damage route is ferroptosis, in which iron fuels a rust-like burning of cell membranes. Blocking that route has become a live strategy.

The review explains how ferroptosis unfolds in sepsis and which control points might be drugged. It then catalogs natural products reported to protect lung and liver by touching those points. The authors are frank about the evidence: nearly all of it is preclinical, from cells and animals, and solid clinical data are scarce. They frame the catalog as a map for the trials that must come next.
pmc-13223973:
Karina Cancino-Maldonado and co-authors present a 2026 single-cell study of ampullary carcinoma, a rare cancer arising where the bile and pancreatic ducts meet the intestine. The tumour accounts for a small share of gut cancers, and its awkward anatomy often makes diagnosis hard. The team profiled gene activity cell by cell in tumour tissue.

Their atlas separates malignant epithelial cells from the surrounding immune environment. Known cancer drivers appeared more active, alongside a gene program specific to this tumour that may yield markers detectable without invasive sampling. Immune cells looked suppressive in character, with macrophage and T cell groups showing limited anti-tumour activity, which may guide later treatment research.
pmc-13227273:
Msellati, Christodoulides, and Dorairaj rebuild an arm destroyed by flesh-eating infection that began at a contraceptive implant site, in a paper dated 2026. Necrotising fasciitis races along tissue planes, and survival leaves enormous wounds. The authors believe this is the first recorded case following insertion of an implantable contraceptive.

Group A streptococcus was the culprit, and the defect in the left upper limb was extensive. Reconstruction used a flap of lower abdominal tissue carried on two pedicles, twin lifelines of blood supply, based on the deep inferior epigastric vessels. The double supply let one flap cover a wound too large for standard options. The limb kept good function and appearance. The report extends the reconstructive playbook for the worst soft-tissue losses.
pmc-13229473:
Tai-Cheng Kuo and colleagues compare in 2026 two layered skin templates for rebuilding injured fingertips and nail beds in Taiwan. Thirty patients with Allen type one to three injuries were treated between 2020 and 2022. Twelve received Integra and eighteen received Terudermis, both used instead of flap surgery.

At six months the two products gave closely similar results across healing, appearance, feeling, and movement. Skin closed fully in about thirty-nine days on average, and satisfaction averaged near the top of a five point scale. Two-point discrimination averaged under six millimeters on the injured side. The findings support either template as a choice that avoids taking tissue from another site.
pmc-13230673:
Yudai Murayama and colleagues review in 2026 eight cases where the drug eribulin was given after surgery for soft tissue sarcoma. Most patients were older or had other health problems that made standard anthracycline chemotherapy risky. Records from one hospital captured dosing, side effects, and cancer outcomes after curative surgery.

Blood side effects such as low white cell counts were fairly common but were handled with dose changes and support care. Nerve tingling and taste changes stayed mostly mild to moderate, and no treatment deaths or major heart events occurred. Six patients stayed free of cancer during follow-up, while two died of the disease. The small series suggests the drug is workable after surgery, though benefit size cannot be judged from eight cases.
pmc-13231073:
Xiaojie Yao and Ziqing Cheng review in 2026 a nursing model meant to turn gum disease advice into lasting daily habits. Gum disease affects more than a billion people and needs steady self care, yet knowing what to do rarely changes behavior. The model follows a chain from information to knowledge, then attitude, then practice.

Care unfolds in three phases covering digital preparation before visits, skill building and motivational talks in the clinic, and remote follow-up afterward. Trials gathered in the review show better gum measures such as shallower pockets and less bleeding. Patients also reported stronger self-management skills, confidence, and quality of life. Joining behavior science with ongoing nursing contact may close the gap between intention and action.
pmc-13233473:
Jing Chen, Fei Chen, and Shuang Qiu published a 2026 questionnaire study of test anxiety among medical students in China. Drawing on surveys from 1,067 students at three medical universities, the team weighed academic stress, social support, and two kinds of perfectionism, healthy striving versus harsh self-judgment. Psychological resilience, the capacity to recover from pressure, sat at the center of their model.

Academic stress and maladaptive perfectionism raised test anxiety, while social support and adaptive perfectionism lowered it. Resilience carried part of every effect, transmitting over half of the benefit linked to social support. pmc-13240073:

pmc-13242373:

pmc-13242773:

pmc-13243373:

pmc-13244273:

pmc-13245573:

pmc-13246373:

pmc-13250873:

pmc-13252573:

pmc-13258173:

pmc-13259273:

pmc-13259973:

pmc-13260173:

pmc-13261073:

pmc-13261373:
