pmc-13261773:
Kaneyuki Tsuchimochi and Hiroe Tsuchimochi report a 2026 case of long-term sequential therapy for pregnancy- and lactation-associated osteoporosis. This rare condition weakens bones during late pregnancy or after delivery and can fracture several vertebrae. Evidence on long-term treatment sequences combining bone-building and bone-protecting drugs is limited.

Their patient was a 37-year-old woman who developed low back pain three months after delivery, with multiple acute and chronic vertebral fractures. Her lumbar spine Z-score stayed low at −3.0 despite early improvement on a bisphosphonate. Therapy then moved in sequence: daily teriparatide for two years, romosozumab for one year, then denosumab for maintenance. Over five years and seven months, bone density rose 53.4% at the spine and 26.1% at the femoral neck. No new fractures occurred. The authors credit shared decision-making and patient education for the sustained gains.
pmc-13261873:
Elizabeth Phillips and co-authors measured in 2026 how isotope ratios shift as microbes break down two chlorinated ethane pollutants in groundwater. These solvents are common contaminants, and isotope analysis can reveal how they transform. Their study is the first to track both carbon and chlorine isotopes for both compounds in a cleanup culture.

Each compound showed its own fractionation strength, with the dichloroethane shifting more than the trichloroethane. Yet dual-isotope plots gave the same slope for both, matching values known from chemical rather than biological breakdown. That match points to a masking effect, where a hidden step mutes the isotope signal. Product molecules also carried heavier chlorine than the starting material, a pattern the authors propose as a fingerprint of masking. The work sharpens how field isotope data should be read.
pmc-13261973:
Janika Bolz and co-authors report a pilot study, published in 2026, of the ParaGym exercise app for people with paraplegia, meaning paralysis of the lower body. The app uses an algorithm, a set of computer rules, to tailor and advance workouts without help from health staff. The team tested whether the training was workable, safe, and easy to use.

Twenty-three adults with long-term paraplegia did three app-led sessions a week for six weeks. The team tracked diaries, interviews, a standard ease-of-use scale, and any harm. Users kept up 70 percent of sessions, 88 percent stayed to the end, and the ease score averaged 84. No harmful events occurred, though users disliked frequent moves between wheelchair and floor work.
pmc-13262073:
Bakr F Abdel-Wahab and colleagues describe new drug-like compounds in a 2026 chemistry and biology article. They built a series of hybrid molecules that join a beta-keto ether part to a triazole ring, a common drug building block. The aim was one compound family that could fight both germs and cancer cells.

The team made the hybrids in one step and checked their shape with lab spectra and crystal studies. One compound blocked 97 percent of biofilm growth by resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a hard-to-treat germ. Another killed liver cancer cells in lab tests while harming normal cells far less. Traits linked to dissolving in water or fat helped explain which compound did which job.
pmc-13262173:
Mosayeb Rostamian and colleagues tally how often unusual mycobacteria infect people with bronchiectasis, airways widened for good. These wild microbes thrive where lungs are already damaged. Their 2026 review and meta-analysis pools studies of how common this is from the major sources.

About one in six bronchiectasis patients carried nontuberculous mycobacteria, and a similar share had full pulmonary disease from them. The M. avium complex led the species list by a wide margin. M. kansasii sat at the opposite extreme, rare everywhere. The authors warn doctors that these infections are common enough in bronchiectasis to need routine care.
pmc-13262473:
Zhong Qiu and colleagues report a rare case of abnormal blood vessel links in a 2026 case report. A 34-year-old woman had repeated coughing of blood, called hemoptysis. Scans showed fistulas, direct links between body arteries and the lung artery, fed by four separate vessels. Such links are uncommon, and cases with this many feeders are rarer still.

Doctors first suspected a sealed-off piece of lung tissue, but detailed CT vessel imaging showed the fistulas and no such tissue. The team treated her by blocking the abnormal vessels from inside, a method called embolization. Her symptoms were controlled, and she left the hospital in stable condition with no complications. A later partial lung removal had been planned as a staged step.
pmc-13262573:
Yingjie Lin and colleagues test whether premium trifocal implants let cataract patients out-read people who never had cataracts. Reading speed decides real-world satisfaction after lens surgery. Their 2026 prospective study at two Chinese eye hospitals implants PanOptix trifocals in forty-two patients and matches them with cataract-free controls.

Three months after surgery, the implanted group read Chinese texts aloud measurably faster than controls reading without near glasses. Speeds averaged roughly two hundred twenty characters a minute against about one hundred seventy-five. Age and education were matched, so the lens itself earns the credit. For presbyopic patients, implants may beat their natural aging lenses.
pmc-13263173:
Nasrullah Jan and Mokhtar Rejili propose dressing tiny drug carriers in nature's own camouflage instead of the industry standard. PEG coatings have long kept carriers moving in the blood, but anti-PEG antibodies are undoing them. Their 2026 essay surveys living stand-ins for the stealth layer.

Cell membranes and the natural protein corona can cloak the carriers so the body reads them as its own. Taken membranes may even add active aim to the disguise. The authors weigh longer runs in the blood and kind treatment by the body against hurdles in making them the same way each time. Their roadmap aims at long-circulating carriers that the immune system reads as self rather than man-made.
pmc-13263373:
Wesam Ibrahim Abo Elenien and co-authors present a 2026 bibliometric study, a statistical map of publications, on adoptive cell therapy for triple-negative breast cancer. This aggressive breast cancer lacks the three usual drug targets. Cell therapy trains or engineers a patient's own immune cells to attack it. The team analyzed Scopus records from 2011 to 2025.

Output grew at over sixty percent per year, and their search found 8,496 publications, with a sharp rise after 2020. China and the United States produced over sixty percent of the work. Hot topics included CAR-T cells, the tumor microenvironment, and checkpoint inhibitors. The authors note persistent hurdles such as tumor diversity, unstable targets, and safety concerns.
pmc-13263573:
Darcy T Fay, Nam V Huynh, and Aaron J Buckland traced in 2026 how opioid use before neck surgery echoes through recovery. Their Melbourne series covered 61 patients of one surgeon having front-approach cervical fusion or disc replacement between 2020 and 2024. Pharmacy records split them into 28 opioid-sensitized patients and 33 opioid-naive ones.

Sensitized patients needed opioids far more often at six weeks and at six months after surgery. Even under a month of prior prescribing raised the odds of use in the early months. Longer prior exposure stretched the effect to a full year and raised total morphine-equivalent doses. Pain and disability scores, though, ended the same in both groups, so extra opioids bought no better reported outcome. The authors press prescribers to weigh duration of preoperative use as a warning flag.
pmc-13263773:
The editors and publisher of Cancer Management and Research retract a twenty nineteen colorectal cancer paper by Hong and colleagues. The article claimed the protein IRF1 blocks tumor growth and spread by suppressing a RAS-RAC1 pathway. A third party raised integrity concerns in twenty twenty-three, triggering this 2026 notice.

Investigators found a figure panel unexpectedly similar to one in the group's earlier paper, supposedly showing different samples and conditions. Western blot data in three more figures raised concerns the authors never addressed. Although the authors supplied original data for the first figure, the blot questions stood. The article stays online, watermarked as retracted on every page.
pmc-13263873:
Julie Marie Haabeth Brox and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on what Norwegian dental hygienists know about erosive tooth wear in young adults. This wear is chemical loss of tooth mineral from acids, mainly in drinks, rather than from bacteria. A questionnaire went to 1,084 hygienists, and 266 who work with fifteen- to thirty-year-olds were analyzed.

Ninety-six percent said they record this wear in patient charts, with public services recording more than private ones. Sports drinks, energy drinks, and soft drinks were named the main risks across all groups. The most common preventive steps were dietary advice and fluoride rinses or tablets. The authors conclude hygienists know the condition well and see clear room to improve prevention work.
pmc-13264073:
Yi Lin and colleagues use deep neural networks to trace how people experience visual beauty in a 2026 study. Aesthetic response mixes quick perception, higher-level ideas and final liking, yet models rarely link those stages together. The team used human-aligned convolutional networks, which process images in layers from fine detail toward abstract features, and measured how layer patterns relate to fluency and preference.

Early layers best predicted how easily paintings felt to process, especially for fine spatial detail. Deeper layers, carrying style and concept information, predicted liking more accurately. Paintings and natural scenes showed different layer patterns. The work offers a step-by-step account that separates feeling fluent from actually liking an image, a distinction future art and design research can test.
pmc-13264173:
Roberto Cruz-García and Felipe Amezcua develop a standard method for finding microplastics in shark and ray gut tissue in a 2026 protocol paper. Gut tissue is fatty and tough, and small particles are easily lost during handling. Their sequence digests tissue with potassium hydroxide, clears leftovers with peroxide when needed, splits particles in strong salt fluid and filters them for microscope sorting and infrared checks.

Spiked tests recovered most added plastic particles, and blank checks did well. Real samples yielded one hundred seventy-two particles, mostly fibers, with plant-based cellulose most common beside several man-made polymers. Firm finding limits and clear exclusions for very small or dense particles are stated. Other labs can adopt the steps for matching wildlife tracking.
pmc-13264273:
N. Segond and colleagues test how to deflate an aortic rescue balloon after cardiac arrest in a 2026 animal analysis. The balloon, placed inside the aorta, supports circulation during resuscitation with a head-up positioning device. Once the heart restarted in pigs after prolonged arrest, teams compared two ways of letting the balloon down. One way released it fully at once, and the other released it halfway. Aortic, brain and heart perfusion pressures were watched around the change.

Full deflation caused large pressure drops across all measures. Partial deflation kept drops small and pressure far steadier in comparison. Thirteen of twenty animals regained circulation and entered the comparison. Gentle staged release after resuscitation may protect brain and heart perfusion, a practical point for emergency protocols using this device.
pmc-13264373:
Julena Maurer and colleagues interview people experiencing homelessness about the overdose reversal drug naloxone in a 2026 qualitative study. Overdose is the leading unintentional killer nationally, and unhoused people face elevated risk. Twelve adults recruited at a clinic inside a low-barrier shelter shared views on using and reaching the nasal spray between January and March 2024. Transcripts were coded by grounded theory methods to build themes from participants own framing of barriers.

Themes included distress and mistaken beliefs about substance use, confusion about supportive steps after an overdose and a striking gap between wide availability and real accessibility. Supplies may sit nearby yet remain out of reach through physical or social obstacles. Programs should design distribution around lived constraints, not shelf counts.
pmc-13264673:
Abhijit Biswas and Devanjan Sinha propose a fruit fly mutant as a living model for stress-tolerant brain tumors in a 2026 article. The mutant develops rapidly expanding brain tumors in larvae, enlarging over days in a measurable way. As tumors grow, production of the protective chaperone Hsp70 rises in step with size. That protein helps cancer cells survive stress and is linked to poor outlook in human gliomas, making its behavior in a simple animal valuable.

The fly system is genetically easy to manipulate, cheap to maintain and fast to screen compared with mouse models. Researchers can test which genes or drugs change stress tolerance and tumor growth in the whole brain environment. The authors position the model as a discovery platform, not a direct substitute for human study.
pmc-13264873:
Lina Zhao and a large team published a 2026 study on a simple blood measure that may warn of severe lung failure in sepsis. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, can flood the lungs, a state called ARDS. The measure, estimated plasma volume status, reflects fluid overload in the blood and can be worked out from routine labs.

The team studied 3,854 adults with sepsis at many centers in China. Higher plasma volume values linked strongly to later ARDS in every model they ran, and the measure sorted patients fairly well on its own. Patients who developed ARDS died more often and needed breathing machines and kidney support more. Plasma volume also tracked ARDS severity. Paired with a standard severity score, it sharpened death risk prediction, and the authors back it as a warning marker.
pmc-13264973:
Mengmeng Xu, Jie Sun, and Menghan Sun wrote a 2026 study on whether low albumin, a blood protein that reflects nutrition, predicts lung problems after keyhole lung surgery. The operation removes a defined part of the lung, often for cancer, and lung complications are common afterward. The team reviewed cases at one Nanjing hospital from 2020.

Of 1,192 patients, 26.7 percent had a lung complication, and pneumonia was the most common. Low albumin before surgery affected 224 patients, 18.8 percent. After balancing the groups by matching, low albumin patients still had more complications, and the protein level stood as an independent risk factor in adjusted models. They also stayed in hospital longer. The authors say checking and fixing nutrition before surgery may cut risk.
pmc-13265173:
Liu Gao and colleagues examine a collagen gene called COL10A1 in breast cancer, in a 2026 study. The gene is raised in several cancers, though its role in breast cancer lacked systematic study. The team combined database analysis with patient samples and cell experiments. Mouse tumour tests were also included.

COL10A1 was higher in breast tumours across subtypes, and higher levels linked to poorer survival. Patient tumour samples confirmed the rise and tied it to clinical features. Cell experiments probed self-eating processes, called autophagy, and vessel-like channels formed by tumour cells. Changing COL10A1 altered growth, movement, and invasion. The authors link the gene to worse outcomes through these pathways.
pmc-13265673:
Tai-Li Chen and colleagues examine whether a blistering skin disease raises the risk of atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 Taiwan cohort study. Bullous pemphigoid mainly affects older adults and involves chronic inflammation. Shared inflammation suggested a possible heart rhythm link. Insurance records from 2011 to 2019 were analysed.

New atrial fibrillation occurred more often in patients with the skin disease than in controls. The adjusted risk was close to double. The link persisted across age and sex groups and in sensitivity checks. Missing lifestyle and severity data limit the study. The authors advise prompt rhythm checks when these patients show suggestive symptoms.
pmc-13266073:
A J Ashbaugh, H A Jamniczky, and J M Theodor study how premolar teeth became molar-like in hoofed mammals, published in 2026. Cheek teeth carry rich evolutionary information. Most work treats single tooth positions rather than the whole row. Molarization, where premolars match molar complexity, was the focus.

A two-dimensional landmark scheme captured shape across the premolar-molar boundary. Two hoofed groups, even-toed and odd-toed, were analysed with family-tree-aware methods. Both supported modular organisation across the boundary, with more variation in upper teeth. Developmental cascade models framed the hypotheses. The framework links tooth shape evolution to growth rules.
pmc-13266173:
Alessandra Andrade Fantinelli and the team study treatment adherence for syphilis in pregnancy (2026). Complete treatment requires three penicillin doses plus partner treatment. Talks and records covered 325 pregnant women diagnosed while pregnant. Number and network methods explored linked factors.

Full course completion occurred in under half of women and partners. Babies of mothers who finished scored higher on newborn scores. Early finding, good early care, planned pregnancy, a job, and higher income aided completion. Substance misuse, abuse in childhood, violence faced, and prior detention hindered it. Network analysis grouped factors into violence, substance, and money-and-schooling clusters.
pmc-13266873:
Huixiang Su and colleagues compare in 2026 two bypass strategies used alongside mitral valve surgery in patients who need both operations. Stopping the heart for bypass is standard, but keeping it beating, on or off the pump, may shorten clamp time and spare organs. Their study reviewed 473 patients and used statistical weighting to balance the groups.

The beating-heart group had shorter aortic clamp times and lower peak markers of heart muscle and kidney strain afterward. New strokes were also less common in that group. Operating time, ventilation time, and death in hospital did not differ clearly. The authors suggest the beating approach may soften organ injury in this high-risk combined surgery.
pmc-13267073:
Sophia Sburlati, Afton Gustafson, and Bart Kahr test in 2026 whether flat pairs of molecules can twist light, a gap in a classic method for reading molecular handedness. The exciton chirality method ties light twisting to how paired electric dipoles sit, and it tends to ignore magnetic and quadrupole effects. Their computer models used pairs of a long carbon chain placed between two extreme layouts.

The light response peaked for in-between layouts in some directions, and it matched what the full set of transition moments predicted. A tiny symmetry-breaking nudge then produced the paired signals the classic method is known for. Flat systems, the authors show, fit the standard framework once all moment types are counted.
pmc-13267573:
Pengyu Li and colleagues present a 2026 study of lab-grown tumor copies for mouth cancer. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is the main mouth cancer, and patients answer chemotherapy very unevenly. The team grew organoids, small 3D copies of tumors, from 10 patients. The copies kept the look and gene traits of the original tumors.

Drug tests on the copies mirrored how each patient actually responded to treatment. Gene, activity, and drug data together found patterns tied to drug resistance. The copies also pointed to a signaling pathway, called JAK-STAT, as a target that might break that resistance. The authors argue that such copies can guide personal treatment choices. They may help doctors avoid drugs that will not work for a given patient.
pmc-13267673:
Roberto Colangeli and Fiorenzo Conti show in 2026 that the brain's own cannabis-like signals can tune a steady form of braking in cortex cells. Alongside brief braking pulses at synapses, neurons also feel a constant background brake from receptors outside synapses. Recording from single cells, the pair briefly excited pyramid-shaped cortex neurons and watched that background brake respond.

Short excitation briefly strengthened the background brake. Blocking the CB1 cannabis receptor, or stopping the cell's own cannabinoid release, prevented the change. The effect did not come from more transmitter drifting around the cell. It needed the cell to make neurosteroids, hormone-like molecules built inside neurons. Activity, cannabinoids, and neurosteroids thus work together to fine-tune steady inhibition.
pmc-13268873:
Fei Yang and co-authors review in 2026 the models built to predict a racing, irregular heartbeat complication after lung cancer surgery. This problem, postoperative atrial fibrillation, raises illness and death after operations, and many prediction models exist with unclear quality. Their review searched Chinese and English databases to May 2024 and included six model studies, checking bias with a standard tool.

Most models used logistic regression, leaning on age, sex, heart conditions, and surgical factors. Accuracy scores ranged widely, and the pooled value suggested good separation between patients who did and did not develop the complication. Every study, however, carried a high risk of bias, and results varied greatly between studies. Without outside validation, the authors caution against routine clinical use yet.
pmc-13269573:
Chanelle Warton and Danya F Vears published a journal article in 2026 on genetic counsellors in Australia and non-invasive prenatal testing, a blood test in pregnancy that screens the unborn child. Counsellors support parents' free choices, yet their own values can clash with that duty. Interviews explored how they handle such clashes.

Twenty-three counsellors who provide the testing were interviewed. All shared a clear sense of their main duties, but differed on what to do when personal values conflicted. Tensions arose most when testing targeted conditions seen as mild. Some reported colleagues refusing care over abortion objections. Counsellors agreed that values blocking patient access clash with free choice, and suggested careful wording can ease disability concerns.
pmc-13270073:
Hunter Geneau, Hailey C Lewis, and Sean P Holmes published a review in 2026 on adding eustachian tube widening to ear tube insertion for chronic fluid in the middle ear without infection. The eustachian tube connects the ear to the throat, and its failure helps cause the fluid. Four databases were searched for combined-treatment studies.

Four cohort studies covering 294 ears were pooled where possible. All main outcomes appeared to favor the combined treatment, though studies varied. Symptom recurrence averaged 9.9 percent with the combined approach against 24.9 percent with tubes alone, a significant gap. The authors say the added procedure looks clinically worthwhile in adults, but better controlled studies are needed for confidence.
pmc-13270873:
Rashid Menhas led a 2026 systematic review and meta-regression on virtual reality nature scenes for older adults with cognitive impairment. A meta-regression pools past trials and adds extra analysis. Cognitive impairment means problems with memory and thinking. The interventions used simulated nature as the main treatment.

Across 24 randomized trials with 1,534 people, the programmes improved depression, anxiety, stress, apathy, loneliness, and agitation scores, and raised quality of life and sleep quality. Engagement also favoured virtual reality. The authors urge caution, though: effects were large, results varied a lot between studies, and small-study effects may inflate the gains. Longer programmes linked modestly to bigger effects.
pmc-13271273:
Welbeck Danquah is lead author of a 2026 journal article on a new antibody combination meant to make T cell engager drugs work better against solid tumours. Engagers drag immune T cells onto cancer cells, but in solid tumours they cause dose-limiting side effects and lack the second, costimulatory signal T cells need.

The team built a bispecific antibody, one that binds two targets, aimed at HER2 on tumours and CD2 on T cells, and paired it with a standard engager. In a mouse model with human tumours, the pair cleared tumours fully in eight of nine mice at a low engager dose that alone cleared only one. The helper also produced far lower cytokine release than a CD28-based rival.
pmc-13271573:
Eric Ofori is lead author of a 2026 prospective study of fetal blood flow patterns by sex in a Ghanaian pregnancy cohort. Ultrasound Doppler measures track blood flow in the cord, the fetal brain artery, and the fetal aorta. They may differ between male and female fetuses. But African data on this question are limited.

Among 239 low-risk singleton pregnancies, 53.6 percent of fetuses were male. Pooling all pregnancy stages, no Doppler index differed clearly by sex. Before 25 weeks, though, female fetuses showed higher cord artery resistance measures, suggesting tighter flow through the placenta, while males showed higher aorta resistance measures. The authors present these early patterns as sex-specific physiology worth tracking.
pmc-13271973:
Xiang Lin and coauthors review in 2026 wearable devices for tracking recovery around lung cancer surgery. Recovery programs stress early movement, yet clinic visits capture that progress only in snapshots. Wrist or body sensors could record activity and body signals continuously at home and in hospital.

The review gathered eight reports covering seven patient groups, from randomized trials to usability studies. Searches spanned three databases for studies since 1996, with bias and certainty checks applied to each report. Because designs differed so much, the authors summarized findings in words rather than pooled numbers, weighing where wearables genuinely help discharge planning.
pmc-13272073:
Miguel Mansilla-Polo is lead author of a 2026 case article on detecting circulating tumour DNA during treatment of in-transit melanoma metastases. Tumour DNA means fragments of cancer DNA in the blood. In-transit deposits spread between the original tumour and nearby lymph nodes. Such blood tests, called liquid biopsies, often fail in this setting because DNA levels are undetectable despite clear disease.

The authors report two cases of stage IIIC melanoma treated with imiquimod, a cream applied to the skin, in which tumour DNA became detectable only during treatment. They suggest the cream may release tumour DNA by destroying cancer cells, letting genetic material spill into the blood. One case began with an 84-year-old woman with a thick, ulcerated melanoma.
pmc-13272573:
Grégory Andreoli and colleagues presented a dataset on removable urban pavements in a 2026 data article. These pavements use interlocking hexagonal slabs that crews can lift quickly to reach pipes and cables below. Knowing their surface and subsurface state helps cities plan repairs.

The dataset records a version with a draining porous concrete surface, meant to stop standing water. Measurements came from several tools: drone images to map each slab, ground photos from a phone standing in for a robot, and radar that peers below the surface. Together they classify slabs and flag faults above and below ground. The authors aim to build a growing database that a learning model can use to spot damage over time.
pmc-13272773:
Sang-Seok Oh leads a 2026 study of why dust storms have grown stronger over the Mongolian Gobi in early spring, even as dust has fallen across most of East Asia. The team focused on March, when snow cover and land-air links are sensitive to climate. They used 24 years of observations, from 2000 to 2023, plus weather reanalysis data.

Snow loss and soil drying made the surface easier to lift, while persistent air instability and strong upper winds kept conditions ripe for dust. Over the Loess Plateau, by contrast, weaker winds offset drying and held dust down. The authors call the Gobi pattern an unmitigated climate penalty, where land and air changes amplify each other.
pmc-13273473:
Eusondia Arnett and a large team showed how tuberculosis bacteria exploit a zinc transporter in immune cells in a 2026 study. The bacterium lives inside macrophages, the cells meant to kill it, in a pocket called a phagosome. Hosts often poison such pockets with zinc, yet the bacterium needs traces of it too.

The transporter ZIP8 was the only zinc carrier strongly switched on by infection in human macrophages, and it gathered at the bacterial pocket. It pulls zinc out of the pocket into the cell body, which spares the bacterium from poisoning. That extra zinc also dulled inflammatory signals while raising tissue cutting enzymes. Mice and cells lacking ZIP8 handled the bacterium differently, which confirms the route. The findings matter where diet zinc is low.
pmc-13273773:
Esther J. Hutloff and co-authors analyzed what shapes hair steroid levels in babies in a 2026 study. Hair captures long term hormone exposure, yet almost nothing was known about what drives these readings in the first two years of life. Their prospective study collected hair four times from three weeks to two years.

Six steroids were measured by advanced chemical analysis in samples from more than two hundred children at each visit. Cortisol, cortisone, and progesterone peaked just after birth, fell sharply by eight weeks, then eased down slowly. Most background factors mattered little. Birth mode linked to early cortisol and season to one hormone at age two, even after strict correction. Weight and pandemic exposure showed no link. The authors judge hair analysis promising for early life research.
pmc-13273873:
Estermann and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for growing single fetal mouse gonads outside the body. The paired design lets one gonad receive treatment while its pair serves as control. The method screens inhibitors, metabolites, and signaling modulators.

Steps cover gonad dissection and paired culture setup. The team uses 3D-printable molds for single-gonad culture. Standard 48-well plates hold the cultures. Downstream checks include immunostaining of the tissue. Multi-omics analyses are also described. Metabolic measurements use both tissue and culture media. Pairing the gonads from one fetus cuts variability. The protocol suits short-term screening during sex differentiation. That window is narrow in mouse development.
pmc-13273973:
Helene Johansson and co-authors present a 2026 qualitative journal article comparing how family doctors in the United States and Sweden promote healthy habits. Qualitative work relies on interviews rather than counts. Earlier surveys had found big gaps between the two countries in lifestyle counseling.

The team recorded semi-structured interviews with twenty-eight primary care doctors and sorted their answers by theme. Doctors in both countries called habit change part of their job, covering smoking, poor diet, and low activity. American doctors described more set routines and personal duty, while Swedish doctors leaned more on referrals and shared team duty. Lack of time was a common barrier in both countries.
pmc-13274573:
Mary C Wilding and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on whether viruses worsen long-term sinus disease in children. Pediatric chronic rhinosinusitis means months of inflamed sinuses, and viruses are suspected drivers alongside bacteria. The team collected sinus swabs during surgery at a children's hospital from 2018 to 2022.

Groups covered fifteen children whose sinus disease came with cystic fibrosis, twenty-one without it, and thirty-two controls having nose structure surgery. At least one virus turned up in about thirty-one percent of first samples, most often in the cystic fibrosis group at fifty-three percent. Rhinovirus, the common cold virus, led detections. Virus-positive patients reported far more nasal drainage and showed more discharge on scope exams.
pmc-13274873:
Thomas Sheffield and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on keeping prediction models useful as a virus keeps mutating. Models trained on early SARS-CoV-2 strains fade as new variants drift away from the originals. The team's fix is a loop: machine learning models predict, high-throughput lab tests check the most informative cases, and the results retrain the models.

Their models forecast three properties of the virus's receptor-binding domain: grip on the human ACE2 receptor, protein production, and escape from antibodies. Iterative testing covered over two hundred variants from the original and Omicron strains. Prediction accuracy reached correlation values up to 0.79 for antibody binding, and the models generalized across antibody types, including heavy-chain-only antibodies.
pmc-13275173:
Omar Musbahi and colleagues report a 2026 journal article linking wrist-measured activity after joint replacement to long-term survival. Using UK Biobank data tied to hospital and death records, the team studied 1,769 adults. All had a hip or knee replacement and later wore an accelerometer, a motion sensor, for activity measurement. Survival was tracked for up to twenty years.

Between the ten- and twenty-year marks, more active patients died less often by every measure the team tried. Daily steps, light activity, and moderate-to-vigorous activity each predicted lower mortality after adjustment, with vigorous activity showing the strongest link. The authors call this the first demonstration that objectively measured activity after joint surgery predicts survival, and they stress careful patient selection and activity promotion.
pmc-13275973:
Mariyam Shafiq and Saiqa Tabassum present a 2026 journal article on an unusual source for making silver nanoparticles: the common housefly. Tiny silver particles can fight germs and oxidation, but chemical production pollutes. Plant and microbe extracts offer greener routes, while insect materials remain barely explored.

Extract from houseflies turned a silver solution into particles, signaled by a color change and confirmed by light tests. Microscope views showed mostly round particles, and crystal tests confirmed their silver structure. In lab assays the particles calmed inflammation, lowered sugar-related chemistry, and mopped up harmful oxygen molecules. They performed slightly better than the raw silver solution and the plain extract. The authors call for dose and safety studies before any medical use.
pmc-13276173:
Stephanie Zika and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how the infant brain insulates its wiring. Myelination wraps nerve fibers in fatty sheaths so signals travel fast. It races ahead in early infancy, but whether the cortex and the white matter tracts develop in step was unknown.

The team used two brain-scan measures linked to myelin. One dataset covered more than two hundred seventy infants; a smaller one used a more precise measure in twenty-one babies. Software traced twenty-six white matter bundles to the cortex areas they serve. For both measures, average levels and growth rates in cortex and white matter moved together. Babies whose tissue growth was more in sync tended to show better motor skills as toddlers. Premature birth and age since conception shifted that synchrony.
pmc-13276273:
Min-Su Jung and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on catheter ablation for a stubborn heart rhythm disorder. In persistent atrial fibrillation, the heart's upper chambers quiver instead of beating steadily. Burning small areas inside the heart can restore rhythm, but results beyond the standard step remain uneven.

The team treated fifty-seven patients with a tailored approach guided by dense electrical maps of the heart. They compared them with fifty-seven similar patients who got the standard procedure alone. After one year, about seventy-nine percent of the tailored group stayed free of the rhythm disorder, versus about sixty percent of the standard group. When related fast rhythms were counted too, the gap shrank and was no longer clear-cut. No extra harm was reported, and the authors see promise in the personalized strategy.
pmc-13276573:
Angelita Costantino and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a testing platform built from patients' own colon tissue. Miniature gut models called organoids mimic human intestinal lining far better than flat cell lines or animals. Nutraceuticals, food-derived compounds with health claims, are usually screened on those cruder models.

Their platform grows organoids from non-tumor colon samples in two states, growing and matured. Instruments weigh and measure single organoids while gene sequencing and sensitive counting methods profile their activity. The two states ran distinct gene programs, and structural measures captured shape changes. As a pilot, the team applied an oxidative insult, then a nutraceutical treatment. Gene and physical responses moved together in a coordinated way. The authors offer the system for patient-specific screening of dietary compounds and stress responses.
pmc-13276673:
Ridvan Sakir and co-authors report a 2026 journal article mapping high blood pressure across Türkiye over fourteen years. Hypertension is the world's leading fixable driver of heart disease and stroke. Updated long-term national figures for Türkiye were lacking, so the team pooled seven national health surveys.

Nearly one hundred thousand adults aged nineteen and older took part between 2008 and 2022. About nineteen percent reported having hypertension. Prevalence rose modestly to 2016, then leveled off. Risk tracked strongly with older age, higher body weight, bigger waist size, inactivity, and having a spouse or parent with the condition. Women reported it more than men, and rates differed by region. Two findings cut against expectation: graduate-educated adults showed higher prevalence than the least educated, and regular smokers showed slightly lower prevalence than nonsmokers.
pmc-13276873:
Jasmijn O Heijman leads a 2026 review of why many people feel overwhelmed by sound, light, or touch after a brain injury. The review looks at the problem through neuropsychology, the study of how brain damage affects thinking and behavior. Such sensitivity can affect most patients after injury, yet it has drawn little research.

The authors propose that weak filtering of signals, slow processing, poor memory, anxiety, and fatigue may all play a part. Their model frames the problem as a mismatch between what a person can handle and what the setting demands. That mismatch varies by person. The review sets out testable ideas and points toward teaching and rehabilitation plans to ease daily life.
pmc-13277173:
Mohamed Gamal Ibrahim leads a 2026 survey of how health workers view patient safety culture in three public hospitals in Beni-Suef City, Egypt. Safety culture means the shared habits and attitudes that keep patients from harm. A total of 497 workers, from nurses to office staff, filled in a standard safety survey.

Nurses rated safety culture higher than office staff did, and government hospitals scored higher than the university hospital. Working longer hours and direct patient contact also shaped scores. Higher workplace safety scores went with higher patient safety scores, while burnout went with lower ones. The authors urge better workplace safety, less burnout, and support aimed at younger staff to lift safety culture.
pmc-13277773:
Zhenyan Lu leads a 2026 study that builds computer models to predict fatty liver using a painless liver scan and routine health data. Fatty liver, called hepatic steatosis, means excess fat stored in liver cells. The team used United States national survey data for 12,177 people and trained six machine learning models, programs that learn patterns from data.

One model, called XGBoost, sorted fatty liver cases best. Fourteen factors fed the models, and body mass index, a blood sugar marker, age, and a cholesterol type mattered most in the winning model. An explanation tool showed how each factor pushed each prediction. The authors say such a model could help flag risk early in clinic checks.
pmc-13278573:
Olav N L Aga leads a 2026 study that maps how drug resistance evolves in Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium that causes many hospital infections. Resistance is a growing global burden, and predicting its paths could guide policy. The team used resistance features predicted from about forty-seven thousand bacterial genomes across 102 countries and a sampling method that infers likely evolutionary routes.

Some resistance behaviors were consistent worldwide, while resistance to two key drug classes varied by country. Those differences tracked with regional groupings and drug use policy. Newly sequenced African data across several decades matched the roadmap's predictions. Linking resistance forecasts to policy and social factors could strengthen responses, the authors hope.
pmc-13278673:
Charles Micou, Timothy O'Leary, and Tim Kietzmann study how brain codes drift over time in a 2026 neuroscience paper. Neurons representing the same stimulus slowly change their tuning across days and weeks. Reading brain areas must somehow keep extracting the right information despite that drift.

Drift can build from many tiny changes or from sudden jumps in a few cells at a time. The authors show that a simple adaptive reader exploits jump-like drift to stay accurate. Recordings from parietal and visual cortex in animals confirmed that real drift comes in sudden jumps, not a smooth random walk. The finding motivates a search for adaptive decoding circuits in the brain.
pmc-13278973:
Pengfei Dai and co-authors evaluate internet-based team care after haemorrhoid surgery in a 2026 cohort study. Mixed haemorrhoids often need surgery, and recovery at home can go wrong without follow-up. Records covered 186 patients treated between 2023 and 2025 at their centre.

Ninety-four patients received online multidisciplinary continuity care, while ninety-two had conventional follow-up. Wounds healed about four days faster in the online care group. Complications were far rarer there, and pain scores at one and two weeks were lower. Quality of life, satisfaction, and self-care ability all scored higher, while anxiety and depression fell further. The authors back the model for routine postoperative management.
pmc-13279673:
Paula Alcazar and colleagues report a 2026 case of extra breast tissue on the back of a child as a sign of spine defect. Extra nipples or breasts form when a fetal milk line fails to shrink back. They sit most often on the line from armpit to groin. Back sites are rare and can link to spine closure defects. Their patient was an eleven year old girl.

A back midline swelling present from birth was first called a lipoma, a fat lump. Growth and a dark centre spot led to closer checks, which proved a nipple and areola complex. Spine MRI showed a fat tumour inside the spine cover at chest level, with a fibrous tract to the skin lump. The cord was tethered, or held tight, by the tract. Teams removed the tissue and did spine surgery in one plan. Back midline marks in children merit spine scans.
pmc-13279873:
Thaer A. Tumar and colleagues report a 2026 case of a low grade brain tumour in a young infant with a gene fault. Child low grade gliomas grow slowly and often end well. Early infancy cases in the back brain with wide spread are rare. Their patient was a four month old girl with signs of high skull pressure and sunsetting eyes. Scans showed a mass on the medulla, the low brain stem, with a large cyst.

The mass blocked fluid flow and swelled all four ventricles. A shunt drained fluid and surgery eased pressure. Tissue tests proved a low grade glioneuronal tumour with low growth rate. Gene tests found an FGFR1 mutation, a growth gene fault, plus a chromosome arm loss. Despite benign tissue looks, the tumour spread to neck cord and spine linings. Targeted therapy was started. Gene class can warn of fierce acts that tissue grade hides.
pmc-13281173:
Enayat Mohsenzadeh and three co-authors model a plastic sensor for a cattle drug in a 2026 paper. The drug, clorsulon, is toxic to fish and water insects, so finding traces of it matters. The sensor design uses polypyrrole, a plastic molded around the drug so that fitted cavities remain, like a lock shaped for one key.

Using quantum chemistry methods and fast simulations, the team worked out the best recipe for the plastic. A mix of sixteen building blocks per drug unit in water worked best. They also compared how the plastic chains link up, since the linking pattern changes the sensor's electrical behavior. The study is a blueprint for building the real sensor.
pmc-13281873:
Yiwei Zhang and colleagues followed women after pelvic support surgery for over seven years in a 2026 study. Pelvic organ prolapse lets the womb or bladder sag into the vagina. The surgery lifts the top of the vagina with its own ligaments through small cuts, alongside womb removal. Thirty-four women had the operation at a Beijing hospital from 2015 to 2019. Thirty-one stayed in follow-up past seven years. Checks joined exams with standard questionnaires.

By strict joint rules, about four in ten women counted as full successes. By body measures alone, more than three in four held up. No sag returned at the lifted top. Returns clustered in the front and back walls instead. More than nine in ten women never needed a second fix. The authors call the support durable, while noting strict success rules flatter no one.
pmc-13282173:
Maria Papaefstathiou and co-authors describe a 2026 wearable sensor made wholly from fabric that tracks body posture during yoga. The sensor is a stretchy capacitor, a device that stores charge and changes its signal when stretched, woven into clothing in a comb-like pattern. It is light, comfortable, and washable. Lab tests showed it kept working through six thousand five hundred stretch cycles.

Built into garments, the sensor recorded electrical signals during four yoga poses: two lunges, a squat, and a tree pose. A machine learning program, which learns patterns from examples, sorted the poses with about ninety-four percent accuracy. Signals linked to capacitance, the stored charge, carried the most useful information. Other signal types added detail on how each pose moved the fabric. The authors say such clothing sensors could support digital fitness coaching and home movement checks without stiff hardware.
pmc-13282473:
Perihan Kubra Akman and co-authors report a 2026 food study on fermenting reduced-calorie sour cherry drinks with lactic acid bacteria. Fermentation can raise how much of a food's useful compounds the body can access. The team used three single probiotic strains and one mixed culture, comparing the drinks with unfermented controls over twenty-eight days of cold storage. They tracked acidity, colour, plant compounds, antioxidant power, and bacterial survival.

Fermented drinks ended more acidic and kept live bacteria above the probiotic threshold for three weeks. Their key plant compounds were identified, though most declined in storage. Despite higher starting plant compound levels, controls were beaten on recovery after simulated digestion, meaning better bioaccessibility. Calorie cuts reached nearly half in the best recipe. Antioxidant capacity stayed higher in fermented drinks. The authors present fermentation as a practical upgrade for functional cherry beverages.
pmc-13282673: Adwall and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their 2022 study of complications and risk factors in breast cancer surgery. One sentence in the limitations paragraph of the Discussion was wrong. It explained why neoadjuvant chemotherapy, treatment given before surgery, was excluded, citing an earlier department cohort study and a hazard ratio for surgical site infection. The corrected sentence cites instead a 2014 to 2015 department study, gives an odds ratio near one, and marks the data as unpublished. The authors apologise for the error.
pmc-13282873:
Atom-by-atom maps for chemical reactions get a rigorous theoretical treatment from Marcos E Gonzalez Laffitte and collaborators, writing in 2026. Such maps link each atom in starting compounds to its place in products. Databases often lack these links, yet synthesis planning and isotope studies need them.

The authors focus on partial maps that cover only the reaction center, where bonds change. Using the Imaginary Transition State graph, they prove a clear rule for extension. A full unique map exists exactly when the partial map covers the reaction center. They also extend the result to cases where hydrogen atoms are not shown. Algorithms follow from the proof.
pmc-13283173:
Chicago's school stock inhaler rollout is audited for fairness in a 2026 district-wide analysis under Mariya Patwa. Stock inhalers are shared rescue inhalers kept for breathing distress at school. Asthma is common in the city, but access gaps hit Black and low-income students hardest.

Data covered 517 district schools and more than 266,000 students in total. High schools had higher asthma rates than elementary schools in the data. Black students had higher asthma odds than Hispanic students in adjusted models. Yet they had lower odds of a formal support plan for asthma. Low-income and unhoused students also had higher asthma odds. The rollout itself was judged fair across schools.
pmc-13283373:
Ultrasound stiffness of the cervix outpredicts the classic Bishop score before labor induction, Ping Li's prospective team shows in 2026. Failed induction raises risks for mother and baby alike. The Bishop score relies on hand exam and can vary between examiners.

A total of 106 first-time mothers with single babies joined from January 2024 to August 2025. Ultrasound measured neck length, angles, and tissue stiffness of the cervix. Of the group, 83 had successful induction and 75 had vaginal births. Ultrasound traits differed clearly between outcome groups in the analysis. Bishop traits showed no clear gaps in this study. Tissue stiffness alone predicted both outcomes best.
pmc-13283473:
Uncertainty bands make GPT-4o death forecasts from ICU notes more honest, Fatemeh Shah-Mohammadi's conformal study shows in 2026. Clinical notes hold rich detail but are hard to use in structured models. Large language models can read notes, yet their confidence per patient is unclear.

Notes from the first 24 hours of intensive care were fed to GPT-4o. Cases came from the MIMIC-III set for kidney failure patients admitted via emergency care. A conformal method wrapped predictions with patient-level uncertainty ranges. The model spotted death cases well, with high recall in that class. Survival calls were weaker by comparison in the test results. Clear uncertainty bounds may make AI forecasts safer for clinical use.
pmc-13283873:
Yi Zhong and a large team built a prediction chart in 2026 for death risk in children with moderate-to-severe head injury. Brain injury is a leading cause of child death and disability, and spotting high-risk cases early guides care. Records of 289 children admitted with such injuries were reviewed, and statistical selection pulled out the strongest predictors of dying in hospital within thirty days.

Four factors made the final chart: the Glasgow Coma Scale score, which grades consciousness, blood lactic acid, blood albumin, and trauma-driven clotting failure. Half the children were under about five years old. The chart sorted risk with high accuracy and matched observed outcomes well in checks. Decision analysis suggested value across a wide range of risk thresholds. The authors offer it for early risk sorting at admission.
pmc-13284773:
David Baud and co-authors report a 2026 cohort study on sexual function twelve years after childbirth injury to the anal sphincter. Such tears can cause pelvic floor problems, and short-term work has found more pain and less pleasure after injury. Long-term evidence was scarce, so the team re-surveyed the same women with a standard sexual function questionnaire.

Replies came from 52 women with injury and 141 controls, a high return rate for this long follow-up. Total and domain scores were alike between groups overall. Still, women with injury more often reported poor lubrication and pain on penetration. A past gap in reaching orgasm had faded by year twelve. The authors show broad recovery with some lasting symptoms.
pmc-13284873:
James Muscat and co-authors give a 2026 case report and literature review on a rare open midfoot injury. A 30-year-old woman fell six meters and suffered an open fracture-dislocation of the medial cuneiform bone, plus tearing of the tibialis anterior tendon from its anchor. Such cuneiform injuries are uncommon and often hide within wider foot trauma.

Urgent care included washing and cleaning the wound, realigning and fixing the midfoot, and repairing the tendon through a bone tunnel with strong sutures. At six months, X-rays held the alignment with no hardware failure. Pain was minimal, no infection appeared, and she walked on her own. The authors call this the first report of this exact pairing.
pmc-13285073:
Yaping Liu and co-authors describe, in a 2026 case report, a newborn who developed group B streptococcus sepsis and meningitis even though the mother screened negative at thirty-nine weeks. Screening plus antibiotics during labor have cut this early-onset disease sharply, but no screen is perfect.

The term baby showed breathing trouble, poor feeding, and floppiness soon after birth. Blood culture grew the bacterium, and spinal fluid confirmed meningitis. Seventeen days of antibiotics, adjusted for brain coverage, cured him. Brain scans showed small bleeds that later cleared. The case urges clinicians to trust symptoms over a reassuring screen and treat fast.
pmc-13285173:
Rumaisa Riaz and co-authors give a 2026 overview of drug care for Alzheimer disease, centered on the newly approved antibody donanemab-azbt. Older drugs lift a brain chemical or calm a receptor, easing symptoms but with side effects such as nausea or dizziness. New antibodies aim at amyloid clumps, yet can cause imaging faults tied to swelling or bleeding.

Trial data show donanemab-azbt lowers amyloid load and slows thinking decline in early symptomatic disease, the authors report. That gain comes with a need for close clinical and scan monitoring during treatment. The overview weighs donanemab beside standard drugs and the earlier antibody aducanumab to guide early-stage care choices.
pmc-13285273:
Theodorus van Schaik and co-authors describe a 2026 case where smart software helped repair a burst belly artery through a catheter. Such repairs are demanding because time is short and the vessels are distorted by bleeding. The software overlays a prior scan onto live X-ray images to guide the team.

Many teams feared the overlay step would cost precious minutes in a burst case. The case shows the setup was workable within the emergency pace. Better guidance could shorten the procedure and cut X-ray dose and dye use, which matters since kidney harm is common after these bleeds. The report offers proof of concept for wider emergency use, from a single case.
pmc-13285373:
Greener straw pulping with soda ash help is the advance in a 2026 study by Qixi Xu and co-authors. Normal oxygen-alkali pulping of wheat straw runs hot, chews up cellulose, and lets silicon foul the process. Their low-heat method adds sodium carbonate and recycles the alkali mix.

At set heat and alkali levels, pulp yields rose over the standard method, and the test paper grew stronger on both pull and crush measures in the trials reported here. Far less dissolved silicon stayed in the waste liquor than under the old method, easing a key snag. The authors say the route gives steady, high-grade straw pulp with less waste strain.
pmc-13285473:
Dhaka and seven co-authors unify screening methods for water splitting catalysts, in work from twenty twenty-six. The oxygen evolution reaction is the slow half of splitting water for green hydrogen. Faster discovery needs screening that is both quick and mechanistically sound.

Their test case is cobalt oxide doped with transition metals. They built a volcano style approach that resolves mechanism and depends on voltage, joining scaling relations with multiple reaction paths. Descriptor methods alone can misrank catalysts when the mechanism changes. A unified screen should cut wasted lab trials and focus synthesis on the most promising doped materials.
pmc-13285573:
A tail stretch of viral RNA steers how well Getah virus grows, sickens, and rides mosquitoes, Tongwei Ren and co-authors show in a 2026 study. This mosquito-borne virus threatens farm stock and people, with fresh outbreaks growing harsher. The team snipped parts of the tail stretch, called the 3 prime untranslated region, and watched each mutant.

The tail proved bendy: cutting up to three hundred ten letters still left live virus. Losing repeat bits slowed growth in some cells and blunted illness in mice. The biggest cut crippled spread to mosquitoes and caused only brief sickness, with no deaths. Joint gene reads tied the softening to immune path shifts. A weakened vaccine seed is the goal.
pmc-13285673:
Yuhai Dang and Jinliang Kong describe an 80-year-old woman in rural Guangxi, China, who carried two infections at once, in a 2026 case report. She had coughed and run a fever for a month. Her lungs were already scarred by past tuberculosis, and she had eaten raw rodent meat, a known route of exposure to a tropical fungus.

Standard tests found nothing, although a nose swab detected the COVID-19 virus. Gene sequencing of fluid washed from her lungs identified both that virus and the fungus Talaromyces marneffei. pmc-13285973:
Reda Amrani Souhli and colleagues compare four laboratory tests for tuberculosis in Tangier, Morocco, in a 2026 study. Fast, accurate diagnosis limits spread and guides treatment. The team ran smear microscopy, a rapid molecular test, and two culture methods side by side on the same samples, using liquid culture as the reference.

The study covered 386 specimens over nine months, from lungs and from other body sites. The molecular test found more cases than microscopy in both sample types while staying highly specific. Solid culture landed between the two in sensitivity. Results for drug resistance matched well between the molecular test and standard methods. The authors recommend combining molecular testing, microscopy, and culture rather than relying on one method.
pmc-13286073:
Elizabeth R Boskey and co-authors run a 2026 randomized trial on whether readers notice gender-inclusive health writing. The trial handed adults paired versions of teen handouts, one inclusive and one gender-specific, in random order.

The study held 454 adults assigned female at birth, about a third of them LGBTQ+. Most readers never spotted a difference between the paired sheets, even in the first pair they saw. Many who said they favored gender-specific wording still picked the inclusive sheet as the one they liked better. Those who favored inclusive wording chose it far more often when they did notice. Quiet inclusion, the authors conclude, passes without friction across the political range.
pmc-13286373:

pmc-13286573:
Megan S Laham and a large team refine a fingerprinting assay for liver X receptor drugs in a 2026 pharmacology study. pmc-13286673:
Giuseppe Dell'Anna and colleagues describe fishing a stray gallbladder stent out through a second one in a 2026 case vignette. The team converted her to internal drainage under ultrasound guidance, seating a 10 by 10 millimeter metal stent through the gut wall into the gallbladder.

A month later, checks showed the stent had slipped entirely inside the gallbladder. Rather than operate on a frail patient, the team placed a second stent beside it, widened the passage, and pulled the migrated stent out with grasping forceps through the new channel. A large gallstone followed with a basket tool in the same session. No complications ensued, and the authors commend the rescue route for expert centers.
pmc-13286873:
Chukwuka Elendu and co-authors recount a goat saved by timely surgery in a 2026 veterinary case report. A proven mother doe under smallholder care strained in active labor for about fourteen hours with nothing to show for it. Examination found an alert but exhausted animal, weak contractions, and a cervix that stayed firm and barely open, admitting at most two fingers despite the long labor.

Gentle manual stretching failed, and the team deliberately skipped drugs that would strengthen contractions against a closed cervix, fearing rupture. An emergency cesarean through the left flank under local anesthesia resolved the obstruction directly. The report's lesson targets field practice: when a rigid cervix ignores both time and manipulation, earlier surgery, not more tugging, protects both doe and kid.
pmc-13286973:
Ting Lei and colleagues report long-term results for a modified hip operation in children born with a dislocated or poorly formed hip joint. The modification ends the cut a few millimeters above a notch in the pelvis, hinging above the Y-shaped cartilage instead of through it. Average follow-up exceeded seven years. Socket angle measures improved dramatically and stayed stable. Roughly nine in ten hips earned excellent or good ratings on both function and imaging scales. Bone death in the femoral head affected about one hip in nine, within historical norms.
pmc-13287073:
Yue Fei and colleagues lay out the protocol for a randomized trial comparing two sedatives in older patients having both upper and lower digestive tract endoscopy in one session. Published in 2026, the protocol responds to a real risk: sedation in the elderly can drop blood oxygen and blood pressure. Ciprofol, a newer relative of the standard propofol, may keep breathing and circulation steadier.

One hundred eighty-four patients aged sixty-five and over will be assigned evenly to one drug or the other, with neither patients nor assessors told which. The main outcome joins oxygen dips and blood pressure drops during sedation. Secondary measures cover airway help, recovery times, drug totals, and satisfaction. The registered trial aims to give firm guidance for a common procedure.
pmc-13287773:
Qian Zhou and co-authors find a bodyguard protein that keeps a leukemia alive in a 2026 study. The team shows a second protein, PELI1, shields the driver from destruction.

The driver itself raises PELI1 levels through a signaling chain, and the raised PELI1 grabs and protects it, a self-reinforcing loop that also pushes cell growth. Blocking PELI1, by gene edits or a drug, slowed both drug-sensitive and drug-resistant leukemia cells and even the stubborn stem cells that seed relapse. Mouse disease burden eased as well. The authors pitch PELI1 as a target that could break resistance.
pmc-13287973:
Sultan M Alsharif and co-authors sequenced bacteria in 2026 from soil hugging the roots of four date palm varieties grown near Madinah in Saudi Arabia. A marker gene survey named the resident groups, and a prediction tool inferred what growth-helping jobs those bacteria might carry.

One large bacterial phylum led in most samples, while a second led in one variety. Known helper genera appeared throughout, including Bacillus and Paenibacillus. Predicted genes for moving phosphate and sulfur, grabbing iron, and handling oxidation were plentiful. The authors present the root zone as a rich source of helper microbes that could support greener date farming after strain-level testing.
pmc-13288973:
Xinyan Chen and colleagues give a 2026 trial plan for pain drugs after heart surgery. The trial sits at one center in China. It deals with small-cut valve replacement. Pain care after such surgery is tricky. Strong pain drugs can cause side effects.

The trial will enroll 130 patients in all. Half will get oxycodone by a pain pump. Half will get sufentanil instead. Neither side will know their drug. The main test is pain on coughing at 24 hours. Staff will also track drug use and side effects. The goal is to match, not beat, the standard drug.
pmc-13289373:
Tracey Smythe and coauthors ran a 2026 pilot in Luuka district, Uganda, on group work to improve health care access for people with disabilities. Barriers to care are steep in low-resource areas, and few community fixes have been tested. The Participatory Learning and Action for Disability approach lets groups name local barriers and act on them together.

Five groups ran from May 2023 to March 2024, each with roughly 35 to 48 members, totaling 204 people meeting every two weeks. Trained facilitators led 11 sessions per group cycle. Interviews, group watching, activity logs, and surveys before and after checked appeal, demand, and early effects. Members found the groups relevant and wanted them to continue, though mentor support for facilitators lagged at times.
pmc-13289473:
Saad Alghamdi and ten co-authors published a transplant outcomes study in twenty twenty-six on liver replacement for Wilson disease, the inherited disorder that overloads the body with copper. Transplant is the definitive cure, but experience is limited, especially where living donors dominate. Their center reviewed every case from twenty oh one to twenty twenty-three.

Forty-one patients, median age twenty-three, received new livers for causes from sudden liver failure to brain involvement. Living donors supplied over half the organs. Rejection struck about thirty percent but was always manageable, and nobody needed a second transplant. Most patients with neurological symptoms improved. Survival reached ninety-four percent at five years and eighty-two at ten.
pmc-13289673:
Louisa Horvath and Silke Pawils explored a 2026 mixed-methods study on trauma-sensitive obstetrics from the provider side in Germany. Most providers defined traumatic birth through loss of control and negative emotions for the patient. Poor communication and information topped causes at 97.1 percent, followed by lack of emotional support as reported. Emotional support also ranked as the top preventive step by mean score. Lack of time and staff shortages were the main barriers named.
pmc-13289773:
Shivangini Duggal headed a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on infection after cholangioscopy, a scope procedure that views bile ducts directly. The method helps with complex bile disease but seems to carry higher infection risk than standard duct procedures. Blood infection pooled near 6.68 percent, with wide uncertainty and high variation across studies as reported. Duct inflammation and pancreas inflammation pooled lower. Technical success was very high and clinical success also high overall. Study design explained part of the variation.
pmc-13289973:
Muhammad S Shabbir, Mary Ayad, and Christian S Jackson compare two treatments for bleeding vessel tangles in the upper gut, in 2026. These tangles, called angioectasias, often cause anemia, hospital stays, and transfusions. Using the TriNetX database, the team sorted patients into endoscopic therapy or drug therapy with somatostatin analogues. Outcomes were tracked at six months, three years, and five years.

Endoscopic treatment led on nearly every measure at six months. Its patients had lower hospitalization, fewer repeat scopes, and lower death rates than the drug group. The gap persisted at three years, including fewer transfusions for the scope group. At five years the endoscopic advantage still held across the same outcomes. Average hemoglobin also ran higher in the endoscopic cohort at every checkpoint. The authors call for randomized multicenter trials to confirm the pattern. Their data favor treating the lesions directly over drugs alone.
pmc-13290573:
Testing whole blood, not just plasma, catches more infections in patients with blood disorders, a 2026 real-world cohort study from northern China by Cuicui Lyu and colleagues shows. Infection is a leading killer in this group, and standard blood culture misses most culprits.

The team reviewed 231 blood samples from patients with suspected infection who received metagenomic sequencing. Whole-blood sequencing, which reads plasma plus blood cells, detected pathogens far more often than culture and found 13 organisms that plasma-only testing missed among its 101 detections. Its agreement with final clinical diagnoses was also the highest of the methods compared. Treatment improved for most patients as a result, with needless antibiotics stopped and therapy better aimed. Lyu and colleagues back the combined sample for early infection care in these fragile patients.
pmc-13291073:
Yiwei Chen and colleagues report a 2026 case where gene sequencing of spinal fluid found the true cause of meningitis after standard treatment failed. Their patient was a 67-year-old man with chronic lung disease who arrived with four days of high fever and confusion, and first antibiotic cover with meropenem brought no gain.

Metagenomic sequencing named Listeria monocytogenes, a foodborne germ that strikes hardest at older and weakened patients, as the cause of meningitis alongside a flare of his lung disease. Care switched to ampicillin-based treatment plus gentamicin for set courses, and his symptoms and blood markers improved fast afterward. The case backs early use of broad sequencing when brain infections resist usual diagnosis.
pmc-13291273:
Xiaochan Wang and co-authors measure how grass roots change water entry into loess soil, in a 2026 study. Loess covers China's Loess Plateau, where rain is scarce and restoration planting is widespread. The team grew tall fescue in soil columns and tested infiltration at five growth stages up to ninety-nine days. Root mass grew steadily across those stages. Water behavior was then modeled with a standard flow equation.

Older root systems let water finish infiltrating much faster than bare soil did. Saturated conductivity rose in a straight line with the root-to-soil mass ratio. Other water traits followed smooth exponential curves as roots grew. The team folded those relationships into the Richards equation for unsaturated flow. Simulations with the HYDRUS program matched measured wetting fronts and moisture profiles closely. The work gives modelers growth-stage parameters for vegetated loess slopes.
pmc-13291473:
Remote rehab may beat home exercise for sore tendons. Shijie Fan leads a 2026 review of telerehabilitation trials. Tendon pain often gets exercise care without surgery. Remote coaching could add support that home plans lack.

Ten trials with 412 people were pooled. Remote care cut pain more than home exercise alone. Function also improved more with remote support. Against in-person therapy, remote care tied on both scores. No clear gap showed for pain or function. Study quality and bias were graded with care. Remote care thus looks like a fair swap for clinic visits. It may widen access for rural patients.
pmc-13291773:
Theodore Z Cook and co-authors present a 2026 data paper assembling the first specimen-backed occurrence dataset for stoneflies across West Virginia. Stoneflies signal clean water, and the state holds unusually rich diversity for the eastern United States. The team merged museum specimens, fresh statewide collecting, and trusted literature records, with funding from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and northeastern states.

The dataset holds more than 4,500 records from all 55 counties, spanning 134 years and drawn from 17 institutions and private collections. Checking specimens confirmed 150 species from all nine eastern North American families. Fourteen species reported earlier could not be found again, most likely because of naming changes. The records will anchor a planned distribution atlas and checklist.
pmc-13291873:
Suqing Zhou and colleagues stop DNA origami pieces from clumping in a 2026 study. DNA origami folds a long strand into precise shapes that can dock onto patterned chips. The team worked with an asymmetric right triangle meant to land in a chosen orientation. Instead, triangles stuck to each other at one corner, cutting single-piece placement sharply. Microscopy traced the clumping to the hypotenuse arm's vertex.

Twisting along that arm exposed loose staple ends that grabbed neighboring triangles. Trimming short staples at that corner softened the vertex and hid the sticky ends. Single, unclumped triangles rose from about seventy-two to about eighty-seven percent. A competing fix, adding poly-T tails, helped only slightly, ruling out simple base stacking. On patterned surfaces, correctly oriented placement jumped from about thirty-three to seventy-seven percent. Tiny local tweaks can rescue placement fidelity.
pmc-13292573:
Lidan He and co-authors trace a 2026 protective circuit in the placenta that fails in preeclampsia, the dangerous pregnancy disorder. The deubiquitinase USP22 runs low in preeclamptic tissue while the necroptosis machinery, RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL, runs high. In oxygen-starved trophoblast cells, necroptosis proved the dominant death route among several tested with targeted blockers.

Removing USP22 worsened the necrotic signaling, while restoring it revived histone acetylation marks and calmed cell death. Gene scans after knockdown found 1,186 changed genes, including the silenced Wnt antagonist SFRP1. The mechanism: USP22 grips the acetyl writer KAT2A and shields it by snipping off K48-linked ubiquitin chains, keeping SFRP1's promoter acetylated and active. A rat model induced with L-NAME backed the pathway in living tissue.
pmc-13292773:
R. M. G. van Vuren and co-authors ask whether the COVID-19 pandemic widened income gaps in Dutch surgical cancer care, in a study published in 2026. Using national quality registries, they compared patients operated on for lung, esophageal, stomach, pancreatic, or liver tumors during the pandemic with a group treated in the two years before it. Social position was estimated from postal code scores.

Nearly thirty thousand operations were analyzed across both periods. The mix of patients by social position stayed much the same, and the median wait for treatment held at twenty-seven days in both groups. Rates of surgery for advanced tumors also showed no income pattern. The authors credit near-universal coverage and pandemic prioritization of cancer care for keeping access fair under pressure.
pmc-13293373:
Benjamin N Rome and colleagues test, in a 2026 validation study, whether live prescription fill data can stand in for slow official insurance counts by state. Coverage data often lag, which delays judgment of new health policies.

Quarterly state coverage and fills by payer type were compared from 2013 to 2024 for Medicaid, private cover, and uninsured groups. Medicaid fills tracked Medicaid coverage closely, while cash-pay fills tracked uninsured rates fairly well, and both links were stronger for adults than children. Private cover links were weak. The authors suggest fill data could give fast early reads on policy effects, above all for Medicaid.
pmc-13293473:
Junghee Yoon and co-authors build, in a 2026 expert study, a first framework for virtual reality health literacy in clinical care. Headset-based virtual reality can teach and treat patients, yet the skills patients need to use it well had not been defined.

A three-phase Delphi process ran from January to April 2024, starting with a literature scan and a panel of 15 experts in health care, virtual reality, and health literacy. Two survey rounds rated draft parts, and 13 experts stayed for round two. The final framework holds 5 domains and 14 subdomains, covering expected benefit, effort, and other readiness traits. The work gives clinics a shared language.
pmc-13293673:
Aparna Meher, Riya Chaudhary, and Himanshu Kumar identify a circular RNA that helps the body fight influenza A, in a 2026 laboratory study. Circular RNAs are ring-shaped molecules that fine-tune gene activity, yet their role in the first-line immune defense against flu was poorly defined. The molecule they studied, circCPSF6, normally falls during infection, and the team probed what happens because of that drop.

Experiments in cells and animals showed the ring works through two routes at once. It soaks up a small RNA that otherwise suppresses several antiviral defenders, freeing those defenders to act. It also binds a protein that normally restrains a key signaling hub, keeping interferon responses switched on. Together these actions raise cytokine and interferon-driven gene activity, marking the ring as a possible target for antiviral therapy.
pmc-13294273:
Jun-Chen Liu and coauthors pool early evidence on albumin-bound paclitaxel for advanced small cell lung cancer in a 2026 single-arm meta-analysis. Later-line options have improved survival, but the best regimen stays debated and trials of this drug were small and uncontrolled. Four databases yielded nine studies with 334 patients, covering response, survival, and side effects.

Pooled response rate was 25.0% and disease control rate was 62.5% in the reported figures. Median-style pooled survival values reached 3.16 months without progression and 7.23 months overall. Low white cell counts and anemia dominated side effects. Adding immunotherapy looked numerically better in subgroup checks, a lead for controlled trials.
pmc-13294373:
Ziqiang Ding and coauthors build a nanobody T cell engager that can reach targets inside cancer cells in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. Standard engagers only grip surface markers because inner proteins stay hidden, and bulky fragments clump easily. Their two-headed nanobody joins T cells via CD3 while the other head mimics a T cell receptor, reading peptide scraps displayed on HLA-A2 from WT1 or GPC3 proteins.

Lab tests showed strict target-only T cell firing and killing, sparing marker-free cells. In mouse grafts from cell lines and patients, tumors shrank, survival lengthened, and T cell entry rose, with no reported treatment harms. A modular route to inner targets opens many cancers.
pmc-13295873:
Julie Werenberg Dreier and colleagues measure lost working life among people with epilepsy in Denmark in a 2026 register study. They compare losses by the cause behind the seizures, from injury and stroke to unknown origin, against the wider population.

Following more than five million adults, the team find epilepsy after head injury cost the most working years, at just over ten on average. Tumour-related and stroke-related epilepsy also cut working life heavily, and even epilepsy of unknown cause cost over five years. Disability pensions and early death drove most losses, prompting a call for stronger job support.
pmc-13295973:
Mark Kalinich and colleagues propose, in 2026, using simulation to estimate how risky medical chatbots built on large language models really are. Device safety rules were made for predictable tools, yet these systems can give unsafe replies in ways that are hard to count directly.

Fourteen open models were tested on spotting suicidal thoughts and therapy-like requests using made-up datasets judged by psychiatrists. Failure rates fed into estimates of how often a hazard turns into harm, and those estimates spanned a wide range.
