Rates of liver injury were similar between groups at 21, 30, and 60 days, and overall side effect rates matched after baseline. Controls, however, showed larger rises in several liver enzymes, and treated patients had fewer overall liver-related side effects, driven by fewer mild enzyme changes. Severe events stayed similar. The drug may soften mild liver strain during treatment without adding clear risk.
pmc-13350173:
Qilong Wang and colleagues compared eight large language model chatbots in 2026 on public mental health information. With mental illness burdens rising and professional help scarce, people increasingly ask chatbots, whose quality, clarity, and warmth in this sensitive area needed testing.

A bank of 48 questions from literature, search trends, and clinic consultations was put to each model. Scores covered information quality, source openness, reading level, and empathy as judged by psychiatrists and from a user's view. Two models led on quality, but none wrote at the recommended easy reading level, and models rarely volunteered their sources. The results urge caution and better design before chatbots advise on mental health.
pmc-13350573:
Ana González-Cordón and a Barcelona team reported real-world results in 2026 for long-acting injectable HIV treatment, cabotegravir plus rilpivirine given every two months. The prospective study followed people switching to the injections at one hospital from February 2023 to February 2025 and gathered their own ratings of the experience.

Women made up only 8 percent of switchers, 57 of 741, against 14 percent among those staying on other therapy, a gap the authors highlight. Virus control was checked several ways, split by sex. Replacing daily pills with six injection visits a year suits many, but who gets offered the switch matters.
pmc-13350673:
Taishi Yonetsu discussed in 2026 where optical coherence tomography adds most value in complex coronary intervention, in an editorial titled Complexity Within Complexity. Intravascular imaging has moved from adjunct to core tool in complex stenting. Trials show better outcomes for imaging-guided work, most of all for long lesions, bifurcations, and chronic total occlusions.

Rules now back OCT-guided work next to ultrasound-guided work. Yet added gain over angiography alone varies by lesion type. Discussing a study that extends OCT versus standard guidance, Yonetsu asks which hard settings justify OCT most. The editorial helps interventional cardiologists place imaging where it shifts picks and outcomes, rather than using it with no discrimination.
pmc-13351673:
Ya Dai leads a 2026 narrative review of behaviour-based vision training for childhood amblyopia, often called lazy eye. Standard care with patching or drug blurring often suffers from poor adherence and weak gains in two-eye vision. Training built on brain plasticity offers another route, and the review covers its basis, main forms, and results.

PubMed and Web of Science were searched for work from January 2015 to December 2025, and 100 studies were included. Forms covered include perceptual learning, two-eye training, digital treatments, and virtual reality. The review compares training with standard therapy, looks at combined plans and adherence, and notes wide differences in study designs that block pooled analysis.
pmc-13352473:
Yiran Deng and co-authors sort mixed anxiety and depression patterns in older Chinese adults and link them to thinking scores in 2026. Anxiety and depression often occur together in later life, but their combined forms vary. A survey covered 5,116 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older, using standard anxiety and depression scales plus a brief dementia screen.

Latent class analysis found four groups: high mixed symptoms at 7.41 percent, moderate mixed at 8.64 percent, high depression at 13.94 percent, and low symptoms at 70.01 percent. Mixed and depression-led groups scored lower on thinking tests, with all P values below 0.001. Adults with both anxiety and depression showed the steepest thinking disadvantage.
pmc-13352873:
Emmanuel Kwang and three colleagues published a scoping review in two thousand twenty-six on teamwork in health emergencies in poorer countries. Local health authorities and community leaders must pull together when crises hit. Evidence on how that teamwork actually works was scattered.

The reviewers searched five sources for studies from the COVID-19 years. Only three studies, from Bangladesh and the Philippines, met their rules. Teamwork often joined health offices with charities, universities, and community groups, sometimes through formal coordination bodies. The review maps the strategies those studies reported. The authors note how thin the evidence base is and where new research should look.
pmc-13353073:
Praveen Baskaran, Abigail S Bower, and Ashley I Simpson review early care for lower brachial plexus injury after shoulder trauma in 2026. The uncommon injury follows shoulder dislocation or upper arm fracture and can disable the arm. The axillary nerve is hit most often after dislocation, but multi-nerve damage signals cord-level harm with slower, partial recovery.

Emergency care centres on early, repeated nerve exams mapped to cords and branches, plus prompt gentle relocation of dislocated joints when deficits show. Pain relief should ease exams without masking the baseline picture. Blood vessel injury is a critical red flag needing fast escalation, since it can starve nerves and threaten the limb. UK trauma standards stress documented nerve checks and fast specialist referral.
pmc-13353173:
Giuseppe Campo, Armando Guglielmi, and Vanessa Manni analyse accidents that kill several workers at once in Italy in 2026. In 2022 the European Union logged more than 3,000 deaths at work and close to 3 million non-fatal accidents. Data came from the INAIL database and the Infor.MO surveillance system, which probes accident dynamics with a multi-factor model.

Deep review covered 181 multiple-fatal events from 2008 to 2022. Road crashes caused many, joined by collapses, fires, explosions, and suffocation in confined spaces. Construction and manufacturing were hit hardest. Weak training, poor work organisation, and missing safety devices led the causes. The authors press for a stronger safety culture built on real risk understanding.
pmc-13355273:
Robert J Valenzuela and co-authors ran a 2026 pilot of a heat-based radiofrequency treatment for men with mild to moderate erectile dysfunction. The noninvasive treatment uses a handheld device and is meant to help restore function, but proof was thin. Nineteen men aged 40 to 80 had six weekly sessions and filled in standard function surveys over three months.

Scores for erectile function rose from about 16 to near 24 by three months, and hardness scores also improved. Nearly all men still reported gains at three months, and no treatment harms were recorded, with pain near zero. As a small study with no control group, the authors call results early and urge sham-controlled trials.
pmc-13355373:
John Sauer, Kathleen Jedruszczuk, and Adriana Ros describe a case of widespread shingles in a patient taking an immune-damping drug. Shingles comes from the chickenpox virus waking up in the body. It stays in one stripe of skin in most people. In people with weak immune defenses, it can spread across the body.

The patient was taking upadacitinib, a drug that blocks immune signals and is known to raise shingles risk. The case followed exposure to tear gas. The report sets out how the rash spread beyond the usual single band. Spread-out shingles can lead to lung, liver, or brain problems, so early care matters. The authors add this case to what doctors know about infection risks on this drug class.
pmc-13356673:
Theodora Wingert and J Robert Sneyd write a 2026 editorial on remimazolam, a fast, short-acting sedation drug, and the gap between its license and its real use. A large United States health system reported more than nine thousand cases, with fast recovery and a critical event rate under one percent. The drug is licensed in the United States only for procedural sedation.

Yet hospitals widely used it to start general anesthesia, above all in sicker patients, and often mixed it with other anesthetics. The writers trace the drug's slow, narrow development path and argue that its best role is still unclear. They call for work to match rules to real clinical practice.
pmc-13359573:
Marcel Figueras and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on a urine test for bladder cancer that may cut the need for scope checks. A scope is the standard way to find and watch this cancer, but it is invasive. The test reads chemical marks on DNA in urine. The team ran it in two groups: people at first diagnosis and patients watched for return.

The test caught about three quarters of first cancers and just over half of returns. For the harsh high-grade kind, it caught close to nine in ten. False alarms were near the rate for the older cell check, which it beat in both groups. Its score rose with risk class, and high scores tracked worse disease. The test may let some patients space out scope checks.
pmc-13359973:
Yool Lee and co-authors review a fat-handling protein in brain tumors in a 2026 paper. FABP7 helps glial cells manage lipids and follows daily rhythms. In gliomas, aggressive brain tumors, it appears at abnormally high levels. The review gathers how this protein may help tumors adapt their metabolism, act like stem cells, resist oxidative stress, and hide from the immune system.

It also maps the protein's links between tumor cells and the brain's own networks. Because these threads converge on one molecule, blocking it might open several weaknesses at once. The authors argue for combined strategies that pair metabolic and immune treatments against this target.
pmc-13360073:
Qunhui Xiao and co-authors published a 2026 study of a rare fish in the upper Yellow River on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. The fish, Schizopygopsis pylzovi, is at risk, and the team wanted to learn how healthy its gene pool is. They took samples from 11 spots along the river and read two stretches of DNA passed down from the mother.

Most gene differences sat inside local groups rather than between them, so fish from far apart places still seem to mix and breed. Natural blocks in the river may still cause small splits between some groups. Some groups also showed signs of past growth or sharp drops in numbers. The authors say the results give river managers a firm base for protecting this fish and its home waters.
pmc-13360873:
Yuqi Wang and Changmin Hu review tiny carrier beads for stem cell therapy in a 2026 paper. Stem cells can renew themselves and turn into many cell types, which suits them for repairing tissue. But growing enough of them is hard: flat lab dishes drain their power, and planted cells often wash away or take the wrong path. Small beads that carry the cells, paired with moving 3D culture, offer a way around these blocks.

The review compares new ways to make such beads, including microfluidics and spraying methods. It explains how bead traits steer cell sticking, growth, and the type of cell they become. Beads can be programmed, meaning their cues can be set in advance. The authors see them as a path to large-scale, controlled stem cell production for real treatments.
pmc-13361573:
Delfino Pérez-Ugarte and co-authors studied surgery for carotid body tumors in a 2026 paper. These rare neck tumors sit on the carotid artery, and removing them risks heavy bleeding and nerve damage. Blocking the tumor's blood supply before surgery, called embolisation, can reduce those risks. The team compared 68 patients: 24 with embolisation first and 44 with direct surgery.

The embolisation group had larger, harder tumors, yet bled less during surgery, with median blood loss clearly lower. Their raw quality-of-life scores after surgery were lower, reflecting the tougher cases they started with. Adjusted analysis weighed that starting gap. The study speaks to working-age patients who need both a safe operation and a good life after it, and it adds patient-reported outcomes to a debate often run on surgical numbers alone.
pmc-13361673:
Tulsi Suchak and co-authors studied how meals and time of day sway blood chemistry in a 2026 paper. Chemical levels in blood shift with food and the daily clock, which can confuse studies hunting for disease markers. The team first checked 100 published studies and found over half did not control for food intake or sampling time. That gap can waste money and blur real findings.

To give designers a reference, they analyzed a controlled lab study of 24 young, healthy adults. Blood was drawn every two hours over 34 hours, with fixed meals at set times. The team measured how strongly each chemical jumped after meals and which ones follow a daily rhythm. The resource can help future studies plan sampling that keeps markers clean.
pmc-13362473:
Teresa Chianese and co-authors present a 2026 lab study on how plastic microbeads affect female Mediterranean mussels, a species often used to gauge sea health. They kept mussels for two days in water with two low doses of polystyrene beads, then checked the ovaries, blood cells, and body chemistry for signs of harm.

Even that short contact hurt the eggs: more of them broke down, and the harm grew with dose. Stress proteins rose, and the fuel and amino acid mix in the ovaries shifted in ways that point to strained energy use. The results warn that brief plastic exposure can chip away at mussel breeding, with knock-on risks for coastal food webs.
pmc-13362973:
Jakub Pulka and colleagues report a 2026 lab study on biodrying mixed food waste that still holds bits of plastic packaging. Biodrying uses the heat of rotting microbes to dry waste into a fuel. The team dried four mixes, from plain food waste to blends with added plastic, in small reactors and tracked heat, moisture, and the fuel value of what came out.

All mixes heated past 70 degrees, and plastic blends ran hotter than the plain control. The recovered plastic gained the most fuel value, and the compost part settled to a stable state that stores well. Plastics did not hinder the process and may have helped air flow. The authors call the single-run results early and ask for repeat trials.
pmc-13363373:
Linhui Gao and colleagues report a 2026 materials study on making glowing microspheres with less rare-earth material. Their phosphor, an yttrium borate spiked with europium, lights up displays and lamps but uses costly rare earths. By spraying a mist through a hot zone in one step, with organic additives in the mix, they steered the spheres from solid to porous to hollow. The same crystal form held throughout.

Hollow spheres used far less rare-earth material with little loss of glow. Shell thickness and cavity size could be tuned by the recipe. The authors offer the one-step spray method as a route to large-scale, shape-controlled phosphor production that stretches scarce rare-earth supplies further.
pmc-13363873:
Xingcai Qin and colleagues present a 2026 device study that turns a cheap glass rotameter into a smart, programmable gas flowmeter. A webcam watches the float from the side, avoiding the scale blocking the view, and software maps float height to flow. A small motor valve, driven by a pre-set step table, sets the flow, and users can run it from a PC or a small embedded board.

The prototype answered in a fifth of a second, held readings steady, and kept mean error under three percent, while still allowing hand control and eye reads. Cost is the point: commercial programmable meters are pricey. The authors expect the design to speed lab automation and gas sensor testing on tight budgets.
pmc-13366573:
Jason Wu and co-workers give in 2026 a new way to turn alcohols and alkyl parts into carbon pairs with plain olefins, a core shape in chem goods. Their route uses a small ring diazene to spark a two step swap: join, then split, which trades parts and forms the pair bond.

The swap builds styrene type goods and spice scent esters from plain starts. It grows from the team's past work on like swaps with carbon oxygen pairs. The route adds a fresh tool for bond swaps that skips harsh metal or waste rich steps of old ways.
pmc-13367973:
Arren Ramsey and co-workers grow in 2026 mini brain mods from stem cells to show how a guard gene fault drives front brain waste ill. The fault cuts a cell clean and feed protein. Their mods show star cells wake too soon and stir stress in nerve cells, with link loss.

Gene reads show a growth cue path runs hot in the star cells. Ill marks clump in them, a hall mark of the ill. Block that cue path and star wake and clump marks ease. The path may be a drug aim to slow this brain waste.
pmc-13370273:
Romy Moukarzel and co-workers read in 2026 the germs that live in dandelion seeds across a climb from low to high land in New Zealand. The weed thrives in many lands, and its seed germs may aid that spread. The team reads germ genes in seeds from sites at ten steps of height.

Germ kind counts fall as height climbs, and mixes shift in clear groups by height. High sites hold more alike, more thin mixes. Six germ types lead, some at all sites and some at set heights. Height acts as a sieve on seed germs, with spread gains still to prove.
pmc-13370773:
Christopher Randolph and co-workers give in 2026 a plain way to coat tiny spheres with a made skin that can hold working proteins. Such spheres serve in many lab tools, but most coats lack a skin, though many proteins need one to work right. Their skin bears hooks for more bits and whole proteins.

Coated spheres take a glow bit and a DNA grip protein and keep both at work. Light traps let them weigh the pull of the grip at play. Near all spheres take the coat. The way opens build of rich, skin clad lab tools.
pmc-13371173:
Ngo Duc Hiep and co-authors report a rare trauma case from Vietnam in a 2026 case report. A man aged 52 hurt his pelvis and groin in a bad motorbike crash in 2022. The crash tore away the left half of his pelvis and badly hurt his leg, bladder, and bowel.

Care teams stopped the bleeding, removed the lost half of the pelvis, and moved urine and stool to new openings. Later steps used skin flaps and grafts to close the wounds. He left the hospital after 112 days in stable health. The case shows that even this grave harm can be survived with fast, joint care.
pmc-13371673:
Xuemei Yang and colleagues study readiness for advance care planning among younger adults with advanced cancer in China in a 2026 paper. Advance care planning lets patients state future care wishes, yet readiness varies widely. The team surveyed 432 inpatients aged young to middle-aged at a tertiary cancer hospital in Guangxi between late 2024 and late 2025.

Machine learning methods, including LASSO and random forest, first narrowed the factors linked to readiness, which were then tested in regression models with bootstrap checks. Mediation analysis tested whether a sense of benefit from illness carries part of the link between social support and readiness, with gender subgroups compared. The work points to support and benefit perception as levers for helping younger patients engage with future care talks.
pmc-13371773:

pmc-13373173:

pmc-13374273:

pmc-13374373:

pmc-13376773:

pmc-13382773:

pmc-13382973:
Capucine Januel and colleagues align cat and human ages by matching brain and health changes across the lifespan in 2026 work. They drew on 3,754 observations, plus brain scans from pet and colony cats. Shared patterns of brain shrinkage let the team build a cross-species age scale.

pmc-13385773:
Melkamu Tulbake and colleagues measure use of preconception care among HIV-positive women in southern Ethiopia in 2026 work. pmc-13386473:

pmc-13386773:

pmc-13389473:

pmc-13390373:

pmc-13390473:

pmc-13391373:

pmc-13392073:

pmc-13392173:

pmc-13393273:

pmc-13393773:

pmc-13394373:

pmc-13394973:

pmc-13395473:

pmc-13395573:

pmc-13396073:

pmc-13396473:

pmc-13396573:

pmc-13396773:

pmc-13396873:

pmc-13397473:

pmc-13397573:

pmc-13399773:

pmc-13400173:

pmc-13400273:

pmc-13400673:

pmc-13403373:

pmc-13403473:

pmc-13405073:

pmc-13407473:

pmc-13407573:

pmc-13407673:

Nitrogen dioxide emerged as an additional culprit, with a hazard ratio of 1.12 per doubling of exposure for decline in the survival models. Specific chemical components of fine particulate matter also showed new associations with faster decline in the wider analysis reported. The authors argue the replication across independent exposure datasets strengthens the case that air quality is a modifiable driver of glomerular disease outcomes.
pmc-13455373:

Salt damage limits wheat on China's northern coast, and growth-promoting root bacteria offer one remedy, yet their effect on native soil microbes at fine detail was unclear. The team ran pot and field trials, reading soil bacteria with long-read sequencing that resolves species far better than short reads.

Proteobacteria, Acidobacteria and Bacteroidetes led across treatments, with Proteobacteria richer near roots. Bacillus treatment shifted community structure, raised diversity and narrowed gaps between groups, above all in pots, and enriched a Pseudomonas strain that appeared to cooperate with Bacillus. Genes for phosphorus and nitrogen cycling rose, and microbial networks grew more resilient. pmc-13457073:
Yu Chen and six colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether cheap inflammation scores from a routine early pregnancy blood test can warn of preeclampsia months ahead. The condition, marked by dangerous blood pressure in pregnancy, strikes three to eight percent of mothers and still lacks a useful early predictor. Blood drawn between weeks six and twelve was compared for 109 women who later developed it and 177 who did not.

White cell families ran higher in the future cases, while two cell types stayed level. All four combined inflammation indices were significantly raised in the women bound for preeclampsia. The signal tied mainly to the late-onset form of the disease. Severity, once the disease arrived, did not track the early scores. The authors present the indices as candidate early flags drawn from a test clinics already run, pending wider validation.
pmc-13457573:
S Kamalakannan and colleagues compare five hybrid controllers for solar panels under patchy shade in a 2026 simulation study. Partial shade creates many false power peaks, so ordinary trackers settle on a local peak and waste energy. The team simulated five hybrid maximum power point methods with a SEPIC converter at 10 kHz and a 250 W panel in MATLAB and Simulink. Panel voltage and power plus output voltage and power were tracked under varied shading.

Two hybrids, PSO-PO and GWO-PSO, converged fastest at first, but the grey wolf plus fuzzy method, GWO-Fuzzy, tracked most accurately with smaller steady oscillations and steadier voltage control. The study thus favours GWO-Fuzzy for reliably finding the true global power peak as sunlight shifts. Results come from simulation only, so hardware tests under real shade, temperature and ageing must confirm the ranking.
pmc-13458373:
Jiahan Cheng and colleagues ask whether symptoms before diagnosis say anything about survival after surgery for the earliest stage of lung cancer. Stage I non-small cell tumors are usually found by scans, yet some patients arrive with cough or pain, and nobody knew whether that distinction mattered once the tumor was out. Their 2026 analysis draws 9,205 resected stage I patients from a West China Hospital registry covering 2011 to 2021.

Bloody sputum stood out, carrying a hazard ratio of 1.71 on both outcomes even after adjustment. The authors propose symptom status as a free, instant cue for flagging stage I patients deserving closer surveillance after curative surgery.
pmc-13458573:
Christine Moshe and colleagues check whether a paravertebral block, local anesthetic injected beside the spine, meaningfully eases recovery from robotic kidney-sparing surgery. Their 2026 retrospective review covers 200 patients of one surgeon operated between 2018 and 2022, 81 with the block and 119 without, comparing pain scores, morphine use, and recovery-unit time.

The groups matched on age, sex, and anesthesia type, and adjusted models kept the same small effects. The authors' verdict is blunt: the differences, while real, are too small to matter clinically, and routine blocks for this operation should wait for stronger prospective evidence.
pmc-13458773:
Ziwei Li and colleagues build a preoperative MRI model reading iron and fat inside prostate tumors to judge how dangerous the cancer is. The improved fusion model reached an area under the curve of 0.920, with sensitivity of 0.952. Stripping out the fat and iron measures dropped performance to 0.819, a statistically significant loss, which pins predictive value on the metabolic signals. The authors render the model as a nomogram and propose it as a noninvasive way to sharpen risk conversations and spare some men unnecessary biopsies.
pmc-13459173:
Guojun Yue and co-authors tested whether a simple nutrition and immunity blood score, tracked after lung cancer surgery, can flag patients heading for recurrence. The score, the prognostic nutritional index, combines albumin, a blood protein, with lymphocyte counts. Their 2026 study enrolled 119 patients having curative surgery for stage I to III non-small cell lung cancer. By three months, 51 patients had recovered their score to target levels and 43 had not. During follow up, recurrence or death events struck 41.9 percent of the non recovered group against 17.6 percent of the recovered group. Two year recurrence free survival was 59.2 percent versus 82.3 percent in the comparison reported. Failing to recover the score more than doubled the recurrence hazard after adjustment. Adding the recovery measure improved the prediction model's accuracy.
pmc-13459273:
Marisa Iborra and co-authors surveyed gastroenterology trainees across Spain about their training, skill gaps, and well-being, on behalf of the national society SEPD. Burnout was reported by 63.5 percent of respondents, a strikingly high share. Inadequate rest strongly raised burnout risk, while satisfaction with working conditions protected against it. Nearly nine in ten wanted an extra training year.
pmc-13459373:
Arlene Jiang and co-authors describe how they built the statistical starting assumptions for a children's emergency trial without ever meeting in person. Their 2026 study ran three remote workshops, each with two survey rounds separated by group discussion. The topic was two steroid doses for croup, the barking cough childhood illness, in a planned trial comparing a low dose with the standard dose.

pmc-13459773:
Ruyue Fan and colleagues profile drug fight-back and genomes of runny-belly Salmonella in Shandong, China, in a 2026 study. Twenty-eight types and 30 sequence types appeared, most commonly ST34 type 1,4,[5],12:i:-, with 63 fight-back genes and 171 harm genes overall. pmc-13460173:
Zi-Wei Zhang and Qiu-Hua Wan combined in 2026 a global literature map with a bedside test of the SAVE score. That score predicts survival for patients on veno-arterial ECMO, a machine that takes over heart and lung work in refractory shock. Bibliometric tools charted publications from 1988 to 2024, while a separate check ran the score on 101 intensive care patients drawn from the MIMIC-IV database.

At the bedside the score disappointed: discrimination was weak, predicted survival was badly calibrated against actual hospital deaths, and decision analysis showed little net benefit. The pairing warns clinicians that celebrated scores need local validation before guiding real ECMO decisions.
pmc-13460673:
Mary Curtin and colleagues explore how doctors deliver tailored care to high-risk women during labour in a 2026 talk study. Tailored care anchors kind birth care, yet evidence for high-risk women in labour was thin. Twelve midwives and birth doctors took part in half-set online interviews, analysed by constant matching with open, axial and picked coding.

People described tension between duty to one woman and ward duties to many births, with standard guidelines invoked for the group. Knowing the woman before labour made them more likely to honour her wishes. Wards gain a lesson: staying with her and knowing her ahead may be the lever that lets own requests survive set processes.
pmc-13461173:
David Alsina and co-authors modeled in 2026 two disease-causing variants of POLRMT, the sole enzyme that copies mitochondrial genes in mice, mirroring mutations recently found in patients. Mice with the dominant variant lived, with depressed mitochondrial transcripts yet normal DNA levels, matching patient biology. The comparison separates two jobs of the enzyme: starting fresh transcription versus priming DNA copying.
pmc-13461373:

The authors conclude that muscle loss alone should not disqualify these drugs for obesity, while insisting that protein intake and exercise accompany treatment to protect strength and function.
pmc-13461573:
Dergaa and colleagues mapped in 2026 the evidence on generative artificial intelligence in sports medicine, where chatbots are already used for training plans, rehab, nutrition, mental health support, and writing. Made-up content, called hallucination, was rated a critical risk for general chatbots but much lower for systems tied to retrieved sources. The authors call for governance matched to the fast uptake.
pmc-13461873:

pmc-13462073:
Dsouza and Mendon ran a 2026 school-based study of digital exposure and health behaviours in South Indian adolescents. Dsouza found most students scored in the neutral middle range for eating behaviour overall. Activity split sharply, with about fifty-five percent highly active and about forty-five percent in the low activity group. Between fourteen and twenty percent reported two or more hours of screen time daily across domains. Activity linked significantly to sex, family type, exercise status, and age.
pmc-13462873:

The authors offer the model as a transparent aid for tailoring follow-up and extra treatment.
pmc-13463973:
Mosaddeghi-Heris and colleagues studied in 2026 how oxidative stress, mood, and thinking skills interact in people with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis who have mild to moderate disability. Disability level and years of schooling were the strongest predictors of thinking scores, with more disability tied to slower processing and weaker working memory. The authors stress support for cognition even at low disability.
pmc-13464273:

pmc-13464873:

pmc-13465473:

pmc-13465573:

They built a plain Cox hazards model as a baseline, then a DeepSurv deep-learning model, using records for 3,266 patients drawn from the RADCURE collection held in The Cancer Imaging Archive.

On held-out test data the two models scored close together, and the small gap between them was not statistically clear. Older age and more advanced tumors pointed to higher risk, while people who had quit smoking or never smoked fared better than current smokers. The authors stress that the outputs are decision support, not proof that one treatment causes a better outcome.
pmc-13466273:

Cell density averaged a little above two thousand per square millimeter, and small deposits called guttae appeared in about fifteen percent of eyes. Older age tracked with fewer lining cells. Models adjusted for age and sex, and separate looks by eye length tested whether long or short eyes changed the pattern.
pmc-13466373:

pmc-13466673:

pmc-13468373:

pmc-13469273:

pmc-13469373:

pmc-13469473:

pmc-13470373:

Minor grammatical fixes were also made, and the authors confirm the corrections in the journal record dated 2026.
pmc-13471173:

pmc-13471473:

pmc-13471673:

pmc-13471773:

pmc-13473073:

pmc-13473473:

pmc-13474373:

Added notes explain the choices behind key steps in testing and dosing. Doctors gain a structured path for a lifelong condition that needs close early care.
pmc-13474673:

pmc-13474773:
