pmc-13474873:
Zhou and colleagues present a computer model in 2026 that predicts growth traits in Duroc pigs from DNA alone, aiming to speed up breeding choices. Their model, named TKOA-GPNN, first narrows the genome to the markers most tied to growth, then feeds those markers into a neural network, a pattern-learning program loosely modeled on brain cells. Two selection stages use correlation screening and an optimization search inspired by Kepler's laws of planetary motion.

Tested against 14 existing prediction models, the new framework gave the best accuracy while also running efficiently on the study's pig data. It held up on offspring records, on cheaper genotyping array data, and on full genome sequencing data, which the authors cite as proof of robustness. Growth traits such as days to reach 100 kilograms matter economically in China, the world's largest pig producer with about 700 million pigs a year.
pmc-13475573:
Nihira and a large team of co-authors traced an inflammation switch in macrophages for this study from twenty twenty-six. Macrophages are immune cells that drive many inflammatory diseases. A signal called interferon gamma switches them into attack mode. The team tracked which proteins rush into the cell nucleus when that signal lands.

A protein kinase named RSK1 stood out in the unbiased screen. The signal marks RSK1 for action, and RSK1 in turn marks a partner that drives inflammatory genes. Silencing RSK1 cut the release of inflammatory messengers in human cells. Mice carrying human immune cells without RSK1 also responded weakly. The authors name nuclear RSK1 a key mediator of macrophage activation.
pmc-13475973:
Meng and six co-authors tested a gene-silencing drug candidate for fatty liver disease in human organoids in twenty twenty-six. The disease, called MASH, scars the liver, and animal models predict human results poorly. Their drug is a small interfering RNA, a molecule that switches off one target gene, HSD17B13.

The RNA carries a sugar tag steering it to liver cells, plus chemical tweaks for stability. The lead candidate stayed stable in human serum and liver extracts and showed few off-target risks. In three-dimensional human liver organoids mimicking fat buildup and scarring, it lowered disease markers. Its effect matched a clinical-stage rival. The authors offer both a candidate and a testing route that reduces animal use.
pmc-13476273:
Zehan Liu and co-authors present, in a 2026 paper, a way to make skin-like electronic films that are extremely thin yet still easy to handle. Films only hundreds of nanometers thick cling to skin and pick up body signals well, but they curl on their own and tear easily.

Their fix adds a slightly thicker frame around the edge of the film. The frame gives strength during making, wearing, and reuse, while the thin middle keeps close, light contact with skin. The frame also lets the film lift off its base in plain water, with no harsh chemicals. Tests include a body signal electrode and a fast temperature sensor.
pmc-13477073:
Silvia Mariani and colleagues compared in 2026 outcomes for patients needing life support after bypass surgery alone versus bypass plus left heart valve surgery. They studied 639 adults across 34 centres between 2000 and 2020 who required postcardiotomy extracorporeal life support.

Valve-surgery patients were older, more often had lung artery hypertension, and needed longer bypass times and more reoperations. In-hospital death ran 63.1 percent with valve surgery against 54.8 percent without, a gap that held after adjustment. Five-year survival after discharge did not differ. Early recognition of patients likely to need support after valve surgery may improve outcomes.
pmc-13477373:
Kyle J. Bourassa and colleagues present a 2026 study testing whether a DNA-based pace-of-aging measure can predict future heart and metabolic disease. The measure, called DunedinPACE, estimates how fast the body is aging from chemical marks on DNA. Participants were 2,062 United States military veterans who were free of cardiometabolic disease at the start.

Health records followed the veterans for an average of about 14 years. Faster pace of aging predicted new disease even after standard measures like blood sugar, blood pressure, pulse, and body weight were counted. Adding the measure improved prediction beyond demographics and beyond a fuller clinical model. The authors suggest such aging markers could help target prevention toward people most likely to develop disease in the coming years.
pmc-13478473:
Xinyu Yan and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study from the TwinsUK cohort linking diet, fatty acids stored in body fat, and heart-metabolic health. Fat under the skin is the body's largest fatty acid buffer, yet most research uses blood measures instead. The team measured 18 fatty acid proportions in fat tissue from 569 participants alongside diet records and clinical traits.

Daily rhythm proxies, such as fasting hours and visit timing, showed no link with fat tissue composition. Eight dietary pattern scores did relate to stored fatty acids, with the Healthy Diet Indicator showing the most connections. Healthier diet scores generally tracked with more polyunsaturated fatty acids stored. The study also tested whether fat tissue composition sits on the pathway between diet and disease risk markers.
pmc-13479573:
Wang and co-authors developed a fast blood test in 2026 for colistin, a last-resort antibiotic whose dosing in critically ill patients is a tightrope between curing infection and damaging kidneys. Their method uses liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry to measure both active parts of the drug, colistin A and colistin B, in serum. Sample preparation is a single solvent crash step, keeping the assay cheap enough for routine monitoring.

Each run takes five minutes, and calibration stayed linear across the working ranges for both components, with fit values above 0.99 in validation. The team then applied the test in intensive care for about a year and used the outcomes to set a danger line for kidney injury. A trough level, the lowest point between doses, of 2.22 micrograms per milliliter marked the preliminary cut-off above which kidney injury risk climbed.
pmc-13479673:
Britta K Matthes and seven colleagues published this 2025 study of how tobacco and nicotine industry actors argued against the United Kingdom's Tobacco and Vapes Bill of 2023/4. The Bill proposed a generational ban, phasing out tobacco sales by birth year, plus restrictions on youth products. The authors analysed 43 consultation and evidence submissions from industry-linked actors, mapping ties to transnational tobacco companies and coding their arguments.

Companies and linked actors accounted for 42 percent of submissions through known current ties alone. Submissions painted industry as the good actor and public health champions, while casting policymakers and non-compliant sellers as the villains. Industry opposed the generational ban as evidence-free, economically harmful and a trigger for retail violence, proposing a sales age of 21 and exemptions for heated tobacco. It fought flavour and display restrictions, blaming irresponsible individuals for youth use. The authors urge policymakers to pre-empt these strategies.
pmc-13483173:
Qayyum and team proposed a way to grade disaster-response technology before a real emergency tests it. Their 2026 paper models sensor networks as layered graphs, where devices and control layers become linked points, then scores the design for complexity, recovery, and reuse. Most earlier work judged these systems only by prediction accuracy, leaving design flaws hidden until floods or earthquakes struck.

A flood-response case study from Pakistan tested the framework by varying sensor density and gateway connections. Designs with backup links between devices recovered better and kept detection simpler than sparse designs. Thinly connected layouts let disaster severity ripple further through the network model. Qayyum argues that grading structure early lets planners compare rival systems fairly and fix weak points while changes are still cheap.
pmc-13483573:
Xin Du and co-authors measure how often the right side of the heart weakens in people whose heart failure comes with preserved pumping fraction. Published in 2026, the retrospective review covers 163 patients seen between January 2022 and January 2024. Heart ultrasound measures and a blood marker of heart strain were tested as predictors of right-sided weakness.

Right ventricular dysfunction affected 41.7 percent of patients, a figure tied to notably higher levels of the strain marker NT-proBNP. Six ultrasound measures each predicted weakness on their own, with right ventricular free wall strain performing best as a single test. A model combining all six separated affected from unaffected patients very well, even after internal validation. Adding the blood marker to ultrasound review could sharpen risk sorting for this heart failure group.
pmc-13483673:
Didem Yüzügüllü and co-authors study how eating in response to emotions relates to body fat in women seeking weight counseling. Their 2026 cross-sectional study includes 271 women whose body fat was measured by electrical impedance testing of body composition. Blood fats, blood sugar control markers, and activity levels were examined alongside emotional eating scores.

About half the women counted as emotional eaters and a further share counted as very emotional eaters. The strongest emotional eating group showed lower protective cholesterol and higher harmful cholesterol values. Emotional eating scores rose together with triglycerides and a long-term sugar marker, and fell as protective cholesterol and activity rose. Emotional eating also strengthened the link between certain blood fats and body fat share. Counseling that ignores emotional triggers may miss a driver of the numbers.
pmc-13486473:
Sheshadri and team blended two industrial wastes into low-carbon pavement concrete and used machine learning to find the best recipe. Foundry sand waste replaced part of the fine aggregate, and rice husk ash replaced part of the slag binder in their alkali-activated concrete. Their 2026 study cast 330 samples across many mix ratios, measured 28-day strength, then trained six prediction models on the results.

More waste generally weakened the concrete, but one mix with 20 percent foundry sand and 15 percent rice husk ash still met pavement-grade strength requirements. Its workability also stayed within acceptable limits for placement. A random forest model predicted strength most accurately, explaining about 92 percent of variation in the test results. Sheshadri says the model lets engineers screen greener mixes on a computer before casting a single trial slab.
pmc-13487173:
Yunchang Zheng trims a smart vision model so it can spot brain bleeds on head scans at emergency speed. Slow reads cost lives, since death and disability climb while scans wait. This 2026 work rebuilds the YOLOv11 model in three ways. A new stem lifts faint bleed traits early. A fusion block pools bleed clues across scales and mutes busy backdrops. A stacked gaze block homes in on small or blurred bleeds.

On the BHX scan set, the rebuilt model beat its base form. It also stood well against rival models in the full test set. Exact gains in hit rate and false alarms sit in the full text. A model that stays sharp at real speed can join live triage queues. Research demos alone won't cut deaths in the emergency room.
pmc-13487673:
Luo and Muffly wrote in 2026 a review of ten year results from CALGB 10403. That trial gave teens and young adults with acute lymphoblastic leukemia a child style drug plan. Old adult plans cured just a third of such patients at three years. The trial's plan lifted that mark a lot in its first read. This fresh read tracks the same 295 patients for a full decade.

At ten years, just over half the group still lived. Most falls back came in the first three years, but some came past year five, all in one cell type. Patients whose blood cleared to no trace after the first block did best by far. The authors flag two flaws: under half the group could end the long plan, and its harms can last.
pmc-13488073:
Sina Saffaran leads a large clinical and engineering team reviewing computer tools for personalizing care in acute respiratory failure in a 2026 narrative review. Patients range from newborns to adults, in settings from ambulances to intensive care, and all need help with breathing. The review spans prediction models trained on large datasets, detailed body models tuned to one patient, and digital twins, which are virtual copies updated as the patient changes.

Prediction tools can flag who may gain or suffer from a given treatment. Body models let clinicians test choices in simulation before touching the patient, including trial designs run entirely in computers. True digital twins remain rare, and the authors map what must improve before bedside use is routine.
pmc-13488173:
Xiaohuang Yang and colleagues search for survival predictors after repeat surgery for tongue cancer in a 2026 cohort study. Patients had recurrent or spread tongue squamous cell carcinoma and underwent removal again, some after drug treatment meant to shrink the tumor first. Clinical, pathology, and scan measures from 114 patients treated between 2017 and 2024 fed survival models checked by repeated resampling.

Nodal status at the first diagnosis and tumor differentiation, meaning how abnormal the cancer cells look, at recurrence each predicted both return of disease and death. In the small subgroup treated before repeat surgery, higher baseline scan uptake values marked patients whose tumors responded well under the microscope. The authors offer the factors for counseling and planning, pending outside validation.
pmc-13488573:
Sibusiso Khombo and Siphathisiwe Foma explore lived experience among transgender adults in Zimbabwe in a 2026 study based on in-depth talks. Being transgender there is heavily stigmatized and lacks legal recognition, and African evidence in strict settings is scarce. Twenty adults reached through a community group in Harare gave in-depth interviews. Their words were read closely to build themes.

Adults described widespread stigma, family rejection, physical and sexual violence, and deep distress. Mismatch between identity papers and appearance blocked access to health care, schooling, jobs, and civic services in account after account. Peer networks and community groups gave respect and practical support, forming the main source of strength. The authors call for services that affirm gender and grasp trauma, linked to community groups.
pmc-13489573:
Sadeghzadeh and colleagues checked the microbial safety of packaged enteral formulas, the liquid feeds given to patients who cannot eat normally, in 2026 food science research. Formulas can pick up contamination during preparation. The team also tested whether a mixture of thyme, saffron, and turmeric extracts could suppress germs and add antioxidant protection, meaning defense against damaging reactive molecules in the feed.

Fifty samples were screened for total microbes, coliform bacteria, Staphylococcus aureus, and Escherichia coli at the start. No Staphylococcus aureus or Escherichia coli appeared, but coliform counts averaged 3.67 colony-forming units per milliliter and total counts 4.29 units, both above United States food safety standards. Follow-up tests on 26 samples showed the plant extract mixture cut microbial load sharply within 24 hours of preparation. The mixture also raised antioxidant activity to 38.7 percent in the standard assay used.
pmc-13489673:
Silva and colleagues seek a way back for head and neck cancers that have stopped answering EGFR blocking drugs. Such resistance often arrives with a shape shift called epithelial mesenchymal transition, which loosens tumor cells. Their 2026 study builds cell models resistant to two blockers, erlotinib and afatinib. It charts what changes and tests drug pairs in dishes and mouse tumors, hunting for a weakness the resistant state creates.

Resistant cells had shifted shape and raised NEDD9, a partner of the division kinase AURKA. In colony tests and in animals, the resistant cells leaned harder on AURKA. They grew more sensitive to its inhibitor, even as short term synergy with the old blockers faded. Pairing the inhibitor, VIC-1911, with adavosertib, which blocks the cell cycle checkpoint WEE1, hit parent and resistant tumors, and the effect held in resistant mouse grafts. A cell cycle blockade is the authors' candidate for trials.
pmc-13489773:
Rana R. McKay and a large cooperative group report the RADICAL trial in kidney cancer spread to bone in a 2026 phase II study. About a third of patients with advanced kidney cancer develop bone spread, bringing pain and skeletal complications. The trial assigned patients at random to cabozantinib, a targeted pill, alone or with radium-223, a bone-seeking radioactive injection, with a planned early stop if results crossed a futility line.

The interim check crossed that line after ninety patients, and enrollment closed at ninety-eight. Time free of skeletal events was similar between arms at a median near seventeen months in both groups in the reported results. Response rates and severe side effects also looked alike, while survival estimates favored neither arm firmly. The combination was dropped.
pmc-13490573:
Fanar Hashum Al-Hashemi and colleagues test fertilizer mixes on marigold, Calendula officinalis, in a 2026 field experiment in Mosul, Iraq. The plant is grown for medicine and ornament, and growers want bigger, richer flowers. Two factorial sections combined liquid NPK fertilizer with moringa leaf extract at several doses, or humic acid with the same extract range. Each treatment was repeated three times under a fully randomized design in 2023.

Combinations beat single inputs across growth, flowering, and flower chemistry in the reported measures. The strongest pairing in the second section joined the highest humic acid dose with moderate moringa extract, topping most traits in a combined ranking analysis. High liquid fertilizer with moringa led several first-section traits, from branch count to nutrient content.
pmc-13490873:
Shen and colleagues report in 2026 a multicenter randomized split-face trial of intelligent microfocused ultrasound for lifting facial laxity without surgery. The device focuses sound energy under the skin to tighten it. Each patient's treated and untreated sides served as the comparison.

Thirty-two patients completed the study, with one side of the middle and lower face treated and outcomes measured at one and two months. On treated sides, the folds beside the mouth shortened by about seven percent and the smile lines by about eighteen percent at two months. Both changes were significant in the trial's analysis of these patients. Side-face and jaw angles opened measurably, skin tone indices improved more than on control sides, and satisfaction scores were significantly higher for the treated side. Apart from one case of toothache, no persistent or serious side effects occurred.
pmc-13493473:
Salvatore Taglialatela Scafati and four colleagues present in 2026 the Octopus Mastopexy, their standardized way of combining breast implants with a lift in one operation. Doing both at once is notoriously unstable, since implants stretch tissue that the lift is trying to tighten, inviting sagging relapse and revisions. Their method places the implant first, trims breast tissue only as needed, and mobilizes tissue pillars in several directions to spread tension evenly.

Ninety-five patients treated by the senior surgeon between 2019 and 2024, average age about thirty-nine, formed the review group. No major complications occurred, and only two small wound separations healed with dressings alone. Six patients later chose revision for renewed looseness or weight change. Standardized questionnaires showed significant gains in breast satisfaction and physical and psychosocial well-being a year or more after surgery.
pmc-13494073:
Carina Heydt and others expose pitfalls in detecting MET exon 14 skipping changes in non-small cell lung cancer. In 2026, the study looks at 379 tumours with mutations around MET exon 14, comparing DNA- and RNA-based reading, and reports the first multi-country outside quality check programs for this testing. These mutations guide aimed therapy, so missed calls change treatment.

Among 171 distinct mutations, two big deletions and one same-meaning splice change appeared only on RNA testing, while seven single-nucleotide variants did not cause skipping. Tissue quality schemes succeeded in ninety-eight percent of cases, but liquid biopsy success lagged, mainly at low allele fractions. The authors urge merged DNA and RNA analysis with better sensitivity, coverage, and bioinformatics.
pmc-13494173:
Kang and a large Ethiopian team tested whether an enhanced nutrition package for pregnant women improves weight gain during pregnancy, a basic marker of whether mother and baby are getting enough. In their 2026 cluster-randomised study in rural Amhara, twelve health centres were assigned to routine care or to the package. The package added a daily balanced supplement for women whose arm circumference flagged undernutrition. Nearly 2,400 women enrolled before 24 weeks of pregnancy, and over 2,100 were followed to birth.

Overall, the package made no measurable difference: weight gain rates in the two arms were statistically indistinguishable in the main analysis. A secondary look offered a hint, since women who actually kept taking the supplement for at least sixty days gained better than those who stopped early. The authors conclude delivery and adherence, not the supplement's content alone, decide whether such programmes work.
pmc-13494673:
Zhang and colleagues traced how heart and aorta problems reach the brain, in a 2026 study of 1,748 UK Biobank volunteers. They tested whether sluggish cerebral blood flow is the connecting mechanism. All participants had heart scans, brain perfusion imaging, and brain scans, and none had cardiovascular disease or dementia. The team scored six heart measures, and measured the volume of blood reaching brain tissue and how long it took to arrive.

Zhang found worse heart and aortic function tracking with lower brain blood flow and slower arrival times. People with both problems carried the heaviest burden of white matter hyperintensities, the bright spots marking small-vessel brain injury, equivalent to five and a half years of ageing. Mediation showed the two flow measures explained over half the link between heart dysfunction and brain injury. The authors propose perfusion imaging as a target for preventing brain damage before symptoms appear.
pmc-13495173:
Hasna Khandekar and co-authors present a 2026 case report of heart valve infection in a 15-year-old after a catheter ablation for a racing heart rhythm. Such infection is a rare outcome of heart catheter work, and rarer still in children. The boy had spina bifida with a bladder that needs catheter care, plus well-kept diabetes.

The ablation, guided by 3D mapping, fixed the rhythm fault at the aortic valve, and he went home the next day. Three days later fever led to a urine infection diagnosis, traced to a germ called Enterococcus faecalis, likely seeded during the long procedure's bladder catheter use. Months on, tiredness and a new heart murmur brought him back, and tests showed the germ had settled on his heart. Major heart surgery followed. The authors urge teams to weigh urine infection risk when a bladder catheter is planned for such patients.
pmc-13495273:
Yajun Zhu and a large team review, in a 2026 article, how macrophages, the brain's cleanup and defense cells, behave after stroke when read one cell at a time. These cells both worsen early harm and drive later repair, and the old two-box scheme for naming their states now looks too crude. Single-cell gene reading has revealed a spectrum of states with distinct fuel use.

The review highlights fresh subsets, among them one defined by coupled sugar and fat metabolism. Sugar-burning states feed inflammation, while oxygen- and fat-burning states favor repair. The authors then survey nano-sized carriers, from fat bubbles to cell-shed sacs, that can steer macrophage behavior at set places and times. They propose a framework joining cell subset, fuel pathway, drug target, and matched nano treatment, and they rank targets for near-term trials while flagging the hard road to clinic.
pmc-13498573:
Martin E Farina and colleagues introduce in 2026 a way to read bird evolution from fossil footprints across Gondwana, the ancient southern landmass. Rather than counting footprint types, they score the variety of foot designs, such as toe number, toe direction, webbing, and size. That variety can signal when bird groups spread into new ways of life, even where bones are scarce.

Twenty-three rock formations spanning the Early Cretaceous to the Late Pleistocene were compared. Early tracks were mostly large, small designs later took over, and no sideways-toed prints appeared at all. Variety stayed high before the dinosaur-ending boundary, peaked again in the Miocene as large running birds returned, and shifted once more in the Pleistocene when a large webbed design first appeared.
pmc-13499173:
Wang and colleagues model whether screening pregnant patients for iron deficiency pays for itself. Their 2026 paper compares ferritin blood-test screening in the second and third trimesters against no screening. It tests two cut-off levels, 30 and 15 micrograms per litre. A Markov model follows women in the United States over a lifetime.

The analysis found screening cost-effective compared with no screening at standard United States willingness-to-pay levels. The higher ferritin threshold performed better than the lower one, catching more iron deficiency while remaining specific enough to be worthwhile. The model counted treatment time and lost patient wages among its costs, taking a broad societal view. The authors support adopting the 30 microgram threshold for later-pregnancy screening, above the level in current diagnostic guidance.
pmc-13499473:
Le Tan Hung and co-authors compare in 2026 how two jaw surgery plans affect the upper airway in adults with a protruding lower jaw pattern. Moving the lower jaw back can narrow the throat airway, which matters for breathing during sleep. Their one-year follow-up covered 40 adults split evenly between lower jaw setback alone and two-jaw surgery that also moved the upper jaw forward. Both followed a surgery-first plan that skips pre-surgery braces.

Airway size was measured by an acoustic method before surgery and at one month and one year after. Both plans shrank the airway at one month, with far steeper losses after lower jaw surgery alone, both in total volume and per millimetre of setback. Partial recovery followed by one year in both groups, yet airway space stayed better preserved in the two-jaw group, a difference surgeons can weigh when planning correction.
pmc-13499873:
Karl Vivoda and co-authors critically review in 2026 how health economic models for high blood cholesterol are built, since such models guide whether health systems pay for treatments. Cholesterol drives heart and vessel disease, and model quality depends on transparent choices. Their search of two databases for work from 1987 to 2025 found model-based economic evaluations. Screening and extraction ran by hand with software checks, and structure and data practices were scored against a recognised checklist.

A total of 154 unique evaluations emerged, dominated by state-transition models that track cohorts through health states over time, with general high cholesterol studied far more than inherited forms. Prevention in people without prior disease was the most common setting. Structure and data use scored as high quality overall, while consistency checks rated only moderate, and data selection was rarely systematic, giving the authors concrete targets for tightening future models.
pmc-13500373:
Mayuka Koike and colleagues present in 2026 the first genetically confirmed case in Japan of Musladin-Lueke syndrome, an inherited connective tissue disorder of Beagles caused by a mutation in the ADAMTSL2 gene. Their patient was a six-month-old male Beagle showing the classic signs, a tiptoe gait, stiff joints, a sideways-shifted eye socket, and undescended testes. Genetic testing settled the diagnosis definitively, which the authors note has not previously been published for Japan.

Surgery for the retained testes at ten months and heart scans at that stage found no heart abnormality. By twelve months forelimb stiffness had progressed, chronic toe abrasions had appeared, and mild enlargement of the left heart chamber showed on ultrasound. No cure exists, so care targeted symptoms, and custom-made orthotic boots substantially improved his quality of life. The authors suspect the condition is underdiagnosed in Japan and call for greater clinician awareness.
pmc-13501573:
Xin Mi leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 study of aged mouse egg cells and a stem cell secretion that slows their rushed maturation. With age, the spindle assembly checkpoint weakens in oocytes, so cell division speeds up and chromosome errors, called aneuploidy, become common. The team added the secretome of mesenchymal stem cells, the mix of factors they release, to cultures of aged oocytes. They tracked division timing, chromosome alignment, and two checkpoint proteins, BubR1 and ZW10.

The secretome slowed the rushed progression and raised checkpoint protein levels at the kinetochore. Its effect ran through the PI3K/AKT pathway, since a blocking drug erased the benefit. The active ingredient proved to be BDNF, a growth factor for nerve cells: antibodies against it removed the effect. A BDNF mimic called 7,8-DHF reproduced it in culture and, injected into aged mice, improved egg quality and embryo development.
pmc-13501673:
Khem Raj leads a seven-author team with a 2026 portrait of the gut microbiome in the Pangwala tribal community of the Pangi region in India. Whole metagenome shotgun sequencing read all the DNA in stool samples, letting the team census bacteria, fungi, and viruses together rather than bacteria alone. Leading bacterial genera included Prevotella, Bifidobacterium, and members of the Succinivibrionaceae family, with similar diversity in both groups studied. The bacterium Prevotella copri emerged as the largest source for the pathways detected.

Fungi were led by the subkingdom Dikarya at 74 percent of fungal species, while viruses were dominated by bacteriophages of the Caudoviricetes class. The resistome, the catalogue of antibiotic resistance genes, held more than 100 candidate genes and high levels of vancomycin resistance in both groups. Despite the wide variety of species, what the microbes do looked stable, with much overlap, suggesting a core set.
pmc-13501773:
Yujing Gu leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 mixed-methods study of kinesiophobia, an excessive fear of movement, in older stroke survivors in Wuxi, China. Between January 2024 and June 2025, 307 patients aged 60 or older in subacute or chronic recovery completed questionnaires on physical function, psychological state, and illness adaptation. Eighteen of them later gave semi-structured interviews, read through a life-course lens that weighs early experiences, relationships, and timing across a lifetime.

Kinesiophobia affected 64.8 percent of the sample, 199 of the 307 patients counted in the survey. Muscle weakness, fear of falling, frailty, and anxiety each raised the likelihood, while being over 81, confidence in exercising, and acceptance of the illness lowered it. Interviews distilled four themes covering historical setting, linked lives, life timing, and personal agency. The authors urge nurses to screen for movement fear routinely and to shape rehabilitation plans around each patient's history.
pmc-13501973:
Alsuwied and co-authors report removing a jaw tumour and rebuilding the bite in a single operation. Their 2026 case report and literature review describes a 36-year-old woman with pain on biting and swelling near her right ear. Examination found facial asymmetry with her chin shifted left and limited mouth opening. She also had an open bite at the back right and a tilted biting plane. All traced to an osteoma, a benign bone tumour, on her jaw condyle.

Rather than staging the work, the team resected the condylar tumour and performed orthognathic surgery, corrective jaw surgery, simultaneously, guided by virtual surgical planning. The authors argue the combined approach restored facial harmony that tumour removal alone would not have achieved, while sparing the patient a second operation and a second recovery. Their review places the strategy among options for condylar osteomas where asymmetry is significant.
pmc-13502773:
Tibenderana and colleagues analyzed a 2022 national health survey to find what predicts cervical cancer screening among Tanzanian women aged fifteen to forty-nine, in a 2026 study. Cervical cancer is the most common cancer in Tanzanian women of reproductive age despite being preventable through early detection, and screening uptake is low. Their weighted sample covered more than fifteen thousand women, analyzed with multilevel models that account for clustering.

Tibenderana found screening odds rising steeply with age and with education. Odds were modestly higher among employed women, contraceptive users, and women who had visited a health facility in the past year. Women living with HIV had more than fivefold higher odds of being screened, likely reflecting their contact with HIV care services. Rural residence cut the odds substantially. The authors call for outreach to younger, less educated, rural, and poorer women, plus access and health literacy, to close the screening gap.
pmc-13502973:
Shyamala Ravikoti and others review in story form germ, viral, and germ mix roles in heart and vessel disease. In 2026, the review joins people-study evidence linking germs to heart and vessel disease beyond classic risks such as high blood pressure, blood sugar illness, and daily habits. Heart and vessel disease causes about eighteen million deaths yearly worldwide.

Named germs include Helicobacter pylori, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and gum germs, plus herpes germs, flu, CMV, hep C, and HIV. Put-forward paths run through chronic swelling, tiny copycat action, vessel lining trouble, direct tissue spread, and gut breakdown products such as trimethylamine-N-oxide. The authors map gaps and future research paths for germ-aware blocking.
pmc-13503473:
Lucrezia Rizzelli studies why Indonesia has fought the global push toward ending the death penalty. In 2026, the article traces the death penalty from the empire era through freedom to the new crime code of 2022, reading history, politics, religion, and culture through a post-empire lens. More than seven hundred people now sit on death row.

The claim centers on empire habits: keeping the death penalty asserts self-rule over home policy. It resists moral pressure from former empire rulers, including for drug crimes not seen as the most serious crimes worldwide. Islam and Pancasila, the five tenets holding up the Indonesian state, also shape keeping. The death penalty thus works as death power, a symbol of taking back state rule.
pmc-13503773:
Svenja Stolz and co-authors ran a small trial of a visual aid meant to help lung patients inhale their medicine correctly. People with chronic obstructive lung disease depend on inhaled drugs, but poor technique wastes the dose. The aid uses a chest-imaging method that draws a live picture of air moving in the lungs, shown to the patient as feedback. Twenty-nine patients took part; half inhaled with the picture and half without.

The feedback group showed a clear drop in air trapped in the lungs after breathing out, while the control group barely changed. Standard flow measures and patient questionnaires showed no clear gap. The authors say feedback may improve technique and ease hyperinflation, but changed breathing patterns could also explain the shift. They call for trials of repeated feedback over time.
pmc-13503873:
Fan Ding leads a team that made carbon nanodots glow red for minutes after the light stops, in a 2026 study. Long afterglow in red is prized for imaging and light devices, yet most materials fade in seconds at room heat. Carbon dots are cheap and safe, but their red glow has been short-lived.

The team tuned the dots' energy states with help from machine learning searches. The best dots kept glowing for more than 4,000 seconds, with a glow life of 353 seconds by the standard measure. Light studies showed two decay paths, one fast and one very slow; the slow path rules the long tail of light. As a test, the team built a wearable lamp marker that keeps signaling after power is cut.
pmc-13504373:
Ryota Tozuka and ten co-authors grade a deep learn auto-draw tool for ray care plans on real ward cases. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. True line draws guard cure worth, but odd forms and gear marks can trip code tools. Sixty-nine chest and male hip cases were picked to span odd forms and marks like pace gear and fake joints.

In plain cases the tool held high truth marks. In odd packs truth fell, most with fake hip joints and one-side lung falls. Eye checks laid most flaws to form and marks. One dose miss was caught. Hand checks stay a must.
pmc-13504973:
Souleymane Ouedraogo leads a team reporting a patient carrying two water-linked parasite infections at once, in a 2026 case report. The man, aged 37 and visiting France from Djibouti, had belly pain and a cough that had lasted three months. Both parasites favor regions with poor water safety.

Blood tests showed a surge in allergy-linked white cells and mild liver strain. Scans found odd tube-like liver lesions. Parasite eggs in samples, plus positive antibody tests for both liver fluke and blood fluke, confirmed the pair. He recalled eating local greens and bathing in fresh water years before. Two drugs, one for each parasite, were given together. He improved with no side effects. The authors urge checking for both when liver signs and travel history align.
pmc-13505073:
Ryuichi Nakayama and colleagues asked whether long use of high-flow nasal oxygen before intubation predicts worse outcomes on lung-support machines. The patients had severe ARDS, a lung failure syndrome, and all later received veno-venous ECMO, a machine that oxygenates blood outside the body.

Registry data covered 209 adults treated between 2012 and 2022 who had high-flow oxygen before ECMO. Each extra day on high-flow oxygen raised the odds of death within 60 days by a factor of 1.22 after adjustment. Patients on it three days or more, 69 people, faced about double the death risk and freed themselves from ECMO less often. Nakayama reads long high-flow use as a risk marker of delayed escalation, not proof the oxygen itself harms.
pmc-13505573:
Lei Zhou and colleagues built a generative computer model that mimics how tumour-associated macrophages shift between attack and support states during immunotherapy for digestive cancers. Only a minority of patients respond to such therapy, and fixed biomarkers miss these moving immune changes. Their digital-twin platform learned from more than a million single-cell profiles, tissue maps, and clinical records covering 2,847 people with five cancer types.

Attention-based links between cells and time-aware modules let the model simulate immune state changes and search for patient-specific moves that push macrophages toward the anti-tumour state. It predicted therapy response more accurately than standard biomarker models in their tests. Among 156 cases where its advice clashed with doctors' choices, model-guided care coincided with higher response rates and longer time before progression. The authors flag possible selection bias in that comparison and call for randomised prospective trials before clinical use.
pmc-13508273:
Ying Zhang and eight co-authors compare two surgical routes for putting a slipped jaw joint disc back in place, in 2026 work. The disc can slide forward and fail to return, locking the jaw in later stages of the disorder. The study reviewed 132 patients with 218 affected joints treated at a Guangzhou hospital in 2023 and 2024. Surgeons reached the joint either in front of or behind a bundle of nerves and blood vessels on the temple. Scans and early outcomes were compared between routes.

Scans after surgery confirmed the disc was back in place in 211 of 218 joints. The behind route bled more and took longer, and it brought more fevers and infections. The front route caused more temporary facial nerve weakness and a few skin flap injuries. The study gives jaw surgeons a clear trade-off table when choosing how to reach the joint.
pmc-13508373:
Sara Farinone leads a nine-author letter from an Italian kidney center arguing that pain alone does not explain lost quality of life in polycystic kidney disease, in 2026 correspondence. The letter answers a study linking kidney size to worse physical quality of life, with mental effects flowing largely through kidney pain. Enlarged organs can squeeze the gut, causing early fullness, indigestion, and constipation. Survey data they cite put about three in ten clinic patients at nutritional risk, with kidney and liver size the strongest predictor.

Body measures in cited work show low muscle mass with extra body water, a wasting pattern appearing even when kidney function holds up. Women face more liver enlargement over time, and body image strain seems stronger in women, which may deepen mental health effects. The letter urges sex-split analyses and nutrition-aware thinking in future studies of this disease.
pmc-13509373:
Francesco Paolo Lo Muzio and eight co-authors test whether heart sounds can reveal how the left side of the heart works under stress, in a 2026 pig study. The group studied twelve minipigs in three groups: healthy ones, animals with a weak pumping heart, and animals whose hearts relax poorly while pumping strength stays near normal. Sensors recorded heart sounds, heart rhythm, and oxygen levels while direct pressure readings gave the reference values.

A computer model learned to predict the pressure-based measures from the outer signals and sorted the three groups with high accuracy in standard tests. Accuracy stayed strong in a tougher test that left one animal per group out of training entirely. The poor-relaxation animals showed the most change in sound features as heart rate rose. The authors say the method could aid diagnosis, though human testing still lies ahead.
pmc-13510273:
Bo Lyu, Zhixuan Liu, and Xiaozi Gao report a longitudinal study, published in 2026. It tracks how executive function and motor skills influence each other in preschool children. Executive function covers the mental skills for goal-directed behaviour. More than two thousand children were assessed. They were aged three, four, and five. Parent reports supplied the data. The team modelled the two-way links over time.

Early executive function predicted its own later levels. Fine motor skills did the same. This was as expected. The striking result ran from fine motor skill. It significantly predicted later executive function at every step. It also predicted later gross motor skill. The reverse paths were weaker. The authors argue for combined motor and thinking training in preschool programmes.
pmc-13511973:
Jiahui Zhang and Dongxin He investigate how silicone gel used to seal power electronic devices fails under high voltage and high heat, in 2026 work. The gel insulates modules that convert electric power, and long service under harsh loads eats into reliability and lifespan. The team aged samples under combined electrical and thermal stress, varying pulse edge speed and aging stage.

They tracked tree-like damage channels, breakdown strength, charge-driven molecular vibration, leakage current, and softness by cone penetration. Failure traced to two forces acting together: fast pulse edges drove repeated charge damage inside the gel, while heat broke down its part-solid, part-liquid structure. Each force alone explained only part of the decline. The authors say the paired mechanism gives a base for reformulating the gel and redesigning modules for longer sealing life.
pmc-13512673:
Zhu and colleagues proposed GLUQ, a system for judging the quality of ultra-high-definition images without a reference copy, in a 2026 computer vision study. Scoring such huge images directly is computationally expensive. Shrinking or chopping them into independent patches loses distortions that only appear at certain scales and disconnects local flaws from the whole scene's context.

Zhu instead samples patches aligned to the image's aspect ratio and links them as nodes in a graph. The graph is built from spatial closeness and feature similarity, letting information flow between regions through graph convolution, a method that pools data across connected nodes. Attention-based pooling then weighs patch evidence into one quality score, trained with a combined loss balancing accuracy, correlation, and ranking. On the standard ultra-high-definition benchmark the system achieved the lowest prediction error among compared methods with competitive correlation scores, supporting graph relations as the key improvement.
pmc-13514373:
Jiajia Lu, Yue Shen, Xu Wang, and Fuyang Ke present a robotics study, published in 2026. It improves SLAM for self-driving in cities. SLAM lets machines locate themselves while mapping their surroundings. Single sensors drift or fail in built-up areas. The team tightly combined three data sources. They used laser scanning, motion sensing, and GPS data.

Their system extracts features from laser scans. These include lines, surfaces, and ground. It corrects height drift frame by frame. Motion and GPS data are fused with an error-state filter. GPS-checked loop closure avoids false matches. In tests, average position error fell by nearly half. This was against laser-only methods. Against laser-inertial methods, the cut was about a quarter.
pmc-13516073:
Juan Mauricio Ramírez-Vidal leads a ten-author team testing an essential oil against two parasites in a 2026 study. The oil comes from Plectranthus amboinicus, a medicinal plant grown in Mexico City. Chemical analysis found forty-six compounds, led by camphor at about thirty-one percent, with several aromatic oxides and carvacrol behind it. The team then exposed amoebae that cause gut disease and the Chagas-disease parasite Trypanosoma cruzi to the oil.

The oil killed amoeba trophozoites at moderate strength. Against the blood form of the Chagas parasite it worked better, landing near the potency of the reference drug benznidazole, while the insect-stage form needed a stronger dose. Tests on monkey kidney cells gauged collateral harm to host tissue. Ramírez-Vidal's team plans to trace the oil's molecular effects and test its parts singly, in mixes, and beside standard drugs.
pmc-13516773:
Hossein Omidian, Sumana Dey Chowdhury, and Luigi X Cubeddu argue, in a 2026 review, that inhaled RNA medicines must be designed as whole products, not just clever molecules. Breathing RNA into the lungs can place gene-silencing, protein-making, or editing cargo exactly where lung disease sits. The authors survey cargo types and the carriers that ferry them, from fatty nanoparticles to polymer bundles and dry powders.

Progress is real but patchy, they find. Many studies show a carrier can work, yet few prove it survives the inhaler, crosses mucus, enters the right cells, and stays tolerable on repeat doses. The review urges target-first design: define the patient, cell, and outcome, then gate each manufacturing and device step with hard measures. Success, in their framing, means RNA still working after production, spraying, landing, and cell entry.
pmc-13517973:
Haupt and colleagues reported a 2026 case of hepatopulmonary syndrome, a liver-driven cause of low blood oxygen, in a ten-year-old boy whose breathing tests had looked normal. The boy, who had obesity, sleep apnea, and asthma, arrived with low resting oxygen and drops during exertion. Yet his lung examination and outpatient lung function were unrevealing, and inhalers did not help.

Haupt describes how the workup instead uncovered liver cirrhosis and an enlarged liver and spleen. It found swollen veins in the food pipe. There was a widened gap between oxygen in the air sacs and in the blood, the signature of blood bypassing oxygen pickup through dilated lung vessels. A liver center confirmed the syndrome, whose only established cure is transplantation, and the boy underwent liver transplant. The authors urge emergency physicians to consider this liver-lung connection when a child's low oxygen defies the usual explanations.
pmc-13518373:
Vivien Min Er Lee and eight colleagues study disabled patients who teach medical students in a 2026 qualitative paper. Patient educators bring lived experience into family-medicine training, yet nobody had asked those with physical disabilities how the role feels from inside. All seven educators from a workshop on communicating with disabled patients gave in-depth interviews, and reflexive thematic analysis sorted their accounts.

Each educator blended three roles: patient, teacher, and advocate, in personal proportions. The team sketched four types, from patient-led to advocacy-led, with the middle types, where teaching stood equal, proving most confident and best aligned with course aims. Pure advocacy sometimes pulled sessions off the lesson plan. Lee's team recommends structured training and guided reflection to help educators balance story, advocacy, and syllabus, so disabled voices strengthen teaching instead of being flattened into a single testimony role.
pmc-13518973:
Kartick Bag and four colleagues build a 2026 learning system for managing hospital outpatient queues as demand swings through the day. Fixed staffing models assume steady arrivals and identical servers, while real clinics see surges plus different handling for first-time and returning patients. Their model separates those two provider types and lets arrivals follow a time-varying pattern.

A Q-learning agent, guided by a supervised exploration rule, decides when to add or move providers. Separate value tables for arrivals and departures capture their different costs and rewards, which also shift over time. Simulations showed clear cuts in total waiting time and system cost versus conventional uniform queue models. The design extends to wider hospital resource planning.
pmc-13519273:
Fonseca and colleagues reviewed drug treatment for olfactory reference disorder in a 2026 analysis. The disorder is the conviction that one emits a foul body odor others barely notice. The analysis also traces how prescribing changed over decades. Following standard review guidelines, the team extracted patient, symptom, and treatment details from every report they could find on medicines for this condition.

Fonseca located 52 studies covering 87 patients, almost all single case reports or small series, with no controlled trials at all. Serotonin reuptake inhibitors were used in about three fifths of cases and antipsychotics in about half. These inhibitors are a class of antidepressants. The reported response rate ran above eighty percent, which the authors discount for publication bias. Antipsychotics dominated earlier decades, while serotonin drugs took over after the nineteen nineties as the disorder was reclassified within the obsessive-compulsive spectrum, and no patient feature reliably predicted response.
pmc-13519773:
Tom Duchemin and colleagues test whether French health databases can reliably find major birth defects. Their proof-of-concept study from twenty twenty-six uses a national mother-child register. Registries track defects, but databases cover every birth. Medication safety in pregnancy needs that complete coverage.

Seventy-two specific defects in eleven organ groups were defined. Hospital diagnoses, procedures, and death causes supplied the signals. Over ten million births from twenty ten onward were scanned. Roughly two percent of live-born infants had a defect flagged. Rates were compared against the European registry network. A known drug exposure served as a validity check. Database surveillance could complement registries at national scale.
pmc-13520273:
Gabriel Cubillos and nine colleagues train machine learning models in 2026 to predict which babies will be born large for their gestational age. Such size is a risk factor for delivery injury to mother and child. Twelve algorithms were tuned and tested using routine prenatal variables, with data augmentation and feature selection to sharpen performance.

The leading model balanced sensitivity and specificity at 0.84 each using 14 variables, while a leaner 10-variable model reached 97 percent specificity, beating the classic ultrasound formula's balance of errors. Maternal body mass index, maternal weight at first and last checkups, and estimated fetal weight drove predictions most. Cubillos's team argues standard clinic data, gathered early, can flag risky pregnancies in time to act.
pmc-13520373:
Wu and colleagues compared in 2026 human-led and ChatGPT-assisted analysis of the same nursing interview data. Artificial intelligence tools promise faster coding and tidier organisation for qualitative research, but nursing stories carry emotion, context, and culture that software may flatten. The team ran both methods side by side on interviews from a larger nursing project and compared where the results agreed and split.

Wu found the software helped with rapid sorting, first-pass coding, and spotting clear, surface themes. Its output read smoothly yet simplified context, missing tacit nursing know-how and the feel of experience-based stories. Four ethical themes emerged: privacy and data safety, loss of emotional and contextual grasp, algorithmic narrowing with cultural bias, and shifting roles for researchers. The authors treat the tool as a support for human judgement, not a replacement for it in nursing inquiry.
pmc-13520473:
Haijia Tang and colleagues review in 2026 how support cells around tumours and lymphoid-like clusters inside tumours jointly shape anti-tumour immunity through their layout in tissue. Support cells can block immune entry and fuel resistance, while lymphoid clusters help prime immune cells locally and track with better outcomes.

Recent single-cell and spatial studies show varied support-cell states, some of which even help organise lymphoid clusters. The authors frame outcome as a balance between stromal restriction and lymphoid organisation. That balance may guide tumour classification, patient grouping and combination treatments that reprogramme stroma or encourage lymphoid cluster growth.
pmc-13520873:
Soufyane Elkadiri and colleagues review in 2026 twenty patients treated surgically for eyelid cancers at a university hospital in eastern Morocco over three years from 2023 to 2025. Eyelid tumours demand full removal while preserving eye function and appearance.

Average age was about 63 years, with women slightly outnumbering men. Long sun exposure appeared in nine of ten patients, while the lower lid was the commonest site. Basal cell tumours made up three quarters of cases, with squamous tumours making up the rest. All patients had wide removal with margin checks, mostly rebuilt with local flaps, and no return of cancer was seen during follow-up.
pmc-13522473:
D Rex Mitchell and colleagues study how extinct armored fishes from Devonian Australia crushed hard prey in a 2026 analysis of eight species. Fossils came from the Gogo Formation, a site known for detailed preservation. Computer models simulated biting stresses in the lower jaw, while tooth surface complexity was measured to infer how each species handled resistant food.

Species with broad, flat teeth showed low strain, suiting them to crushing armored prey small enough to swallow whole. The largest species paired a very strong jaw with complex teeth able to pierce and tear prey too big for its mouth. Medium-sized forms seemed suited to slicing softer tissue. Feeding therefore depended on prey size relative to the predator, not on predator size alone.
pmc-13522573:
Li and co-authors report in 2026 that a splicing factor called CELF2 drives production of the 4R form of tau, a brain protein whose abnormal buildup marks several dementias. Splicing decides which protein version a gene makes, and too much 4R tau is linked to disease. The team found that CELF2 works not as scattered molecules but by gathering into clusters inside the cell nucleus.

These clusters form through the protein's intrinsically disordered region, a floppy segment that lets molecules assemble, and one residue, D388, proved essential for clustering and for the splicing effect. Two other splicing factors, NOVA2 and SFPQ, joined the same clusters. In animal tauopathy models, the capacity for this nuclear assembly tracked with 4R tau levels and with movement and thinking performance. The authors identify CELF2 clustering as a possible drug target for tau diseases.
pmc-13523073:
Robbe Wils and co-authors present a 2026 profile of irritable bowel patients in family doctor care. Most such patients are seen in primary care, yet that group is the least studied. The team re-read data from the DOMINO study of 483 adults newly diagnosed by their family doctors. Scores covered gut patterns, symptom weight, life quality, mood, and body-wide symptoms.

About 70 percent met the strict Rome IV bar for the disorder. Mixed and diarrhea patterns were the most common kinds. Mean symptom weight sat in the high range, with over a third of cases severe. Patients who met the strict bar felt worse and carried more mood load than those who did not. The profile gives family doctors a truer picture of their daily caseload.
pmc-13523173:
Christos Psevdos and Giovanni Ianniruberto analyze how friction falls as polymer melts flow in a 2026 theoretical study. Recent experiments on three unentangled polystyrene melts of different chain lengths showed complex thinning and stress patterns under fast shear. Single-chain simulations that let friction drop as chain segments align were compared with the measurements and with many-chain simulations.

The analysis confirmed that the friction coefficient must fall significantly as segment alignment rises. The extracted relationship matched earlier results from stretching experiments for the two longer-chain melts, while the shortest melt showed a weaker dependence. Single-chain models missed some effects that many-chain simulations captured, especially in stretching flows. The authors conclude that interactions between chains still hold part of the missing physics.
pmc-13523273:
Sherin Khamis Hussein and colleagues investigate serum IL-38 and a related gene variant as biomarkers for childhood idiopathic nephrotic syndrome. Their 2026 case-control study concerns the most common chronic glomerular disorder in children.

Eighty-eight child patients and seventy-four matched healthy controls took part. Serum IL-38 was measured by an enzyme assay, and a specific gene polymorphism was typed by real-time PCR. IL-38 levels were significantly lower in patients than controls. Levels also correlated negatively with age, systolic blood pressure, and urinary protein. Diagnostic performance was moderate. The authors explore whether this anti-inflammatory cytokine could help identify disease or predict treatment response.
pmc-13523573:
Kenji Yamaji and co-authors test whether anatomy predicts side effects of a heart rhythm treatment, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Nerve clusters closer to the vein junction changed more often after the procedure. Upper clusters changed more than lower ones. The measured distance sorted likely from unlikely change with fair accuracy. Knowing the distance in advance may help doctors predict nerve effects and tune the procedure.
pmc-13523973:

Their workflow joined three-dimensional QSAR modeling, which relates molecular shape to activity, with absorption and toxicity profiling, docking into the enzyme, molecular dynamics simulation, transport checks, and retrosynthesis planning. The best model showed strong fit and predictive power. The ligands fit the enzyme active site from a known crystal structure, stayed stable in hundred-nanosecond simulations, and showed sound drug-like profiles. A lead compound emerged, with a synthesis route sketched, ready for lab testing.
pmc-13524073:
Rahpeyma and colleagues probed the purpose of stromules in 2026, the thin fingers that plastids, the plant cell's energy and chemical factories, extend under stress. Blocking the cell's microtubule rails stopped the response, while blocking a jasmonate-making step prevented one hormone's effect. When finger growth was suppressed, hormone-driven gene switching grew stronger, hinting the fingers temper the signal. pmc-13524973:
Kaijun Gu and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on when the seam between the two halves of the upper jaw hardens. The threshold landed at 11.2 years, nearly the same for boys and girls, with strong accuracy. Maturation tracked age tightly, and girls ran ahead of boys through the teen years. A middle grade proved distinct enough to keep its own stage. The authors say the cutoff can spare young children needless scans.
pmc-13525173:
Dokos and colleagues investigated in 2026 prescription errors inside a regional psychiatric hospital in Germany. They identified errors by a modified EQUIP method, then interviewed prescribers in a double-blind way and built a codebook of error themes.

From 6,020 treatment plans, 150 errors were detected, an error rate of about two and a half percent. A Delphi consensus process clarified the nature of each error type. The authors argue that psychiatric prescribing has its own error profile shaped by ward routines and drug mix. Understanding those circumstances, they say, is the first step to targeted safety work in mental health facilities.
pmc-13525373:
Five authors report a study dated two thousand twenty-six on a form of inflammatory arthritis of the spine. The condition is axial spondyloarthritis. Some patients do not respond to a first biologic drug, secukinumab, and doctors must pick the next drug with little guidance on who will benefit.

The team re-read immune data from eighteen patients who had not responded. Eight were switched to a different class of biologic, and ten had their dose raised. Falls in two sets of helper T cells during the first drug marked the patients who later did well. Disease activity was checked at week twenty-four to judge the response.
pmc-13525573:
Raphael Fernandes Casseb leads a large team in a 2026 study of a free deep-learning tool that automatically outlines the cavity left after epilepsy surgery on brain scans. The tool reached the highest median overlap score with manual outlines, beating three rival automated methods after statistical correction. Volume agreement was comparable with the best rival, but that rival falsely marked cavities in three control scans while the new tool marked none. The authors offer the software freely for surgical research.
pmc-13525773:
Ziqian Tang and four co-authors report a rare late snag of a neck-of-womb stitch band, in this 2026 case. The band, set by keyhole surgery, holds a weak cervix shut in child-bed. Bands can, in rare years-later cases, eat into near organs, most oft the bladder. A move into the bowel had not been told of before this case.

The patient was a woman of forty-four with no signs at all. She came to have the band out by choice. Scans before the cut showed no hint of the truth. In surgery, two bands sat wholly in her bowel's last stretch. The team fixed the bowel and brought out a side vent for stool. Three months on, a scan for the vent's close found a leak path from bowel to womb. She chose watch and wait over a big fix, with a team on call.
pmc-13526073:
Leyun Pan and colleagues ask, in a 2026 prospective study, whether dynamic PET imaging adds value for liver metastases from uveal melanoma. This eye cancer's liver spread can be faint on standard scans. Three image sets were compared, parametric maps, standard static images, and delayed static images. Total lesion detection did not differ significantly between approaches. One true liver metastasis appeared on the parametric map and was confirmed by MRI after being unclear on static images. Quantitative contrast ratios were measured for every lesion.
pmc-13526473:
Naidu and colleagues mapped in 2026 the United Kingdom's research output on artificial intelligence in medical imaging. They analysed Scopus-indexed papers from 2017 to 2025 on generative and foundation AI methods. Globally they found 13,452 publications with about 195,000 citations. UK-affiliated papers numbered 889, about seven percent of the world total, and the UK ranked fourth by volume.

UK papers averaged twenty-one citations each, higher than several larger producers, despite the UK's smaller share. Output grew roughly eighteen-fold across the nine years, with a citation lag in recent years because new papers need time to be cited. The authors describe a fast-growing, high-impact national ecosystem. They note the analysis shows where UK imaging AI concentrates and how its themes connect internationally.
pmc-13527473:
Shabnam Afzal and colleagues report a 2026 dermatology case of a rare pigmented purpuric disorder appearing during pregnancy. These disorders leak red blood cells into the skin, leaving brown patches from iron pigment. The Majocchi variant forms ring-shaped or geographic plaques, reported more often in young women, usually on the legs.

A twenty-nine-year-old woman developed painless darkened patches during pregnancy eighteen months earlier, which enlarged, darkened, and then stabilized without fading. Examination found well-demarcated violet-brown, slightly thinned ring plaques across both lower legs and feet, and over-the-counter moisturizers had not helped. A punch biopsy of the ankle showed escaped red blood cells and iron pigment in the upper skin layer, matching the clinical picture. The authors stress biopsy plus clinicopathologic correlation to confirm this uncommon diagnosis.
pmc-13528073:
Laura Kirkpatrick and four colleagues interview pediatric clinicians about sharing hard newborn screening results in a 2026 study. The team interviewed twenty-five clinicians in western Pennsylvania.

Clinicians named three big barriers. They knew little about Krabbe disease. Their schedules had no slack. Specialists were hard to reach. Helpful factors included past training in breaking bad news and trusted online resources. Requests were practical: fact sheets, scripts, and care pathways. Education bundled with the result notice was another idea. Better links with specialists would help too. The authors say primary care can play this role if systems support it.
pmc-13529673:
Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 study of how a malaria parasite protein punches holes in cell membranes. Plasmodium parasites must cross several cell types, and perforin-like proteins do the piercing. One, PLP2, is essential for bursting out of red blood cells at the sexual stage. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team resolved its shape on membranes.

The protein assembles into arcs and rings of varying size on fat membranes. One complete pore held seventeen copies: the pore-forming domains line up as a central barrel through the membrane, while tail domains anchor the ring to the surface. A locked mutant form caught the complex just before insertion, showing the steps of the attack. The pore's build gives drug designers a concrete structure to block.
pmc-13530173:
Wojciech Piasecki and colleagues give a fresh account of a widespread freshwater fish parasite in 2026 using modern imaging and DNA tools. The tiny crustacean has been cited in fish disease writing for nearly two centuries, yet its form and identity stayed fuzzy. Specimens came from ide fish in a Polish lake.

Electron microscopy revealed fine details on mouthparts, legs, and other structures never shown before. DNA barcodes, the first for this species, confirmed its separate identity and close kinship with a relative. Two names long treated as distinct species were folded into this one, and the group diagnosis was rewritten.
pmc-13531273: Lowe and co-authors address lung disease tied to early birth in this 2026 paper. Children born early can carry lasting lung problems, yet the best way to spot and treat the condition is unsettled. The paper describes a method to find at-risk children who might benefit from inhaled therapy. Its focus is on breathing test cut-off points that best predict a good response to a bronchodilator, a drug that opens the airways. Clear cut-offs could help doctors choose which children should receive inhaler treatment.
pmc-13531973:
Isobel K Dunstan leads a 2026 chemical profile of blood and spinal fluid in osteoarthritis, hunting molecules tied to pain. Modeling separated the groups with high accuracy in both fluids.

Two amino acids, histidine and glutamine, ran low in patient blood across every subgroup. Lower levels meant stronger pain, disability, sleep trouble, and overall symptom burden. Women showed the deepest drops and the heaviest symptoms. The pair emerges as candidate markers for sorting patients and targeting pain pathways.
pmc-13532073:
Thanapat Chaisudhiphongskul and co-authors race two wound dressings against each other on skin graft donor sites in this 2026 trial. Thirty patients each wore both: one half of the donor site got foam, the other half the superabsorbent pad, assigned by chance. In bench tests the lighter superabsorbent pad drank ninety-three milliliters of salt water against the foam's seventy-five. On patients it absorbed clearly more fluid on days three, six, and nine. Pain scores leaned lower with the new pad without reaching firm proof. Skin regrowth matched between sides, and no infections or reactions appeared. The authors rate the superabsorbent pad the stronger drinker with equal healing.
pmc-13534373:
Ilker Sengul, Demet Sengul, and Cagri Akalin discuss in 2026 why HER2-positive breast cancer splits into two distinct groups by hormone receptor status.
