The double-positive group showed richer drug-processing pathways, which may explain better response to hormone therapy. Immune cell mixes in tumours also differed by group, while key gene mutations stayed similar. Readers are urged to treat the two groups as separate diseases in trials.
pmc-13534673:
Tengfei Long and colleagues track in 2026 how changes in estimated glucose disposal rate, a stand-in for insulin resistance, link to death in middle-aged and older Chinese adults. Single baseline measures miss how risk shifts over time. Data from a national ageing study held 5,966 people with measures in 2012 and 2015.

Four change patterns emerged, and patterns with falling values carried higher death rates than the steadiest group. Total exposure over time linked inversely to death risk in follow-up. Readers see why repeated and cumulative checks add warning value beyond one reading.
pmc-13534773:
Rebecca Lievesley and colleagues chart in 2026 treatment pathways for people convicted of sexual offences who take medication to manage problematic sexual arousal in the United Kingdom. The service is little studied beyond before-and-after outcome reports. Service records covered all 139 users at the first evaluation site.

Six distinct pathways emerged from starting drug class, dose or drug changes, and stopping patterns. Each pathway paired with positive shifts in arousal problem measures, while journeys varied a lot between users. The team also offers an ethical prescribing frame that weighs benefit and user experience.
pmc-13535973:
Binyang Zhu and seven co-authors test whether heart ultrasound measures can forecast the return of atrial fibrillation after ablation, in a study from 2026. One hundred patients had standard and in-depth ultrasound of the left atrium and its appendage before a catheter procedure that burns faulty heart circuits. Strain measures show how well the chamber walls stretch and contract.

Over one year, a third of patients saw the faulty rhythm return. Those patients had worse chamber function on many strain measures at the start. Two appendage strain values stood out as predictors. Adding them to standard data may help pick patients most likely to benefit.
pmc-13536573:
Wenqiang Liu and colleagues clone in 2026 DT1, a cytochrome P450 gene that boosts drought tolerance in rice. Drought limits rice output worldwide, and new protective genes aid breeding of hardier varieties. Near-isogenic lines narrowed the trait to a small stretch of chromosome 3 with several candidate genes.

Gene tests singled out one candidate: knockout plants became more drought sensitive, while overexpressing lines tolerated dry spells better. The gene acts mainly in stems and leaves, and one form common in japonica rice looked favourable. Breeders gain a fresh genetic resource for drought-resistant varieties.
pmc-13536673:
Usama Yaseen and co-authors report a 2026 field experiment on black soybean grown in poor, low-fertility soil called Inceptisol. Plants received organic soil additions, either biochar or vermicompost, alone or with two helpful microbes. One microbe helps roots fix nitrogen from the air, while the other helps roots absorb nutrients. Growth, nutrient uptake, and root colonization were tracked across treatments.

Plants given both organic additions plus both microbes grew the tallest and fullest canopies. Biochar with both microbes gave the largest shoot and root mass and the highest root colonization, reaching 80 percent of roots. Phosphorus uptake also rose, and nitrogen-fixing bacteria were most numerous under the combined treatment. The authors conclude that pairing biochar with both microbes offers a practical route to stronger soybean growth with less reliance on chemical fertilizer.
pmc-13537573:
Graziosi and co-authors published a 2026 report of repeated failures to replicate famous experiments on awe. Earlier studies claimed that inducing awe makes people detect agency more, act more generously, and feel better. The team tried to reproduce these effects in online and lab settings, using videos, writing tasks, and virtual reality to spark awe. The classic effects generally did not appear.

Three direct replications followed, with samples two and a half times the originals. The past findings still did not reproduce. The authors discuss what this means for emotion research done online, where induction tools may be weaker than in the lab. They close with advice for future awe studies, including stronger inductions and pre-registered designs.
pmc-13538673:
Pinzhen Wu and colleagues released a long, fine-grained global dataset of grassland plant mass. Published in 2026, the dataset spans 2000 to 2022 at 0.005-degree steps, built with a tuned random-forest model trained on 11,265 field samples worldwide. Grasslands anchor the carbon cycle and feed livestock, yet steady high-detail global plant-mass records were scarce.

Inputs mixed greenness readings, weather, air carbon dioxide, and land shape. The model scored 0.60 on both holdout and fresh checks, with errors near 86 and 94 grams per square meter, and 0.93 across all samples with errors near 52. Its year-to-year paths matched other sets and sat closer to field readings. The set gives carbon workers and herders a base for tracking grassland health and grazing limits.
pmc-13539373:
Angela Cristina Nicola and co-authors study panic and breathing in a 2026 rat study tied to the menopause transition. The stage before menopause brings hormone swings and higher risk of panic disorder. The team compared female rats with regular cycles against rats in a stage like that transition, exposing both to normal air, low oxygen, and extra carbon dioxide.

Both gases raised breathing in both groups, and body temperature responses were alike. Low oxygen, though, triggered stronger panic-like behavior in the transition-stage rats. It also raised the number and size of immune cells in a brainstem hub tied to panic. Breathing control itself stayed intact. The authors link the stage's hormone shifts to a sharper panic response and brain immune change.
pmc-13539673:
Youran Lee and co-authors published this diet study in 2026 on adults with high blood pressure. The DASH diet, rich in plants and low in salt, is known to cut pressure, yet few people stick to it. The team asked whether eating style sorts people into groups. They drew on intake data from 301 adults in a United States trial.

Scores showed low DASH habits on the whole. A grouping method found three camps: low adherence, high adherence, and a mixed camp. The camps differed in how they ate by feel: trust in hunger cues, freedom to eat, and matching food choice to body needs. Low scorers leaned more on hunger cues, while high scorers matched food to their bodies more. The authors say diet advice should fit each camp's habits, not just hand all patients one score to chase.
pmc-13539873:
Megan Gow and six co-authors built a frame to pull lived experience into pregnancy and parenting research with care. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, deals with young researchers in this field. Such staff are keen, and more oft bound, to bring in people who have lived the topics. But tight rules and thin means can push that work to token form. Then the tie in feels forced yet out of reach, and trust dies.

Their VOICE frame sets safety first steps for true joint work, drawn from practice. It is aimed at early and mid career staff who must thread fund, ethics, and care lines. Readers get a path from tokenism to togetherness that guards the people who share their lives.
pmc-13540173:
Qing Li, Mingrong Cheng, Xiaoyue Wang, Weiwei Li, and Feng Zhang published a 2026 review on why drugs stop working in inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD. Resistance to modern precision treatments is a major barrier for patients. Older studies usually blamed a single molecule or pathway.

The authors describe a web of three interacting systems: the gut microbiota, the immune system, and epigenetics, the chemical marks that control gene activity. They review resistance to key medicines, including anti-TNF biologics, vedolizumab, and JAK inhibitors. Their model casts disturbed gut microbes as the initiator, immune disorder as the amplifier, and epigenetic change as a third loop. Seeing resistance as a system may reveal new ways to restore drug response.
pmc-13540273:
High blood pressure drives heart and kidney damage worldwide, yet control stays poor. Kamlesh Khunti and co-authors drew on a global registry to profile patients whose hypertension travels with diabetes, kidney disease, or heart failure. The analysis covers over twenty-three thousand people in twenty-nine countries. Three quarters had uncontrolled pressure by modern cutoffs, even though nearly nine in ten were prescribed pressure lowering drugs.

Most patients had diabetes, about two fifths had kidney disease, and obesity and abnormal blood fats were common. Patients with uncontrolled pressure were younger, heavier, and more likely to show heart wall thickening. They were treated less intensively, with fewer combinations, than patients whose pressure was controlled. The authors argue the gap is not mainly drug failure but under treatment. They point to combination therapy and kidney and heart risk care as the fixes health systems should push.
pmc-13541873:
Noah Bunkley and co-authors map the research on whether reflective cool roofs protect health, in this 2026 scoping review. Heat threatens millions living in flimsy housing, and a pale roof is a cheap, passive defense. The team searched six databases across four decades and kept fourteen studies that compared cool and normal roofs on health or wellbeing outcomes. Every one turned out to be a modeling study.

Most work targeted city heat island relief in rich countries. Projected health gains swung widely with local setting and method. No study measured real people, and low-resource settings were barely touched. The authors say the promise is plausible but unproven where it matters most. They call for field trials in vulnerable communities before policy leans on the idea.
pmc-13542073:
Muhammad Shazib Hameed and colleagues write a 2026 mathematics paper. The topic is fairer ways to merge expert judgements. The judgements are fuzzy and uncertain by design. The formalism is called intuitionistic fuzzy Z-numbers. It grades both support and doubt about a claim. Group decisions in e-learning form one test case.

New aggregation operators anchor the paper. They rest on proportionate weighting of support and doubt. Weighted versions serve groups where experts carry different weight. Worked examples apply the machinery to multi-criteria choices. A grey relational analysis step double-checks the rankings. The authors claim more accurate results than existing models. They also claim more consistent results across comparisons.
pmc-13542173:
Hasti Nouraei and colleagues test a laboratory risk in 2026. The subject is the yeast Candida albicans. Labs regrow this yeast again and again for experiments. The team asked whether that routine strips away dangerous traits. If it does, research findings may mislead. Ten clinical isolates went through twenty passages.

Adhesion gene activity fell steadily across passages. Two genes, ALS1 and ALS3, both declined. Biofilm building weakened in nearly all isolates. Most isolates had lost biofilm growth by the final passage. Surface water-repellence slid as well. Every isolate scored low on that trait by passage fifteen. The authors urge low-passage isolates for realistic work.
pmc-13542673:
Karimwabo writes to press health leaders to give rehabilitation a full place in care and policy. Rehabilitation helps people regain daily function after stroke, injury, or long illness. Across much of Africa, and in Rwanda, such care stays low in funding and planning.

Many patients leave hospital with no referral to rehabilitation and no follow-up plan. That gap can turn a survivable illness into lasting disability and lost work. Karimwabo asks ministries to fund rehabilitation inside main health budgets. He also asks that rehabilitation staff join care teams and policy talks. Training for doctors on what rehabilitation offers forms part of the plea.
pmc-13543073:
Dikra Suleyman George and colleagues published a 2026 case report of endemic Kaposi sarcoma disguised as morphea, a skin-hardening condition, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Kaposi sarcoma ranks among the most frequent cancers in sub-Saharan Africa and is driven by human herpesvirus-8. Its endemic form mainly affects children and younger adult men in the region, often without HIV infection, and usually appears as nodules or swollen limbs rather than flat hardened patches.

Their patient was a 28-year-old HIV-negative man with four months of skin hardening on both sides of the groin. The authors state they found no earlier description of morphea-like Kaposi sarcoma in an HIV-negative person. The case matters because endemic Kaposi sarcoma in Africa is classified into recognised patterns, and a hardening presentation that mimics a benign skin disease risks delayed diagnosis and treatment.
pmc-13543373:
M van der Ven and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of SPICE, a Dutch workplace programme teaching trainee doctors to collaborate across the primary and secondary care boundary during a geriatrics rotation. Learning to hand patients smoothly between family medicine and hospital care matters for older adults with complex needs. Instead of a standard survey, the team used an effects forum: residents, supervisors, and patients together built a timeline of learning moments from the programme and the six months after it.

Seventeen people took part in two forums. Residents said they understood the patient's whole care journey better and understood each other's worlds, which led to more proactive handovers. They also carried the habits into new settings through reflection and conversation, a ripple effect beyond the original placement. The authors present collective evaluation as a way to see how workplace learning becomes changed practice over time.
pmc-13543473:
Yassine Kallel and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a stab wound that pierced the common bile duct straight through. Such injuries appear in only a small fraction of penetrating abdominal trauma and are easily missed at first. A 35-year-old man arrived two hours after being stabbed in the upper right abdomen, stable, with a scan showing a liver laceration and abdominal fluid. Care began non-operatively, but within six hours fever, racing pulse, and abdominal tenderness forced a change of plan.

Exploration found bile-stained fluid and a through-and-through injury of the duct above the duodenum. Surgeons repaired the back wall through the front opening, widened it carefully, placed a T-shaped drainage tube, and added a drain. Recovery was smooth, and dye studies on day eight and at two months showed no leak or narrowing. A year on, the patient remained well.
pmc-13543573:
Gobeille and colleagues compared three visual function surveys in low vision patients to judge which best suits clinic use, in a 2026 study. Seventy-four patients completed the Activity Inventory, a veterans' low-vision questionnaire with forty-eight items, and the vision subscale of a National Eye Institute questionnaire. Testing ran before and six months after a low vision exam, with Rasch analysis applied to the scores.

Gobeille found each tool flawed in a different way. Two surveys showed ceiling effects, bunching patients at the top. The third subscale targeted ability best yet mixed dimensions, with the most responses that fit. Scores tracked each other across tools. On ease of use, the veterans' questionnaire was answered fastest per item before the exam. The authors conclude no questionnaire wins on all counts and recommend the veterans' survey when patient ability sits below its ceiling, while calling for fixes to all three.
pmc-13543873:
Klouda and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of pulmonary vein stenosis returning after a double lung transplant in a young child. The disease narrows the veins that carry blood from the lungs to the heart. Transplant is the last-resort cure for severe forms of this disease that resist other care. The girl had the transplant at 17 months of age after many earlier procedures, on top of other birth conditions.

Klouda describes how early checks showed open veins, but about 34 months after transplant tests revealed severe narrowing again in several veins of the new lungs. Flow scans showed the left lung getting far less blood than the right. Doctors used balloon widening, which eased pressure in the heart, and switched her to sirolimus, a drug that slows tissue growth, instead of placing stents. The authors urge counselling families that the disease can return, plus close monitoring after transplant.
pmc-13544173:
Aubrey and co-authors reviewed a 2026 decade of lung transplants at one centre, comparing recipients aged seventy and above with younger patients. Whether an upper age limit should exist is controversial, since guidelines flag age over sixty-five as high risk. The review covered all transplants performed over the ten year period.

Of 380 transplants, seventy-three went to patients seventy or older and 307 to younger patients, Aubrey reports. Older recipients more often received a single lung and more often had restrictive lung disease as their diagnosis. Length of stay, early graft dysfunction, and kidney injury did not differ between the age groups postoperatively. One, three, and five year survival were statistically indistinguishable, and age seventy plus was not an independent predictor of death.
pmc-13544573:
Alexander Aarvold and co-authors published this 2026 surgical study on a simpler operation for babies born with dislocated hips. In developmental hip dysplasia, the socket is too shallow, and open reduction puts the ball back in place. The socket itself still needs help to grow into shape, which standard bone surgery achieves with bigger procedures.

Their add-on, a minimal growth-stimulating acetabuloplasty, is meant to spark that growth with far less cutting. The paper reports 167 hips in 154 infants, followed for four to sixteen years after surgery. At final check, over 98 percent of hips rated excellent or good, with socket angles back to normal. Only about four percent later needed the bigger pelvic operation.
pmc-13545373:
Sujay Jaju and colleagues reported in 2026 on whole-exome sequencing for 113 people with retinitis pigmentosa seen through an eye disease registry in South India. Retinitis pigmentosa slowly destroys the retina, and many families in this region have parents who are related, which raises the share of recessive disease. The team sequenced the protein-coding genome and judged each variant by standard clinical rules.

Among 109 unrelated patients, testing found 186 rare variants across 92 retinal genes and settled a molecular diagnosis for about 46 percent. Recessive inheritance dominated, and even patients without related parents often carried two identical copies of a variant. Three genes, EYS, USH2A, and ADGRV1, appeared most often, giving counselors a region-specific picture to work from.
pmc-13546573:
Priyadarshini Pathak and colleagues mapped in 2026 how gastrointestinal cancers escape targeted drugs, using DNA shed into the blood after treatment stops working. They reviewed 106 patients with bile duct, colorectal, and other gut cancers who had tumor profiling before treatment and a blood test at progression. The drugs involved targeted a range of growth switches, including EGFR, HER2, and KRAS.

A likely resistance change appeared in just over half the patients, and a third carried two or more. About half the changes altered the drug's own target, while the other half opened a bypass route, most often through RAS and MAPK signaling. Colorectal cancers favored bypass routes, whereas bile duct cancers more often changed the target itself. The authors support blood testing at progression to guide next steps.
pmc-13546873:
Jun-Ze Zheng and co-authors present a cheaper, simpler method for editing genes in Fusarium oxysporum, a fungus that attacks crops and threatens health. Editing this fungus requires first making protoplasts, cells stripped of their walls, and older methods use costly enzymes and fussy steps. The standard editing tool also limits which DNA sites can be targeted and needs complex guide molecules. The team's method makes protoplasts at small scale with a filter column, using far less enzyme. Their editing system uses a different cutting protein with shorter guides and staggered cuts that favor clean repair.

Short DNA arms for the repair template cut the cloning work further. The team verified successful targeting with molecular checks and standard tests of how the edited fungus infects plants. They offer the platform as an affordable toolkit for labs studying how this fungus causes disease, and for screening work in farm biotechnology.
pmc-13547073:
Teng Zhao, Nan Zhang, Yong Tian, and Zhengqiang Yang ask if treating hypothyroidism also repairs kidney function, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. An underactive thyroid can in a quiet way drag kidney performance down. That loss is often misread as ordinary chronic kidney disease. The team set out to see what care for the thyroid does to the kidneys.

Their single-center retrospective study tracked forty hospitalized adults newly diagnosed with hypothyroidism. All of them got levothyroxine as routine care. Blood tests were tracked at admission, when thyroid hormone levels normalized, and when creatinine normalized. Serum creatinine was the main kidney outcome. The title states the top line: hormone replacement was associated with improved renal dysfunction. The team urges clinicians to check thyroid function before they label kidney damage as permanent.
pmc-13547173:
Scott Ling and co-authors show that a normally minor sea snail, swarming in one Tasmanian bay, stripped kelp beds into bare patches, in work from twenty twenty-six. Grazing sea animals can raze kelp forests when they surge. Usually one dominant grazer takes the blame.

Cage experiments on a patchy barren ran for one hundred seventeen days. Where periwinkles were shut out, fleshy algae covered nearly half the ground, many times the cover in open or snail stocked plots. During the study, legal snails were harvested nearby and algae rebounded everywhere except inside the stocked cages. Over sixteen months the kelp crept back as snail weight fell. The authors suspect urchin harvesting released the snail.
pmc-13547273:
Qianqian Bai and colleagues reported in 2026 that a cellular helper protein, HSPA8, fuels the inflammation behind a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The protein was more abundant in the spinal cords of sick mice, in step with disease severity, and concentrated near microglia, the brain's immune cells. Lowering it through spinal injection eased the illness, calmed inflammation, and reduced damage to nerve insulation and fibers.

Cell experiments traced the effect to an internal alarm complex, the NLRP3 inflammasome, which HSPA8 helps both prime and assemble. Without enough HSPA8, inflammatory messengers and a fiery form of cell death fell. Restoring the protein partly reversed the protection. The authors nominate HSPA8 as a drug target for multiple sclerosis and related inflammatory brain diseases.
pmc-13547373:
Tingxing Wu and colleagues built in 2026 a prediction model for how fast the protective epoxy coatings on power equipment break down in humid substations. First they studied how failed coatings change shape and chemistry over service time. Then they fed six environmental and operating factors into a gradient boosting model whose settings were tuned by an automated search method. The factors included peak temperature, daily temperature swing, vibration, humidity, ultraviolet exposure, and service age.

The tuned model explained about 96 percent of the variation in degradation rates and beat support vector and random forest rivals. It matched a far heavier neural network's accuracy while running much faster. Repeated checks across time periods held up, and the authors propose the model for lifespan planning of grid equipment.
pmc-13547473:
Robert Figlin and seven co-authors wrote a health systems article in two thousand twenty-six about patient flow in cancer care. Demand for outpatient cancer care is set to grow, while staff stay scarce and cases grow more complex. Single fixes, such as new clinics or new schedules, have not ended delays in starting treatment.

The authors treat access as one flow, not a set of split scheduling events. Their plan groups the work into entry, throughput, and transition, from referral and tests through to treatment. They argue for one owner for access, and for measures tied to how patients move. The plan uses current resources first, though it still needs record system and staffing support.
pmc-13548273:
Betül Özgan and co-authors present a 2026 study checking how closely feeding practice in Turkish intensive care units follows the guidelines. Malnutrition worsens outcomes for the critically ill, and tube feeding into the gut is preferred over vein feeding because it works with the body. Guidelines spell out timing, rates, and monitoring, but wards drift.

The multicentre study took a one-day snapshot across six intensive care units, recording what each adult patient was actually fed. Comparing practice with the recommendations exposes the common gaps, such as late starts or underfeeding. Point prevalence designs like this give hospitals a cheap mirror: one day's honesty about routine care.
pmc-13548473:
Resta Emanuela and colleagues modeled in 2026 the mental health of Italian regions from 2016 to 2023, blending lifestyle behavior data with environmental, social, and governance indicators drawn from national statistics. The country's mental health index held fairly steady nationally while regional gaps persisted, with the north and center ahead of the south.

Inactivity, smoking, and living with several chronic conditions tracked consistently with worse regional mental health, while good nutrition and city green space looked protective. Job security and effective courts also played a part, which the authors read as mental health being shaped by institutions and surroundings, not only personal habits. Calabria and Campania bucked the southern pattern with notable gains. Policy advice joins lifestyle programs with green investment and better governance.
pmc-13549173:
Elaheh Ghods, Razieh Bandari, and Ali Montazeri translate and test a Persian tool to grade foot self-care in people with diabetes. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Foot sores are a grave risk in diabetes, and a sound local tool is needed to track daily care acts. The team used a forward and back translate, then expert checks and patient chats to fit the tool to local life.

Two patient groups, one near three hundred and one of two hundred fifty, took the tool. Results fell into three parts: upkeep, watch, and response. Scores for trust and steadiness were high, and the shape fit held well. The authors urge more checks before wide clinic use.
pmc-13550573:
Xiaohua Xu, joined by five colleagues, presented a 2026 remote sensing model for picking water bodies out of satellite images. Finding lakes and rivers automatically supports flood control, city planning, and environmental monitoring, yet tangled shapes and limited labeled data cause errors in older methods. Their design, called ResDDSCUNet++, rebuilds a familiar segmentation network for this task.

New building blocks widen the area each decision can draw on, an attention module highlights key information, and a lighter convolution design cuts computing cost. Training mixed labeled examples with self-supervised learning on unlabeled images. In experiments the model beat rival methods, raising two standard accuracy scores by modest margins that the authors report in full.
pmc-13551073:
Dong Luo and Haibo Hu laid out an X-ray-free fix for leaks around man-made mitral valves. Published in 2026, the step-by-step guide covers a skin-through, X-ray-free closure steered only by throat sound scans. Valve-edge leak after valve swap can drive heart failure or blood breakdown.

The guide walks through scan-based sizing, throat-guided septal puncture, sheath placement in the left atrium, wire crossing, and plug drop-off clear of valve discs. Success leans on crisp ultrasound views, and murky or heavily chalky leaks may still need X-ray help. The authors call the approach workable and exact, cutting rays while holding safety in picked patients. Readers get a copy-ready recipe for picked leak closures.
pmc-13551673:
Eugene Ham, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 study asking whether a signaling protein in immune cells drives liver cancer. Hepatocellular carcinoma grows amid many infiltrating myeloid cells, and focal adhesion kinase, called FAK, links adhesion and inflammatory signals. Human tumor data showed higher FAK gene activity in myeloid-rich tumors tied to worse survival, with the strongest pattern in one macrophage type.

The team bred mice lacking FAK only in myeloid cells and triggered liver tumors with an established model. Baseline livers looked normal, and tumor survival, burden, and growth did not change significantly without myeloid FAK in the reported results. Macrophage accumulation inside tumors did fall, so the authors conclude FAK recruits macrophages yet its loss alone cannot slow this cancer.
pmc-13551773:
Franco Poma-Soto, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 benchmark of software that decodes DNA barcodes when copying errors are heavy. Barcodes tag molecules in pooled sequencing, and light-printed arrays reach huge library sizes yet err on ten to twenty percent of letters. The team tested three decoders on simulated and real data across barcode lengths, library sizes, and error rates up to about a third of letters.

A GPU-accelerated tool called QUIK recalled the most barcodes while keeping precision above 99.5 percent at medium error rates in the reported runs, and it processed reads far faster than its rivals. Longer barcodes helped every tool, and on real array data QUIK assigned the most reads with perfect precision, leading the authors to recommend barcodes of at least 34 letters.
pmc-13551873:
Ruohang Sun and co-authors present a 2026 study of a gut worm that calms body-wide inflammation in mice. Parasite worms can tune host immunity, but whether they rewire gut nerve chemicals was unclear. The team infected mice with the worm Trichinella spiralis, then sparked inflammation with a bacterial toxin. Gut tissue chemicals and blood signals were read two weeks after infection.

Worm-infected mice showed lower levels of two flame signals and less lung harm after the toxin. Their gut chemical mix shifted as a team, with some nerve signals up and others down at rest. Under toxin attack, prior infection raised a fresh set of nerve-linked chemicals. The worm thus resets the gut's chemical weather, which may be part of how it calms the host.
pmc-13551973:
Fusel oil is a leftover stream from bioethanol making, rich in rough alcohols. Yuchen Luo and co-authors upgrade it into levulinate esters, valued as green solvents and fuel additives. Their route uses an immobilized enzyme instead of harsh chemistry, and no solvent. Levulinic acid from plant biomass meets the fusel alcohols under mild heat. Under tuned conditions the acid converted almost fully within five hours, with yields near 98 to 99 percent.

A bulkier alcohol reacted less, as docking simulations predicted. The enzyme kept working across five reuse cycles. A run at 100-gram scale also succeeded. The authors present the process as a clean use for a waste stream.
pmc-13552173:
Sourav Lal Das and co-authors compare, in a 2026 study, the Ponseti casting method across two kinds of clubfoot. Clubfoot turns a baby's foot inward, and the Ponseti method corrects it with a series of casts. The team asked whether the method serves feet whose cause is known, such as nerve or syndrome conditions, as well as feet with no clear cause.

Seventy-five children with 105 clubfeet were followed for four years. The unexplained group needed a median of five casts; the explained group needed eight. Tendon release rates were alike. Return of the deformity hit about eight percent of the first group and twenty-one percent of the second. Final success was high in both, near ninety-nine and ninety-five percent. The authors call the method reliable for both, with extra procedures rescuing returns.
pmc-13554273:
Asia Othman Aljahdali presents a federated learning system that spots cyber attacks across spread-out networks without pooling raw data in a 2026 study. Each site trains a small local detector on its own traffic. A central step merges the local models by averaging, while a regularizer keeps local and global models aligned. Calibrated noise added to updates gives formal privacy protection.

On a public benchmark of network traffic, detection accuracy reached near ninety-eight percent. That beat standard federated rivals by about five points. Precision and recall both ran high and balanced. Message costs fell by more than a third, and privacy loss shrank compared with baselines. The author pitches the system for live defence in linked device networks.
pmc-13555073:
Christian-Hendrik Heeger and co-authors report a combined heart procedure study in a 2026 paper. Two procedures for atrial fibrillation, isolating the pulmonary veins and closing the left atrial appendage, are increasingly done alone. They share the same access route, so combining them in one session could benefit patients. The registry study gathered 155 patients from twenty two centers in nine European countries.

The combined procedure succeeded in isolating all veins in every patient and closing the appendage in nearly all. Serious adverse events occurred in about two percent of patients. Follow up imaging found no device movement or device related clots, though small gaps around devices appeared in some patients. Most patients with rhythm follow up stayed in normal rhythm past six months. Readers see one session do the work of two.
pmc-13555873:
R V Shravya, A I Ananthakrishnan, and Ranajit Das compare inherited risk for autoimmune diseases in Indians with and without type 2 diabetes in a 2026 study. Their group held 474 people from Gujarat, ninety-nine of them diabetic. Polygenic scores summed many small gene effects for eleven autoimmune diseases. Two diseases separated the groups clearly.

People with diabetes carried higher genetic risk for lupus. People without diabetes carried higher genetic risk for rheumatoid arthritis. Genes behind the patterns clustered in immune pathways covering antigen display, helper T cell growth, and responses to viruses. The authors frame the split as a clue to how diabetes reshapes immune inheritance, useful for future risk sorting and tailored care.
pmc-13555973:
Wanyue Xu leads a six-author team revealing how skin cells help prune fruit fly nerve branches during development in a 2026 study. Young neurons grow excess branches that later get trimmed for precise wiring. Skin cells were known to eat the trimmed debris afterward. The team found a scaffolding protein, Patronin, working earlier in those skin cells, before any eating begins.

Lowering Patronin in the skin left sensory neuron branches unpruned. The protein normally restrains a surface receptor in skin, which keeps the neuron's own copy working and triggers branch breakage near the cell body. A growth enzyme inside neurons also joined the chain. The work recasts skin as an active signalling partner, not just a cleanup crew.
pmc-13556073:
Xuan Chanh Tran and five colleagues validated in 2026 a built-in dialysis monitor and a machine learning predictor for patients in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Dialysis adequacy is usually judged by a formula-based measure called Kt/V, while machines can estimate the same quantity live through online clearance monitoring. Data from Southeast Asian patients were scarce, so the team compared both measures in 97 people on maintenance dialysis.

The monitor's readings tracked the reference formula very closely, though they ran slightly low on average. Two thirds of patients met guideline adequacy targets. Machine learning models that combined the monitor reading with age and body mass index predicted the continuous value well, and a classification model separated adequate from inadequate treatments almost perfectly in testing. With local calibration, the live monitor could guide sessions in real time.
pmc-13557173:
Dimitra-Danai Varsou and nine co-authors build a joined pipeline that predicts whether a chemical can cause gene mutations, using a cloud platform. Such checks guard health and can swap for animal tests on new materials. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Data came from the Ames test, a bacterial mutation assay, with care for mirror form inputs where needed. The pipeline blends many chemical views, from finger print patterns to 3D traits and molecule graphs. It also blends many model kinds, from classic structure activity models to read across and deep learning. A boost based model and a graph network are part of the mix, with clear reasons for each call.
pmc-13557473:
Audrey Beaufils and a large international group of colleagues built in 2026 an image-based marker that aims to predict which chemotherapy a pancreatic cancer patient will benefit from after surgery. Choice between the two standard regimens, gemcitabine and a modified FOLFIRINOX combination, is usually guided by how fit the patient is rather than by tumour biology. The team trained deep learning models on routine microscope slides from 231 patients treated at several centres.

The score was then checked in a randomised trial cohort of 313 patients, where it separated outcomes within both treatment arms. The authors propose that tumour appearance on ordinary slides carries treatment-relevant information that current practice ignores.
pmc-13558373:
Eef Hoeben and co-authors modeled a leukemia drug for liver cancer in a 2026 study. The drug is a long-acting form of an enzyme that starves cells of a key food building block. It is approved as part of care for a blood cancer of the young, but its worth for solid tumors is far less explored.

Fresh reports hint the enzyme may also work on liver cancer, a hard and fast-growing tumor. The team built a math model that links drug dose to drug action, tuned on lab and animal data. Such a model can forecast how the drug might act in people. It helps pick doses and schedules for first trials in liver cancer.
pmc-13558573:
Alessandro Mondanaro and twelve colleagues rebuild past chimpanzee movements and mixing. Common chimpanzee subspecies show strong geographic separation today, yet their history holds several past introgression events of unknown date and place. Their 2026 study rebuilds past biogeography from cranial morphology and genetics. Western chimpanzees emerge as the most derived lineage.

Cranial shape tracks genetic splits, consistent with western isolation punctuated by contact with other subspecies. Contact moments coincide with warming periods that grew tree cover across the Dahomey Gap, the barrier now separating western chimpanzees from the rest. Past climate swings and vegetation change thus shaped present-day distribution and genetic differences. The work offers a climate-mediated view of chimpanzee evolution.
pmc-13558673:
Mohammad Tahami and three colleagues ground copper ore concentrate in acid in 2026 to break the crust that normally stalls its leaching. Chalcopyrite resists chemical attack because a passivation layer seals its surface. Their mechanochemical approach mills the concentrate in sulphuric acid without oxidants, and one variant uses pyrite itself as the grinding medium so abrasion and galvanic chemistry work together.

Optimised milling recovered about twenty-seven percent of the copper in three hours, seventy percent better than still leaching, while activation energy fell and rates rose several fold. Microscopy confirmed stripped surfaces and fresh mineral exposed. Pyrite media pushed recovery to about forty percent in six hours. Grinding too fine backfired by choking later leaching, so particle size needs control. The authors see industrial promise once periodic milling and oxidant dosing are tuned.
pmc-13558773:
Laura Ospino and five colleagues epoxidised sesame oil in 2026 using solid acid resins instead of dissolved catalysts, a greener route toward bio-based plastics ingredients. Epoxidised vegetable oils feed polymer production, and the trick is converting double bonds into reactive oxygen rings without wrecking them. Two commercial ion exchange resins were compared across three temperatures and three reaction times, with hydrogen peroxide and acetic acid generating the active oxidant in place.

Falling iodine values confirmed the double bonds were consumed, and spectra verified the new oxygen rings. Eighty degrees proved best for both resins, and four hours gave the highest conversions, above ninety-five percent for the stronger resin. Stretching to six hours gained nothing and likely fed side reactions that degrade the rings. The authors map the sweet spot where conversion and ring stability balance.
pmc-13558873:
Siti Nafisah and four colleagues asked in 2026 which ordinary patient traits travel with more worrying ultrasound grades in thyroid nodules. A Korean reporting system sorts nodules into risk classes by their scan appearance, and why some patients land in higher classes was unclear. Their cross-sectional study at a Banda Aceh hospital in Indonesia gathered 109 patients holding 171 nodules, recording age, sex, body mass, and thyroid hormone levels beside the scan grade.

Most patients were women with a median age in the mid forties, and most nodules fell in the two middle risk classes. Age alone tracked with higher grading in first-pass analysis, and it survived in the adjusted model that accounts for several nodules sharing one patient. Sex, body mass, and hormone level showed no clear link. The authors suggest age deserves weight when clinicians judge how hard to chase a nodule.
pmc-13560773:
After a stroke clot is pulled out under general anesthesia, doctors must decide when to remove the breathing tube. Jingjing Fan and co-authors studied one hundred thirty-three such patients to see how intubation time related to recovery. About half the patients had a poor outcome at ninety days, meaning real disability or death, and more than half caught pneumonia in hospital. The analysis adjusted for other risk factors.

Each extra six hours on the tube came with higher odds of a poor outcome and clearly higher odds of pneumonia. Bleeding inside the skull and death were also tracked. The authors read intubation time as a warning marker: patients who stay tubed longer do worse. They are careful that the study cannot prove the tube itself causes the harm, since sicker patients also stay tubed longer. They call for prospective trials to test whether earlier removal improves recovery.
pmc-13561073:
Emrah Işıktekin told of a rare and dangerous face injury in a case report from twenty twenty-six. A nineteen-year-old man hurt the right side of his face during farm work. The cut was stitched shut with no deep check, and two days later he came to hospital with headache and fatigue. Scans told the true story.

A large, crescent-shaped piece of metal sat inside his face, its tip lodged below the skull base, through a sinus and under the brain's hormone gland. Its base reached toward the nose, close to branches of a major face artery. Surgeons took it out through the old wound, under full anesthesia, with a careful turning move. The author warns that face cuts must be fully checked and imaged before they are closed, since a mild-looking wound can hide metal near vital parts.
pmc-13562273:
Jeanette Koeppe and colleagues ask how treatment choice after a shoulder-end fracture shapes older patients' long-term care dependency. Their 2026 propensity-matched analysis uses nationwide German insurance data to compare non-operative care, locked-plate fixation, and reverse shoulder replacement. Most studies of this fracture chase X-ray results; this one chases independence.

Reverse replacement carried a higher risk that a patient's formal care level would deteriorate within a year of the fracture. Locked-plate fixation showed no such difference from non-operative care in the matched comparison. Surgery overall was associated with lower death rates, yet no strategy changed progression to severe dependency or nursing home entry. The authors advise weighing care-level consequences beside survival when choosing treatment for an older patient, and framing the choice around geriatric priorities rather than the fracture film alone.
pmc-13562573:
Verónica Santos-Pulpón and ten colleagues publish a dataset on breathing support in intensive care, built for teams who study how patients and ventilators interact. Waveform-level data from ventilators is rarely kept in standard hospital records, which limits work on mismatches between a patient's effort and the machine's push. The 2026 resource, called RAMIC-I, covers 155 critically ill adults treated at Hospital Universitari Parc Taulí in Sabadell, Spain, between 2015 and 2019. Names were removed before release.

Inside are 13,433 hours of mechanical ventilation from each patient's first eight days, grouped in ten-minute blocks. Clinical details travel alongside: treatments, bedside measures, severity scores, vital signs, and survival outcomes. Derived measures flag patient-ventilator asynchronies, the clashes that can harm lungs. The set follows FAIR sharing principles through a shared repository. The authors aim it at prediction models and at safer, better-tuned ventilation.
pmc-13563573:
N Martínez-Lago and co-authors published this cancer study in 2026 from routine care in Spain. A drug pair, short-named FTD/TPI plus bevacizumab, had already won a large trial in bowel cancer that had spread and resisted two prior rounds of care. The team asked how the pair fares in daily practice. They tracked 549 patients across nineteen Spanish hospitals.

Median survival came to 10.8 months, and the span before the cancer grew again was five months. About half the patients kept the disease in check for a time. Gains did not hinge on sex, gene marks, or past use of like drugs. Patients with less spread and better strength fared best. Low white cell counts were the chief harsh side effect, and two deaths were tied to care. The authors back the pair as a sound late option.
pmc-13563773:
Aylin Taghipour and four colleagues follow 390 patients through the Whipple operation, the sweeping surgery for pancreatic and nearby cancers, with lymph node clearance included. The operation cures some and burdens many, so knowing who gains matters. Their 2026 retrospective study covers one tertiary centre's cases from 2019 to 2023, all of one cancer family to keep the group clean. Follow-up reached 299 patients, about three-quarters, through records and structured phone calls.

Median survival came to 3.5 years, with 69.2 percent alive at one year and 50.6 percent at three. Four traits predicted death: age 65 or over more than doubled the hazard, as did cancer in the lymph nodes, while pancreatic origin and removing fewer than twelve nodes also hurt. Chemotherapy after surgery cut the death hazard by about a third. Recurrence struck hardest in the first three years. The authors press two levers: count and clear nodes properly, and get eligible patients to chemotherapy.
pmc-13566373:
Lara Lewis and colleagues ask, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether moving stable HIV patients to community medicine collection also improves clinic care for people just starting treatment. Those new patients cannot yet use the community option. Records from 112 clinics in KwaZulu-Natal covered 36,865 people who began therapy between February 2022 and September 2023.

When a clinic's community referral share rose from twenty to thirty percent, new patients became slightly more likely to complete key blood tests. The clearest gain was for six-month virus checks. No gain appeared for staying in care at six months. The spillover benefit looks real but small, a useful calibration for claims about freeing clinic capacity.
pmc-13567073:
Mingliang Guo and co-authors published this 2026 study of a rice gene family that shapes plant growth. The genes, called OsEPF and OsEPFL, guide the making of leaf pores, seed husks, and flower clusters. Their roles in fighting stress and disease in rice were far less clear.

The team mapped switch regions ahead of each gene and tracked all family members under heat, cold, drought, and salt. Two genes switched on fast and stayed on under all four stresses, and most members rose under salt. Four genes also jumped within twelve hours of attack by the rice blast fungus. One gene, OsEPF2, proved to matter for disease resistance when tested directly.
pmc-13568073:
Watching a classroom by camera means spotting small, varied behaviors against cluttered backgrounds. Jintao Sun, Jian Wang, and Ming Yu upgrade a detection network for that job in a 2026 paper.

Their Hyper-YOLO variant tackles three problems at once. An attention module in the backbone cleans up features so key behavior channels stand out. A two-way weighted pyramid in the neck balances fine detail against overall meaning across scales. A smarter loss function softens the damage done by poor-quality training samples. On a public classroom data set, the system reached a mean precision score of about seventy-four percent at the standard overlap bar. The authors frame the work as scene-driven tuning, not a new architecture.
pmc-13568173:
Zhao and three co-authors teach a small net to read face moods through blocks in this twenty twenty-six study. Hands, shades, and masks can hide the face cues a mood read needs. Hard drill on fake blocks can fix that, yet it can also blunt reads on clean faces.

Inside, their drill hangs on clean faces as the fixed base for all tests. Fake blocks of set and random shapes are mixed in with face-zone weights. A frozen guide net from a prior stage keeps score spread steady through the drill. The end net scored high on both clean and blocked face sets in trials. Its size stays small, which suits live cam use on light gear.
pmc-13569873: Kim Wouters and co-authors report a heart case in which a phone app helped read a warning ECG, in this 2026 paper. A fifty-three-year-old man arrived with chest pain brought on by effort. His heart tracing showed no classic ST elevation, a pattern that can hide a blocked artery. The tracing and the PMcardio app flagged ischemic changes. Urgent imaging found a clot blocking the main right coronary artery near its start. Doctors opened the vessel, placed two drug-coated stents, and restored blood flow.
pmc-13570073:
Esther Salama, Michael Wolfowicz, and Badi Hasisi set out a plan to review deterrence-based counterterrorism in a 2026 protocol paper. Their question: do government interventions meant to deter domestic terrorism in wealthy OECD countries actually work? The review will follow Campbell Collaboration standards for systematic evidence gathering.

If data allow, multilevel meta-analysis will pool effects while handling studies that report several results. Moderator analysis and meta-regression will probe why effects differ across settings. The authors stress the stakes: findings should steer evidence-based policy and expose where research is thin. As a protocol, the paper fixes the questions and methods before results are gathered, guarding against cherry-picking.
pmc-13571273:
Kiyoto Nishi and co-authors trace how a protein called nardilysin controls a sugar gate gene in insulin-making cells, in a study from 2026. The gene builds GLUT2, the main sugar doorway of these cells. When the doorway fades, insulin release falters and diabetes follows. Mice lacking nardilysin in these cells showed exactly that pattern, but the chain of cause was murky.

The team mapped open DNA regions near the gene and found four enhancer stretches. One conserved enhancer, far downstream, answered to nardilysin in lab tests. The protein sits on that enhancer and helps recruit a second factor, ISLET1. Without it, the helper arrives poorly and the gene quiets. The effect does not run through the usual master switch. The work adds a second control route for a key diabetes gene.
pmc-13571373:
Arturo Giacaman and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a 79-year-old man with torrential leakage of the tricuspid valve whose catheter repair succeeded only after the team switched entry route. They moved from the leg vein to the neck vein. His history included a protein-deposition heart disease, atrial fibrillation, lung hypertension, kidney disease, and repeated heart failure admissions.

The standard leg approach failed because a prominent ridge inside the right atrium pushed the delivery tube off line. Entering through the right internal jugular vein gave a straight path, and two clips reduced the leak from torrential to mild with no harmful narrowing. The case offers a backup route when anatomy blocks the usual one.
pmc-13571673:
A team led by Hanan AlRayes studied rheumatoid arthritis that stays active despite proper drug treatment, a state called difficult to treat. They drew on a registry of nine hundred twenty-eight patients at major centers in Saudi Arabia. Patients were classed by a European standard as difficult to treat or well controlled.

About one in seven met the hard-to-treat mark. Compared with controlled patients, they had worse joint scores, more deformity and swelling, greater disability, and a longer wait before first seeing a doctor. They also stuck to treatment less well. Age at diagnosis, disease length, and activity scores linked to the state on their own. The authors map who needs closer care.
pmc-13571773:
Jonathan Lam and co-authors ask clinicians and data staff what they need from drug harm risk tools. Such tools read patient data to flag who may suffer medication harm. Hospitals adopt them slowly due to workflow and trust snags. The team held semi-structured talks with twenty-two staff in three Australian digital hospitals.

Doctors, pharmacists, and informaticians named trust and felt worth as top drivers. Wanted traits were automation, feedback loops, and fit with daily workflow. Poor links with current systems and doubt about tool soundness blocked uptake. Good feedback systems and sound resource plans helped adoption. The authors map the findings to a known implementation frame for hospitals.
pmc-13571973:
Emine Celiker, Gregory Sutton, and Natasha Mhatre model the tree cricket ear as a sound interferometer in a 2026 paper. Finding sound sources is vital for insects, yet their tiny size blocks the time and loudness cues mammals use. The team used computer models to test how the cricket ear handles sound. Sound splits into two paths that reach two membranes on the front and back of the ear.

The split waves meet again at a shared wall, where their reunion creates interference sensitive to microsecond delays. That is the same principle light based instruments use to measure tiny differences. In sound form, it could let a tiny ear locate sources with striking precision. Readers see a fresh physical account of insect hearing.
pmc-13572573:
Payman Raise-Abdullahi and six co-authors show that stress hormone signals in a brain reward area shape morphine reward in rats, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. The area, the dorsal striatum, helps link places with rewards. Rats learned to favor a chamber paired with morphine, a standard test of drug reward. Before training, the team infused the area with a stress hormone or with drugs that block its two receptor types.

Each of the three infusions blocked the place liking and saved the transporter, with no change in how much the rats moved. The authors say unsettling this hormone system dulls opioid reward at its root.
pmc-13573173:
Eight physicians measure flat feet in children with a Fontan heart circulation in a paper from 2026. After this surgery, the muscle system helps keep blood moving, yet foot shape in these patients was unstudied. The single-center study examined forty-seven patients with a median age of thirteen. Flat feet were checked by physical exam, and body measures were compared between groups. More than half the children had flat feet, across all ages.

Those with flat feet were shorter for their age. Lean mass also tended to run lower, though adjusted analysis fell short of significance. The authors call flat feet an overlooked trait of this population. They urge follow-up work on causes and meaning.
pmc-13573673:
Zhuanhuai Wang, Hengjun Huang, and Hui Li summed up work on an RNA-binding protein in two thousand twenty-six. The protein helps run RNA use in cells. Future studies can build on the comparison.
pmc-13574473:

pmc-13574673:
Songqing Zhao and co-authors profile social alienation among older adults with cognitive frailty in a 2026 study. Readers see why screening belongs in geriatric nursing checks.
pmc-13574773:

Multi-scale handling is central, since a nodule may span a few pixels or a broad patch in the same scan. Sharper calls at low compute cost would suit mass screening, where scans pile up fast. The authors frame the work as a step toward screening that catches cancer while it is still curable.
pmc-13575773:

Vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and calcium form one regulatory circuit, and insulin function depends on calcium signaling. The twenty twenty-six multicenter snapshot covers a multicultural population rarely represented in vitamin D research.
pmc-13575973:

The fifty-one-year-old came in with left testicular pain, and ultrasound showed a mass. Removal of the testicle revealed a Leydig cell tumor, a rare type making up only one to two percent of testicular tumors. Staging scans then found a large mass at the front of the chest. pmc-13577173:
Jiao Han, in a 2026 essay, questions how purpose in life is measured in older adults after work ends. Drawing on work about goals, time views, and retirement, the essay finds later-life purpose to be varied and many-sided. It can rest on close ties, daily acts, faith, or simply feeling that one matters. Some older adults find purpose in the present rather than in long plans, and some see it as not relevant at all.
pmc-13577273:
Nienke Bosma and colleagues ask women who disclosed sexual assault to a gynecologist or midwife what helped and what hurt, in this Dutch qualitative study from twenty twenty-six. Second, initiative: women want the clinician to raise the subject, explain how assault can connect to symptoms, and arrange follow-up, rather than waiting for a confession. Third, control: over how much detail to share, what words are used, what enters the record, and who is in the room. The authors turn the themes into teaching points for trauma-informed gynecology and midwifery.
pmc-13577973:
Anthony Grey and six co-authors build local models to turn a quick burn test into a gauge of carbon in sea mud. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Split models for high-mud and low-mud samples fit better than one pooled model, though the low-mud one stays less sure. They urge clear reports of range and error.
pmc-13578173:

Some gene-defined groups still fare poorly, among them forms with extra gene loss, a key guard gene changed, or too few chromosomes. Early use of immune drugs can deepen response. Relapse remains the hard problem. The review maps the new risk lines and the open choices in care.
pmc-13578273:
Inga-Liina Järvinen and colleagues give a 2026 chemical sketch of oak acorns gathered in Finland, where the nuts are plentiful yet little used. Fresh acorns stood out for plant sterols and vitamin E type compounds. Dried nuts held more long waxy chains, while dried shells showed sterols plus long chain scent compounds. The water loving side held tannins, plant acids, and pigment compounds. The work is a map, not a measure, since amounts were not counted. pmc-13579073:
Ligia Goes Endo and six co-authors present a 2026 study of hidden fentanyl exposure among users of synthetic cannabis like drugs in São Paulo, Brazil. Brazil has long had low opioid use, but seizures of fentanyl keep rising. The lab made drugs these users take have erratic contents, so exposure can happen without their knowledge.

The team recruited 65 people who had used the drugs within the past four days, from treatment and community care centers. Spit samples were tested for fentanyl and compared with what each person said they had taken. The study measures the gap between self report and lab proof in this group.
pmc-13579373:
Ayper Onal Alkan and Ukke Karabacak translate a scale for risk of pressure injury, and check that it works, for Turkish patients in intensive care. Their 2026 study is methodological. It adapts the CALCULATE tool, made to make risk checks in critical care more easy.

About twenty percent got pressure injuries in the study. Agreement among experts on content validity was full. Agreement between the two raters was strong, by standard statistical measures. How well it could forecast was read for the first and seventh days, with standard curves. Pressure injuries can, in large part, be stopped in advance. pmc-13579773:
Peng Fang and colleagues teach computers to tell generalized anxiety apart from major depression using resting brain scans, in a 2026 study. Five learning methods were raced inside a strict nested testing frame to keep scores honest. Sorting was fair to good: the tools separated depressed patients from healthy adults best, and the two patient groups from each other least well. One hub region at the back of the brain, the precuneus, stood out as the sharpest divider. Its activity rose with anxiety severity yet fell with depression severity, a mirror pattern the authors flag for diagnostic tools.
pmc-13579873:
Fengqian Yang and colleagues harvest a fructose rich slime from a salt loving bacterium found in Qinghai saline soil, in a 2026 study. It held together until a high heat near two hundred seventy six degrees, dissolved well in water, and soaked up more than three times its weight in oil. Under the lens it formed a dense, layered web. The authors suggest trials as a stabilizer for hot food processing and as a helper for healing salty, alkaline soils.
pmc-13580273:
Jialin Li and colleagues grow a porous ceramic skeleton to host better cathodes for proton carrying fuel cells, in a 2026 study. Baking heat governed how well the sponge linked up. The praseodymium based catalyst won clearly, posting very low resistance at seven hundred degrees in damp air. A full cell with that cathode peaked near half a watt per square centimeter and ran steady for over seven hundred hours. It also survived one hundred hours of switching between power making and splitting modes.
pmc-13582073:

After one year, filtration rose in four of six cilostazol patients but fell in all aspirin-only patients, and the yearly decline ran slower with cilostazol. Over about 6.7 years, dialysis started in two cilostazol patients versus four on aspirin alone, and strokes hit two aspirin-only patients versus none with cilostazol. The authors call for larger trials to confirm these early signals.
pmc-13582473:

Lab tests showed that treated germs held more of a dye that the pump would often expel. The authors present the compound as a candidate helper for the drug ciprofloxacin. pmc-13582973:
Wang and colleagues present in 2026 MindTS-MMD, a Chinese multimodal dataset for studying emotional expression in children with Tourette syndrome, the condition marked by involuntary tics. Resources for this pediatric clinical group barely exist in any language.

The dataset holds 10,034 samples from 60 children aged six to twelve, recorded during semi-structured tasks designed to elicit emotion. The team checked annotation reliability, signal quality, and synchronization, and supplies baseline computer models showing the released representations can be used for analysis.
pmc-13583673:
