Side effects were mild, though results varied with syndrome rules, treatment type, and course length.
pmc-13583773:
Paul Matte and others surveyed cancer care workers in France and Belgium in two thousand twenty-six. Health care emits large amounts of greenhouse gas. Oncology's own footprint is poorly known. A nameless survey ran through professional networks. Hundreds of workers answered a full survey. Roles ranged from cancer doctors to nurses and others.

Two-thirds saw cancer care as worse for the planet than other fields. Most of those who answered worked in large cancer centers. Views on greener practice were asked about broadly. Whether they would change choices hinged on proof from science. Age and role patterns were noted for context. The survey maps how ready the field is for greener cancer care. Evidence will decide how far practice changes.
pmc-13584273:
Jian Liu, Yuqin Wang, Min Wu, and Hui Wang study a special class of immune cells in ovarian cancer in this 2026 paper. The cells, called Vγ9Vδ2 T cells, can be grown in large numbers and kill tumour cells, so doctors hope to use them as a living treatment. In solid tumours such as ovarian cancer, though, they often lose their punch for reasons that are not yet clear.

Working with public cancer databases and lab cultures, the team focused on a tumour protein named BTN3A1. High levels of that protein switched the T cells on at first, then pushed them toward wear-out and death. Blocking the cells' own receptor removed that wearing effect. The authors propose that easing this pathway could make T-cell transfer work better for ovarian cancer.
pmc-13585073:
Ana Cerón-Zapata and two co-authors follow in 2026 children born with a cleft lip and palate in Medellín, Colombia. Children diagnosed before birth may get a head start, since mothers can prepare and babies receive a shaping device early. Both study groups got that device plus personal coaching for mothers on oral care.

Teeth were checked over the first three years of life. Cavities appeared in both groups despite the coaching. At age two the early-diagnosed group showed more hollowed lesions; at three the later group showed more early ones. Neither gap was statistically firm, and cavity risk scores matched. The authors call tooth decay in these children a public health problem needing stronger programs.
pmc-13585273:
Amanuel Gebrekidan and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, how wealth gaps shape newborn care after birth in Tanzania. Good postnatal care cuts newborn and child deaths, yet national data on care that is both received and of real quality were scarce.

Using the 2022 national health survey, the team analyzed more than four thousand mothers who had given birth in the prior two years. A standard concentration index measured how effective care tilts toward richer families. A decomposition then split that tilt among its drivers, such as education, residence, and service access. The breakdown tells planners which levers could narrow the gap fastest.
pmc-13586073:
Tobechukwu Ndika and co-authors pool studies on kidney cancer that has spread to the spine, in work from 2026. They ask whether survival and symptom relief improved in reports from 2017 onward, a period of newer drugs and radiation methods. Pain and nerve deficits are the top reasons such patients seek care.

The pool held sixty-three studies and 1,968 patients treated from 1986 to 2024. Later reports showed better median survival across surgery, radiation, and drug care than earlier ones. Gains were large in the radiation and drug groups. Relief of pain and nerve signs was also weighed by era. The authors say modern combined care has shifted outlook for this hard group.
pmc-13586773:
Yi-Jui Liu and colleagues use a special MRI method to study a slim strip of tissue beside the brain's top center line. That strip, the parasagittal dura, sits where fluid pathways, drainage channels, and veins meet, and it may help clear waste from the brain. Standard scans cannot easily separate its water movement from the fluid and brain around it. Ten healthy volunteers underwent high-detail scans at a strong field strength.

The method, called IVIM imaging, splits water motion into true spreading and flow-like motion. The dura strip landed between spinal fluid and brain tissue on plain spreading, while showing stronger flow-related signals than brain tissue itself. Two ways of running the scan agreed closely, one with less warping and one with cleaner signal. The authors offer the measures as a no-dye way to probe brain fluid movement.
pmc-13587073:
Jiayan Ding and colleagues reviewed studies comparing how accurately doctors and trainees diagnose skin disease on light skin versus skin of colour. Skin tone changes how rashes and spots look, so the same training may not serve every patient equally.

The team screened 3,724 articles and kept 16 studies, all from North America or Europe. Most studies used image quizzes or written cases rather than real clinic visits, and only three tracked real misdiagnosis rates. Eleven studies found worse diagnostic accuracy on skin of colour than on light skin overall. Certainty in the pooled evidence rated very low, so Ding calls for stronger, real-world studies of the gap.
pmc-13587373:
Siyi Liu and colleagues show how stomach cancer uses a surface protein to hide from the immune system's garbage collectors. The protein, CD90, sits high on gastric cancer cells, a cancer that ranks among the world's top killers and often surfaces late. Macrophages should eat such cells, but a signal pair called CD47 and SIRP alpha tells them not to. This 2026 study ties CD90 to that do-not-eat signal.

CD90 acted as a scaffold that shielded a second protein, IGF2BP2, from being tagged for disposal. With that shield in place, IGF2BP2 steadied the message that builds CD47, so the do-not-eat order stayed strong and macrophages held back. Tumors rich in CD90 also drew in more macrophages. Breaking any link in this chain, the authors suggest, could unmask the cancer for immune clearance.
pmc-13587473:
A team including Ghyslain Mombo-Ngoma asks whether past malaria bouts raise the risk that a standard treatment fails. The study re-reads data from a large trial in Gabon of a two-drug malaria cure used in real-world care. Near two thousand patients, most of them children, were included in the main count. Prior bouts were drawn from study records rather than memory, which can mislead.

In the strict count, about eight in each hundred patients saw the malaria return. The team weighed whether the count of past bouts predicted that return, with other traits taken into account. The paper gives a firmer read on a risk factor that clinics often guess at.
pmc-13587573:
Weihai Shi and co-authors relate body weight to lung trouble after spine surgery in children in a 2026 study. Straightening a scoliotic spine is long surgery, and lung complications afterward are common. Charts for 1,165 young patients at three Chinese hospitals were analyzed for whether starting body mass index predicted those complications.

About twenty-eight percent of patients developed a lung complication. Surprisingly, each step up in body mass index came with lower odds, and thin patients fared worst, a pattern that held after adjusting for other risks. Possible middlemen, nutrition score, blood loss, and fusion length, were probed, and a prediction model gained only a little from adding body mass. The finding flips the usual worry that heavier patients face more risk.
pmc-13588273:
Haotian Chen and co-authors present a 2026 study of a protein that helps bladder cancer grow. The protein, PYCR1, helps cells manage building blocks, but it may also drive tumors in ways past work missed. The team mapped how much of it sits in bladder tumors and what it partners with inside the cell.

Tumor data and lab tests showed PYCR1 runs high in bladder cancer and boosts cell growth and spread. Mice carrying the tumors showed the same push. The team found the protein binds a partner, NUDT5, which helps make energy units inside the cell core. That link switches on a growth signal chain in the tumor cells. Blocking the pair could offer a fresh drug angle for a common cancer.
pmc-13589373:
Zheng and colleagues validated in 2026 a Chinese version of a scale measuring nurses' attitudes toward telehealth. Telehealth lets nurses monitor and guide patients remotely, but no trusted attitude tool existed for China. The team translated and adapted the Nurses' Attitudes Towards Telehealth Scale, then tested it on 452 nurses from large hospitals in Hubei Province. The scale has nineteen items in three dimensions: satisfaction, rejection, and development.

The Chinese scale proved reliable, with strong internal consistency and stable scores on retesting. Experts rated its content as sound, and factor analysis confirmed the three-part structure fit well. Fit indices all met standard thresholds for a good model. The authors conclude the scale works well for measuring Chinese nurses' attitudes toward telehealth.
pmc-13589873:
Wang and co-authors trace a copper-driven cell death pathway in children whose sepsis injures the lungs. Their 2026 paper studies cuproptosis, a recently described death process controlled by the protein FDX1. Blood cells came from 40 healthy children, 30 with sepsis alone, and 30 with sepsis plus acute lung injury, backed by cell and mouse experiments.

FDX1 and two partners, the transcription factor SF1 and the regulator cJUN, were all raised in sepsis, and highest when lungs were injured. Forcing FDX1 up worsened cell injury, inflammation, and cuproptosis, while silencing it protected the cells. Mechanistically, SF1 binds the FDX1 gene's promoter to switch it on, and SF1 physically partners with cJUN so the two amplify that activation together. Removing cJUN cancelled the SF1 effect. The authors name this axis as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13590473:
Yi Chen and ten colleagues report, in 2026, that a sleep drug may fight glioma, a harsh brain tumor with few good treatments. The drug, tasimelteon, is approved for sleep rhythm disorders and reaches the brain well. In lab tests it slowed glioma cell growth in step with dose and time. The team traced the effect to ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fat damage.

Tasimelteon raised a gene called ACSL4 by steadying its switch, a protein named SP1, the team found. In mice with glioma grafted into the brain, the drug curbed tumor growth and lengthened life. No clear harm to major organs showed up. Chen and colleagues offer the drug as a candidate worth testing in patients.
pmc-13591173:
Adam Friedman and colleagues reviewed shockwave therapy for patellar tendinopathy, the jumper's-knee tendon disorder. Focal and radial extracorporeal shockwave therapy are noninvasive options, but their evidence needed synthesis. Their systematic review and meta-analysis searched three databases to May 2025 and kept 13 studies totalling 899 participants, measuring pain on a visual scale and function on the VISA score.

Shockwave cut pain by 2.53 points, from 5.24 to 2.71, and raised function by 20.22 points, from 54.65 to 74.86, both beyond clinically meaningful thresholds, with large effect sizes. Randomised trials were mostly low-bias, and evidence certainty ranged from high to low across studies. The authors present shockwave as a viable option when conservative care fails, while calling for standardised protocols.
pmc-13591273:
Van Trung Hoang and five colleagues report a rare cause of sharp belly pain in a 57 year old woman. She arrived with two days of pain low on her right side, a classic sign of appendicitis. Scans instead showed a swollen epiploic appendage, a small fat pouch on the gut wall, sitting at the base of her appendix. The pouch had twisted and died, with mild swelling of the appendix itself.

Surgery confirmed what the scan suggested, and she recovered after the operation. Epiploic appendages hang along the large gut on thin stalks, so they twist easily and can mimic far more common ills. Hoang and the team stress that a careful scan read can spare patients a wrong call and guide the right treatment.
pmc-13592173:
Sara Ascenso studied orchestral players who lead community music in a 2026 paper. Community projects have spread fast, and they build joy, purpose, and social skill in the people who take part. The players who run them, though, have rarely been asked what the work does for them.

Ascenso drew on two London projects where players from two major orchestras made new music with primary school children. Through close interviews she traced how the work feeds a player's own flourishing. Gains such as purpose and fresh pride came through. The study gives arts funders a look at the giver's side of the gift.
pmc-13592473:
Lara Bücheler and colleagues compared two MRI morphometry algorithms for finding focal cortical dysplasia before epilepsy surgery. They retrospectively analyzed high-resolution 3-Tesla scans from 32 patients with 34 histologically confirmed lesions. The volume-based MAP18 program and the surface-based MELD program were judged against lesion masks for detection, precision, and recall.

MAP18 found 33 of 34 lesions and MELD found 32 of 34, with agreement on 32 lesions. MELD proved significantly more precise at both cluster and voxel level, with a median of zero false-positive clusters per patient against three for MAP18. Both algorithms matched the seizure onset zone well, and 87.5 percent of patients achieved seizure freedom. Combined use may sharpen presurgical planning.
pmc-13594473:
David T. Zhang, Abhijeet Singh, Eric J. Rashba, and Roger Fan present a rare rhythm puzzle in which one heartbeat from the atria produced two ventricular beats. Their 2026 report explains the double ventricular response, a sign of dual pathways through the atrioventricular node, occurring alongside the common circling rhythm known as AV nodal reentrant tachycardia.

Ordinarily a single impulse chooses either the node's fast road or its slow road. Here it traveled down both at once. The authors show this is possible when the slow pathway conducts almost not at all in the upward direction. That leaves it free for the downward trip. One treatment settled both problems: ablating the slow pathway abolished the double response and the tachycardia together. The case gives clinicians a tidy mechanism for an otherwise baffling tracing.
pmc-13595473:
Grant Creaney and co-authors study health system factors in late diagnosis of head and neck cancer in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Late stage at diagnosis worsens outcomes for this cancer. The study drew on interviews in two city cancer centers, Glasgow and Montevideo.

Twenty-nine patients and clinicians were interviewed in depth, and themes were drawn from the transcripts with a set frame. Sixteen themes and forty-five subthemes came out of the work. Key points were public grasp of risk and signs, how well patients can reach and move through care paths, gaps tied to wealth and place, and how teams work across services. The authors aim to guide service changes that catch the cancer sooner.
pmc-13595673:
David Lerma-Irureta and colleagues compared eighty-five adults with long COVID against eighty-five recovered peers in Spanish primary care to find what drags quality of life down most in the lingering illness. Their 2026 matched study measured quality of life alongside depression, fatigue, sleep, pain attitudes, walking capacity, and daily functioning.

The long COVID group scored dramatically lower on quality of life. They also scored worse on nearly everything else. Fatigue and depression scores were far heavier, sleep was poorer, and the six-minute walk ran roughly seventy-five meters shorter. Fewer than four in ten were employed, against eight in ten controls, and more carried additional post-COVID conditions. Modeling within the long COVID group then singled out the factors independently tied to the worst quality of life. The authors say care should treat the whole biopsychosocial cluster, not chase single symptoms.
pmc-13595773:
Qian Gao and four co-authors show that a small RNA strand worsens severe pancreas swelling by driving an iron linked cell death, in a 2026 journal article. The severe form of the illness brings whole body swelling and organ failure. Small RNA strands that tune genes have been tied to the damage.

Blood from 130 patients and one hundred healthy adults showed the strand ran high in the illness, and higher still in severe cases. Its level tracked a standard severity score and split severe from mild cases well. In lab pancreas cells, a toxin raised the strand and set off the iron death, marked by iron build up and lost guards. Blocking the strand eased the harm. The strand acts by muting a gene that feeds the cell's shield.
pmc-13596973:
Singh and seven colleagues study gallbladder surgery outcomes by ethnicity in twenty twenty-six. Hispanic patients get gallstone disease more often than others. Emergency gallbladder removal carries higher death risk than planned surgery. The team asked whether ethnicity links to surgery type and death.

A national surgical database held nearly four hundred eighty thousand cases from two thousand five to twenty nineteen. Hispanic patients had higher odds of emergency rather than outpatient surgery. They also had more unplanned operations overall. Yet their odds of dying within thirty days were much lower. That advantage held for both planned and unplanned surgery. The authors flag the access pattern as a disparity worth fixing.
pmc-13597173:
Nicole Jackson and Laura Tafe review duties to the unidentified dead in the US. Their review from twenty twenty-six deals with remains in examiner offices. Thousands of remains lie unnamed across the land.

Naming is step one to closure for kin and to justice. Forensic artists and photographers work to retell each story. Sketches serve both naming and remembrance at once. Respect, dignity, and no harm guide this post death work. Gaps between the missing and the found are also probed. The scale is called a silent mass disaster.  Families wait on those names for closure.
pmc-13597973:
Tomohiro Takeda and co-authors report a rare case of rectal cancer coming back in the skin, in a paper from 2026. A man aged seventy-seven had surgery for low rectal cancer. The surgery removed the rectum and the anus through a combined approach, and tests showed the cancer had not spread to lymph nodes.

Scans three months later showed a soft spot near the tailbone that stayed stable and was judged a normal change after surgery. More than two years later, bleeding led doctors to find a sore lump in the skin of the perineum. Tests showed it was the same cancer type, and it was cut out with clear edges. The authors stress that follow-up after such surgery should include close checks of the skin in that area.
pmc-13598073:
Jialin Xiang and co-authors pooled ninety brain imaging studies of local activity synchrony. The studies covered 3,764 patients with depression, bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia. They also covered 3,590 healthy controls. The team asked what these three diagnoses share in the brain and where they part ways. Their 2026 meta-analysis searched the literature to March 2025.

One shared signature emerged: heightened local synchrony in the right inferior frontal gyrus across all three disorders. The differences spread by diagnosis. Depression-specific changes sat mainly in the default mode and subcortical networks, bipolar changes concentrated in the default mode network, and schizophrenia showed the broadest dysfunction, reaching into frontoparietal and movement networks. The authors argue the blend of one common node and distinct network fingerprints supports a transdiagnostic view, useful for precision diagnosis and for choosing treatment targets patient by patient.
pmc-13600473:
Sajan Pandya sets out a step-by-step protocol for replacing a lead investigator mid-trial in a 2026 report. Multi-site studies of high-risk devices run under a strict federal exemption framework. Every site needs an unbroken chain of investigator authorization, which a sudden departure breaks.

The protocol splits each handover into four gates. First comes a continuity review of the study's state, then qualification of the successor. Authorization transfer follows, and a final verification gate releases the site to resume. Poorly run handovers stall enrollment and leave approval lapses that regulators love to find. The method grew from long cardiovascular device trials, where such swaps are routine. Sponsors gain a checklist where the literature offered almost none.
pmc-13600773:
Miranda Cumpston and co-authors present a 2026 report on a living guideline program for pregnancy and newborn care in Australia. Static guidelines age fast as new proof lands. The LEAPP program, set up in 2023, turns the national pregnancy guide into a living one and builds a fresh living guide for care after birth. A wide team of health groups and colleges backs the work.

Questions are ranked with clinician and parent input. For each, proof is reviewed by set methods, and context such as cost and fairness is weighed. Draft advice passes parent and clinician panels, and all 25 partner groups must agree before release. Watch teams keep scanning for new proof. The model aims to keep national advice current month by month.
pmc-13600873:
Xiaoli Zhang, Peiwen Dong, Minfang Lian, and Lin Li link early famine to adult liver disease in a 2026 paper. Poor nutrition early in life reshapes the body and raises later disease risk. The team studied people examined at a hospital in western China.

They sorted 4,188 adults by their age during the Great Chinese Famine. Those exposed before birth had higher rates of fatty liver disease, both mild and worse grades. Exposure during childhood showed no clear link. The models adjusted for weight, blood sugar, blood pressure, and blood fats. Extra checks on the famine birth years backed the finding.
pmc-13601473:
Debbie Chung and colleagues lay out a trial testing whether better sleep plus exercise can slow Alzheimer's risk. Dementia affects over 55 million people, mostly Alzheimer's, and no cure exists, so modifiable risks matter. Their protocol, called CASE, runs eight weeks at one site with 60 adults aged 55 to 80, with or without mild cognitive impairment, randomised to exercise only, sleep only, or both.

Sleep gains will be tracked against thinking scores and blood markers of brain and heart-metabolic health, as will exercise effects and any combined synergy, with light exposure as a possible sleep modulator. Programs mix in-person sessions with headbands, Fitbit trackers, and light sensors. Chung and colleagues aim to inform larger multi-site trials of scalable digital prevention.
pmc-13602373:
Baibhav Barbaruah, Rahmadani Airlangga, and Hidetaka Ito study a jumping gene in a small plant that wakes up under heat. The gene stretch, called ONSEN, is normally kept quiet by chemical marks on its DNA. Its end regions carry many docking sites for heat shock factors, the switches that fire under heat stress. The team mapped those sites and compared them with other jumping genes.

ONSEN's ends held far more switch sites than its peers, and heavier silencing marks at rest. Computer tests showed no simple swap keeps the heat response. Across plant strains, the sites stayed in place even as the letters changed. The paper shows how heat response, silencing, and variation meet in one stretch of DNA.
pmc-13603873:
Machado and co-authors evaluated a 2026 set of quinoidal compounds, redox active molecules, against Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind African sleeping sickness. New treatments are needed because current drugs are limited, toxic, or hard to deliver in rural settings. Twenty-four previously described derivatives were tested in cell culture.

Several compounds killed the parasite potently, Machado reports, but most also harmed human kidney and liver cells in parallel tests. Only quinone-triazole hybrids showed significant antiparasitic activity as a class in the whole series of compounds. One compound stood out with strong potency plus the best selectivity margins over both human cell lines tested. Computer analysis confirmed the novelty of its scaffold against this parasite, and the authors propose it as a platform for safer analogues.
pmc-13605173:
Yao Yao and four co-authors measure retinal blood vessels in children at high altitude in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Retinal vessel width may reveal how eyes and bodies grow together. Children in Lhasa, living high above sea level, had not been charted.

Over fourteen hundred children, near age eight, gave fundus photos and eye measures. Longer eyes went with narrower retinal arteries and veins, and myopic children showed the same pattern. Lower blood oxygen tracked wider arteries. Once the team corrected for eye magnification, the length links faded away. Girls had longer vessel widths than boys on both measures. The authors stress that magnification correction is essential in such studies.
pmc-13606473:
Ioannis Voutsadakis wrote a 2026 study of the genomic patterns of well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. These tumors can grow slowly for decades, but their course is unpredictable and sometimes aggressive. The two markers used to grade them, the Ki67 index and the mitotic index, cannot capture an individual patient's trajectory.

Voutsadakis downloaded data from two genomic series of these tumors from the cBioPortal database. He looked for subsets of tumors with divergent genetic characteristics. Distinct genomic patterns could serve as better prognostic biomarkers. They could also point to rational drug targets matched to each subset. The study addresses an unmet need for therapies shown to extend survival in this uncommon cancer.
pmc-13607173:
Ulugun and eight co-authors measure cell death gene activity in resected lung cancer, in work from twenty twenty-six. Necroptosis is a regulated, inflammatory form of cell death run by three proteins named in the title. Its clinical relevance in lung cancer was uncertain.

Tumor tissue from forty-one patients who had complete surgical removal of non small cell lung cancer was tested. Transcript levels of the three genes were linked with survival outcomes. The single center study is exploratory: small, but it tests whether a death pathway that tumors may suppress leaves a measurable signature tied to prognosis.
pmc-13607573:
Joanna Wojciula and co-authors follow patients who had genital or throat warts removed and began HPV vaccination at the same time, in a study from 2026. All 350 patients also carried HPV type 16 or 18, types tied to cancer risk. Some had weak immune systems, which can make HPV disease more severe.

Patients got either a two-type or a four-type vaccine, starting on the day of surgery and finishing over 12 months. Checks ran at set points for years, in some cases past 15 years. At three years, only 5 percent needed wart removal again, with no gap between the vaccine groups. No pre-cancer cell changes or cancers were found, and tests found none of the tracked HPV types. The authors note the study had no untreated comparison group.
pmc-13608173:
Omar Hassan, Hadi Hassan, Shuvam Prasai, Fiza Rajput, and Julio Garcia published a study in 2026 on swirling blood flow inside the heart's left atrium in patients with atrial fibrillation. The erratic rhythm lets blood stagnate and clot, and a vein-isolation ablation is the standard fix. How the treatment changes the atrium's vortex patterns, not just its stagnation, was unclear.

Four-dimensional flow MRI measured vorticity and vortex size in 107 patients before ablation, 56 after, and 19 healthy controls. Before treatment, vorticity ran low; after ablation it matched the controls. Vortex volume, though, stayed enlarged in both patient groups. Spin strength recovers while the swollen swirl remains, the authors note, so the two measures report different sides of the remodeling.
pmc-13608373:
In dry salt-lake regions, rock salt is close at hand while good soil and gravel are scarce, so builders compact salt into fills. Liyang Wang and six co-authors studied how such fills gain strength as they dry, in a 2026 paper. They varied water, brine content, and packing level, then crushed samples to measure strength.

Strength rose slowly at first, then fast at low water, as salt bridges replaced water bridges between grains. Saltier mixes started weaker but ended far stronger once dry, and mid-to-high packing gave the best result. The team built a formula that predicts strength from these factors for field use.
pmc-13609273:
Jiangyong An and colleagues show that feeding a medicinal herb more nitrogen makes it grow bigger and heal weaker, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Persicaria capitata is a prized Miao medicine from Guizhou, valued for its flavonoids. Farmers had noticed that nitrogen fertilizer cut those compounds, but the machinery was unknown.

In pots, nitrogen stretched stems, multiplied branches, and raised yield, peaking at a middle dose. Gene and metabolite profiling explained the cost. Over ten thousand genes changed activity, most switching down, and one hundred sixty-eight flavonoids shifted. Core flavonoids fell as nitrogen rose, because the assembly-line genes for making them were dialed down. The pathways involved center on phenylpropanoid and flavonoid production. The authors frame a trade-off growers must manage: nitrogen buys bulk at the price of potency.
pmc-13610273:
Chatchaya Ponsuremas and four co-authors build a paint-on film that feeds a plant compound through skin, in this twenty twenty-six study. The compound, found in vine tea, fights cell damage and may refresh skin, but it barely dissolves in water and crosses skin poorly.

Their mix is spread as a liquid and dries in place into a film, using a pharmacy polymer as the film base. The team tuned the recipe by testing drying time, stretch, vapor flow, and skin passage. The aim was more compound into the skin and less into the blood. The work may serve creams that need steady, local dosing.
pmc-13610773:
Sweetened drinks are tied to many health problems, and the two authors asked whether they also track with mental distress. They used the 2013 to 2016 Nutrition and Health Survey in Taiwan, covering 3,787 adults aged 19 to 64. A food frequency questionnaire measured how often people drank sugar-sweetened beverages, and a 24-hour recall captured nutrients. Logistic regression linked drink frequency to psychological distress.

Distress risk was higher at every level of weekly intake. The adjusted odds were 1.75 for one to six drinks a week, 1.56 for seven to thirteen, and 1.99 for fourteen or more. The heaviest drinkers also ate fewer whole grains, vegetables, fruits, and nuts, and more fried foods, desserts, and snacks. The authors conclude that sweet drink intake is positively tied to distress, and they call for intervention studies to test which way the link runs.
pmc-13614273:
Daniela Silva Gonçalves and three co-authors set a standard lab protocol for testing natural products on bacteria that shun oxygen. Their 2026 paper targets microbes that die in open air. Such germs live in the human gut and can cause infections when chances arise. Testing drugs on them is often skipped, since keeping air out is hard.

The protocol finds the lowest drug dose that stops growth in tiny wells of broth. All steps run in a sealed chamber with no oxygen at all. Small volumes let staff screen many samples at once. Tweaks to older guidelines keep the germs alive from start to finish. The method suits labs hunting new drugs from plants and other natural sources. Results repeat well, with no air spoiling the test.
pmc-13614473:
Alycia Galindo and five co-authors grow spinal interneurons inside an injectable hydrogel designed to mimic central nervous system tissue, in a two thousand twenty-six biomaterials paper. V2a interneurons relay motor signals and are a hopeful treatment for spinal cord injury.

The hydrogel crosslinks hyaluronic acid and alginate through hydrazone bonds, and its stiffness was tuned to match neural tissue. Cell-adhesive peptides derived from extracellular matrix proteins were added to support neurons. Mouse embryonic stem cell aggregates embedded in the gel differentiated toward V2a interneurons, doubling expression of the marker Chx10 versus controls. Peptide-bearing gels also made longer neurites, supporting future repair applications.
pmc-13614873:
Bruno Costa Poltronieri leads a team asking whether more hours of digital brain training give older adults longer-lasting gains in thinking and daily function. Participants were aged 60 or older and had mild neurocognitive disorder, a stage of thinking decline beyond normal ageing. In a double-blind trial, groups received either the training or standard computer games as a control, stepping up from 10 to 20 hours of practice.

Sixty-seven people finished the training and were tested before, after each dose, and at follow-up visits. The 20-hour group improved in daily function and satisfaction, plus processing speed, word fluency, and self-control, and kept much of the gain at three and six months. The 10-hour group improved in narrower areas. The results suggest dose matters: enough practice may be what turns short gains into lasting independence.
pmc-13614973:
A rare, slow cancer of the parotid saliva gland has too few cases for trials, so pooled case data carry the evidence. Francesco Chiari and co-authors gathered sixty-eight patients from twenty-three studies spanning nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-five. The average age at diagnosis was about fifty-nine. Five-year disease-free survival reached about eighty-four percent, and disease-specific survival about ninety-three percent. About thirty-one percent of tumors came back, mostly at the first site.

Missing extra therapy after surgery and tumor growth along nerves each cut disease-free time. Positive cut edges hurt disease-specific survival. Late returns past five years are on record, so long follow-up is advised. The pooled numbers give surgeons firmer ground for advising patients.
pmc-13615473:
Erica L Kenney, Matthew M Lee, Rebecca S Mozaffarian, and Eric B Rimm published a study in 2026 on keeping toddlers enrolled in a food support program. The WIC program feeds low-income mothers and young children, but many families drift away after infancy as paperwork piles up and benefits feel thin. Two changes, remote services in twenty twenty and a richer fruit and vegetable benefit in twenty twenty-one, aimed to reverse that.

The team tracked Massachusetts enrollment month by month from twenty seventeen through twenty twenty-two, covering nearly two hundred forty thousand children. They measured whether children certified as infants were still active at each later age, and whether families actually redeemed food benefits. Comparing the trend before and after each change tests whether easing access, raising value, or both keeps families in.
pmc-13615673:
Young and five co-authors studied in twenty twenty-six how hoverflies react when a shape seems about to hit them. A fast-growing dark shape on the eye can mean a crash, a foe, or a rival fly is near. Nerve cells that sense this threat fire most for shapes low in the view.

The team showed tied flies shapes from above or below at four speeds. Shapes from below, at mid speeds, drew far stronger moves from the flies. Shapes from above drew weak moves by contrast. The acts match the nerve cells, but speed and height still shape the result.
pmc-13616473:

pmc-13619073:

pmc-13619673:

pmc-13623273:

pmc-13623373:

pmc-13626173:

pmc-13626473:

pmc-13626673:

pmc-13627273:

pmc-13627873:

pmc-13628173:

pmc-13628573:

pmc-13630273:

pmc-13630473:

pmc-13631273:

pmc-13631473:

pmc-13633073:

pmc-13633873:

pmc-13633973:

pmc-13634273:

pmc-13635873:

pmc-13637273:

pmc-13637373:

pmc-13638873:

pmc-13641773:

pmc-13643773:

pmc-13645573:

pmc-13645773:

pmc-13646173:

pmc-13646873:

pmc-13647173:

pmc-13647973:

pmc-13648273:

pmc-13650573:

pmc-13650973:

Overall incidence is rising, led by spider bites and caterpillar contacts, and spider case fatality is projected to climb if trends hold. Surveillance quality, risk mapping, clinical readiness, and follow-up of lasting damage all showed weaknesses, and antivenom output, purchasing, and actual use often mismatched the burden for each envenomation type. Regional cooperation has sharpened coordination, yet access gaps persist, and the authors lay out strategic fixes.
pmc-13651773:
Jintao Song and four co-authors show that the visual system files spatial relations between objects into topological categories, such as inside versus outside and connected versus separate. Geometry treats these relations as the deepest invariants, unchanged by stretching, and the team asked whether perception honors those boundaries while hunting for targets.

Search performance jumped whenever the difference between target and distractors crossed a topological category line, even with distances held equal. Control experiments stripped away a depth-from-overlap explanation and showed that removing the inside-outside boundary restored a smooth dependence on plain metric distance. The categorical edge reappeared across several forms of connectivity. The authors read the results as evidence that vision represents relations abstractly and categorically. That would explain why a phone in a basket and a knife in a cup feel similar at a glance despite sharing nothing else.
pmc-13651873:
Frank Förster and five colleagues report a laboratory study of how weathered volcanic rock affects reef-building corals. Working with material collected on the island of St. Vincent, the team exposed three coral species to weekly additions of untreated tephra and its leachate over six weeks. The question was whether long-term contact with remobilized sediment helps or harms the animals that build reefs around volcanic islands.

Every exposed colony showed stronger photosynthetic light harvesting, while most other measures of coral health stayed unchanged. Chemical analysis found that the tephra released small amounts of dissolved trace metals into the seawater, including iron, manganese, and copper. The authors argue that this slow supply of metals may quietly support reef growth near volcanic coasts, a role for eroded volcanic sediment that earlier work had largely overlooked.
pmc-13654373:
Shuhong Wang led a 2026 case report on using extracorporeal membrane oxygenation to rescue a young worker with a ruptured main airway after severe chest trauma. Major airway rupture is rare and often fatal, since the patient can suddenly lose effective ventilation and standard treatments may fail. The patient, a twenty-eight-year-old freight worker, fell twenty meters with a car. He sustained bilateral pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, lung contusion, and multiple rib fractures, with oxygen saturation that could not be maintained.

A multidisciplinary team urgently started ECMO to secure gas exchange, then completed airway repair surgery and abdominal exploration. The patient recovered well, left hospital after thirty-five days, and continued to do well at one to six months of follow-up. Trauma teams get a rare success story and a practical lesson: early ECMO can buy time for definitive airway repair when ventilation collapses after major thoracic injury.
pmc-13664573:
Yang Wen and co-authors map, in a 2026 study, the shrinking welcome that one Chinese river basin offers the Siberian crane, a critically endangered migrant. The Erlongtao basin, on the Songnen Plain, is a key stopover where the cranes refuel. The team combined migration-season field surveys from 2020 to 2024 with three decades of land data, a habitat quality model, and a species suitability model.

Wetlands have shriveled and swamps fragmented, degrading feeding grounds, even as some land conversions back to water helped. In 2020, truly high-suitability habitat covered less than two tenths of one percent of the basin, and much of it was dry farmland in poor condition. Two thirds of the best habitat lay outside the two national reserves. The authors call for targeted restoration of the richest water and swamp patches, and feed their numbers into planning for a proposed crane national park.
pmc-13669273:
Juan He and co-authors present a study the catalog lists under 2026. The topic is liver cancer and a gut bacterium, Alistipes. Gut germs shape cancer growth, and Alistipes counts as a helpful genus. Its role in liver cancer was undefined. Gene surveys of stool find Alistipes scarcer in patients than in healthy controls. The same drop appears in mouse models. One of its fatty products, iso-15:0, also runs low in both groups.

Feeding the fatty acid tests whether it fights the tumor. The team traces its action to a signaling chain inside cancer cells, the G-beta-gamma, PI3K, AKT path. Blocking it slows the cancer's advance. Oncologists get a microbe-derived molecule with a mechanism, not a correlation. Gut-based add-ons to liver cancer care are plausible if the molecule proves safe. The patient-plus-mouse pairing strengthens the claim before human dosing.
pmc-13669373:
Ruiming Liu and co-authors published this materials study in 2026. It builds a soft electrode material for ear-based brainwave recording, a discreet way to track mental states. Polymer electrodes are comfortable and stick well to skin, but they slowly creep under steady strain, and that drift corrupts the signal. The team attacked the creep problem at the molecular level, designing a polymer whose structure repays the entropy lost when it is stretched.

Their copolymer mixes flexible links, held by electrostatic coordination, with a minority of rigid covalent bridges locked in a twisted shape. Scattering tests and simulations confirmed the rigid parts stop chains from slipping. The result stretches past two hundred percent, springs back almost fully, and creeps less than 0.4 percent over twelve hours. Built into an ear device, it enables long, stable recordings in everyday settings.
pmc-13672673:
Birkas and six co-authors test a short personality survey for screening, in work from twenty twenty-six. The survey is the brief form of the Personality Inventory for DSM-5. It measures maladaptive traits under a newer, graded model of personality disorders.

Proof of how well the short form spots true cases, and what cut scores to use, has been thin. The team studied more than a thousand Hungarian adults in three groups: people with a personality disorder, clinic patients without one, and people outside clinics. They compared trait levels and profiles across groups. They also tested accuracy and best cut scores, to judge if the short form can screen with care.
pmc-13672773:
Yi Lu and ten colleagues review how long-running bowel inflammation can turn into colon cancer. Steady inflammation wears the gut lining and opens the door to malignant change. The review gathers the known drivers of that path. Gut microbe imbalance, a leaky gut barrier, and constant immune firing all play parts.

Ongoing inflammation floods tissue with damaging oxygen byproducts. DNA takes hits, genes switch wrongly, and the tissue around tumors reshapes itself. Together these steps help cancers start, grow, and dodge the immune system. The review also covers warning markers, prevention drugs, and targeted treatments now in reach. Certain chemical signal paths stand out as both markers and targets. The authors stress the hard step: turning lab insight into care that fits each disease stage.
pmc-13677573:
Mansoor Khaledi and co-authors review a way of killing cancer cells by rusting their membranes from within. The process, ferroptosis, is a regulated cell death driven by iron and by peroxides that build up in cell fats. The review walks through the machinery: how cells import and store iron, the glutathione defence line guarded by the enzyme GPX4, and a backup pathway found more recently.

Therapies that trip this death are the focus. Classic small molecules can trigger it, nanoparticles can deliver iron and drain defences to force it, and even cold atmospheric plasma shows promise as a physical trigger. The authors also examine how this death interacts with immune cells in the tumour, and how markers might select the patients likeliest to benefit, including cancers that resist standard chemotherapy.
pmc-13680773:
Bal, Patel, Doan, Liang, and Cassarino present a study from twenty twenty-six on a gene test for hard-to-call skin growths. Some pigmented lesions defy clear diagnosis under the microscope alone. A twenty-three-gene test sorts them as likely benign, in-between, or likely malignant. The team track two hundred sixty-seven such lesions tested at first workup. Follow-up runs a median of six years for recurrence or spread. The test yields a firm diagnosis in near nine of ten cases.

Event rates rise steeply from benign to malignant test results. Benign results pair with low event rates over long follow-up. Malignant results pair with rates near nine times higher. Results hold in the subset with at least five years of follow-up. The authors back the test for guiding care.
pmc-13683473:
Stanislava Voběrková and nine colleagues compare four home food-waste composting devices, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Each device was run three times with the same food waste mix. The team tracked heat, chemical traits, compost maturity, and germ safety. Electric units mixed and heated on their own but did not finish the compost faster.

All four devices turned out half-stable material that still needed a curing stage. Costs, energy use, and waste diverted pulled in different directions across devices. Checks found no drug-resistant germs among the cultured samples, though wild germs were not covered. The authors advise matching the device to the household and adding a maturation step.
pmc-13688373:
Bauer and six co-authors adapt a swallowing score into German in work from twenty twenty-six. The score, DIGEST for endoscopy, grades how safe and efficient swallowing is in throat cancer patients. Endoscopy is one of two gold standard tests for swallowing trouble.

No proven summary score existed for this test until recently. The team translated the tool with forward and back translation, patient interviews, and expert review with the original makers. They then validated it on a hundred recorded exams. A trusted German version lets clinics score swallowing in the same way and track change after treatment.
pmc-13689073: Ibrahim Ahmed and co-authors present a draft genome sequence in a 2026 announcement. The bacterium Staphylococcus aureus was isolated from a patient with an ear infection. Its genome assembled into twenty six contigs, totaling about two point eight million base pairs, with a low GC content typical of the species. The sequence encodes roughly two thousand seven hundred eighty genes, including several associated with virulence. Such reference data support later work on this clinical isolate.
pmc-13693973:
Katherine Ann McCusker, Betsy Kennedy, and Abby Parish offer nursing teachers a guide for judging which exams AI can undermine, in this 2026 article. Students can now draft answers with chatbots, threatening the honesty of competency checks in a field where skill gaps endanger patients. Educators had no shared way to grade that risk.

Graduate nursing faculty built the guide by backward design, anchoring its criteria on assessments known to resist AI misuse and testing it across many exam types. It scores each assessment on setting and method, then points to fixes matched to the weak spots. The authors aim to spend redesign effort where stakes are highest, while leaving room for AI where its use mirrors real practice.
pmc-2836773:
Webb, Joseph, Yardley, and co-authors review internet programmes that aim to change health behaviour. The internet is used ever more to deliver such interventions, from quitting smoking to eating better. Earlier reviews had not sorted out, in a systematic way, which features make online programmes work.

The team pooled results across studies and linked effectiveness to three things: the theory behind a programme, the behaviour change techniques it uses, and how it is delivered. Their findings give designers evidence for building online health tools that do more than inform; they actually shift habits.
pmc-3163573:
Alikhan, Petty, Ben Zakour, and co-authors present BRIG, the BLAST Ring Image Generator, for comparing microbe genomes. Seeing genome matches as pictures is of great use for spotting genetic differences between closely related microbes. Fresh ways to draw genomes were needed to check, read, and share sequencing results well.

BRIG draws genomes as ring-shaped bands, aligning shared and missing regions at a glance. Differences that signal new traits, such as resistance or virulence, become easy to point to. The simple format made genome comparison accessible to labs without specialist graphics skills.  Doctors use such matches when a familiar microbe behaves in a new way in patients.
pmc-3599573:
Akbarzadeh, Rezaei-Sadabady, Davaran, and co-authors review liposomes: their kinds, how they are made, and their uses. Liposomes are sphere-shaped vesicles made of one or more fat-like layers, much like cell membranes. First described in the mid-1960s, they have become useful models, reagents, and tools in many sciences.

The review covers fields from physics and chemistry to medicine, where liposomes carry drugs inside their shells. Sorting types and making methods helps researchers choose the right carrier. Liposome delivery now supports approved medicines and vaccine tools used worldwide.  Cosmetics and food science also use liposomes, a breadth the review covers.
pmc-3933873:
Zhang, Kobert, Flouri, and co-authors present PEAR, a fast and accurate tool for merging Illumina paired-end reads. Illumina paired-end technology reads DNA fragments from both ends at once. When fragments are short enough, the two reads overlap and can be merged into one longer read.

Tools for merging already existed for some cases, but accuracy and speed varied. PEAR was built to merge reads reliably at scale. Longer, cleaner merged reads improve assembly and variant detection in sequencing projects of every kind.  Amplicon studies merge reads first, so merger quality shapes all downstream ecological conclusions.
pmc-4081273:
Van der Walt, Schönberger, Nunez-Iglesias, and their team presented scikit-image in 2014. Scikit-image is a library for image processing in the Python language. It supplies algorithms and helper tools for work in research, teaching, and industry.

The library is released under a liberal open source license, so anyone may use and adapt it. Its interface is well documented, which lowers the bar for new users. Tasks range from cleaning and filtering images to finding edges and shapes. As part of the wider Python science stack, it helps labs build image workflows that others can run and check.
pmc-4261873:
Bardou, Mariette, Escudié, and their colleagues built jvenn in 2014, an interactive viewer for Venn diagrams. Venn diagrams are a common way to compare lists, showing what is shared and what is unique. Biologists use them often to compare gene lists from different analyses.

Unlike a static picture, jvenn lets users click and explore the overlaps directly in a web browser. Lists from different conditions or species can be swapped in and compared at once. The shared part often holds the genes most worth studying further. A clear, hands-on view saves time and helps teams agree on what a list comparison really shows.
pmc-4839673:
Talevich, Shain, Botton, and their colleagues built CNVkit in 2016. Copy number variants, where a DNA stretch is deleted or repeated, matter in inherited syndromes and in cancer. Targeted DNA sequencing is increasingly used to infer such changes from read depth.

CNVkit detects genome-wide copy number changes and draws them for inspection. It works with the targeted panels that clinics use for cancer and genetic testing. Clear plots help analysts judge whether a change is real and where its edges fall. Reliable copy number calls from standard sequencing panels widen access to this layer of diagnosis.
pmc-5014473:
Martin, Murrell, Golden, and their co-authors released RDP4 in 2015. RDP4 is the latest version of a recombination detection program for sequence alignments. Recombination, where viruses swap genome pieces, can distort evolutionary trees if it goes unseen.

The Windows program runs a wide array of methods to detect and visualize recombination in virus genomes. It can also strip the evidence of recombination from an alignment so other analyses run cleanly. Viruses such as HIV recombine often, which affects vaccine and drug work. RDP4 helps researchers spot those events and judge how virus families truly evolved.
pmc-5267473:
Sekhon, Cartwright, and Francis studied the acceptability of healthcare interventions in 2017. Acceptability, whether patients and staff find an intervention suitable, is increasingly seen as something to consider when designing, evaluating, and putting care into practice. The literature gave almost no guidance on defining the term or measuring it.

The authors reviewed existing reviews on the topic and built a theoretical framework for acceptability. A clear framework gives trial teams questions to ask before and during a study. Interventions that patients dislike fail in real life, however well they work in theory. The framework helps designers catch that problem early and improve uptake.
pmc-7296073:
Bianca Parker and co-authors surveyed in 2020 a genus of gut bacteria called Alistipes, a group scientists are only beginning to understand. Members of this genus were first isolated mostly from medical samples, and they belong to the Bacteroidetes, a large bacterial phylum with a strong role in gut imbalance and disease. Interest grew as studies began linking these bacteria to conditions well beyond the gut.

The review gathers evidence tying Alistipes to inflammation, to cancer, and to mental health, and weighs where the links look protective and where they look harmful. The authors are candid that findings conflict and that context seems to matter a great deal. Their summary gives researchers a clear starting map of a microbe whose story is still being written.
pmc-7319273:
Xiandong Chi and colleagues reported in 2020 that they had found a human antibody able to block SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19. Their target was the viral spike protein, the three part structure the virus uses to latch onto cells and fuse with them. Most antibody work at the time aimed at the spike's receptor binding region, the part that grips the cell.

This antibody instead attaches to a different stretch of the spike, its N-terminal domain, and still stops the virus from infecting cells. That result mattered because it showed the spike has more than one vulnerable spot. Drugs and vaccines that press on several spots at once are harder for a changing virus to escape.
pmc-7619273:
Stephen Potter and Mark Hawley survey what older people living independently actually think about digital technology. Services delivered through apps and connected devices are often proposed as the way to help people age well at home, yet uptake among older users is patchy. The researchers questioned 230 people aged fifty-five and over, drawn from independent-living schemes and local communities, and compared attitudes across generations within that group.

Views were more varied than the stereotype of the reluctant older user suggests, with experience and perceived usefulness shaping opinion more than age alone. Missed chances to help, the authors argue, come from services designed around assumptions rather than these stated attitudes. For councils and care providers rolling out technology-enabled care, the survey offers a corrective: ask first, and build around the answers people actually give.
racine-athaliah-donkersley-1873:
Athaliah, Racine's last tragedy, stages a child king hidden in the Temple of Jerusalem. J. Donkersley's 1873 English blank verse renders the biblical drama of Joash and the high priest Jehoiada. Queen Athaliah, who seized the throne by blood, dreams of a child she cannot name.

The priest guards the boy until the hour comes to crown him before the people. Racine drew the tale from scripture and gave it the tight, singing form of French classical tragedy. In English dress the play completes a shelf of Racine's tragedies, and many judge it his most sacred work.
ralston-russian-fairy-tales-1873:
W. R. S. Ralston, a Scots scholar at the British Museum, made this first great English set of Russian tales in 1873. He read Russian well and drew from the best stores of tales in that tongue. No such set had been made for English readers before his work.

The tales hold the rusalka, the water maid of Slav lore, in her gay and grim forms. House spirits, wood demons, and bold young heroes fill the rest of the rich store. Ralston's set gave the English world its first true sight of the fairy lore of Russia.
riemann-hypotheses-geometry-clifford-187:
Bernhard Riemann gave his famous lecture on the foundations of geometry in 1854, though it was printed only after his early death. William Clifford's 1873 English version brought it to a wider world. Riemann asks what we truly know about space itself.

He argues that space need not be flat, and that its shape is a fact to be measured, not assumed. Curved spaces of many kinds become open to math for the first time. Einstein later took Riemann's tools to build general relativity. Few short lectures have changed physics and math so deeply. Clifford, himself a fine geometer, kept the translation close and clear.
stowe-palmetto-leaves-1873:
Palmetto-Leaves, printed at Boston in 1873 with pictures, gathers Stowe's sketches of Florida. She wintered at Mandarin on the St. Johns River and wrote as a delighted newcomer. The contents open with Nobody's Dog and A Flowery January in Florida.

Orange groves, alligators, and steamboat trips fill the bright early pages. She also describes freed Black families building new lives after the end of slavery. Part travel book and part gentle sales pitch, the sketches urge Northern settlers south. Historians credit the book with helping to spark Florida's first great land boom in the years that followed its release.

Only the front matter of the reprint is present here: the series page, the names of the society's editors, and the note that the text was lithoprinted at Ann Arbor in 1949. No scene or speech from the play itself shows up in these pages.
